title: Western Arkansas hospital joining initiative to expand access to doulas
description: Mena Regional Health System is joining a state initiative to integrate doulas into maternal healthcare, the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences announced Thursday. Doulas provide emotional, physical, educational and logistical support to parents-to-be and serve as middlemen between them and other medical professionals. As of September, doulas can ser[...]
text:
The UAMS medical sciences campus on Markham Street in Little Rock. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)Mena Regional Health System is joining a state initiative to integrate doulas into maternal healthcare, the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences announced Thursday.
Doulas provide emotional, physical, educational and logistical support to parents-to-be and serve as middlemen between them and other medical professionals. As of September, doulas can serve Arkansas Medicaid recipients.
The UAMS Institute for Community Health Innovation launched the Advancing Doulas and Perinatal Teams Toolkit earlier this year at Mercy Hospital in Rogers. The program trained 45 Mercy employees to include doulas in prenatal care teams, leading to a 47% increase in “understanding of a doula’s scope of practice among staff,” according to the UAMS news release.
UAMS began co-managing the Mena Regional Health System earlier this year. The west Arkansas hospital’s administrators expressed appreciation for the system’s adoption of the doula initiative in Thursday’s news release.
Facing financial headwinds, rural Arkansas hospitals turn to partnerships

“We believe every mom deserves to feel supported, informed, and cared for throughout pregnancy, childbirth, and beyond,” Amber Williams, a registered nurse and the Mena hospital’s director of women’s services, said in the news release. “Through this partnership, we look forward to working together to create a more positive birth experience and better outcomes for mothers and babies in our community.”
The Mena hospital is one of the few that deliver babies in western and southwestern Arkansas. Eight labor and delivery units have closed in Arkansas since 2020, including in Magnolia, Fort Smith and Camden, though one of Fort Smith’s two hospitals still has a maternity ward. Studies show the closures have increased Arkansans’ drive times to delivering hospitals, putting mothers and newborns at risk.
The Mena hospital’s co-management agreement with UAMS makes the facility better equipped to care for high-risk pregnancies, CEO Paul Ervin said, thanks to UAMS’ perinatology and maternal-fetal medicine specialties.
Last year, the UAMS Institute for Community Health Innovation enrolled more than 50 people into a comprehensive doula training program, and it added 25 more people this year.
Arkansas consistently has high maternal and infant mortality rates. More than 90% of Arkansans surveyed by Heartland Forward in October want the state to increase its investment in maternal and infant healthcare, according to data released Wednesday. Heartland is a Bentonville-based nonprofit founded by family members of Walmart founder Sam Walton.
Arkansas is the only state that has not taken the federal option to extend postpartum Medicaid coverage from 60 days to 12 months after birth. Legislation to create this policy did not pass the Arkansas Legislature in 2023 or 2025. Lawmakers will begin their 2027 session on Jan. 11.

title: Indiana won’t implement Medicaid work requirement grace period
description: Indiana won’t participate in a six-month grace period to delay enforcement of Medicaid work requirements set to take effect in January. The federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services updated its guidance last week creating an optional “hold-harmless” period, during which states could delay enforcement for up to six months as they update systems trackin[...]
text:
The Indiana Family and Social Services Administration determined it cannot participate in an optional six-month grace period for enforcing Medicaid work requirements, which take effect Jan. 1.Indiana won’t participate in a six-month grace period to delay enforcement of Medicaid work requirements set to take effect in January.
The federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services updated its guidance last week creating an optional “hold-harmless” period, during which states could delay enforcement for up to six months as they update systems tracking compliance and exceptions to Medicaid work reporting rules created by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Both state and federal law will require most working-age adults between the ages 19 and 64 who are insured through the Healthy Indiana Plan to work, volunteer or be in school for 80 hours a month starting Jan. 1, unless they meet an exception or monthly income threshold.
The work reporting rules do not apply to traditional Medicaid.
After reviewing the CMS guidance, the Indiana Family and Social Services Administration determined the state cannot participate because “Indiana law does not provide the agency with the authority to delay implementation of these requirements,” said Marcus Barlow, an agency spokesperson.
“While the updated federal guidance affords states additional flexibility, FSSA’s actions must remain consistent with state statutes that require implementation of the work requirements by January 1,” he said.
The agency, which estimated last month that 58,000 Hoosiers were not in compliance with the forthcoming rules, is urging HIP members to create a benefits portal account and check online for updates and deadlines to maintain coverage.
“The agency remains committed to providing clear information, resources, and support to help members successfully navigate implementation and avoid unnecessary disruptions in coverage,” Barlow said.
While enforcement won’t begin until January, some Hoosiers must already be in compliance to maintain their coverage next year as the state will use a three-month look-back window for eligibility determinations.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Van der Vaart resigns from NC Utilities Commission with 4 1/2 years left in his term
description: Donald van der Vaart has resigned from the North Carolina Utilities Commission, with the announcement coming two days after the commission approved rate hikes for Duke Energy customers.  The rate increases start Jan. 1, 2027, the same day van der Vaart’s resignation becomes effective.  State Treasurer Brad Briner announced van der Vaart’s resignation Wednesd[...]
text:
Donald van der Vaart resigned from the NC Utilities Commission. (Photo: NC DEQ)Donald van der Vaart has resigned from the North Carolina Utilities Commission, with the announcement coming two days after the commission approved rate hikes for Duke Energy customers. 
The rate increases start Jan. 1, 2027, the same day van der Vaart’s resignation becomes effective. 
State Treasurer Brad Briner announced van der Vaart’s resignation Wednesday, but did not give a reason. Van de Vaart’s resignation email to the commisssion didn’t offer a reason, either. He had about 4 ½ years left in his 6-year term. 
Briner was given a Utilities Commission appointee in a 2024 law passed during a lame duck legislative session. He appointed van der Vaart, who was serving at the time as the state’s chief administrative law judge and director of the N.C. Administrative Office of the Courts. 
In June, Van der Vaart was barred from voting on Duke Energy’s long-term resource plan, WFAE reported, because he had missed two weeks of testimony in the case. He disagreed with his exclusion, which was announced by Utilities Commission Chairman Bill Brawley after parties to the case objected to his participation.
Van der Vaart also did not participate in the Duke Energy Carolinas rate hike case. He partially dissented from the Duke Energy Progress case. 
Electricity rates will increase more than 9% over two years for residential customers. 
Van der Vaart was secretary of the N.C. Department of Environmental Quality under former Gov. Pat McCrory. He demoted himself to a position in the agency’s air quality division before Roy Cooper, who defeated McCrory, took office. The governor appoints the DEQ secretary, and van der Vaart would have lost his leadership position under the Cooper administration. He resigned after less than a year at that job.

title: GAO prods ICE for new immigration detention plans
description: The nonpartisan Government Accountability Office urged federal immigration authorities to plan immigration detention costs more carefully to avoid more wasted taxpayer funds, in a new report released Thursday.  Immigration and Customs Enforcement budgeted $2.8 billion for detention in the 2025 fiscal year, more than 40% above the previous year, but then scal[...]
text:
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement vehicle is parked outside a Roxbury, N.J., warehouse slated to become a migrant detention center. The nonpartisan Government Accountability Office urged federal immigration authorities to  plan immigration detention more carefully to avoid more wasted taxpayer funds, in a new report. (Photo by Benjamin Leynse/New Jersey Monitor)The nonpartisan Government Accountability Office urged federal immigration authorities to plan immigration detention costs more carefully to avoid more wasted taxpayer funds, in a new report released Thursday. 
Immigration and Customs Enforcement budgeted $2.8 billion for detention in the 2025 fiscal year, more than 40% above the previous year, but then scaled back an unpopular move to buy 11 warehouses and convert them to hold detainees. That pullback resulted in millions of dollars in waste, according to a previous GAO report, and ICE has yet to make a new plan for the money, the new GAO report stated. 
Millions of dollars of waste found in Trump administration push for immigration detention

Costs per prisoner range from $85 a day for state and local jails to $180 a day for federal prisons, and ICE needs to make a new plan to “reduce potential waste and help ensure the cost effective use of taxpayer dollars,” the report states.  
Not all the warehouse conversion plans will be reversed.
As recently as Nov. 5, ICE informed New Jersey that it still plans to convert a Roxbury warehouse into an immigration detention center after environmental review. Another proposal in Arizona is open for public comment until Dec. 9. 
ICE, however, has announced plans to sell other warehouses in Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Texas and Utah. 
There have also been purchases of private prisons — such as one in Minnesota that drew fire for its high price compared with an earlier offer, and a deal announced this week to buy a private prison in Washington state. 
Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org.

title: Facing new DOJ threats, Slotkin uses anniversary of illegal orders video to decry intimidation
description: While facing new threats of legal action from members of the Trump administration’s Department of Justice, U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) joined four of her congressional colleagues to decry what she described as “intimidation” and threats from the president and his allies against those speaking out against him. The press conference was hosted almost exa[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan) speaks to reporters in Washington D.C. on Nov. 19, 2026 along with four of her congressional colleagues to decry what she described as “intimidation” and threats from the president and his allies. (Screenshot)While facing new threats of legal action from members of the Trump administration’s Department of Justice, U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) joined four of her congressional colleagues to decry what she described as “intimidation” and threats from the president and his allies against those speaking out against him.
The press conference was hosted almost exactly one year after the group of legislators, all military veterans and former intelligence officers, posted a video reminding military servicemembers of their responsibility to refuse illegal orders. 
In the press conference Thursday afternoon, Slotkin recounted the past year of military and intelligence actions taken by President Donald Trump, including federal immigration enforcement deployments in Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis, as well as the ongoing war in Iran and military strikes against boats in the Caribbean.
“It was important for us to come together a year later to say: number one, we stand behind the video we made. Number two, we won’t be intimidated out of calling out threats to our democracy,” Slotkin said. “We stand behind our men and women in uniform for the amazing work that they do, and I think we feel strongly that if this is the thing we need to do to stand up for the country we love, we have no problem doing that.”


Slotkin’s statements at the press conference come a week after a letter directed towards her was posted on X by Aaron Reitz, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas, alleging that her statements in a public podcast taping, which said that congressional oversight could send a “deterrence message” to those considering working in the Trump administration, were unconstitutional and potentially opening her up to a criminal investigation. 
“Your comments reflect soon-to-be-realized fantasies about weaponizing congressional investigations for the purpose of personal aggrandizement and punishment of people close to the President. In other words, your ’oversight’ plans seem to have no legitimate legislative purpose and may therefore be unlawful,” Reitz wrote in the letter. “The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action. Your stated intent to ‘deter’ Americans from associating with President Trump may run afoul of this constitutional right.”
Slotkin responded Thursday with a letter of her own and a press release telling the Department of Justice to “bring it on.”
Slotkin noted in a video posted to social media that, in addition to the constitutional freedom of speech rights that all Americans have, sitting senators enjoy further privileges and responsibilities for oversight that protect her and her colleagues in investigating Trump.
“The Constitution’s Speech or Debate clause bars prosecution of a legislator for conducting an investigation or performing other legislative acts. As such, your threat of investigation is baseless, and you should withdraw your letter immediately,” Slotkin wrote in her letter. “Your public threats to prosecute a sitting Senator for speech and legislative oversight also violate Justice Department policy. Your breach of these rules — publicly posting your letter instead of providing it to me, my attorney, or Senate Legal Counsel — is evidence that your threat of investigation is more about publicity and your political ambitions than any sort of legitimate inquiry.”
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a radio interview in response to questions about Slotkin’s statements being potentially illegal, “what the senator said in and of itself is absolutely not a crime.” NBC News has also reported that Blanche said at a press conference last week that there were “no ongoing investigations, criminal investigations, into words that incoming senators or congressmen have said.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Slotkin referred, throughout her letter in response to Reitz and in Thursday’s press conference, to the result of an investigation into the video that was the subject of the press conference, and the failed criminal indictment from the federal government of Slotkin and her colleagues, as demonstrating that her speech is constitutionally protected.
“It’s again similar, just going after someone for basic freedom of speech, and then on top of that, for speech and debate, for those of us who are legislators, we’re sort of doubly protected against that,” she said in the press conference. “It’s just a demonstration again that what began a year ago of the weaponization of the government continues.”
U.S. Sen. Mark Kelly, a Democrat from Arizona, who was also featured in the 2025 video, similarly said at the press conference alongside Slotkin, “Donald Trump is trying to fundamentally change the nature of this country, it hasn’t worked on us. I will tell you that none of us are backing down.”
“Just like the service members who have a duty to uphold the Constitution and refuse illegal orders, we have a duty in Congress to hold this president accountable and always stand up for the Constitution and the American people,” he continued. “That’s our job, and no amount of threats from Donald Trump or the people around him are going to stop us from doing that.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Scott Colom’s election is tied to the legacy of 1964 Freedom Summer, says writer-in-residence at the University of Mississippi
description: A Freedom Summer volunteer speaks with a Mississippi family about voter registration.
text:
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful ideas to be shared about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.

“Like other Southerners, Mississippians are obsessed by their sense of the past, but this does not ensure the accuracy of their historical picture,” historian James W. Silver once wrote as an analysis of the cultural ethos of the Magnolia State in his book “Mississippi: The Closed Society.”
He went on to note that when looking at their past, Mississippians “see legend rather than history.” Written in 1962, Silver, then a faculty member at the University of Mississippi, compiled his observations of Mississippi in the aftermath of the violence that occurred during the integration of Ole Miss. His painfully accurate depictions of the culture of Mississippi prompted state officials to launch an effort to fire him from the university even though he was a tenured faculty member. In the aftermath of the book’s publication, Silver found himself harassed, threatened and ostracized, and eventually he left Mississippi.
James Silver’s mid-20th-century portrait of the worldview of segregated Mississippi has been on my mind of late as Democrat Scott Colom was elected as the first African-American U.S. senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction.
‘Lost Cause’ mythology
While it is an historical fact that Colom will be the first elected Black senator since Blanche K. Bruce in 1881, Bruce’s service as Mississippi’s senator has been seen by most Mississippians more as legend than historical fact. The story of Reconstruction in the South has been wrapped in a narrative of failure, warped by images from D.W. Griffith’s “Birth of a Nation” and the Dunning School of historians who framed the service of senators like Bruce as illegitimate. This interpretation came to be the basis of the “Lost Cause” narrative that rationalized lynching and led to a Jim Crow system of segregation that controlled Black citizens economically, socially and politically.
In a culture that prizes memory of the Civil War through the lens of the Lost Cause over the realities of the Reconstruction era – Mississippi still observes Confederate Heritage Month each April – Bruce’s time as Mississippi’s senator is surrounded with forgetfulness and consigned to a footnote.
Mississippi Summer Project 
There is a stronger connection between Colom’s win and the goals of the Mississippi Summer Project in 1964, commonly known as Freedom Summer. White Mississippians long took pride in the effective practice of the art of politics. Part of that practice meant excluding Black people from the political process, beginning with the disenfranchisement of African Americans in its 1890 Constitution to the use of literacy tests and poll taxes to prohibit voting until the enforcement of the Voting Rights Act of 1965. 
The political activism put into motion by Freedom Summer sought not only to change the way Black Mississippians thought about their position in society but also to break down the barriers that kept them from participating in politics.
For nearly a century, segregation prevented most African Americans in Mississippi from voting or holding public office. The ingrained culture of segregation – which extended to housing, schools, workplaces and public accommodations – denied Black Mississippians access to political or economic power. Many Black Mississippians lived in dire poverty, indebted to white banks or plantation owners for whom they worked as sharecroppers.
Their daily life was kept in check by police and white supremacy groups such as the Ku Klux Klan as well as by the Mississippi Sovereignty Commission, a group that operated as a state-run spy agency during the Civil Rights Movement. African Americans who dared to challenge the condition imposed on them by white society were often killed, tortured, raped, beaten, arrested, fired from their jobs or evicted from their homes.
The organizers of Freedom Summer believed that bringing well-connected white volunteers from northern colleges to Mississippi would expose the conditions that Black Mississippians lived under. They hoped that media attention would make the federal government enforce civil rights laws that local officials ignored. Most important of all, Freedom Summer sought to educate Black Mississippians about their rights under the U.S. Constitution. To that end, the student volunteers launched Freedom Schools to teach children and adults black history, social studies, reading and math, as well as develop leadership skills, preparing them to become voting citizens.
Freedom Democratic Party
They also planned to help Black Mississippians organize a new political party that would be ready to compete against the mainstream Democratic Party after voting rights had been won. That was the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party.
Because Black Mississippians were barred from Democratic Party primaries and caucuses, they challenged the right of the party’s all-white delegation to represent the state at the Democratic National Convention (DNC) in August 1954. And since Black Mississippians were not allowed to vote, they held a parallel “Freedom Election” in November 1964 and challenged the right of the all-white Mississippi congressional delegation to represent the state in Washington in January 1965.
Fannie Lou Hamer after being beaten in jail, June 1963. Credit: FBI
Activist Fannie Lou Hamer’s impassioned plea for voting rights at the DNC was seen on national television by millions and epitomized Freedom Summer to many viewers. Hamer concluded her speech by saying “if the Freedom Democratic Party is not seated now, I question America. Is this America, the land of the free and the home of the brave where we have to sleep with our telephones off of the hooks because our lives be threatened daily because we want to live as decent human beings, in America?”
Despite Hamer’s valiant speech, as well as the strategic actions of other participants, including Freedom Summer leader Bob Moses, the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party was not seated at the Democratic National Convention in 1964. President Lyndon Johnson feared a white southern backlash if they were seated, and he used everything in his power to get the Freedom Democratic Party to stand down.
Political changes in the South
The backlash Johnson predicted did come, just not immediately. Eventually the Republican Party’s Southern Strategy led white Mississippi Democrats to change their party affiliation. Mississippi has not been represented in the U.S. Senate by a Democrat since January 1989, when John C. Stennis left office.
But the activism that was set in motion by the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party continued despite the setback from the party establishment. One of the places that spurred the activism of Freedom Summer was the town of Hattiesburg in Forrest County.
In 1964, Hattiesburg resident Victoria Gray Adams challenged Stennis for his seat, even though she did not have the right to vote. Stennis was a hardline segregationist as well as the last Democratic senator elected in Mississippi in 1982, before the state became a Republican stronghold. Although this challenge was ridiculed as a mock election by the Mississippi press, it was a very real challenge to Black Mississippians who took part. People like Victoria Gray Adams wanted to make the point that Mississippi would be a different place with Black voter participation.
Although the mock election or “Congressional Challenge” was dismissed as stagecraft, it did make white Mississippians aware that Black Mississippians would no longer accept a subservient role in the state’s politics. During Freedom Summer, more than 60,000 Black Mississippi residents risked their lives to attend local meetings, choose candidates and vote in the “Freedom Election” that ran parallel to the regular 1964 national elections.
Three Freedom Summer volunteers – Andrew Goodman, Michael Schwerner and James Chaney – were murdered because of their voter registration efforts. Despite the dangers, several hundred African-American families also hosted some of the nearly 1,500 volunteers who worked in Mississippi Summer Project offices scattered across the state. The volunteers were not just students: some were clergy sponsored by the National Council of Churches, attorneys recruited by the National Lawyers Guild and the Lawyers Constitutional Defense Committee and medical professionals from the Medical Committee for Human Rights.
Victoria Gray Adams, Freedom Summer, 1964, Herbert Randall Freedom Summer Photographs. Credit: University of Southern Mississippi
When news broke that Colom had won in Forrest County, many saw that win as significant since the county is named for one of the Ku Klux Klan founders, Nathan Bedford Forrest. Instead, I saw more of a connection to Freedom Summer as well as the activists who came out of Hattiesburg and Forrest County: Vernon Dahmer, whose house in Forrest County was firebombed, leading to his death, because he demanded the right to vote; sisters Joyce and Dorie Ladner, who participated in the Freedom Rides and sit-ins while students at Tougaloo College in Jackson; and of course, Victoria Gray Adams, a woman whose bravery and foresight about the power of the political process should be celebrated more.
But I also thought of Theron Lynd, the circuit clerk and registrar of voters for Forrest County, who systematically denied Black residents the right to vote by avoidance, hostility and dishonesty. Black residents were sometimes asked “how many bubbles in a bar of soap” on a literacy test in Forrest County.
It is equally important to examine the actions of the people like Lynd who resisted the changes the Civil Rights Movement demanded as it is to look at the work of activists. That is because there is a direct connection between those who sought to stop Black voting rights in the past and those who seek to reduce Black voter strength in the present. And the delays in Colom being declared the winner in this Senate race have everything to do with modern-day voter suppression.
Moving voters to inactive status
Before this year’s midterm elections, Mississippi’s secretary of state, Michael Watson, worked with the credit bureau Experian to “strengthen the integrity of elections” by moving people from the active voter rolls to inactive status in the state’s 82 counties. Yet, errors were rampant in the data used to remove voters from the rolls, according to reports.
In the days leading up to the elections, a coalition of national and state civil rights organizations warned Secretary of State Watson about this problem and requested that voters mistakenly ruled as invalid be reinstated. But in a manner much like the way Theron Lynd reacted to Black voters seeking to register in 1964, Watson never responded to the request. As a result, many voters were forced to use “affidavit ballots,” which delayed the final vote count in the Senate race. It is this thinly veiled attempt at voter suppression that may have led to the record turnout that led to Colom’s win.
While contemporary forces have sought to keep elements of Mississippi’s closed society in place, Mississippi was never absolutely closed off from the rest of the country, despite its politicians’ best efforts. There were always dissenters who kept Mississippi moving forward, many of them losing their lives in the process.
A long line of organizers and dissidents have been hard at work since Freedom Summer. Many of them have been at work since the Reagan era made Mississippi into a Republican stronghold, when he launched his presidential campaign by delivering a speech on states’ rights in the very county where the murder of three civil rights workers took place in 1964.
Colom’s election as senator shows that the legacy of Freedom Summer is very much alive in Mississippi. And while Colom alluded to the Civil Rights Movement and its martyrs, such as Medgar Evers, in speeches and his advertising, he maintained a campaign focus on the issues of the present, revealing, as the poet Charles Wright once observed, that living in history without living in the past is what the task is.

W. Ralph Eubanks is faculty fellow and writer-in-residence at the Center for the Study of Southern Culture at the University of Mississippi. He is the author of “When It’s Darkness on the Delta: How America’s Richest Soil Became Its Poorest Land,” as well as three other works of nonfiction.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: ACLU seeks stronger privacy protections in RI’s license plate camera policy
description: The American Civil Liberties Union of Rhode Island is calling for significant changes to the state’s recently proposed rules for automated license plate reader cameras, arguing they leave too much latitude for police to collect, retain and access data on motorists. In an eight-page analysis sent to Rhode Island State Police Superintendent Col. Darnell Weaver[...]
text:
A Flock automated license plate reader records data on Point Street in Providence on Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)The American Civil Liberties Union of Rhode Island is calling for significant changes to the state’s recently proposed rules for automated license plate reader cameras, arguing they leave too much latitude for police to collect, retain and access data on motorists.
In an eight-page analysis sent to Rhode Island State Police Superintendent Col. Darnell Weaver, the ACLU found the guidelines unveiled by Gov. Dan McKee in mid-October are too broadly written, offer inadequate safeguards against misuse and leave significant gaps in protecting motorists’ privacy.
“Given the significant capabilities of these systems, the policy’s shortcomings warrant careful attention and modification before serving as a model for legislation or ordinance,” wrote Madalyn McGunagle, a policy associate for the ACLU of Rhode Island.
The ACLU sent letters to Weaver, McKee, Gov.-elect Helena Buonanno Foulkes, Providence Police Chief Col. Oscar Perez, the Rhode Island Police Chiefs Association, the League of Cities and Towns, and the Rhode Island Police Accreditation Commission.
McKee ordered a statewide pause on new automated license plate reader installations in August, giving state police 60 days to review how the technology was being used and recommend standards for its use amid growing resistance to Flock Safety cameras.
The review was conducted in consultation with the Rhode Island Police Chiefs Association, the Rhode Island Police Accreditation Commission and the League of Cities and Towns. Privacy advocates, including the ACLU, criticized the process for excluding them from those discussions.
State Police ultimately produced a model policy McKee unveiled Oct. 19, offering local departments voluntary guidelines for using the technology. McKee extended the installation pause indefinitely and left it to the General Assembly to establish binding statewide rules.
McKee extends pause deadline on Flock cameras indefinitely

McKee’s office did not  immediately respond to a request for comment on the ACLU’s letter.
Jon Carvalho, a spokesperson for Foulkes’ transition team, said the governor-elect supports keeping the statewide pause on Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers in place until questions about security, privacy and transparency are addressed.
“Once all of those are clear, the state can determine if and how to move forward with any related technology for law enforcement agencies,” Carvalho said in an emailed statement to Rhode Island Current Thursday.
The League of Cities and Towns confirmed receipt of the analysis and said it planned to review the ACLU’s recommendations. Christine Crocker, executive director for the Rhode Island Police Accreditation Commission, wrote in an email to Rhode Island Current Thursday that she received the ACLU’s letter but has not yet reviewed it.
Sid Wordell, executive director of the Rhode Island Police Chiefs Association, said the group stands by the policy and disagrees with many of the ACLU’s recommendations, arguing the guidelines already address most of the concerns raised.
“We stand by what has been presented,” Wordell said in an interview.
Under the state’s model policy, police can use the cameras and access the data only for specified law enforcement purposes. Searches for federal immigration enforcement, traffic violations, outstanding fines and civil infractions, or conduct that is not a crime under Rhode Island law are also prohibited.
The policy further bars uses that violate First Amendment rights, discriminate against protected groups or interfere with reproductive rights.
Police can search the database as part of a criminal investigation when there is reasonable suspicion that a state or federal crime has been committed. The policy requires departments to delete collected data after 30 days unless it is preserved as part of an investigation.
But the ACLU warns the policy gives police too much discretion over how the cameras are used and the data accessed.
Among the organization’s central concerns is the policy’s broad definition of a “valid law enforcement purpose,” which includes open-ended goals such as crime prevention and public safety. 
“This essentially allows the ALPR system to proactively track just about any individual or groups of individuals with the most meager of rationales for virtually any suspected criminal offense, as police can almost always justify access to the system based on such open-ended standards,” McGunagle wrote.
Wordell said the association recognizes the definition may need some clarification but considers a range of investigations — including hit-and-run crashes and property damage — legitimate law enforcement purposes, even when they may not involve a crime.
The ACLU also questioned why the policy allows data to be retained for 30 days, noting that Flock Safety recently revised its default retention period to seven days. Flock made the change on Aug. 13. 
Wordell defended the retention period, saying investigations can take time to surface and even longer access to the data can help police solve cases.
“There’s often times that cases are not learned about a day, two days or three days in,” he said.
The ACLU called for tighter restrictions on data sharing between police departments, stronger auditing requirements and more explicit protections against using the cameras to monitor constitutionally protected activity. The ACLU also raised concerns about Flock-recorded images of people possibly being used for possible facial recognition purposes. 
“While these suggested revisions are admittedly extensive, we believe they are essential if the policy’s goal is to ensure that use of this surveillance technology appropriately balances safety interests and the privacy rights of this state’s residents,” McGunagle wrote.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico legislative analysts lay out pathway to universal primary care
description: Healthcare analysts for the Legislative Finance Committee on Thursday presented a three-year plan for lawmakers’ consideration that aims to reduce healthcare costs, expand access and potentially provide all New Mexicans with primary care, even if they’re uninsured.
text:
State lawmakers could establish universal primary healthcare for all New Mexicans by boosting direct funding to federally qualified health centers, Legislative Finance Committee Director Charles Sallee said in a presentation to lawmakers Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo by Getty images) Healthcare analysts for the Legislative Finance Committee on Thursday presented a three-year plan for lawmakers’ consideration that aims to reduce healthcare costs, expand access and potentially provide all New Mexicans with primary care, even if they’re uninsured.
The plan seeks to leverage the state’s position as the biggest statewide purchaser of healthcare, as well as money in the state’s Healthcare Affordability Fund, to improve health outcomes in New Mexico, which regularly ranks among the lowest in the country for healthcare access and affordability. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Prominent New Mexico Democrats, including Gov.-elect Deb Haaland, campaigned this year on major expansions of healthcare access and coverage, including creating a public option, which would allow all New Mexicans access to a government-funded healthcare plan that competes with the private market. 
LFC Director Charles Sallee told lawmakers Thursday that the LFC was not recommending a universal healthcare law, which would cover all types of healthcare regardless of a patient’s insurance status, due to high anticipated costs, the unlikelihood of receiving federal approval and lack of evidence that such a law improves healthcare outcomes. 
Still, he said the Legislature could, over the next three years, greatly reduce costs and expand access to care by consolidating public employee insurance pools, better targeting state subsidies and exerting more control over prescription drug negotiations. 
He also described how the state could move closer to universal primary care by bolstering funding to federally qualified healthcare centers across the state. Primary care refers to most patients’ everyday health checkups, treatment for minor illnesses and preventative care.
The centers already serve all patients regardless of whether they are insured, Sallee noted, and the state has hundreds of millions of dollars set aside in the Healthcare Affordability Fund to directly pay the centers for primary care visits.
The Legislature in 2021 created the fund, which is financed through surcharges on insurers and state funding. Lawmakers have used the fund in recent years to pay for expiring federal tax credits for residents who receive coverage through the state’s healthcare exchange, as well as other healthcare initiatives. 
A previous LFC analysis warned that the fund could be insolvent due to rising healthcare costs and other changes that drive people to the heavily subsidized exchange. Still, the fund has hundreds of millions of dollars set aside that could pay for primary care visits, Sallee said, and it would serve as the “prime mechanism” for universal primary care. 
Lawmakers from both parties weighed in on the idea and proposals for universal care more broadly. State Sen. Nicole Tobiassen (R-Albuquerque), who has spoken publicly about her late husband’s challenges accessing medical care in the state, said she remains concerned about the number of providers statewide, even if patients can access care for free. 
New Mexico US Rep. Stansbury touts state’s universal healthcare push during Albuquerque visit

“When you need a doctor desperately to live, you may not find one here, and so we can talk about universal care, whether it’s primary or not,” she said. “But then we have the bigger challenge of who’s left to help us, who’s left to do the job.”
State Rep. Liz Thomson (D-Albuquerque), who chairs the Legislature’s interim Health and Human Services Committee, previously told Source NM that she expects lawmakers to start “laying the groundwork” at the 60-day session beginning Jan. 19, with the goal of having a fully funded universal healthcare program by 2029. 
Tobiassen urged lawmakers to meet again before the session begins to do a “deep dive” into the finances of universal care provisions and other healthcare measures. LFC Chair Rep. Nathan Small (D-Las Cruces) said he would organize such a meeting.
Tobiassen said the additional meeting is necessary to ensure lawmakers “come armed with the most well-thought-out plan and viable solutions” possible “for all of New Mexico.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Commentary: Editor’s notebook: The Niceley Awards, election version
description: More than two weeks after the midterm elections, the dust is starting to settle in Tennessee politics, a welcome respite before the Tennessee General Assembly gavels into session in January, full of new members and optimism about what can be accomplished before political jaundice sets in.  But over or not, politicos like almost nothing better […]
text:
(Illustration by John Cole.)More than two weeks after the midterm elections, the dust is starting to settle in Tennessee politics, a welcome respite before the Tennessee General Assembly gavels into session in January, full of new members and optimism about what can be accomplished before political jaundice sets in. 
But over or not, politicos like almost nothing better than to rehash the coulda-woulda-shoulda from recent elections, who might have won had a few more dollars been raised and how mistakes nearly sabotaged campaigns. 
The late Sen. Frank Niceley, a longtime Republican who died in 2025, was known for his colorful phrasing and sometimes controversial statements, including the equating of toll roads with fascism, arguments against outlawing cockfighting and his once holding Adolf Hitler out as an example for people living in homelessness. 
There’s no substitute for Niceley, who at least could be counted on to keep the legislature interesting, but in his name, we began writing an end-of-session wrap up to recognize those lawmakers doing their best to emulate him. 
In that spirit, we give you “The Niceley Awards: Election 2026 edition.”
Photo finish
After a May special legislative session redrew Tennessee’s 9th Congressional District to make it much friendlier to Republicans – Democrats have held it for almost 50 years – GOP state Sen. Brent Taylor was poised to take the seat, despite a strong challenge from Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson. 
And when the votes were counted on Nov. 3, Taylor won, despite an October surprise that came through his own unforced error. 
Nashville Scene writer Eli Motycka got a tip: Taylor had, as recently as 2021, allegedly sent unsolicited nude pictures of himself to at least one woman. The woman, who asked for anonymity, didn’t have the photos anymore. Taylor hadn’t been in office at the time. Motycka’s tip could have remained just that, a story that could have been but wasn’t. 
Tennessee congressional candidate responds to allegations he sent unsolicited nude pics

But Taylor picked up a call from Motycka, and once he started talking, he couldn’t stop. He interviewed with Matt Murphy, a conservative radio host for 99.7 Supertalk, saying the photos were a product of “youthful indiscretion,” though Taylor was 51 at the time of the alleged photo bomb. He talked to Action 5 News in Memphis, admitting that yes, he did send the photos. 
He sent a statement to the Memphis Flyer, a weekly alternative paper. He just. Couldn’t. Stop. Talking. 
Pearson issued his own statement saying, “Men of faith — let alone men who are married, in their fifties, and in public office — have no business sending unsolicited nude photos to women.” 
The outcome, in addition to Taylor’s win, could be “cyberflashing” legislation, which newly-elected Democratic Rep. Jesse Huseth says he plans to file. 
Camo controversy
Most political candidates say yard signs are the bane of their existence. 
Are there enough of them? Are they in the right prominent locations? Will there be large signs? Is someone stealing the signs? 
But the race for Congressional District 7 brought forth a new complaint: who had the right to use a camouflage design for signs? 
The brouhaha began when Democratic nominee Darden Copeland created a yard sign featuring his campaign logo on a background of muted brown hunting camo, as an addition to his basic blue sign repertoire. 


 










View this post on Instagram






















 
A post shared by Darden Copeland (@dardenfortn)



“It has absolutely triggered my opponent,” said Copeland, speaking of Republican U.S. Rep. Matt Van Epps. 
And indeed, during an interview on “Inside Politics” with Nashville NewsChannel 5, Van Epps, a former U.S. Army helicopter pilot, raised the issue, seemingly implying Copeland’s use of different signs for Nashville and for more rural Dickson County was dirty pool.
Copeland campaign manager Kevin Teets said the camo signs were available across the 7th District, not just in Dickson, and the Copeland team leveraged Van Epps’ angst for social media laughs, pointing out a sitting congressman should have more important issues on which to focus. 
Van Epps edged Copeland out. The camo likely wasn’t the cause.
Old Hickory, we hardly knew ye
Andrew Jackson, son of Tennessee and seventh U.S. president, is a controversial figure because of many issues, including his ownership of enslaved people and, perhaps chiefly, his role as the architect of the nation’s Native American removal policies. In 1830, Jackson pushed for the creation of the Indian Removal Act, which led to the ethnic cleansing of five tribes.
So when independent gubernatorial candidate Lauren Pinkston posted a video from Jackson’s Jonesborough, Tennessee home on Sept. 22 that she called her “hottest Andrew Jackson take,” viewers interpreted it as a spit take. 
“When you have a lot of trauma and you don’t know how to process it, you end up doing things that are very risky and actually sometimes very harmful to other people,” Pinkston, a former professor at Lipscomb University in Nashville said, after noting that Jackson was an orphan with childhood trauma. 
After people weighed in as they are wont to do on social media, Pinkston took the video down, but the internet lives forever.

name: California
title: Prop. 4 fails, ending latest effort to allow taxpayer funding of California political campaigns
description: Supporters of Prop. 4 argued it would have curbed private money in politics and encouraged poorly funded candidates to run. Critics doubted its effectiveness.
text:
In summary
Supporters of Prop. 4 argued it would have curbed private money in politics and encouraged poorly funded candidates to run. Critics doubted its effectiveness. 


California’s ban against public funding for most state and local candidates running for office will remain in place now that the defeat of Proposition 4 is official. 
The Yes on Prop. 4 campaign conceded Thursday, after weeks of trailing by a thin margin.
The proposition would have lifted the 1988 ban and allowed state and local governments to set up public campaign financing. 
With 99% of the votes counted as of Thursday morning,  50.2% of voters opposed the measure, with  49.8% in favor. 
“The razor-thin margin shows just how close California is to embracing a democracy where running for office doesn’t require personal wealth or connections to wealthy donors,” said Jenny Farrell, executive director of the League of Women Voters of California and co-chair of the Yes campaign. 
She said the campaign would not hesitate to bring the issue back to voters.
Other good government groups and Democratic leaders also backed Prop. 4, arguing it would make it easier for candidates without wealthy donors to run for office. They argued it would boost competition and counter the influence of major donors, especially as statewide elections in recent years have grown more expensive. 
“We need to change the way we finance election campaigns so candidates can run and win without having to raise big money, and they can spend their time listening to voters rather than their donors,” said Trent Lange, president of California Clean Money Campaign and co-chair of the Yes campaign.
Voters ‘quite clear’ 
“The voters have been quite clear they don’t want taxpayer money being used for politics,” said Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican. “Unfortunately, politicians simply can’t take no for an answer.”
Critics said the public should not subsidize political campaigns, period. Others argued that fraudulent candidates could scam the system, and taxpayers could end up subsidizing candidates or types of political speech they don’t support. Some were also skeptical that public campaign financing could curb private spending in politics, saying there’s little evidence it works.
Voter confusion?
The ballot measure may have been confusing to voters, which could be why the race was so tight, said Mindy Romero, founder and director of the nonpartisan Center for Inclusive Democracy. Even though polling consistently shows that voters think there’s too much money in politics, there’s no consensus on how to address it, she said.
“I think people want to know what that means. Does it mean directly from my pocket? Does it mean additional taxes? Like, what does that look like?” Romero said. 
Seven charter cities in California, including San Francisco, Berkeley and Oakland, were spared from the 1988 ban and already have public campaign financing. Prop. 4 would have given state and other local governments the option to set up similar systems if they choose to. 
The funds wouldn’t have been available to just anybody: To qualify, candidates would have had to prove they had a certain number of small donors or agree to cap how much they would raise and spend on their campaign.

name: Michigan Advance
title: As Dems claim U.S. House majority, Dingell will continue to helm policy and communication committee
description: As Democrats prepare to take control of the U.S. House in the next congressional term, caucus members are finalizing leadership roles, reelecting one Michigan representative to her role as head of the caucus’s communications and policy arm, and another to advocate on behalf of swing seat voters. The office of U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Ann […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Ann Arbor) speaks at a press conference on water affordability and the need for federal aid to low-income families on June 16, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)As Democrats prepare to take control of the U.S. House in the next congressional term, caucus members are finalizing leadership roles, reelecting one Michigan representative to her role as head of the caucus’s communications and policy arm, and another to advocate on behalf of swing seat voters.
The office of U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Ann Arbor) announced Thursday that she would once again serve as chair of the Democratic Policy and Communications Committee, continuing a tenure that began in 2024.
“The most important work we will do with our new Democratic majority is pass policies that lower costs and help people who are hurting. But our work is unfinished if people never hear about it, cannot see how it changes their lives, or do not believe anyone in Washington is listening,” Dingell said in a statement. “That’s why it is critical Democratic leadership provides the support, resources, and tools our members need to effectively communicate with their distinct districts across the county. And that’s the work I will continue to do in the new Congress.”
U.S. Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Bay City) also secured a position as House Democrats’ Battleground Leadership Representative, after making the case to her Democratic colleagues in a letter on Nov.5.
U.S. Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet, D-Bay City, speaks at her swearing-in ceremony in Flint, Mich., on Jan. 27, 2025. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
McDonald Rivet will succeed Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nev.), who created the role in 2022 to ensure Democrats representing hotly-contested congressional districts across the county have a seat at the leadership table.
McDonald Rivet represents Michigan’s 8th Congressional District, which was a key target for Democrats and Republicans alike during the 2024 election. 
She was recently elected to a second term, defeating retired GM engineer Thomas Smith, who dropped out of the Republican primary weeks before voters selected him to represent the party in the general election. 
“The American people have demanded real change that will actually make their lives better. They sent us an amazing class of members for the 120th Congress,” McDonald Rivet said in a statement. “It’s my honor to serve as this group’s representative to leadership. Now the work begins: to do everything we can to deliver on the opportunity we’ve been given.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Incoming Secretary of State Penny Brown Reynolds announces bipartisan transition team
description: Secretary of State-elect Penny Brown Reynolds has named the transition team that will help her step into the role of election chief.  Democrats flip statewide offices up and down the ballot in Georgia; state House is in play Brown Reynolds, a Democrat, defeated Republican state Rep. Tim Fleming of Covington earlier this month in the […]
text:
Secretary of State-elect Penny Brown Reynolds debuts her transition team at the state Capitol on Nov. 19, 2026. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderSecretary of State-elect Penny Brown Reynolds has named the transition team that will help her step into the role of election chief. 
Democrats flip statewide offices up and down the ballot in Georgia; state House is in play

Brown Reynolds, a Democrat, defeated Republican state Rep. Tim Fleming of Covington earlier this month in the race to become Georgia’s next top elections officer, amassing roughly 56% of the vote, according to unofficial results from the secretary of state’s office.
“Our task is not simply to inherit this office,” she said at a Thursday press conference at the state Capitol. “Our task is to prepare for it, strengthen it and ensure that it continues to serve the people of Georgia.”
The full transition team will have more than 120 members, including business executives, elected officials, faith leaders, veterans and advocates from voting rights and labor organizations. Former Democratic Gov. Roy Barnes, for whom Brown Reynolds once worked as executive counsel, will chair the committee. Co-chairs include Georgia’s two U.S. senators, Democrats Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff, civil rights leader Andrew Young and Georgia’s last Democratic secretary of state, Cathy Cox, among others.
The team will also include members from across the aisle, including Ryan Germany, the former general counsel for Republican Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger’s office.
“It was very, very important to me that [the transition team] represented the people who voted for us, and even the people who did not,” Brown Reynolds said. “So you will have independents and Republicans and Democrats on this transition team.”
The 2026 midterms are heating up, but this election panel is focused on 2028

Among her priorities upon assuming office will be working closely with the state Legislature to oversee the implementation of Georgia’s next election system, rebuilding trust in Georgia’s elections and bolstering the state’s protections against business fraud and scams.
She also extended her thanks to Raffensperger’s office for their cooperation with the transition. 
“I want to express my sincere appreciation for your graciousness, your willingness to meet with us, and your cooperation in providing information and resources that will help us prepare for this responsibility,” she said.
Robert Sinners, a spokesperson for the secretary of state’s office, pledged to continue working with the incoming administration to make the transition as seamless as possible.
“Our office has been in coordination with the secretary-elect and will continue to assist to ensure a smooth transition for the people of Georgia,” Sinners said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Grinnell College reports $272 million annual impact on Iowa economy
description: A new economic impact analysis of Grinnell College details how its contributions to the state of Iowa and its communities have grown in the 2020s, through employment, community partnerships and student programming. The Grinnell private college announced in a news release Thursday its 2026 economic study, conducted by Decision Innovation Solutions in spring 2[...]
text:
Grinnell College has released data from an economic impact report showing its impact has grown by more than one-quarter from 2020. (Photo courtesy of Grinnell College)A new economic impact analysis of Grinnell College details how its contributions to the state of Iowa and its communities have grown in the 2020s, through employment, community partnerships and student programming.
The Grinnell private college announced in a news release Thursday its 2026 economic study, conducted by Decision Innovation Solutions in spring 2025, shows a 28.7% increase in the college’s contributions to the state economy from the first study in 2020, reaching $272.3 million annually.
As more Iowa institutions report data on their economic impacts, Grinnell College President Anne Harris said in an interview they want to “demonstrate their value in all sorts of ways,” not just for students but for the communities where they are housed.
“It has been said to me, you know, you hate higher (education), but you love your local college because that’s where you can swim, that’s where you can go see sports events, and that’s where the students are volunteers in your school, things like that,” Harris said. “So I think demonstrating the value … for us at Grinnell that has really meant pushing ourselves and being more visible, inclusive, available to be partners — partners, not experts, but partners — and we’ve got several different avenues to do that.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Over the past 25 years, the economic study states, the college invested nearly $500,000 annually in local priorities, totaling $12 million for health and safety, education, downtown development, public infrastructure including road maintenance, and placemaking.
Four out of five Grinnell College faculty members live in the 9,000-person town, Harris said, and the college is the source of 1,761 jobs in the state. The economic impact report also totals the number of Grinnell graduates living and working in the state at more than 1,700.
Initiatives like mini grants for local nonprofit projects and dining dollars for students to spend at local businesses, totaling $173,000 in the 2025-2026 academic year, as well as a new residence space and community pavilion opened by the college in downtown Grinnell, are evidence of the college’s work to be a good neighbor, Harris said.
When asked about the effect of state and federal policies bringing more scrutiny to higher education, Harris said she doesn’t believe Grinnell’s work or its impacts have been hampered but the political climate has brought more visibility, and maybe importance, to the work.
“I think it’s made us want to be a more visible good neighbor, and what I mean by that is again not just like, ‘Hey we’re here contributing money,’ you know,” Harris said. “I don’t want to be the big neighbor, I want to be the good neighbor.”
Grinnell College students and visitors bring $6.9 million annually to the Poweshiek County economy, according to the release, with $4.4 million stemming from student spending and the rest from visitors. Total economic impact on the county, which has a population of 18,368 people, rose from $96.2 million in 2020 to $109.1 million in the most recent analysis.
One of Harris’s goals for building off this data is to expand the college’s relationships at the county level, going beyond Grinnell’s town borders to see where the institution can make an impact. She’d also like to isolate the data on Renfrow Hall, the student residence and community hub in downtown Grinnell, to see its specific impact on the town.
While they’re still digging into the numbers, Harris said she attributes the growth in economic impact to better understanding the college’s role in its community long term, not just with year-over-year support, and changing financial structures to ensure initiatives and projects align with that.
“We are all embedded in all these different communities, and I think with rural communities, there’s a special kind of impact because we’re partners for the roads in a way that in a big city you wouldn’t need … our pool is used by everyone at the high school…” Harris said. “It is a trend of saying, ‘Hey, we’re here as economic partners, economic stimulants, we’re here as good neighbors.’”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: How to know if you qualify for a free grocery card in Hartford
description: Did you recently lose SNAP benefits? You may qualify for the state-funded grocery gift card program. Here’s how to get one.
text:
Around 25,000 Connecticut residents who lost their monthly Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program, or SNAP, benefits due to federal changes are eligible to receive a $300 one-time grocery store gift card.
Gov. Ned Lamont released state funds for this temporary relief program over the summer to try and alleviate some of the financial burden of grocery costs in Connecticut. Distribution of the cards started in August but the roll-out has been slow. In late October, the Department of Social Services said that only 2,000 of 25,000 cards had been distributed.
There are nine Community Action Agencies, or CAAs, across the state distributing the gift cards. In Hartford, the Community Renewal Team, or CRT, is responsible for the city’s efforts.
Because of the slow rollout, DSS recently extended the deadline to get a card to Dec. 31. It was previously Nov. 30. Officials at CRT in Hartford say that there are still a lot of unclaimed cards.
Here’s what to know about the gift card distribution in Hartford.
Who qualifies?
Not everyone who receives SNAP benefits is automatically eligible. 
The program is targeting people who have lost SNAP benefits in recent months due to new federal work requirements for “Able-Bodied Adults Without Dependents.” If you have been able to re-enroll in benefits, you’re not eligible to receive a card.
“In order to receive a card, residents must receive notification from the Department of Social Services or from CAFCA that their SNAP benefits have changed, and that they are now considered ABAWD, ‘Able-Bodied Without Dependents,’” Stephen Bigler, director of community service and veteran affairs at CRT, told The Connecticut Mirror.
Bigler also mentioned that CRT sent out physical mailers to “over 4,000 residents in the Hartford and Greater Hartford area that are eligible for the cards.”
Those unsure if they qualify can contact DSS to ask, Bigler said. CRT can also be contacted online or by calling 860-560-5600 to speak with a staff member.
Also, in light of the extended deadline, DSS stated that it’s sending out text messages to eligible people.
Where can the cards be picked up?
The $300 cards must be picked up in person from a CAA location, like CRT. Bigler said there are two CRT offices in Hartford residents can go to: 395 Wethersfield Ave. and 330 Market St.
The offices are open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. No appointments are needed. Residents outside of Hartford can locate the CAA operating in their town online.
While all that’s needed to pick up a gift card is a valid photo ID, Bigler said it could be helpful for residents to also bring any mailers they received from CRT or DSS stating their eligibility for the gift card to show staff members.
Bigler said it takes a few minutes to get the card, but residents should be prepared to wait in case there is a line.
“You may have to wait due to the sheer number of people coming in for cards at each location,” Bigler said.
How does the card work?
The card was previously virtual but now DSS is providing physical cards to CAAs. They are loaded with $300 and work like a debit card. Residents will be able to use it at the same places that accept SNAP benefits.
“It would work just like their SNAP card,” Bigler said. “There would be the same requirements as the SNAP card on what you can and cannot use it for. Like you can’t buy alcohol or cigarettes with it.”
Residents can check the card’s balance online, according to Bigler. He added that instructions of use will come with the card.
At this point, no additional money will be added to the card after the $300 is used up. But Lamont has previously said he would consider further action next year after the gift cards are exhausted.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma added millions in children’s literacy funding. Schools are still waiting for it.
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — While ratcheting up pressure on third-grade reading scores, Oklahoma lawmakers more than doubled state funding for early literacy support, but public school leaders complain they’re still waiting to receive the money. District leaders said the timing of the $43.57 million Strong Readers Act funding, usually delivered in December or January, n[...]
text:
A student reads a graphic novel at Hills Elementary in Santa Fe South Charter Schools on Aug. 4 in Oklahoma City. The Oklahoma Legislature more than doubled funding dedicated to K-3 reading instruction this year, but school districts haven't yet received the funds. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — While ratcheting up pressure on third-grade reading scores, Oklahoma lawmakers more than doubled state funding for early literacy support, but public school leaders complain they’re still waiting to receive the money.
District leaders said the timing of the $43.57 million Strong Readers Act funding, usually delivered in December or January, no longer suits the high-stakes nature of Oklahoma’s literacy laws. 
Had the funding — or at least a projection of each district’s allocation — been delivered by the time classes began in August, multiple superintendents said their schools would be better equipped to prepare students before the 2027-28 academic year, when third graders’ performance on state reading tests will determine whether they advance to fourth grade.
“Right now our second graders need the support,” Tulsa Public Schools Superintendent Ebony Johnson said during a Nov. 12 education forum hosted by Oklahoma Watch. “Our first graders need the support in order to get ready for second grade, and we do not have the resources yet. I know they’re coming, but it’d be great if they were here already in order for us to get the reading interventionists, the reading specialists and all of the additional resources that we need to prepare for ’27-28.”
Tulsa Public Schools Superintendent Ebony Johnson speaks at an Oklahoma Watch education forum Nov. 12 at Oklahoma City Community College in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Tulsa, the largest district in the state, received just under $1.17 million from the Strong Readers Act last year, state records show, and could see its allocation increase with the added funding.
Children who score “below basic” on the third grade state reading test and fail a second literacy assessment would be held back, unless they meet narrow criteria for an exemption. This spring, 44% of third graders scored below basic on the state reading exam, indicating they are well behind their grade level.
State lawmakers passed the new law intending for Oklahoma, which scored near the bottom in the country in fourth-grade reading, to emulate Mississippi, which rocketed up national rankings with similar legislation.
The Legislature also added $26 million to the Strong Readers Act budget. These funds support remediation, diagnostic assessments and learning materials for struggling readers in grades K-3. They also fund teacher professional development and salaries for reading interventionists and instructional coaches.
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, said he’d be open to changing the timing of when reading funds are paid or when projections are provided to districts. 
Hilbert, an author of the literacy legislation, said the Oklahoma State Department of Education could adjust its administrative policies to move up that timeline or the Legislature could change state laws.
He said he’s not concerned, though, that the current system will negatively impact implementation of the new law, and there’s “no chance” he would consider postponing student retention from taking effect.
“If they got the funds a couple of months quicker, would it change anything? It shouldn’t,” Hilbert said. “Because at the end of the day, the job of our public schools is to educate our kids, and reading is essential to that. So, teaching kids to read should be the fundamental job of every elementary school in the state. And so, if they’re not doing that, then what are they doing?” 
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, bangs a gavel to begin a swearing in ceremony Nov. 17 at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
Lawmakers also changed how the Strong Readers Act budget is distributed, designating 40% for general reading instruction, 30% for students needing more intervention and 30% as an incentive for districts that show improvement. 
The recent changes have made it difficult for district leaders to calculate how much their schools might receive this year, said Steven Stefanick, superintendent of the Harding Charter Preparatory School District in Oklahoma City.
Without knowing how much his district will be allocated, Harding Charter Prep was able to put reading supports in place based only on what last year’s funding levels could afford, he said.
State records show Harding Charter Prep received $7,900 from the Strong Readers Act last school year, when the state’s total budget for it was $17 million.
“We’re being asked to do a Mississippi miracle on dollars from last year,” Stefanick said. “How are schools going to hire additional reading supports and specialists and things without that funding being put in place?”
Strong Readers Act funds are typically doled out in December or January because the distribution relies on the annual Oct. 1 count of every district’s enrollment, said Tara Thompson, chief communications officer for the Oklahoma State Department of Education. 
It also factors in a Strong Readers Survey due Oct. 1 in which districts report how many of their students are behind in reading.
“The data will need to be verified before we move forward, but once the reports are verified, payments are sent to districts,” Thompson said.
Pre-K dual-language teacher Laura Porras speaks to students in her classroom at Adelaide Lee Elementary on Aug. 11 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
That means the added funding arrives after most districts have already hired their staff and implemented instructional plans. 
The end result, Stefanick said, is the extra reading dollars will primarily be put to use in the following school year. Receiving an early estimate of his district’s annual allocation could have sped up preparations, he said, but instead pressure will mount even higher on 2027-28.
“Most districts are just going to pocket the money and wait until August to spend it, but now we just wasted an entire year of a second grader’s academic ability,” he said.
Clinton Public Schools hasn’t received notice of what its Strong Readers Act allocation will be, either, but that hasn’t caused any issues for the western Oklahoma district, Superintendent Nathan Meget said.
Clinton schools provides reading coaches from the elementary level up to seventh and eighth grade. Meget said it’s been a longtime goal of the district to do so.
The added reading funding “will definitely help us out,” he said, but “as of now it has not affected us in a negative manner.” 
Clinton received $59,388 in the 2026 fiscal year, according to state records.
In Tulsa County, Jenks Public Schools collected $178,405. Jenks Superintendent Stacey Butterfield said she’s been suggesting to state lawmakers that, if the literacy law has changed, the timing of its corresponding funds should, too.
The football stadium at Jenks High School is pictured Nov. 13, 2024, in Jenks. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Other education dollars are paid sooner. The largest source of state funds for public schools, the state aid funding formula, provides an initial allocation at the beginning of the year based on the previous year’s numbers and is adjusted later once enrollment reports are finalized.
However lawmakers want to make the change, Butterfield said “we need the funding earlier” now that students face possible retention.
“We need that funding at the beginning of the year so that we can hire the reading interventionists, so that we can hire the reading specialists, so that we can begin intervening and remediating student deficits in reading at the beginning of the year because they are going to be held accountable,” she said. “We’ve got to be able to work earlier.”
