name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Higher Duke Energy bills are coming to NC households already struggling to afford them
description: For Midori Brooks, a part-time community health worker in East Durham, the cost of keeping the lights on is already a strain on her tight household budget.  Brooks said her most recent Duke Energy bill totaled $900, the highest she has seen in recent months.  She lives in a three-bedroom house with her three grandchildren, […]
text:
Residential electric meter (Photo: Douglas Rissing/Getty Images)For Midori Brooks, a part-time community health worker in East Durham, the cost of keeping the lights on is already a strain on her tight household budget. 
Brooks said her most recent Duke Energy bill totaled $900, the highest she has seen in recent months. 
She lives in a three-bedroom house with her three grandchildren, and said the fluctuating electricity costs make it difficult to plan for other household expenses.
“I still have other bills, and I still have to eat,” she said. “I have to make sure that they have food, still have clothes on their back and just day-to-day stuff.”
Brooks said high utility bills have forced her to make changes to her grocery shopping, including buying store-brand products and discounted meat. She doesn’t know where she’ll find the money for another rate hike. 
“You can’t afford it, you just can’t afford it,” she said. “Your bills are going higher, but your money is not going any higher.”
Her situation mirrors that of many North Carolinians who’ve seen their energy bills rise much faster than the rate of inflation over the past few years. The average utility customer in the state saw their electric bill climb by more than 23% between 2019 and 2024. 
Now, they’re about to increase again. 
On Tuesday, North Carolina utility regulators approved a two-year rate increase for Duke Energy customers and imposed new data center rules amid growing energy demand.  
The N.C. Utilities Commission approved the increase, which will affect customers of both Duke Energy Progress and Duke Energy Carolinas. 
Duke Energy Carolinas serves the western portion of the state while Duke Energy Progress covers the eastern half of North Carolina. (Graphic courtesy of Duke Energy)
Residential customers of Duke Energy Progress will see a combined 9.3% increase in monthly bills by 2028. Duke Energy Carolinas customers will see a higher increase of 9.5%.
Industrial users will see a lower increase than residential customers under the approved plan. 
To illustrate the impact on household bills, Duke Energy used a typical residential customer consuming 1,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity per month as its baseline. 
For Duke Energy Progress customers, the increase will translate into a monthly increase of $9.62 starting Jan. 1, 2027. Duke Energy Carolinas customers will see a $6.53 increase. 
A second increase will begin Jan. 1, 2028. Progress customers will see another increase of $5.89 a month, while Carolinas customers will see another $4.66 increase. 
New requirements for data centers
The increases come as Duke Energy faces growing electricity demand in North Carolina from population growth, economic development and data center usage. 
In its review, the Utilities Commission said the pace and scale of data center growth create new risks for existing customers.
If a planned data center doesn’t materialize, reduces its electricity consumption or leaves the system before infrastructure costs are recovered, other customers could be left paying for the investments instead. 
Under the new order, data centers with electricity demands of at least 50 megawatts will be subject to a separate electricity rate schedule instead of a broad, large-load rate structure. 
Data centers threaten energy affordability, NC task force says

Data centers will also be required to provide funding for dedicated infrastructure built to serve their facilities and pay demand charges based on at least 75% of their contract power demand, even if they use less. 
In response to questions from NC Newsline, Duke Energy declined to say how much of the approved residential rate increase, if any, is due to data center development.  
Duke Energy’s North Carolina President Kendall Bowman said customer affordability is important to the company. 
“We know families and businesses are watching their energy bills closely, and we take that seriously,” she said. 
Consumer advocates criticized the commission’s decision. 
Claire Williamson, energy policy advocate at the North Carolina Justice Center, said the organization has urged Duke Energy and regulators to extend the company’s payment assistance program to help customers ahead of the rate increase. 
“This decision sadly still locks in rate increases for all North Carolinians, while at the same time offering insufficient assistance for those already struggling most to pay their electric bills,” she said.

name: VTDigger
title: A more resilient, more affordable Vermont is within reach
description:
Gov. Phil Scott’s sixth term should be spent enforcing Vermont’s climate law, expanding cheaper clean power and setting firm limits on data centers.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A more resilient, more affordable Vermont is within reach.
text:
This commentary is by Elena Mihaly, vice president for Vermont of the Conservation Law Foundation.
As we congratulate Gov. Phil Scott on his reelection, we face a moment of opportunity for our state. Vermonters are grappling with rising costs, growing threats to public health and the impacts of severe storms and heat waves. Meanwhile, our federal government is rolling back vital environmental protections. 
These challenges are deeply interconnected. Protecting our environment goes hand in hand with making life more affordable, improving public health and building a stronger future for Vermont families and communities. The governor has the chance during his next term to work with the Democratic and Progressive supermajority in the House and Senate to address some of the most pressing challenges facing our communities. 
There are three key priorities that should be at the forefront of his next administration.
First, expanding affordable, reliable clean energy. Vermonters face higher energy bills when household budgets are already stretched thin. Preserving our Renewable Energy Standard can help bring affordable, clean power online, reduce reliance on fossil fuels with unpredictable prices and create jobs across the state. The Renewable Energy Standard requires Vermont distribution utilities to gradually ramp up the percentage of renewable sources of power — wind and solar, for example — in their energy mix to move away from polluting and price-volatile fossil fuels. We must reduce unnecessary barriers to allow for responsible renewable energy development. From installation of solar and increased home insulation to adoption of clean, modern heat pumps to heat and cool homes, these investments create jobs while helping households reduce energy waste and manage their bills.
As temperatures climbed this summer, Green Mountain Power relied on its virtual power plant of residential batteries, utility-scale storage and other clean energy sources, which helped save $6 million from our peak electricity costs. Expanding these resources can lower costs, strengthen grid reliability and help Vermont better withstand the stronger storms and extreme weather we face.
Second, Vermont needs to meet its climate mandates. Vermont’s elected leaders took important action years ago when they passed the Global Warming Solutions Act, establishing requirements to reduce climate-damaging pollution. But we have fallen short on turning those commitments into action. The law is our path forward to cut pollution. Its citizen suit provision gives the public a way to hold the state accountable.

READ MORE

Also, the Agency of Natural Resources must take the necessary action to ensure we meet our mandates and protect the people and places that make this state special. We have endured deadly and devastating floods, prolonged droughts, shrinking winters and harmful algae blooms in our lakes and streams. These changes threaten our state’s iconic industries, our farms, ski areas, tourism economy, wildlife and treasured spaces. We cannot let the status quo continue.
Scott should make meeting our climate mandates a priority, protecting both today’s communities and future generations.
And third, guardrails are needed on data centers, which were on the ballot in many states. One of the biggest upsets from the election was in Texas, where Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa drove out incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott after campaigning on a data center moratorium and criticizing Abbott for selling out to the tech industry. That’s because this is an industry that is having enormous harmful impacts on land use, energy, water, noise and air pollution. Voters want their leaders to protect them.
Our existing environmental and utility regulations were not designed to fight the vast financial resources backing the development of large-scale data centers across the country. The Vermont Legislature has already crafted legislation to establish sensible guardrails so that Vermont communities don’t bear an unfair burden from the development of these massive facilities. This is what it looks like to get ahead of this industry, rather than waiting for its consequences to hit us.
Just in time for election season, Scott shifted his stance on data centers and expressed some support for a moratorium. The Legislature should compel him to follow through on this recent conversion by putting another bill on his desk to protect Vermonters from massive artificial intelligence data centers. 
As the governor alluded to in his victory speech, the political pundits weren’t sure if he’d win even the day before he was elected. His margins were thinner than they’ve ever been. That’s because many Vermonters are dissatisfied with the status quo. Our energy is too expensive, and the impacts of climate change are hurting our families and communities. The good news is that Scott has the opportunity to lead Vermont in a direction that responds to those concerns. By supporting clean energy, reducing pollution and establishing guardrails for data center development, he can protect our natural resources, lower electric bills and build a healthier, more resilient future.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: No charges for Madison cop who shot Corey Ruiz
description: No charges will be filed against Kiel Baitinger-Peterson, the Madison police officer who shot and killed Corey Ruiz at the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin streets on July 22, Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne announced Thursday.  Officers responded to the area after receiving reports that someone had been looking into parked cars. When four [...]
text:
Hundreds of people crowded the intersection of Baldwin and Williamson Streets on Madison's East Side on July 23 for a vigil in honor of Corey Ruiz, who was killed by a Madison Police officer July 22. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)No charges will be filed against Kiel Baitinger-Peterson, the Madison police officer who shot and killed Corey Ruiz at the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin streets on July 22, Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne announced Thursday. 
Officers responded to the area after receiving reports that someone had been looking into parked cars. When four officers tried to arrest Ruiz in the intersection, a struggle ensued and officers reported that he had pulled a knife. Ruiz was tased before being shot at close range. 
Ruiz’s killing sparked weeks of protest in Madison this summer, including the occupation of the busy intersection by activists. In the months since Ruiz was killed, Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway announced she would not be running for re-election, citing threats she’d received following the shooting. City officials have also been in an ongoing fight with Madison’s independent police monitor since Ruiz’s death. That fight has included disputes over the role and authority of the position to investigate the shooting and the firing of the interim monitor by the city’s common council. 
On Thursday, Ruiz’s family met with Ozanne and the county medical examiner and were informed of the  decision not to file charges. In a statement, the family’s attorney Ben Crump argued the available video of the incident shows an excessive use of force. 
“There is nothing in the videos the district attorney showed us that justifies this officer stepping back, pulling his gun, and firing three shots at point-blank range at Corey Ruiz after he had been tased and was on the ground, hitting him once in the chest and with the kill shot to his head,” Crump said. “The medical examiner told the family that if the officer had not fired that shot to his head, Corey would have survived. It was clearly an excessive use of force. This police killing in Madison, Wisconsin, was unjustifiable, unreasonable, unnecessary, and unconstitutional.”
In a news release, Ozanne said that the shooting was justified because Ruiz had pulled a knife and therefore Baitinger-Peterson had a genuine fear that Ruiz presented a deadly threat.
“A knife can be used as a dangerous weapon and may pose a grave danger of bodily harm and/or death to an individual. A person fleeing from police who, when contacted, physically resists and produces a knife from their person does pose a threat of great bodily harm and/or death to the officers,” Ozanne said. “Responding to that threat with deadly force is permitted under the law. A person does not have to like and/or agree with the law, however I am sworn to apply the law to the facts at hand. The law applies equally to members of law enforcement and to those who are not.”
2026-November-19—District-Attorney-Decision-Regarding-Criminal-Liability-for-the-Death-of-Corey-Ruiz-as-the-REsult-of-an-Officer-Involved-Shooting-on-July-22–2026
At a press conference Thursday afternoon at Madison’s Center for Black Excellence and Culture, Ruiz’s family, including his siblings, mother and daughter, expressed disappointment and frustration that the officer won’t be held accountable for what they see as a miscarriage of justice.
Crump said he and the family would explore “every possible legal remedy” available to them, adding that “when you look at that video, this video cries out for a civil rights lawsuit.”
Some local elected officials also criticized Ozanne’s decision. State Sen. Kelda Roys (D-Madison), whose district includes the shooting site, said the decision not to file charges shows a broken criminal justice system.
“The Dane County District Attorney’s decision not to prosecute the officer who killed Corey Ruiz is deeply disappointing, and yet another example of a justice system that fails to hold the powerful to account,” Roys said. “This is not an isolated failure by prosecutors to uphold the rights of every citizen. Rather, it reflects a broader pattern of policing and prosecutorial decisions that deny those harmed by police violence equal treatment under the law and accountability when their most fundamental rights are violated. I am committed to public safety and real justice for all – and to reforming our broken criminal justice system that is not serving Wisconsinites well or fairly. A miscarriage of justice against one of us is an injustice to us all.”
This is a developing story and will be updated.

title: Oklahoma’s governor-elect plans to celebrate with 3 inaugural balls
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – Gov.-elect Mike Mazzei on Thursday announced that he will hold three separate inaugural balls in January to celebrate the start of his first term. The balls will be held in Oklahoma City, Tulsa and Durant. Mazzei, a Republican, will be inaugurated Jan. 11 in Oklahoma City, ahead of the final inaugural ball, […]
text:
Republican Mike Mazzei and his wife, Noel, address supporters on Nov. 3, 2026, at a watch party in Tulsa after Mazzei won the general election for Oklahoma governor. (Photo by Ace Cuervo/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Gov.-elect Mike Mazzei on Thursday announced that he will hold three separate inaugural balls in January to celebrate the start of his first term.
The balls will be held in Oklahoma City, Tulsa and Durant.
Mazzei, a Republican, will be inaugurated Jan. 11 in Oklahoma City, ahead of the final inaugural ball, which is scheduled for 6:30 p.m. to 9 p.m. at the National Cowboy & Western Heritage Museum.
The oath of office is usually administered on the south steps of the Capitol and includes an inauguration speech.
That ball will be preceded by a Jan. 9 ball at the Expo Square Exchange Center in Tulsa from 6:30 p.m. to 9 p.m.
Mazzei’s first inaugural ball will be from 6:30 p.m. to 9 p.m. Jan. 6 at the Choctaw Event Center in Durant.
“Oklahoma’s tribal nations are the crown jewels of our state, making this opportunity to partner with the Choctaw Nation and celebrate together in Durant especially meaningful,” Mazzei said.
On Oct. 1, President Donald Trump held a rally there and reiterated his endorsement of Mazzei, who defeated former Rep. Cyndi Munson, D-Oklahoma City, and three independents in the Nov. 3 general election.
It is common for governors to hold three inaugural balls in the state’s two largest cities and one in an outlying community.
Gov. Kevin Stitt’s first inauguration included balls in Tulsa, Oklahoma City and Lawton.
The balls also can include well-known entertainers.
Mazzei on Thursday did not announce performers, but late country music star Toby Keith performed at one of Stitt’s inaugural balls, while the late Wanda Jackson, known as the Queen of Rockabilly, and pop band Hanson, performed at one of former Gov. Mary Fallin’s.
Former Democratic Gov. Brad Henry included Pulitzer Prize winning author N. Scott Momaday, who died in 2024, at one of his inaugural ceremonies. Internationally known soprano Leona Mitchell during his interfaith prayer service.
The balls are paid for with private money generated by ticket sales and sponsorships.
Stitt raised just under $1.5 million to pay for his 2023 inaugural balls, NPR-affiliate KGOU reported at the time. He raised nearly $2.37 million to pay for his 2019 events, the outlet reported.
General admission tickets for Mazzei’s events will go on sale next month. Additional ticketing information, including cost, will be announced later.

title: Wisconsin sues TikTok as addictive and harmful to its young users
description: Wisconsin is suing the social media video platform TikTok, charging that its operators knowingly addict and profit from young people at the expense of their mental health. The lawsuit charges that TikTok “knowingly deploys features that addict and harm Wisconsin children,” Wisconsin Attorney General Josh Kaul said at a press conference Thursday. “We’ve alleg[...]
text:
Josh Kaul announces a lawsuit Thursday that Wisconsin has filed against the TikTok social media app. (Photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)Wisconsin is suing the social media video platform TikTok, charging that its operators knowingly addict and profit from young people at the expense of their mental health.
The lawsuit charges that TikTok “knowingly deploys features that addict and harm Wisconsin children,” Wisconsin Attorney General Josh Kaul said at a press conference Thursday.
“We’ve alleged that TikTok is doing this while deceiving parents and the public about the dangers of the app, thereby contributing to the children’s mental health crisis that kids in Wisconsin and throughout the country face,” Kaul said. “Our lawsuit alleges that TikTok knowingly uses addictive design features to target kids as intended users and to get them to spend as much time as possible on TikTok.”
The lawsuit, filed in Dane County Circuit Court, charges TikTok has violated Wisconsin’s deceptive trade practices law and created a public nuisance. It asks for a court injunction and payment that would provide restitution; cover civil forfeitures; an amount “to remedy the harmful effects” the suit alleges; abate the nuisance; reimburse the state and cover costs and fees for investigating and prosecuting the company.
The lawsuit doesn’t assign a dollar value to the prospective damages. Kaul said that would be determined in the course of the case against the company.
“Kids, and frankly adults as well, now spend large amounts of time on social media platforms,” Kaul said. “And those platforms have an interest in keeping our kids scrolling — taking away time that kids have to learn and to socialize. It’s critical that we curb the negative impact that social media is having on our kids.”
In a statement, a TikTok spokesperson said the company “will vigorously defend against the State’s claims.”
The suit “relies on misleading and inaccurate claims and ignores the concrete safety measures TikTok has voluntarily implemented to support the well-being of our community,” according to the statement. The statement cited more than 50 “present safety, privacy and security settings” in the app’s teen accounts, and a “Family Pairing” feature that “helps parents and guardians customize the experience for their teens.”
Kaul said the suit follows an investigation conducted by a bipartisan group of states working together. He declined to say how long ago the investigation began. Following the investigation, other states are also suing the company, he said.
“TikTok’s model, like those of other social media companies, is based on the monetization of its users: sell access and information about its users to advertisers and companies so they can sell their product and services,” the 67-page lawsuit states. “In addition to selling targeted ads, TikTok runs an ecommerce platform. Every user, and every minute that user spends on TikTok’s platform, helps generate revenue for TikTok.”
The lawsuit cites documents from TikTok showing that algorithms such as the app’s recommendation engine “are designed to ‘maximize engagement, and can lead users to filter bubbles of harmful content.” The recommendation engine directs users to videos that might interest them.
“TikTok’s business model is predicated on taking advantage of addictive behaviors which children and teenagers are particularly vulnerable to experiencing,” Kaul said. In addition to the recommendation engine, the lawsuit cites the app’s infinite scroll, autoplay and push notification features as well as TikTok LIVE — through which users can broadcast or watch live videos.
Live videos are only available when they are livestreamed, which “encourages users to visit and remain on the platform longer,” the lawsuit charges. A similar feature presents short videos that disappear after 24 hours.
After Meta settlement, Wisconsin lawmakers say there’s still a lot to be done to protect kids online

“By design, this rapidly disappearing content pressures users to check the TikTok platform more frequently,” the suit charges.
The live feature is supposed to prevent users younger than 18 from broadcasting, but the lawsuit charges that “TikTok knows its lax age verification measures allow kids access.” And all TikTok users are able to view the videos using the live channel, the lawsuit states.
The lawsuit cites reports and other documents from TikTok that acknowledge compulsive usage and its negative effects on mental health and emotional skills of young people, contributing to depression, anxiety, dissatisfaction with one’s own body and eating disorders.
“TikTok has been aware of the dangers of its platform to children for years, but has misled the public about its platform’s safety,” Kaul said. The lawsuit also charges that despite TikTok’s advertisement that its content is appropriate for children 13 years and older, “sexual content and drug and alcohol content are frequently encountered by these users,” Kaul said.
Kaul said that any specific changes to how TikTok operates will be up to the court, but the suit seeks “limiting time” on the app as well as limiting the features referred to in the complaint.
“It’s easy to say that you don’t want your kids to be on these apps,” Kaul said. “But when other kids are, it makes it very difficult as a parent. Having universal policies in place that are going to apply to kids throughout the state of Wisconsin is something that we’re looking for as well.”
A settlement in August with Meta, owner of the platforms Facebook and Instagram, illustrates the sort of resolution the state would seek in the case, he said. The Meta lawsuit and settlement involved 47 states, including Wisconsin, and is worth between $219 million and $313 million to the state.
Under the Meta settlement the apps are to block children from accessing the platforms at night, limit push notifications during school hours and limit the total number of hours children can spend on the app in a single day. Kaul said the terms of the settlement are in the process of being implemented.
In addition to the outcome of the lawsuit, Kaul said he would like to see additional state legislation that would “provide stronger guardrails” to protect children.
“I do hope we will see policies in place in the state of Wisconsin that help to keep our kids’ mental health safe from the potential harms of social media,” Kaul said.

title: Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly pardons man convicted in 1971
description: LAWRENCE — Gov. Laura Kelly granted a pardon to a man who was convicted of criminal non-support of a child or spouse more than 50 years ago. Gary West was convicted in 1971 in Cowley County and sentenced to five years of probation. “Before deciding on a request for a pardon, a thorough vetting and […]
text:
Gov. Laura Kelly appears during a June 26, 2026, recording of the Kansas Reflector podcast. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)LAWRENCE — Gov. Laura Kelly granted a pardon to a man who was convicted of criminal non-support of a child or spouse more than 50 years ago.
Gary West was convicted in 1971 in Cowley County and sentenced to five years of probation.
“Before deciding on a request for a pardon, a thorough vetting and review process must take place,” Kelly said. “This review considers whether individuals requesting a pardon have made amends for their actions and have made positive impacts on their community. Individuals who have long maintained their law-abiding behavior and positive community impact are good candidates for the second chance a pardon can provide.”
In the pardon, Kelly referenced West’s honorable discharge from the U.S. Army and service to the Federal Aviation Administration. West was convicted when he was 23 years old and had no prior offenses. 
The pardon was granted after review from the Kansas Department of Administration, the governor’s legal team and the Prisoner Review Board. The governor’s office said she takes into account a person’s criminal history, behavior while incarcerated, evidence of rehabilitation and contributions to society following release from prison.
Kelly has used authority outlined in the Kansas Constitution to pardon sentences twice as many times as the state’s four previous governors combined. Earlier this year, Kelly granted a pardon to Chung Pham in a 1993 case of aggravated battery in Lyon County.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Civil rights complaint filed against Cheboygan County officials over Islamophobic posts
description: A Cheboygan County planning commissioner’s recent social media post, which called anyone who voted for a Muslim in the Nov. 3 election a “treasonous traitor,” has been referred to state civil rights officials and criticized as Islamophobic by the head of a prominent Muslim civil rights organization in Michigan. At least two complaints have been […]
text:
Michigan Department of Civil Rights office in Lansing. July 23, 2026 | Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceA Cheboygan County planning commissioner’s recent social media post, which called anyone who voted for a Muslim in the Nov. 3 election a “treasonous traitor,” has been referred to state civil rights officials and criticized as Islamophobic by the head of a prominent Muslim civil rights organization in Michigan.
At least two complaints have been filed over the Nov. 5 Facebook post from Cheboygan County Planning Commissioner John Studer, which quoted another post from a community group unaffiliated with the county. The post was also liked by Cheboygan County Commissioner Tom Eustice, who shared a separate video of fitness influencer Jillian Michaels criticizing U.S. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and then offering an extremist interpretation of Sharia law.
Studer responded to Eustice’s repost of Michaels’ video by saying, “So many are clueless!! This is a battle older than we can comprehend.”
On Nov. 16, almost two weeks after El-Sayed’s election and following the post by Studer, a county resident filed a complaint that was sent to both the Cheboygan County administrator’s office and the Michigan Department of Civil Rights.
“As you know, there is no religious test for public office under the United States Constitution,” the complaint said. “It is also unconstitutional, under the United States Constitution and the Constitution of Michigan, to discriminate against someone on the basis of race, ethnicity, or religion. I demand a full and independent investigation.”
The complaint said that should the investigation determine that Studer made the post and that Eustice liked it, the full county Board of Commissioners should, at a minimum, censure Eustice and remove Studer from his appointed position as a planning commissioner.
“This cannot and must not be tolerated by Cheboygan County,” the complaint added.
Email and social media messages seeking comment from Studer and Eustice were not returned at the time of publication. Comments from either Studer or Eustice will be added to this article once they are received.
What is Sharia law, and why is it so controversial in the United States?

Tessa Roy, the public information officer for the Michigan Department of Civil Rights, confirmed for Michigan Advance that they had received the email complaint and that the department is evaluating the allegation, “as we would in any other similar situation.”
“Since this matter is pending, we cannot comment on it any further,” Roy told the Advance.
Cheboygan County Administrator Jeff Lawson, in an email to the Advance, also acknowledged the receipt of the complaint, but said there may be little that it can do officially because the comments were made on Studer’s and Eustice’s personal social media pages.
“Cheboygan County takes any complaint alleging discrimination including, but not limited to, religious discrimination very seriously,” Lawson said, adding that the alleged statements in question were made on the individuals’ personal social media account, “outside of any official municipal meeting, event, activity, or communication.”
Lawson added members of municipal boards and commissions, “like all individuals, retain the right to express personal opinions in their private capacity.”
“Individuals’ personal statements do not necessarily reflect the views, policies, opinions or positions of Cheboygan County,” Lawson wrote. “Cheboygan County is committed to treating all individuals equally and with dignity and respect, regardless of their religious beliefs, ethnicity, national origin or affiliations. Cheboygan County firmly rejects all forms of discrimination including religious discrimination or intolerance.”
Studer is a member of the Michigan Republican Party’s 1st Congressional District executive committee, and also ran for county sheriff in 2024. He serves on the county’s planning and zoning board, as well as the county Soil Conservation District Board.
Several posts on Studer’s personal Facebook page contain anti-Muslim sentiments, along with criticisms of El-Sayed and other Muslim officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, that are focused on their religion.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
El-Sayed will become the nation’s first Muslim member of the U.S. Senate when he is sworn into office early next year. He was the most prominent Muslim candidate on the statewide Michigan ballot.
Dawud Walid, director of the Michigan chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the nation’s largest Muslim civil rights and advocacy organization, has also called for an inquiry “into the bigoted post and the sharing of it by one of its planning commissioners, as well as one of its own members.”
“Government officials, who were elected to serve residents and visitors irrespective of religious affiliation, should not be impugned as traitors for voting for fellow Americans that are Muslims,” Walid said in a statement.
Meanwhile, CAIR-MI said it was also contacted by a concerned Cheboygan County resident, who is not Muslim, regarding the comment. Although a majority of Cheboygan County voters chose former Republican nominee Mike Rogers over El-Sayed, CAIR-MI did note that more than 2,300 county residents cast ballots for El-Sayed.
El-Sayed defeated Rogers statewide by seven percentage points.
While his election was historically significant, Walid said that there has been an increased amount of fearmongering and vitriol against Michigan’s Muslim population “due to millions of dollars recently poured into advertisements attempting to defeat Senator-elect El-Sayed in the 2026 midterm election.”
CAIR’s latest civil rights report also documented more than 8,600 instances of anti-Muslim bias complaints last year, which was the highest number recorded of such incidents since CAIR began publishing its civil rights report in 1996.

ʻO Todd Apo nō paha ka Luna Hoʻokele Hoʻokō hou o ke Keʻena Kuleana Hawaiʻi. (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2026) (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2026)
Ma mua aku nei o kēia makahiki, ua kaʻawale ka manaʻo o ka Papa Kahu Waiwai ma luna o ke ʻano i holo ai kahi hihia kānāwai i hoʻokomo ʻia na ka Luna Hoʻokele Hoʻokō ma mua ʻo Stacy Ferreira, i hoʻokuʻu ʻia mai kona kūlana i kēlā Kepakemapa aku nei. Hāpai kona hihia kānāwai i ko ke keʻena a me ko nā lālā kahu waiwai kūʻē ʻana iā ia no ka hōʻike ʻana i ka hana hewa a ka Luna Hoʻomalu o ka Papa ʻo Kai Kahele i nā ʻelele hoʻokō mokuʻāina ma luna o kona mālama ʻana i ka moʻohelu o ke keʻena.
ʻŌlelo nā loio o ke Keʻena Kuleana Hawaiʻi, ʻo kekahi mole o kā Ferreira hana ka hōʻalo ʻana i kahi loiloi e puka pono ʻole ai paha ʻo ia. E pau kona ʻaelike ma ka lā 31 o ʻOkakopa.
Ua puka hou mai ia kaʻawale ʻana ma luna o ka hihia kānāwai i ka Poʻakolu, a ʻo kekahi māhele i alakaʻi ʻia na Kahele e kākoʻo ana iā Sylva. Ua komo pū ka Lālā Papa Kahu Waiwai ʻo John Waiheʻe IV me nā lālā kahu waiwai ʻē aʻe a he ʻehā ma ke kūʻē i kona inoa, me ke kākoʻo i ka hui e kākoʻo ana iā Apo.
Ua kākoʻo ʻo Kahele, ka Luna Hoʻomalu Kākoʻo Keoni Souza, a me nā Lālā Papa Kahu Waiwai Brickwood Galuteria a me Dan Ahuna iā Sylva.
Ua kākoʻo nā Lālā Papa Kahu Waiwai ʻo Carmen Hulu Lindsey, Luana Alapa, Kalei Akaka, Keliʻi Akina, a me Waiheʻe iā Apo.
Ma ka walaʻau kelepona ma hope o ke koho pāloka ʻana, ua ʻōlelo ʻo Apo, ʻaʻole ʻo ia makemake e walaʻau a holo pono ka ʻāpono piha ʻana i ka lā ʻāpōpō.
Ua noho ʻo Apo he ʻeono makahiki he lālā o ka ʻAha Kūlanakauhale o Honolulu he ʻelele no ka ʻaoʻao Komohana ma mua o ke komo ʻana ma nā kūlana ma Disney a me Ward Village.
ʻO kahi wahi i kū aʻe ai ʻo ia ma luna o nā moho ʻē aʻe no ke kūlana Luna Hoʻokele Hoʻokō ʻo Kakaʻako Makai, kahi e kaʻa nei he 30 ʻeka ʻāina ma lalo o ke Keʻena Kuleana Hawaiʻi me ka hiki ʻole nō naʻe ke kūkulu i nā wahi noho ma muli o kahi pāpā ʻana i ia ʻano kūkulu ʻana e ka ʻAhaʻōlelo.
Ua ʻōlelo ʻo Apo, kekahi mea i hana no Ward Village i ka wā e kūkulu ʻia ana nā hale noho waiwai pākela ma kekahi ʻaoʻao o ke alanui, e aho ko ke Keʻena Kuleana Hawaiʻi nānā ʻana e kūkulu i ka mea e hiki ma loko o nā lula kūkulu. ʻOluʻolu pū kona manaʻo i ka ʻimi e kuapo ʻia ka ʻāina me ka mokuʻāina i ʻoi aʻe ka maʻalahi no ke kūkulu ʻana.
He mea kēia kuanaʻike e ʻokoʻa ai paha kona manaʻo i ko nā lālā papa kahu waiwai e kū nei, ka poʻe hoʻi e ʻiʻini ana e kūkulu i kahi hale noho ma ka hana pū me ke Keʻena ʻĀina Hoʻopulapula Hawaiʻi.
ʻO kona hana pū ʻana me nā pāʻoihana kūkulu ma Kakaʻako ka mea i kākoʻo ai ʻo Lindsey iā ia, nāna i hāpai i kona inoa he moho.
“Aia he pilikia ma Kakaʻako,” i ʻōlelo ai ʻo Lindsey ma kahi nīnauele kelepona. “Ke lana nei koʻu manaʻo i ka hiki iā ia ke kōkua ma ka hoʻoholomua i kā kākou hana.”
Ua ʻōlelo ʻo Lindsey, ua kūlanalana kona manaʻo ma waena o Park a me Apo, ua manaʻo naʻe ʻo ia, ʻoi iki aʻe ko Apo ʻano he ikaika aʻe “no ka pono e hana pū me Kai Kahele” — he kanaka nona kahi ʻano ikaika aʻe nāna i kipaku iā Lindsey mai ke kūlana luna hoʻomalu o ka papa he ʻelua makahiki aku nei.
Ua ʻāpono ʻia ko ka Luna Hoʻomalu o ka Papa Kahu Waiwai ʻo Kai Kahele noho ʻana he lālā kahu waiwai ma Kekemapa 2024. (David Croxford/Civil Beat/2024) David Croxford/Civil Beat/2024
E kākoʻo ana ʻo Kahele i ko Sylva noho moho ʻana ma ka hālāwai a ka papa. ʻŌlelo ʻo ia, he koʻikoʻi ko Sylva alakaʻi ʻana ma kēia wā loli nui o ke Keʻena Kuleana Hawaiʻi. Ua hoʻohālike ʻo ia iā ia me kahi hoʻokele ma luna o ka waʻa a me nā hihia kānāwai e ʻalo nei nā Hawaiʻi he ʻino weliweli e hōʻea mai ana i ke ʻalihi lani.
“ʻAʻole nō hoʻohala manawa kahi hoʻokele ʻoi a hōʻea pono ka ʻino i mua pono o ka waʻa no ka hoʻomākaukau ʻana,” wahi āna. “Heluhelu ka hoʻokele mākaukau i nā hōʻailona, ka makani, ke kai, a hoʻomākaukau i ka waʻa a me nā kānaka no ka huakaʻi.”
Ua ʻōlelo ʻo De Mont Manaole, kahi mea hoʻopaipai pono kaulike ma ke kānāwai, nāna i hāpai manaʻo ma ke kākoʻo iā Sylva ma ka Poʻakolu, ua pūʻiwa ʻo ia i ka manaʻo hoʻoholo o ka papa.
“Me he mea lā, ʻaʻohe mana o ka manaʻo o nā ʻōhua,” wahi āna i ʻōlelo ai.
Ua manaʻo ʻo ia, ʻo Sylva a me Park nā moho ikaika aʻe no kā lāua hana ma ka hoʻopaipai no nā Hawaiʻi. ʻO Sylva, wahi āna, he mea ʻo ia e ʻimi ana e kū i mua o ke Kiaʻāina Josh Green a koi e ʻoi aku ke kūlana o ka Hawaiʻi ma ka hoʻoholo ʻana me ka ʻoihana pūʻalikoa ma luna o nā ʻaelike ʻāina. A ua alakaʻi ʻo Park i ke Keʻena ʻĀina Hoʻopulapula Hawaiʻi.
No Apo, wahi āna, he “kanaka ʻo ia o ke Alanui Bishop” a Manaole e manaʻo nei, ʻaʻole i kū kāna hana he hana e hoʻopaipai ana no nā Hawaiʻi.
He mea ke kaʻawale o ka papa e hōʻike ana i ka hemahema i ke ākea, wahi āna, a me he mea lā, he “politika keiki.”
Ma kona ʻaoʻao ʻo ia ka Luna Hoʻokele Hoʻokō hou, e komo ʻo Apo ma kahi wā e piʻi aʻe nei nā hihia kānāwai no nā papahana Hawaiʻi. A e hālāwai pū ʻo ia me nā manaʻo hoʻoholo no ke ʻano e ʻimi aʻe ai i ke “ea” — he mea i kāpae ʻia he pahuhopu ma ko ke keʻena papahana hikiāloa i kekahi mau makahiki aku nei a i hoʻolauna hou ʻia e kekahi mau lālā papa kahu waiwai.
Ua ‘ōlelo ʻo ia, ʻo kāna makakoho mua ke kūkulu pilina me nā lālā papa kahu waiwai ʻē aʻe a me nā limahana o ke Keʻena Kuleana Hawaiʻi. Ma kahi hālāwai hōʻike manaʻo o kēlā Poʻahā aku nei, ua ʻōlelo ʻo ia no kona ʻike ʻana i kona kūlana he kūlana hoʻokuanaʻike i nā limahana o ke Keʻena Kuleana Hawaiʻi ma waena o ka “hūhā o waho.”
Ua wehewehe pū ʻo ia iā ia iho he alakaʻi hana pū e ʻimi mālie ana i ka hoʻolohe i ka poʻe ma mua o ka lele ʻana. I mea e kōkua ai i ka hoʻokaʻaʻike kūloko ma ke Keʻena Kuleana Hawaiʻi, ua hāpai ʻo ia i kahi palapala “ʻoiaʻiʻo hoʻokahi” e hiki ai i nā limahana a manakia ke kiʻi no ka hoʻomaopopo ʻana i ka hana a ka hui me ke aʻo pū no nā papahana hou.
Ma ka hōʻuluʻulu i kahi manaʻo mai ke kiʻiʻoniʻoni ʻo “Lilo & Stitch,” ua wehewehe ʻo ia i nā kime āna i hana pū ai ma ke ʻano he ʻohana.
“ʻAʻohe lālā e waiho ʻia i muliwai,” wahi āna.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Task force dives into possible changes to Kansas school funding as current formula is set to expire
description: TOPEKA — A legislative committee resumed the challenging task this week of examining possible new school funding models to replace the one the state was forced to use by the courts.  Since 2016, the state has used a formula set after the settlement of a lawsuit that challenged the state for not fully funding education, […]
text:
Leah Fliter, assistant executive director of advocacy for the Kansas Association of School Boards, shown here testifyign in February, watched the Education Funding Task Force  with interest to track how possible changes to the public school funding formula would affect school districts statewide. (Kansas Reflector screen capture of Kansas Legislature video)TOPEKA — A legislative committee resumed the challenging task this week of examining possible new school funding models to replace the one the state was forced to use by the courts. 
Since 2016, the state has used a formula set after the settlement of a lawsuit that challenged the state for not fully funding education, said Leah Fliter, lobbyist at Kansas Association of School Boards.
With legislation that adopted the formula set to expire June 30, 2027, lawmakers are looking at how they can adjust the formula. 
The Education Funding Task Force considered more than 15 models with a variety of scenarios at its Tuesday and Wednesday meetings. Discussions ranged from pulling gifted education from special education funding to its own category to how weightings could be changed to support better literacy education in kindergarten through third grades.
Fliter said she watched the proceedings with interest to make sure the Legislature continues to fund at the current level. 
Task force members haven’t shown interest in cutting school funding overall, but the many models they considered would affect funding by school district whenever the formula changes, she said. Each district has different mixes of students with different needs. 
“Whenever you tweak the formula, you do end up with districts that gain money and districts that potentially lose money, so a winners-and-losers thing that plays out when you start to push and pull the levers and the buttons in the school formula,” she said. 
The “levers” are pieces of the funding formula that support services like special education, at-risk students and high or low enrollments. Each student gets base state aid and then, depending on extra needs, additional monies, Fliter said. 
“The formula was built to have these different weightings in place to to help make sure that everybody is getting an equitable and adequate education, regardless of where they live in the state,” Fliter said. 
The concept of whether a formula might lower or raise the amount school districts receive was one that caused disagreement within the task force. Rep. Nikki McDonald, D-Olathe, said she couldn’t foresee accepting a formula that gave any school districts fewer dollars than what they currently receive. 
Sen. Renee Erickson, R-Wichita, said any changes to the formula were certain to affect districts in a variety of ways. 
“The reality is that when we start making any change, no district is probably going to get exactly the same amount,” she said. “If that’s our goal, give everybody the same amount, then we just wasted two years of talking about what are some changes we can do better on the school finance formula.”
The current funding formula already has its own challenges, including how it accounts for inflation, Fliter said. Lawmakers in 2019 satisfied the Kansas Supreme Court by agreeing to automatically increase funding each year by the average increase in the Midwest consumer price index for the past three years.
“It was developed under a set of factors that really are no longer true,” she said. “They were not taking into account that inflation was going to do what it did, especially around the COVID pandemic.”
The inflationary adjustment doesn’t account for the actual increases in personnel costs, such as insurance and other benefits, Fliter said. 
The task force is scheduled to meet again in December.

title: Jackson is a no on Schumer, but still holding out support for Van Hollen
description: Even before U.S. Sen.-elect Troy Jackson defeated outgoing Sen. Susan Collins, he said he would not back Chuck Schumer as caucus leader. But Jackson has not committed to supporting Schumer’s only declared challenger. Jackson told Maine Morning Star that he spoke with Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., earlier this week and was pleased with his […]
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson answers questions at a campaign event in Brunswick on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)Even before U.S. Sen.-elect Troy Jackson defeated outgoing Sen. Susan Collins, he said he would not back Chuck Schumer as caucus leader. But Jackson has not committed to supporting Schumer’s only declared challenger.
Jackson told Maine Morning Star that he spoke with Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., earlier this week and was pleased with his vision for Senate Democrats. 
“I haven’t done anything more than had that conversation with him, but it was a good conversation,” he said. “At the same time, I want to make damn sure that my vote counts.”
Jackson’s counterpart, independent Sen. Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats, has said he will support Schumer during the closed door leadership vote, which is slated for Dec. 1. 
Schumer, who has led the caucus since 2017, helped fund many of the candidates whose wins flipped the chamber blue in the midterms. But, he had also backed moderate challengers over progressives who ended up winning primaries, including Gov. Janet Mills, who dropped out of Maine’s U.S. Senate race when former insurgent candidate Graham Platner had still been in the running.  
Some Democrats say the party’s significant midterm wins reflect voters’ desire for change, criticizing Schumer as not being aggressive enough in pushing back on President Donald Trump and being too friendly with Israel, among other policy stances. 
Regardless of who is chosen to lead when Democrats become the majority in January, Jackson, a former logger and state Senate president, said it won’t make a difference to how he approaches his work. 
“I’m going down there to fight for Mainers and people that need government to work for them, and from what I’ve seen so far there’s another group of people that feel the same way,” Jackson said of meeting other newly elected Democratic senators during a trip to Washington, D.C. 
“Hopefully leadership gets on board,” he added. “If not, I think we’re going to push them to get on board. That’s just the way that I think it should be. Leaders don’t decide the policy. I think the overall group does.”
During a recent caucus meeting, Jackson said he made his priority of affordable, quality health care known. “I don’t really care if people think I’m pushing too hard or not,” he said. 
U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont who had campaigned with Jackson, has vowed to focus on Medicare for All when he takes over as chairman of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year. 
As Jackson prepares for the new U.S. Congress to begin, he said he is focused both on coalition building in Washington and on constituent services at home. 
He said the most surprising thing he learned during his trip to the nation’s capital was that in-state office space is capped by a square footage formula tied to state population for U.S. senators. In light of that, he is considering how to have smaller but more offices in more parts of the state so people do not have to travel as far to speak with his staff. 
As for building alliances, Jackson was glad to hear many of the other newly elected senators shared his priorities, he said. But he’s also begun having conversations with senators skeptical of certain aims, including those nervous about Medicare for All.
“My biggest thing has always been I’m happy to lead on an issue; I’m also happy to be a partner with other people that are pushing forward on things I care about,” he said. “It’s about getting results.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi enhances income verification for SNAP recipients
description: Food is stored on pantry shelves at Johnson Elementary School in Jackson on Wednesday, Oct. 5, 2025.
text:
Mississippi is rolling out new income verification software for food assistance as state officials say they seek to reduce errors that could cost taxpayers. 
The so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act, passed by Congress and signed into law by President Donald Trump in 2025, requires states with high payment error rates to pay a share of the cost of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits beginning in 2027. How much a state pays is based on its error rate for SNAP, which measures how accurately each state determines eligibility and benefit amounts. 
The Mississippi Department of Human Services’ new software, called Truv, will help caseworkers verify income faster, calculate benefits more accurately and reduce the state’s error rate, said Mark Jones, the department’s chief communications officer. 
“It’s all part of a comprehensive plan to see what we can do to keep the SNAP program moving forward to the benefit of the clients, but also to make sure that there wasn’t a substantial drag on the state’s finances because of these new provisions,” Jones said. 
People receiving SNAP benefits can already digitally submit documents that verify their income, but the new tools seek to automate the process further. Applicants and recipients can choose to connect a participating payroll account and authorize Truv to share income and employment information with MDHS. 
Jones said clients are expected to have the choice to opt in to most Truv features.
The software can help caseworkers review applications, renewals or reported changes more efficiently, but households still have to report certain changes. Mississippi uses “change reporting” in its implementation of the federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. This requires SNAP recipients to report changes in their income, household size or home address within 10 days.
Mississippi is the only state that exclusively uses change reporting. 
Critics say this system creates administrative burdens, causes eligible families to lose food assistance and could cost the state millions of dollars by contributing to its high error rate. 
Some lawmakers during the 2026 legislative session attempted to ease these requirements by adopting “simplified reporting,” which requires recipients to report only major changes in income immediately, like a salary change that exceeds the program’s income threshold or large lottery winnings. Most states use this reporting method. The proposal failed. 
From the 2025 to 2024 fiscal years, Mississippi reduced its error rate from 10.69% to 9.51%, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. 
When state cost sharing for SNAP benefits begins next October, Mississippi can use its 2025 or 2026 error rate to determine how much it will pay in the first year. If it uses its 2025 rate, the state would pay 10% of benefit costs. The highest share is 15%.
Jones said Mississippi’s error rate has continued to fall. If the rate used to calculate the state’s share is between 6% and 8%, Mississippi would pay 5% of benefit costs.
“We’ve been working hard to lower our performance error rate,” Jones said.  
Lawmakers in 2026 appropriated $6 million to MDHS for income verification software. 
Jones said the agency has also renewed an employment and income verification tool contract with Equifax, and expanded a service called Promise that sends text messaging reminders for work reporting, recertification deadlines and documents for timely processing.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pennsylvania U.S. Sen. McCormick previews a Congress with a GOP minority
description: For the first time since being elected in 2024, U.S. Sen. Dave McCormick will be in the minority congressional party.
text:
U.S. Sen. Dave McCormick spoke in Harrisburg at the Pennsylvania Press Club on May 18, encouraging the commonwealth's stakeholders to lean into an exciting time in human history. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)As Republicans contend with an election rout earlier this month that pushed them out of power in Pennsylvania and Congress, GOP U.S. Sen. Dave McCormick reflected Thursday on future opportunities for his party and home state.
“We got thumped,” the state’s junior U.S. senator summarized. “As a collegiate athlete, when you get beat badly or fail, you need to step back and say, ‘What happened? What did we learn?’”
The big message from voters, he continued, was that they disliked the lack of his party’s focus on the high cost of gas, healthcare and housing. 

New US House Democrats — including two from Pa. — reinforce push for congressional stock-trading ban


“I think lesson one is more focus, more attention … that we heard you and we have a plan to deal with that,” he said. Secondly, he added, concerns about public corruption or selfishness from elected leaders benefitting from their roles — with stock trading, for example — eroded voter confidence in the party. 
For the first time since being elected in 2024, McCormick will be in the minority after Democrats clinched 56 of the Senate’s 100 seats. 
“In terms of my day-to-day way I operate, I don’t think it’s going to change much, to be honest with you,” McCormick said. “I look for opportunities to get things done with my colleagues in the Democratic Party. Even if I disagree with them on 80% of the stuff, I look for the 20%.”
“The one thing I am 100% sure of is that people elected me with an expectation that I was going to work with whoever I needed to work with to get things done, and that’s what I promised them,” he added. 
He pointed to his conservative voting record, but also noted he’s built a reputation for working in a bipartisan fashion, putting himself in a good position to work on common ground issues that elevate Pennsylvania as a place for innovation.
“I think I’m going to be able to continue to do that, and I think that’s a big part of the job,” McCormick continued. 
 Priorities for new elected officials

Democrats on both the state and national level have named increasing the minimum wage from $7.25 as one of their priorities as part of their promise to tackle affordability. 
McCormick said employers had to have higher wages to be competitive, adding that he was “open-minded” about an increase. 
“I think it’s not the main thing that’s going to help folks in Pennsylvania,” he continued. “I think the thing that we really need to do that’s going to change the landscape is bring down gas prices. We got that message loud and clear in the election.”
McCormick detailed three priorities for Republicans during the lame duck session, since the GOP still has a majority in both congressional chambers until Democrats take power in early January.
