He said he hoped a permitting reform bill would be on President Donald Trump’s desk before the new year, an effort that aims to streamline the process for building infrastructure and energy. Additionally, senators would work to confirm Trump’s judicial nominees and finalize a reconciliation bill “that funds our military.” 
“I’m very worried that, because there are different views with the Congress on the Iran War, that the Democrats in particular are going to use funding for the military as a way to show their lack of support for operations there,” McCormick added. “Whether you agree or disagree with the operations in Iran, we have to have the financial support, the resources for our men and women in the military to protect them … to make sure we remain the most lethal military in the world.” 
Sharing that he will “likely” be the ranking minority member of the Senate Energy Committee, he said that he’d recently dined with the new chair and talked about accelerating nuclear power, small modular reactors and other power sources. 
“I think Pennsylvania is really uniquely positioned to be a leader in this,” he added, pointing to natural gas and nuclear resources. “We’ve got a lot of assets, a lot of expertise, and I expect we’ll be at the forefront of many of the things that happen.”
 Optimistic about Pennsylvania’s future

McCormick highlighted several recent economic investments on his radar, including Eli Lilly’s $3.5 billion investment in Lehigh County to build an advanced pharmaceutical manufacturing facility.
“They could have put this anywhere in 50 states. They chose Pennsylvania,” he said. “It’s an example of the kind of focus on advanced manufacturing and reindustrialization that’s happening here in Pennsylvania that I’m such a champion of.”
He said attracting projects like that required bipartisan support. Getting Democrats like Gov. Josh Shapiro and his Pennsylvania olleague U.S. Sen. John Fetterman would also boost the state’s application to be the site of the new U.S. Space Academy.

Pennsylvania pitches plan for U.S. Space Academy with $285 million state investment


“We think … southwestern Pennsylvania has the talent, technology and industrial strength to help America win the race for space dominance,” McCormick, a West Point graduate, continued. “We have the strength to really have a great facility, or really ecosystem, to train the next generation of leaders.” 
The school would be the nation’s sixth service academy and is expected to eventually enroll up to 4,000 students. The site, adjacent to Pittsburgh International Airport, is paired with a $285 million investment from the commonwealth.
“We think we have a lot of things that make this an attractive application,” McCormick said, naming the state’s proximity to other major cities and higher education opportunities.
He added that Pennsylvania’s status as a purple state is important. “It’s not a political decision, but it’s certainly a benefit,” the senator said. “I think that Pennsylvania is well represented by Democrats and Republicans in putting this proposal forward.”

name: Delaware
title: When do Delaware schools tell parents about a student’s new name or pronouns?
description: A federal investigation named a Colonial district in Pennsylvania. In Delaware, Christina and Red Clay have written policies on how staff address students at school and what names and pronouns they use when contacting home. WILMINGTON, Del -The Colonial School District named in a federal student privacy investigation Wednesday is in Montgomery County, Pennsy[...]
text:
A federal investigation named a Colonial district in Pennsylvania. In Delaware, Christina and Red Clay have written policies on how staff address students at school and what names and pronouns they use when contacting home.
WILMINGTON, Del -The Colonial School District named in a federal student privacy investigation Wednesday is in Montgomery County, Pennsylvania. The U.S. Department of Education’s announcement named no Delaware districts, including the Colonial district based in New Castle.
The inquiry raises a question for Delaware families. When does a school tell parents that a student has asked to use a different name or pronouns? Delaware’s school nondiscrimination regulation leaves that question open. Two New Castle County districts, Christina and Red Clay Consolidated, spell out how staff should address students in class and when they contact home.
What federal officials are investigating
The department’s Student Privacy Policy Office opened investigations into five districts. Along with Colonial in Pennsylvania, it named Eau Claire Area in Wisconsin, Thompson in Colorado, Community Unit School District 300 in Illinois and St. Paul Public Schools in Minnesota. The investigations will determine whether the districts violated federal law. Forth
Federal officials pointed to forms often called gender support plans that ask students which names and pronouns they want to use and whether their families know. The department also raised concerns that some districts keep those plans in separate files that parents may be unable to access. Jessica Lester, a spokesperson for Pennsylvania’s Colonial district, told The Philadelphia Inquirer that the policy had been in place since 2019 and was intended to foster a welcoming school community.
The office is examining two laws. The Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, known as FERPA, generally gives parents the right to inspect education records a school maintains about their child. The Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment gives parents rights concerning certain surveys or evaluations that ask students for sensitive information, including consent rights in specified circumstances. Protecting Student Privacy
What Delaware’s regulation says
Delaware’s Regulation 225, amended in April, bars unlawful discrimination in programs that receive approval or financial assistance from or through the state Department of Education. It incorporates protections in the Delaware Equal Accommodations Law, which includes gender identity. The regulation is silent on names, pronouns and parent notification. regulations.delaware.gov
Delaware considered a more specific rule in 2017. The initial proposal would have allowed schools in some circumstances to honor a student’s request to use a different name without notifying parents. WHYY reported that the state received more than 11,000 comments, most opposing that provision. Then-Education Secretary Susan Bunting revised the proposal in June 2018 to require permission from a parent or guardian before granting a minor’s request. The state dropped that version in August after receiving more than 6,000 additional comments. WHYY
What Christina and Red Clay put in writing
Both districts allow students to use names and pronouns at school that reflect their gender identity. When staff contact a parent or guardian, the policies say staff should use the student’s legal name and the pronoun corresponding to the sex assigned at birth, unless the student, parent or guardian has specified otherwise. Both districts keep the student’s legal name in the official permanent record. christinak12.diligent.community
The policies also direct staff to protect private information about a student’s gender identity unless disclosure is legally required or the student authorizes it. Neither published policy describes a gender support plan form. Whether either district uses one remains unconfirmed. christinak12.diligent.community
Christina adopted its policy in 2021 and revised it in June 2023. Red Clay’s board approved its policy by a 4-3 vote in December 2021 after removing a parental approval requirement from an earlier draft. Supporters cited student safety and privacy. Then-board President Cathy Thompson, who voted against the policy, argued that schools should involve parents as much as possible. christinak12.diligent.community
What’s known about other districts
Delaware Public Media reported in May 2024 that Christina and Red Clay were the only two of Delaware’s 19 school districts it found with formal policies on the treatment of transgender and gender-nonconforming students. Current practices across all 19 districts remain unverified. Delaware Public Media
Individual plans have been used elsewhere. Spotlight Delaware reported in April that a Cape Henlopen district lawyer’s letter described a gender support plan reviewed with a middle school student’s teachers and school nurse at the start of the 2018-19 school year. Separately, a Cape Henlopen parent told Delaware Public Media in 2024 that the district suggested a plan for her child and later revised it to include his preferred name and pronouns. Cape Henlopen’s current approach to notifying parents remains unconfirmed. spotlightdelaware.org
In a separate California case, the U.S. Supreme Court in March allowed a lower court injunction to take effect for parents challenging that state’s school gender identity policies while the appeal proceeded. In its interim ruling, the court said the parents were likely to succeed on their religious exercise and due process claims. supremecourt.gov
To Go Box

Ask your principal or district office what happens when a student requests a different name or pronouns. Ask whether staff notify parents, whether they seek consent and whether the district uses a written support plan.
To inspect your child’s education records under FERPA, send a written request to the school or district records office. Identify the records you want to see, including any support plan the school maintains for your child. Schools generally must provide access to covered records within 45 days of receiving the request. Federal student records guidance
Find your district through the Delaware Department of Education’s public school directory. Delaware’s Colonial district office in New Castle can be reached at 302-323-2700. Delaware public school directory · Colonial district contacts
Parents who believe their federal student privacy rights were violated can find complaint instructions through the U.S. Department of Education. Federal complaint instructions

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: FCC approves cellphone jamming in state prisons, a longtime priority for SC leaders
description: The decision came a day after South Carolina officials called for the regulation to pass, following more than a decade of advocacy.
text:
Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr, surrounded by South Carolina law enforcement officials, talks about cellphone jamming at the attorney general's office in Columbia, S.C., on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)States can ask the federal government for permission to jam cellphone signals in prisons after a federal commission vote Thursday.
The Federal Communications Commission’s vote came a day after South Carolina’s top law enforcement officials called for the regulation to pass, following more than a decade of advocacy from state leaders.
Chairman Brendan Carr and Commissioner Olivia Trusty voted in favor of the change in regulation, which will allow state prisons and local jails to block cellphone signals. Commissioner Anna Gomez agreed in part and dissented in part, raising concerns that the regulation didn’t do enough to ensure prisoners still have access to people on the outside.
After years of advocacy in SC, FCC poised to allow cellphone jamming in state prisons

South Carolina is ready to apply as soon as the rule is officially added to the Federal Register, said state prisons director Joel Anderson. That could take up to a few weeks, Carr said.
The Department of Corrections plans to implement the technology one facility at a time, starting with the Broad River Road complex, which includes five separate prisons, Anderson said Wednesday.
“South Carolina is ready to move forward and institute this crucial public safety technology,” Anderson said in a statement to the Daily Gazette on Thursday. “We will work methodically and strategically to make sure the public, our staff and inmates are safe.”
To start using the technology, the Department of Corrections will need more state funding, said spokeswoman Chrysti Shain. How much is unclear, since that will depend on which companies can prove their jamming technology works, she said.
Over the past two years, legislators spent $18.5 million on technology that tracks cellphones in prisons, allowing officials to report illegal phones and get them turned off. The same technology should be able to block cellphone signals, but that aspect is untested because jamming was previously illegal, Shain said.
Before a state prison or local jail can start jamming cellphone signals, officials must get permission from the FCC. Agencies must prove the technology works and won’t affect communications outside the prison before getting approval.
After that, the FCC will issue annual certificates to make sure the technology is still working as planned, said Wireless Telecommunications Bureau attorney Andrew Ware.
The commissioners agreed contraband cellphones are a major public safety issue. Prisoners have used the phones to have people killed, run scams, and traffic guns and drugs, officials have said.
In South Carolina, prisoners used cellphones to orchestrate a hit on contraband officer Capt. Robert Johnson in 2010, kicking off state leaders’ push to flush phones out of prisons. Johnson survived six bullet wounds from close range.
The largest crime ring in state history also relied on inmates with cellphones, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office.
“While there is no dispute that this is a problem worth solving, one question has been how to effectively do so while protecting legitimate communications,” Trusty said.
The regulation does that through the specific requirements laid out, she and Carr said.
Despite the safeguards, Gomez still had concerns, she said.
Gomez worried jammers becoming widely available could get them into the hands of bad actors, who might sell them for use outside of prisons, leading to more crimes and other chaos.
“I want to make sure that we don’t harm public safety in the name of helping public safety,” she said.
The regulation addressed many of Gomez’s fears, she said. The change includes strict requirements about notifying nearby communities, proving jammers won’t interfere with other signals, and alerting the FCC immediately if a jammer is taken off prison property.
However, she felt the regulation didn’t do enough to ensure prisoners can still communicate with their families outside the prison walls. The FCC’s primary job in prisons is to ensure access to communication, not block it, she said.
“While correctional facilities should have safety and security services like jamming to prevent criminal activity, it is not the responsibility of the families of incarcerated people to pay the costs of these measures,” Gomez said.
Inmates aren’t spending thousands of dollars on contraband cellphones to talk to their families when they can do so on the prison-provided phones, Carr said.
States, including South Carolina, have tried other methods of keeping phones out of prisons, but none have proven as effective as jamming, Carr said. Prisoners will continue to get contraband and commit crimes without cellphones, but stopping the signals will make that more difficult, he said.
“This itself is not going to be a silver bullet, but I think it’s time that we stop denying this tool to state and local officials,” Carr said.

name: California
title: California ordenó a las escuelas que se aseguraran de que los niños fueran al dentista. Pero nadie revisó que se cumpliera
description: La Evaluación de la Salud Dental en el Jardín de Infancia de California exige a los centros educativos que realicen encuestas a los alumnos, pero una auditoría reveló que muchos de ellos no disponían de datos fiables.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Una iniciativa que lleva 20 años en vigor y que exige que los alumnos más jóvenes de California sean examinados para detectar caries y deterioro dental antes de entrar en la escuela pública no está dando los resultados esperados.
 El estado creó la Evaluación de Salud Bucal para Niños de Jardín de Infantes en 2006 para garantizar que las familias se conecten con dentistas, identificar las necesidades dentales de los estudiantes y detectar obstáculos para acceder a la atención. Sin embargo, según un nuevo informe del Auditor Estatal de California que se centró en seis distritos escolares y el Departamento de Salud Pública de California, esta iniciativa se ha visto obstaculizada por dificultades.
 La caries dental es en gran medida prevenible, sin embargo, es la enfermedad crónica más común en niños en todo el país. Alrededor del 61% de los estudiantes de tercer grado padecieron caries durante el año escolar 2018-19, según un informe estatal de 2021, y los expertos señalan que la salud bucal infantil ha empeorado aún más desde el inicio de la pandemia.
 Los problemas dentales no tratados pueden provocar ausencias escolares. La Encuesta de Entrevistas de Salud de California del Centro de Investigación de Políticas de Salud de la UCLA reveló que cerca del 7% de los niños de 5 años o más que asisten a la escuela faltaron a clase debido a problemas dentales en 2025.
 La revisión de los distritos reveló que no mantenían datos fiables sobre todos los aspectos del programa y que reportaban información incorrecta al estado. Los distritos auditados son el Distrito Escolar Unificado de Los Ángeles, el Distrito Escolar de la Ciudad de Merced, el Distrito Escolar Unificado de Milpitas, el Distrito Escolar Unificado de Oakland, el Distrito Escolar Unificado Costero de San Luis y el Distrito Escolar Unificado Conjunto de Woodland.
 Ninguna agencia estatal supervisa el programa de salud bucal para niños de preescolar, según reveló la auditoría, y ni el Departamento de Educación de California ni el Departamento de Salud Pública supervisan las actividades del programa. El departamento de salud estatal, responsable de las iniciativas estatales para mejorar la salud dental, no ha verificado los datos reportados por los distritos, según la auditoría, y no los utiliza para medir el progreso del estado en la mejora de la salud bucal infantil.
 El departamento no publica análisis anuales de los datos en su sitio web; los datos más recientes del programa disponibles en línea, correspondientes al año escolar 2020-21, se encuentran en el sitio web de la Asociación Dental de California . La auditoría también reveló que la fuente de financiación del programa —un impuesto de 2016 sobre los productos de tabaco— está disminuyendo.
 “Hemos determinado que los datos poco fiables que presentan los distritos y la supervisión estatal insuficiente de los requisitos del programa [Evaluación de la Salud Bucal en el Jardín de Infancia] ponen en peligro los objetivos del programa”, escribió el auditor estatal Grant Parks en un informe del 5 de noviembre.
 La portavoz del Departamento de Salud Pública, Kristine Tuzon, citando el código de educación estatal , afirmó que la agencia no es responsable de dar seguimiento a las solicitudes del programa de salud bucal para niños de jardín de infantes ni de notificar a las oficinas de educación de los condados cuando los distritos no informan los datos. Tuzon indicó que la ley no otorga al departamento de salud la autoridad para exigir a los distritos y a las oficinas de los condados que cumplan con el mandato de presentación de datos del programa.
 Según la auditoría, una forma de reducir las barreras para que los niños accedan a evaluaciones dentales es realizar más en los centros escolares, como se hace con las pruebas de visión y audición obligatorias por ley. Esta solución también ha presentado dificultades en cuanto a la recopilación de datos.
 Esther Yepez es la directora asociada de programas de bienestar y salud bucal en The Los Angeles Trust for Children’s Health, organización que coordinó exámenes de salud bucal en las escuelas del Distrito Escolar Unificado de Los Ángeles durante cinco años. Tras completar las evaluaciones, su equipo entregaba los formularios a las escuelas. Sin embargo, según Yepez, a menudo las escuelas no registraban esos exámenes en el sistema del distrito, lo que generaba una discrepancia entre el número de estudiantes examinados y el número reportado al estado. Además, no estaba claro quién era el responsable de recopilar los datos en cada escuela.
 “Fue frustrante”, dijo Yepez, “porque teníamos información de que se habían realizado las pruebas de detección, pero las escuelas no tenían esos datos”.
 El Distrito Escolar Unificado de Los Ángeles no respondió a las preguntas de CalMatters sobre la exactitud de los datos del programa de salud bucal para niños de kínder. En respuesta a la auditoría, publicada como parte del informe, Joel Cisneros, director ejecutivo de los servicios de salud mental y bienestar estudiantil del Distrito Escolar Unificado de Los Ángeles, indicó que el distrito planea capacitar al personal escolar sobre los procedimientos de ingreso de datos y los requisitos de documentación del programa, así como establecer un proceso estandarizado para registrar todos los formularios y exenciones devueltos. 
Dientes podridos y un dolor insoportable
 La Academia Estadounidense de Odontología Pediátrica recomienda que los niños visiten al dentista cuando les salga su primer diente, o a más tardar en su primer cumpleaños.
 Las visitas dentales en la primera infancia son “sumamente importantes”, afirmó el Dr. Francisco Ramos-Gómez, jefe del departamento de odontología pediátrica de la Facultad de Odontología de UCLA y director del Centro de Salud Bucal Infantil de UCLA. Sin embargo, señaló que muchas familias no acceden a la atención debido a problemas de transporte, barreras lingüísticas y la escasez de profesionales que atienden a niños de bajos recursos.
 “Si empezamos a ver a estos niños a los 3 o 4 años”, dijo, “ya llegan con dientes podridos, abscesos y un dolor intenso”.
 El programa de jardín de infancia exige a los distritos escolares que notifiquen a las familias que se matriculan por primera vez en la escuela pública (preescolar, jardín de infancia o primer grado) que deben presentar un comprobante de una evaluación de salud bucal. La ley estatal permite a los padres eximir de este requisito debido a dificultades económicas, falta de acceso a un dentista o negativa a dar su consentimiento.
 El programa exige que los distritos presenten datos específicos a las oficinas de educación de sus condados o a un sistema designado por el director de odontología del estado, que desde al menos 2021 ha sido el Sistema de Informes de Salud Bucal de California . Asimismo, ordena al departamento de salud que evalúe periódicamente los requisitos del programa de jardín de infancia.
 Sin embargo, la auditoría reveló que ninguno de los distritos proporcionó a las familias toda la información necesaria sobre el requisito de evaluación. Los seis distritos auditados también carecían de procedimientos formalizados para dar seguimiento a las familias que no devolvieron los formularios de evaluación o que devolvieron exenciones que indicaban un impedimento para obtener la evaluación.
 La auditoría reveló que cinco distritos reportaron datos al sistema estatal que diferían significativamente de sus datos locales. Por ejemplo, el Distrito Escolar Unificado de Los Ángeles, el más grande del estado, incluyó erróneamente a todos los alumnos de primer grado en su conteo de estudiantes sujetos a los requisitos del programa para el año escolar 2024-25, en lugar de solo a aquellos que no se habían inscrito previamente en kínder en el distrito, según la auditoría. El distrito también sobreestimó la cantidad de estudiantes que presentaron comprobante de la evaluación, agregó la auditoría.
 «La magnitud de los errores de información cometidos tan solo por el Distrito Escolar Unificado de Los Ángeles», escribió Parks, «distorsiona cualquier análisis estatal de los datos colectivos».
 La auditoría recomendó que los distritos proporcionaran a los padres toda la información requerida sobre el programa y que reportaran datos completos y precisos al sistema estatal. En sus respuestas al estado, los distritos de Milpitas y Oakland indicaron que implementarían las recomendaciones de la auditoría, mientras que los distritos de Los Ángeles y San Luis Coastal compartieron planes de acción para abordar algunas de las conclusiones del informe. Los distritos de Merced y Woodland no presentaron respuesta. 
 ¿De dónde viene el dinero?
 La auditoría también reveló que la financiación del programa de salud bucodental está disminuyendo.
 El departamento de salud pública estatal otorga fondos de la Proposición 56 —generados por un impuesto a los productos de tabaco— a los departamentos de salud de los condados y les exige que apoyen iniciativas de salud bucal, incluido el programa de jardín de infancia. Sin embargo, según la auditoría, los ingresos provenientes de este impuesto están disminuyendo drásticamente, y a partir del próximo año, el departamento de salud ya no exigirá a los condados que reciban fondos de la Proposición 56 que apoyen el programa de jardín de infancia.
 Tuzon afirmó que el departamento de salud está evaluando estrategias para mantener y mejorar el cumplimiento del programa, dada la disminución de la financiación procedente de los impuestos al tabaco.
 A pesar de los problemas con los datos, Eileen Espejo, directora general sénior de salud de Children Now, dijo que los responsables políticos deberían considerar cómo financiar el programa de salud bucal de jardín de infancia en el futuro.
 “Los programas de salud locales van a tener menos capacidad para realizar algunas de estas tareas”, afirmó. “Es necesario debatir: ‘¿De dónde saldrá el dinero para ayudar a aumentar el cumplimiento de las normas?’”.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Brown Health was supposed to expand primary care access. Instead, it lost providers.
description: Fourteen months after Brown University Health committed to a long-term expansion plan that includes hiring 15 more primary providers by the end of 2027, the healthcare operator has lost — not increased — total clinicians and only added a fraction of the 40,000 new patients required.  The lackluster preliminary performance was laid bare in a […]
text:
An exam room at Brown University Health Middletown Primary Care. (Courtesy of Brown University Health)Fourteen months after Brown University Health committed to a long-term expansion plan that includes hiring 15 more primary providers by the end of 2027, the healthcare operator has lost — not increased — total clinicians and only added a fraction of the 40,000 new patients required. 
The lackluster preliminary performance was laid bare in a July 1 report, which was released by Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha’s office on Wednesday. 
“I am deeply concerned by Brown Health’s insufficient progress, and in my view a repeat performance in the next reporting session would warrant a significant response from this Office,” Neronha said in a statement.
AG leverages regulatory review to tackle Rhode Island’s primary care shortage

Neronha negotiated the aggressive, four-year growth mandates in September 2025 as a condition for letting Brown University Health, the state’s largest hospital operator, merge with Brown Physicians, Inc, a 500-physician nonprofit specialty practice.
The marriage between the two similarly named but unrelated healthcare giants would normally have to undergo rigorous scrutiny by state regulators for potential antitrust violations. Neronha agreed to suspend the state review process in September 2025, in exchange for a series of conditions meant to soothe the state’s primary care crisis.
Under the seven-page agreement, signed days before the Oct. 1, 2025  merger closed, the healthcare system agreed to take on 40,000 new primary care patients by the end of 2029 and hire at least 27 new primary care providers, including 15 by the end of 2027.
But as of June 1, 2026, the healthcare system had three fewer primary care providers than when the agreement took effect. The net reduction in providers — with 17 clinicians leaving and 14 hired — also made it harder to add more patients, since the providers who retired or took other jobs were responsible for a combined 15,000 patients, according to the report.
Five more providers are expected to leave by the end of the year.
The healthcare system added 260 net new patients during the nine-month reporting period, representing less than 1% of the 40,000 it needs to add by Dec. 31, 2029. Despite the gargantuan gap that remains, Brown Health remains confident it can meet the benchmarks set by the AG’s office, including a net increase of 15 clinicians by the end of next year.
“The recruitment of primary care providers is a top priority to ensure Rhode Islanders have timely access to care,” Jessica Wharton, a Brown University Health spokesperson, said in an emailed response to the Current Wednesday. “We are backing our recruitment efforts with significant investments in competitive compensation, technology, clinical support, and resources that allow physicians to focus on caring for patients.”
The performance report and supplemental materials released by Neronha’s office offer some signs of progress. At the time of the July 1 report, Brown Health said it was interviewing 10 more primary care physicians, projecting a net increase of four total providers by Dec. 31.
Despite losing clinicians, Brown University Health still projects it can meet the provider and patient expansion requirements set in a 2025 agreement with the Rhode Island Attorney General’s office. (Courtesy of Brown University Health)
Waiting list: zero 
Meanwhile, Brown Health has whittled down its waiting list from a 14,000-person high on the heels of the June 2025 closure of Anchor Medical Associates, to 1,200 people as of June 1, and now, completely cleared of primary care patients. Decreasing wait times such that new patients would be seen within 14 days of calling for an appointment was also a requirement of the agreement with the AG’s office.
Neronha acknowledged the incremental achievements while noting the underlying structural challenges standing in the way of results: uncompetitive reimbursement rates compared with neighboring states, an aging workforce and the lure of concierge medicine with better pay and reduced workload.
But Brown Health knew about those problems at the time of the agreement, and made the commitment anyway, Neronha said. 
And, maybe they should not have, according to Dr. Michael Fine, a former state health director and vocal primary care advocate.
Fine said Thursday he was “absolutely not surprised” by the poor performance in Brown Health’s expansion plans.
“There aren’t any primary care clinicians available,” Fine said. “Unless there are consequences for missing the goal, I think you can expect a report like this every year.”
Neronha’s office did not respond to questions regarding potential sanctions for missed benchmarks in the agreement.



Quotation







Unless there are consequences for missing the goal, I think you can expect a report like this every year.


– Dr. Michael Fine, president of Primary Care for All Americans and former Rhode Island health director


Brown Health blamed an aging workforce and lower Medicaid reimbursement rates for hindering its ability to hire more primary care providers. 
Eight of the 22 providers who left or are expected to leave by Dec. 31 took jobs in a different state, according to the report. Another seven people retired, while four moved to private, membership-based practices.
But Fine also pointed to the reported workloads for Brown Health physicians — 1,766 patients per adult physician, and 1,339 patients per pediatric physician — as a deterrent.
“You’re asking people to do the work of three to five clinicians,” Fine said.
Research suggests fewer patients per provider can improve health outcomes and reduce physician burnout. The concierge medicine model increasingly luring doctors into private-pay practices also offers smaller patient loads of 300 to 500 people on average, promising a more individualized approach for those who can afford it. 
On the flip side, reducing providers’ patient rosters means more clinicians are needed to fill the existing provider shortage, Fine acknowledged. 
And even raising Medicaid reimbursement rates, as recommended by the Rhode Island Office of the Health Insurance Commissioner, doesn’t translate to better pay for providers, Fine said.
Brown University Health providers gather in the Rhode Island State House library on Thursday, May 14, 2026, to show support for a package of bills meant to ease rising costs and provider shortages. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)
Money talks 
Brown Health in the report says it has “refined our physician compensation model,” to incentivize clinicians to take on more new patients. A second report on July 16 answering follow-up questions from Neronha’s office provides information on payroll expenses by provider type, but the numbers are redacted. 
The company also spent more than $19 million in technology and “PCP support” in the first six months of its fiscal year, from Oct. 1, 2025 to April 1, 2026, according to the supplemental report. The breakdown of how money was spent is also redacted.
Wharton did not respond to requests for comment on how higher Medicaid reimbursement rates would be spent if awarded. But Brown Health has already made clear its balance sheet is in trouble, with alarming rises in insurance denials, debt and charity care cutting into its third-quarter bottom line, and even bigger losses projected from federal budget cuts.
“If they’re investing a lot of money into IT and overhead, as it appears they are, there is very little left over for physicians,” Fine said. “Until primary care physicians are paid about 70% of the compensation of high-income specialties, almost no one is going to choose primary care.”
Meanwhile, preliminary efforts to start a medical school at the University of Rhode Island — creating a new pipeline of healthcare providers to ease staffing shortages — will take at least $175 million and a decade to start producing results, according to analysis by a state Senate panel, on which Fine served.
Neronha suggested higher pay, modern practice models and “minimizing unnecessary workload burdens” as ways to attract and retain new primary care solutions.
Fine’s take on solutions to help Brown Health meet its mandates by 2029: “There’s no way to give us the volume of improvement we need on income, and address the workforce we need.”
While Fine lauded Neronha for an “unprecedented” focus on healthcare during his eight terms as state prosecutor, he didn’t think the terms set by the AG’s office in the 2025 agreement were realistic.
“I’m not sure lawyers should be setting healthcare policy,” he said. 
A spokesperson for Attorney General-elect Kim Ahern, who will succeed term-limited Neronha in January, acknowledged but did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The next progress report from Brown Health is due in July 2027.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Federal judge in Colorado holds ICE officials in contempt over ‘re-detention’ policy
description: A federal judge in Denver on Wednesday held senior U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials in contempt of court over a policy of immediately re-arresting individuals who had been ordered by the court to be released. In a scathing 15-page order, Judge Charlotte Sweeney of the U.S. District Court of Colorado wrote that the conduct […]
text:
The Byron G. Rogers U.S. Courthouse, home of U.S. District of Colorado, in downtown Denver is pictured in 2021. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)A federal judge in Denver on Wednesday held senior U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials in contempt of court over a policy of immediately re-arresting individuals who had been ordered by the court to be released.
In a scathing 15-page order, Judge Charlotte Sweeney of the U.S. District Court of Colorado wrote that the conduct of Nichole Black, the assistant field office director for ICE’s Denver Enforcement and Removal Operations, and other agency higher-ups “should — and, in the Court’s opinion, must — shock any reader.” But she declined to impose sanctions on the respondents following sworn testimony that the policy is no longer in effect.
The order concerned proceedings in a habeas corpus case filed by Ramon Quintero Alvarez, a longtime U.S. resident born in Mexico who was detained by ICE in February, and instructions that Black received to “immediately re-detain” Quintero Alvarez and other individuals “following their release pursuant to court orders.” In Quintero Alvarez’s case and at least 18 similar cases Black was aware of, detainees were processed for release, given their personal property and then re-arrested moments later in a “public area” outside the detention facility.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Sometimes, behavior stuns and renders a listener speechless,” Sweeney wrote. “To the extent any reader may be lost for words as to what ICE and Respondents did in this case and others in this judicial district like it — and the ridiculous nature of the justification for their behavior — turn to what the Supreme Court has said repeatedly over the course of our Nation’s history. ‘The government of the United States has been emphatically termed a government of laws and not of men.'”
“Any reader — and chief among them, Respondents — would do well to keep these binding statements in mind,” she concluded.
At least two other federal judges in Colorado have clashed with ICE officials in recent weeks over the policy, which Black characterized as a “direct order” from agency leaders to re-arrest individuals “that had some type of criminality.” Quintero Alvarez, who has lived in the U.S. for more than 30 years since entering the country with his mother and is the father of two children who are U.S. citizens, was arrested on criminal charges prior to his detention by ICE, but those charges were later dropped.
Sweeney said she wasn’t convinced by testimony from Nathan Rasper, ICE’s acting field office director in Denver, suggesting that there had been a “misunderstanding” about the new policy, characterizing the agency as exhibiting “unconstitutional behavior that runs top to bottom.”
She ruled that Black and other agency officials “were in clear contempt” of her earlier order, but that the cessation of the re-detention policy has “essentially cured” that contempt finding.
“The single thing that saves Ms. Black and Respondents (from sanctions) is Mr. Rasper’s unequivocal representation that ICE has “ceased” its immediately re-detain them ‘approach’ as a result” of a Nov. 4 hearing, Sweeney wrote.

title: Alabama Rep. Patrick Sellers indicted on federal fraud charges
description: A grand jury indicted an Alabama state representative Thursday morning on fraud charges. Rep. Patrick Sellers, D-Pleasant Grove, surrendered himself to the police Thursday morning. He is being charged with four counts of federal wire fraud. Phil Williams, the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Alabama, said at a press conference Thursday that Sellers[...]
text:
Rep. Patrick Sellers, D-Birmingham, stands on the floor of the Alabama House of Representatives on April 23, 2024 at the Alabama Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama. Sellers was indicted Thursday morning on federal wire fraud charges. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)A grand jury indicted an Alabama state representative Thursday morning on fraud charges.
Rep. Patrick Sellers, D-Pleasant Grove, surrendered himself to the police Thursday morning. He is being charged with four counts of federal wire fraud.
Phil Williams, the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Alabama, said at a press conference Thursday that Sellers was charged with fraudulently seeking and obtaining over $240,000 in COVID-19 relief funds and spending it on personal needs while working as chief of staff for the Alabama State Missionary Baptist Convention in 2020 and 2021. 
“Seven of the eight grants that he obtained and loans were intended to provide COVID-19 relief to a pair of nonprofit entities that he had assumed control over. One being the Alabama State Missionary Baptist Convention,” Williams said. “With regard to the ASMBC, the evidence indicates that Sellers did not have the authority to solicit grants and loans on behalf of the ASMBC. He did so without the knowledge of the ASMBC’s leadership. And then thereafter, Rep. Sellers took those funds that he had fraudulently obtained, and he used them for his own personal benefit.”
Attempts to contact Sellers were not immediately successful Thursday. He is scheduled to make an appearance Thursday afternoon in the Hugo L. Black United States Courthouse.
Sellers, a pastor, was first elected to the Alabama House of Representatives in 2022. He was re-elected without opposition earlier this month. 
The indictment includes a redacted email from Jan. 2024 from the president of the ASMBC saying he received notice of an Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL) that he was “not aware of nor did I approve.”
“In checking with the executive board of the convention they did not authorize any such application,” the president said in the email. “It was determined that Patrick L. Sellers, the former chief of staff for the convention, and the sole person with access to the 501(c)(3) account had surreptitiously applied for and received the loan and used the funds without any notification or authorization from the president or executive board.”
According to Williams, Sellers used the EIDL loan, totaling $20,000, for personal payments including “credit card payments and water bill payments.”
Williams accused Sellers of filling out two more grant applications from the state of Alabama on behalf of ASMBC and using the money, worth $15,000 and $20,000 each, for “personal spending such as automobile loan payments for himself and college tuition payments for his daughter.”
The last piece of evidence shown during the press conference was Sellers’ application for a Paycheck Protection Program Loan under the business Sellers Lawncare.
“The application falsely represents that Sellers Lawn Care had done $98,000 in gross income the previous year, and that was part of the application process was to establish the value of the business based on previous year’s gross receipts,” Williams said. “But yet the IRS indicates that there is no evidence of any filings on behalf of a seller’s lawn care, despite the fact that in order to apply for this loan, this PPP loan, he had to provide an IRS 1040 Schedule C, which he did, which the IRS has no record of.”

name: California
title: Becerra podría enfrentar déficit presupuestario de 2 mil millones de dólares si explota la burbuja de la IA
description: California apostó por un mercado bursátil impulsado por la inteligencia artificial para obtener miles de millones de dólares en ingresos fiscales inesperados. Pero si esa burbuja estalla, podría generar un déficit anual de 35 mil millones de dólares para el año fiscal 2028-29, advierte la Oficina del Analista Legislativo, un organismo no partidista.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
California está recaudando miles de millones de dólares en ingresos fiscales extraordinarios gracias a un mercado bursátil en auge impulsado por el entusiasmo por la inteligencia artificial.
 Pero no hay que contar con ello para solucionar los profundos problemas presupuestarios estructurales del estado, especialmente cuando la burbuja de la IA muestra signos de estar peligrosamente cerca de estallar, advirtió la Oficina del Analista Legislativo, un organismo no partidista, en su pronóstico económico anual publicado el miércoles.
 Si el mercado de valores comienza a desacelerarse el próximo año, el estado enfrentará un pequeño déficit de 2 mil millones de dólares para finales del año fiscal 2027-28, según estimaciones de la oficina. Sin embargo, ese déficit podría aumentar a 15 mil millones de dólares anuales para el año fiscal 2028-29, afirmó el analista legislativo Gabe Petek.
 Según Petek, para cubrir un déficit tan grande, los líderes estatales tendrían que desechar prácticamente todas las ampliaciones de servicios implementadas desde el año fiscal 2019-2020, incluida la extensión de Medi-Cal a los adultos inmigrantes indocumentados. O bien, explicó, se necesitaría un nuevo impuesto mayor que el actual impuesto sobre la renta del 10% al 12% para los contribuyentes de mayores ingresos, que los votantes acaban de hacer permanente mediante la Proposición 3.
Según la oficina, un desplome repentino del mercado podría desencadenar déficits presupuestarios aún mayores —un déficit anual de 35,000 millones de dólares para el año fiscal 2028-29— y el estado no tendría suficiente dinero en el banco para cubrir esa brecha.
Los ingresos aumentan, pero también el déficit
 El pronóstico del miércoles marca el quinto año consecutivo en que el estado proyecta un déficit a pesar del crecimiento de los ingresos.
 El informe ofrece un primer vistazo a los desafíos financieros que enfrenta el gobernador electo Xavier Becerra, quien presentará su primer presupuesto en enero junto con una perspectiva económica actualizada del propio departamento de finanzas del estado, que podría ser drásticamente diferente del análisis de la LAO.
 Pero si se cumplen las previsiones de la LAO, Becerra heredará un panorama financiero mucho más sombrío que el que había prometido su predecesor: en junio, el gobernador Gavin Newsom firmó un presupuesto que, según él, equilibraría las finanzas estatales durante dos años consecutivos y reduciría a la mitad los déficits futuros. Sin embargo, el presupuesto de Newsom dependía en gran medida de los ingresos derivados del auge de la IA para retrasar importantes recortes en los servicios de salud, especialmente para los inmigrantes indocumentados. Dichos recortes entrarán en vigor el próximo año a menos que Becerra encuentre nuevos fondos para mantener esos servicios.
 Becerra ha dicho poco sobre sus prioridades presupuestarias. Indicó que estaría abierto a nuevos impuestos, como un impuesto de “participación equitativa” para los ricos y un polémico cargo a los conductores por kilómetro recorrido para financiar la reparación de carreteras. Becerra también afirmó que buscaría revertir los recortes al acceso a la atención médica para los inmigrantes indocumentados, pero no ha dado detalles al respecto.
 En un comunicado emitido el miércoles, el portavoz de Becerra, Jonathan Underland, afirmó que el gobernador electo está “trabajando arduamente” en la preparación de su propuesta de presupuesto para enero.
 “Sigue comprometido con la elaboración de un presupuesto responsable y equilibrado que proteja los servicios de los que dependen los californianos y que se centre en la reducción de costes.” 
El riesgo exige respuesta
 Cualesquiera que sean las soluciones presupuestarias que Becerra esté considerando, deben implementarse rápidamente: el riesgo de una recesión del mercado exige que la administración entrante “reconstruya la resiliencia presupuestaria” mediante un ahorro agresivo, el pago de las deudas pendientes y la implementación de recortes a largo plazo o aumentos de ingresos, dijo la Oficina del Auditor General de la Unión (LAO).
 En respuesta a las previsiones, los líderes demócratas de la Asamblea celebraron la aprobación de la Proposición 2 a principios de este mes como una directriz para que la Legislatura sea prudente con los fondos públicos. La medida electoral permite al estado reservar hasta el 20% de sus ingresos fiscales generales para imprevistos, un aumento con respecto al 10% anterior, y exige que el estado ahorre más durante los períodos de auge económico.
 Los demócratas del Senado afirmaron que buscarán maneras de revertir o compensar algunos de los recortes a Medi-Cal implementados por la administración del presidente Donald Trump, que se estima que dejaron a 2 millones de californianos sin cobertura médica. A principios de este año, los demócratas del Senado propusieron un impuesto a las grandes corporaciones cuyos empleados estén inscritos en Medi-Cal y utilicen los ingresos para financiar la atención médica. Becerra, quien respaldó la idea, debe presentar un plan antes de marzo . 
 Un llamado a “afrontar la realidad”
 El líder republicano del Senado, Roger Niello , quien funge como vicepresidente del comité de presupuesto del Senado, instó a la administración de Becerra a “afrontar la realidad”.
 “Que el mercado de valores vuelva a niveles más normales es solo cuestión de tiempo”, declaró Niello en un comunicado. “Equilibrar el presupuesto estatal de manera que funcione tanto en épocas de bonanza como de crisis nos ayudará a evitar las consecuencias de realizar cambios aún más drásticos en la vida cotidiana de los californianos. De lo contrario, cuando el mercado finalmente se corrija, las consecuencias de los problemas presupuestarios actuales nos alcanzarán”.
 Desde 2023, una economía sólida impulsada por el entusiasmo por la IA ha generado importantes ingresos fiscales para el estado, incluso cuando economistas y analistas legislativos advirtieron sobre un posible colapso.
 Según Petek, los estadounidenses ahora poseen un 175 % más de acciones que el promedio histórico, y los inversores han pedido prestado el doble en los últimos tres años para comprar acciones. “Esto roza la euforia”, afirmó. 
 ¿Podría el auge convertirse en crisis?
 Pero eso no significa que los expertos se equivocaran al preocuparse.
 «Podría resultar tentador concluir que esto significa que estas señales son erróneas esta vez. Pero advertimos que podría ser cierto lo contrario: el riesgo de un cambio de tendencia en el mercado es aún mayor ahora», señala el informe de la LAO. «El riesgo que enfrentan ahora los ingresos estatales es que este auge, como muchos en el pasado, termine abruptamente en una crisis».
Por ahora, los analistas esperan que el auge de la IA genere 11,000 millones de dólares más en ingresos de lo que estimó el departamento de finanzas del estado en junio, suponiendo que el mercado se enfríe gradualmente en lugar de desplomarse en 2027, dijo Petek.
 Pero según la constitución, todos los nuevos ingresos —e incluso más— deben destinarse a la educación y a las reservas estatales, sin que quede nada para gastar en otros programas.
Aproximadamente 4,000 millones de dólares de los nuevos ingresos deben destinarse a las escuelas primarias y secundarias y a los colegios comunitarios, según la Proposición 98, que los votantes aprobaron en 1988 para establecer un nivel mínimo de financiación para la educación.
En virtud de la Propuesta 2, los líderes estatales deben depositar otros 9,000 millones de dólares en las reservas estatales este año, lo que exige un ahorro más agresivo cuando el mercado está tan agitado.
 El estado también gastará aproximadamente 600 millones de dólares más de lo previsto en junio en programas como Medi-Cal, a pesar de la disminución en la inscripción. Esto se debe principalmente al aumento de los costos de la cobertura de Medi-Cal y de los servicios sociales, según señaló la Oficina del Fiscal General. 
 Se avecina un déficit estructural
 El riesgo de un desplome del mercado hace que la ya volátil situación presupuestaria de California sea aún más precaria.
 El estado depende en gran medida de los salarios y las ganancias de las inversiones de sus residentes más adinerados, que fluctúan al ritmo del mercado de valores. Con el paso de los años, el gasto ha superado los ingresos, ya que los líderes estatales ampliaron el alcance de programas como Medi-Cal y los costos para brindar dichos programas se dispararon.
 En respuesta, los líderes estatales recurrieron principalmente a herramientas temporales, como el endeudamiento interno, el uso de las reservas estatales y la suspensión de nuevos gastos para evitar recortes drásticos en los servicios sociales.
 Pero ninguna de ellas logró restablecer el equilibrio. Como resultado, el estado ahora tiene una deuda de casi 30 mil millones de dólares, según la Oficina del Analista Legislativo (LAO).
 “Esto significa que el desequilibrio subyacente se ha mantenido y el nivel de servicios en curso no se ha ajustado a la baja para reflejar esta capacidad más limitada, lo que sugiere que el tamaño ampliado del gobierno estatal era insostenible”, dijo la oficina en un informe a principios de este mes.

title: Mike Sherzan announces independent run for Iowa Senate District 14
description: Mike Sherzan, a businessman and former candidate for Congress, announced Thursday he will run as an independent for the Iowa Senate seat left vacant by Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott’s election to Congress. Sherzan ran for Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District seat as a Democrat in 2014, 2016 and 2018. He withdrew from the race before the […]
text:
The state flag waves in front of the Iowa Capitol on May 8, 2025. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Mike Sherzan, a businessman and former candidate for Congress, announced Thursday he will run as an independent for the Iowa Senate seat left vacant by Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott’s election to Congress.
Mike Sherzan is running as an independent in the special election for Iowa Senate District 14. (Photo courtesy of Mike Sherzan)
Sherzan ran for Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District seat as a Democrat in 2014, 2016 and 2018. He withdrew from the race before the 2014 and 2018 primary; he lost to Jim Mowrer in the 2016 primary.
Sherzan said in a news release that while he is a longtime Democrat, he is running as an independent for Iowa Senate District 14 because in a special election, major-party nominees are chosen by “party insiders” at convention rather than by party voters.

“А full primary would be my first choice, but the special election process is what we currently have. I believe the people of Iowa’s 14th District should have a say about who their representative will be,” Sherzan said in a statement. “I respect the Democratic Party and the policies it stands for. However, after careful consideration, I’ve decided to take an independent path.”
Sherzan said in the release that “a world-class public education system, clean water, a fair property and income tax structure, an increase to the minimum wage, and an end to corruption in government and business is what voters in Iowa want and deserve.” He said he also would support state legislation to restrict corporate spending on elections through political action committees.
Sherzan is the third candidate to announce plans to run in the special election, which has yet to be scheduled by Gov. Kim Reynolds. Democrat Wendy Marsh, a Waukee school board member and intellectual property attorney from Waukee, announced her plans to run on Nov. 11. Republican Dave Roszak, a financial professional from Dallas County and 2026 candidate for Dallas County supervisor, announced his candidacy on Nov. 13.
Senate District 14 in southeast Dallas County includes parts of Adel, Van Meter, Waukee, and West Des Moines.

title: New bird flu cases appear in dairy herds as state ag, vet officials seek vaccine urgency
description: More states are seeing new cases of bird flu in cattle as state agricultural officials urge the federal government to prioritize approving vaccines for dairy cows. The virus, highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1, known commonly as bird flu, has been affecting poultry flocks for years, but in 2024, it began infecting milking cows after wild […]
text:
Cows from a non-suspect herd are seen at the Cornell Teaching Dairy Barn at Cornell University in 2024 in Ithaca, N.Y. States are seeing new cases of bird flu in cattle as state agricultural officials urge the federal government to prioritize approving vaccines for dairy cows. (Photo by Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)More states are seeing new cases of bird flu in cattle as state agricultural officials urge the federal government to prioritize approving vaccines for dairy cows.
The virus, highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1, known commonly as bird flu, has been affecting poultry flocks for years, but in 2024, it began infecting milking cows after wild birds spread it to cattle. The virus is deadly to poultry and milder in cows, but cows with the virus pose a risk to dairy herd workers.
While cases peaked in 2024, states are still seeing new infections in cattle this year. The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service reported that there are cases in states this year that previously hadn’t seen infections among dairy herds: Last Saturday, Oklahoma saw its first case since the outbreaks among cows began that year, according to data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Oregon also detected its first diagnosis at a dairy herd last week, as did Indiana, earlier this month, bringing the total number of states where the virus has been detected in dairy cattle to 22.
Colorado, Idaho, Texas and Washington state have also reported cases among cattle over the past month.
As bird flu spreads, feds might undercut states by firing scientists, removing data

This year so far, there have been at least 146 dairy cattle infected with the virus, with more than 1,200 cases among cattle since the outbreak began.
On Nov. 6, the National Association of State Departments of Agriculture, which represents agricultural officials across all 50 states, and the National Assembly of State Animal Health Officials, wrote a letter to the USDA urging the agency to prioritize developing an emergency vaccination framework for cows, “to take additional action to control and ultimately eradicate” the virus in dairy cattle. Cattle can develop short-lived immunity to the virus but can get re-infected, the groups wrote.
The USDA says it supports rapid development and timely approval of a vaccine for dairy cattle, and several are undergoing field trials or awaiting final approval for emergency use. Developing and approving a vaccine has its own regulatory structure, and that can make for slow testing and implementation.
Bird flu in livestock “poses an urgent threat to public and animal health, national agricultural stability, international market access, and the economic viability of the dairy and poultry industries across the U.S.,” the associations wrote. “… Without a proactive, coordinated eradication strategy, H5N1 risks becoming an endemic disease in U.S. dairy cattle, requiring USDA, State Animal Health Officials and industry to manage the disease for years while continuing to respond to costly spillover events in poultry.”
The risk to humans and the general public is low, but dairy workers who work closely with herds are at highest risk. Washington state has seen roughly three dozen new cases among cattle over the past month, and one dairy worker there died earlier this month, bringing the total deaths among humans contracting the virus to three nationwide. United Farm Workers, a workers union, said they think officials are undercounting cases among farmworkers in Washington state, and that immigration enforcement activity is hindering workers from interacting with public health systems.
Last year, federal officials announced a $1 billion plan to fight the outbreak among poultry flocks in an effort to lower egg prices, with research into a vaccine for poultry as part of the plan.
“Veterinary and state government leaders need every available tool to protect the agricultural economy in their states and empower their farmers in combating this virus to protect their dairy herds and poultry flocks. We are asking USDA for their support in helping our farmers,” Dr. Alex Hamberg, president of the National Assembly of State Animal Health Officials, said in a joint press release.
Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein can be reached at nhassanein@stateline.org.

name: WyoFile
title: Can ‘direct primary care’ help Wyoming’s healthcare woes? Powell doctors think so.
description:
307Health clinic has operated without taking health insurance for 11 years. Its doctors explain how this unorthodox primary care model works. 
The post Can ‘direct primary care’ help Wyoming’s healthcare woes? Powell doctors think so. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Back in 2014, Powell doctor Mike Tracy was asked to speak to a legislative committee about the high cost of healthcare in Wyoming. Along with serving as president of the Wyoming Medical Society, he had been a hospital-employed primary care physician for 16 years. 
In preparation for his presentation, Tracy learned about direct primary care, a model in which patients pay a membership fee directly to a doctor or clinic, bypassing traditional insurance. The idea is that by removing the burden of insurance-related paperwork, doctors can give patients more personalized care, more time and more direct access. 
“It made a lot of sense to take out the middleman and to be able to take care of people directly instead of having to work through a machine where so much of it is not transparent and not patient centered,” Tracy said. 

The 307Health clinic in Powell is a direct primary care facility that doesn’t rely on health insurance. (Mark Davis/Powell Tribune) 

That research was so convincing that Tracy went on to establish a direct primary care clinic in Powell with Dr. Robert Chandler. Eleven years later, 307Health has added a third provider, Dr. Dean Bartholomew, as well as family nurse practitioner Randy Baxter. Each physician cares for a pool of up to 600 patients. 
Meantime, the Wyoming Legislature is still wrestling with the high costs and barriers to healthcare. A health insurance affordability task force was convened this year for reasons similar to the ones that spurred the study 12 years ago.  
“It sounds like deja vu,” Tracy said.  
While the task force touched on direct primary care at its October meeting, it’s still a relatively novel model and thus is lacking large-scale studies on its benefits and drawbacks, Wyoming Medical Society Executive Director Sheila Bush told the panel.
“It’s early, and they’re fairly new within the context of everything else in healthcare,” Bush said. 
307Health’s doctors are happy to share the lessons they’ve learned in traditional and direct primary care medicine, they say. They believe the model holds promise for Wyoming communities. 
“We’d just like to be part of the conversation to help,” Chandler said. “I mean, we’ve all spent our whole careers in Wyoming practicing medicine, trying to help improve the health of our state.”
The principle physician
A primary care provider is meant to be the first contact and point person for a patient. The doctor will monitor the patient’s overall health, refer them to specialists and coordinate continuing care — be it an MRI for a knee injury or a biopsy on a suspicious sunspot. 
Primary care is instrumental in keeping healthcare costs down, experts say, because routine check-ups and screenings can catch issues before they escalate into major medical emergencies requiring hospitalization, surgeries or transport flights. 
“Primary care physicians are the front-line of prevention,” Bush told the task force. 
Despite this, primary care visits have dropped nationally. Experts believe that could stem from factors ranging from workforce shortages to decreasing ability to pay. 
Near the end of his time as a hospital employee, Tracy said, he watched three patients in fairly rapid succession declare bankruptcy because of healthcare bills. 
If their health issues could have been treated upstream, he felt “they could have been handled on an outpatient basis.” Instead “they ended up going to the emergency department, having a huge bill, and they just declared bankruptcy because that was the only solution they could see.”
It made Tracy realize that “even patients who are fully insured are getting really hurt by the high cost of healthcare,” he said. It was a tipping point to break away and go to direct primary care. 
He reached out to Chandler, who had practiced in Douglas, Powell and Colorado, to join him. The idea made a lot of sense, Chandler said. He remembers thinking that “it’d be much better for patients and much better for us in terms of being able to spend a significant amount of time with patients, get to know patients better, and not feel like we’re just constantly on a treadmill with no time to to really take care of our patients the way we felt we should.”
Dr. Dean Bartholomew speaks with doctor of nursing practice Randy Baxter in the main office at 307Health, in Powell. (Mark Davis/Powell Tribune)
Bartholomew previously owned a small clinic in Saratoga with his wife. Trying to make ends meet and operating the practice as a small business owner was tough, he said. When the opportunity to join 307Health arose, “it was kind of a no-brainer.”
At his Saratoga clinic, he spent a tremendous amount of time and resources billing insurance, collecting payments and navigating Medicare. Direct primary care, he said, “flips that [model] its head.” 
Here’s how it works: Patients pay a monthly membership fee, which gets them round-the-clock access via text or phone to their doctor, as well as no-copay visits and a menu of procedures and diagnostics that include simple sutures, EKG or a rapid strep test. The clinic’s monthly fees depend on age, with the most expensive being $75. 
Several local businesses cover memberships for their employees, and those workers make up a large chunk of the clinic’s patients.  
By avoiding the work required by traditional insurance, the clinic cuts costs and doesn’t need to generate visits to generate income, Bartholomew said. Instead, “we’re doing whatever’s going to be the best and the quickest for the patients.”
When their patients experience emergencies or need specialist care to treat more severe illness or chronic disease, they will act as navigator and advocate, they say. They recommend people have a method for paying for those high-cost items, be it traditional insurance, catastrophic plans or alternatives like healthshare ministries. 
Still, patients rely on them to help guide them through what can be a byzantine maze of decisions with quick answers, same-day appointments and an approach geared toward what’s best for the patient. 
“I tell them, ‘I don’t work for that health system, I don’t work for this health system, I don’t work for the hospital down the street. I work literally for you,’” Bartholomew said.
Still selling it
Despite what they feel is proof of concept, the doctors of 307Health still find they have to sell it to many prospective patients, they said. Amid a rise of concierge or boutique-style practices, there is a lot of confusion about what exactly direct primary care entails. 
At the October meeting, Bush said benefits of the direct primary care model include reduced administrative burden, more time with patients and burnout mitigation. 
“Physician satisfaction within [direct primary care] is unbelievably high,” she said. Because doctors oversee smaller pools of patients, patients see benefits like longer visits and same-day services, she added. 
However, she said, those smaller physician panels can also reduce the system-wide primary care capacity, leaving a larger burden on the doctors remaining in the traditional care models. Other skeptics worry it will further fragment care by creating gaps between providers. 
Drs. Tracy, Chandler and Bartholomew, however, say that in their experience, the opposite is true. 
“I think it’s working because it helps patients,” Tracy said. “If it didn’t, I think we would be out of business.”

title: FEMA chief, US House members push for emergency management changes
description: WASHINGTON — Federal Emergency Management Agency Administrator Cameron Hamilton testified before a U.S. House panel Thursday that he hopes to make significant alterations in the years ahead, though he didn’t share details. “The president's vision is clear: Stronger states make a more capable, ready and resilient nation,” he said. “While FEMA is ready to meet[...]
text: WASHINGTON — Federal Emergency Management Agency Administrator Cameron Hamilton testified before a U.S. House panel Thursday that he hopes to make significant alterations in the years ahead, though he didn’t share details. “The president's vision is clear: Stronger states make a more capable, ready and resilient nation,” he said. “While FEMA is ready to meet the current and future challenges, we must be reformed in an immediate, commonsense and lasting way.”A review council created by President Donald Trump released a report in May that called for local, state and tribal governments to “lead disaster response with the federal government in a supporting role,” but so far neither the administration nor Congress has taken action to implement the proposed changes. Alabama Republican Rep. Dale Strong, chairman of the Homeland Security  Committee’s Emergency Management and Technology Subcommittee, said during the hearing “the need for meaningful reform has become increasingly clear.”“In recent years, we've seen the challenges that FEMA and the state governments face when responding to multiple major disasters,” he said. “In 2024, Hurricanes Helene and Milton struck within weeks of each other, followed by devastating wildfires in Southern California. These events underscored the importance of ensuring FEMA has the capacity and resources to respond effectively when communities need assistance most.” New York Democratic Rep. Tim Kennedy, ranking member on the panel, raised numerous grievances with how FEMA has managed counterterrorism grants and how it has responded to severe storms. “I want to say from the outset that I'm deeply concerned about the direction of FEMA under the Trump administration and your leadership,” he said. “Since January of 2025, you've helped set in motion a series of decisions that undermine the agency and weaken our nation's disaster preparedness, making it harder for Americans to get help when they need it the most.”Kennedy said the administration “unlawfully shut down” the Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities, or BRIC, program that helps local and state governments prepare ahead of natural disasters. He mentioned that the agency gave U.S. Doge Services access to people’s information. And he said the agency was trying to move “disaster responsibilities onto states and local communities, even though FEMA's own research shows that they lack the resources and capacity to manage them.”Despite a promise from Trump to restore counterterrorism funding to New York state, Kennedy said the administration still owed $87 million, hampering the city’s police and fire departments. “Without this funding, the NYPD's counterterrorism and intelligence operatives will lose critical capabilities. FDNY will have to cut their hazmat team, their search and rescue team, and special operations command,” he said. “And it places into serious jeopardy emergency management for Erie and Niagara counties in western New York.”Hamilton testified during the hearing that FEMA planned to distribute the funding for fiscal year 2026, which concluded at the end of September, “shortly.” He said the amount the state would receive should be similar to previous levels.Katrina recovery ongoingLouisiana Democratic Rep. Troy Carter thanked Hamilton for approving a deadline extension “for several remaining Hurricane Katrina recovery projects, including the city of New Orleans Joint Infrastructure Recovery Request Program.”“This extension will allow the city to finish repairing some 10,000 blocks of streets and drainage systems damaged by catastrophic flooding,” he added. “Projects like these are critical for communities throughout south Louisiana, where the effects of Hurricane Katrina remain visible more than 20 years later.”Carter then asked Hamilton to commit to helping local and state officials move forward on about 20 other projects that are related to Hurricane Katrina, which struck in August 2005. Hamilton said he would “be happy to work with you in ways to ensure that these programs, which are awarded, can move forward in a successful manner.”Response based on governor’s party?Illinois Democratic Rep. Delia Ramirez didn’t receive such a commitment from Hamilton when she questioned him about why her home state was denied three times following a severe storm in 2025, but neighboring Indiana, which was struck by the same weather system, was approved for federal assistance from FEMA. “What I can tell you is, as a public servant, we support the decisions of the president,” Hamilton said. “The entirety of the Stafford Act declarations are at his discretion. The president is a very intelligent, very dynamic individual.”Ramirez then asked Hamilton to explain what “statutory criteria” Indiana met that Illinois hadn’t. He responded that FEMA had looked at “damages to roads, damages to power infrastructure, damages to fuel distribution centers, damages to corporate and public buildings.”Ramirez told Hamilton that Illinois was able to prove the state incurred similar damage three times, but was denied repeatedly. “What I'm really concerned about is that having a Republican governor seems to be a statutory requirement for getting FEMA assistance, not actually responding to emergencies that every state deserved to have a response to,” she said. Ramirez added that during the next Congress, when Democrats will take control of both chambers, there will be a significantly different approach to oversight of the Trump administration, including FEMA. “We are going to do a lot of oversight,” she said. “And one of the things that we have to do is to ensure that FEMA, (the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) and the Coast Guard are able to protect their mission and not be politicized.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Company eyeing LEAP District site says its plans won’t include nuclear power generation
description: A California company considering the central Indiana LEAP District for a medical radiopharmaceuticals plant is saying it won’t include nuclear power generation.
text:
An image from an Indiana Economic Development Corp. promotional video for the LEAP District in Lebanon. (Screenshot from IEDC website)A California company considering the central Indiana LEAP District for a medical radiopharmaceuticals plant is saying it won’t include nuclear power generation.
The possibility of Oklo Inc. using the site near Lebanon for nuclear power drew questions from legislators as the State Budget Committee last week reviewed an Indiana Economic Development Corp. request regarding the project.
Information distributed at a public open house in Lebanon this week said the company is working on plans for a $1.5 billion facility that would include a reactor to produce radioisotopes for medical use.
“Oklo does not plan to build an electricity-producing nuclear reactor in LEAP,” the Lebanon Reporter quoted the information packet as saying.
The Santa Clara, California-based company did not immediately reply Thursday to a request for comment from the Capital Chronicle. Oklo has not yet announced a decision about proceeding with the project.
A company spokeswoman told the Indianapolis Business Journal that its proposed Lebanon project would focus on isotope production and not include commercial power generation.
Oklo has also revised its agreement with the IEDC to reduce its possible land purchase from up to 440 acres to a maximum 220 acres, the IBJ reported.
An IEDC spokeswoman told the Capital Chronicle that the agency could not provide a copy of the updated agreement and did not answer questions about the project.
The initial contract with IEDC from September listed several possible uses by Oklo for the site near Lebanon, including “nuclear power generation, radioisotope production, research and development.”
State Budget Committee members last week approved an IEDC request to allow $20 million in agency funding to go toward expanding the LEAP District by 185 acres for the Oklo project. 
Democratic legislators criticized the IEDC for insufficient public disclosure about Oklo’s development plans. They also questioned whether it was creating the chance for nuclear generation for data centers in the LEAP District, including Meta’s  $10 billion data center campus now under construction there.
The district aimed at attracting high-tech businesses now spans some 6,700 acres and has faced persistent public criticism as the state has poured about $1 billion into its development.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Full 3rd Circuit rejects McIver’s appeal
description: The full appeals court's 10-3 ruling allows a prosecution the congresswoman has called political to continue.
text:
Rep. LaMonica McIver speaks outside of Delaney Hall after she, Rep. Rob Menendez, and New York Rep. Yvette Clarke visited the Newark migrant jail for an oversight visit on Dec. 23, 2025. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)The full U.S. Third Circuit Court of Appeals denied Rep. LaMonica McIver’s request to overturn an earlier appellate ruling that found the U.S. Constitution did not shield her from charges stemming from a scuffle outside an immigrant detention facility in Newark.
Only three of the circuit court’s 13 judges who participated in the vote moved to grant McIver’s petition for a rehearing, and the decision will keep in place an August appellate ruling that found the U.S. Constitution’s Speech and Debate Clause did not shield the congresswoman from at least two of the three charges against her. 
“The petition for rehearing by the panel and the Court en banc, is denied,” Judge Cindy Chung wrote in the Circuit Court’s one-paragraph ruling.
McIver, who represents portions of Essex, Hudson and Union counties, is accused of forcibly impeding and interfering with federal officers during a scuffle outside the Delaney Hall immigrant detention facility in Newark last May.
The congresswoman, who was conducting an oversight visit alongside other members, argued the Speech and Debate Clause, which shields lawmakers from prosecution over legislative acts, barred the charges.
In a statement Thursday, she repeated her claim that the charges against her were politically motivated.
“Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison. Now, due to the disappointing decision by the Third Circuit, we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for,” McIver said.
The charges against McIver stem from a scuffle outside Delaney Hall last May where immigration agents arrested Newark Mayor Ras Baraka after he complied with directives to leave a fenced portion of the detention facility’s property.
Prosecutors moved to drop the charges against the mayor only days later, earning a rebuke from a federal judge for an apparently political prosecution. They charged McIver that same day.
Security and other footage showed McIver pushing agents during the scuffle that erupted when federal authorities moved to arrest Baraka. She faces up to 17 years in prison if convicted but won reelection earlier this month.
Judge Emil Bove, a former senior Trump Department of Justice Official, did not participate in the court’s ruling.

title: Reynolds appoints attorney Michael C. Richards to Iowa Board of Regents
