text:
Michael C. Richards, son of Mike Richards, has been appointed to the Iowa Board of Regents by Gov. Kim Reynolds.  (Photos by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch. Logo via Iowa Board of Regents)Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds has selected the son of a former Iowa Board of Regents president to join the university governing body, bringing the board back to nine members.
The governor’s office announced in a news release this week that Reynolds has appointed Michael C. Richards to the Iowa Board of Regents, with his appointment beginning Nov. 18. His term will expire in 2031.
“Mike’s distinguished legal career reflects his deep commitment to excellence, integrity, and public service,” Reynolds said in the release. “His experience and sound judgment will be a tremendous asset to the Iowa Board of Regents, and I’m confident he will serve the state well in this important position.”

Richards previously served as secretary of law firm Dentons Davis Brown PC and is currently a shareholder with the firm, according to his online biography, and the news release states he “practices all stages of complex civil litigation, with an emphasis on defense litigation.” He also chairs the firm’s Iowa Insurance Defense Department.
Board President Robert Cramer said in an emailed statement that he is excited to “have a person the caliber of Michael Richards” on the board of regents.
“Everyone who has worked with him tells me his intelligence, thoughtfulness, and judgment are among the qualities that make him a huge asset,” Cramer said in his statement. “He has a great knowledge of our state, and I look forward to working with him on higher education issues, as we continue to keep our public universities among the best in the nation.”
He holds a bachelor’s degree in business administration from the University of Iowa and a law degree from Drake University. His father, Mike Richards, served on the board of regents from 2016 to 2024 and held the role of board president for most of that time.
“Our state’s universities play an enormous role in shaping the future of Iowans and our communities,” Michael Richards said in the release. “I’m honored that Governor Reynolds has appointed me to serve on the Board of Regents and I look forward to working with my fellow board members to help strengthen and guide these vital institutions into the future.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Proposed Jackson movie studio faces legal trouble over neglected property
description: A view of the proposed home of film production soundstages as part of a $250 million movie studio development in Jackson on Monday, April 6, 2026. Film production was announced to begin on this site as early as October, but construction has yet to begin. The development is led by Jackson business owner and multiple-time mayoral candidate Charlotte Reeves and[...]
text:
Twelve years ago, Jackson business owner Charlotte Reeves set out to build a state-of-the-art movie studio in the city’s Historic Farish Street District, complete with educational centers, advanced soundstages and an on-site hotel.
Now, she’s facing jail time after pleading guilty in Jackson Environmental Court on Tuesday to allowing her property to fall into disrepair. Judge Jeffery Reynolds sentenced Reeves to 10 days in the Hinds County Detention Facility and ordered her to pay $500 in court fees.
A view of the proposed home of film production soundstages as part of a $250 million movie studio development in Jackson on Monday, April 6, 2026. Film production was announced to begin on this site as early as October, but construction has yet to begin. Credit: Aaron Lampley/Mississippi Today
The judge suspended jail time and court fees contingent on Reeves demolishing the dilapidated property and removing all debris by Jan. 12.Reynolds set an additional $2,500 cost bond and $1 million secured appearance bond in the event that Reeves decides to appeal. The bonds would cover court and demolition costs if Reeves fails to comply with court orders.The multimillion dollar project is a proposed 20-acre film studio and “entertainment destination.” The company was first registered in 2014, with Reeves calling it a “lifelong dream” for her and her husband.
The studio sought to transform parts of Hooker Street, which sits a few blocks from the Capitol, into a film production set. The site was also set to have outdoor stages and a cinema.Mill Street Studios, also referred to as Movie Garden Studios, was first slated to open late this year. However, progress on the production has been slow, pushing the launch date further back as debris piled up.In an April interview, Reeves attributed the snail’s pace to “snags.”
Reeves told reporters Wednesday that her current demolition contractor had equipment issues that delayed efforts for three months, but would get the job done, “weather permitting.”
The parcel currently houses several decaying mill houses and were meant to serve as soundstages as a part of Reeves’ Mill Street Studios.This is not the first time Reeves has faced litigation regarding the studio. Reeves is being sued in Hinds County Circuit Court over allegations of fraud and breach of contract from her former business partner and film studio owner, Rob Schnitzer.
Reynolds’ ruling is one in a laundry list of recent litigation against dilapidated property owners. Grand Chateau apartment owner Ramesh Ramchandran was recently sentenced to 630 days in the Raymond jail for seven code enforcement violations to his West Capital Street property.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: ‘2028 starts now’: NC Dem Chair Anderson Clayton eyes future after historic wins
description: Two weeks after the Nov. 3 midterm election, Anderson Clayton apologizes for her voice. The North Carolina Democratic Party Chair was still hoarse from celebrating a blue wave that saw her party capture a U.S. Senate seat, flip seven U.S. House seats, secure a critical state Supreme Court seat and retake the North Carolina House […]
text:
North Carolina Democratic Party chair Anderson Clayton speaks to supporters protesting the state's new Republican-drawn congressional map outside the old State Capitol building on Oct. 21, 2025 in Raleigh. (Photo by Galen Bacharier/NC Newsline)Two weeks after the Nov. 3 midterm election, Anderson Clayton apologizes for her voice. The North Carolina Democratic Party Chair was still hoarse from celebrating a blue wave that saw her party capture a U.S. Senate seat, flip seven U.S. House seats, secure a critical state Supreme Court seat and retake the North Carolina House of Representatives.
Unlike a lot of political observers, Clayton doesn’t think the blue wave gets all the credit.
“I think that a lot of what happened on election night is owed to 16 years of Republican oppression in the state,” Clayton said in an interview with NC Newsline. “I also think it’s because of the incredible volunteers and candidates that stepped up to run for office.”
Clayton, who became the youngest state Democratic Party chair in the country in 2023, is quick to recognize high-caliber candidates who agreed to run for seats they didn’t expect that they would win.
“These people to me are heroes in their communities,” said Clayton. “They wanted to make sure that there was a name on the ballot.”
That’s a stark contrast to 2022, when Democrats left 44 state legislative races uncontested.
Democratic Party Chair Anderson Clayton, pictured here in 2024, holds up a pamphlet of down-ballot candidates shortly before a get-out-the-vote canvassing event. (Photo by Ariana Figueroa/States Newsroom)
This year, first-time candidates were willing to step up because they believed in the need for accountability both at the federal and state level, Clayton said.
Clayton credits members of the House and Senate caucuses, including Sen. Lisa Grafstein, D-Wake, and Rep. Eric Ager, D-Buncombe, with meeting with candidates one-on-one to discuss what it meant to run for public office.
“It was someone they could call while they were on the job,” said Clayton. “Everybody in the caucuses this year really stepped up to make it possible so that no one felt alone. They felt like they had people to lean on.”
Clayton points to candidates like Claire Kempner, a mother of three, who lost her race to Rep. Dr. Tim Reeder (R-Pitt) in 2024 by more than 5,700 votes. With support, Kempner signed up for a rematch this year, and defeated Reeder to win House District 9.
Clayton, who grew up in Roxboro, ran for chair on the promise of expanding Democratic political power in rural parts of the state, instead of settling for winning only in conventional urban strongholds for Democrats. She preaches the importance of connecting with North Carolina’s rural residents and giving them a reason to vote for Democratic candidates.
She points to the success of Dennis Allen, a retired deputy, who unseated Republican “Skeet” Wilborn to become Person County’s first Black sheriff.
“It’s incredible to see the type of community that he brought around him – Republicans, Unaffiliated and Democrats that all came out to say that ‘We want to see a good person in office,'” said Clayton.
She notes Allen notched a win in a race in a deep red county that saw voters vote for Republican Michael Whatley by five points over Democrat Roy Cooper in the U.S. Senate race.
NC Democratic Party leader Anderson Clayton runs to the problem – engaging voters

Making the case for the South

Days after the election, Clayton was in Denver for a post-midterm conference where party strategists were celebrating the Nov. 3rd outcomes and looking ahead to 2028.
Clayton told the conference, hosted by Majority Democrats, that the midterm victories delivered two important lessons: invest in organizers and infrastructure, and don’t write off the South.
“Black Americans right now, 50% live in the South,” said Clayton. “When we’re looking at the investments that we make as a party, and we say that Black voters are the base of our party, then I ask, why are we not investing in a region of the country that on Tuesday just proved everybody wrong?”
In North Carolina, Democrats took a mid-decade redistricting map that Republicans carefully crafted to deliver an 11-3 GOP delegation and flipped seven of those U.S. House seats. Democrats will hold an 11-3 advantage come January.
‘They took districts for granted’
David McLennan, a retired political science professor from Meredith College, says while 2026 investments paid huge dividends for Democrats up and down the ticket, Republicans put themselves at a disadvantage.
“The president’s approval was just really an anchor around the Republicans’ neck,” said McLennan. “They took districts for granted.”
U.S. Rep. Tim Moore in the 14th Congressional District didn’t aggressively campaign until the last weeks of the election as his race against Democratic newcomer LaKesha Womack appeared to tighten. (Photo: House.gov)
McLennan points to U.S. Rep. Tim Moore in the 14th Congressional District. The former state House speaker didn’t campaign until the final weeks of the election as his race against Democratic newcomer LaKesha Womack appeared to tighten.
“I think one of the things that Republicans will decide in their autopsy is, ‘We can’t not campaign hard in every district,’ even in years that are favorable for them,” said McLennan.
McLennan said heading into 2028, Democrats will still be facing Republican-drawn districts at the congressional and legislative level, making it hard to duplicate this year’s success. They also won’t have Cooper at the top of the ticket.
But Clayton is optimistic. After 16 years in the wilderness, she says Democrats in the state House are prepared to deliver on their promises to address affordability.
“Raising the minimum wage from $7.25 in North Carolina has got to be a priority,” said Clayton.
Healthcare costs are also high on the radar.
“It’s going to be on our state legislatures and our state governments while Congress is figuring out the best way to repeal some of the ACA cuts to offer immediate relief,” said Clayton.
Clayton believes the departure of Senate Leader Phil Berger, R-Rockingham, may open the door to more bipartisanship in some areas, including making private school vouchers more accountable.
‘2028 starts now’
Jason Simmons, the N.C. Republican Party chairman, said on social media that the party will take an honest look at the results and identify where improvements need to be made.
NCGOP chairman Jason Simmons, left, looks on as Michael Whatley speaks outside the NCGOP headquarters in Raleigh. Whatley lost the U.S. Senate race by nearly 20 points to Democrat Roy Cooper. (Photo by Galen Bacharier/NC Newsline)
“We owe that to our candidates, our supporters, and the millions of North Carolinians who share our commitment to conservative leadership,” Simmons wrote. “We cannot afford to sit back. The work of rebuilding, organizing, and preparing for the next election starts now. 2028 starts now.”
Clayton is also readying her party for 2028. She held regional post-election debriefs this week in Martin, Duplin, Cabarrus, and Wake Counties. The meetings are not only a chance to thank volunteers, but also to look at recruiting potential candidates for down-ballot races for district attorney and county commissioners as a way to build the party’s bench.
“To be honest, there were wins that I think we should have had this year,” said Clayton.
Her boundless energy and success over the last three years has led some political observers to suggest Clayton could be tapped to help the party nationally, perhaps at the Democratic National Committee, in the next presidential cycle.
“She’s a rock star right now,” said McLennan. “It’s not only her dynamism and enthusiasm, but it’s how she goes into rural North Carolina or districts that are exurban areas and chooses women or women of color, when 10 years ago, Democrats probably would not have done that.”
Western Carolina University political scientist Chris Cooper writes at his Substack that when the new legislature is sworn in in January, it will include about twice as many women as it did in 1983. Women will make up more than 52% of the Democratic House delegation and 62.5% of the Democratic Senate delegation, according to Cooper.
National media appearances aside, Clayton dismisses talk of moving to greener pastures.
“I love North Carolina,” Clayton said. “I love coming home every day to Roxboro to touch the grass and remind Republicans I’m sitting in their backyard.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Parole again denied for Susan Smith, 32 years after she killed her 2 sons
description: The SC parole board again denied parole for Susan Smith, a mother convicted of murdering her two young sons in the Upstate.
text:
Susan Smith appears via livestream from Leath Correctional Center in Leath before South Carolina's Columbia-based parole board on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Parole is again denied for Susan Smith, a mother convicted of murdering her two young sons in a case that garnered national attention more than three decades ago.
The state parole board voted unanimously Thursday, with one member recusing herself: Geraldine Miro was a warden in the prison where Smith was originally housed.
On Oct. 25, 1994, Smith left her sons — 3-year-old Michael and 14-month-old Alex — buckled in their car seats and rolled her car into John D. Long Lake, located in South Carolina’s Upstate.
For nine days after, Smith claimed a Black man carjacked her and drove off with her sons. She tearfully pleaded on national television for their return, before eventually admitting to investigators what she had done.
“I want to say I’m sorry to Michael and Alex. They were innocent children. They did not deserve to die,” Smith told the board during her hearing Thursday. “I dropped to my lowest when I let that car go into that lake.”
Smith also apologized to her ex-husband, David Smith, who did not get to see his sons grow up.
“He didn’t get to see them ride a bike or go to school, and I’m really, really sorry for that,” she said. “I would go back and change all of that if I could.”
David Smith told the parole board her apology doesn’t change the grief he feels.
David Smith, ex-husband of Susan Smith, appears before South Carolina’s parole board in Columbia Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Screenshot of Court TV press pool livestream)
“Is 32 years enough for what she did?” he asked.
Prosecutors sought the death penalty for Smith. The jury ultimately opted for life in prison.
But in 1995, when Smith was tried, a life sentence did not mean life. She could seek parole after 30 years.
Legislators changed the law the next year, making those with life sentences ineligible for parole.
Smith, who is now 55, made her first plea for parole in November 2024. Thursday’s hearing marked her second attempt. She has the option to reapply every two years.
That’s something state Speaker Pro Tem Tommy Pope, who was the chief prosecutor for Smith’s trial, hopes to change. He told the parole board he wants to introduce legislation that would extend the time between hearings to three to five years.
“I’m going to do everything possible to change that,” he said.
In South Carolina, the outcome of a parole hearing is almost always “no.”
In 2024, the Palmetto State granted parole at the lowest rate in the country — just 4% — when compared to other states that offer discretionary parole.
And data from the state Department of Probation, Parole and Pardon Services, which reports numbers quarterly, shows the board approved just 6% of the cases it heard between April and June. Of those denied, 71% were non-violent offenders.
The parole board has a list of official reasons it can cite for denying parole.
It cited three of them Tuesday: risk posed to the community, seriousness of the crime, and Smith’s attitude toward her family and authority in general.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Cruise ship strike confirmed as cause of death for Alaska fin whale
description: A pregnant fin whale found dead on the bow of a Royal Caribbean cruise ship in June was killed by blunt force trauma, a federal agency has concluded. The final necropsy report concerning a whale found on a cruise ship that sailed into the Kenai Peninsula port of Seward on June 19 provided conclusive evidence […]
text:
A necropsy team examines a deceased female fin whale near Seward, Alaska on June 20, 2026. The photo was authorized by NOAA Fisheries permit #24359. (Photo by Kaiti Grant/Alaska SeaLife Center)
A pregnant fin whale found dead on the bow of a Royal Caribbean cruise ship in June was killed by blunt force trauma, a federal agency has concluded.
The final necropsy report concerning a whale found on a cruise ship that sailed into the Kenai Peninsula port of Seward on June 19 provided conclusive evidence that the animal had died from a vessel strike, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said.
The results of the necropsy were released on Monday by NOAA Fisheries. The necropsy found that the whale was freshly dead and in good nutritional condition, the agency said.
“Our necropsy findings are consistent with blunt force trauma, in this case from a vessel strike, as the cause of death for both the adult whale and her unborn calf,” Dr. Emmanuelle Furst, the Alaska SeaLife Center veterinarian who conducted the necropsy, said in a statement released by the agency.
NOAA Fisheries law enforcement agents came to the Seward scene shortly after the dead whale was discovered and conducted an investigation, the agency said.
“Accidental collisions with vessels are a serious threat to this endangered species,” Dr. Anne Marie Eich, leader of NOAA Fisheries’ Alaska regional protected resources division, said in the statement. “We are committed to working with vessel operators to increase awareness of the risks of whale strikes and the importance of reducing vessel speed where practicable in areas with concentrations of whales, as well as investigating other ways to help avoid such incidents.”
In a statement, Royal Caribbean Cruises said it is making changes to reduce the chances of future ship strikes.
“We remain heartbroken by the whale strike involving one of our vessels and recognize its profound impact on the Seward community, our guests, and all who care about the marine environment,” the emailed statement said. “Protecting marine life is a serious responsibility across our fleet. All shipboard officers receive specialized whale awareness and detection training and follow bridge protocols to identify and avoid marine mammals wherever possible.”
The statement said Royal Caribbean Cruises is working with NOAA Fisheries to introduce “an enhanced, layered approach widely recognized by marine scientists and regulators.”
The case of another dead fin whale found this year on the bow of a different cruise ship remains under investigation, according to NOAA Fisheries. That whale was found on the bow of a Norwegian Cruise Line ship as it pulled into Sitka on Sept. 17.
There have been 11 confirmed cases of cruise ships striking whales in Alaska since 2001, though not all resulted in fatalities, according to NOAA Fisheries.

title: New Mexico Film Office announces the return of Pluribus
description: Pluribus will film its second season of the sci-fi show in Albuquerque, the New Mexico Film Office announced on Nov. 19.
text:
Rhea Seehorn stars in Vince Gilligan's "Pluribus," which is filming its second season in New Mexico. (Photo courtesy of Apple TV)The Emmy-award winning sci-fi television series Pluribus will return to New Mexico to film its second season, the state Film Office announced on Thursday.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The show, from Apple TV, marks writer and director Vince Gilligan’s third for Albuquerque, following “Breaking Bad” and “Better Call Saul,” the latter which he co-created. He also wrote and directed the Netflix film, “El Camino: A Breaking Bad Movie,” which was made in Albuquerque as well.
Gilligan, Film Office Director Steve Graham said in a statement, “found his creative family in New Mexico and has used our landscapes as a setting for making great stories for nearly 20 years.”
Pluribus, in a nutshell, tells the story of “the most miserable person on Earth,” (Carol, played by Rhea Seehorn), who “must save the world from happiness.” For a little more context, the New York Times in reviewing season 1, notes that “something” has happened and now “suddenly the human race is not what it once was.” Except for Carol,  “the cynical author of a best-selling series of cheesy romantasy novels, who finds herself left outside this change and fighting to save humanity.”
In a news release, the Film Office said the show’s second season, the timing for which has not been announced, is expected to employ more than 500 New Mexico crew members, 100 New Mexico actors and stunt performers and 800 New Mexico background actors. The first season won six Emmy Awards, including for Seehorn as lead actress (she also won a Golden Globe Award and Critics Choice Award for the role), along with writing for a drama series, original main title theme music, production design, picture editing and sound mixing.
The Film Office in August produced a report acknowledging a drop in film and television production in New Mexico and nationally. New Mexico offers a film production tax credit, which a study presented to state lawmakers in May found generates pennies on the dollar for every dollar the state invests.

name: WyoFile
title: Former Wyoming Boys’ School resident suing for alleged abuse told staff they were ‘like family,’ witness testifies
description:
While acknowledging positive aspects of the school, witnesses and attorneys suggest Blaise Chivers-King suffered trauma from his time at the state facility.  
The post Former Wyoming Boys’ School resident suing for alleged abuse told staff they were ‘like family,’ witness testifies appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
CASPER—Blaise Chivers-King, the former Wyoming Boys’ School resident suing school staff for alleged abuse, stands out as a memorable student to the employees who worked with him. 
He was the first resident who was quarantined when he arrived at the state facility during the COVID-19 pandemic. The 15-year-old needed a lot of attention. Chivers-King had a history of trauma, and he often struggled to manage his emotions, boys’ school staff testified at the trial spurred by the former resident’s lawsuit. Staff described doing various activities with him like watching movies, designing custom shoes, playing card games, folding origami, looking at World of Warcraft characters and just talking. At one point, Chivers-King wanted to try different kinds of hot sauce, so staff members picked some up for him in town. 
“The kid wanted somebody to love him and care about him, and that’s what we tried to do,” Bryan DuPree, a Wyoming Boys’ School supervisor, testified Tuesday. 
Chivers-King is one of six former boys’ school residents who sued school staff in 2024. The school, which detains delinquent boys ages 12 to 21, is a 38-acre residential facility near Worland that’s overseen by the Wyoming Department of Family Services. 
Chivers-King, who spent time at the boys’ school between 2020 and 2022, alleged staff violated his 14th Amendment rights by placing him in prolonged isolation, using excessive force and infringing on due process. He is suing in part for days he spent locked in 7-by-10-foot cinderblock rooms under conditions that his attorneys consider solitary confinement. One of those stints lasted two weeks.
Several employees testified that Chivers-King kept in touch after he left the boys’ school. He talked with them about dogs, boxing, getting a job and visiting a haunted house in Denver. He sent videos of himself doing figure eights on his new motorcycle and pictures of a visit to a zoo. 
Their testimony paints a broader picture of how students were treated at the school that adds to depictions offered by other witnesses, who described staff forcing kids to shave their heads, walk in single-file lines, look forward without talking and refrain from communicating with one another. A former boys’ school employee testified that staff “would make degrading comments to escalate a kid.” Stuart Grassian, a Massachusetts psychiatrist who testified at the trial as an expert witness, described the school as having “a culture of total control and domination.” 
But the former student’s attorneys and witnesses have acknowledged there were also positive aspects of Chivers-King’s time at the boys’ school. Asked about staff taking Chivers-King to the Humane Society to walk a dog, Grassian, the psychiatrist, commented that he “thought that was terrific,” adding that not everything at the boys’ school is “evil.” 
Chivers-King’s attorneys have emphasized that his claims only concern select incidents and time periods. One pointed to a day outside of the claims in which a logbook indicates Chivers-King was let out of the detention room for several hours to watch “Miss Peregrine’s Home for Peculiar Children” and a Marvel movie. Another suggested that just because not everything at the boys’ school was “horrible” doesn’t mean the former resident didn’t suffer trauma from his time there. 
While many spoke fondly of Chivers-King, boys’ school employees called to testify in the trial described challenges they faced in managing his needs while keeping the school safe. 
Among the witnesses defense attorneys called were two Wyoming Boys’ School employees whom Chivers-King testified about becoming close with during his time at the facility. Neither are defendants in the case. 
“A lot of people knew that me and Blaise were tight,” Craig Jones, a boys’ school dorm director, testified. “When Blaise was having a hard time, they asked me a lot of times to come over and help.” 
John Schwalbe, a dorm supervisor, said Chivers-King would keep in contact almost on a weekly basis before the lawsuit. “He would tell us that we were like family to him and he missed us.” 
During cross examination, Chivers-King’s attorneys probed dynamics that might incentivize the employees to offer testimony that reflects positively on the school, including that they work for the facility and their colleagues are defendants in the case. 
Boys’ school staff testified that they continued to interact with Chivers-King frequently even when he was confined in detention rooms at the facility, including going into the room to talk with him and offering him exercise, reading materials, therapy and schoolwork, though they said he often rejected these services. 
“I believe that the strict definition of solitary confinement pertaining to Blaise Chivers-King was not met,” Dr. Dominique Sotelo, an associate professor of clinical mental health counseling who worked in juvenile justice for 22 years, testified. The expert witness explained that the services staff were supposed to provide for Chivers-King while he was confined would require them to open the detention room door. Sotelo said that “even the attempt or the approach” to offer things like school would fall “under the definition of meaningful contact.”
But dorm logbooks, which staff use to record their checks of students in isolation, don’t reflect such interactions or that staff regularly offered Chivers-King schoolwork, reading, therapy or exercise. Mike Nelson, a defendant in the case who worked as a risk management officer, a dorm director and a dorm supervisor when Chivers-King was at the school, testified that the logbooks are “incredibly incomplete.” Other employees also testified that they wouldn’t log every interaction they had with Chivers-King while he was locked in a detention room. 
“What I saw is the logbooks at times would meet the standards in terms of documenting the detail,” said Sotelo, who used American Corrections Association standards to form his opinion about the boys’ school’s detention practices. He also noted times when there wasn’t very much detail in the logbooks. “You want a good record of what’s going on when someone is placed in isolation,” he said. 
Chivers-King’s attorneys have pointed to numerous times when video and school records show that the former resident had calmed down but was not released from a detention room. Records also show that staff expected Chivers-King to demonstrate a “credible” commitment to being safe by having two consecutive days of good behavior in detention before he could be released. This predetermined amount of detention time is central to attorneys’ argument that staff violated the 14th Amendment, which protects detained people from arbitrary punishment.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: KY judge calls misconduct allegations calls them ‘politically motivated’
description: A Kentucky judge facing allegations of misconduct has asked a state panel to dismiss the charges, arguing in part that the prosecution is politically motivated as he awaits confirmation as a federal judge. Circuit Judge Dan Ballou said in a response to the charges that the matter is “an improper selective prosecution” and is “improperly […]
text:
A Kentucky circuit judge is disputing misconduct allegations.
(Stock photo by Greenleaf123/Getty Images)A Kentucky judge facing allegations of misconduct has asked a state panel to dismiss the charges, arguing in part that the prosecution is politically motivated as he awaits confirmation as a federal judge.
Circuit Judge Dan Ballou said in a response to the charges that the matter is “an improper selective prosecution” and is “improperly motivated by political and free speech affiliations.”
Ballou did not specify those affiliations. However, he has long been close to Republican U.S. Sen. Rand Paul.
Ballou publicly supported Paul in his initial 2010 Senate race – drawing a reprimand from the state Judicial Conduct Commission given that Ballou was a judge at the time – and Paul endorsed Ballou when he ran unsuccessfully for state Supreme Court.
When President Donald Trump nominated Ballou to be a federal judge in August, Paul called Ballou, a U.S. Marine veteran and longtime state judge, a “Great American.”
Ballou has not yet been confirmed to a federal judgeship in Kentucky by the full U.S. Senate, though a committee forwarded his nomination this month.
Circuit Judge Daniel Ballou (Photo courtesy Administrative Office of the Courts)
Laura Hendrix, executive secretary of the commission, said the agency could not comment on the claim that the prosecution is politically motivated.
Dispute with attorney
The misconduct allegations against Ballou come against the backdrop of his federal nomination.
The Kentucky Judicial Conduct Commission (JCC) notified Ballou in late October of formal charges that he committed misconduct.
The charges arose from an interaction Ballou had with a lawyer in his court. He is a circuit judge for McCreary and Whitley counties.
The lawyer, Kerri Bartley, had filmed a video in the courthouse in McCreary County in late August with a caption that said, “How I feel when I’m trapped in a musty courtroom surrounded by pictures of the old yt (white) male judges knowing the current old yt (white) male judge is going to disagree with everything I say.”
The video showed Bartley’s face with portraits of former judges in the background, according to the JCC complaint.
Bartley had a case before Ballou that day, according to the record.
Bartley posted the video on social media.
Ballou’s staff told him about the video, and he directed Bartley to appear before him.
At that appearance, Bartley apologized, called her behavior thoughtless and said she intended no disrespect.
Ballou allegedly interrupted her to ask if she was aware of any other judges allowing attorneys to make videos in the courtroom, then interrupted her again when she began responding.
Ballou asked Bartley where she attended law school and told her she “might want to look into a refund if (she) didn’t learn any better than to come into a courtroom and make videos,” according to the JCC charges.
Before Bartley could respond, Ballou told the bailiff to hand her an order he had prepared and dismissed her from the courtroom, rolling his eyes, according to the charges.
According to the complaint, Ballou drafted an order before Bartley’s appearance that alleged she had “for some bizarre and inexplicable reason chose to make a childish, unprofessional, disrespectful, belligerent, immature, and extraordinarily arrogant video.”
The order barred Bartley from using or possessing any electronic device in the McCreary County Courthouse and the Whitley County Judicial Center, and directed that the notice be distributed to more than a dozen local officials and the Kentucky Bar Association.
The JCC said Ballou decided on disciplinary measures for Bartley before she even appeared and did not give her a chance to respond.
The order also used language about Bartley indicating a possible bias, “including a statement regarding the courtroom being turned into ” ‘Romper Room,’ ” the conduct commission said.
The commission alleged that Ballou violated a number of ethics rules.
Those included rules requiring judges to perform all duties fairly and impartially; prohibiting judges from manifesting bias or prejudice, or engaging in harassment by words or conduct while doing their judicial duties; requiring judges to accord to every person who has a legal interest in a proceeding, or that person’s lawyer, the right to be heard; and requiring judges to be patient, dignified, and courteous to lawyers and others with whom the judge deals in an official capacity.
In his response filed Nov. 9, Ballou denied engaging in any misconduct and said he had not pre-judged discipline for Bartley before she appeared.
Bartley violated prior orders barring the use of cell phones in the court, according to Ballou’s response, though the JCC charges noted that some other attorneys had their phones out during her court appearance.
Ballou raised more than a dozen defenses altogether, including that his handling of the issue was within his duty to maintain order and decorum in the court; that his decisions were in good faith; that the charges infringe on the independence of the judiciary; that the JCC violated confidentiality rules; and that the charges violate his free-speech rights.
Ballou also argued in his response that the process the JCC uses, in which the panel both issues accusations and then decides on them, violates his constitutional right to due process.
Ballou said in his response that the commission has proposed issuing a public reprimand for him, which he argued is inappropriate and excessive.
Ballou asked in his response for the charges to be dismissed.
One of Ballou’s attorneys, John G. Prather Jr., of Somerset, said the JCC did not adequately investigate the allegations against Ballou.
“It’s certainly nothing to raise an issue like this,” Prather said of Ballou’s handling of the issue.
Attorneys Howard Mann of Corbin and Christopher Wiest of Covington also represent Ballou.
The next formal step in the case would be to schedule a hearing before the conduct commission.
Ballou is among several conservative nominees to federal judgeships the Trump Administration hopes to push through before Democrats take over the U.S. Senate in January.
If confirmed Ballou would replace former U.S. District Judge Gregory F. Van Tatenhove, who left the bench to head the law school at the University of Kentucky.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Nike giving shoes to valedictorians after plea from Scott Colom
description: U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom, center, takes photo with law enforcement after his news conference at the Hinds County Sheriff’s Office in Jackson on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026.
text:
Nike is gifting high school valedictorians across the country with a pair of custom sneakers after Mississippi’s incoming senator appealed to the company on social media.
Scott Colom, who is poised to become the state’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction, called on the sneaker giant to honor his historic election by giving every high school valedictorian in his state a pair of custom Air Force 1s — his favorite style. The sneakers cost between $90 and $180 on the company’s web site.
“It would encourage MS students to hit the books the rest of the year! #justdoit,” the Democrat suggested Monday on X, referencing Nike’s famous slogan.
The company accepted the challenge and took it one step further.
“The athlete mindset makes things possible, including this idea,” Oregon-based Nike responded Tuesday on X. “@scott_colom, we’ll do you one better… For this year, 2026/2027 high school valedictorians from across the U.S., let’s go!”
Nike said more details would be forthcoming, but Colom has already suggested the custom sneaker should give a nod to Hiram Revels, a fellow Mississippian who was the first African American to serve in Congress when he took office in 1870.
“I’m so proud of @Nike for stepping up to motivate students across the country in this historic moment. This is the #justdoit mentality that makes your company great,” he wrote on X on Tuesday. “Please consider honoring Hiram Revels in the design.”
Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, narrowly defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in this month’s midterm elections.
When he takes office in January, he’ll become the state’s third Black senator, following Revels and Blanche Kelso Bruce, who was the only formerly enslaved person to serve in the U.S. Senate when he took office in 1875.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: People Still Sick 5 Years After Fuel Leak Into Oʻahu Water
description: Five years after nearly 20,000 gallons of fuel leaked from the Navy’s Red Hill depot into the drinking water supply at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam, some of the area’s current and former residents are still experiencing serious health issues. The spill on Nov. 20, 2021, polluted a water system that serves over 90,000 people. Jamie […]
text:
Five years after nearly 20,000 gallons of fuel leaked from the Navy’s Red Hill depot into the drinking water supply at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam, some of the area’s current and former residents are still experiencing serious health issues.
The spill on Nov. 20, 2021, polluted a water system that serves over 90,000 people. Jamie Simic, a former military spouse who lived on the base on two separate occasions, started experiencing concerning symptoms at around that time — and still does today.
She was hospitalized twice in the first four months after the spill. Doctors diagnosed her with subacute hydrocarbon toxicity exposure, a sign that she had likely been poisoned by the jet fuel. Simic relocated to Florida with her two children in 2022, and her health has gradually improved since then. But she still experiences tremors in her legs, arms and hands as well as other symptoms.
“I will break out in rashes on my hands, and I have gastrointestinal issues, headaches, loss of balance,” Simic said last week. Her children both have similar symptoms that flare up when they overexert themselves or when they’re exposed to other environmental toxins. 
Simic is one of around 500 people who have documented their lingering health issues in a registry that tracks ongoing symptoms, which was created specifically for people impacted by the Red Hill water crisis. 

Jamie Simic was hospitalized and lost 30 pounds after being exposed to jet fuel in water after the Red Hill spill in 2021. (Courtesy: Jamie Simic)  (Courtesy: Jamie Simic)

Facilitated by the University of Hawaiʻi’s Office of Strategic Health Initiatives, the Thompson School of Social Work & Public Health and other related groups, the Red Hill Registry began collecting data from participants back in August 2025. This fall, the team behind the registry presented its early findings at the Military Health Research Symposium and other major scientific conferences across the United States and Canada.
Similar registries exist to track the medium- and long-term health impacts of other environmental disasters, including the Maui wildfires, the Flint, Michigan water crisis and air pollution caused by the explosion of the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001. The goal, in all those cases, is to track the health of affected populations over time as acute illnesses come and go and chronic illnesses emerge. They help scientists and researchers understand the possible trajectories of such an exposure. 
Those behind the Red Hill Registry are still working to enroll people and will begin a second survey for existing participants in the coming months, said Rosana “Sanie” Weldon, the register’s director. 
Early data shows “people still reporting symptoms in every bodily system,” Weldon said. “We see things like fatigue, sleep problems, headaches, memory problems, anxiety and ear problems. A lot of these symptoms look a lot like long Covid or chronic fatigue syndrome.”
Dr. Rosana “Sanie” Weldon, director of the Red Hill Registry, in her office Thursday in Honolulu. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
It’s still too soon, however, to say much about what those symptoms mean about the longer term effect on people’s health, she said. For now, the registry staff “feel it’s important to show our community that we’re looking at the data, we’re honoring the time that it took them to fill out our questionnaires and that we’re paying attention and looking for patterns,” she said.
Weldon and others hope to get the word out about the registry to more people who have lived on the base — even if that’s not an easy task, given the fact that military families tend to be far more transient than others. She said 70 percent of those who have already responded have left the state.

Like Simic, Meredith Wilson left the island in early 2022 and hasn’t been back. Now based in North Carolina, she spent over a year seeking out care from specialists there, including a neuro-ophthalmologist who has helped with her vertigo, nausea, dizziness and vision problems. Many of those symptoms have dissipated for now, but she wanted to contribute to the data regardless. 
“A lot of providers didn’t understand what to do with us. When you tell someone you’re exposed to JP-5, they have no idea what that is,” Wilson said, referring to the type of jet fuel that spilled at the base. 
When she and others were exposed, they went in search of data from similar incidents and came up empty handed. “God forbid if this happened again, we are going to be the studies that someone looks to for help, for what kind of conditions to monitor for, and guidance on how to get better. That can’t happen until there is a registry,” Wilson said.  

Jamie Simic, seen here in a recent photo, said she still experiences flare-ups of various symptoms including hand, leg and foot tremors. (Courtesy: Jamie Simic) (Courtesy: Jamie Simic)

Simic echoed that sentiment. “These symptoms are hard to diagnose. There is not a lot of direct data, so this registry is vital in helping establish that data long term,” she said. 
Weldon said the registry has begun receiving inquiries from researchers interested in using the registry’s data to investigate the links between exposure to jet fuel in water and various health effects. 
“Hopefully there will be more information soon,” she said. 
Attorney Kristina Baehr, who represents people sickened by the water at Red Hill, said she has encouraged her clients to participate. 
“It’s important to know what happened here. It’s important to track the health outcomes, and I believe that they will be very real,” Baehr said. She added that she has so far seen families dealing with seizures, neurological damage and developmental delays.
Baehr compared the situation at Red Hill to what happened at Camp Lejeune, a military base in North Carolina. Although residents there were exposed to chemicals in drinking water in the early 1980s, they didn’t know until much later. A court found that there was not enough evidence to prove a connection between the pollution and long-term outcomes such as birth defects, cancer, and other chronic diseases when they arose years later, because epidemiologists weren’t tracking their early symptoms. 
In the case of Red Hill, more than 3,000 plaintiffs are in the process of receiving settlements of $27,000 from the federal government, while another 3,000 are holding out for a larger payout. 
“The judge issued an order on damages that found that $76,000 was the baseline for adults,” Baehr said. “The government undercut the judge’s order in the settlements for our clients. The people that remain are enforcing the court’s order. They’re holding out in hope that number will be recognized.”

Civil Beat: 
$17 Million In Court Settlements Is Coming To Red Hill Families

Baehr’s firm is also working on two appeals related to the suit. One is in response to a judge who issued what she considers a very low damages award for babies and toddlers compared to older children. The other found the government did not need to compensate active service members because they were harmed in the line of duty.
Michelle Tiemeyer, director of public affairs and engagement for the Navy’s Red Hill Closure Task Force, did not respond directly to a request for comment on the registry but she said the task force “remains focused on our mission to safely and deliberately decommission the Red Hill Bulk Fuel Storage Facility.” She recommended the Defense Health Agency as a public resource for health information related to Red Hill.
In addition to sharing their data with the registry, Simic and Wilson both said they wanted to make sure the fuel spill isn’t forgotten, even as the Navy has moved to reopen the wells in the area. Simic is pushing for better healthcare coverage for military families, and both of them are advocating for more investigation into what may have spilled into Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam’s water system before November 2021.
Wilson said she still sees a neurologist to manage her migraines and expects to be dealing with the mental health impacts on her mind and body for years to come. 
“Not a day goes by when I don’t think about it,” she said. “And really it’s more like not 15 minutes goes by without me thinking about it.”

text:
Families can pick up a frozen turkey and a box of sides while supplies last. A $25 donation sponsors one dinner.
NEWARK, Del. — The Delaware Regional Dream Center will hand out free frozen turkeys and Thanksgiving sides Saturday, Nov. 21, at its annual drive-through giveaway at 310 Ruthar Drive, Unit 11. kidsfiles.delaware.gov
Families can receive one 12-pound turkey and one Box of Hope while supplies last. The box includes stuffing, mashed potatoes, canned vegetables and gravy, according to the center’s campaign flyer. kidsfiles.delaware.gov
The volunteer-run nonprofit is asking donors to sponsor the meals. The campaign lists $25 for one dinner, $50 for two and $100 for four.
Food assistance year-round
The Rev. Chris Dito founded the Dream Center in 2020. The center says it provided more than 2,000 Thanksgiving meals in 2025 and distributed about 190,000 pounds of food through its work that year.
The center distributes Boxes of Hope with shelf-stable groceries on the last Friday of each month and reserves home deliveries for Delaware residents who lack transportation. It also provides backpacks filled with school supplies and runs an after-school reading program for fourth and fifth graders.
To Go Box

What: Delaware Regional Dream Center’s annual Thanksgiving drive-through giveaway. One free turkey and one Box of Hope per family while supplies last.
When: Saturday morning, Nov. 21. The public pickup flyer lists 9 a.m. The donation flyer lists 8 a.m. to noon. Call 302-286-7406 to confirm the pickup time before heading out.
Where: 310 Ruthar Drive, Unit 11, Newark, DE 19711, at the rear of the complex.
Donate: Make a check payable to Delaware Dream Center and mail it to the address above, or use the Dream Center’s online giving page.

title: UW-Madison names University of Illinois engineering dean as next chancellor
description: Rashid Bashir, dean of the engineering school at the University of Illinois Urbana Champaign, is set to become the next chancellor of the University of Wisconsin-Madison.  Bashir’s hiring was approved by the University of Wisconsin Board of Regents in a special meeting on Wednesday.  An immigrant from Pakistan who moved to the United States when […]
text:
Rashid Bashir was named the next chancellor of UW-Madison. (Photo courtesy of UW-Madison)Rashid Bashir, dean of the engineering school at the University of Illinois Urbana Champaign, is set to become the next chancellor of the University of Wisconsin-Madison. 
Bashir’s hiring was approved by the University of Wisconsin Board of Regents in a special meeting on Wednesday. 
An immigrant from Pakistan who moved to the United States when he was 15, Bashir got a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering from Texas Tech University. He received his master’s and PhD from Purdue University. His research as a bioengineer has been focused on developing new technology to diagnose and treat illnesses. 
Bashir has been the author or co-author of more than 340 academic papers, according to a UW-Madison news release, and holds more than 65 patents. 
“Serving as UW–Madison chancellor is about serving the people of UW–Madison – faculty, staff and students – and the state at large,” Bashir said in a statement. “The Wisconsin Idea, the idea that the work of our campus influences the state and world beyond, and the importance of access to the university, that resonates deeply with me because those were the opportunities that were also given to me. I want to give back, and I will do that through service leadership, with empathy, kindness and community-building. I am very honored, humbled and excited to serve.” 
Bashir is set to take over the job from interim chancellor Eric Wilcots in February. He’ll take the helm of Wisconsin’s flagship public university after years in which the state’s public universities have frequently been demonized by Republican lawmakers and the administration of President Donald Trump has made massive cuts to federal spending on universities and research programs. 
Bashir starts the job shortly after Democrats take total control of state government, including next year’s state budget process. 
UW officials said Bashir was the right person to lead the school during this time. 
“Dr. Bashir is exactly the leader for this moment,” UW Regent Amy Bogost said. “He is an exceptional scientist and accomplished leader whose own journey embodies the promise of the American Dream. He understands both the possibilities that education creates for individuals and families and the responsibility that comes with leading an institution of this stature. He brings a compelling vision for the future, and I am confident he will build on UW–Madison’s extraordinary legacy. As Wisconsin’s flagship university and a source of tremendous national pride, UW–Madison has an essential role to play in shaping the future of our state. I can think of no more important responsibility or opportunity.”

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Newly Elected Kaua‘i County Council Chooses Leadership
description: Incumbents Arryl Kaneshiro and Fern Holland were selected to lead Kaua‘i's County Council.
text:
Newly elected members of the Kaua‘i County Council have unanimously selected incumbents Arryl Kaneshiro as chair and Fern Ānuenue Holland as vice chair.
Kaneshiro replaces the current chair Mel Rapozo, who will take over as mayor next month, and Holland replaces KipuKai Kuali‘i, who is terming out. 
Kaneshiro has been a council member on and off for 10 years and was the third highest vote-getter in the Nov. 3 general election with 11,501 votes. Holland, who is serving her second term, was the top vote-getter with 12,425 votes.
Newly elected council members, from left, Paul Noboru Applegate, Todd Ozaki, Addison Bulosan, Arryl Kaneshiro, Fern Ānuenue Holland, Michelle Kaleiohi Correa and Dane Smith at their first council-elect meeting on Tuesday.  Screenshot/2026
The seven-member council-elect met for the first time Tuesday to discuss the body’s leadership, what committees they’ll have and who will lead them, and the council’s operational rules. The members will be inaugurated on Dec. 1. 
Altogether, the meeting lasted roughly 15 minutes, and no community members testified. The brief discussions were led by the three incumbents. The four other council members will be serving their first terms. 
The newly elected Hawai‘i and Maui county councils are also forming their leadership structures in the coming weeks. The Honolulu City Council selected their new chair at the beginning of this month.
Kaneshiro, who is the son of former council member Darryl Kaneshiro and a fourth-generation farmer from Kōloa, was nominated as chair by Holland. He previously served as council chair from 2018 to 2022 and currently chairs the council’s Finance & Economic Development Committee.
He said he’s excited to be chair and hopes to provide good leadership and help speed up the learning curve for all the first-time council members.
“Hopefully I can provide the leadership and institutional knowledge for the new guys and just for everybody,” he told Civil Beat. “I think we have a good team.”

Arryl Kaneshiro will chair the Kauaʻi County Council. (Courtesy: Kauaʻi County) Provided: Arryl Kaneshiro/2026

Incumbent Addison Bulosan said at the meeting that he thought the council and broader community would benefit from Kaneshiro’s previous council experience.
He nominated Holland to serve as vice chair, saying her way of engaging the community while working on legislation, as well as her knowledge and experience, will benefit the community. 
Kaneshiro said at the meeting that Holland showed she’s a hard worker during her first term and thinks that they’ll work well together, even when they may not agree. He added that he’s excited about the council’s makeup and believe it can move the needle on the county’s challenges.
Holland is an ecologist and community advocate who grew up on Kaua‘i and currently chairs the council’s Parks & Recreation and Transportation Committee. 
“I am humbled and grateful for this opportunity to help lead our new council and very much looking forward to working with my colleagues to tackle major issues and move our county in the right direction,” she told Civil Beat. 
The new council also voted on the council’s organizational rules, its committees and who will lead those committees after members are inaugurated. Kaneshiro told Civil Beat that he made the assignments based on members’ experience and interest. 
He will lead the Committee of the Whole, Holland will chair the Public Works & Veterans Services Committee, and Bulosan will chair the Planning Committee again. 

Fern Ānuenue Holland will serve as vice chair. (Courtesy: Fern Ānuenue Holland/2026) Provided: Fern Ānuenue Holland/2026

Michelle Kaleiohi Correa, who manages the county’s Waimea Neighborhood Center, will chair parks and recreation; Dane Smith, an affordable housing project manager for The Hanalei Initiative, will chair housing; retired police captain Paul Noboru Applegate will chair public safety; and Todd Ozaki, executive assistant to the mayor and Capital Improvements Program manager, will chair finance. 
“I think we’re going to continue to move forward and do good things as a council,” Kaneshiro said.
