name: Kentucky Lantern
title: After mild blue splash, some Kentucky Democrats wonder if state party could have done more
description: After November elections brought a blue tsunami to places like Texas and North Carolina, some Kentucky Democrats are wondering where that wave was in the Bluegrass state.  Ned Pillersdorf, who ran against incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Hal Rogers in Eastern Kentucky, took to social media last week to say Kentucky Democrats’ had “an abysmal failure” […]
text:
Supporters of Rep.-elect Zach Dembo, a Kentucky Democrat who flipped a Republican seat, cheer during Dembo’s victory speech in Lexington on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Brian Simms for Kentucky Lantern)After November elections brought a blue tsunami to places like Texas and North Carolina, some Kentucky Democrats are wondering where that wave was in the Bluegrass state. 
Ned Pillersdorf, who ran against incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Hal Rogers in Eastern Kentucky, took to social media last week to say Kentucky Democrats’ had “an abysmal failure” compared to other states this year. During the Nov. 3 election, Kentucky Democrats flipped control of a Central Kentucky U.S. House seat with candidate Zach Dembo and gained control of nine seats in the General Assembly in suburban areas of the state. Yet, the last remaining Democratic-held state House seat in Eastern Kentucky is now held by Republican Tanner Hesterberg. In his race, Pillersdorf lost by 46 points to Rogers. 
Pillersdorf wrote on Facebook that in addition to running against Rogers, he also helped legislative candidates in Eastern Kentucky this cycle and accused party officials of slighting them. He said he and four legislative candidates were denied entry to a fundraising reception held during a party gathering in Lexington and were not discussed during the main public event later that evening, the Forward Together dinner, which was open to media. A staffer later said in a comment the event required purchased tickets. 
“The good news is that thanks to the wonderful blue tsunami help is on the way from elsewhere thanks to the Democratic parties in other states who saw the blue wave coming and didn’t do what the Kentucky Democratic Party did — abandon many of their candidates,” Pillersdorf said. “As far as the Kentucky Democratic party is concerned – we might as well be in West Virginia.”
In response to Pillersdorf, Democratic officials, organizers, past candidates and more chimed in to debate how effective the party is. 
Democratic congressional candidate Ned Pillersdorf speaks to voters in Knott County. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)
Asked more about his comments, Pillersdorf told the Kentucky Lantern that he felt like the lack of visibility for him and other candidates from the state party labeled them as non-viable candidates.
“They sent the clear signal that I was not viable,” he said. “And suddenly, all these people who were going to help me stop. My network dried up.”
On if party leadership should change, Pillersdorf said yes. 
“Compare Kentucky to Tennessee or Texas. Look what happened there, and look what happened to us,” he said. “They swung and missed, and it was because they completely missed the ball.”
Another Democratic Congressional candidate, Megan Wingfield, told the Lantern that “anybody who would disagree with what Ned has to say is being disingenuous.” She challenged Republican U.S. Rep. Brett Guthrie in the 2nd Congressional District and lost by 28 points. 
Wingfield said Kentucky Democrats have organizational issues in rural areas, which meant voters did not see visibility from the top of the state party in those places. 
“They’ve spent, in my humble opinion, a lot of their time and resources with Zach Dembo in the 6th District,” she said. “Well, we saw how those results went, and Zach ran a good race and he did a good job, but they are supposed to be getting out to vote everywhere, and it’s really difficult for folks to feel like the party is behind them and fighting for them if they don’t even come into rooms where they are.”
‘Support isn’t always a check’
Kentucky Democratic Party Executive Director Morgan Eaves told the Lantern that “support isn’t always a check.” It can also include advice, gathering volunteers and organizers to help candidates, directing party staff to review and make campaign materials, connecting candidates with reporters and more.
“It’s no secret, I think, at the state and national level that Democrats are the party of fewer resources, particularly here in Kentucky, and that’s a consequence of being in the minority, for now, a long time, and having to be hard-scrabble about our politics. So we work within the resource allotment that we have, but we provide a lot of people power and a lot of training and a lot of other non-monetary resources to candidates.” 
She added that “we provided those opportunities to Mr. Pillersdorf and candidates up and down the ballot across the state.” Emails between Pillersdorf and party officials that were reviewed by the Lantern showed discussion about his campaign as far back as the summer of 2025. 
“I think it’s interesting that when party leaders deliver more Democrats going to Frankfort and to Washington than they have in over a decade, people are calling for change. I think this election cycle was a case test in exactly how strong our party leadership is,” Eaves said. “It’s not our job to tell everyone they can win. It’s not our job to run campaigns. It’s our job to create an infrastructure and to prepare candidates to do the work to flip seats.”
Kentucky once had a Democratic supermajority for decades, but lost control of the Senate in 2000 and the House in 2016 to Republicans. In July 2022, registered Republican voters outnumbered Democrats for the first time in state history. 
Eaves said after losing the majority, many Democrats were “demoralized” for a while and have only restarted their work in the last few election cycles. She credited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear for that renewal. 
“The credit is at his feet. He has excited Democrats in Kentucky in a way that they have not been excited in a really long time, and he has proven that if you mobilize and you organize and you have the right message, you can win anywhere,” Eaves added. 
Robert Kahne, a Jefferson County legislative district chair and member of KDP’s state central executive committee, said the party “does a lot to make hard decisions about which candidates to support, but there is a level of support that is available to all candidates, including and especially candidates in Eastern Kentucky.” 
When it comes to comparing Kentucky to places like Texas, Kahne said the blue wave in Texas had “been building for a long time, and the demographics of it aren’t surprising for the people that pay attention.” That state has four of the top 10 biggest cities in the country and large demographics of voters that supported Democrats this year, including Black, Latino and suburban voters, he added. He also pointed to redistricting that favored Republican candidates. 
Kahne said voting trends showed that Democrats’ “most fertile ground” was in areas like Louisville, Lexington and Northern Kentucky this year. 
“You have to be judicious about where you’re going to spend your money,” he said. “And I do think that there’s a lot to be celebrated.”
Eaves said work is already underway for 2027 and 2028 election cycles. Next year, statewide offices, including governor, are on the ballot. Legislative seats will be decided again in 2028. 
“We had a really strong class of candidates this year, even if we did not contest as many races as we wanted. We had an incredibly amazing class of candidates, and I think because of the work they put in and the seats that we were able to flip this cycle, and the fact that all 120 counties voted more blue this year than they did just two years ago in 2024, more people are going to run in 2028,” Eaves said, adding that people are asking now about candidate training and other steps to take.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: With weeks until federal law changes, here’s what you need to know about hemp-based THC
description: With just three weeks until a strict new federal definition of hemp takes effect, business owners and consumers are scrambling to understand what the changes will mean for the availability of the intoxicating hemp-derived products like gummies and drinks that have been widely available for years. Minnesota’s top cannabis regulator said his office is preparin[...]
text:
A change in federal law coming next month could change the market for hemp-based THC drinks, seen here at a St. Paul market. (Photo by J. Patrick Coolican/Minnesota Reformer)With just three weeks until a strict new federal definition of hemp takes effect, business owners and consumers are scrambling to understand what the changes will mean for the availability of the intoxicating hemp-derived products like gummies and drinks that have been widely available for years.
Minnesota’s top cannabis regulator said his office is preparing for either possibility: that the law takes effect, or Congress delays or overturns it. 
DFL U.S. Sen. (and Gov.-elect) Amy Klobuchar introduced a bill Tuesday with GOP Sen. Tim Sheehy of Montana that would loosen the definition of hemp and create a regulatory framework for intoxicating hemp products.
If things feel like they are in flux, it’s because they are. Here’s what you need to know about the new hemp law, what could yet happen and what it means for you. 
How did we get here?
It all started back in 2018 when the federal Agriculture Improvement Act – better known as the Farm Bill – legalized hemp products containing up to 0.3% by weight of delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary compound in marijuana that produces a high. 
That meant all sorts of hemp-derived THC products, such as gummies, beverages and topical ointments, were legal nationwide, as long as they met that 0.3% THC threshold. These products quickly became available in stores nationwide, but Congress did not create any mechanism to regulate them, leaving that to the states. 
Some states, like Minnesota, created their own regulations for hemp. But many others did not, and these products were essentially unregulated in many places. 
In November 2025, Congress attempted to put the toothpaste back in the tube by passing a new definition of hemp that will outlaw most intoxicating hemp products in much of the country. Under the new rules set to take effect Dec. 11, any product containing more than 0.4 milligrams of THC per container will be considered marijuana under federal law. That standard is so strict that many nonintoxicating products, such as a topical balm containing the cannabinoid CBD, along with trace amounts of THC, will also become federally illegal.
What happens next in Washington?
Without further congressional action, the new law goes into effect next month, though a handful of bills have been introduced to either postpone or rewire the new rules. The legislation introduced this week is Klobuchar’s third hemp-focused bill of the session. So far, none have moved forward.
But some industry insiders are cautiously optimistic about the Klobuchar-Sheehy bill, also known as the Hemp Guardrails Act. The bill would raise the potency threshold for hemp products to a maximum of 1% by weight total THC (which includes all forms of tetrahydrocannabinol, not just delta-9); empower the Food and Drug Administration to regulate hemp products and producers; prohibit sales of hemp-derived products to those under the age of 21; create packaging and marketing standards; ban synthetic cannabinoids; and allow states to enact stricter regulations.
“Minnesota is a national leader in hemp, and our state has shown that we can protect kids and support responsible hemp businesses,” Klobuchar said in a statement, adding that the measure “would keep safe hemp products on store shelves, protect consumers from dangerous products, and ensure that farmers and small businesses can continue to operate, grow and create jobs.”
Outgoing Sen. Tina Smith of Minnesota also supports reversing the new law, citing a conversation with a Minnesota brewer. The industry has embraced hemp-based drinks but faces a challenging future in that market segment if the law goes into effect.  
“I was just at an event with Utepils where the owner and I agreed that this federal ban is misguided and will hurt our brewers if it isn’t delayed, or better yet, reversed altogether,” Smith said in a statement. 
A major potential roadblock remains: A pair of Republican senators — who are still in the majority during the lame-duck session — are vowing to block any bill that “extends, delays or builds a regulatory framework” around hemp products.
It’s possible that no deal is reached before the new Congress is sworn in next year. With large Democratic majorities in both houses and a White House that has signaled support for regulating hemp, the law could get an update in 2027, but passing laws is typically more difficult than blocking them.
What does this mean for Minnesota?
Because Minnesota has its own statutory definition and regulations for intoxicating hemp products, they will remain available in Minnesota regardless of whether the new federal definition takes effect, according to Eric Taubel, director of the state Office of Cannabis Management. 
But these products will likely be stocked by fewer retailers who will face new challenges to carry them.
Because recreational cannabis remains a Schedule I controlled substance under federal law – the most-restricted category, reserved for drugs like heroin, LSD and MDMA – companies that make or sell marijuana (and, if the new law takes effect, intoxicating hemp products) are prohibited from writing off many business expenses. They also have limited access to banking services from federally regulated financial institutions. 
Minnesota hemp companies will lose access to markets in other states, and out-of-state products will disappear from local store shelves.
That means many businesses will likely have to get creative to continue selling hemp products, said Taubel, the state’s cannabis regulator. Alcohol retailers could build a “store-within-a-store” — similar to the small Minnesota liquor stores within Trader Joe’s or Target locations that are physically separated from the rest of the operation. They may add ATMs or “cashless ATMs” like those found in many cannabis dispensaries so customers can pay without using credit or debit cards. Breweries might continue selling THC beverages, but stop producing them at their own facilities.
Some may simply forge ahead with business as usual and hope for the best, Taubel said. 
“Every business is going to make a series of calculations about what risk they’re willing to tolerate,” he said.
Taubel said that his office has not received any guidance from the federal government on how it intends to interpret or enforce the new law and is forging ahead regardless of the outcome. 
“What we’ve tried to do is less predict what the federal government is going to do … and more just construct a smart, well-regulated system for our businesses, with the hope that a licensed, regulated market puts our operators in the best place to succeed,” he said.
How are Minnesota businesses preparing for change? 
Ryan Kopperud, vice president of growth for Minneapolis’ Wild State Cider, maker of the Birdie and Odder brands of hemp-derived THC beverages, said he has a “substantial amount of hope” that lawmakers could take action before Dec. 11. He pointed to a recent letter from a coalition of veterans groups to Congress in support of reversing the looming ban as a reason for optimism.
“Those big voices that are not hemp trade groups speaking to how valuable hemp has been … are really crucial for getting Congress to understand the depth and breadth of the [industry] and how many people are going to be negatively impacted,” Kopperud said.
Wild State plans to continue producing, distributing and retailing its hemp-derived products statewide, he said. ATMs are being installed in taprooms across the state so people can pay cash for THC beverages — necessary given the federal banking restrictions — while manufacturers are looking for new distributors so they can continue shipping product. 
“Every tier of the three-tier system is putting in contingency plans and modifying their business models to be able to sustain a Minnesota-only market,” Kopperud said, referring to the producer-distributor-retailer model for the sale of alcohol in the U.S., upon which Minnesota’s hemp regulations are modeled.
While some alcohol distributors are likely to exit the hemp business entirely, others are looking for ways to remain in the market. Keith Donovan, general manager of liquor and wine wholesaler Bellboy Corporation, said the company is planning to spin off its hemp operations into a new company.
Donovan said he believes any ban on intoxicating hemp products won’t be permanent, but he’s “not feeling very good about something happening prior to January.” 
As demand from retailers cratered with the ban approaching, Bellboy has reduced its inventory of hemp products to a manageable level, Donovan said. Sales of hemp products fell by about 75% in just one month between September and October, he said. 
In Washington, D.C., Beecher Vaillancourt was in a taxi on Tuesday during a “hill climb” trip to lobby legislators on behalf of the U.S. Hemp Roundtable. Vaillancourt, who owns the Minneapolis-based Foundry Nation and BLNCD Naturals brands of hemp-derived products with his wife, Allison, said his sales to distributors have also dropped off precipitously in recent months. But it’s been counteracted a bit by a spike in online sales, he said.
Vaillancourt’s companies held two “warehouse sales” to move unsold product in recent months. They’re working to build up wholesale and dispensary sales in Minnesota to compensate for the potential loss of out-of-state sales. They’re also in the process of getting an adult-use cannabis license to expand their product lines into the recreational marijuana market, he said.
In the event a deal is reached, Vaillancourt has stocked up on ingredients so they can immediately ramp up production again. 
“We’re hedging our bets, optimistically,” he said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Federal officials propose new nutrition requirements to infant formula
description: Infant formula is in place on shelves at Mac's Fresh Market in Ridgeland, Miss., Thursday, May 5, 2022. The U.S. is currently experiencing a shortage in infant formula.
text:
Federal officials are weighing changes to nutritional requirements for infant formula for the first time in nearly three decades. Experts say those changes could have the biggest impact on Mississippi, which has one of the lowest breastfeeding rates in the country.
Initial proposed changes include lowering, raising or maintaining mandated levels for eight vitamins and minerals already required in formula. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has said that “subsequent phases will assess the remaining required nutrients, potential new nutrient requirements and carbohydrate sources.” All changes will be consolidated into a final rule, and the FDA has not set a date for when the rule will take effect. 
Experts agree the review is overdue and that the changes proposed so far are positive. But they also said they hope new regulations are created and implemented in a thoughtful way. Increasing safety around infant formula could heighten nutritional standards, but also preserve families’ access to formula without delays, shortages or skyrocketing prices.  
“If you’re going to ban the old formula, you have to make sure there’s a new formula in place right behind it, so that the shelves aren’t empty,” said Dr. Cris Glick, a retired neonatologist and former director of Mississippi Lactation Services, a freestanding breastfeeding clinic in Jackson that closed in 2024.
Glick said she hopes the federal government discusses with formula companies about feasible timelines for changing their ingredients. Glick added she worries because she believes President Donald Trump’s administration has a track record of moving “rashly and erratically.” This effort is part of the broader Make America Healthy Again campaign. 
If implemented as written, the White House’s proposed changes would take place over multiple phases. The first phase of the revision would change acceptable amounts of vitamin A, vitamin D, iodine and manganese and reaffirm specifications for chloride, potassium, selenium and sodium. Comments are due by March 2, 2027. A second and third phase will propose changes to other ingredients and will also have comment periods, with a final rule taking effect 60 days after publication. Manufacturers would then have three years from that effective date to comply. The federal government hasn’t announced when final changes would go into effect. 
Glick worries if formula companies can’t reformulate their products in time, it could lead to shortages like the one four years ago. 
In 2022, four U.S. babies fell ill – two fatally – after consuming powdered formula manufactured at an Abbott Nutrition plant in Michigan. The company voluntarily recalled 5 million units of powdered formula and closed operations for five months. Along with post-pandemic supply chain issues, the closure led to nationwide shortages and price surges. 
During that time, Delta-based Brittany Reed-Isler worked as a designated breastfeeding expert for the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children. She remembers dozens of families in her Bolivar County area having trouble finding formulas covered by WIC at their local grocer. The WIC program contracts primarily with two formula companies nationwide – Abbott Nutrition and Mead Johnson –  making supply-chain hiccups more consequential for the low-income families that rely on the federal nutrition program. 
“That was a scary time,” Reed-Isler said. “Because you have to think about everything – it’s not just about the formula. It’s about the mom who may not have a car. She’s able to go down the street to go to her local grocery store. But what if she can’t find it there? How will she get a ride to another town?”
‘The reality of the market’
Dr. Patricia Tibbs, president of the Mississippi chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said she’s been surprised and impressed with the way the administration has handled the rollout of these proposed changes. Tibbs said it’s a refreshing reminder of how leaders can work together to advance health policy – which she said she hasn’t seen enough of under this administration. Now, she has hopes for the future. 
“What has struck me is how correct the process has been for everything,” said Tibbs, applauding the agency for mobilizing on an important issue and for the concerted efforts to glean insights from experts and stakeholders. 
Tibbs said this initiative represents the kind of organization and science-backed policy change she would like to see brought to the table on vaccine issues. 
“To not do that with the vaccines is horrifying,” she said, adding her disappointment that the U.S. lost its measles elimination status this week. 
Tibbs highlighted the change to iodine as an important update in the proposed ruling on infant formula. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services seeks to tighten the window of iodine levels from 5-75 micrograms to 15-50 micrograms. Tibbs said this change is good because iodine deficiency can be detrimental, while excess iodine can be toxic. 
The National WIC Association was among dozens of groups to submit comments to HHS. 
“With the last comprehensive assessment of infant formula taking place in 1998, NWA appreciates the opportunity to consider new scientific data and information related to (commercial milk formula) nutrient requirements,” the letter states. 
While the organization is largely in favor of the proposed changes, Ali Hard, director of public policy at the association, said she hopes White House officials consider the “reality of the market.” 
Because a handful of companies control the market, it is vulnerable to collapse, said Hard. 
Hard said changes to formula nutritional requirements may make it easier for international companies to enter the U.S. market. One example of a meaningful change that would help achieve that, Hard said, is placing a maximum iron level requirement on formulas, the way other countries have. 
Current U.S. standards outline a minimum – but no maximum. HHS asked stakeholders to submit input on an iron level maximum but have proposed no change yet, said Hard. 
“Anemia is certainly a concern, but you also need to think about how iron also competes with calcium for absorption,” said Hard, who is a registered dietitian nutritionist. “So we can’t just say ‘Iron, iron, iron.’”
Different standards across countries complicates the entrance of international companies if the U.S. has a formula shortage, Hard said. She worries what will happen if federal regulations put international companies even further out of reach. 
“The nutrition science is really important and that should be the number one thing,” Hard said. “But we also need to think about the reality of the market and make sure that we’re not setting ourselves up for a situation where we have even further consolidation and vulnerability with access to formula. Because it is a really unique food – there is no safe substitution besides breastmilk.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: 71 NH disability care providers haven’t yet revalidated with Medicaid, risking their funding
description: Seventy-one of the more than 100 provider agencies that make up New Hampshire’s developmental disability care network haven’t yet revalidated with Medicaid as of Wednesday, a state official said, a necessary step to receive funding. In New Hampshire, people with intellectual and developmental disabilities are legally entitled to services, such as in-home car[...]
text:
In New Hampshire, people with intellectual and developmental disabilities are legally entitled to services. (Getty Images)Seventy-one of the more than 100 provider agencies that make up New Hampshire’s developmental disability care network haven’t yet revalidated with Medicaid as of Wednesday, a state official said, a necessary step to receive funding.
In New Hampshire, people with intellectual and developmental disabilities are legally entitled to services, such as in-home care, group homes and day programming, paid for through Medicaid. The services are provided by private agencies. Under federal law, the agencies, like other types of Medicaid providers, must revalidate their enrollment information every five years to continue receiving funds for the care they provide.
Jessica Gorton, chief of the state’s Bureau of Developmental Services, said if the agencies don’t revalidate by the end of the month, their Medicaid claims would start getting suspended. If they don’t revalidate following that, they could be disenrolled as a Medicaid provider. That could significantly affect client services. 
“We are trying to get the word out as much as we can,” Gorton said during a meeting of the state’s Developmental Services Quality Council Wednesday, “give people calls, share some awareness to any member, particularly senior leadership, of any agencies, to make sure it’s on their radar. (It’s) likely communication errors if they thought someone else was handling it.”
Gorton said she didn’t know exactly how long it takes agencies to revalidate.
“My understanding is that it’s not super in-depth, that they have a pretty streamlined process to get that work done. But again, that’s anecdotal,” she said.
Gorton said the state’s “program integrity office, of course, wants continuity of services, so (they’ll make) every effort to make sure that happens.” She said they’ve sent out email blasts urging agencies to revalidate.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Two of Alaska’s legislative races are within five votes after ranked choice tabulations
description: One Republican member of the Alaska House of Representatives is losing his re-election bid by three votes, and another is winning by four after the Alaska Division of Elections conducted ranked choice runoff calculations Wednesday. According to Wednesday’s preliminary results, independents have won 7 of the 40 seats in the state House, Democrats have won […]
text:
Rep. Kevin McCabe, R-Big Lake, talks with Sen. Bill Wielechowski, D-Anchorage (right) during a joint session of the state House and Senate on Tuesday, May 7, 2024. At left is Rep. Zack Fields, D-Anchorage. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)One Republican member of the Alaska House of Representatives is losing his re-election bid by three votes, and another is winning by four after the Alaska Division of Elections conducted ranked choice runoff calculations Wednesday.
According to Wednesday’s preliminary results, independents have won 7 of the 40 seats in the state House, Democrats have won 17 and Republicans won 16. 
The state-level results appear to reflect the “blue tsunami” of Democratic-leaning outcomes in elections nationwide this month. 
Two years ago, Republicans won 21 seats in the state House, and the swing means the House will remain controlled by an emboldened coalition majority of Republicans, Democrats and independents.
The races will be certified Nov. 25, and recounts are possible afterward.


The two tight elections — both in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough — were among a handful of close races decided by Wednesday’s ranked choice tabulation.
In Alaska, all candidates for a particular office run together. The top four vote-getters in the August primary advance to the November general election, and voters are asked to rank the candidates in order of preference.
If one candidate gets at least 50% of the first-choice votes, they win. If none reach that threshold, the lowest finisher is eliminated, and votes for them go to their voters’ second choices. The eliminations continue until only two candidates are left, and the person with the most votes wins.
In the state Senate, where 10 of 20 seats were on the November ballot, Republicans still hold 11 seats, Democrats hold nine, and there is one independent — Sen.-elect Bryce Edgmon, I-Dillingham, whose election was confirmed by Wednesday’s tabulation. Edgmon replaces longtime Democratic Sen. Lyman Hoffman of Dillingham.
The Senate will be governed by an 11-person coalition majority, a smaller version of the coalition that has controlled it since 2023. 


All of the state’s closest legislative elections were in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, where Democratic voters played an influential role in races with multiple Republicans.
In House District 30, which covers the western Mat-Su and the Denali Borough, Republican candidate Doug Massie is leading Republican Rep. Kevin McCabe by three votes.
McCabe led Massie in first-choice votes, but voters who backed Democratic candidate Sandra Loomis strongly favored Massie once Loomis was eliminated: Almost a fifth of her votes transferred to Massie, giving him a narrow lead. 
Next door, in the eastern Mat-Su’s House District 29, Republican Rep. Garret Nelson leads Republican challenger Steve Menard by four votes.
Nelson led Menard by fewer than 50 first-choice votes, but unlike in House District 30, the few Democratic-leaning voters who ranked at least one of the Republicans split evenly between them, allowing Nelson to preserve his advantage.
A similar pattern happened in House District 28, covering Wasilla. Republican Rep. Elexie Moore trailed Republican challenger Stephen Wright in first-choice votes but finished ahead of Democratic candidate Kit Kennedy. When Kennedy was eliminated, most of her supporters chose to rank neither Republican. A small plurality preferred Moore, but not enough to erase Wright’s advantage. He recorded a 46-vote win as of Wednesday night.
In Alaska, the state will pay for a recount if the margin is 20 or fewer votes, or less than 0.5% of the total of the votes for the two closest candidates. The recount must be requested by a candidate or 10 qualified voters in the area covered by the election.
McCabe said by text message that he intends to request a recount. It was not immediately clear whether Menard would do so.
Among the Mat-Su’s closely contested state Senate seats, Republican Sen. George Rauscher — appointed by Gov. Mike Dunleavy to replace Sen. Shelley Hughes, R-Palmer, after her resignation to run for governor — won election on his own merits in a ranked choice runoff.
Dunleavy also appointed Sen. Cathy Tilton, R-Wasilla, to replace Republican Sen. Mike Shower after he resigned to run for lieutenant governor. Tilton lost a ranked choice runoff to fellow Republican Ryan Berry by 467 votes.
Unlike in the close state House races, the elimination of Republican candidate Zane Vrvilo was enough to give Berry the edge; the subsequent elimination of Democratic candidate Pat Chesbro increased Berry’s lead via transfer votes.
Elsewhere in the state:

Sen.-elect Louise Stutes, R-Kodiak, was elected to replace Sen. Gary Stevens, R-Kodiak, in a three-way ranked choice runoff. Stutes had 49.9% of the first-choice votes, just barely short of the margin needed to avoid the runoff against two other Republicans.
Independent Brent Johnson defeated Republican Rep. Sarah Vance, R-Homer in a head-to-head race that was unresolved until Wednesday because of late-counted absentee ballots. Of 10,128 votes, Johnson defeated Vance by 59 according to the preliminary total.
In Anchorage, Republican Rep. Julie Coulombe defeated Democratic challenger Danni Hall by 131 votes out of 8,499 cast in House District 11. Democrats had spent heavily to boost Hall’s campaign.
Also in Anchorage, Democratic candidate Denny Wells confirmed his victory over Republican Rep. Mia Costello, winning in House District 15 by 669 votes in uncertified results Wednesday.
In Eagle River, Republican Rep. Jamie Allard won re-election in a four-way ranked choice runoff election that saw her leading in first-choice votes.
For the other Eagle River state House district, former Republican Rep. Ken McCarty won the election to replace retiring Republican Rep. Dan Saddler by defeating moderate Republican challenger Gina Wall. Though there were only two candidates, ranked choice tabulation was still used because neither had more than 50% of the vote, there were more than 100 write-in votes, and McCarty was leading Wall by just 19 first-choice ballots. The tabulation confirmed McCarty’s victory.
Rep. DeLena Johnson, R-Palmer, won re-election after a three-way ranked choice tabulation. She had led in first-choice votes.
North Pole Republican Rep. Mike Prax was re-elected after a three-way ranked choice runoff in House District 33. Republican challenger Barbara Haney was eliminated first, and Prax defeated independent Pepper McFarland in the final matchup. 
Democratic candidate Evelynn Trefon won the race to replace Edgmon in House District 37. She had 58.8% in the final tabulation, ahead of Republican candidate Brenda Wilson.
In House District 38, incumbent Democratic Rep. Nellie Unangiq Jimmie was re-elected after a ranked choice runoff. She had 58.2% in the final tabulation, ahead of second-place finisher and former Democratic Rep. CJ McCormick. 
Democratic incumbent Rep. Neal Foster, who had 49% of the first choice votes in House District 39, won in ranked choice tabulation. Independent candidate Tyler Ivanoff was second.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Veteran WA state senator enters race for Snohomish County executive
description: Democratic state Sen. Marko Liias, a veteran lawmaker and influential chair of the Senate Transportation Committee, launched his campaign Wednesday to lead Washington’s third most populous county. Liias, of Edmonds, will vie in 2027 for Snohomish County Executive, resetting his political sights fresh off winning a fourth term in the Senate, where he’s been a[...]
text:
Democratic state Sen. Marko Liias of Edmonds on Wednesday began his 2027 campaign for Snohomish County executive. Here is speaking on the Senate floor in the 2026 session.  (Photo by Bill Lucia/Washington State Standard)Democratic state Sen. Marko Liias, a veteran lawmaker and influential chair of the Senate Transportation Committee, launched his campaign Wednesday to lead Washington’s third most populous county.
Liias, of Edmonds, will vie in 2027 for Snohomish County Executive, resetting his political sights fresh off winning a fourth term in the Senate, where he’s been a driving force on statewide transportation policy and an unyielding voice for the rights of LGBTQ children and adults. 
“It’s a really important job,” he said of the executive post. “For nearly two decades, I’ve been proud to represent Snohomish County in Olympia, working to bring home investments that strengthen our communities, create jobs, and improve people’s lives. The relationships I’ve developed will be essential to my ability to deliver for our county.”
He joins Democratic Snohomish County Councilman Jared Mead as the first entries in the competition to succeed County Executive Dave Somers, who cannot run again due to term limits.
Jared Mead, a Democratic Snohomish County Council member in Washington state, is running in 2027 for county executive. (Courtesy of Mead Campaign)
Mead, a former Mill Creek City Council member, served one term in the state House of Representatives representing the 44th Legislative District in Snohomish County.
He won his seat in 2018, then two years later was appointed to a vacancy on the Snohomish County Council. Mead was elected to his first full council term in 2021 and re-elected in 2025. He said he will remain on the council if he is not elected county executive.
“Senator Liias, myself and others who I expect to get in this race are going to bring our own history and our own vision. Voters should have a broad array of options,” Mead said. “To the extent it is a state senator, a county council member, or anyone else, they’re going to want us to prove to them that we care about making their lives better.
“People who have spent their lives here should be able to afford to stay, including seniors living on fixed incomes. Working families need room to get ahead, and people just starting out deserve a real chance to build a life here. This community gave me that chance, and I’m not willing to watch it slip away for others,” Mead said.
Two other Snohomish County Council members, Democrat Megan Dunn and Republican Nate Nehring, are also eyeing the contest.
Dunn, in an email, said she is “strongly considering this opportunity and look forward to expanding on my years of leadership and dedication to the County as the County Executive.”
Nehring, considered the most viable Republican candidate for the countywide race, said he had “no news to share at this point. I’m still exploring my options.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Liias, 45, of Edmonds, enters with the backing of Somers and Democratic state Reps. Lillian Ortiz-Self and Strom Peterson, who serve with him in the 21st Legislative District. Peterson is also a Snohomish County Council member. Former governors Jay Inslee and Chris Gregoire are backing Liias too. 
A former Mukilteo City Council member, he was appointed to the state House in 2008 representing the 21st Legislative District. In 2014, he filled the vacancy created by the retirement of Democratic Sen. Paull Shin. 
He has won four Senate elections, the most recent on Nov. 3. He said he will remain in the Senate if he is unsuccessful next year.
Liias has shown ambition for higher office before. He briefly considered a run for Congress in 2011 and lost bids in 2016 for state treasurer, and in 2020 for lieutenant governor.
On the transportation committee, he’s worked to fund major projects such as constructing new bridges on Highway 9 and the U.S. 2 trestle and pushed for Sound Transit’s extension of light rail service into Snohomish County.
“Transportation is the place where I feel I’ve had the biggest impact,” he said.
Named chair in late 2021, he was an architect of the $16 billion, 16-year  transportation package known as Move Ahead Washington, passed in 2022. It laid out a slew of spending commitments including $1 billion apiece toward the purchase of new state ferries and the replacement of the Interstate 5 bridge connecting Washington and Oregon. 
It was controversial at the time, as Democrats used their majorities in the House and Senate to pass the package without a single Republican vote. It also was unusual because it did not increase the state’s gas tax, relying instead on a buffet of higher fees, receipts from the sale of pollution allowances under the cap-and-invest program created by the Climate Commitment Act, and transfers from the general fund and other accounts.
In the 2025 session, Liias led the effort to pass another transportation funding package. This one contained increases on July 1, 2025 of 6 cents per gallon in the gasoline tax and 9 cents per gallon for diesel. The legislation, which did garner some Republican support, also mandated annual bumps in the fuel tax based on inflation.
Liias earns an annual salary of $72,494 as a lawmaker. He is also employed by Snohomish County as a senior advisor to Somers with an annual salary of nearly $147,999. However, in 2026, Liias earned less than the maximum as he took two months of unpaid leave during the legislative session. He also teaches courses at Everett Community College.
Somers, the term-limited current executive, will earn $250,283 in 2027. His successor will earn 3% more in 2028.
Liias said the “complexity and scope” of his work in local government and the Legislature will inform his approach to creating good-paying jobs, building more housing, keeping neighborhoods safe and making life more affordable for residents.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri delays paid family caregiving program as home nursing shortage persists
description: A program designed to train and pay parents, guardians or their designees to provide skilled nursing services to Missourians with medical complexities has stalled for a second year because state officials don’t know if there will be money in next year’s budget to support it. Missouri lawmakers have approved $11 million in each of the […]
text:
Tommy Smith, who is 10 and loves Batman, was born with a genetic condition that interferes with his body's autonomic nervous system, which controls involuntary functions like respiration (photo submitted).A program designed to train and pay parents, guardians or their designees to provide skilled nursing services to Missourians with medical complexities has stalled for a second year because state officials don’t know if there will be money in next year’s budget to support it.
Missouri lawmakers have approved $11 million in each of the past two state budgets for a program that would pay family members to provide complex medical care at home.
But the program has yet to launch, and state health officials say uncertainty about future funding will likely delay it for another year.
The current state budget includes $3.8 million in state general revenue and $7.2 million in federal matching funds to launch a complex care assistant program, which is designed to ease a shortage of home nurses and provide financial relief for families who step in to provide life-sustaining care. The fiscal year 2026 budget included the same amount of funding.
Proponents of the Medicaid program argue it would compensate families for care they already provide and help keep individuals with medical complexities or disabilities out of institutions. They also contend the state would save money by avoiding preventable hospitalizations.
But as Missouri faces growing pressure on its budget, Lisa Cox, communications director for the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, said the department doesn’t expect the program to launch during the current budget year.
“Regrettably, the uncertainty around sustainable funding for an ongoing project has resulted in an implementation timeline that would make it unlikely that any service would be paid before the next fiscal year, which is beyond the authorization of our current budget,” Cox said in an email to The Independent.
The department’s budget request for fiscal year 2028 includes the same level of funding for the program as the current year.
The program would allow parents, guardians, other family members and people with close relationships to Medicaid recipients to be employed through a private duty nursing agency and provide designated services, such as tube feedings and ostomy care, under the supervision of a registered nurse who would be required to visit in person every 60 days.
Complex care assistants would have to be certified nurse assistants or home health aides and undergo additional competency training, Cox said. 
Carol Hudspeth, executive director of the Missouri Alliance for Care at Home, told The Independent her organization is “disappointed” that implementation of the program has stalled.
“While we understand the importance of fiscal responsibility, we also believe it is important to consider the long-term value of programs that can help prevent gaps in care and support for families who are already carrying an enormous responsibility.”
When Martha Smith’s grandson, Tommy, first came home from St. Louis Children’s Hospital at 10 months old, it wasn’t uncommon for him to stop breathing multiple times a day.
Smith, of Lebanon, told The Independent she and her husband would manually resuscitate Tommy using a bag valve mask, squeezing the self-inflating bag to force air into his lungs.
Tommy, now 10, was born with congenital central hypoventilation syndrome, a rare genetic condition that disrupts many of the body’s automatic functions, including breathing and sensing oxygen and carbon dioxide levels. 
This hasn’t been necessary as often recently, Smith said — it’s been eight months since Tommy has needed this intervention. He now uses a diaphragm pacer, which stimulates his breathing with electric pulses delivered beneath his skin.
But Tommy still needs around-the-clock supervision, and Smith said it’s a struggle to find consistent nursing coverage for the 112 hours a week Medicaid has approved for his care.
Under the complex care assistant program, Smith said her family could have more financial stability and fewer sleepless nights. She and her husband can’t work regular jobs because they never know when one of them will need to step in to care for Tommy, so they work shifts around his care to make ends meet.
Some family members learn to perform complicated medical tasks from hospital staff before bringing their loved ones home. Once home, however, families can struggle to find nurses to provide the care Medicaid has authorized.
Stacy Atwood, of Springfield, said that after her daughter Brinley was diagnosed with a rare genetic condition called mosaic trisomy 13, her family was approved for 24-hour home nursing through Medicaid. But multiple weekslong stays at Cardinal Glennon Children’s Hospital in St. Louis during Brinley’s first year made it difficult to retain nurses to work those hours.
Atwood told The Independent she and her husband were able to shoulder the responsibility of gradually reducing the narcotic medications prescribed to Brinley, now 6, after heart surgery because their doctors were supportive and accessible — and because she could work remotely from the hospital and learn from her daughter’s medical team.
Brinley Atwood, 6, has been more mobile since switching to a feeding tube that is less bulky (photo submitted).
When Brinley was discharged, the Atwoods had to continuously monitor her breathing and follow a precise feeding and medication schedule through a tube connected to her stomach and small intestine. Tapering the narcotics too quickly could have sent Brinley into withdrawal.
“No training, no experience,” Stacy Atwood said. “It was just what we learned at the hospital. Thank goodness we had a doctor that literally allowed us to email every day, call every day and be able to get some guidance and tell us what we were listening for.”
Atwood said Brinley is now thriving. She’s nonverbal but learning to communicate with a device, and she hasn’t been hospitalized since her heart surgery. 
“She’s made it leaps and bounds beyond what (her doctors) ever expected, and that’s because we’ve been able to give that close care for her,” Atwood said.
But Atwood said if her job had been less flexible, Brinley might have had to stay in the hospital much longer. 
Brinley’s experience is hardly unique.
Shawn Dryden, CEO of Ranken Jordan Pediatric Bridge Hospital in Maryland Heights, told The Independent it’s “very common” for kids to face prolonged hospitalization because of a lack of home-based care.
Out of the 45 or 50 children in the hospital at any given time, Dryden said, it’s not unusual for five or more to have “a discharge barrier either related to private duty nursing or broader caregiver team support and availability.”
Dryden said the team at Ranken Jordan, which specializes in preparing kids and families who to go home after transitioned from acute care hospitals, was “thrilled and excited” about the complex care assistant program because “we think it expands and grows the care team that trained and qualified to take care of these children.”
“We’re all anxious for the day when the service is up and running and available,” Dryden said.
 Years of delays

Home care agencies have long struggled to attract nurses, partly due to low Medicaid reimbursement rates, and families, advocates and nursing agencies have been seeking solutions for years.
Lawmakers in 2020 approved funding for a pilot program that would have allowed up to 100 parents in the St. Louis metro area to be trained and paid, according to previous reporting by The Independent. But the program was called off after discussions between MO HealthNet and the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services determined it would violate private duty nursing regulations.
The following year, lawmakers and then-Gov. Mike Parson signed off on rewritten language placing a 50-person pilot in the Department of Social Services’ Home Health Program, but state officials instead spent the money on pandemic response, according to reporting from The Kansas City Star.
In 2022, the department agreed as part of the settlement of a federal lawsuit to expand efforts to help parents find nurses, raise private duty nursing reimbursement rates and explore “innovations that will increase the availability of private duty nursing to children.”
Missouri last raised Medicaid reimbursement rates for private duty nursing in 2024, from $55.04 to $60.80 per hour. That’s the rate nursing agencies are paid by MO HealthNet before  deducting administrative costs and overhead. Wages paid to nurses are considerably lower.
A MO HealthNet program compensating “families as caregivers” was one of 12 action steps identified during a July 2023 provider capacity meeting mandated by the settlement, according to a report obtained by The Independent. 
Multiple states have Medicaid programs that pay relatives to perform skilled care tasks, including Arizona, Florida, Oklahoma and Massachusetts.
Missouri officials have already drafted regulations and an amendment to Missouri’s Medicaid plan to launch the program, Cox said. The “current barrier” to implementation is an “internal approval process” requiring “a review of state funding to sustain the program long-term.” 
The department would then have to conduct a contracted rate setting analysis and update its systems to be able to process claims through the program, Cox said. The regulations would also need to be approved by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.
Hudspeth, from the Missouri Alliance for Care at Home, urged the state “not to lose sight of the families this program was intended to help.”
“Budget uncertainty should prompt us to look for responsible solutions, not necessarily abandon programs that address significant gaps in care.”
For family members like Atwood who have been advocating for the program, the delays are disheartening. 
In 2025, Atwood said, “it was a very long approval process that it had to go through, and then here we are at it again. If it doesn’t go through, we’re going to be back in the same boat.”
Smith said when she and her husband first brought Tommy home, she and Tommy’s auntie alternated caring for Tommy and working shifts while her husband “pretty much worked around the clock.”
“Whatever it took to make it work,” she said. “But there’s a better way. There’s got to be a better, humane way.”

name: California
title: Is the Democratic supermajority bad for us?
description: We had a hot story last week on the hack some part-time college professors found to make big-time money in online education, and California’s community colleges noticed. Check out how the system chancellor responded to our investigation. In other news, we learned Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra is probably going to have to make some hard budget […]
text:
California senators on the Senate floor in the state Capitol in Sacramento on Aug. 31, 2026. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters




We had a hot story last week on the hack some part-time college professors found to make big-time money in online education, and California’s community colleges noticed. Check out how the system chancellor responded to our investigation.
In other news, we learned Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra is probably going to have to make some hard budget choices right away. He won’t have to worry much about Republicans blocking his plan. It turns out they’ll hold just one in six seats in the Legislature.
Stay dry out there, friends. 
Republicans already were a superminority in the California Legislature. This month’s election results shrank their numbers even further. 
When the Legislature swears in new members next month, Republicans will hold just 20 out of 120 seats in the Senate Assembly. That’s a decrease from 29. 
That means for the next two years at least, Republican lawmakers will face the largest Democratic supermajority in 150 years, and Democrats will face fewer checks on their power, reports CalMatters’ Kate Wolffe.
Republicans already didn’t have enough seats in the Legislature to block certain tax and urgency measures, nor pass policies Democratic lawmakers didn’t like. But with nearly a third of its seats lost, the GOP is even more likely to be excluded from big decisions. 
And while Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas touted the incoming Assembly Democratic Caucus as the “most diverse in the history of the California Legislature,” several political scientists agree that having more ideological diversity via a strong opposition party makes for a more robust democracy.

Eric Schickler, co-director of UC Berkeley’s Institute for Governmental Studies: “Competition keeps politicians honest. It pressures them to deliver.”

Armed with a bigger supermajority, Democrats may have less incentive to fix pressing issues or scrutinize bad policy proposals pushed by their colleagues, experts said.
As the Republican party regroups and strategizes for 2028, what would GOP lawmakers do to counter Democrats’ power until then? Likely, much of the same things they’ve done before: Put Democrats on blast on social media, on the Capitol floor and in press conferences.

Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican: “It’s no different than when we were 20 (assemblymembers). We have no … leverage when it comes to the traditional legislative process.”

Read more.



Your favorite state, in photos: CalMatters has teamed up with CatchLight on “California in Pictures,” a monthly newsletter that highlights compelling photojournalism from across the state. See the latest edition here. Sign up to receive the next one. And read more about it from our engagement team.

Other Stories You Should Know


CA economy OK — if AI doesn’t go bust


Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra speaks at an election night watch party at Drake’s: The Barn in West Sacramento on Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters




For the fifth year in a row, California is projected to have a budget deficit despite growing revenue, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
As CalMatters’ Yue Stella Yu explains, the office’s latest economic forecast offers a sneak peek into the financial challenges Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra will face as he prepares for his first state budget in January. 
The state is raking in billions of dollars in taxes due to an AI-driven stock market, but if a downturn begins next year, California will face a deficit of $2 billion, according to the office. That deficit could grow to $15 billion the following year, which could then soar to $35 billion if there’s an abrupt market crash.
With the risk of a ballooning deficit, state leaders would have to cut programs or raise taxes. 
A spokesperson for Becerra said he is committed to delivering a “balanced budget that protects the services Californians depend on.” But Sen. Roger Niello, a Roseville Republican and vice chairperson of the Senate budget committee, urged Becerra’s administration to “face reality.”

Niello, in a statement: “When the market eventually corrects, the consequences of today’s budget problems will catch up with us.”

Read more.



Colleges respond to CalMatters investigation


A student looks through their class schedule on their laptop in Stockton on May 7, 2026. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters




California’s head of community colleges is assessing whether online professors are providing a quality education to students, after CalMatters found that some part-time faculty took on extreme courseloads, write CalMatters’ Adam Echelman and Mohamed Al Elew.
CalMatters’ report, published last week, described how some professors were teaching more than a dozen online classes at a time across several California public college and university campuses. The highest earner was an ethnic studies professor who made nearly $800,000 in 2024.
In response to the story, California Community Colleges Chancellor Sonya Christian emailed campus chief executives, saying “some of the practices described in the article are deeply troubling and warrant further scrutiny.”
Under state, federal and accreditation standards, online instructors must interact with students regularly, and Christian said her office will examine whether colleges are complying with these rules. If they do not, schools, and ultimately students, are at risk of losing federal financial aid.
Read more.



And lastly: Newsom touts an AI ‘kill switch’


Attendees gather at the OpenAI DevDay 2026 conference in San Francisco on Sept. 29, 2026. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo




Saying the state is stepping in to fill what he sees as a lack of federal regulation, Gov. Gavin Newsom unveiled Wednesday a sweeping set of policy recommendations to curb the risks of AI. A panel of experts the governor brought together earlier this fall drew up the recommendations, which include enabling state officials to order an immediate emergency shutdown, or “kill switch,” of AI systems they deem dangerous. Read more from CalMatters’ Khari Johnson.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Former foster parents’ attitudes sour toward Kansas child welfare system
description: TOPEKA — Kansas foster care parents who left the system described themselves in 2022 as “glorified babysitters” and pointed to a lack of respect from the state’s foster care agency. A year later, the Legislature passed the Gail Finney Memorial Foster Care Bill of Rights, which attempted, in part, to establish caregivers as primary members […]
text:
Sen. Beverly Gossage, a Republican from Eudora, says a report on the feelings of former Kansas foster parents "is very telling,” and legislators ought to listen to them. She appears here on March 31, 2025. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas foster care parents who left the system described themselves in 2022 as “glorified babysitters” and pointed to a lack of respect from the state’s foster care agency.
A year later, the Legislature passed the Gail Finney Memorial Foster Care Bill of Rights, which attempted, in part, to establish caregivers as primary members of a foster care team.
But a 2026 survey of former foster care parents found “an alarming rise” in perceptions of institutional pushback and retaliation.
The state Office of the Child Advocate presented this year’s survey results Tuesday at a joint bipartisan child welfare committee meeting, where lawmakers discussed priorities ahead of the upcoming 2027 legislative session.
Kansas lost roughly 1,000 licensed foster homes between 2020 and 2025, according to data from Who Cares, a national count of foster homes and families. The number of youths in care has decreased during that time, too, from more than 7,200 to 5,600.
“Parents didn’t leave because they stopped caring about kids,” said Brook Town, the lead case investigative analyst for the child advocate office. “They left because the system made it too hard for them to stay.”
More than 51% of survey respondents said they didn’t feel valued as members of their foster child’s planning team. More than 31% reported experiencing retaliation from the child welfare system. In 2022, only 18% of respondents said the same.
The office sent the survey this summer to more than 1,000 former foster parents, and 312 responded, which was about half of the number of parents the office surveyed in 2022. 
Town likened the child welfare system to a vehicle in need of maintenance. 
“That foster parent attrition is kind of like that check engine light,” Town said. “It tells us something is going on, but where is it?”
This year’s respondents said inadequate communication, training and flexibility needed improvement. Town pointed to survey results that indicated quick turnover rates early on. Roughly 60% of homes closed within three years. More than 20% of homes closed within the first year. 
Parents said in the survey they felt unequipped to deal with foster children’s trauma. More than 51% said initial foster care training adequately prepared them for a foster child, which was a 10-percentage-point drop from 2022.
More than 100 respondents cited unresolved conflict or lack of agency support as a direct cause of closing their homes to foster children.
“I think this report is very telling, and we need to be able to listen,” said Sen. Beverly Gossage, a Eudora Republican.
The full report is expected to be available Friday.

name: National
title: Now in charge, state Democrats plan climate agendas that focus on affordability
description: Climate change was largely absent as a campaign topic during this year’s midterm elections. Democrats gained power in many states by focusing on issues such as the cost of living and healthcare.  But many state lawmakers believe environmental policies will be key to delivering on those promises.  Democrats want to use their newfound power to […]
text:
With newfound power in many state legislatures and governor’s offices, Democrats say their focus on climate and clean energy can deliver on their campaign promises to help residents with cost of living concerns. (Photo by Marga Buschbell-Steeger/Getty Images)Climate change was largely absent as a campaign topic during this year’s midterm elections. Democrats gained power in many states by focusing on issues such as the cost of living and healthcare. 
But many state lawmakers believe environmental policies will be key to delivering on those promises. 
Democrats want to use their newfound power to promote clean energy, rein in data centers and regulate utilities — priorities they believe could help with voters’ skyrocketing electricity bills. And they want to enact new safeguards for clean air and water, pointing to the healthcare burden caused by pollution. 
“Affordability absolutely does tie into our climate and energy agenda,” said Arizona state Sen. Priya Sundareshan, who will serve as Senate president next session after Democrats gained a majority. “I’m excited to see what we can do now that Republicans are no longer able to block any action.”
Across the country, Democrats flipped control of 12 legislative chambers and six governorships. They will hold trifectas — controlling both chambers of the legislature as well as the governor’s mansion — in at least 22 states. And in several other states, the party will have newfound leverage with a majority in at least one legislative chamber or a Democratic governor. 
“Even though environment and climate did not reach the top level for most voters, they were deeply embedded in affordability conversations,” said Dylan McDowell, chief executive officer of the National Environmental Caucus, a collaborative forum for state lawmakers. “There is a higher sense of awareness around how energy and climate and environment are tied to kitchen table issues.”
Tackling energy costs
Lawmakers in newfound positions of power say they want to accelerate their states’ transition to clean energy — but with a message focused more on utility bills than carbon emissions. 
“Clean energy is more affordable and healthier,” said Pennsylvania state Sen. Carolyn Comitta, a Democrat who served as minority chair of the Environmental Resources and Energy Committee during the previous session. 
With Democrats now holding a trifecta in the state, Comitta expects lawmakers to craft an update to the state’s clean energy law to accelerate the buildout of renewable power. Other priorities include giving residents more access to rooftop, balcony and community solar projects, as well as promoting battery storage projects to bolster the electric grid. Comitta has also called for a moratorium on data centers amid concerns about rising energy costs. 
Some Republicans have sought to blame rising energy prices on Democratic climate policies. Pennsylvania state Sen. Gene Yaw, who will lose his chairmanship of the Environmental Resources and Energy Committee when the Democratic majority is sworn in, said during the campaign that the Biden administration’s pollution rules were driving up electricity bills. 
Voters across the country reject data centers

“Pennsylvania families should not be asked to sit in the dark so someone else’s climate timeline can be met on paper,” Yaw said in a statement at the time. 
In Georgia, Democratic state Rep. Eric Bell said lawmakers want to regulate electrical utilities to promote efficiency, instead of the current system where they earn returns from building costly infrastructure. One approach could include the use of grid-enhancing technologies, which allow more power to flow through existing infrastructure. 
As energy demand rises, Bell also said lawmakers will consider bills to regulate the power and water use of data centers to ensure they don’t drive up costs. 
Bell, who serves as Georgia’s state lead with the National Environmental Caucus, said he is also focused on restoring an electric vehicle tax credit, as gas prices remain high. 
While Democrats now control the Georgia governor’s office and state House, Republicans have a slim majority in the state Senate. 
In Arizona, where Democrats have a newfound trifecta, lawmakers are also looking at regulating utilities. Sundareshan, the incoming Senate president, wants to consider limiting utilities’ political spending. 
“We said we would be holding corporations accountable and lowering costs for people,” she said. “Is it appropriate to use ratepayer money for things like lobbying and campaign contributions?” 
Arizona Democrats will also focus on limiting data centers’ impact on energy bills and improving residents’ access to solar energy programs, she said. 
Utility spending was also a major issue in Michigan, where more than 81% of voters approved a ballot proposal to prevent electric and gas utilities from making campaign contributions. 
“We saw a real repudiation of utilities,” said Ben Poulson, state government affairs director with the Michigan League of Conservation Voters. “Michiganders are really concerned about rising energy bills, and they see those political contributions as standing in the way of reforms.”
Environmental activists there are pushing Democrats, with a new trifecta in state government, to realign utilities’ investor incentives to be tied to reliability and bill savings rather than capital spending, while opening up more customer-owned generation such as community solar projects. 
Meanwhile, Michigan Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson has pledged to put a moratorium on data center construction until the state issues rules requiring them to pay for their own power and restricting their tax breaks. 
Michigan Democrats were able to retake control of the House from Republicans, who had argued that state climate policies were the real culprit in driving up energy costs. Republican state Rep. Pauline Wendzel, who will lose the chairmanship of the House Energy Committee, proposed legislation earlier this year that would have repealed the state’s clean energy mandates. 
States are counting on battery farms. Some towns don’t want them.

“For too long, energy policy has focused on restricting what we can produce instead of making sure families have the power they need at a price they can afford,” Wendzel said in a statement last month. 
In Minnesota, lawmakers need to make sure the state is on track to meet its target of 100% clean electricity by 2040, said Democratic state Sen. Nick Frentz, who chairs the Energy, Utilities, Environment, and Climate Committee. He noted that severe weather caused by climate change is already driving up insurance bills. 
“Minnesotans are saying, ‘I can’t have my costs go up, but I do think it’s a priority to reduce carbon emissions,’” he said. “We’re spending billions of dollars right now on climate change through property insurance.”
Frentz said Democrats may use their new trifecta to advance battery storage projects, facilities that can harness surplus electricity and redeploy it when demand is high. 
And in New Hampshire, Democrats now hold majorities in the House and Senate, while the governor’s office will continue to be held by Republican Kelly Ayotte. State Rep. Peter Bixby, a Democrat who serves on the Environment and Agriculture Committee, said lawmakers are likely to propose bills to increase solar access, battery storage and energy efficiency incentives. The legislature will also consider a moratorium on data centers, he said. 
Air and water protections
Many lawmakers are also focused on air and water issues, from pollution to drought to flooding. 
“Voters were telling us that water is one of those top three to five priorities,” said Sundareshan, the Arizona lawmaker. “Water sustainability is really a concern for a state like Arizona.”
She said legislators will seek to enact a new groundwater management plan for the state’s rural areas, where some residents have seen their wells run dry, while strengthening groundwater protections for urban areas. 
In Georgia, Democrats will seek to expand cleanup efforts for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, the “forever chemicals” commonly known as PFAS. Bell, the state legislator, said he was hopeful that priority will earn bipartisan support.
“Whether you’re a Trumper or the president of Al Gore’s fan club, you don’t want to breathe dirty air or drink contaminated water,” he said. 
States sue feds over endangered species rollbacks

Bell also plans to advocate for an extended producer responsibility bill, an approach that forces manufacturers to take responsibility for the disposal and recycling of plastic packaging. 
Comitta, the Pennsylvania lawmaker, and Frentz, the Minnesota lawmaker, said state investments in pollution regulation programs have become increasingly important as President Donald Trump’s administration has rolled back federal rules for a variety of pollutants. 
“Pennsylvania has been that backstop protecting our citizens and we will continue and expand that work,” Comitta said. 
Minnesota lawmakers will likely consider a number of proposals to protect the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness, Frentz said, following congressional Republicans’ vote this year to rescind a mining ban in nearby national forest land. 
In Michigan, environmental advocates are pushing lawmakers to invest in water infrastructure. 
“We have a severe investment problem when it comes to all types of water infrastructure, whether it’s lead service line replacement, dam failure or old septic systems,” said Poulson, with the Michigan League of Conservation Voters. 
Meanwhile, New Hampshire lawmakers need to invest in dam repairs and flood protection, Bixby said. He’s also hoping to see bills supporting an extended producer responsibility program and PFAS cleanup. 
Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand, a Democrat, made water quality a major campaign issue, tying the state’s agricultural runoff and high levels of nitrates in drinking water to its fast-growing cancer rate. His proposals include investments in water quality monitors, manure management plans and restoring wetlands to harness their natural filtration benefits. 
McDowell, with the National Environmental Caucus, said voters are recognizing how environmental issues are linked to public health. 
“We’re not just saying this is bad for fish and wildlife, this is bad for people,” he said. “There’s very clear data and it’s scary. People are understanding the realities.”
Stateline reporter Alex Brown can be reached at abrown@stateline.org.
