The St. Mark Spartans and the St. ... Rea[...]
text:
The St. Mark’s boys soccer team poses for a group photo after earning a spot in the 2026 DIAA Division Two Boys Soccer State Championship game. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
The St. Mark’s Spartans defeated the Tower Hill Hillers, 3-1, and the St. Andrews Saints defeated the Sussex Academy Seahawks to advance to the 2026 DIAA Division Two Boys Soccer State Championship game. 
 
FREDERICA, Del. — The two teams competing in the 2026 DIAA Division Two Boys Soccer State Championship are set. The St. Mark Spartans and the St. Andrews Saints will meet for the first time this season on Friday, November 20, to crown a division two state champion.
St. Mark’s defeats Tower Hill, 3-1
Spartan junior Dylan Solomon spun the ball and placed it on the turf, standing closer to the midfield line than the goal. Solomon took a few steps back, raised his hands in the air and booted the ball toward the net where many of his teammates awaited the pass. Solomon’s kick went high into the evening sky. 
The pass started to descend as it neared the box and by the time senior Brady McMann leaped into the air the pass was already placed perfectly in the front of the net. McMann headed the ball past the Tower Hill goal keeper and to the back of the net for the first goal of the game.
St. Mark’s scored two more goals in the second half to defeat the Tower Hill Hillers, 3-0, in their semifinal matchup Wednesday night.
“I thought it was going over,” McMann said about his first goal. “And then I jump up and I realized I was up there and I just kind of flicked it back and it helped us.” 
McMann scored the Spartans first goal of the second half three minutes into the frame. McMann scored from the left side of the net on a left footed shot from just in front of the goalie box. The score was set up by a pass from senior Justin Baxley that passed through a pair of Tower Hill defenders, perfectly to the feet of McMann. Baxley scored the Spartans third goal in the 58th minute off a long assist from junior Nicholas Cirillo. 
Cirillo made the pass from about midfield with the initial intention of clearing the ball to protect a Tower Hill counterattack, but the ball floated toward the goal. The ball hung up in the air long enough for Baxley to dash toward the ball and beat the Hiller goalkeeper to the spot. Baxley tapped it in for a Spartan score. 
Cirillo’s impact on the game was felt as much on defense as it was with the long assist. Cirillo spent a majority of the game matched up with Tower Hill senior Chase McDonald and helped hold the Hillers’ leading goal scorer without a goal.
“Just stay in front of him,” Cirillo said about the defensive focus. “I know most his moves, I’ve played against him a lot so I just stayed in front of him, hope I can catch up with him.”
McDonald assisted on the Hillers goal in the 77th minute with a through ball to senior Sam Perny which Perny knocked in, to the right of the net. 
The Spartans are returning to the state championship game for the second season in a row and will try to earn their second straight state championship win. The last time the Spartans won back-to-back boys soccer championships was in 2000-2001. Those championships were a part of six straight won by the Spartans between 1996 and 2001.
St. Andrews defeats Sussex Academy, 1-0
St. Andrews and Sussex Academy during a brief pause in the action in their semifinals game, November 18. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
St. Andrews senior Gabriel Musa stood out of bounds right in front of the Sussex Academy bench, the ball in hand and ready to deliver the throw-in with just over 17 minutes remaining in regulation. The whistle sounded and Musa threw the ball in toward the left side of the box. The ball was headed by a fellow Saint and landed at the feet of junior Luke Robinson.
Robinson took his touch near the goal line on the left side of the net but faced strong resistance from a pair of Sussex Academy defenders. Robinson was forced to bring the ball out a bit, but as he did he created a passing lane to get the ball to junior Max Newman. The pass was deflected a bit, but landed right in front of Newman and he fired without wasting a second. His rocket shot flew to the back right of the net.
Newman’s goal in the 63rd minute was the game’s first and only goal helping the Saints beat the Seahawks, 1-0, Wednesday night.
“It means the world,” Newman said postgame about reaching the state championship. “We’re a family and I know that every single person here is good enough and I think we all know that we have what it takes.”
The Seahawks offense picked up their aggressiveness after the goal trying to find the equalizer before the game ended. Sussex Academy created a couple of strong scoring chances, but the Saints defense was able to keep those chances from hitting the back of the net. 
Senior goalkeeper Liam Wilson was integral to the late defense leaping into the air to corral a Sussex Academy corner kick near the net.
“I mean that was a great moment, but it was only possible because we put ourselves, 1-0, up and we fought hard as a team,” Wilson said. “That moment is a result of hours and hours of the practice we put in this week. Everyone on this team deserves to be on this field and so when I caught that ball … I was happy because I did it for the boys, I did it for the team and we’re on our way to the state [championship].”
The Saints held the majority of possession throughout the game earning multiple shot attempts in both halves. A couple of St. Andrews shot attempts went just high or just wide, while a bunch of others were turned away by Sussex Academy goalkeeper, freshman Benjamin Figueroa-Morales. Figueroa-Morales finished the game with over five saves.
St. Andrews is returning to the state championship game for the first time since 2024 and will play the St. Mark’s Spartans in the first ever championship game between the two. The Spartans beat the Saints in the semifinal round last season. St. Andrews last state championship win came in 1981. 
The 2026 DIAA Division Two Boys Soccer State Championship game will be played at DE Turf Sports Complex on Friday, November 20. The game will start at 5:00 p.m.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Commentary: SC’s mothers need more than congratulations
description: I was sitting in my OB-GYN’s waiting room after having my fourth baby when I overheard a conversation I still cannot shake. A new mother was on the phone, pleading with the receptionist to sign her return-to-work paperwork. The receptionist said she could not legally sign it. At two weeks postpartum, it was not safe. […]
text:
State law guarantees workers of state agencies, colleges and K-12 school districts up to six weeks of paid leave to care for their newborns. Many new moms in South Carolina get no paid leave. (Diane Macdonald /Stockbyte/Getty Image)I was sitting in my OB-GYN’s waiting room after having my fourth baby when I overheard a conversation I still cannot shake.
A new mother was on the phone, pleading with the receptionist to sign her return-to-work paperwork. The receptionist said she could not legally sign it. At two weeks postpartum, it was not safe.

To read more commentaries in this series, click here.

But the mother would not accept that answer. She needed to go back. She had to go back.
I understood her desperation. But I worked from home, with flexibility and help. Even then, I pumped during Zoom meetings, paced through phone calls with a baby strapped to my chest and scheduled therapy for perinatal depression and anxiety, all while working and caring for a newborn.
If it was hard for me, with every advantage, what must it have been like for the mother who had none?
I keep thinking about what she needed that day: time to recover and enough income to stay home with her baby. Instead, she was pleading for permission to return to work two weeks after giving birth.
SC law extends paid parental leave to temporary workers, ensures time off for stillbirths

South Carolina has begun to address the issue.
In 2022, legislators guaranteed eligible state employees six weeks of paid leave after giving birth. School district employees were included in that protection in 2023.
South Carolina also requires pregnancy-related workplace accommodations and protections for expressing breast milk at work.
We should celebrate these meaningful advances.
Unfortunately, the House’s effort to expand leave to 12 weeks did not pass the Senate.
And public-employee benefits do not guarantee paid leave to mothers who are employed in the private sector.
An estimated three out of four South Carolina workers do not have access to any employer-provided paid family leave, according to an analysis released in February by the National Partnership for Women & Families.
In South Carolina, paid family leave remains the exception.
One study found that paid leave reduced mothers’ postnatal depressive symptoms by nearly 30%. Research also links it with longer breastfeeding, fewer infant hospitalizations and greater employment stability, reports the Society for Research in Child Development.
SC House tries again with 12 weeks of paid parental leave for state workers

Access follows a stark economic divide.
Nationwide, only 5% of the lowest-paid workers have employer-provided family leave. Among low-income working mothers, 76% lose pay when they miss work to care for a sick child, twice the rate among mothers with higher incomes.
The women who can least afford to miss a paycheck are the least likely to receive paid time to care.
In my work alongside vulnerable families, I’ve seen how quickly the bills pile up after a baby is born.
Without paid leave, a mother may fall behind on rent or face having her electricity shut off while she is still recovering from childbirth. Returning to work brings other expenses, especially
childcare, and missing a shift to care for a sick baby can put her job at risk. It feels impossible to recover when you’re worried about keeping your family housed and fed.
The event meant to celebrate new life becomes the beginning of a crisis.
South Carolina’s maternal and infant health outcomes are devastating.
In 2024, we lost 441 babies before their first birthday; a shocking toll in a state with one of the nation’s highest infant mortality rates.
Based on data from 2020 to 2024, South Carolina ranked 40th out of 47 states with available data on maternal mortality.
In a separate review of pregnancy-related deaths in 2022–23, the state found that 86% were preventable.
As maternal mortality rises, SC report suggests ways of increasing health care access

Our mothers and babies are desperately in need of more support.
Scripture repeatedly uses the relationship between a mother and her child to describe the faithfulness of God.
In Isaiah, God asks, “Can a mother forget the baby at her breast?”
The image is familiar to anyone who has cared for a newborn who needs to be fed and held around the clock. Yet the caregiving that Scripture elevates as sacred is the same work our society expects mothers to squeeze around paid time-off balances, shift schedules, unanswered emails, and bills that cannot wait.
The image draws its power from a bond we instinctively understand: a newborn is utterly dependent, and a mother’s care is constant.
We celebrate babies. We congratulate new parents. We call children our greatest blessing.
Then we accept an economy that treats a newborn’s dependence as an inconvenience and caring for another human being as less valuable than almost any other work.
Caregiving has never been secondary work. It makes all other work possible. Every teacher, physician, mechanic and elected official was once an infant whose life depended on someone willing to feed, comfort, protect and love them.
On the Jericho Road, the Samaritan did not simply stop to bandage a stranger’s wounds. He paid for his continued care and promised to return for whatever more was owed. He tethered
himself to another person’s recovery.
Perhaps that is the deeper lesson: care is not only compassion in a moment of crisis. It is the willingness to remain connected; to recognize that healing requires time, security and someone
prepared to share the cost.
I think again of that mother in the obstetrician’s waiting room, pleading to return to work because she had no other choice.
And I wonder what it would mean for a community to tether itself to the well-being of both mother and child.

name: Nevada Current
title: Age-old real estate strategy raises fair housing, affordability concerns
description: The time-honored practice of allowing real estate agents to keep some listings private and determine which homes potential buyers see is facing pushback as the industry becomes more consolidated. Privately held listings, which are not advertised publicly, affect affordability, allow agents to engage in racial discrimination, and render home sale data used by[...]
text:
Pocket listings, also known as private listings or exclusive listings, are getting more popular as ownership of real estate companies is consolidated. Several states and both houses of Congress are now taking a look at the controversial practice. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)The time-honored practice of allowing real estate agents to keep some listings private and determine which homes potential buyers see is facing pushback as the industry becomes more consolidated. Privately held listings, which are not advertised publicly, affect affordability, allow agents to engage in racial discrimination, and render home sale data used by appraisers incomplete, say critics. 
Private listings, also known as pocket or exclusive listings, are properties that are kept off the Multiple Listing Service, the database that is the source for houses and condominiums listed for sale on platforms such as Zillow and Redfin. Instead of being available to the public, the listings are known only to select agents and their colleagues. 
Pocket listings are getting more popular as ownership of real estate companies is consolidated.
This year, Compass Inc. paid $1.6 billion to acquire Anywhere Real Estate, which owns  national brands such as Coldwell Banker, Century 21, Sotheby’s, ERA, and Better Homes and Gardens.
Critics contend the practice allows agents to ‘double-end’ more of their transactions – earning a commission from the buyer and seller by keeping the transaction within the brokerage. 
A Consumer Policy Center analysis found that 41% of Compass’s transactions in Washington, D.C. were double-ended deals. 
Compass contends multiple listing services are the problem. Last week, it filed 15 antitrust lawsuits against MLS in eight states. 
Flouting the rules?
The National Association of REALTORS®’ Clear Cooperation Policy, adopted in 2020, requires a broker to enter a listing in the MLS within one business day of advertising it publicly. 
The policy states “significant growth in the use of pocket listings and misuse of various limited exposure marketing tactics” are to the “disadvantage of homebuyers and sellers,” and “generally have been perceived as benefitting the listing firm more than the client.”
Nevada REALTORS®, the state association that has until now spoken for local groups, says the rules are flexible.
“MLS listing requirements vary based on the circumstances of the listing and the policies established by each individual MLS,” association consultant Julie Walburn of Red Rock Strategies said via email.
Real estate experts say association rules are no longer sufficient to protect consumers. Some are advocating for legislation. 
Nevada law does not regulate private listing networks. 
Three states – Wisconsin, Connecticut, and New York – have passed laws requiring that sellers sign notarized disclosures acknowledging they are aware that their home won’t be advertised publicly for sale.  
Washington’s law prohibits private listings except in exceptional cases to protect an individual’s health or safety. 
“Nevada can do the same,” says Geoff Lavell of The Brokerage in Las Vegas. “Privacy calls for withholding an address or photos. It does not require that only one company’s clients may buy the home.”
Nevada REALTORS®, which generally conducts policy campaigns for Nevada real estate associations, is wary of enacting laws regulating private listings.
“Nevada’s real estate licensing laws establish enforceable duties for licensed professionals, including disclosure obligations, reasonable skill and care, and accountability to the consumers they represent,” NVR CEO Tiffany Banks said via email. “Those protections remain in place regardless of how a property is marketed or whether an MLS policy is challenged.”
George Pickard, CEO of the Northern Nevada Regional Multiple Listing Service says the organization, which is owned by Sierra Nevada REALTORS®, has hired its own lobbyist for the first time and is hoping the Nevada Legislature will take up the issue when it meets in February. 
He says while not perfect, his organization is more in line with the Washington state legislation.
“I think the most important part is that there’s a conversation happening about the issues posed by private listing networks to consumers, and that the MLS perspective is represented in those conversations,” he said. 
Pickard says no lawmaker has yet agreed to sponsor the legislation. 
Las Vegas REALTORS® did not respond to a request for comment. 
Lavell contends that a buyer’s ability to find an unadvertised home requires them to “hire the ‘right’ brokerage. That is a fair housing problem, a pricing problem and a market power problem.”
Private sales, Lavell says, deny small brokerages the level playing field that the MLS provides. Agents tend to flee for the larger companies “because that’s where the action is.”
The lack of competition results in higher costs for buyers. Large firms, he says, are unlikely to offer the discounted commissions that are common among smaller brokers. 
Large firms, however, can afford to incentivize agents to keep deals within the brokerage. 
Compass, according to the Consumer Policy Center, has a new program that offers any Compass agent a 10% commission if the referral of a seller or buyer to another Compass agent results in a sale.
While agents benefit from the arrangements, sellers are often left holding the bag. Private listings tend to sell for less than properties advertised on the MLS, say experts. 
Research from Zillow found that homes sold without being advertised on the MLS reaped 1.5% less than comparable homes that were listed, amounting to about $4,975 lost to the seller per transaction. 
Pickard says NNRMLS research indicates the difference can be as much as 17%. 
Additionally, private listings reduce the pool of available homes to buyers.
“A buyer on a tight budget needs to see every home in her price range,” says Lavell. When homes are hidden in private listing networks, choices are limited to what’s available to the agent.  
The practice also tends to accelerate white flight – the migration of white people from ethnically diverse urban areas to suburbs – by steering buyers to properties in predominantly white neighborhoods.
Another study by Zillow found that homes in predominantly white neighborhoods were more than two times as likely to be in a private listing network as homes in urban areas.
“The growing acceptance of private listing networks by powerful real estate interests signals a shift in how the market operates, with selective access becoming a central feature rather than an exception,” Derrick Johnson, president of the NAACP, wrote in August.
Appraisers and lenders rely on public sales data to justify home prices. The dearth of data resulting from private listings – such as the number of days on the market and price changes – dilute that history, says Lavell. Prices, he says, “get harder to trust” as a result. 
“Public accountability suffers,” he adds. “Researchers, fair housing testers and reporters use open listing data to spot discrimination. They cannot audit what they cannot see.”
Both houses of Congress are now taking a look at the controversial practice.
“Nevada REALTORS® recognizes the significant value of the MLS in promoting transparency and broad market exposure,” says a statement from the association. “Equally important is ensuring that consumers receive accurate information, understand their options, and can make informed decisions when buying or selling a home.”
Proposed legislation, NVR says, “should be evaluated carefully, with a clear understanding of existing protections, demonstrated consumer needs, and potential unintended consequences, including potential antitrust implications.”

name: California
title: California told schools to make sure kids see a dentist. Then the state didn’t follow up
description: The state created the Kindergarten Oral Health Assessment in 2006 to ensure families connect with dentists, and to identify students’ dental needs and reveal roadblocks to care.
text:
In summary
The state created the Kindergarten Oral Health Assessment in 2006 to ensure families connect with dentists, and to identify students’ dental needs and reveal roadblocks to care.


A 20-year-old initiative requiring California’s youngest students be screened for cavities and untreated tooth decay before they enter public school is falling short.
The state created the Kindergarten Oral Health Assessment in 2006 to ensure families connect with dentists, and to identify students’ dental needs and reveal roadblocks to care. But the effort has been dogged by challenges, according to a new California State Auditor report that focused on six school districts and the California Department of Public Health.
Tooth decay is largely preventable, yet it’s the most common chronic disease in kids nationwide. About 61% of third grade students had tooth decay during the 2018-19 school year, according to a 2021 state report, and experts find that children’s oral health has declined further since the start of the pandemic. 
Untreated dental problems can lead to missed school days. The California Health Interview Survey from the UCLA Center for Health Policy Research found nearly 7% of children 5 and older who attend school missed class due to dental problems in 2025.
The review of the districts found they did not maintain reliable data about all aspects of the program and reported incorrect information to the state. The audited districts are Los Angeles Unified School District, Merced City School District, Milpitas Unified School District, Oakland Unified School District, San Luis Coastal Unified School District, and Woodland Joint Unified School District.
No state agency is assigned oversight of the kindergarten oral health program, the audit found, and neither the California Department of Education nor the Department of Public Health oversees program activities. The state health department, which is responsible for the state’s efforts to improve dental health, hasn’t verified the data reported by districts, the audit said, and isn’t using the data to measure the state’s progress in improving kids’ oral health. 
The department doesn’t publish annual analyses of the data on its website; the most recent program data available online, from the 2020-21 school year, is on the California Dental Association website. The audit also revealed that the program’s source of funding — a 2016 tax on tobacco products — is dwindling.
“We determined that unreliable data reported by districts and insufficient statewide oversight of the [Kindergarten Oral Health Assessment] program’s requirements threaten the goals of the program,” State Auditor Grant Parks wrote in a Nov. 5 report.
Department of Public Health spokesperson Kristine Tuzon, citing state education code, said the agency isn’t responsible for tracking kindergarten oral health program submissions or notifying county offices of education when districts don’t report data. Tuzon said the statute doesn’t give the health department authority to require districts and county offices to comply with the program’s data reporting mandate.
One method of reducing barriers to kids’ obtaining dental assessments, the audit found, is to conduct more on school campuses, as is done for state-required vision and hearing screenings. That solution, too, has had data-reporting challenges.
Esther Yepez is the associate director of wellness programs and oral health at The Los Angeles Trust for Children’s Health, which coordinated oral health screenings at L.A. Unified schools for five years. After completing the assessments, her team left the completed forms with the schools. But oftentimes, she said, schools didn’t enter those screenings in the district’s system, resulting in a mismatch between the number of students screened and the number reported to the state. It was unclear, she said, who at each school was responsible for compiling the data.
“It was frustrating,” Yepez said, “because we had information that the screenings had happened, but the schools didn’t have that data.”
L.A. Unified did not answer CalMatters’ questions regarding data accuracy in the kindergarten oral health program. In a response to the audit published as part of the report, Joel Cisneros, executive director of L.A. Unified’s student mental health and wellness services, said the district plans to train school staff on data-entry procedures and program documentation requirements and establish a standardized process for recording all returned forms and waivers.
Rotten teeth and huge pain
The American Academy of Pediatric Dentists recommends that children see a dentist when their first tooth appears, or no later than their first birthday. 
Early childhood dental visits are “extremely important,” said Dr. Francisco Ramos-Gomez, UCLA School of Dentistry’s pediatric dentistry chair and director of the UCLA Center for Children’s Oral Health. But he said many families don’t access care due to transportation challenges, language barriers and few providers treating low-income kids.
“If we start seeing these children by age 3 or 4,” he said, “they already come with rotten teeth, abscesses and huge pain.”
The kindergarten program directs school districts to notify families enrolling in public school for the first time in transitional kindergarten, kindergarten or first grade that they need to present proof of an oral health assessment. State law allows parents to waive the assessment requirement due to a financial burden, lack of access to a dental provider or nonconsent. 
The program mandates that districts submit specific data to their county education offices or a system designated by the state’s dental director, which since at least 2021 has been the System for California Oral Health Reporting. It directs the health department to periodically evaluate the kindergarten program requirements.
But the audit found none of the districts provided families with all required information regarding the assessment requirement. The six audited districts also lacked formalized procedures for following up with families that didn’t return assessment forms, the audit said, or that returned waivers indicating a barrier to obtaining an assessment.
The audit found that five districts reported data to the state system that was “significantly different” from their local data. For example, L.A. Unified, the state’s largest school district, for the 2024-25 school year incorrectly included all first-graders in its count of students subject to the program requirements, instead of only those who had not previously enrolled in kindergarten in the district, the audit said. The district also overreported the number of students who presented proof of the assessment, the audit said.
“The magnitude of the reporting errors by Los Angeles Unified School District alone,” Parks wrote, “skews any statewide analysis of the collective data.”
The audit recommended that the districts provide parents with all required program information and report complete and accurate data to the state system. In responses submitted to the state, the Milpitas and Oakland districts said they would implement the audit’s recommendations, while the L.A. and San Luis Coastal districts shared action plans to address some of the report’s findings. The Merced and Woodland districts did not provide a response.
‘Where is the money coming from?’
Funding for the oral health program is also declining, the audit found. 
The state public health department grants Proposition 56 funds – which are generated by a tax on tobacco products – to county health departments, and requires them to support oral health initiatives, including the kindergarten program. But revenue from the tax is plummeting, according to the audit, and starting next year the health department will no longer require counties receiving grant funds to support the kindergarten program.
Tuzon said the health department is assessing strategies to maintain and improve compliance with the program, given declining funding from tobacco taxes.
Despite the data issues, Eileen Espejo, senior managing director for health at Children Now, said policymakers should consider how to fund the kindergarten oral health program moving forward.
“Local health programs are going to have less capacity to do some of the work,” she said. “There needs to be that conversation of, ‘Where is the money coming from to help increase compliance?’”

name: California
title: Why students might lose access to financial aid because of ‘low-quality’ online courses
description: Colleges — and ultimately students — risk losing access to state and federal financial aid after a CalMatters investigation found online professors teaching over a dozen classes across multiple campuses.
text:
In summary
Colleges — and ultimately students — risk losing access to state and federal financial aid after a CalMatters investigation found online professors teaching over a dozen classes across multiple campuses.


After CalMatters reported last week on the heavy courseloads of some part-time faculty, California’s community college chancellor is reviewing whether online professors are providing a quality education to students. 
CalMatters found that some professors were teaching more than a dozen online classes at a time at several California community colleges, California State University and University of California campuses. In some cases, they were earning well over $340,000.
On Nov. 13, California Community Colleges Chancellor Sonya Christian sent an email to  campus chief executives in response to the CalMatters story. “We should not characterize faculty as doing something inappropriate simply because they teach at more than one college,” she wrote. “At the same time, some of the practices described in the article are deeply troubling and warrant further scrutiny.”
She said her office will examine whether colleges are complying with state, federal and accreditation standards, which require online instructors to interact with students regularly, such as by facilitating a group discussion or responding to student questions. 
Mac Powell, the president of the organization that accredits California’s community colleges, said he reached out to all the schools mentioned in the CalMatters story, asking about their compliance with those quality-education standards. “The issue of who teaches how much and when — that’s not what we’re most interested in,” he said. “We’re interested in the education that students get.”
The highest earner, ethnic studies professor Thien-Huong Ninh Villarreal, made nearly $800,000 in 2024 by teaching at nine community college districts, Cal State Sacramento and UC Berkeley, according to a CalMatters analysis using public payroll records, university course listings and hiring documents. She has a similar course load this fall, encompassing about 1,100 students across 30 classes. 
Some faculty and college leaders say it’s impossible to provide students a quality education when a professor has such a large courseload. But technically, teaching multiple classes or holding multiple jobs, by itself, doesn’t prove anything about the quality of the instruction. 
If online professors are not regularly interacting with their students in the ways the law and the accrediting body require, then schools — and ultimately students — could lose access to federal financial aid. 
A ‘personal perspective’ from the state chancellor
It’s no secret that part-time faculty, or adjuncts, at California’s colleges and universities often work multiple jobs. By law, part-time faculty in the community college system can teach only about three classes per district each semester. They are paid less than full-time faculty and have fewer, if any, benefits. 
“I bring a personal perspective to this discussion,” wrote Christian. “When I first graduated, I taught at three California community colleges. I didn’t own a car, so I rode the RTD bus from campus to campus to teach in person, piecing together assignments and barely making rent. I remember those days well. I understand firsthand why adjunct faculty teach at multiple institutions. For many, it is an economic necessity.”
Part-time faculty outnumber full-time faculty at every one of the state’s community college districts, sometimes by more than 5-to-1, but the total number of adjuncts statewide is unknown because professors who teach at multiple campuses are often counted repeatedly in the data. 
In her email to college leaders, Christian acknowledged that there’s an “absence of a systematic way” to track faculty who teach at multiple campuses or across the community college, Cal State and UC systems. She said her team is looking into how college districts handle faculty with multiple jobs and what information about outside work faculty disclose. “The objective is to determine whether additional guidance, improved data sharing, or a common approach would strengthen institutional oversight.”
To find instructors who teach at multiple campuses, CalMatters used public payroll records gathered by Transparent California, a nonprofit organization advocating for limited government. CalMatters looked only at professors who taught at  five or more community college districts, Cal State or UC campuses in 2024, the most recent data available. 
Of the 72 professors who taught at five or more districts or universities, the median pay was about $190,000, though a few instructors made much more. CalMatters found 10 professors who made more than $343,000, which was the median salary of a community college president or chancellor in the same year. Most of the highest earners had full-time jobs along with numerous part-time gigs. Ninh Villarreal currently has at least two full-time tenured community college positions, along with other adjunct roles elsewhere. 
Christian said these 72 professors are a “small group” compared with the tens of thousands of faculty employed by the state’s public higher education systems, and the highest earners “an even smaller one.”
Are online professors interacting with students enough?
Because the federal and state governments dole out billions of dollars in financial aid to students, they regulate the kinds of courses and institutions where students can qualify for aid, and online courses in particular have undergone increased scrutiny in recent years. 
The general rule that accreditors and state and federal lawmakers all share is that online professors need to interact with their students regularly. Research shows students are more likely to succeed when they interact with their professors.
Many online courses are asynchronous, meaning that the lectures are prerecorded and students can listen at any time. In these courses, and in many in-person ones, quizzes and tests are often graded automatically by computers. 
Christian said that “prerecorded lectures, automated quizzes, and other instructional technologies” can be valuable in online classes, but professors must do more than that to meet the legal requirements. “Low-quality instruction is unacceptable, and we will not tolerate practices that compromise the education our students deserve.”
After the story was published here, online professors who taught at fewer than five districts or colleges shared their perspectives.  
William Mead is a full-time lecturer in design and web development at UC Davis who also teaches part-time at two community college districts. He said his online courses are prerecorded but that doesn’t mean he is disengaged — quite the opposite. “My lectures take many hours to produce before a term begins,” he wrote in an email. “That front-loaded work is what frees me, during the semester, to focus on what matters most: individual feedback on student work and time with students. I hold a regular weekly office hour plus three additional appointment blocks each week (one morning, one afternoon, one evening) so that working students can meet with me on Zoom when it fits their lives.”
Jonathan Horn, who teaches one asynchronous online journalism course at San Diego Mesa College, said he writes his students “paragraphs and paragraphs of feedback on their assignments, sometimes worrying if it’s too much.” He said it would be impossible to provide the same level of feedback for 30 or 50 classes.

name: California
title: Los Angeles elected more democratic socialists, but don’t expect a revolution at City Hall
description: All three elected citywide offices at Los Angeles City Hall will be occupied by democratic socialists. But voters may expect more than the candidates actually promised.
text:
As Nithya Raman prepares to become the first mayor of Los Angeles affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America, that connection reveals a lot about the city electorate and surprisingly little about what we can expect from her.
In terms of the electorate, the voting base that has defined Los Angeles for generations is officially yesterday’s news. The coalitions of Jewish and Black voters that elected Tom Bradley, or Latinos and conservatives that elected Richard Riordan, or San Fernando Valley moderates and Black liberals that favored James Hahn are all passe now. They have been supplanted by an energized base of young people, many of them renters, who cross demographic lines but share a demand for something new.
The strength of that coalition is evidenced not just by Raman’s solid win over incumbent Mayor Karen Bass. It shows up in an astonishing fact: With this year’s elections, every one of Los Angeles’ three citywide elected officials is a democratic socialist. Marissa Roy, a 34-year-old former California deputy attorney general, was this month elected city attorney, after City Controller Kenneth Mejia’s successful reelection bid in June.
This, in a city where the publisher of the Los Angeles Times once could boast of never having met a union leader and where California’s Republican politics once were anchored.
No more.
Surely, then, a city so thoroughly in thrall of socialist officeholders must be perched on the edge of something truly revolutionary. 
Not so much. Raman’s victory put a democratic socialist in office, but she comes to her post so at the edge of that movement that it’s difficult to tell how much of its program she will implement. 
She is not a West Coast replica of New York’s Zohran Mamdani, as was often observed during the campaign. She does not propose rent freezes or free public transit or city-owned grocery stores or a pied-à-terre tax on second homes — the pillars of Mamdani’s New York platform. 
Raman’s ambitions are far less sweeping. She talks like the urban planner she is, trilling over the nuts and bolts of government, promising accountability and transparency. She vows to patch potholes and fix streetlights. She supported the city’s so-called “mansion tax” but also believes it needs amending to correct some of the downward pressure it has put on new housing construction.
All of that is easy to support, but there’s nothing about a program of pothole filling and modest reform that suggests the unveiling of a radical, socialist agenda. With those positions, Raman sounds more like former Mayor Eric Garcetti than a zealous activist.
Even the goal she most seeks — a significant uptick in the city’s capacity to build new housing — is one she wants to pursue, not through a socialist program of government intervention, but by decreasing regulation and clearing the way for the market to do its work. She promises to create a city where “it takes weeks, not years, to get permission to build housing during a housing shortage.” That’s under the banner of eliminating “red tape” to “build faster.” 
Not exactly Trotsky.
Raman’s program of back-to-basics tinkering, modest social reforms and reduced government intervention may satisfy the electorate for now. They signal a gentle shift in emphasis away from Bass, and Raman herself represents the emergence of a younger generation: She is 45 and replaces the 73-year-old Bass. 
But the electorate’s historic move to the left may test even Raman’s socialism-lite, underscored by the uneasy relationship the mayor-elect has with the Democratic Socialists of America. The Los Angeles chapter endorsed her in September, but the organization’s national committee came within one vote of rescinding that endorsement just days before the election because it questioned whether Raman was, well, socialist enough.
One test: Will Raman deliver an overhaul of the Los Angeles Police Department, starting with the removal of its chief, as many of her allies demand? Or will she opt for stability in the run-up to the 2028 Olympics, as many of her more moderate supporters would like to see?
That’s not to say that a more ambitious, liberal agenda is out of reach for Raman or her new colleagues in city leadership. 
Mejia is the young, activist city controller who was elected in 2022 and a rare City Hall incumbent to support Raman’s mayoral bid. Her council colleagues, for varying reasons, sided with Bass — including the three other democratic socialists. As controller, Mejia has occasionally clashed with Bass, releasing audits that questioned some of her programs and warned that the city’s spending could force “wrenching choices” down the line.
As that history suggests, a controller can be an irritating foe — or a powerful ally — and Mejia will welcome the changing of the guard under Mayor-elect Raman.
Roy, meanwhile, won her first election to city office this fall and brings a background and commitment to consumer protection to the city attorney job. She ran as a “champion of justice,” determined to thwart the Trump administration and to defend city residents who are “victimized by businesses engaging in unlawful, unfair, or deceptive conduct.” Her priorities fall neatly alongside those of Raman.
Altogether, the DSA-supported city leadership has an unmistakable mandate to pursue novel programs that make the city more affordable, more protective of residents and more aggressive in defiance of federal authority, particularly on immigration.
The bigger question may be whether Raman and her colleagues can deliver as much as their electorate may demand. As renters and young people look to their government for stronger cost-of-living solutions and new ideas, the energy unleashed by this month’s victories place Raman, Mejia and Roy in a position to lead — or to be led.

name: California
title: California Dems just super-sized their statehouse supermajority. What’s next for a fractured GOP?
description: Republican lawmakers in California are becoming an endangered species. The already-sparse caucus lost about a third of its seats in this month’s election. Former lawmakers and political scientists say the shrinking opposition means fewer checks on Democrats’ power.
text:
In summary
Republican lawmakers in California are becoming an endangered species. The already-sparse caucus lost about a third of its seats in this month’s election. Former lawmakers and political scientists say the shrinking opposition means fewer checks on Democrats’ power.


In the San Joaquin Valley, a 28 year-old Democrat with a thin campaign resume unseated the Republican party Assembly leader. 
In the Palm Springs area, a Democrat making her first run at elected office won decisively over a well-financed, two-term Republican incumbent.  
And in once-reliably Republican Orange County, a candidate with an “enthusiastic” recommendation from the Democratic Socialists of America leads in a race that still hasn’t been called, while nearby, the Democratic owner of a DEI consulting business beat out the Vietnamese Republican incumbent who represents Little Saigon, a traditional GOP stronghold. 
This month’s blue tsunami swept away nine of the Republican Party’s 29 seats in the 120-member state Legislature. The magnitude of the upset surprised statehouse leaders, but most agree that divisions within the GOP didn’t help. 
Democrats won every statewide office, right down to the Board of Equalization, continuing a trend that began in 2010, when Gov. Jerry Brown replaced the termed-out Arnold Schwarzenegger. In California and across the country, voters turned out to voice disapproval with the Trump presidency, and to flood Congress with Democrats to counter his power.   
For the next two years at least, Republicans will have to represent their constituents while facing the largest Democratic supermajority in 150 years. And Californians, meanwhile, will have to contend with a Democratic body that has fewer checks on its power.
Why so many GOP losses?
Experts told CalMatters they believe most of the losses stemmed from the “nationalization” of the down-ballot races.
“It was about voters sending Republicans a message,” said GOP strategist Duane Dichiara, whose candidates had mixed results in the election.
He said with the majority of media focusing on Republicans in the federal government, it’s difficult for state-level Republicans to differentiate themselves.
Eric McGhee of the Public Policy Institute of California agreed. Across the country, he said, “voters are responding more to how they’re feeling about the broad parties nationally, and not to how the parties are delivering locally,” he said. 
In competitive districts, Democrats won resoundingly. Republicans survived mostly in traditional strongholds.
Hard for a fractured party to win
And although nationalization was a factor, legislative leaders agreed that the fracturing of the state Republican Party in recent years contributed to their woes. 
A few months after California GOP chair Corrin Rankin took the helm in March 2025, Republican leaders in the Assembly and Senate signaled their displeasure with her leadership and broke a longstanding joint fundraising agreement with the party. In a letter, they asked lobbyists to donate to a separate super PAC, the Legislative Action PAC, administered by Republican political strategists instead of the party. 
Further dividing the conservatives is San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, which also courted tens of thousands of small-donor dollars that might otherwise have contributed to the party. 
“The California Republican Party has been a complete dumpster fire for a long time now,” said DeMaio. 
The state party was barely a factor in the legislative races, if it was there at all. Between January and mid-October, campaign filings show it spent less than half of what Legislative Action PAC did.
“We cannot afford to be fractured by rogue organizations, grifters, and selfish commentators,” CA GOP leader Rankin wrote in a statement lamenting the losses on social media. “Republicans have too little power in California to be divided and too little resources to be inefficient.”
Rankin announced last week that she would not seek reelection after her term is up in February. Tony Strickland, a Huntington Beach Republican who lost his bid for re-election to the state Senate, is favored among several candidates to succeed her. 
How will fewer Republicans affect lawmaking?
Most Republicans agree they have little or no power in the Capitol. 
The new delegation would need 15 more members in the Assembly and six more in the Senate to be able to block certain tax and urgency measures, dozens more to reach the majority needed to pass policy unpopular with Democrats. 
The additional losses mean Republicans are even more likely to be locked out of the rooms where significant decisions are being made, such as the call to not move forward with a wildfire liability package at the end of the recent legislative session. 
“It’s no different than when we were 20 (assemblymembers)” said DeMaio. “We have no involvement, no leverage when it comes to the traditional legislative process.”
Even so, DeMaio and several other Republicans try to counter Democrats’ power by calling them out on social media, on the Capitol floor, and in press conferences around Sacramento. Occasionally, they can get a faction of Democrats to break off with them  — as they did in several successful efforts to increase penalties for sex crimes against minors. 
Less committee representation
But Republicans won’t have much of a bully pulpit in the Legislature’s standing committees, where policy proposals are scrutinized. 
Assemblymember Tom Lackey, a Republican from Palmdale, speaks during a press conference against Gov. Gavin Newsom’s call for a special session to regulate gasoline prices in the state, at the state Capitol, on Sept. 18, 2024. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters
Former Republican Assemblymember Tom Lackey served on the public safety committee for his entire 12 years in the Legislature. Lackey, a former California Highway Patrol officer from Palmdale, said he was painted as “hateful” for pushing back on Democratic proposals in committee. 
“The left perspective focuses so much on rehabilitation that it dismisses the impact to victims,” he said. “Victims become ghosts.”
Now, with even fewer Republicans on the committee, he said Democrats won’t have to consider the victim’s perspective as often. 
Public safety committee chair Nick Schultz, a Burbank Democrat, said Lackey was a “value-add” to the committee, but stressed that moderate Democrats and progressives can diverge widely on the subject of public safety, and that lawmakers will continue to look at all sides of an issue. 
It’s unclear how the 12 Republicans in the Assembly will be distributed across its 32 standing committees, which have all traditionally had a Republican vice chair. Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas’s spokesperson Nick Miller declined to discuss the topic.
“Voters just elected the largest and most diverse Assembly Democratic Caucus in California history, and under Speaker Rivas’ leadership, it will deliver,” he said in a text. 
Less incentive to get things done?
Several political scientists say the increasing Democratic supermajority means there may be less incentive for Democrats to fix pressing issues.  
“Competition keeps politicians honest,” said Eric Schickler, co-director of UC Berkeley’s Institute for Governmental Studies. “It pressures them to deliver.”
“To the extent that you don’t face a viable opposition party in California, the pressure on politicians to actually solve big, complicated problems is reduced somewhat.”
Thad Kousser, a political science professor at UC San Diego, says politicians are “hard-wired” to scrutinize policy proposals by the other party, but face huge pressure not to vote against their party colleagues. 
“That brings up this concern that committees, and lawmakers, when they’re voting on the floor, might not screen out bad policies as aggressively as they should,” he said.
‘Blindly following the president’
While he agrees it would be good to have more of an opposition party, Napa state Sen. Christopher Cabaldon said Republicans’ refusal to acknowledge the impact of ICE raids and federal healthcare cuts means they are naturally left out of conversations around governing. 
“Republicans haven’t been doing the job of the opposition party, and instead have been more or less blindly following the president,” he said. 
Some California Republicans have pushed back against ICE tactics – last year six Republican legislators wrote to President Trump asking him to focus on targeting violent criminals, not everyday people. 
Cabaldon pointed to Roseville Sen. Roger Niello as an example of a Republican invested in bipartisanship. The two often work closely together on the budget committees, where legislators oversee oft-overlooked state agencies.
State Sen. Roger Niello holds a news conference in the rotunda of the state Capitol in Sacramento on March 13, 2025. Niello requested more transparency from Gov. Newsom as to why they need $3.5 billion to keep Medi-Cal solvent. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters
“Even when we’re not agreeing, we’re both taking seriously the fact that we’re running the government here, and the public deserves to get answers,” he said.
Niello barely held onto his seat this year. Democratic challenger Sean Frame lost to the longtime legislator from the Sacramento area by about 5,000 votes. 
Republicans plot their path forward
Given the fundraising success of DeMaio’s Reform California operation, some in the party see him as the captain they have, for better or worse, to steer the GOP ship back on course. It’s a role he doesn’t necessarily want, he said. 
“The only reason why we’ve had to step into the void is because the California Republican Party has been completely inept; it’s been AWOL,” he said.  
Still, DeMaio has a plan. Unwind the alternative fundraising efforts, restructure party leadership, and create a “shadow caucus” of Republican candidates who get to know constituents and weigh in on state policy long before they’re voted on at the polls. 
“We have to act like a larger opposition party, and that’s how we’re going to grow our ranks,” he said.
Niello, who became Senate Republican leader on Nov. 5, is more circumspect. 
When the session reconvenes, he said, “the first thing is looking at 2028.”  He added the focus will be on quality candidates and positioning their image in contrast with Democrats.  
However, with the nationalization of party politics, it might be an uphill battle. 
The question, UC Berkeley political science professor Paul Pierson says, might boil down to how Republicans plot their post-Trump future. 
“I think a lot is going to depend upon how the Republican Party nationally evolves,” he said.

name: Nevada Current
title: Commentary: 4 takeaways from an editor’s retirement
description: As I announced last month, tomorrow is my last day as editor of the Nevada Current.  After  a couple stabs at drafts and much dithering, I had concluded a farewell column is exactly the sort of thing I would execute poorly, and had decided not to write one. Alas, the Nevada Current staff, to whom […]
text:
Just a couple old guys waiting for the light to change. (Photo: Hugh Jackson/Nevada Current)As I announced last month, tomorrow is my last day as editor of the Nevada Current. 
After  a couple stabs at drafts and much dithering, I had concluded a farewell column is exactly the sort of thing I would execute poorly, and had decided not to write one. Alas, the Nevada Current staff, to whom I am deeply indebted and of whom I’ve grown very fond, more or less ordered me (not unprecedented) to write one whether I wanted to or not. 
Being so appalled at my aforementioned drafts, alternating as they did between dreadfully sentimental and even more dreadfully ponderous, but bound to do as told one last time, I resorted to a journalism trope: the “here are X takeaways” listicle, the X in this case being four. 
Here they are:
Surprise. I had never imagined that I would someday “announce” my retirement. Before I was hired to edit the Current in 2018, I’d spent most of the previous 20 years blogging (blogs used to be a thing) and freelance writing/editing, doing some TV work, pulling a stint with a D.C.-based policy advocacy organization, and teaching college intro history courses. That sort of stuff. None of it amounted to a conventional full-time job that would warrant a retirement announcement. Over that time I never really gave much thought to retiring, except for a little while at one point thinking maybe I already was semi-retired ha ha. I guess I just assumed that eventually I’d work less, and then a little less than that, and then stop.
Editor’s note: I’m retiring. April’s going to take over

So actually announcing my retirement, publicly no less, and then having people congratulate me and wish me well  and say they were going to miss me wasn’t something that had crossed my mind when making and timing my decision. And it’s been great! Thank you. You’re too kind.
Irony. If there’s one angle, one “take” I’ve written more than any other over the last 30 years or so, it has been chronicling the Democrats’ go-to move: Planting their tails between their legs, surrendering to the right’s economic narratives, sucking up to the party’s corporate wing and soaking in polite incrementalism. It’s been as if they didn’t want to stop the polarization of wealth by which the rich and corporate gobble up greater shares of prosperity while everybody else’s share dwindles. Democrats, it seemed, just wanted to let that happen a little more slowly than Republicans did.
Now Democrats have had historically big election wins, and the public is screaming for life to be more affordable — a desire which necessarily involves a more fair and equitable distribution of prosperity. And a whole lot of Democrats, steeped in Clintonism basically, will “fight,” as they’re fond of saying, to slow that roll.
Hammering on Democrats who think they have to be like that has been my jam. And now I’m retiring. Ironic, right? 
On the bright side (where I’m always looking), the Overton window on wealth distribution policies has opened up a lot in the 30 years since Bill Clinton, who rarely met a right-wing economic narrative he didn’t want to capitulate to, declared the era of big government over. Now there is no shortage of people making the case for more progressive economic policies.
And while some Democratic politicians, especially the traditional mainstream Nevada variety, may be comfortable playing footsie with oligarchs and apologizing for virtually any and every industry that flashes them a campaign contribution-accompanied smile, it sort of looks like the public is not. One case in point: 66% of U.S. adults favor Medicare for All. That’s interesting, seeing as how politicians tend to be followers, not leaders.
Luck. Through no effort or worthiness of my own, I was born an upper middle class white protestant male in the U.S. in 1961 — in other words, on second base, maybe third. Contacts I made in college helped me land my first job at a newspaper. I’ve never made a lot of money, but I’ve never gone hungry.
And though it’s been iffy at times, I got to carve out a career that has consisted mostly of working on what I wanted to work on and writing what I wanted to write. My spouse is a lot smarter than I am (which of course I’ve always thought reflects very well on me), and her qualities include (but are not limited to) powerfully sensible judgment, as well as a sense of empathy that I can sometimes lack. She has saved me from making stupid mistakes countless times. My mother (bless her), a successful businesswoman of integrity and strength and a force of nature, told me about 25 years ago she didn’t understand how I could have political views so different from hers. I reminded her that she hammered into me the importance of thinking for myself. (And she liked the TV show.)
I’ve been very fortunate.
Finally, the most important thing you, as Nevada Current readers, need to know. I learned a lot more from the Nevada Current staff — Michael, Jen, Dana, and April  — than they learned from me. As I said, I’ve been fortunate, and I’m grateful.
Their interests and areas of expertise, not mine, are and have been the Current’s heart and soul. To reiterate what I wrote in October when we announced that I would be retiring and the amazing April would be taking over, I’m excited to see what the Current does and where it goes over the next few months and beyond.

name: Nevada Current
title: Rosen introduces bill to limit ICE operations at airports
description: Federal immigration enforcement operations have played out at airports across the nation this year, including in Las Vegas and Reno, and Nevada Democratic U.S. Sen. Jacky Rosen is seeking to stop federal agents from arresting immigrants without criminal records at or near airports. The Travel Without Fear Act — introduced by Rosen and California Sen. […]
text:
Monday afternoon security lines were short at Harry Reid International Airport on March 23, 2026. (Photo: Hugh Jackson/Nevada Current)Federal immigration enforcement operations have played out at airports across the nation this year, including in Las Vegas and Reno, and Nevada Democratic U.S. Sen. Jacky Rosen is seeking to stop federal agents from arresting immigrants without criminal records at or near airports.
The Travel Without Fear Act — introduced by Rosen and California Sen. Alex Padilla on Wednesday — would prevent U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) from carrying out civil enforcement operations at airports without judicial warrants. 
The bill would also ban information-sharing between ICE and the Transportation Security Administration for civil immigration enforcement unless there’s a judicial warrant for a specific target. 
Rosen said the bill was spurred by a July incident involving masked ICE officers trying to violently arrest an elderly man in Las Vegas’ Harry Reid International Airport.
In July, a video of masked and plain-clothed ICE officers attempting to violently arrest an elderly man at Reid airport was widely shared across social media. 
It was only later that the public learned the masked men were ICE agents, and that the target of the immigration operation had no outstanding criminal warrants, said Rosen.
“In the moment, no one knew what’s going on. The man himself is seen in the video asking what’s going on. He’s yelling for help. Bystanders got involved because no one had any idea of what was going on, and when bystanders began to record the incident, the undercover ICE officers, well, they quickly left,” Rosen said in a press call Wednesday announcing the bill. 
A month later, a pregnant woman was arrested by immigration officers at Reid Airport as she attempted to fly to Connecticut after a vacation.
“It’s clear that ICE needs to be reined in,” Rosen said. 
The widely publicized incidents spurred Rosen to lead a Senate letter condemning immigration enforcement activity at airports and calling on Trump administration officials to disclose TSA cooperation with ICE at airports.
In addition to requiring ICE agents to have a judge-issued warrant before arresting someone at an airport, the bill would also prohibit ICE from accessing passenger data without a warrant, require ICE to notify airports and airlines in advance of an enforcement action and require updates to online databases that track detainees’ locations within six hours of their change in custody.
Rosen stressed that warrantless arrests harm civil rights and tourism.
“Their actions are instilling fear in entire communities, and when they conduct violent arrests in our airports, they’re hurting states like Nevada even more by discouraging the public from traveling at a time when tourism is already down,” Rosen said. 
“International travelers are afraid that they’re going to be profiled, knocked down, and just taken away somewhere,” Rosen said.
It’s unclear how many immigrants without criminal records have been arrested at Nevada’s airports, Rosen said.
“We’ve seen and heard other things are going on at the airport, not only in Las Vegas but up north in Reno,” Rosen said. 
However, ICE arrests of immigrants without criminal records have skyrocketed in Nevada, according to data collected from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.
While the bill focuses on limiting immigration enforcement at airports, Rosen said she believes other sensitive locations should be protected from ICE enforcement, including schools, churches, and hospitals. 
“In the meantime, I believe that stopping these broad ICE operations in airports is an important place to start and a needed action to protect our economy and, more importantly, our communities,” Rosen said.
The bill is unlikely to move forward in the Republican-controlled Congress. Rosen said she plans to reintroduce the bill whenDemocrats will control Congress after the first of the year.Still, the bill would still need four Republican Senators to vote with Democrats to break a filibuster. 
“My plan is to continue to put everything we can up for vote after vote. And I challenge my Republican colleagues to veto it. I challenge the president to veto it then take those receipts to the next election because people are watching,” Rosen said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Psychedelic mental healthcare for veterans wins bipartisan backing from US House panel
description: Federal regulators could be on the cusp of approving psychedelic-assisted mental health treatment for veterans.
text:
WASHINGTON — Federal regulators could be on the cusp of approving psychedelic-assisted mental health treatment for veterans, but lawmakers asked tough questions Wednesday of Trump administration officials over whether the Department of Veterans Affairs can meet patients’ needs, and if federal law enforcement and health agencies are on the same page.
Just over 2 million veterans suffer with treatment-resistant depression, and approximately 180,000 of them would likely meet the criteria for treatment with psychedelic compounds, including MDMA, psilocybin, LSD, DMT and ibogaine, according to the Veterans Health Administration.
Members of the House Committee on Veterans Affairs Subcommittee on Health grilled officials for roughly two and a half hours during an afternoon hearing contemplating how the VA should implement the labor-intensive treatments if given the green light by the Food and Drug Administration.
If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. You are not alone. Call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. Support is free, confidential, and available 24/7.
Nearly 6,500 veterans died by suicide in 2024, according to the latest Veterans Affairs Suicide Prevention Annual Report, published in September.
“Something needs to change,” said subcommittee chair Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, who said despite prevention efforts, the numbers have remained “stubbornly stagnant.”
“When I came to Congress in 2021, I didn’t think I’d be sitting here today advocating for these emerging breakthrough therapies, but in meeting with veterans from all walks of life, I have found the effectiveness of these treatments and am willing to advance it as potential hope,” said Miller-Meeks, who recently lost her bid for reelection.
Miller-Meeks, an Army veteran and ophthalmologist, cited randomized clinical trials for MDMA-assisted therapies that commenced this year at VA facilities in Rhode Island and Connecticut, both of which resulted from funding allocated in 2024. 
Miller-Meeks also praised President Donald Trump’s April executive order directing the FDA to work with other agencies, including the VA, the Drug Enforcement Administration, and the Department of Health and Human Services to remove barriers, like drug enforcement classification, that complicate testing the treatments.
The possibility of new treatments was met with optimism on both sides of the aisle.
The subcommittee’s ranking member Rep. Julia Brownley, D-Calif., said the clinical trials are “extremely welcome news and will change lives for the better.”
“At the same time, we must not lose sight of the fact that this treatment, much like the ones already in use today, will not be a panacea for everyone,” she said. “Even as VA works to build its capacity to provide access to these drugs, we must continue to maintain and strengthen the continuum of mental healthcare at VA.” 
Staff reductions present problem
During questioning Brownley expressed concern about VA’s ability to implement the new treatments in the wake of staff reductions under the Trump administration, if the FDA moves forward.
“Will VA be hiring additional workforce to meet the expected demand for these treatments and ensure existing workforce is not overtaxed if these treatments are approved in the next several months?” Brownley asked.  
Andrew Gradison, a Veterans Health Administration senior adviser who testified, acknowledged the treatments are “extremely labor intensive” and that along with preparation protocols, “dosing sessions alone can last six to eight hours.”
“We’ve conducted extensive analysis of the amount of staff time that goes into these treatments,” Gradison said. “We want to make sure that all of our initial implementation sites have the resources they need, not to have a detrimental impact on mental health access at large.”
Gradison told the panel that VA has identified 10 initial sites where treatment could occur, but would not publicly divulge every location. He said he would provide a list to all committee members within 30 days.
Rep. Herb Conaway, D-N.J., said “most of them are on the coast.”
“I see a lot in California. I see New Haven, Connecticut. I don’t see any in the Southeast. New York is on this list as well. Do you believe that you have, even with those that you’ve established as possibly being ready, that you’re sufficiently covering the country?” Conaway, a medical doctor, asked.
Dr. Ilse Wiechers, deputy assistant under secretary for health for patient care services with VA’s Veterans Health Administration, told Conaway,  “The reason you see the selected sites that you do is because those are the sites that we have evaluated to be the most likely to be successful in implementing this early on. 
“We are going to use that experience from those experienced sites,” she added.
Working with DEA
All the drugs under review remain categorized as Schedule I substances by federal law enforcement. 
Michigan Republican Rep. Jack Bergman, a retired U.S. Marine Corps lieutenant general, asked the expert panel, “What should VA be working out with DEA now, and where do you expect control substance requirements to cause the most delay?”
Marion Coe, director of clinical development and postmarketing surveillance at the healthcare industry consulting firm Pinney Associates, Inc., said the research involving these chemical compounds, particularly being able to legally store them, is a “complicated process.”
“VA and DEA ideally would work together to reduce these bureaucratic hurdles to make research easier,” she said. “This will all be made simpler after approval and rescheduling of these drugs.”
This story was first published Nov. 18, 2026 by States Newsroom.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah lawmakers introduce bills expanding where high-level nuclear waste is allowed
description: The U.S. Department of Energy hasn’t released its final decision on sites for “nuclear lifecycle innovation campuses,” but Utah, one of the finalists, is preparing its regulatory framework with a set of bills proposed for next legislative session. Fountain Green Republican Sen. Derrin Owens is sponsoring a bill on regional nuclear lifecycle campuses. The dra[...]
text:
The Capitol in Salt Lake City is pictured on the final night of the legislative session, Friday, March 6, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The U.S. Department of Energy hasn’t released its final decision on sites for “nuclear lifecycle innovation campuses,” but Utah, one of the finalists, is preparing its regulatory framework with a set of bills proposed for next legislative session.
Fountain Green Republican Sen. Derrin Owens is sponsoring a bill on regional nuclear lifecycle campuses. The draft isn’t publicly available yet, but Owens said it will lay out the state’s involvement in safety practices for the site proposed in Tooele County.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Utah currently has strict regulations on high-level spent nuclear fuel waste storage, but has made exceptions for test reactors in state facilities, like the one at the San Rafael Energy Lab. If the bill becomes law, state restrictions on high-level nuclear waste won’t apply to the designated campus zone.
“Before the U.S. Department of Energy can commit to Utah, state law needs to be adjusted and cleared, and limited exceptions for that type of handling of fuel needs to be allowed, or made legal in the state,” Owens told the Public Utilities, Energy and Technology Interim Committee on Wednesday.
Utah may be home to a nuclear innovation campus, Department of Energy announced

Shipments of the material would also need to be allowed, Owens said. But that would need both federal and state legislation.
That exception may also be extended to commercial nuclear reactors under another bill sponsored by Richfield Republican Rep. Carl Albrecht. That draft would also update the high-level waste law in Utah, providing exceptions for nuclear power reactors located in the state and licensed by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, including commercial plants, which currently aren’t allowed to store high-level waste on site.
Meanwhile, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright acknowledged earlier this month that before a nuclear lifecycle campus could take shape, Congress would need to approve a new nuclear waste disposal site.
What would Utah’s campus allow
Owens’ bill would also list activities allowed within the nuclear innovation campus, which, he said, would include advanced nuclear reactors, nuclear fuel fabrication and enrichment, recycling and reprocessing of used nuclear fuel, storage and disposal of nuclear material, and medical and industrial isotope production, as well as research, manufacturing, workforce training, and the needed infrastructure to support all of those activities.
The campus impact could be comparable to 10 times that of Kennecott’s copper mine, “if you did some weird math,” Owens told the committee. “So we are approaching this strategically and carefully and slowly and trying to get it right.”
Utah leaders, including Gov. Spencer Cox, have made a big push to become one of the Department of Energy’s choices for the campuses, saying in a June statement the state’s nuclear efforts would strengthen national security and help secure energy independence for the country.
However, environmentalists from the nonprofit Heal Utah said in a news release in August that the proposal would position the state “to become a destination for not only testing of new nuclear reactors, but also to become the nation’s high-level radioactive waste dumping ground.”
Utah Gov. Spencer Cox announced Utah will be applying with the U.S. Department of Energy to host a “nuclear lifecycle innovation campus” in a remote area in northwest Tooele County during a news conference there on March 27, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
