name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri spent nearly $65 million keeping children in hospitals with nowhere else to go
description: ST. LOUIS — The teen’s hospital stay began in room 3005. The room didn’t feel like home at first. Back then, Jaloni didn’t have posters on the wall or snacks on the shelf, and he hadn’t learned about the morgue yet. He just wanted to survive. Fresh gunshot wounds filled the 14-year-old’s body with unbearable […]
text:
Jaloni and his aunt Deborah talk in his hospital room at SSM Health Cardinal Glennon Children’s Hospital in St. Louis during one of his three stints at the facility. He spent more than 475 days total at the hospital in the three years after he was shot in 2023 (Cara Anthony/KFF Health News).ST. LOUIS — The teen’s hospital stay began in room 3005.
The room didn’t feel like home at first. Back then, Jaloni didn’t have posters on the wall or snacks on the shelf, and he hadn’t learned about the morgue yet.
He just wanted to survive. Fresh gunshot wounds filled the 14-year-old’s body with unbearable pain. That first night, Jaloni said, he could barely move.
But in his own way, Jaloni could fly. His pain medication was so strong that the teenager said he felt like he was soaring in a dream.
In reality, though, Jaloni was a teenager caught between two worlds. Around his friends he had been a fearless risk-taker who knew how to steal without getting caught. Inside the hospital, Jaloni was now a boy who needed his grandmother to tell him that everything would be OK and that somehow life would get better as soon as he was released from the hospital.
But she couldn’t make that promise. No one could.
He ended up staying in the SSM Health Cardinal Glennon Children’s Hospital for more than 475 days over the next three years, his medical records show. Some of that time was not because he needed the hospital’s medical care but because he had no safe place to go. The now-18-year-old asked KFF Health News to use only nicknames or first names to protect his family’s safety.
Like thousands of children throughout the country, Jaloni experienced what is called a social stay. The practice also known as hospital boarding, in which children remain in hospitals “beyond medical necessity,” has become a costly and intractable issue nationwide.
A shortage of suitable foster care homes can mean children with mental health issues, chronic physical conditions, or disabilities that require special accommodations get stuck in hospitals. One study from Minnesota found that boarding a child with a complex medical condition in a hospital cost about $3,932 a day in 2017.
It is not clear how much of Jaloni’s hospitalization was beyond what was medically necessary or how much those extra days in the hospital cost. The hospital system declined to comment on the details of Jaloni’s stay. In a statement, SSM Health spokesperson Liz Sharpe-Taylor said that the health system is committed to its “mission of serving those who are in need” and that when “patients remain hospitalized due to an absence of discharge options, hospitals like ours often bear a burden of extensive uncompensated costs.”
In the past five years, state records show, Missouri has spent more than $64.7 million boarding children in state custody in hospitals because they had nowhere else to go. But Missouri Hospital Association spokesperson Dave Dillon said that’s a substantial undercount of the problem and that hospitals often don’t always have staff to log and request reimbursement for housing children.
And those numbers also don’t account for the toll that living in this limbo takes on the kids.
 ‘Well, y’all almost killed him’

Jaloni slept a lot during his first stint at the hospital, starting in June 2023. Bullets had pierced his right arm and the right side of his chest, cutting through his torso. He was glad to be alive.
The teen already knew a lot about death — he had been surrounded by it. An older sister died after getting shot, as did his 17-year-old brother. He’d lost a few cousins to gun violence, as well, in and around St. Louis.
He had continued to walk in the shadow of death for the next few years. “It was a lot of dying going on,” Jaloni recalled. “People were dropping like flies.”
He didn’t want his name added to that list. But he came close one summer evening when the war happening in his community erupted in a gunfight. He was injured, and a 22-year-old died. A 16-year-old was charged in the death.
“I felt like I was Superman with my gun,” Jaloni said. “But when you get older, you realize that it’s just stupid.”
In the hospital, Jaloni tried to focus on healing from the bullet wounds and what his doctors said was a spinal cord injury. After three weeks, he was discharged to a rehabilitation facility, then he was sent home.
There his mother and grandmother struggled with caring for the teen, who now needed a wheelchair.
His grandmother, who had been his legal guardian since he was little, was a double amputee and in a wheelchair herself. His mother was juggling his care and her job as a paid caregiver for another family. Changing Jaloni’s bandages, cooking, cleaning, and turning him every four hours as instructed to prevent bedsores was just too much for anyone to handle, his mother said she repeatedly told hospital officials.
“I just couldn’t take care of him anymore,” said his mother, Quette. “It was something that I was not ready for.”
She said she begged hospital officials for assistance that never arrived. Jaloni was in bad shape with what seemed like an infection on the November day they called 911 for help. He had bedsores. He felt sick and weak.
Jaloni then found himself back at Cardinal Glennon Children’s Hospital, less than five months after he’d been released.
“They were like, ‘Well, y’all almost killed him,’” his mom recalled officials telling her.
The family was accused of neglect. Because they lived just across the river from St. Louis in Illinois, Jaloni became a ward of that state.
That meant he couldn’t go home to his mother and grandmother. Jaloni’s mother thought about asking her ex-boyfriend to watch over her son. She considered asking other relatives, too. A social worker mentioned the idea of sending Jaloni to a home in Chicago where he could get the kind of attention he needed.
Chicago? “I’m not going,” he recalled thinking.
He wanted to go home, not 300 miles away. So he remained in the hospital while the adults in his life sorted out where he could go.
This time, his hospital stay was longer than anyone could imagine: 250 days.
 Searching for a place to call home

Jaloni had known life would be different in a wheelchair. But he didn’t think about how his new condition would make it harder for him to find somewhere to live. A place with ramps or an elevator for his wheelchair. A place where he could keep all his medical equipment and medicines. A place where someone could care for him safely.
Thousands of kids nationwide are in similar situations. In the fiscal year ending in June 2025, the Illinois Department of Children and Family Services logged 304 young people staying in psychiatric hospitals beyond medical necessity, according to an annual state report, while 312 spent more than 24 hours in hospital emergency departments awaiting a safe place to go.
The problem also is well documented in Missouri: 648 youths in the state’s custody were boarded in hospitals during the fiscal year that ended in June, according to data obtained by KFF Health News through a public records request.
Missouri lawmakers have introduced multiple bills over the years to try to end the practice, without success.
Unaware of the politics or the growing costs, Jaloni was stuck waiting on the hospital’s third floor, with the busy medical center effectively becoming his new home.
For most of his life, Jaloni’s grandmother had provided a safe space for him to land. She taught him how to cook his favorite meal, fried tilapia served with spaghetti. She kept him company in his early days at the hospital. She kept his secrets.
But then in 2024, while he was hospitalized, his grandmother died.
Jaloni wasn’t sure what would happen, until his aunt Deborah agreed to be Jaloni’s foster parent. Taking on the role brought back memories for Deborah, or Tete, as he called her, because Jaloni lived with her during his first year of life. But this time was different. Jaloni wasn’t a baby anymore, and he was harder to bring home than a newborn.
Deborah had to move into a first-floor, one-bedroom apartment with a ramp for his wheelchair. He needed a specialized hospital bed. While his aunt rearranged her life, Jaloni remained hospitalized until she was ready to receive him at their new home.
In the hospital, members of his care team had given him presents, braided his hair, and tried their best to connect with the teen. But for Jaloni, the third floor still felt like a different world.
“If you’re in the hospital for a whole year just doing nothing, it’s going to be the worst year of your life,” Jaloni said. “I was mad I was in there for so long.”
 ‘My kingdom’

By his third stint at the hospital — this time for a bone infection, starting in October 2025 — Jaloni had a change of heart. As he healed, Jaloni explored almost every corner of the hospital. He played his favorite video game, Fortnite, at the nurses’ station. Sometimes he ate in the cafeteria instead of his room. He occasionally went outside for fresh air. He eventually learned about a place in the hospital that was totally off-limits.
“They have a basement downstairs with a morgue in it, lots of dead bodies,” Jaloni said while at the hospital in March. “Somebody just died the other day. She was 13.”
The girl made a bracelet for Jaloni before she died. A nurse brought it to him, Jaloni recalled.
A bevy of nurses, a friendly custodian, and a chatty cook decided to look out for the teen while he was there for so long. A teacher who works for Cardinal Glennon visited five days a week to help with his online high school classes.
And, he took care of them, too. “I hear about relationships, dates, Valentine’s Day,” Jaloni said. “It’s like I’m a therapist, for real.”
To help him avoid cabin fever and allow for deep cleaning, the hospital moved him into a new room every 30 days. He said he slept in almost every room on the third floor. He said hospital workers once asked whether he wanted to avoid room 3005. After all, it was the first room he slept in after he was shot, and they thought it would bring back too many bad memories.
“Some people think it’s like a trauma room, but it’s a good room for me,” Jaloni said with a smile, noting “how much I accomplished since that day.”
Yet he watched the seasons change inside his room as traces of Halloween, Christmas gifts, and Valentine’s Day treats piled up, reminding him of what he was missing.
“I don’t make friends,” Jaloni said while still in the hospital. “I don’t have any friends.”
He had plenty of stuffed creatures, some with sewn-on smiles.
“This is my favorite: Bruno,” Jaloni said, holding a stuffed dog, then pointing out another. “Everybody knows who this is: Snoop!”
A “fish tank” in his room was filled with small plastic neon fish. With the push of a button, he could make it glow.
“This is my kingdom,” the teen said from his hospital bed. “I’ve got a good mindset.”
 Cologne, Doritos, and a night at the prom

In March, big shiny black letters spelled out “J-A-L-O-N-I” outside the door to his hospital room. Above his name, a “STOP” sign on the door instructed visitors to knock and wait for a response before entering the space that could easily be mistaken for a college dorm room.
He had photographs taped to his bathroom door — including an image of the brother he lost. The sink in his room had everything he needed for grooming: castor oil for his hair, a jar of Shea Moisture mud mask for his face, Old Spice deodorant, and a small bottle of Dior cologne.
He doesn’t wear the cologne often, but he did the night this spring that Cardinal Glennon staffers put on a prom for patients past and present. He found a YouTube tutorial and taught himself how to tie the necktie someone gave him for the occasion. His cousin came to the hospital to twist and style his locs. He invited his aunt to the big dance. She happily confessed it was her first prom, too.
Deborah is the type of person who bounces into the room, filling it with enough positive energy to fix any situation.
“Heeeeey, Jaloni,” she sang one afternoon as she visited him. “How you doing today? You hungry?”
While most young patients on his floor ate the regular hospital food on the menu, Jaloni had more options after he had a conversation with a cook. The man wanted to know if Jaloni liked the food there.
“It could be better,” he recalled saying.
After that exchange, Jaloni called the cook whenever he wanted to order something special: lemon pepper wings with cheese fries, Philly cheesesteaks with crushed Doritos on top, or a meat lover’s pizza with a tortilla-shell crust.
Another hospital worker gave him an air fryer as a gift. He used it to keep his french fries crispy. And as often as she could, his aunt would bring in his favorite meal from a nearby restaurant: cheese fries, six chicken wings, and a lemon-lime soda.
Many kids stuck boarding in hospitals don’t get private rooms, special food, tutoring, fresh air, or such attention. Even so, Jaloni’s world felt narrow.
When the door to his room was open, Jaloni observed all the events that unfolded on any given day on the hospital floor. The outside world sometimes intruded, too. On an otherwise quiet Friday in April, he said, he could hear gunshots. A 15-year-old boy was shot at a nearby gas station. Jaloni said the teen ended up at the hospital for treatment.
“He was actually on this floor,” Jaloni said. “We hear people shooting all around here.”
Still, he felt safer in the hospital than outside it.
 Heading to a new home

When he was discharged in May — after his aunt found a larger, two-bedroom apartment — Jaloni needed time to adjust to what he calls “the real world.”
To make sure he had enough room for his bed and plenty of space to move around, his aunt gave him the larger of the bedrooms in their new apartment, a modest place with a homemade wheelchair ramp outside.
His bedroom at his aunt’s home is much different than the hospital rooms he rotated in and out of for months. He gave his mom a tour when she came to visit him at the new place. She helped make up his bed, then he showed off a crisp white pair of Nike Air Force 1s that he keeps in a box under his bed. A cluster of prescription drug bottles sat on the shelf under the television in his room. It’s his job to keep up with his meds now.
He’s become his own chef, too. He uses an air fryer to make meals while his aunt is at work.
While his peers were getting ready to embark on their senior year of high school, he had another milestone on his mind — turning 18. He celebrated his birthday in August at the St. Louis Aquarium, a far cry from the tank with plastic neon fish he had in room 3005.
His aunt also quietly celebrated the first time Jaloni took out the trash. “He wasn’t going outside at first,” his aunt whispered while Jaloni took a phone call a few feet away.
He’s trying to enjoy life outside the hospital, but he still largely stays inside. He gets anxiety around a lot of people, and he fears more violence. To stay safe, the teen tries to make himself invisible, usually going out when it’s dark and wearing a black hoodie.
On a recent Sunday afternoon, Jaloni sat in his dimly lit bedroom watching YouTube videos while his aunt opened a new air freshener in the living room. She’s trying to cut back on her smoking, but the stress of caregiving, work, and taking care of herself makes it hard to quit.
She’s doing her best to help Jaloni fly. This time, she wants him to soar toward his dreams of getting his GED, learning a trade, and becoming a business owner.
In the meantime, Jaloni just wants to stay out of the hospital — and stay alive.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Commentary: Kids Can CEO: After-school programs are where ‘Nebraska skills’ are made
description: When we talk about preparing students for the future, we typically think of what happens inside the classroom. We talk about grades, literacy milestones and graduation rates. But something else deserves our attention: What happens after the school bell rings at the end of the day? After-school programs are much more than a place for […]
text:
Children enjoy hands-on learning experiences at the Luminarium during Omaha’s Lights On Afterschool program in October 2023. (Cary Mohiuddin/Collective for Youth)When we talk about preparing students for the future, we typically think of what happens inside the classroom. We talk about grades, literacy milestones and graduation rates. But something else deserves our attention: What happens after the school bell rings at the end of the day?
After-school programs are much more than a place for children to go while their parents are working. They are places where they discover their strengths, explore new interests, build relationships and develop the skills they will carry into adulthood and the workforce.
These skills — communication, teamwork, problem-solving and leadership — have had many different names over the years. They have been called soft skills, life skills or even durable skills. I like to call them “Nebraska skills” because they are valuable in every career in our state.
Technology and industries will continue to change. We know the jobs we hold today may not even exist in the future. But having the ability to collaborate, navigate challenges, learn from mistakes and work with others will always matter to the Nebraska workforce.
Our community recently celebrated Lights On Afterschool, a nationwide day to celebrate our after-school programs, for both the students who attend and the staff who support them. It is a day to raise the awareness and importance of our out-of-school programs. Like many things, we sometimes take these for granted until they are gone.
More than ever, we need to acknowledge that after-school programs give young people opportunities to practice these “Nebraska skills” and not just learn about them.
Consider one of our students participating in one of Kids Can’s after-school STEM projects. The project may involve science and technology, but the learning goes far beyond the finished product. Students must share ideas, listen to others, work through frustration and find solutions together. Another student may be participating in our mentoring program, learning how to set goals and build confidence. Another may be involved in a group sports activity and discover what it means to work as a team.
These experiences may seem like small moments, but they are important building blocks for future success. They are the “Nebraska skills” that help young people understand not only what they can do, but who they can become.
The Afterschool Alliance’s America After 3PM research highlights the key role after-school programs play for families. Yet access remains a challenge — millions of children whose parents want after-school opportunities cannot participate because programs are unavailable or inaccessible. That should concern all of us.
For Nebraskans, investing in after-school programs is an investment in our future workforce. Employers need people who can communicate effectively, solve problems, work across differences and adapt to change. Schools cannot, and should not, be expected to build these skills alone. We all have a role to play.
As a nonprofit leader working alongside children, families and educators, I believe our responsibility extends beyond helping our children succeed today. We must help them prepare for the opportunities and challenges of tomorrow.
The next generation of Nebraska workers and leaders is already in our classrooms and community centers. Every afternoon presents an opportunity to help them grow.
The school day may end with a bell, but the future does not stop there.

name: WyoFile
title: ‘My job’s gone’: Southwest Wyoming braces for impact of trona layoffs
description:
Wyoming's trona and soda ash industry has driven Sweetwater County's economy for decades. Now, workers and residents are preparing for an economic "disaster."
The post ‘My job’s gone’: Southwest Wyoming braces for impact of trona layoffs appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Help, resources for workers
Workers facing unemployment can contact the Department of Workforce Services.
The agency is also coordinating rapid response, in-person meetings this week at Western Wyoming Community College in Rock Springs.
If you or someone you know is having suicidal thoughts, you can call or text the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988.
To find a local food bank near you, go to the Food Bank of Wyoming website. Go to the same website to learn how to help.
Because there are so many different social service organizations in each Wyoming town, one of the best ways to find help or to learn how to help is to visit the Wyoming 211 website or dial 2-1-1. The call center can connect you to services and organizations in your community.


SWEETWATER COUNTY—Trona miner Jarred Weiss was up by 4:30 a.m., packed a lunch for work — a cup of hummus and a couple pieces of naan bread — and arrived at the Rock Springs Family Recreation Center at 5:15 a.m. Way too early, he said, as usual. But it’s a calming time to scroll through his phone before catching the company bus for the 40-minute drive to WE Soda’s trona mine and soda ash complex.
“I’m kind of a worrywart,” he said. “I don’t like to rush.”
Weiss, 45, has a lot on his mind these days. His company announced earlier this month that it will lay off 350 workers over the next two years, with most of the pink slips coming in January.
“I know my job’s gone. I’m only number 20 from the bottom,” said Weiss, who has worked above ground at the powerhouse for the past three years. Soon after the layoffs were announced, the company cut his pay and reassigned him underground to “basically do whatever they want me to do,” he said.
Instead of the 12-hour shifts he used to work — with a guaranteed full week off once a month — he’s now working eight-hour shifts. That means he can’t join his son for lunch at school or take care of personal business on weekdays — minor inconveniences, he said, compared to what’s to come.
“I’m not sure what my future holds,” Weiss said. “Southwest Wyoming is my home now, and I hate to leave. The thought of having to learn something new, maybe find a new trade or a different lifestyle — it’s hard to know how to make sense of this.”


WE Soda worker Jarred Weiss. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)


WE Soda worker Jeremy Litz. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)


Pointing to a flood of new soda ash fed onto the global market from China and Mongolia, London-based WE Soda says it’s been losing money on every ton of Wyoming soda ash — which is derived from trona — that it ships out of state. To regain a competitive edge, and to ensure its trona and soda ash operations in Sweetwater County remain viable into the future, the company plans to shift from underground mining to less labor-intensive drill-and-pump “solution” mining. 
It will require flooding the mine and trimming its Wyoming workforce from 850 to 500, WE Soda said. It also means the company will cut its Wyoming soda ash production by more than 1.5 million metric tons annually as it focuses less on global markets and more on North American customers.
“This repositioning is necessary to strengthen the long-term competitiveness of the company’s Wyoming operations in response to the significant impact which low-cost Chinese soda ash exports have had on the pricing of American soda ash in export markets,” the company said.
The move and impending layoffs are a gut-punch to workers and southwest Wyoming communities, residents say. By shifting to solution mining, locals worry, WE Soda might force three neighboring trona mining operations into the same drill-and-pump method, resulting in hundreds more layoffs.
“It’s a disaster,” WE Soda worker Jeremy Litz, 44, told WyoFile after a union meeting last week. “Talking to friends and family and co-workers, this is going to affect our community top to bottom.” Families will likely have to move, sending the economy into a tailspin, he added. Meantime, people are already taking drastic measures to cut their spending, like forgoing a haircut, to prepare for the loss of their livelihoods. 
“We’ve already had [WE Soda workers],” Litz said, “who have had to take their kids out of daycare and out of preschool because of the unknown — what they’re going to be able to afford.”
‘All of a sudden, you have your world torn apart’
Wyoming’s trona and soda ash industry consists of four separate operations clustered west of Green River in Sweetwater County, each including mining operations and processing plants. Combined, last year they supported about 2,500 workers and produced 10 million tons of soda ash worth $1.3 billion, according to industry figures.
Once brought to the surface, trona is crushed and baked into a fine powder: soda ash. That’s used to make myriad products, from toothpaste to beer bottles, car windshields and large industrial batteries. 
For decades, the “trona patch” has been the primary economic driver in the region, locals say, supporting big-box stores and mom-and-pop businesses, a robust community college, as well as amenities like parks and state-of-the-art recreation centers.
The economic hit from the WE Soda layoffs, and potentially others, “is huge,” Green River Mayor-elect Stan Blake said.
“You’re going to see people not paying their taxes, houses up for sale,” the former lawmaker added. Enrollment at public schools will decline, which means less funding and possible school closures. “It’s all a trickle-down effect,” Blake said. “Especially if this knocks down some other dominoes [forcing other trona mines] to go to solution mining.”
A miner in a lunchroom at Tata Chemicals’ underground trona mine in southwest Wyoming. Tata is a WE Soda competitor. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
Dozens of support companies stretching from southwest Wyoming to Casper and Gillette — suppliers, welding and machine shops — will also feel the pinch, especially if there’s an industrywide shift away from traditional underground mining operations, Blake said. “Solution mining is a big fear.”
Locals have always regarded the trona patch as a source of steady, good-paying jobs with excellent benefits to support a family — a sort of blue-collar brass ring within reach without requiring a college degree.
“I left the oilfields for the job security of the trona mines,” WE Soda worker Tyler Pehrson said. “You look for these mining jobs because they were sustainable. They were something you could build a future on and feel safe. And now, I don’t think there’s a trona mine in the patch that can feel safe after this.
“My oldest child graduated [high school] last year,” added Pehrson, 42. “I have a 12-year-old son, a mortgage, a truck payment. You can’t prepare for it. You wake up one morning, come in joking with your friends, and all of a sudden you have your world torn apart.”


WE Soda worker Tyler Pehrson. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)


WE Soda worker Ryan Heikes. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)


Ryan Heikes, 27, has worked at WE Soda as a mechanic for almost four years, and he guesses he’ll probably receive a pink slip. “It’s been great money,” he told WyoFile. “I can go and buy all the toys and live comfortably. But now it’s all going up for sale.”
Accepting his likely fate at WE Soda, Heikes said he’s preparing for his next steps and somewhat grateful to find out now — while he’s still young — he probably can’t count on the trona patch for a career.
“If they’re going to do this now, what’s going to keep them from doing it again later?” he said.
WE Soda worker Litz said he’s especially concerned for a couple of fellow workers on his crew who have children with special needs. “Now they’re going to lose their insurance,” he said. “How in the world are they going to make those bills?”
Union workers fear for safety
Hundreds of WE Soda workers, many accompanied by family, flooded a meeting hall Thursday evening at the Sweetwater Events Complex in Rock Springs to get the latest information from United Steelworkers Local 13214 — the union that represents about two-thirds of the company’s Wyoming workforce.
Union officers, the first to arrive, casually chatted about who might try to retire soon in light of the layoffs. “I think about it all the time, then I remember I’m too young to retire,” one union officer said. 
As workers arrived, a woman picked up a young girl and told her, “I remember when you were born. Your daddy was on my crew.” Workers and spouses discussed Thanksgiving and Christmas plans, asking each other questions like, “how much does unemployment [insurance] pay?”
WE Soda workers, accompanied by family members, attend a union meeting Nov. 12 in Rock Springs. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
Getting to the business at hand, union officials, noting “the union is not in agreement with any of these proposals,” read through WE Soda’s provisional list of job cuts. 
“The hoist relief is a mess,” United Steelworkers Local 13214 President Marshal Cummings said. “Hoist relief goes from two relief guys and three [supply/storage shop] people and two cagers to one guy. So he would receive, do the cager job and the storage job. So congratulations.”
Reading from WE Soda’s provisional layoff plans department by department, Cummings described jobs being eliminated along with how the company would reassign duties to remaining workers, frequently eliciting guffaws and disgusted chuckles. Union officials and workers in the audience detected a theme: As WE Soda cuts positions, it doesn’t appear to be cutting duties. Many of the remaining employees after the initial round of layoffs are expected to take on the workload of two, three, sometimes four workers.
“The good news,” Cummings said sarcastically, “is they didn’t offer any pay rate [increases] for you to take on additional responsibility.” 
The crowd audibly moaned.
Though the company’s proposals are merely a starting point before official negotiations with the union kick off, United Steelworkers Staff Representative William Wilkinson suggested WE Soda officials are setting the stage for an uphill bargain. Both Wilkinson and Cummings noted that, in their discussion with company representatives earlier that day, they consistently had to correct them about who works where in the complex and how adding additional assignments poses safety questions.
“If they have the legal right to make stupid decisions, we really need to worry about the safety [risks] and try to save as many jobs as possible,” Wilkinson said. “A bunch of people that don’t do work at all made a bunch of dumb decisions. Now, it’s really hard to sit here today and be like, ‘What about this? What about that?'”
“They’re going to take this one guy,” Wilkinson added, “and they’re going to give him four more jobs to do. It’s not realistic.”
United Steelworkers Local 13214 officials prepare for a meeting Nov. 12 in Rock Springs. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
Cummings implored workers to follow task protocols and safety procedures “to a T.” If a worker is asked to break the rules, “find a [union] steward, file a grievance.
“Don’t take any shortcuts,” he added. “Don’t risk your safety.”
Reached by WyoFile for response, WE Soda provided a statement: “The safety of our employees and our operations is our top priority, and any changes to work assignments are being evaluated with safety in mind.”
After the meeting, while people were still milling about, workers bemoaned the challenges ahead.
Heikes, the 27-year-old, resigned to his fate at the company, told WyoFile, “I don’t want to be there with the ones left that are going to be running around like chickens with their heads cut off. It’s going to be way too much work on one person.”
Officials respond
Local elected officials have said they’re seeking more details from WE Soda while working with state offices to coordinate workforce services for employees facing joblessness. Gov. Mark Gordon and Gov.-elect Eric Barlow launched a coordinated response among the Department of Workforce Services and state unemployment insurance staff, as well as Western Wyoming Community College. 
Staff from those agencies are hosting in-person information sessions this week at the college in Rock Springs for those affected. (See the infobox at the top of this story.)
Gordon on Monday paused a $13 million state grant that had been recommended for a natural gas pipeline connection at WE Soda’s operations. While reconsidering the grant, Gordon instructed state officials “to conduct an expedited thorough examination of the economic impacts to Sweetwater County and the state from the shifting global dynamics affecting Wyoming trona production.”
The Wyoming Energy Authority this week began soliciting proposals from third-party entities to take on the research, demanding it be completed by the end of January.
Gordon and Barlow traveled to Sweetwater County on Tuesday to visit with industry and community officials about the impacts of the pending layoffs.
“Sweetwater County is an economic powerhouse for Wyoming,” Gordon said in a prepared statement. “Trona is central to that story, as are the miners, their families and all the businesses that depend on a robust mining economy.
“I came because I wanted to hear from the people most affected by the news and get the conversation going about what the state can do,” Gordon added, “what we need to do and how we can work together to keep these mines healthy and employment full.”
Barlow, also in a prepared statement, said his team will stay engaged to ensure a seamless transition of state efforts to help the miners and their communities. “Families in Sweetwater County are facing difficult questions about their next paycheck and their future. They deserve our attention and a coordinated response.”
Wyoming’s senior U.S. Sen. John Barrasso, during a Senate Finance Committee hearing this month, demanded assurances from Trump administration nominees for Assistant Secretary of Commerce and Under Secretary of the Treasury for Domestic Finance to do all they can to help Wyoming’s soda ash industry and push back against China’s efforts to flood the global market.
“They’re rigging the market against our producers,” Barrasso said. “They’re flooding global markets with their subsidized soda ash.
“Our miners,” he added, “can beat anyone on a level playing field. But Communist China has no interest in fair competition.”
WE Soda, in a statement to WyoFile, said it is cooperating with state and local officials in efforts to help employees.
“We continue to meet with state and local elected officials to keep them informed and to find the best ways to help affected families and communities,” WE Soda said. “We are also working closely with Wyoming Workforce Services and we have met with local community groups and Western Wyoming Community College to work together on retraining efforts.”
But workers remain uncertain about how they and their families will navigate the loss of their economic livelihoods.
“There’s not many jobs out there,” Litz said. “There’s going to be so many people fighting for the five or six that are there; the majority of the guys are going to have to go somewhere else or take a substantial wage and benefits cut.”

title: Something about guns
description:
Columnist David Romtvedt writes that we seem to accept a society awash in guns as ordinary, perhaps even desirable.
The post Something about guns appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Opinion

One day, early on in my work life with my father-in-law at his ranch, he turned and pointed out the two rifles hanging just above our heads in the cab of the pickup. “You see a coyote, you take one of these and shoot it,” he said. “They’re always loaded.”
I spent much of my childhood on my grandmother’s dairy farm where I learned to shoot with a .22 rifle my uncle had given me. We’d set tin cans on a rock or a chunk of wood or a fence post and he’d coach me. I didn’t mind the shooting. In fact, I liked trying to be good at it. But I didn’t connect it to killing and when it was time to hunt rabbits, I told my uncle I’d rather not.
It wasn’t just the killing of animals. I felt cautious about guns in general, about accidents, and about the way some of the men got into a rage with a recalcitrant cow or a disobedient dog. Even as a young boy, I was aware that many shootings occur in moments of sudden anger when, if there’d been no gun available, things might not have gone so wrong. And I knew how often guns had a role in suicides.
So as an adult, my inclination has been to favor pretty vigorous gun control. For much of our history, U.S. courts have largely supported this view even as many of us have disagreed on how much gun control is appropriate. The arguments have often swirled around the brief but maddeningly unclear language in the Second Amendment to the Constitution: “A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.”
That’s not very helpful. In 1792, Congress passed the Militia Act, requiring that “every free able-bodied white male citizen, who is or shall be of age eighteen years, and under the age of forty-five years” be enrolled in the Militia. But the Militia is long gone, and we don’t have Militiamen with guns in the house to be used in times of active duty. Could the language now pertain to National Guard members keeping a gun at home with its use limited to analogous times of active duty? What exactly about the people’s right to bear arms shall not be infringed? And who are the people — free able-bodied white males?
In the 1939 United States v. Miller case, the Supreme Court, in an 8-0 decision, ruled that the National Firearms Act, which required registration of short-barreled shotguns, was constitutional. The eight justices, speaking unanimously, wrote that a militia was composed of civilians sometimes acting as soldiers who were expected to report for service bearing arms supplied by themselves and of a type in common use by the military at the time. With this in mind, the justices held that in the absence of any evidence pointing to the use of short-barreled shotguns in the maintenance of a well-regulated militia, the Second Amendment did not protect such weapons from regulation. Later Supreme Court rulings upheld this view, notably in the 1980 Lewis v. United States case, when by a 6-3 vote the court ruled that it was constitutional to prohibit a convicted felon from possessing a firearm that does not have “some reasonable relationship to the preservation or efficiency of a well regulated militia.”
These and other judicial precedents have been repeatedly overturned in the past two decades, with courts interpreting the Second Amendment as guaranteeing the right of all individuals to keep and bear arms of just about any kind in just about any circumstances and just about anywhere with little or no regulation. And we have an epidemic of mass shootings and killings in this country. In schools, in churches and synagogues, in bars and nightclubs. 
The Mass Tracker database defines a mass shooting as one in which four or more persons are shot in one incident, at one location, at roughly the same time. Using this definition, there were 454 mass shootings in the United States between Jan. 1 and Oct.28, 2026. That’s slightly more than 1.5 mass shootings per day. Five hundred people were killed and 1,865 wounded. Given these numbers, I’m surprised by our reluctance to control the manufacture, distribution, sale, use and permitting of guns. Indeed, we seem to accept a society awash in guns as ordinary, perhaps even desirable.
Where I live, a local pharmacy promotes itself as “Mixing guns and drugs since ’22” and offers 20-minute in-and-out sales of firearms suppressors — silencers. And to raise funds this year, my local Arts and Humanities Council raffled off a DPMS Panther Arms AR-10 (6.5 Creedmoor) tactical rifle with 20-round magazine.
I think that’s where I’ll end. You decide what to do.

title: Conservation programs in the Colorado River’s Upper Basin inch forward, despite thorny questions
description:
Four upriver states are planning to use $100 million in federal grants to do the work. But it’s unclear whether the federal government will bank the water for them.
The post Conservation programs in the Colorado River’s Upper Basin inch forward, despite thorny questions  appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.
New voluntary water conservation programs in the Upper Colorado River Basin appear on track after the 320th meeting of the Upper Colorado River Commission concluded last week. But Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, Wyoming and the federal government have yet to agree on how any conserved water would be credited and stored.
These questions, experts say, may not come with easy answers.  
This June, the federal Bureau of Reclamation put $100 million on the table for the four states in the Upper Basin to fund their own voluntary water conservation programs, which usually entails paying ranchers and farmers to use less water. Overuse and drought-diminished flows on the Colorado River threaten the water supply of roughly 40 million people, 30 tribes, seven states and Mexico.
Most Upper Basin states are planning to implement programs in 2027 (Utah already has one running), and their success could be crucial to the states’ assertion that they should only have to ease the pressure on the Colorado River through voluntary measures. This fall, the federal government implemented new mandatory reductions on the Lower Basin, and Nevada, later joined by Arizona, sued over the potential for even deeper cuts.
“It’s … important to recognize, and I say this in a positive way, a complimentary way, the audacious ambition of attempting to put this together in the time frame that we have,” Wayne Pullan, the Bureau of Reclamation’s Upper Colorado Basin regional director, told negotiators from the Upper Basin states at the virtual meeting.
Colorado made it clear that its program can only move forward with an agreement from Reclamation that conserved water would remain under the state’s jurisdiction.
“We really need to get some credit for the upper division states through a program like this,” said Amy Ostdiek of the Colorado Water Conservation Board, who presented the state’s conservation program. “What that means in Colorado is seeing that that water is treated as operationally neutral, and not simply passed downstream.” 
“Operationally neutral” water is conserved by one state and stored in federal reservoirs for future use by that state. Arizona, California and Nevada, the Lower Basin states, have banked water in Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the United States, with the option to withdraw it for future use. But the Interior secretary is the legal water master in the Lower Basin and has the ability to allocate surplus water there. The secretary does not play the same role in the Upper Basin. 
Pullan said that Reclamation is “able and willing” to keep working on how the government would credit and handle water conserved by the Upper Basin. Some observers wondered how the Upper Basin’s condition would sit with the federal government, which built and financed the dams that store the water.
“They don’t like to turn over the keys of the car to the states,” said James Eklund, a partner at Taft Law and Colorado’s Colorado River negotiator from 2013 to 2019.
An irrigation headgate in the Green River drainage in Wyoming seen in the spring of 2026. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)
The Lower Basin would also need to agree that water conserved in the Upper Basin could be stored for the upstream states’ use, something Kathryn Sorensen, director of research for Arizona State University’s Kyl Center for Water Policy, had a hard time envisioning. 
The Lower Basin states “would expect some sort of quid pro quo for that type of arrangement,” she said.
The Upper and Lower basin negotiators from each of the seven Colorado River states had years to agree on new guidelines for the federal government to implement. After they missed several deadlines, Reclamation implemented its own new operating plan this year, and the states appear no closer to an agreement.
The possibility of one of the seven basin states suing another before the Supreme Court looms over the basin.
Various conservation programs in the Upper Basin are in different phases of development. Utah’s program saved about 5,500 acre-feet of water in 2025, Amy Haas, executive director of the Colorado River Authority in Utah, announced at the meeting.
One acre-foot of water can supply anywhere from three to six homes for a year, depending on the region’s climate and urban density. 
New Mexico and Wyoming made their programs compatible with other funding sources, like state appropriations or grants from nonprofits, should they become available, state representatives said.
The Upper Basin uses less water than the Lower Basin, which recently reined in its consumption after years of drawing more water than it was allocated, though it has plans to divert yet more water from the river. In its operating guidelines released this summer, Reclamation modeled up to 200,000 acre-feet of voluntary conservation annually in the Upper Basin — if hydrology allows.  
Eklund, who attended the virtual meeting, said it’s disappointing the seven basin states still can’t agree on a solution to the problems plaguing the Colorado River. “If this system collapses, it doesn’t really matter what we’re legally entitled to,” he said. 
“If Phoenix sneezes, the Upper Basin catches a cold,” he added. “We’re very, very connected economically to each other, and if we don’t start governing the system like we’re all part of one country and not seven different sovereign countries, then we’re A: only going to have ourselves to blame, and B: we’re not going to like the results.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho officials request raise for disability caregivers and restoring cuts to mental health services
description: Idaho health officials are hoping to increase the pay rate for disability caregivers by 13% next year.  The raise request — detailed in the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare’s budget proposal submitted to the Idaho governor in September — would bring the pay for personal care service workers up to $27.64 per hour. That’s […]
text:
Hundreds of Idahoans gathered in the rotunda of the Idaho Capitol on Jan. 12, 2026, to protest budget cuts to the state's Medicaid program. The protest, organized by Idaho Voices for Children, took place before the governor's State of the State Address. (Photo by Christina Lords/Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho health officials are hoping to increase the pay rate for disability caregivers by 13% next year. 
The raise request — detailed in the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare’s budget proposal submitted to the Idaho governor in September — would bring the pay for personal care service workers up to $27.64 per hour. That’s up from Idaho’s current hourly pay rate of $24.44.
That could bring the state out of its status as the lowest paying state for the industry in the Northwest for the first time in years. Idaho has, for years, had a shortage of disability caregivers, who often work in low-paid, demanding jobs. 
On the heels of the 2026 legislative session’s deep budget cuts across state government, the request to increase the pay of disability caregivers represents a rare departure from the governor’s office’s instructions for state agencies to continue submitting barebones budgets. 
The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare is calling for the pay increase after recently learning that few caregiving agencies can take new patients, Medicaid Administrator Sasha O’Connell said in an interview last month. Through the research, required by federal regulators as part of the state’s recent cuts to doctor pay rates, the state found — by hiring a secret shopper — that only three personal care service agencies, out of 152 across the state, could take children. Less than a third said they could take new adult Medicaid clients.
“What we found is very concerning,” O’Connell said.
The budget request is only one of the first stops for a change in the state’s budget. 
Gov. Brad Little will next lay out his priorities for state agencies and the state budget during January’s State of the State Address. But it is ultimately up to the Idaho Legislature to set the state budget and weigh which individual requests make the cut.
Across the board, the raises for disability caregivers would cost the state roughly $3.9 million, and the federal government about $8.1 million. That represents a small chunk of the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare’s overall $6.58 billion budget for next fiscal year, which starts in June. The total budget could see about a 2% increase from what lawmakers approved this fiscal year. 
State health officials aren’t expecting to need to ask the Legislature for more money to fund Medicaid for this fiscal year. But they are hoping to ask the Legislature for permission to tap into a recently created rainy day fund, the Medicaid Stabilization Fund, in case costs come in higher. 
But in a year where state agencies were instructed to once again submit barebones budgets, the Department of Health and Welfare had a few new spending areas. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 After Legislature restored mental health budget cuts, agency requests permanent funding

Early this year, within months after a Medicaid contractor cut a set of mental health programs, four patients died. The contractor, Magellan, had had its pay rate cut by the state as part of an early round of budget cuts by Little. 
In the final weeks of the legislative session, state lawmakers had secured temporary funding — through legal settlements with tobacco and opioid manufacturers — to restore the two programs, which included a mobile treatment program for people with severe mental illness, called Assertive Community Treatment, as well as peer support services, which help people navigate mental health treatment.
Heading into the next legislative session, the Department of Health and Welfare requested ongoing state funding to keep providing the programs. 
The state’s estimates for how to maintain those services are tough to break apart. The costs for people on those programs who are on Medicaid are baked into a bigger budget area; this year, it cost the state $8 million to run the program, and it cost the feds $20 million. The costs next year to fund non-Medicaid members of those programs is $2.15 million from the state’s general fund.
Without the program, state officials acknowledged that more patients could die.
Without sustainable funding for these services, “Idaho may see higher utilization of crisis services, hospitalizations, death, and incarceration among individuals with serious mental illness,” state officials wrote in the budget proposal.
Idaho Medicaid Deputy Director Sasha O’Connell presents to the Legislature’s Medicaid Review Panel in Rexburg on Dec. 15, 2025. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
O’Connell said health officials were instructed to bring back programs restored temporarily last year into ongoing funding, through the state’s general fund, the pool of taxpayer funding that lawmakers can freely allocate to different areas. 
But she acknowledged that lawmakers could decide to keep tapping temporary funding for the programs.
“It’s completely up to the Legislature, should they choose to use ongoing funding sources to fill that need or one-time, like they did last year,” O’Connell said.

Have a news tip?

And she stressed that this programs’ inclusion isn’t a sign that they are safe from cuts for good. In budget shortfalls, she said state health officials would still have a similarly small list of options of what they could cut.
“Those are not decisions that we would have made if it weren’t for budget reductions that were necessary,” O’Connell said. “But we also live in an environment where we need to plan according to a state budget. And if we were in a similar position … we would be faced with a similar set of options, where Assertive Community Treatment, adult peer support services, and very few other services would be on the list of things that could be eliminated if we were told that we needed to eliminate services or change our budget to get in line with expectations, given our limited resources.”
 Other new programs: Patients pay more for Medicaid care, and a scorecard for Medicaid contractors that manage health benefits

More parts of big Medicaid changes from a cost-cutting state law in 2025 are rolling out. 
One of the next pieces will essentially be more patient copays, or costs people have to pay per doctor’s visit or treatment session.
The law allowed those payments, called cost-sharing, to be “at least to the levels developed by other states and up to the maximum charged by other states.”
In researching that part of the law, Health and Welfare found that the cap would be about $4 for most services, and $8 for prescription drugs that are not on the state’s preferred drug list. The state asked federal regulators for permission to make those changes. 
Part of implementing this change, the agency says, is developing a tool to ensure that the cost-sharing amounts aren’t more than 5% of the household income. The agency is requesting permission to transfer $1.78 million in mostly federal funds to set up that system from program benefits costs. Long term, the state expects the policy to save money.
As part of the state’s shift to private companies managing Medicaid benefits spurred by the same state law, the state is also preparing to roll out a new federally required tool to monitor those contractors. The model of private companies running Medicaid is called managed care. 
The tool, set to be publicly available by the end of 2028, is expected to include feedback from patients and providers, O’Connell said. In the past, some providers have complained that the two most recent mental health managed care organizations, Magellan and Optum, had delayed payments to providers. 
“The goal is really to share that information publicly, so that managed care organizations have that information transparently as providers and members are making selections about who to contract with or who to receive their care from in a future state where we’re moving to comprehensive managed care,” O’Connell said.
To help set up the tool, the state health agency is requesting $550,000, largely from the federal government.
What wasn’t detailed in Health and Welfare’s budget request was an update on its cuts to doctor pay rates. The agency hasn’t yet received approval from federal regulators on its cuts, which it first implemented in late 2025. But Department of Health and Welfare spokesperson AJ McWhorter said the agency has “no reason to expect that we won’t” receive approval.
Ending the cuts to provider pay rates and cut services would cost $34 million in general funds, and nearly $92.3 million in federal funds, according to estimates the agency provided to the Idaho Capital Sun.

title: Tuberville committee to hold regional inaugural celebrations; will not disclose donors
description: Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville plans to hold regional inaugural celebrations in January under a nonprofit not required to disclose donors, selling sponsorship packages with VIP tickets ranging from $10,000 to $500,000. Elliot Maisel, chair of the Tuberville Transition and Inaugural Committee, Inc., and a distributing company CEO based in Mobile, wrote in an int[...]
text:
Alabama Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville speaks to supporters after declaring victory during an election night watch party at The Hotel at Auburn University on Nov. 3, 2026. Tuberville plans to hold multiple inaugural celebrations across the state, that are open to the public and sponsors that bought access under a nonprofit that is not required to disclose donors. (Larry Robinson for Alabama Reflector)Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville plans to hold regional inaugural celebrations in January under a nonprofit not required to disclose donors, selling sponsorship packages with VIP tickets ranging from $10,000 to $500,000.
Elliot Maisel, chair of the Tuberville Transition and Inaugural Committee, Inc., and a distributing company CEO based in Mobile, wrote in an introductory letter describing the sponsorship opportunity package that Tuberville’s inauguration “belongs to the whole state.” 
“It is the moment Alabamians set the campaign aside, gather as neighbors, and turn to the work ahead,” he wrote in the letter, obtained by Alabama Reflector. “This inaugural is built to reach well beyond the capital city.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Hannah Eddins, communications director for Tuberville, said in a statement Wednesday morning the events will also be open to the public.
“We are working on capacity and availability and will make that information available to the public at the appropriate time,” she said. 
The Tuberville committee is organized as a 501(c)(4) “social welfare” organization, a designation commonly used by dark money organizations. As a 501(c)(4) nonprofit corporation, the sponsors’ identities are not required to be disclosed to the public. 
The letter says the group “will not disclose the identity of donors or the amount donated without donor authorization.”
“It should be noted that the Corporation intends to publish a list of sponsors (by sponsorship level), and if a donor wishes to be included on this list, then the amount donated may be apparent based on the published sponsorship levels,” the letter says.
The committee is led by Maisel, Jonathan Gray – Tuberville’s policy consultant – and Lee Edwards, Jr., a Birmingham car dealer who served on Tuberville’s campaign finance committee. 
The committee is not the same as Tuberville’s campaign committee, which must report all donations to the Alabama Secretary of State’s Office. 
“The committee raises contributions and sells tickets to cover the costs of the transition and the inauguration, and to help the Governor-elect and his staff serve the general interest and welfare of Alabama and its people,” Maisel wrote in the letter. 
The costs of the transition were not specified. 
The committee will host a “Regional Inaugural Celebration” in Mobile on Jan. 12 and one in Huntsville on Jan. 14. A “Private Inaugural Pre-Celebration” will be held on Jan. 17 before the Inaugural Ball, both at the Renaissance Hotel in downtown Montgomery. According to the package, the private celebration is “reserved for sponsors.”
On Jan. 18, Inauguration Day, the committee will host a prayer service before Tuberville is sworn into office in the State Capitol, followed by the traditional Inauguration Parade through downtown Montgomery. 
Maisel wrote that the “sponsors make this week possible.”
“In return, the committee has built six sponsorship levels that place you and your guests at the center of the celebration, from the regional events to the reception with Coach and his Cabinet, the Inaugural Ball, and priority seating at the Swearing-In,” he wrote.
In order to get reserved seating at the ball, swearing-in ceremony and VIP tickets to the regional celebrations, sponsors can pay in tiers. All tiers include acknowledgement in the inaugural program and a “premium” inaugural gift.
Sponsors can choose from six tiers to “take part” in Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville’s inaugural celebrations. (screenshot of Tuberville Transition and Inaugural Committee, Inc. Sponsorship Opportunity Package)
A single $500,000 package includes 50 VIP tickets for each regional event and the ball, 25 tickets to access Tuberville and his cabinet at the ball; 25 tickets to the swearing-in ceremony; a two-page ad in the inaugural program and advertising and sponsorship at the ball.
A single $250,000 package for each regional event includes 32 VIP tickets for each regional event, 30 tickets to the ball, 16 tickets to access Tuberville and his cabinet at the ball, 16 tickets to the swearing-in ceremony, a two-page ad in the inaugural program and advertising and sponsorship at the sponsor’s respective regional event.
For $100,000, a sponsor would receive 24 VIP tickets for each regional event and the ball, 12 tickets to access Tuberville and his cabinet at the ball, 12 tickets to the swearing-in ceremony and a full-page ad in the inaugural program.
For $50,000, a sponsor receives 16 VIP tickets for each regional event and the ball, 8 tickets to access Tuberville and his cabinet at the ball, 8 tickets to the swearing-in ceremony and a full-page ad in the inaugural program.
For $25,000, a sponsor receives 8 VIP tickets for each regional event and the ball, 4 tickets to access Tuberville and his cabinet at the ball, 4 tickets to the swearing-in ceremony and a half-page ad in the inaugural program.
For $10,000, a sponsor receives 4 VIP tickets for each regional event and the ball, 2 tickets to access Tuberville and his cabinet at the ball, 2 tickets to the swearing-in ceremony and a half-page ad in the inaugural program.
The letter also notes that “there is no limit imposed by law on the amount that may be given by corporations or other individuals.”
This is the first statewide inaugural celebration in Alabama. Gov. Kay Ivey held a pre-inaugural party in Gulf Shores in 2019, and former Gov. Bob Riley held an inaugural ball in Birmingham in 2007.

title: The Nature Conservancy announces $2.1M wildfire risk reduction projects in Idaho, Wyoming
description: Officials with The Nature Conservancy announced a $2.1 million agreement with the U.S. Forest Service to expand forest restoration activities and wildfire fuels reduction projects in Idaho and Wyoming.  The Nature Conservancy, or TNC for short, will provide additional workforce to support prescribed fires, ecological thinning and other work to reduce overgro[...]
text:
A wildland firefighter conducts a prescribed burn on Oct. 19, 2023, on the Beaverhead-Deerlodge National Forest in Montana. (Courtesy of the U.S. Forest Service).Officials with The Nature Conservancy announced a $2.1 million agreement with the U.S. Forest Service to expand forest restoration activities and wildfire fuels reduction projects in Idaho and Wyoming. 



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



The Nature Conservancy, or TNC for short, will provide additional workforce to support prescribed fires, ecological thinning and other work to reduce overgrowth that fuels wildfires, The Nature Conservancy said in a press release issued Monday.
Prescribed fires are planned and controlled fires that are intentionally set by land managers or firefighters to remove excess vegetation or dead wood and brush that can fuel wildfires, or accomplish other ecological goals. 
“Hazardous fuels reduction projects remain a critical tool for protecting communities across Idaho and Wyoming from the growing threat of high‑severity wildfire,” Great Basin Geographic Area Fire Director Ben Newburn said in a written statement. “Through the Forest Service’s focus on active management, we are strategically reducing dense vegetation and restoring more natural fire behavior to support the development of healthier, more diverse and more resilient landscapes.” 
“Progress at this scale is only possible through strong collaboration,” Newburn added. “Our partnership with The Nature Conservancy plays an essential role in expanding capacity, aligning scientific expertise, and accelerating work that safeguards both communities and forests.” 
The funding will support fuel reduction projects in the wildland urban interface – the area where human development and undeveloped wild lands meet. Projects will take place in the Caribou-Targhee, Payette and Salmon-Challis national forests in Idaho and the Bridger-Teton National Forest in Wyoming, where existing agreements with the U.S. Forest Service are in place, officials said. 
“Recognizing the vital role of prescribed fire and ecological thinning to restore forests — and the great need for more workforce capacity to accomplish it — TNC has spent years developing strong partnerships with the U.S. Forest Service,” Matthew Ward, The Nature Conservancy Idaho forest and fire program manager, said in a written statement. “This agreement enables us to expand proven, proactive restoration strategies and make an even bigger impact for forests and communities in Idaho and Wyoming.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Before federal indictments, State Auditor left WV education leader in dark about schools’ money
description: Amid intense scrutiny of State Auditor Mark Hunt’s actions, the state education department can’t get clear answers — or even a response — about how the Auditor’s Office is handling delinquent property taxes owed to schools.
text:
Inside a classroom in Bridgeview Elementary in South Charleston, West Virginia. (Lexi Browning | West Virginia Watch)Amid intense scrutiny of State Auditor Mark Hunt’s actions, the state education department can’t get clear answers — or even a response — about how the Auditor’s Office is handling delinquent property taxes owed to schools.
Over the last decade, a school fund dedicated to staff development — like helping teachers improve their instructional skills — has received on average $520,000 in surplus funds from delinquent property sales across the state. The process is outlined in state code. 
Hunt was indicted this week by a federal grand jury on allegations he was involved in a property stealing scheme within his state office. Prior to federal indictments, Hunt’s office had faced scrutiny for hiring a state senator for contract work, an Auditor’s Office employee testing lobbying rules, irregularities in tax sales and a potential conflict of interest with a used car lot. 
In April, West Virginia Department of Education staff met with the Auditor Office’s staff to discuss education officials’ concern about money legally owed to the school fund. 
But State Schools Superintendent Michele Blatt still had numerous questions and concerns.
She sent a letter to Hunt in July laying out several issues. Among Blatt’s requests, she asked for itemized checks and dates of surplus property funds that were ripe to be transmitted to the school fund.
Hunt’s response: a ghosting. 
“ … At this time, there has been no response to those questions, nor the letter dated July 9, 2026,” Christy Day, education department communicators director, said on Nov 16.
On Wednesday, a spokesperson for the Auditor’s Office said in an email, “We are still formulating our response to Superintendent Blatt’s July 9 letter.”
“As it happens, our office recently received WVDE’s annual request to credit this year’s surplus proceeds to the General School Fund, totaling $506,875.10. Those funds have been transferred,” wrote Madlyn Alqutub, a multimedia specialist for the Auditor’s Office.
There are calls from Gov. Patrick Morrisey and House Speaker Roger Hanshaw for Hunt to resign or he will face swift impeachment proceedings.
Hunt said he is innocent of what’s alleged in the federal indictments. 
In the wake of the federal charges, other issues — like the one raised by education officials — have come to light, casting a shadow of doubt over Hunt’s ongoing tenure as auditor. 
‘The law clearly says where the money is to go’
Funding for public schools has been enshrined in the state Constitution since 1872 in an effort to provide a fair and free school system for West Virginia children.
Counties have surplus funds after paying delinquent taxes, and other costs, and if no rightful property owner comes forward to collect the money.
County sheriffs had been required to put the funds in the General School Fund, but in 2022, lawmakers transferred many delinquent land duties to the state auditor. Before the 2022 reforms, a since repealed statute directed surplus from sheriff-run tax sales to be split among local taxing bodies.
That surplus money from delinquent property sales is one of a few funding sources for educators’ professional development, as dictated by the Legislature.
House Education Chair Joe Statler, R-Monongalia, reads legislation on the House floor March 2, 2026. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
House Education Chairman Joe Statler explained that professional development is important as lawmakers try to address education reform, including implementing new ways of teaching reading. 
“Things are changing rapidly in the education world, and if our educators are going to be brought up to date on the new technologies and everything, that’s expensive,” said Statler, R-Monongalia. 
Hunt sent a memo in April to all county commissions — and copied the state superintendent — saying that, after lawmakers’ 2022 tax sale reform, it was his interpretation that unclaimed surplus from tax sales belong in the state’s school fund. He said counties that had improperly spent surplus funds prior to 2022 should pay those amounts to the auditor for the school fund. 
Blatt wrote in her July letter that she was “unaware of any discussions or deliberations that led up to” Hunt’s decision to contact county commissions. 
State code dictates that the school fund is administered by the state superintendent of schools, Blatt noted. She wanted to know what steps Hunt’s office had taken to ensure proper surplus amounts were deposited into the school fund. 
“Clearly, it is my fiduciary duty to ensure the integrity of and the proper management of that fund for the benefit of public education constituents that the people have established that Fund to benefit,” Blatt wrote.  
Hunt, a Republican, began his tenure as state auditor in 2025. His office has continued depositing surplus funds from delinquent property sales into the General School Fund, according to a document shared by the state department of education.
The state’s payment tracker showed that $445,377.95 in surplus funds collected during fiscal year 2026 were deposited into the Strategic Staff Development Fund within school funding. In the 2024 fiscal year, that number amounted to $255,837.72. 
But the education department has no clear answers about whether they’ve received the total amount they are owed or how Hunt has handled the funds. 
With public school funding woes top of mind, Statler said that lawmakers need to take a closer look at the situation. 
“The law clearly says where the money is to go, and the full amount needs to go into that area or have an accounting of it,” he said when reached by phone Wednesday.
House sidelines auditor’s bill to change school funding 
Earlier this year, the Senate unanimously passed a bill — backed by the auditor’s office — that could have changed the process for selling property with delinquent tax liens. 
The measure, Senate Bill 651, was sponsored by Senate President Randy Smith, R-Preston, and other Republican senators.
Among the proposed changes to the state Auditor’s Office, it would have altered the distribution of surplus proceeds from tax sales so that, if the former owner didn’t claim the surplus within two years, 90% would be deposited into the general school fund versus the current 100%. The auditor would keep the other 10% for the land operating fund.
“Certainly, the general school fund will be entitled to the tax dollars,” Auditor’s Office attorney Frederic Caudill told the House Judiciary Committee in March. “But we believe the surplus is a different species, and that the Legislature can do with that money as it pleases, as long as property owners who have lost their property have an opportunity to get that surplus back.” 
Kelli Talbott, general counsel for the education department, told lawmakers in that same meeting that she believed the bill to be unconstitutional.
Del. J.B. Akers, R-Kanawha, is the chairman of the House Judiciary Committee. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
“We believe the Constitution requires all monies to come to the school fund,” Talbott said. 
The House Judiciary Committee voted down the bill, with members unclear about the constitutionality of the measure. 
“At the end, our committee was left with more questions than answers, and the bill failed. At both the time and in hindsight that was the right outcome,” House Judiciary Chairman JB Akers, R-Kanawha, said on Tuesday. 
Caudill was indicted Monday in the property stealing scheme alongside Hunt and others. All five defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

title: Tennessee Department of Safety & Homeland Security questioned on immigration enforcement
description: Democratic lawmakers on Wednesday pressed the Tennessee Department of Homeland Safety & Security for details about its role in cooperating with immigration enforcement and in implementing a new policy to deny driver’s licenses to immigrants with valid federal work permits.  They received few answers. Department leaders, testifying before a legislative subcom[...]
text:
Officers from Tennessee Highway Patrol, Homeland Security Investigations, the U.S. Marshals Service and the FBI responded to a. traffic stop on Lamar Ave. in Memphis, Tennessee on Oct. 7, 2025. Democratic lawmakers are questioning officials with the Tennessee Department of Safety & Homeland Security about its role cooperating with immigration enforcement.(Photograph by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Democratic lawmakers on Wednesday pressed the Tennessee Department of Homeland Safety & Security for details about its role in cooperating with immigration enforcement and in implementing a new policy to deny driver’s licenses to immigrants with valid federal work permits. 
They received few answers. Department leaders, testifying before a legislative subcommittee, cited ongoing court challenges against them in declining to publicly respond to pointed questions.
Rep. John Ray Clemmons, a Nashville Democrat, sought an explanation for the department denying licenses to certain categories of immigrants.  
“Apparently a lot of individuals who are legal residents of the state are being denied licenses in an inconsistent manner,” Clemmons said. “Can you speak to that?”
In recent months, the department began rejecting applications for driver’s licenses and license renewals from immigrants with valid work permits, citing state law. Hundreds of immigrants statewide, including so-called “Dreamers” who were brought to the country as children and are protected from deportation were turned away at driver’s license offices despite being issued Tennessee licenses for many years.
A Nashville judge earlier this month ordered the department to resume issuing licenses to immigrants authorized to work in the country while litigation against the state agency continues.
Court extends order requiring Tennessee to issue driver’s licenses to Dreamers, other immigrants

Russell Shoup, assistant commissioner at the department, cited the ongoing litigation in declining to respond, drawing an immediate rebuke.
“So you can’t speak or reassure the people of Tennessee right now who are legal residents that they are not going to be unlawfully denied their licenses, unable to work, unable to take their children to school, get to church in any way whatsoever now,” Clemmons said. 
“We are very limited on what we can say,” Shoup responded.
Clemmons also questioned the Tennessee Highway Patrol’s decision to enter into a cooperative agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, giving state troopers the authority to enforce federal immigration law. “Public school absenteeism has spiked as families fear to venture out for fear of detention by ICE or cooperating agencies, including the Tennessee Highway Patrol,” Clemmons said.
“A lot of legal residents, law-abiding citizens in my district were targeted, pulled over. It’s not uncommon for the Tennessee Highway Patrol to be on some of these streets….I do not appreciate (immigration enforcement) giving the state of Tennessee I love and that I’m proud of a bad name and instilling fear in children,” Clemmons said. “Please be mindful of the impact you have on people’s lives, whether you’re asked to do it or not asked to do it.”
Shoup cited ongoing litigation for his response that spoke more broadly to the professionalism of state troopers.
Federal judge denies request to block TN Highway Patrol traffic stops conducted in tandem with ICE

“I assure you that Commissioner (Jeff) Long and I love Tennessee in the same way you do,” he responded. “Without speaking to something being litigated, troopers make — in every operation — probable cause traffic laws…We are trained for that. We are for every operation we’ve taken part in.”
State Sen. Sara Kyle, a Shelby County Democrat, questioned the Tennessee Highway Patrol’s presence in Memphis as part of a multi-agency law enforcement presence convened by President Donald Trump that has made thousands of traffic stops and detained hundreds of immigrants.
Kyle noted there was community anger in her district stemming from the presence of hundreds of federal and state law enforcement officers and the detention of immigrants who live there.
“The anger that has been brought by stopping and taking or kidnapping immigrants, it has just changed our city,” Kyle said. “We are getting a bad rap. I want you to be aware the economy is failing because people are not taking jobs. They won’t drive to certain areas.”
“When we’re trying to improve our city, whoever you all need to talk to, the higher ups, the administration…this has got to come to an end,” she said. “The message is, ‘please stop.’”
But Kyle’s comments drew a rebuke from Rep. Justin Lafferty, a Knox County Republican.  “I know you guys can’t talk about some of the stuff going on because of the legal status or what have you, but the mischaracterization that you all are kidnapping people is appalling to me,” he said.
