name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Lawsuit Against DHHL Is Not Just About Housing
description: Much of the public commentary surrounding the Ryan v. Watson lawsuit filed this year has focused on the 50% blood quantum requirement for Hawaiian Home Lands. For our community, this debate touches identity, family histories, and the urgent need to hold the state of Hawaiʻi and the Department of Hawaiian Home Lands accountable to their […]
text:
Much of the public commentary surrounding the Ryan v. Watson lawsuit filed this year has focused on the 50% blood quantum requirement for Hawaiian Home Lands. For our community, this debate touches identity, family histories, and the urgent need to hold the state of Hawaiʻi and the Department of Hawaiian Home Lands accountable to their trust mandates.
Yet the lawsuit raises questions far beyond Hawaiian Home Lands. Brought by Eric Ryan, president of the Hawaii Republican Assembly, and represented by the Pacific Legal Foundation, a national public-interest law firm, it challenges the distinction between Indigenous political and racial classifications.
When the foundational trust instruments of the Native Hawaiian people are treated as mere equal-protection hurdles rather than solemn compacts, we are not just debating real estate — we risk the legal erasure of our standing as a people and the rights secured for future generations.



Ideas showcases stories, opinion and analysis about Hawaiʻi, from the state’s sharpest thinkers, to stretch our collective thinking about a problem or an issue. Email news@civilbeat.org to submit an idea or an essay.


Read More

The Trojan Horse Of “Equal Protection”
In his First Amended complaint, filed Oct. 23, 2026, plaintiff Eric Ryan continues his constitutional challenge to the Hawaiian Homes Commission Act. He invokes the Fourteenth Amendment’s equal protection clause against the State and the equal-protection component of the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause against the federal government, arguing that the HHCA’s ancestry-based eligibility requirements constitute an impermissible racial classification.
The HHCA should not be reduced to a racial preference. It is a federally established remedial trust intended to rehabilitate an Indigenous population that suffered catastrophic demographic decline, widespread land dispossession, and the loss of its independent government.
The Legal Reality
Three legal considerations are central:

The Political Classification: In Morton v. Mancari (1974), the Supreme Court recognized a classification grounded in tribal political status and self-government as political, not racial. In Rice v. Cayetano (2000), the Court struck down ancestry restrictions in state-administered OHA elections under the Fifteenth Amendment but declined to decide whether Mancari applies to Native Hawaiians. The HHCA presents a distinct question involving a federal trust enactment incorporated into Hawaiʻi’s statehood compact.
The Statehood Compact: Section 4 of the 1959 Admission Act required Hawaiʻi to incorporate the HHCA into its Constitution and restricts changes to beneficiary qualifications without federal consent. This binding federal-state compact is central to understanding the HHCA, rather than treating it as an ordinary state housing preference.
Federal Trust Responsibilities: On Jan. 16, 2025, the Department of the Interior issued Solicitor’s Opinion M-37083 addressing federal trust responsibilities concerning Native Hawaiians and Hawaiian Home Lands. Suspended for review on February 28, 2025, it remains a record of legal analysis, not currently operative guidance.

Ryan nevertheless seeks to subject HHCA eligibility requirements to strict scrutiny as a racial classification, notwithstanding the trust’s distinct federal statutory foundation.
The Domino Effect
The constitutional reasoning advanced against the HHCA could have implications beyond Hawaiian Home Lands if courts or future litigants attempt to apply it to other Native Hawaiian institutions.
Consider Princess Bernice Pauahi Bishop, the last direct descendant of the Kamehameha royal line. Her will established a private charitable trust providing for Kamehameha Schools, directing trustees to give “the preference to Hawaiians of pure or part aboriginal blood” in educational support for orphans and others in need.
Pauahi’s bequest reflects her enduring commitment to her people’s future. Although the Bishop Estate rests on a legal foundation distinct from the HHCA, broader arguments concerning ancestry-based protections warrant vigilance. We must safeguard these institutions while recognizing the distinct legal foundations upon which each stands.
The Broader Constitutional Stakes For Water Rights
Ryan v. Watson does not directly challenge water rights, but its legal theories offer a cautionary lesson. Traditional and customary practices, including water uses, are protected under Article XII, Section 7, of Hawaiʻi’s Constitution, subject to state regulatory authority. Article XI, Sections 1 and 7, establish public-trust duties concerning natural resources and water.
The Waiāhole Ditch decisions affirm those duties, including protection of water for traditional uses. Rights involving kalo cultivation, gathering, and cultural practices have independent constitutional and public-trust foundations. We must remain alert to arguments that could undermine them.
A Call For Unity And Action
Prince Jonah Kūhiō Kalanianaʻole initially advocated a 1/32 eligibility threshold to include as many beneficiaries as possible. The 50% requirement emerged from political compromises with powerful sugar and ranching interests.
These interests operated within a plantation-dominated political economy with deep ties to missionary-descended families and business leaders, some of whom participated in the 1893 overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom. Kūhiō’s struggle to secure homelands unfolded within that legacy of land dispossession and concentrated political power.
The Department of Hawaiian Home Lands is under legal threat. DHHL
We cannot allow external legal challenges to exploit internal debates over eligibility to dismantle the trust itself. Those seeking reform and those defending the trust share the same objective: preserving Kūhiō’s legacy of rehabilitating our people on ancestral land.
As litigation proceeds, the Native Hawaiian community must remain informed, engaged, and prepared to defend its rights. We must exercise our political agency to safeguard our inheritance for generations yet unborn. We must do more than defend what earlier generations secured; we must strengthen our political institutions, advance our constitutional development, and protect our vested rights and the international standing of the Hawaiian nation.
Prince Kūhiō did not fight to secure a permanent foundation on ancestral soil only to see that legacy threatened by legal arguments that reduce our political and trust rights to matters of race alone.
E kū paʻa i ka ʻāina — stand firm on the land. It is now up to us to protect that heritage. This is our ʻāina, our wai, and our future. We cannot afford to wait for someone else to defend them.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Commentary: Bookman: Welcome to Bleorgia
description: Is Georgia now blue? With every statewide office in the hands of Democrats, you’d probably have to say yes. And while the abruptness of the transformation has been stunning, it’s also true that it has been coming for a long time. The signs were there. For example, you now have to go back an entire […]
text:
Georgia U.S. Sens. Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock appeared at a rally for Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024. Both senators have now been reelected since originally winning the seats in 2020, with Ossoff winning this month by 18 percentage points. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderIs Georgia now blue?
With every statewide office in the hands of Democrats, you’d probably have to say yes. And while the abruptness of the transformation has been stunning, it’s also true that it has been coming for a long time. The signs were there.
For example, you now have to go back an entire decade, to 2016, to find the last time a Republican won a U.S. Senate race in Georgia. Since then, Democrats have won four consecutive Senate races, two by Raphael Warnock and two by Jon Ossoff. The first two were extremely close, but the margins grew in the more recent two, with Ossoff putting a cherry on top by winning his re-election race by 18 percentage points. 
As they say in the sports world, you are what your record says you are. And the record says we’re blue.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
You also have to consider that Joe Biden carried the state in 2020, and while Donald Trump won it narrowly in 2024, I doubt even the most optimistic Georgia Republican would put big money on winning the state’s 16 electoral votes in 2028. It’s just hard to imagine the trend line reversing so quickly.
So for the state Republican Party, it’s time to stare into a mirror and be honest about what you see. How did you get here, and what do you do next? If your spouse has left you, your kids won’t talk to you, you lost your job and the mortgage is past due, what now? 
Do you keep doing what got you in this situation, or do you alter course?
They got in this predicament because the state of Georgia and the state Republican Party have both changed significantly in the last decade, but they’ve changed in different directions. 
While the state has grown more diverse and less conservative, the state GOP has done the opposite. Instead of making peace with that diversity, instead of embracing it and adapting to it, Georgia Republicans have used it to fuel a backlash against such changes. 
That strategy worked, for a while, and in large parts of the state it still does. Those GOP state legislators who survived the midterm debacle did so because they represent districts that remain deep red to this day, so they may not feel pressured to alter course. 
But in statewide races such as a U.S. Senate campaign, that strategy does not work and never will again. The demographic changes have simply become too profound to overcome: Every voter they win by advocating an aggressive anti-immigrant platform, for example, is offset by two voters who they drive away with that policy.
Look at the Mike Collins campaign for Senate. He took a hardcore, juice-the-base MAGA strategy that ought to work well in his deep-red home congressional district – a district that Trump won by 21 points – then used it as a blueprint from which to run a statewide campaign. 
He lost by more than 700,000 votes. 
The details are even more damning. Even though Collins sat at the top of the ballot, he got 200,000 fewer votes than the Republican candidate for agriculture commissioner. That means even Republican voters went out of their way to reject him and his message. His performance was so bad that he won his own deep-red 10th District by less than a percentage point. Two years ago, he had won re-election in that district by 26 points.
So blue state or not, Georgia is not a MAGA state. In fact, you could even argue that it never was. Our last Republican senator, the one we elected a decade ago, was the late Johnny Isakson, a moderate who today’s GOP base would run off as a RINO. Our three most recent Republican governors, Sonny Perdue, Nathan Deal and Brian Kemp, were all conservative, and were all re-elected to second terms, but none of them governed in the MAGA fashion.
If Republicans fear that Democrats are going to do real harm to the state, they need to become competitive again as quickly as possible. That process begins by understanding that the Georgia they once knew no longer exists, because the people of this state have decided it shouldn’t.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan Court of Appeals affirms unconstitutionality of abortion limitations
description: In a ruling issued Tuesday, a panel of judges on the Michigan Court of Appeals unanimously ruled that limitations on abortion procedures within Michigan’s public health code are unconstitutional, a decision that was celebrated by reproductive rights advocates. The specific mandated limitations in question are a 24-hour mandatory waiting period, uniform infor[...]
text:
A sign at the Michigan Pride rally in Lansing on June 26, 2022. (Photo by Laina G. Stebbins/Michigan Advance)In a ruling issued Tuesday, a panel of judges on the Michigan Court of Appeals unanimously ruled that limitations on abortion procedures within Michigan’s public health code are unconstitutional, a decision that was celebrated by reproductive rights advocates.
The specific mandated limitations in question are a 24-hour mandatory waiting period, uniform informed consent requirements, a physician participation mandate and mandatory screening for coercion.
The suit, which was first heard in the Court of Claims, was brought by the Northland Family Planning Center, alleged that these provisions in the law “unconstitutionally burdened the right to abortion without serving the limited compelling purpose of protecting the health of an individual seeking care, that each provision was inconsistent with accepted clinical standards of practice and evidence-based medicine, that the provisions imposed requirements that intruded on the autonomous decision making of patients, and that the provisions discriminated in the protection and enforcement of the right to reproductive freedom.”
In the decision from the Court of Claims, which was issued in May 2025, the court decided that the mandatory 24-hour waiting period, the uniform mandatory consent requirement and the physician mandate were unconstitutional and issued a permanent injunction enjoining enforcement of those provisions.
Planned Parenthood of Michigan to close three clinics after funding cuts

However, the lower court did not rule that the mandatory screening for coercion was unconstitutional, arguing that it is neutral on the face of the law. The Court of Appeals, on the other hand, ruled that because the statute prohibits only coercion to abort, not coercion to become pregnant or continue a pregnancy, it “risks operating in a manner that discriminates against individuals who seek to exercise the full range of reproductive choices guaranteed by our Constitution.”
The decision goes on to say that the Court of Claims did not fully interrogate the question at hand, “namely, whether the law, as applied, impermissibly discriminates in the enforcement of reproductive rights by creating a disparate impact on those who do not wish to continue a pregnancy, or who are coerced to become pregnant. The absence of such analysis renders the lower court’s decision incomplete with respect to the constitutional issues presented.”
As such the court remanded the decision to the Court of Claims, which “must determine whether the statutory framework, both in its language and in its application, comports with the constitutional mandate of equal protection in the enforcement of the right to reproductive freedom” and must complete “a searching examination not only of the statutory text, but also of the real-world consequences of its enforcement.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Reproductive rights advocates, including Planned Parenthood of Michigan President and CEO Paula Thornton Greear, welcomed the decision. 
“Michigan voters decided that decisions about pregnancy belong to the person who is pregnant, and this ruling holds the state to that,” Thornton Greear said in a press release issued Wednesday. “These laws had nothing to do with patient health, because they delayed care, forced people to read state-written material no clinician would hand a patient for any other kind of care, and limited who could provide that care — and now the courts have said so twice.”
Thornton Greear also encouraged the incoming Democratic-controlled Legislature, which will convene in January, to update the laws in statute, instead of relying on court decisions to prevent the enforcement of the limitations — a priority that she has previously called on legislators to take up in the new legislative session.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: After 32 years, Indiana Libertarians are just shy of the votes they need to keep ballot access
description: A few hundred votes could end the Indiana Libertarian Party’s 32-year run of automatic ballot access – and a new minor party has secured its place on future ballots. Libertarian Lauri Shillings received 38,663 votes in the race for Indiana secretary of state, or 1.987% of the 1,945,765 votes recorded in preliminary returns from all […]
text:
Secretary of state was the top race for candidates this year in Indiana. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)A few hundred votes could end the Indiana Libertarian Party’s 32-year run of automatic ballot access – and a new minor party has secured its place on future ballots.
Libertarian Lauri Shillings received 38,663 votes in the race for Indiana secretary of state, or 1.987% of the 1,945,765 votes recorded in preliminary returns from all 92 counties.
At that vote total, the 2% threshold is 38,916 votes, putting Shillings 253 short. Former Indianapolis Mayor Greg Ballard received 70,068 votes, or 3.60%, for the Lincoln Party.
The final vote and turnout totals could still change slightly. County certified returns were due Tuesday, but counties have until Friday to make corrections, according to the Indiana Election Division.
Stephanie Dasbach, chair of the Libertarian Party of Indiana, said the party is waiting for certified results and will help its 2028 candidates gather signatures if needed. She did not say whether the party would seek a recount or file a legal challenge if Shillings falls short however.
“We cannot know anything until the final certified results are out,” Dasbach told the Indiana Capital Chronicle. “We will pursue any avenues we can to ensure that every vote is counted and that the election is secure.”
The Nov. 3 election drew nearly 2 million Hoosiers, or about 42% of registered voters, up from about 40% in the 2022 midterms. The bigger change was in how people voted. Nearly 45% of ballots were cast absentee, up from about 37% four years earlier.
Absentee in Indiana includes both in-person early voting and mail-in ballots.
Laura Merrifield Wilson, a political science professor at the University of Indianapolis, said losing automatic ballot access would make it harder for Libertarians to field candidates under their party’s name.
“Of course, if they’re able to clinch the 2%, then the conversation is moot,” Wilson said. “But that said, this would be I think a major loss for the party.”
What 2% gets a party
Democrat Beau Bayh won the secretary of state race with 1,007,815 votes, or 51.8%, in the preliminary count. Republican Max Engling received 829,083 votes, or 42.6%.
For the two minor parties, the same race determined how easily they could put candidates on the ballot in future elections.
Indiana allows a minor party whose secretary of state candidate receives at least 2% and less than 10% of the vote to nominate candidates by convention. If the preliminary results hold, the Lincoln Party would gain that option and the Libertarians would lose it.
Libertarian candidates seeking a printed spot on the ballot will have to petition for it. The signature requirement is based on 2% of the vote in the most recent secretary of state race within the district the candidate seeks to represent.
Libertarian candidate Lauri Shillings listens to a question during the Indiana Secretary of State Debate hosted by the Indiana Debate Commission, Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, at WFYI Public Television Studios in Indianapolis. (Photo by Doug McSchooler for Indiana Debate Commission)
The Libertarian Party of Indiana has held ballot access since 1994.
Dasbach said the party expected Shillings to clear 2%. She said Shillings was “largely locked out of the media coverage given to her three opponents” and still drew more than 38,000 votes.
“The results of this election showed that a significant Hoosiers continue to want more options and are dissatisfied with what the Republicans and Democrats are sending them. Nearly 6% of Hoosiers voiced their displeasure with the major party candidates in a very high-profile, high-turnout race in which candidates spent millions of dollars,” Dasbach said. “Obviously, our expectations were to reach the 2% ballot threshold, but this was a uniquely challenging race and environment this season.”
The next secretary of state race in 2030 would give the party another chance to qualify for automatic ballot access.
Dasbach said the party expects to change how it recruits and supports candidates and members regardless of the final tally.
Wilson pointed to a competitive race between the major-party nominees and a second option for voters looking beyond those parties as two factors that may have made it harder for Shillings to reach 2%.
She said Ballard, a former Republican, may have appealed to moderate Republicans who wanted an alternative to their party’s nominee.
Losing automatic access could change where Libertarians put their time and resources ahead of the next election, Wilson said.
Voters make their selections at Allisonville Christian Church in Indianapolis on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
“Now they’re going to have to look at candidate recruitment probably a little bit differently, at the political infrastructure for campaigns a little differently,” Wilson added. “I think they were likely able to rely on a base of libertarian or nonpartisan voters who chose them because they were an alternative to the two primary parties, not necessarily because of what they stood for or that those voters were super loyal or allegiant to the libertarian message.”
About one in three of Ballard’s votes came from Marion and Hamilton counties, which together accounted for about one in five votes in the secretary of state race. Ballard drew 5.9% in Marion County and 5.3% in Hamilton County, compared with 3.6% statewide.
Shillings received at least 2% of the secretary of state vote in 62 of Indiana’s 92 counties, according to preliminary precinct returns.
Chad Kinsella, an associate professor of political science at Ball State University, said it’s hard to know how voters would have voted in a race without Ballard.
“Some of those people could have gone to the Lincoln Party, but I don’t know that if we got rid of the Lincoln Party, that all of those people or even some of those people would have necessarily gone to Libertarians,” he said. “I think there’s a group of people out there that are disaffected. And I have a feeling that this election, it was a lot of Republicans that were very happy to go for any third party because they were really angry with their party.”
More absentee ballots, fewer Election Day votes
Indiana recorded 1,997,142 ballots from 4,768,979 registered voters in this year’s preliminary turnout figures. That’s 115,582 more ballots than in 2022, when 1,881,560 Hoosiers voted. Turnout rose from 39.5% to 41.9%.
The state recorded 892,609 absentee ballots this year, nearly 204,000 more than the 2022 report listed. The reported Election Day count fell from about 1.2 million four years ago to about 1.1 million this year. Indiana’s absentee category includes early in-person voting and voting by mail.
Indiana recorded nearly 204,000 more absentee ballots than the state reported in 2022, even though the overall number of ballots grew by only 116,000. The reported Election Day count fell by about 94,000.
Bayh puts Indiana Democrats back in winning column with secretary of state victory

In Tippecanoe County, about 38% of registered voters cast a ballot, up from 32% in 2022. The county’s absentee share rose from about 47% to 60%.
Marion County recorded nearly 38,000 more ballots than in 2022, with turnout rising from 34% to 41%. Hamilton County turnout increased from 48% to 52%, and its absentee share climbed from 41% to 53%. In Monroe County, turnout jumped from 41% to 47%.
In Johnson County, turnout held at about 39%, but the share of ballots cast absentee rose from 47% in 2022 to 55% this year.
Still, overall turnout remained below Indiana’s last two presidential elections.
State turnout figures show that about 65% of registered voters cast ballots in 2020 and 62% did so in 2024.
Wilson said competitive races can give voters more reason to participate. She also said some of the growth in absentee voting likely reflects people who would have voted on Election Day taking advantage of an earlier opportunity.
“To see increases in terms of early voting and absentee voting certainly speaks to voter enthusiasm,” Wilson said. “I think it speaks to voter engagement.”
Kinsella said the shift in how Hoosiers cast their ballots stood out more than the rise in turnout. He expects more voters to take advantage of absentee options over time.
“I think here, election day voting is still going to be big,” he said. “But I do expect there are going to be more people that are going to be taking advantage of those options for voting absentee.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: 3 more RI nursing homes are about to be sold. The state must act to protect their residents.
description: Rhode Island Department of Health Director Dr. Jerome “Jerry” Larkin is about to decide whether the AdviniaCare chain can buy three more nursing homes in the state: the Respiratory and Rehabilitation Center of Rhode Island in Coventry, Greenville Skilled Nursing and Rehabilitation, and the Warren Center. The Health Services Council, the state advisory panel [...]
text:
In the last two years, more than a third of Rhode Island's nursing home beds have changed hands. (Getty photo)Rhode Island Department of Health Director Dr. Jerome “Jerry” Larkin is about to decide whether the AdviniaCare chain can buy three more nursing homes in the state: the Respiratory and Rehabilitation Center of Rhode Island in Coventry, Greenville Skilled Nursing and Rehabilitation, and the Warren Center.
The Health Services Council, the state advisory panel that reviews ownership changes of licensed health care facilities among other functions, voted to recommend approval on Nov. 10. Attorney General Peter Neronha has urged the health department to deny the sale or attach conditions, citing AdviniaCare’s high debt and its use of companies its owners control. My organization, Advocates for Better Care in Rhode Island (ABC-RI), has asked for conditions too. The director can still add them.
ABC-RI is a volunteer-run group that advocates for Rhode Islanders in long-term care. Reviewing nursing home sales is one part of our work. When someone applies to buy a Rhode Island nursing home, we read the application and check it for inaccuracies, inconsistencies, and omissions. We look up lawsuits, inspection reports, and staffing data for every home the buyers already run, here and in other states. Then we tell the council what we found. Here is some of what we found this time.
AdviniaCare, which lists its headquarters in Lincolnwood, Illinois, already owns eight of Rhode Island’s 70 Medicare-certified nursing homes. Every one has one or two stars out of five from Medicare. Three are candidates for the federal Special Focus Facility program, which is for nursing homes with a history of serious quality problems. If this sale goes through, AdviniaCare will own nearly 1 in 5 of the state’s nursing home beds.
AdviniaCare has been running the Coventry, Greenville and Warren homes since July 1, 2026, under a management agreement approved by the Department of Health. 
Between September and November 2026, state inspectors cited Coventry twice and Greenville once for “immediate jeopardy,” the most serious kind of violation, where residents are at risk of serious injury or death. According to a health department report obtained by ABC-RI, one instance involved the failure of the Coventry facility to restart oxygen for three different residents discharged from the hospital. One resident had to be readmitted to the hospital for respiratory arrest. 
AdviniaCare’s own budgets for the three homes would cut payroll by $3.3 million, based on our calculations from reviewing the application. Meanwhile, a company its owners control would collect 5% of the homes’ revenue, about $1.7 million a year, as management fees.
The seller, Mayflower Healthcare, is based in Tom’s River, New Jersey. When Mayflower started running the Coventry home in January 2024, it had four stars. By the end of the year, state inspectors had cited the home for immediate jeopardy five times and it was rated one star. The Attorney General’s office asked for conditions on Mayflower’s purchase of the three homes. The health department approved the sale in May 2025 without them.



Quotation







If this sale goes through, AdviniaCare will own nearly 1 in 5 of the state’s nursing home beds.


When ABC-RI reached out to the health department to ask why no conditions were set, we were referred back to the council’s report recommending approval. “The Health Services Council did a review that included an analysis of the applicants’ character, competence, commitment, and standing in the community; and the applicants’ ability to provide safe care,” spokesperson Joseph Wendelken said in a statement.
But four more cases of immediate jeopardy at the Coventry home were documented before AdviniaCare took over management. In October 2025, CMS inspection reports show staff performed CPR incorrectly on one resident, and dispensed a medication to another three times a day instead of three times a week as ordered. Both residents died, according to the reports. 
The application shows that Mayflower’s real estate partner, a company co-owned by Mayflower’s CEO, has an option to buy the three buildings for $25 million. It will exercise that option and purchase Coventry and Warren — then sell them to AdviniaCare’s owners for $39.4 million, according to the applications. That is $14.4 million more than its option price. AdviniaCare’s owners plan to borrow most of the money and pay it back with rent from the homes, according to their application. At the Coventry home, Medicaid and Medicare make up about 92% of patient revenue, according to its budget. That is taxpayer money, and it is meant for care.
ABC-RI asked both companies about the problems described here. We emailed three AdviniaCare executives on Nov. 5. That same week, we emailed Mayflower’s chief executive, filled out the Coventry home’s online contact form, and left the company a phone message. Two email addresses listed for the Coventry home bounced. On Nov. 15, we wrote again to both companies and their lawyer, and to Mayflower’s real estate partner, and asked for a reply by Tuesday, Nov. 17, the day the Health Services Council voted to approve their report and formally recommend approval to the health director.
We only heard back from Advinia’s vice president of operations who confirmed the annual rent for the Coventry facility and the terms of acquisition financing. 
Here is how nursing home chains commonly make money: The people who buy the home also own the building, the management company, and other businesses the home pays. ABC-RI analyzed Medicare cost reports for 13 Rhode Island nursing homes that changed hands between 2017 and 2022 and found payments to the owners’ other companies doubled after the sale, from about 7% of patient revenue to 15%. The money leaves, the home looks like it is barely breaking even, and staff are left to care for residents without enough help.
Rhode Island’s rules for licensing nursing homes require regulators to look at a buyer’s record “whether within or outside Rhode Island.” Yet with one exception, the state has not turned down a nursing home sale since at least 2007. Since January 2025, it has approved the sale of 16 homes, and 10 more sales are pending. Counting those, more than a third of the state’s nursing home beds will have changed hands in less than two years.
Industry leaders and regulators say no one else wants these homes, and that turning down a sale could leave residents with no one to run them. That is a real concern, but the state can’t keep approving every sale just because no one else applied. 
Regulators may also worry about being sued. If the health department feels the authority it has is not strong enough to hold up against a legal challenge, it should tell lawmakers what it needs. The attorney general’s office has been raising these same concerns for years.
But the residents of these three homes can’t wait for a new law. 
The director of health can add conditions to this sale now. The Office of Attorney General has proposed six kinds of conditions, including limits on payments to the owners’ own companies, money held in escrow, and independent monitoring. ABC-RI has asked for an independent monitor, paid for by the owners; no cuts to nursing hours; and no more Rhode Island purchases by AdviniaCare until none of its homes here is below three stars.
For the longer term, three changes would help. First, Rhode Island should limit what homes can pay to companies their owners also own, and require homes to spend a minimum share of their revenue on resident care, as New York does. Second, Medicaid should pay what care actually costs. State law already says rates must be “reasonable and adequate.” And third, the state should bring together nonprofit and independent operators, lenders, and funders to line up the money and management that mission-driven owners need.



How a nursing home sale gets approved in Rhode Island

The buyer applies. Anyone who wants to buy or take control of a Rhode Island nursing home must file a Change in Effective Control application with the state Department of Health. Buyers sometimes start running the home under a management agreement before the state votes, as Mayflower and then AdviniaCare did in Coventry, Greenville, and Warren.
The public gets notice. Once the health department accepts an application as complete, state law requires it to notify the public within 10 working days and give people a chance to comment. Applications are posted on the health department’s website.
The Health Services Council reviews it. This state advisory council meets in public, and anyone can attend in person or watch online. By law, it must consider the buyers’ character, commitment, competence, and standing in the community, and whether the home will give safe and adequate care. State rules put the burden of proof on the buyer and require a look at every home the buyer has run in the past five years, in Rhode Island or elsewhere. The council then votes on a recommendation.
The director of health decides. The decision must follow the council’s recommendation unless the director explains in writing why not. The director can approve the sale, deny it, or approve it with conditions. The law sets a 90-day deadline from when the application is accepted.

Any member of the public may send written comments to the health department during the comment period, and attend Health Services Council meetings in person or online. ABC-RI posts notices of new applications and Council meetings on Bluesky at abcri.bsky.social, and tracks every sale at snfsales.abc-ri.org.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Health and Human Services proposes more funding for childcare in next two-year budget
description: Another budget season has officially begun, and more childcare funding could be on the way.  Last month, New Hampshire’s state agencies published their ideal budget for the next two years, marking the first step in the months-long process to fund a new round of state operations.  Constructing the state’s biennial budget starts at individual agencies, […]
text:
Compared to the budget for state fiscal years 2026 and 2027, the department wants to use more state dollars for childcare initiatives. (Photo by Dana Wormald/New Hampshire Bulletin)Another budget season has officially begun, and more childcare funding could be on the way. 
Last month, New Hampshire’s state agencies published their ideal budget for the next two years, marking the first step in the months-long process to fund a new round of state operations. 
Constructing the state’s biennial budget starts at individual agencies, each of which drafts a budget request and presents it to the governor. Budget proposals include funding for employee salaries and benefits, equipment, technology services and money that will be required to satisfy “a particular mission and/or mandated purpose during the current fiscal year.”
On Tuesday, the Department of Health and Human Services, which houses the Bureau of Child Development and Head Start Collaboration, the state’s childcare governance authority, presented its budget to Gov. Kelly Ayotte’s team. There, DHHS Commissioner Lori Weaver advocated for the use of state general funds for the childcare workforce grant. 
“As a prioritized need, there is the 7½ million dollars for the childcare recruitment and retention program that was funded with general funds in the prior biennium,” Weaver said to a room of Ayotte’s budget advisers. 
The childcare workforce grant is a program aimed at improving childcare capacity and availability by giving programs funding to help recruit and retain employees. In its plan for fiscal years 2026-2027, Health and Human Services proposed funding the grant with state general funds.
However, amid a budget shortfall, the Legislature decided to try an unusual maneuver and fund the program using federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families dollars. The method required federal approval, which was denied, resulting in a back-and-forth between the state and federal government that ended with the money never reaching providers. 
The initiative was one of the most important for childcare providers this past legislative session, as they tried to get the Legislature to approve multiple bills that required the workforce grant to be paid for using general funds as originally intended. The department is now making the grant a “prioritized need” for the next biennium. 
Just like last biennium, the department wants to allocate $7.5 million in both 2028 and 2029 for the grant program. 
Additionally, DHHS also proposed increased state funding for the childcare scholarship program. The scholarship program provides eligible, working parents help with their childcare costs by paying a portion of their tuition directly to childcare programs. 
Participation in the program has drastically increased since income eligibility limits rose in 2024. As of June 2026, 5,601 children were enrolled in the scholarship program.
The department’s proposal allocates $183,459,343 to the scholarship program for the biennium. 
Additionally, the Child Care Licensing Unit, which handles licensing for childcare and residential programs, background checks and other health requirements, may also receive a slight budget increase of over $251,000, even though permanent positions within the unit are being reduced from 19 to 17. 
How this proposal is different than 2025
Budget proposals from state agencies include how much of the request should come from state general funds and from the federal government. For childcare, the Child Care and Development Fund is the primary source of federal childcare funding. 
Compared to the budget for state fiscal years 2026 and 2027, the department wants to use more state dollars for childcare initiatives. 
Not all childcare initiatives receive both state and federal funding, but the childcare scholarship does. Since 2020, state funding for early care and education has declined by 11%, including a 19% reduction in state funding for the scholarship program, according to the New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute. In the same period, federal funding increased by 62%. 
The department’s proposal, if approved, would reverse that trend. The Bureau of Child Development asked for over $126 million more in state general funds in the accounting category that includes the childcare scholarship fund compared to last biennium. The amount of federal funds used for this category has also decreased, making the majority of the $183.4 million the department hopes to have for the scholarship program state funding. 
Spending for the child care scholarship program could increase from what spent in 2026 and 2027. (Graphic by Maya Mitchell)
The increase in funding reflects costs that came with the 2024 eligibility changes. The department’s budget proposal for the scholarship program for state fiscal year 2026 was just over $25 million, but more than $52 million was spent, with an average monthly cost of $4.4 million. 
The new proposal also changed the placement of the workforce grant request within the budget. 
The request for the Child Development-Operations category significantly increased from last biennium due to the childcare workforce grant. For fiscal years 2026 and 2027, the department asked for $1,651,009 for its operations budget. For the next biennium, the operations request is $16,918,929 because it includes $15 million to cover the workforce grant. 
The $7.5 million for “payments to providers” was made as part of the operation expenditures for the Bureau of Child Development. In 2025, it had it’s own section of the Bureau’s budget. (Graphic by Maya Mitchell)
Last budget session, the department had to cut about $51 million worth of programs due to a historic back-of-the-budget cut imposed by the Legislature. Funding for workforce grants was housed under a separate part of the bureau’s budget and was the only item in that section. Advocates have said the isolation of the grants budget line item made it easier to cut. 
The increase in funding to childcare this year could create a similar situation. 
In Tuesday’s budget proposal meeting, Weaver said that the “significant increase in general funds” to the Division of Economic Stability, the division within the department where the Bureau of Child Development and Head Start is, is primarily due to increased funding for the childcare scholarship and the workforce grant. Administration of food assistance benefits is also driving the increased request, according to Weaver. Both have been identified as prioritized requests. 
Weaver told officials that her budget request was larger than last biennium’s due to the back-of-the-budget cuts, and increased utilization of programs like Choices for Independence and the childcare scholarship. If Health and Human Services budget cuts need to happen again, childcare funding is a larger expense. 
The new budget is far from being determined. As the agency’s budget presentations have concluded, the governor has until Feb. 15 to present her budget proposal for the House of Representatives to debate and vote on, followed by the Senate. 
Funding for the current biennium ends on June 30, 2027, and funding for the next biennium will need to begin the next day, July 1, the first day of state fiscal year 2028.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Even in replacing two Cape Cod bridges, a fight over natural gas emerges
description: Algonquin Gas Transmission, which owns the pipes delivering gas to Cape Cod, insists the new lines will be merely a required replacement. But environmental advocates are warning that the relocated pipeline could lock in the infrastructure now for a gas expansion later.
text:
IN CASE A long-running effort to replace two aging Cape Cod bridges wasn’t already complicated enough with billions in financing, regulatory hurdles, and dicey eminent domain deals, now they’re also the site of a fight over the future of natural gas. 
State and regional officials are pushing a plan to replace the nearly century-old Sagamore and Bourne bridges, which connect Cape Cod with mainland Massachusetts. The current bridges would stay open during construction, which could kick off next year, to avoid a crippling traffic bottleneck. 
But aside from the tens of thousands of vehicles that cross the Cape Cod Canal every day, the two bridges also carry pipelines that transport natural gas to warm homes and businesses on the Cape.  
That means that before any bridge demolition work can occur, the two pipelines running under both bridges will be decommissioned and replaced with one new pipeline set to be installed beneath the canal.  
Algonquin Gas Transmission, which owns the pipes delivering gas to Cape Cod and is a subsidiary of the larger Canadian company Enbridge, insists the new lines will be merely a required replacement.  
But environmental advocates are warning that the relocated pipeline could lock in the infrastructure now for a gas expansion later.  
The dispute over one of the state’s highest-profile transportation projects underscores how the controversy over a yearslong effort to move off natural gas, part of a sweeping clean energy transition, is widening and growing more contentious, especially as Gov. Maura Healey signals her openness to new gas supply. 
“Enbridge says it’s not an expansion because we’re not allowed to deliver any more gas. And our point is, well, you build a bigger pipeline, you could,” said Chris Powicki, chair of the executive committee of the Sierra Club’s Cape Cod and Islands Group. “We want to avoid that, and that’s what we’re really worried about.” 
At issue is whether the new pipeline under the Cape Cod Canal could in theory be capable of carrying more natural gas than the two current pipes that deliver to National Grid, which then distributes the fuel locally to its more than 100,000 customers on the Cape. 
The plan is for a single new pipeline to stretch for six miles with an 18-inch diameter as it crosses the canal; the current set up has two 10-inch diameter lines each. And the new pipeline, which will be buried in order to comply with recent state and federal safety regulations that disfavor gas lines exposed on bridges, would have a maximum pressure limit at roughly three times the operating pressure of the current lines in order to carry the gas a greater distance through one pipe. 
The state Transportation Department is set to reimburse Algonquin $302 million for the relocation costs. 
Melissa Sherburne, a spokesperson for the parent company Enbridge, said in a statement that the “project is not designed to, and will not, increase capacity.” And the company wrote in state filings that “this is not a system expansion and there will be no increase in transportation capacity as a result of the project.” 
The company is close to getting the necessary greenlights to proceed and start construction in spring 2027, Sherburne said. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission issued its approval late last month, and state environmental regulators endorsed the plan earlier this year, too. 
FERC agreed with Algonquin’s assessment that the project “would not result in a capacity increase” and that it’s “properly sized to deliver to National Grid the same level of service as currently contracted,” the agency wrote in its 33-page order. Pipe diameter and pressure alone don’t determine how much gas will flow through, FERC added. 
That federal approval is proving key in reassuring members of the Cape Cod Commission, which still must give one of the final remaining regulatory signoffs.  
“For me, that eased a lot of the questions that had come up at the prior subcommittee hearing, and made me much more comfortable with the project,” Tom Wilson, chair of the commission, said at a hearing on the project last week. 
But advocates are taking issue with how the company is characterizing its plans. 
Approval for the pipe replacement project alone does not grant the company the ability to increase gas supply to Cape Cod, which would require separate federal approvals. 
Algonquin wrote to state regulators that for it even to be able to deliver more gas to Cape Cod customers, significant expansion “further upstream” of the larger pipeline network in the Northeast would be needed. 
The issue, Powicki says, is that Algonquin is actively working to do just that.  
The company is looking to install a small gas expansion in southeastern Massachusetts known as Project RARE, which would serve about 600,000 customers and already has a DPU-approved contract with Eversource. Healey has supported the project and urged the Trump administration in a recent letter to speed up approval. 
And Enbridge is contemplating a much larger expansion of the pipeline system through Project Beacon, which could increase capacity by about 10 percent. The company plans to place Project Beacon in service by 2030.  
If those other projects pan out, the conditions could be ripe for Algonquin to then seek to send more gas under the Cape Cod Canal with a new pipeline that the Sierra Club estimates would offer more than double the storage and delivery capacity compared with the two current pipes.  
Powicki doesn’t dispute the need to maintain reliable gas service for customers on the Cape or that alternatives aren’t yet widely and cheaply available. 
But he and other advocates are making a last-gasp effort to push the Cape Cod Commission to condition approval of the project on a commitment from Algonquin not to increase gas supply on the Cape. 
Agency officials, however, are cautious about how their regulatory powers are constrained, since FERC has already issued its approval. The Cape Cod Commission can’t “reconsider or override FERC’s determinations” or impose conditions that “conflict with” FERC or “otherwise prohibit or unreasonably delay” the project, the commission said in a staff report last week. 
Massachusetts climate targets require the state to reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Buildings account for 35 percent of emissions statewide, and 6 in 10 Cape Cod homes are heated by natural gas, according to the Cape Cod Commission. The agency’s climate action plan calls for half of all year-round homes to switch to electric heat pumps by 2050.  
“Concern about potential for future increases in greenhouse gas emissions will persist until the project proponent provides a clear and concise statement about the capacity of the proposed pipeline as compared to the current pipelines,” Andrew Gottlieb, executive director of the Association to Preserve Cape Cod, said in written comments to the commission. 
With local commissioners set to vote on the pipe replacement approval as soon as Thursday, state and local officials focused on the pace, timeline, and success of a larger bridge project considered key to the Cape’s economy will at least temporarily be drawn into a gas pipeline scuffle.  
Paul Niedzwiecki, president and CEO of the Cape Cod Chamber of Commerce, said his support for the overall bridge replacement plan doesn’t amount to an endorsement of future gas expansion. He said the commission should ensure that any potential later attempt to increase gas service would face separate review and scrutiny.  
But because the pipeline relocation is a necessary component of the bridge project, the stakes are too high to let the current Algonquin plan get in the way, he said. 
“Let’s focus on the specifics of what’s been filed here, and let’s make sure that we get a project that is conditioned to do what it says it wants to do,” Niedzwiecki, former decadelong head of the Cape Cod Commission, said in an interview. “Let’s not cause a delay in the bridge project, increase costs there, endanger that project, which then brings real public safety and economic concerns to year-round residents of the Cape.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Wisconsin Democratic wins put ag policy focus on small, mid-sized farms
description: Democrats in Wisconsin are set to take complete control of state government at a precarious time for the state’s farmers and agricultural industry. President Donald Trump’s tariffs and war in Iran have raised the prices of seed, fertilizer, equipment and diesel while his immigration policies have hit the immigrant labor force farms rely on. This […]
text:
Cows at a Dunn County dairy farm. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)Democrats in Wisconsin are set to take complete control of state government at a precarious time for the state’s farmers and agricultural industry. President Donald Trump’s tariffs and war in Iran have raised the prices of seed, fertilizer, equipment and diesel while his immigration policies have hit the immigrant labor force farms rely on. This year, for the first time on record, there are fewer than 5,000 dairy farms operating in the state, according to federal data. 
Agricultural groups and Democratic lawmakers say the start of the legislative session in January represents an opportunity to change direction and craft policies that support farms of all sizes — rather than the focus on massive factory dairy farms and commodity crops such as corn and soybeans that defined the past 15 years with the Legislature under Republican control. 
“We’re not going to go back to Old McDonald,” said state Sen. Brad Pfaff (D-Onalaska), who previously served as the secretary of the Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection and is likely to chair the Senate agriculture committee next year. “We know that that’s not going to happen. But it doesn’t mean we have to continue the same trajectory that we’re going. We just don’t have to. And the voters don’t want us to.”
Global market forces and decades of policy decisions have forced Wisconsin farmers to decide between getting larger or shutting down. Pfaff said that leaning fully into those forces has resulted in a decline for Wisconsin’s rural communities and a growing disconnect between consumers and farmers. 
“I do think that people need to recognize that there is value in having different sizes and scales of farms in our communities,” he said. “We have an opportunity to make sure that we’ve got farms of all sizes, and I want to be able to do that. I’ve listened to these large operators. I’ve heard their stuff. I want to make sure that they can succeed as well. But you know it’s not mutually exclusive. One doesn’t have to not succeed for the other one to succeed.”
Rural voters drive Democratic wins
Michelle Ramirez-White, the government relations director at the Wisconsin Farmers Union, said Democratic wins in rural areas across the state show a shift in perspective away from the previous Republican focus on industrial agriculture. 
“The shift in perspective I think will be hugely influential to this session,” she said. “I think for us, an organization working with rural communities, the outcome from this election was really impactful. Democrats were winning seats outside of Milwaukee and Madison, coming in from rural areas, and they may not and probably don’t have identical priorities on agriculture that the previous people in those seats did. So, learning and working with them, trying to find shared goals. I think the support for small and mid-sized family farms couldn’t come at a better time. We are really in this turning point as a state and as a culture to support family farms before we really do lose them.”
Pfaff said he believes whomever Gov.-elect David Crowley chooses to be the next agriculture secretary can play an important role in speaking up for Wisconsin’s cultural identity as America’s Dairyland by standing up for all types of farms as well as pushing for more staffing, budget and capacity at both DATCP and the Department of Natural Resources. 
Supporting small farms
On the legislative side, Pfaff said he plans to work on making it easier for small farms to sell their products directly from the farm; encouraging the establishment of local butcher shops and meat processing plants; broadening the markets available to farmers; promoting farms that grow specialty crops; investing in county-level land and water conservation departments and easing the transfer of farms from one generation to the next. 
He added that in recent years the Republican-led Legislature has “put in breadcrumbs” for successful programs that help farmers be good stewards of their land and support their families. The Senate agriculture committee “rarely met,” he said and “didn’t take on the topics of the moment.” 
Ramirez-White said the Wisconsin Farmers Union’s policy goals for the coming legislative session include expanding healthcare access for farmers, restoring the ability for immigrant workers to obtain driver’s licenses, establishing a right to repair farm equipment, restoring capacity at DATCP and DNR and making it easier for farms to sell their products locally. 
Danny Akenson, an organizer with Grassroots Organizing Western Wisconsin, said that with Democrats in charge, he believes some of the agricultural policy groups that held the most sway with the previous Republican majority will adjust their strategies.
“We think that Wisconsin has a small farming heritage, and it’s about time that the groups that claim that they represent farmers really start representing small farmers first and family farmers first,” he said. “So I suspect that some organizations will maybe change their tune a little bit in the state Capitol.”
Regulating factory farms
In recent years, GROWW has played a major role in fights against data centers and factory farm expansion and contributed to winning several western Wisconsin legislative races that helped Democrats flip control of both legislative chambers. 
In the organization’s 2027 agenda, the group plans to push for increased regulations on the state’s largest factory farms, including a previously proposed bill that would require the DNR to notify neighbors and local health officials when a permitted factory farm has a manure spill or pollution exceedance. The group also wants to establish a second tier of permitting required for “mega-CAFOs” operating with more than 5,000 animal units. Current law requires a permit for any farm to operate with more than 1,000 animal units — which is about 700 dairy cows. 
Both Akenson and Ramirez-White said they want the state to look at overhauling ATCP 65, the rules that guide dairy farm operations, to help small farms compete in the market. 
Akenson referred to a GROWW member who operates a small farm with seven dairy cows and recently built a creamery on his property. Even though the milking barn and creamery are adjacent to each other, Akenson said, the farmer is required by the state to obtain a license to drive a milk truck to operate the creamery. 
“I think that we can take a look at ATCP 65 and actually lessen regulations for small dairy farms that will allow them to have more of a direct access to the marketplace and be able to basically live out the American dream,” he said. “Make it more of a small business, right? Where they’re directly feeding their communities and able to feed their communities, which is what farmers want to be able to do.” 
Akenson said he believes strengthening small farms in the state will have a ripple effect across rural communities. 
“The stronger our small farms are, the stronger our rural communities could be, and the stronger the ability for downtowns to thrive could be,” he said. “What we’ve seen slowly but surely over the last years of ‘get big or get out’ and corporate consolidation in America is that slowly but surely our rural communities are withering away and dying, right? And getting hollowed out. And one way to help that is by supporting small farmers, and supporting small farmers supports small businesses. It supports Main Street. It supports the ability of people to buy a home and live in a rural community. It really is, overall, key to revitalizing and reviving our rural communities.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: At Quivira National Wildlife Refuge, a special setting to commune with Kansas nature
description: Recently, walking through Baker Wetlands, I met a young man from Ohio. He’d left home in the early hours and stopped to stretch his legs before hitting the road again to finish his trek to Quivira National Wildlife Refuge, where he hoped to spot a certain species of shorebird. “Do you know it?” he asked. […]
text:
Sandhill cranes fly above Quivira National Wildlife Refuge. Tall birds with a six-foot wingspan, sandhill cranes are the most abundant of all crane species worldwide, unlike their larger relation the whooping crane, which is one of the most critically endangered. Both species use the refuge as a stopover during migration. (Photo by Shawna Bethell)Recently, walking through Baker Wetlands, I met a young man from Ohio. He’d left home in the early hours and stopped to stretch his legs before hitting the road again to finish his trek to Quivira National Wildlife Refuge, where he hoped to spot a certain species of shorebird.
“Do you know it?” he asked. “The refuge? Do you think I’ll see this bird?”
He handed me his phone, where a photo was displayed. I can’t recall the species, and I couldn’t say if he’d get lucky before he had to return to work on Monday. But I told him what I knew about the refuge, where his best chances might be, and wished him a safe journey.
It was nice to be reminded of the sense of anticipation felt by travelers to Quivira. Recently we’ve been bombarded by headlines and politics surrounding the fight for water on the refuge. But rarely do news accounts discuss Quivira beyond stating it is a stopover for migratory birds, which is true. But it’s so much more.
Designated in 1956 under the authority of the Migratory Bird Conservation Act and the Fish and Wildlife Act of 1956, the refuge comprises just more than 22,000 acres of diverse habitat including mixed grass prairies, sand prairies, fresh water ponds and wetlands, alkali flats, and the rare inland salt marshes that were recognized even then for their conservation value. Over the years came further designations: RAMSAR Wetland of International Importance, Western Hemisphere Shorebird Reserve Network Site and Globally Important Bird Area, to name a handful.
But what does any of this mean if someone hasn’t stood beside a rare inland salt marsh and experienced it for themselves?
For most people, a wetland — a marshland — isn’t going to fill them with the sense of majesty they feel when looking at the mountains, or the sense of eternity as when gazing the sea. No. The wonder held by these unique and highly endangered places is found in the unfolding generations of life they draw to themselves each season.
To stand beside a salt marsh during fall migration is to be immersed in a rush of activity and sound. Multiple species of ducks, including pintails with their daring black-and-white symmetry, or cinnamon teal with their eerily bright red eyes, softly chitter as they dabble and dive, providing an ever-present background music to honking geese as they arrow across the sky from all directions. But the thrill that runs through a body when you hear your first flock of cranes — likely sandhill cranes, but if you’re lucky the mythic, white presence of the endangered whooping crane — is something you do not forget. It is a rush of exhilaration.
“They’re here,” you whisper quietly to yourself.
Whooping cranes stand on the shore of Little Salt Marsh at Quivira National Wildlife Refuge. In the 1940s, there were only 21 whooping cranes in the wild. Thanks to conservation efforts, there are now just over 800, including both wild and captive populations. The sandy-colored individual pictured here with the adults is a juvenile whooping crane. (Photo by Jackie Augustine)
Then, there are the mornings when there is no sound, when the water is as still and reflective as glass. An elegant American Avocet with her head tucked into her feathers stands as graceful as a dancer in the pink dawn light. Those are the moments when you simply breathe. There is never only one sensation felt in these places. Their ever-changing elements sweep you along on a virtual tide of senses.
In the protected grassland habitats that buffer the wetlands, mammals, birds, plants and pollinators also provide visitors a glimpse of the wild. Grassland birds such as the northern bobwhite dart quickly along the roadside, while bright, perching dickcissels tip back their heads to sing their clear, lilting song. Safe habitat for these birds is imperative, as grassland bird populations overall have plummeted by 53% in the past 50 years.
In addition, reptiles and amphibians, some of which are also threatened, make their home on the refuge. A small population of Arkansas Darters, tiny colorful fish that hold a state designation for a Species of Concern, are found in the freshwater springs present at Quivira. There is not a season that does not provide something to celebrate.
So it was in the hope of celebration that I attended this year’s Audubon of Kansas Crane Festival, because for all I have seen at Quivira, I had not yet glimpsed the critically scarce whooping crane in my home state. That changed one morning standing on the shore of Little Salt Marsh.
I had not expected to see any birds that morning, as a thick fog swathed the marsh. Yet through the heavy, gray mist, I could just make out three ghost-white smudges against the far, dark shore. Slowly, those smudges materialized into the elegant forms of cranes. I caught my breath and watched those rare, beautiful creatures.
In the stillness I sent up a note of gratitude, for the birds and for this gift Kansas has been given: a wetland habitat provided by geology and time that has for generations called cranes to its shores.
A pair of cinnamon teal forage in Big Salt Marsh at Quivira National Wildlife Refuge. These birds are not rare, but they are not commonly seen at the refuge as it sits slightly east of their usual breeding and migration range. (Photo by Shawna Bethell)
Shawna Bethell is a freelance essayist and journalist covering the people and places of Kansas, Nebraska and Missouri. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Democratic budget chairs vow collaborative process after 15 years in the minority
description: Incoming Joint Finance Committee co-chairs Sen. LaTonya Johnson (D-Milwaukee) and Rep. Tip McGuire (D-Kenosha) say the next state budget process to be collaborative. text:
“I don't want to let people down,” Sen. LaTonya Johnson said. “People can barely afford their groceries, their housing, gas.” (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)Incoming Joint Finance Committee co-chairs Sen. LaTonya Johnson (D-Milwaukee) and Rep. Tip McGuire (D-Kenosha) say the next state budget process to be collaborative.
The lawmakers were named last week by their respective Democratic caucus leaders to run the most powerful committee in the state Legislature. 
The 16-member committee is responsible for drafting Wisconsin’s two-year budget and deciding how to invest billions in state revenue.
In interviews with the Wisconsin Examiner, the lawmakers said their biggest priority will be providing economic relief for Wisconsinites, but the specifics will have to be worked out through collaboration with Gov.-elect David Crowley, other lawmakers, state agencies and people across the state. 
Both lawmakers have served on the committee in past sessions, but only as members of the minority. Johnson, who was first elected to the Senate in 2016 and has been on JFC since 2018, said she recently told some of the incoming freshman lawmakers that she was jealous of them.
“It feels really, really good to be in this place, especially after being in the minority for forever,” Johnson said. “They just get to walk in and life is good. They didn’t have 13-14 plus years of misery.”
For years, Republican lawmakers cut out Democratic lawmakers from conversations related to budget writing. Members of the minority party were left to try to elevate the concerns of their constituents during meetings and at press conferences. Only in the most recent state budget did Senate Democrats gain some leverage after winning closer margins. Republicans included them in budget negotiations after some Republicans defected from their party’s budget plan.
Johnson said she’s nervous, but prepared to take on the task of leading the budget drafting. 
“I don’t want to let people down,” Johnson said. “People can barely afford their groceries, their housing, gas.”
Johnson said she spoke with McGuire before they were both named to the committee last week during JFC’s final meeting under the leadership of Sen. Howard Marklein (R-Spring Green), who lost his reelection bid, and Rep. Mark Born (R-Beaver Dam). 
McGuire, who previously worked as a Kenosha County special prosecutor and Milwaukee County assistant district attorney, was first elected to the state Assembly in an April 2019 special election. He has served on the state budget committee for the last three legislative sessions. He also told the Examiner that he is focused on helping working families afford their everyday life. 
“It is relatively straightforward what we’re trying to accomplish here,” McGuire said. “We want people to be able to afford to live in Wisconsin. We want people to be able to afford their health insurance. We want them to be able to afford their homes. We want them to be able to afford to send their kids to good schools and be able to send their kids off to college if they so choose, or be able to afford to go to technical college if they so choose. We really want people to be able to be able to choose their own economic future.” 
The process of writing the state budget begins with agencies submitting requests to the governor’s office. 
Crowley will consider those requests before proposing his own budget. After that, lawmakers on the budget committee will consider his proposal and work over several months to draft a budget bill.
The final bill needs to pass the Senate and Assembly before it goes to the governor, who will have the options of signing it, signing it with partial vetoes or vetoing the entire bill. 
Wisconsin enters 2027 with a projected $3 billion budget surplus, but with a variety of competing priorities for investment. Democrats have a tough task ahead. 
“I would love to be able to fund every single ask, but the reality is that we are working with limited dollars, and this is only the first budget that the Democrats will craft where we are in charge,” Johnson said. “We don’t have rigged maps like the Republicans did that kept them in control for 16 years, that also prolonged that suffering, pain and misery for people for 16 years. All we have right now is this one budget that we are guaranteed to be able to do.”
Johnson, a former in-home childcare provider, said making investments in mental health supports, childcare, education as well as local government are some of her top priorities. During her time on JFC, Johnson has often highlighted the enormous gap between how much the state spends on children in school versus how much the state spends on children if they become incarcerated. She says investments in early childhood could help prevent incarceration down the line. 
Still, “I’m only one person,” she said. Democrats will have to agree on their priorities before budget-writing begins.
McGuire said he is hopeful the state can increase the $7.25 hourly minimum wage which has not gone up since 2009. Given recent complications with expanding Medicaid due to changes in federal law, McGuire said he is interested in pursuing the idea of a statewide public option for healthcare to help make healthcare more affordable. He said a public option would serve as “an additional competitive element in the health insurance marketplace to help ensure that the market is competitive.” 
“That’s certainly something that we’re looking at. Obviously, a lot of that again requires collaboration with the Senate and the governor, so I make no guarantees,” he said.
Under split government, the budget process could be combative between lawmakers and Gov. Tony Evers. Republican lawmakers would throw out the majority of Evers’ budget proposals, calling his proposals a “wish list” and starting from scratch to write their own budget draft. Evers in turn angered lawmakers over the years as he threatened to veto their plans and used his powerful partial veto power to shape the budget.
Rep. Tip McGuire speaks in June 2023 at a press conference on childcare. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
McGuire repeatedly said many of the specifics, including raising the minimum wage, would come down to collaboration and discussions among lawmakers and Crowley. 
The process of writing the state budget begins with agencies submitting requests to the governor’s office. Crowley will consider those requests before proposing his own budget. After that, lawmakers on the budget committee will take up his proposal and work over several months to draft a budget bill. The final bill needs to pass the Senate and Assembly before it goes to the governor to sign or veto. 
Crowley has been deferential to lawmakers when answering questions about his priorities, saying he looks forward to working with them. 
Johnson said she wants Republican lawmakers to be involved in conversations about the budget as well, although their influence could be limited.
“I will not treat them the way they treated us. I want them to be a part of this process. I want to hear what they have to say,” she said. 
Incoming Senate Minority Leader Julian Bradley (R-New Berlin) recently said he wants to address affordability and would be open to working on a tax cut. 
Johnson was not enthusiastic about the idea. “We haven’t talked about what it is that we want to do, but I would be kind of reluctant to follow the Republican lead because that’s how they got ousted,” she said. 
Johnson also said Crowley’s team and state agencies will play a big role. 
McGuire said lawmakers have had only informal conversations with Crowley so far. 
“Once the administration starts in earnest, I think that’s when we can kind of sit down and talk through how we’re going to formally approach things,” McGuire said. “I’ll say this: one of the things I really believe is that none of us has a monopoly on great ideas, and so we are willing to listen to friends in the Senate, obviously the governor, and try and craft something.
The latest agency to submit a budget request is the Department of Public Instruction. Under the leadership of state Superintendent Jill Underly, the agency is requesting $2.75 billion — nearly the entire budget surplus — in additional aid for public schools, as well as an overhaul of the state’s school funding formula. 
McGuire said he had taken a cursory look at the proposal and appreciated Underly’s input, but he couldn’t commit to anything.
“Obviously she’s deeply invested in making sure that our public schools can be as strong as they possibly can be. I think we’re going to have to go through and see what has the biggest yield,” McGuire said, adding the state budget addresses a “tremendous” number of issues. 
“I can’t commit to taking just one budget request and putting all the money into it,” he said.
Underly recently told Wisconsin Public Radio that it is lawmakers’ job to find the money to fund public schools, and that it is time the state make public schools a priority. 
Both Johnson and McGuire said they are open to exploring ways of raising revenue and specifically named legalizing and taxing marijuana as one of the ways to do that.
“That’s something that has been glossed over, but could provide some resources for the state, especially as we see so many of our surrounding states having legalized it,” McGuire said. “We should be finding ways to make sure that that’s in a safe, responsible manner, and if the state can collect revenues off that, that’d be great.” 
McGuire said the question about raising taxes on the wealthy comes down to whether it’s needed. He said raising taxes should not be a penalty. 
“Right now, we’re sitting on a surplus,” McGuire said. “My goal is to make sure that Wisconsinites have what they need, and working people have what they need to be successful, and so I’m not going to commit to approaching something like that.” 
Johnson said she wants to see some changes to the budget-writing process to make it more accessible to Wisconsinites outside of state government. She called the Joint Finance Committee’s operation of budget listening sessions under Republicans “barbaric,” “chaotic” and “disrespectful.” 
The budget committee often takes testimony from the public as it gears up to write the budget, including holding listening sessions across the state. Typically at each location, the budget committee sits and listens to testimony all day.
Wisconsinites seeking to testify had to arrive early and often waited all day to deliver a couple of minutes of testimony.
Johnson said she is interested in allowing people to sign up for time slots to testify so they aren’t required to wait for hours; providing evening hours so people who work during the day have a chance to testify; and providing remote options so those with difficulty traveling have an opportunity to testify.
“For too long, we’ve treated the road show like we’re the center instead of the people — like they’re just there at our whim, and we really don’t care what they have to say in the process,” Johnson said. “The second most disrespectful thing that you can do is to have all those people show up and talk about their needs and their wants, and then the budget does not reflect any of it, and we see that all the time. So that I want to change.”
