name: Georgia Recorder
title: With small margins, democratic socialists could have outsized influence in Georgia state House
description: For the first time in two decades, Georgia Democrats will control the state House of Representatives when the General Assembly convenes in January. But Democrats will have a razor-thin majority. Not only will they have to work and compromise with Senate Republicans to get their legislative priorities to the governor’s desk, but they will also […]
text:
Georgia House Representative-elect Mathewos Samson, who identifies as a democratic socialist, is pictured at the state Capitol on Nov. 12, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia RecorderFor the first time in two decades, Georgia Democrats will control the state House of Representatives when the General Assembly convenes in January.
But Democrats will have a razor-thin majority. Not only will they have to work and compromise with Senate Republicans to get their legislative priorities to the governor’s desk, but they will also have to keep their House Democratic caucus united enough to pass bills in their own chamber.
A small but growing contingent of Democratic Socialists of America members may complicate those efforts as they try to push House Democrats further to the left. Democratic state Rep. Gabriel Sanchez, a lawmaker who identifies as a democratic socialist, was just reelected to a second term representing a Smyrna-area House district. Democratic state Representative-elect Mathewos Samson, who also identifies as a democratic socialist, just won an open seat representing Atlanta.
In a chamber where nearly every Democrat will be needed to pass the caucus’ legislative priorities, Sanchez and Samson will have some leverage they can use to advocate for more aggressive policies on housing, healthcare and raising the minimum wage. And they both indicated that they plan to work with their party to get their priorities passed while also pushing policies further left. 
“The reality is that there’s a two, maybe three-person majority, which means our democratic socialists Gabriel and Mathewos will have a lot of power on whether things can or cannot be passed,” said Bryan Ramirez, the co-chair of Democratic Socialist of America’s Atlanta chapter. “So, the (House Democratic) caucus is required to work with our DSA members, and that allows us to push any type of legislation further left if we can.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Democrats needed to win 91 seats to take control of the state House, and that is currently the exact number they hold. Three House races are still unresolved, with one going to a Dec. 1 runoff and two still too close to call – although a hand count just confirmed the lead of a GOP incumbent. Aside from two DSA-endorsed members, there will be 17 House Democrats – 18 if they win the December runoff – who were endorsed by the progressive Working Families Party.
But House Democratic leadership seemed confident that an economic agenda focused on addressing affordability will lessen any ideological friction across the caucus.
“Regardless of titles or labels, there is a lot of common ground and a lot of shared interest, along with a lot of shared understanding of how we need to deliver over these next two years,” said Lawrenceville Democratic state Rep. Sam Park, who was previously minority whip and will now serve as majority whip in the new session.
Rep. Stacey Evans, an Atlanta Democrat, makes a speech during a session of the Georgia House of Representative at the state Capitol in Atlanta on March 3, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
State Rep. Stacey Evans, an Atlanta Democrat who will serve as majority leader, echoed Park, saying that Democrats are united in addressing kitchen table issues.
“We are a big tent party, and whatever part of the spectrum you find yourself on – affordability, healthcare access, education – we all share those priorities,” Evans said. “I see us working on priorities that everyone can get behind, and I think that’ll go a long way toward making everyone feel like they’re contributing, that their voice matters and that their constituents are heard.”
Still, there are stark policy gaps between Democrats and its democratic socialist faction. While there appears to be Democratic unity on issues like Medicaid expansion, repealing the state’s six-week abortion ban and raising the minimum wage to $15 per hour, the Democratic Socialists of America wants to go beyond that.
“Let’s focus on that,” Ramirez said, pointing to House Democrats’ priorities. “But also let’s ensure that it’s not just $15 an hour. Let’s try to get $20 an hour. Let’s not just repeal the (abortion) ban, but provide easy and accessible access to abortion care and trans healthcare to everybody.”
Samson also said that he “definitely plan(s) to work with the new Democratic majority” and is behind longstanding Democratic priorities, but he said he also believes that lawmakers shouldn’t stop there.
“We have to end the abortion ban and also actually codify abortion as a right in Georgia. We have to expand Medicaid, but we should also strive to pass Medicare for all in Georgia,” Samson said.
While Medicare is purely a federal program, Sanchez earlier this year introduced a bill titled “Georgia Medicare for All Act,” which would have created a universal single-payer healthcare program covering all Georgians without any out-of-pocket costs. The bill did not move after it was introduced in the 2026 legislative session.
Rep. Gabriel Sanchez, a Smyrna Democrat, speaks during a session of the Georgia House of Representatives on March 3, 2026, at the state Capitol in Atlanta. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
Sanchez, who easily secured a second term in November, said he intends to work and cooperate with the incoming Democratic majority while advocating for more progressive policies.
“We just elected a new speaker nominee. It was unanimous. We’re ready to fight and work with the Democrats to fight for Georgians. We’re going to do everything in our power to work where we agree, and then if disagreements come about, we’ll have those conversations and see where we go,” he said. 
Sanchez said that he sees much of the Democratic agenda on affordability as a result of democratic socialism policies rising in popularity nationally.
“Who started that? It was Zohran Mamdani and the DSA. We are pushing our party into a direction that’s actually going to center working people and not just those at the top. We’re going to continue to do that because, again, we all agree that we want to help Georgians,” Sanchez added.
Sanchez’s incoming colleague Samson agrees and says democratic socialist policy proposals are gaining popularity with voters despite previous opposition.
Samson said that’s because democratic socialists can be more outspoken about challenges affecting workers since they act independently from corporate donors. The incoming freshman lawmaker said that Americans are listening to their economic messaging and are realizing that “the things we’re advocating for are not actually that radical.”
A number of Republicans on the 2026 campaign trail tried to tie their opponents to democratic socialism, with Congressman Mike Collins saying in his failed run for Senate that Sen. Jon Ossoff wants to “run as the DSA presidential candidate.” But their efforts seemed to flop. Two more major U.S. cities, Los Angeles and Washington D.C., elected democratic socialist mayors, and the faction quadrupled their numbers in the U.S. House of Representatives, and in some cases unseated more moderate Democrats.
“We have a moral clarity,” Samson said, pointing to democratic socialists’ view that some policies and actions by the government largely prioritizes profits over people, pointing to the war in Iran as an example.
“It’s extremely unpopular. It’s extremely undemocratic,” Samson said.
Even if progressives are successful in pushing legislation further to the left in the House, any legislation must still pass the state Senate, where Republicans hold a slim majority. Democratic leaders will have to thread a needle as they try to appease the left wing of their party while drafting legislation that can survive and move through Senate committees, says Tammy Greer, a political scientist at Georgia State University.
Georgia House Speaker-nominee Rep. Carolyn Hugley, a Columbus Democrat, speaks at a press conference on Nov. 12, 2026, at the state Capitol, announcing the caucus’ picks for leadership roles. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
Although House Democratic leaders will have to work differently with more progressive members of their party than with Senate Republicans, “the skill set is the same for the Democrats,” Greer said. 
“The Republicans and DSA may have different reasons and directions for their opposition,” Greer said. “Yet the communication skills and the compromise, or the ability to negotiate, is the muscle that Democrats are going to really flex or learn or enhance this legislative session, this one and the next one, to get anything passed for the governor’s agenda.”
Greer also said that with a fast-paced, 40-day legislative session, it leaves little room for intraparty disagreements.
“They don’t need to spend those 40 days fussing with each other,” she said. “And so, are they prepared to lead, to start January reading from the same book, same chapter, same page, same line? And if they’re not, then that’s going to hamper any progress.”

title: Ohio Senate Republicans pass bill banning diversity, equity and inclusion in K-12 schools
description: Ohio Republican lawmakers in the state Senate passed a bill Wednesday banning diversity, equity and inclusion efforts in Ohio’s K-12 public schools. The bill will have to be passed by the Ohio House, agreed upon by both chambers, and signed by the Ohio governor before the end of the year to become law. Ohio Senate […]
text:
The Ohio Statehouse. (Photo by Megan Henry/ Ohio Capital Journal)Ohio Republican lawmakers in the state Senate passed a bill Wednesday banning diversity, equity and inclusion efforts in Ohio’s K-12 public schools. The bill will have to be passed by the Ohio House, agreed upon by both chambers, and signed by the Ohio governor before the end of the year to become law.
Ohio Senate Bill 113 passed with a 21-10 vote during Wednesday’s Senate session. Ohio Republican Senators Bill Blessing and Tom Patton joined Ohio Senate Democrats in voting against the bill. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The bill would require every local board of education in the state to adopt a policy that would end any current diversity and inclusion offices or departments and ban any diversity, equity, and inclusion orientation or training. 
It would also prevent the creation of any new such offices or departments and using DEI in job descriptions. 
Each school board of education would be required to create a complaint process for an alleged violation of the policy and the board would investigate the complaint with a hearing. 
“This bill is designed to remove politics from the classroom,” said state Sen. Andrew Brenner, R-Delaware, who introduced the bill. 
“Our schools should be places where students of every background and belief feel welcome, without being expected to subscribe to a particular political or social philosophy,” he said.
Brenner added an amendment to the bill on the Senate floor. 
“This amendment makes it clear that nothing in this legislation should be interpreted as requiring school districts to prohibit services for students with disabilities, English learners, or any other services required under federal law,” he said. 
Ohio Senators debated the bill for nearly an hour before voting to pass the bill. 
“Our educators should be encouraged to incorporate diversity, equity, and inclusion into their training and teaching practices,” said Ohio Senate Minority Leader Nickie Antonio, D-Lakewood.
“I can say as a former educator that while strides have been made, this bill’s passage would be a step backwards rather than a progression forward.”
State Sen. Jerry Cirino, R-Kirtland, asserted that diversity, equity and inclusion efforts do not promote diversity, equity and inclusion.
“It promotes preference,” he said. “It is not equitable because it discriminates inherently. It is not inclusive because it classifies people as being either victims or perpetrators.”
Cirino authored Ohio Senate Bill 1, a controversial higher education law that, among other things, bans diversity efforts at Ohio’s public universities. 
“The instruction that we’re giving in the classroom should not be based on one class of individuals is lesser or greater than the other, based upon their immutable characteristics,” said Ohio Senate President Rob McColley, R-Napoleon. 
“That the idea of all of that is distinctly un-American, and we should try to get back to the basics.”
Ohio Sen. Kent Smith, D-Euclid, said the bill is anti-American and bad business policy.
“Diversity, equity, and inclusion is about building an America that respects and works for all of us across all races, all socioeconomic status, all genders, backgrounds, and abilities, faiths, and sexualities,” he said. 
The bill has received lots of backlash. About 100 people testified against the bill compared to less than a dozen people who testified in favor of the bill. 
The bill now heads to the Ohio House for consideration. Ohio House Speaker Matt Huffman, R-Lima, said he thinks his caucus would support the bill. 
“There’s a short period of time to get a lot of things done,” he said. “I think it’s consistent with a number of other provisions that we have passed over the past several years.” 
Any bill that does not pass before the end of the year must be reintroduced in the new General Assembly to be considered.

title: Ohio secretary of state wants to oversee voter rolls in new office as state auditor
description: Frank LaRose was the only Ohio Republican to win a statewide executive office on Nov. 3. Now, as he prepares to become state auditor, he wants to hang on to some of the power over voting he has as secretary of state. That has his Democratic successor, Ohio Secretary of State-elect Allison Russo, crying foul. […]
text:
Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose talks to reporters. (Photo by Susan Tebben/Ohio Capital Journal)Frank LaRose was the only Ohio Republican to win a statewide executive office on Nov. 3. Now, as he prepares to become state auditor, he wants to hang on to some of the power over voting he has as secretary of state.
That has his Democratic successor, Ohio Secretary of State-elect Allison Russo, crying foul.
As secretary of state, LaRose repeatedly purged voting rolls in ways that critics said canceled eligible voters. 
He did that and restricted voting in the name of election security. But LaRose repeatedly failed to show that voter fraud is a significant problem in Ohio.
Now, as he prepares to leave the secretary of state’s office in January, LaRose wants to keep power over the voting rolls when he becomes auditor, an office he won by less than two percentage points.
On Tuesday, LaRose told Signal Statewide that as auditor he wanted the authority to doublecheck voter rolls to protect against errors — and alleged voter fraud.
“It is a huge task to maintain the accuracy of our voter rolls. We’ve done a really good job of it,” LaRose told the publication. “I think having an outside validator to look at that and audit that would be useful.”
LaRose’s office didn’t respond to questions from the Capital Journal — including one asking why, during his eight years as secretary of state, he never proposed that the Republican state auditor doublecheck voting rolls maintained by his office.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
For her part, secretary of state-elect Russo didn’t buy LaRose’s story that he was merely interested in election integrity.
“I share the goal of maintaining accurate and up-to-date voter registration lists, and as secretary of state, I intend to follow the law and uphold the highest standards of integrity and accuracy in that work,” she said in a written statement. 
“But Ohioans deserve to know that the integrity of our elections and the privacy of their personal information will not be compromised for political purposes.”
Russo alluded to LaRose’s controversial decision in March to turn over millions of Ohio voter files to a U.S. Department of Justice run by President Donald Trump, who has a long history of lying about election fraud.
“Maintaining voter lists should never become a political exercise or, even more alarming, a backdoor attempt by Auditor-elect LaRose to continue sharing Ohioans’ private data with the federal government and the U.S. Department of Justice,” Russo said. 
“Ohioans deserve an elections system that is secure, transparent, and free from political interference. That will be my commitment as Secretary of State.”
In the face of losses at the polls, Republicans in the past have moved to strip incoming Democrats of power over elections. 
In North Carolina in 2024, GOP legislators moved to take power to appoint members of the state elections board out of the governor’s office and hand it to the state auditor. At the time, Democrat Josh Stein was about to become governor, while Republican Dave Boliek was about to become auditor.
After being crushed at the polls Nov. 3, Republicans across the United States are trying to change the rules to retain power.
In Ohio, legislative Republicans last week proposed a change that would make it easier to override Democratic Gov.-elect Amy Acton’s vetoes.
In Texas, outgoing Republican Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick is working to change the rules to cut the great power his office wields over the state Senate — one of the few power centers in Texas that the GOP will still control come January. Patrick lost to his Democratic opponent by 6.1 percentage points.
Back in Ohio, House Minority Leader Dani Isaacsohn, D-Cincinnati, mocked LaRose for what Isaacsohn implied was an attempted power-grab. 
“Does Frank LaRose also want some of the governor’s job?” Isaacsohn asked. “Does he want a little bit of the treasurer’s job? Which statewide office does Frank LaRose not want folded into the auditor’s office?”
Isaacsohn added, “Frank LaRose this whole week seems to just have decided that because he squeaked by as the only Republican in Ohio to survive the election, Ohioans want him to have all of the jobs.”
Capital Journal reporter Megan Henry contributed to this story.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio senators consider eliminating data center sales tax exemption
description: With just a few weeks left in the current session, a bipartisan measure nixing Ohio’s data center sales tax exemption got its first hearing in the state Senate. After Ohio voters soundly rejected data centers at the ballot box, there’s little question about the appetite for reining in the industry. Still, the measure faces long […]
text:
Alabamans hold up signs that read “No Data Center” at a County Commission meeting on Aug. 24, 2026, in Hayneville, Alabama, in the Lowndes County Courthouse. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)With just a few weeks left in the current session, a bipartisan measure nixing Ohio’s data center sales tax exemption got its first hearing in the state Senate.
After Ohio voters soundly rejected data centers at the ballot box, there’s little question about the appetite for reining in the industry. Still, the measure faces long odds for passage.
Ohio Senate Bill 374 sponsors Sens. Louis Blessing, R-Colerain Twp., and Kent Smith, D-Euclid, have been trying, one way or another, to roll back the state’s data center sales tax exemption since 2024. Their current bill is very simple: it blocks state officials from awarding new exemptions starting in Oct. 2027.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Smith explained when they initially drafted the bill, official estimates put the tax break’s annual cost at $130 million. In reality, it cost Ohio $1.5 billion in 2025 alone.
“For that reason, there is now bipartisan outcry to end this tax break,” Smith said.
Lawmakers actually eliminated the exemption as part of the state budget last year. Gov. Mike DeWine vetoed the provision arguing it played a role in attracting investment to the state.
“Gov. DeWine himself may have actually had a change of heart,” Smith added, “when he paused the data center tax break while the legislature considers the policy.”
Data centers go 0-for-21 in ballot initiatives around Ohio

Earlier this year, lawmakers tried a different tack, cutting the tax break in half through Ohio House Bill 646. The measure, which makes several changes to data center policy in Ohio, sputtered out before lawmakers left for the summer recess.
Ohio state Sen. George Lang, R-West Chester, acknowledged the tax incentive is unfair, but downplayed its significance.
“I can only speak to one that I know of in Butler County,” he said. “The fees the data center was going to pay up front far exceeded any sales tax that would have been collected over a decade had the sales tax been in there.”
As for the $1.5 billion in foregone tax revenue, Lang said in his opinion the state “doesn’t need the money” and he expressed doubts about how responsibly the state would spend the cash if it had it.
Blessing said one option lawmakers could consider would be backfilling state education funding.
“If we don’t do that,” he said, “we’re just going to continue to see more and more levies, more and more school cuts.”
Lang also asked if they’d accept an amendment trading elimination of the tax break for an end to data center moratoriums. Blessing said to get there, lawmakers would likely need to follow the model of the Ohio Power Siting Board. The state could probably extract better deals, he said, than a township or village.
But given the results of November’s election, it’s far from clear local governments would welcome state control over siting — even in exchange for more local tax revenue.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Measles is making a comeback in Ohio, and everyone is paying for it
description: A year ago, I wrote a commentary on the importance of vaccination. Apparently too many people skimmed it because measles is back in Ohio. According to the Ohio Department of Health, Ohio has had 327 measles cases this year, only 20 of which came from out of state. Compare that to last year’s statewide total […]
text:
Diseases like measles have surged to the highest level in decades in the United States. (Photo by Getty Images Plus)A year ago, I wrote a commentary on the importance of vaccination. Apparently too many people skimmed it because measles is back in Ohio.
According to the Ohio Department of Health, Ohio has had 327 measles cases this year, only 20 of which came from out of state. Compare that to last year’s statewide total and the number of measles cases in the state this year is already seven times as high as it was in 2025. Measles is a serious disease previously eliminated from the United States that can cause pneumonia, hospitalization, and even death among children who contract it.
Measles is also a costly disease that is expensive to treat. Researchers at Johns Hopkins University’s Bloomberg School of Public Health recently conducted a review of 120 studies of the cost of measles outbreaks. They estimated that the average cost of an outbreak was $43,000 per case. Much of that is wrapped up in the cost of initiating a public health response, which they estimate at the cost of about $300,000. Additional cases cost about $16,000 from there in the form of medical treatment and public health costs.
This means Ohio’s outbreaks this year have cost the state economy $5.6 million in a scenario using the fixed- and marginal-cost numbers above and $14 million using the average-cost number, with the latter possibly being closer to the truth since public health efforts have not been centralized in the state. Whatever the exact cost, it’s likely that measles is costing the state economy millions of dollars already.
How can Ohio protect children from measles and polio?

These dollars mean something. Dollars spent treating measles represent health system capacity not spent treating other diseases, caring for our elderly, or spent on preventive medicine. 
One of the tragedies of measles is how preventable it is. Measles had previously been eliminated from the United States due to widespread vaccination. But barriers to access to vaccination and rising vaccine skepticism has led growing numbers of parents to opt their children out of vaccination. 
The social problem with flagging vaccination rates is the spillover effects of skipping vaccination. Denying your child vaccination not only puts your child at risk, it also puts their friends at risk. It’s kind of like driving your kids to school while drunk: you are putting your own children at risk while putting other people’s children’s lives at risk, too. And the further a community gets from total vaccination coverage, the more likely they are to experience a costly and potentially deadly measles outbreak.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Local public health officials have some tools at their disposal to encourage vaccination rates. Targeted outreach to communities with flagging vaccination rates could help get more children vaccinated, protecting them and their classmates. Making sure school-based health centers are a place where children can get vaccinated and parents can learn about the benefits of vaccination can increase access to vaccination and increase uptake rates.
Cities and counties can support local health departments by making sure they have the funding needed to run vaccination programs. While vaccination is a low-cost intervention for staving off costly disease, different approaches to encouraging vaccine uptake should be evaluated and effective interventions should be shared widely. Communities across the country are grappling with this problem and if local communities can learn from one another they could find effective ways to encourage vaccination, save money, and save hospital visits and even lives.
Ohio is going to be spending money on measles either way. The question is whether policymakers would rather spend money treating measles or preventing it. Lucky for us, prevention is cheaper and safer than treatment. If we can find effective ways to encourage vaccine uptake, it’s a win-win for Ohio.

 Catching Our Eye

• Voter rolls. Cleveland.com reports, “Secretary of State-elect Allison Russo rips LaRose proposal that auditor review voter rolls.”
Secretary of State-elect Allison Russo accused incoming state Auditor Frank LaRose of trying to politicize Ohio’s voter rolls after LaRose asked Republican lawmakers to give the auditor’s office authority to review the state’s voter registration lists.
Russo, a Democrat who will succeed LaRose as secretary of state in January, said LaRose has been responsible for maintaining those lists during his eight years as Ohio’s chief elections officer and questioned why he now wants another office to scrutinize that work.
• Max Miller lawsuit. The Washington Post reports, “Judge tosses Max Miller’s suit against ex-wife, says abuse claim ‘substantially true’”
An Ohio judge on Monday dismissed a defamation lawsuit filed by Rep. Max Miller against his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, after concluding that Moreno’s allegation that Miller once doused her with hot water are “substantially true.”
Miller, an Ohio Republican, filed the lawsuit in May after the Daily Mail published an article that detailed Moreno’s domestic abuse allegations against her ex-husband. Among the allegations was that Miller threw hot water at her during an argument in 2024.
Miller and Moreno, the daughter of Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), married in August 2022, had a daughter in November 2023 and divorced in June 2025.
• Provisionals. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Jo Ingles reports, “ACLU says law firm has raised questions about some provisional ballots in Ohio.”
Letters from Taft Law have been received by several county boards of elections, said the American Civil Liberties Union of Ohio. The civil rights group said it’s unsure how many counties may have received the letters, which tell the county boards to set aside provisional ballots from registered Ohio voters who had not updated their voter registrations after a county-to-county move.
“What they are saying is the poll workers and the secretary of state were wrong about the proper procedures, and because of that, thousands of votes should not be counted,” said David Carey, managing director of the ACLU of Ohio in an interview.
Carey said he suspects counties that were targeted are those with close Ohio House races. Taft Law represents some Republican candidates for office.
Democrats flipped at least eight seats in the Ohio House, breaking the Republican supermajority in that chamber. As of Nov. 5, there were four House races that were separated by 134 votes or less. Unofficial results also show there were 102,148 provisional ballots cast statewide.
• 2028. Politico reports, “‘A savagely brutal map’: Senate GOP braces for 2028.”
Sen. Bernie Moreno isn’t sugarcoating things. The incoming chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee will be in charge of defending 19 GOP seats in 2028 — and he’ll need to flip at least six more to regain control of the Senate majority.
“Looking at it right now, it’s absolutely a savagely brutal map,” the Ohio Republican said in an interview on Capitol Hill.
• Old coal. The Guardian reports, “These US coal plants on the Ohio River shut down years ago. Now, residents say their waste is destroying lives.”
Millions of people downstream in Cincinnati and Louisville depend on the Ohio River for drinking water. While coal-powered electricity plants have been phased out in recent years, their presence has cast a long, dangerous shadow in the form of coal combustion residual (CCR) landfills.
The residual material, typically made up of ash, boiler slag, silica and other waste substances, contain dangerous constituents that can cause cancer and neurological illnesses. Communities along this stretch of the Ohio River have been suffering with the fallout for years.
While the national incidence rate of lung and bronchus cancer is 51.8 per 100,000 residents, in Clermont county, it’s 69.6. In the neighboring Hamilton county, from where much of the waste being dumped comes from, the rate is 62 per 100,000.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Alsobrooks backing Schumer over Van Hollen in race for Senate majority leader
description: Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) said she remains friends with senior Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D), but she will support current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) as Democratic leader in January, when Democrats take control of Congress.
text:
U.S. Sens. Angela Alsobrooks and Chris Van Hollen, both Maryland Democrats, in a July 2025 photo. Van Hollen is running to unseat longtime Senate Democratic leader, Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y,), in the next Congress, but Alsobrooks said this week she will vote for Schumer. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D) said she remains friends with senior Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D), but she will support current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) as the Democratic leader in that chamber in January, when Democrats take control of Congress.
“Chris is a friend. He’s a respected colleague. He will continue to be that. He has every right to run in this and I support that,” Alsobrooks told reporters Wednesday.
But Alsobrooks said she had already decided to back Schumer before Van Hollen, at the urging of progressive groups, announced that he would challenge Schumer, who has been the Democratic leader in the Senate since 2017.
Alsobrooks acknowledged when traveling the country to stump for various candidates, voters said they wanted change in the current leadership on Capitol Hill.
“When I hear people say they want generational change, I hear them. I agree with them. We ought to have new ideas, new leaders and new faces at the table. We have a talented caucus,” she said. “But I would like the conversation right now to quickly go back to how do we solve these problems that the American people were abundantly clear that they wanted us to solve.”
A Van Hollen spokesperson said in an emailed statement Wednesday afternoon that the senator continues to talk with Alsobrooks and remains grateful for the support he has received from various Marylanders and community leaders.
Schumer ‘confident’ he’ll lead US Senate Democrats again, despite criticism

“He continues to have conversations with Senator Alsobrooks and is also speaking with a wide range of his colleagues and hearing about their desire for change,” the spokesperson said. “He will keep discussing with them his view for the future of the Democratic caucus, in response to Americans’ call this election.”
Some progressives have long been disenchanted with Schumer, who they say has not done enough to confront the Trump administration and has been too cozy with Israel. They have said the “blue wave” of Democrats that led to them winning control of both chambers of Congress in this election was a call for systemic change in leadership.
Van Hollen has emerged as a leading progressive voice in the Senate, a critic of both Republican President Donald Trump and Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. He made national headlines with a trip to El Salvador last year, where he demanded a meeting with Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Maryland resident who was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and erroneously deported.
Van Hollen hardly represents generational change — he is 67, while Schumer will turn 77 next week. But he began calling for a race for leader, not a coronation, and continues to draw support from progressive groups, like the U.S. Council of Muslim Organizations.
“The American people delivered a resounding mandate for real policy change in the 2026 midterm election,” the council said in a statement Wednesday. “Before it was easy or popular to do so, Senator Van Hollen singlehandedly stood up to the Trump administration and confronted the forces of political corruption that have harmed our nation’s politics here at home and our policies overseas.”
But progressive groups won’t vote in the election for a new leader, the 55 incoming Democratic senators will, in a closed-door meeting of the caucus currently scheduled for Dec. 1. And among senators, the numbers are currently running strongly in Schumer’s favor, according to published reports.
At least a dozen have come out for Schumer, citing his hand in the party’s sweeping success in this year’s elections, compared to just four for Van Hollen. Those include Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats, who has said he’s supporting Van Hollen.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
But a number of senators have said publicly that they will not vote for Schumer, without committing to Van Holler, and the greatest number is just keeping mum for now.
Meanwhile, Van Hollen and Alsobrooks have supported each other throughout the years as they sought various offices, including her successful 2024 Senate primary campaign against former Rep. David Trone (D). Alsobrooks went on to defeat former Gov. Larry Hogan (R) in the general election that year, becoming Maryland’s first Black U.S. senator.
She also made history in 2024 when she and Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) became the first two Black woman elected to serve in the Senate at the same time. They will be joined in January by a third Black woman, Illinois Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton (D), elected to succeed Sen. Dick Durbin, who did not seek reelection this year after five terms in the Senate.
Meanwhile, history was made across the Capitol on Wednesday morning when House Democrats voted 251-11 to nominate Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY.) for Speaker. If Jeffries is elected in January, he would become the first Black speaker of the House.
All seven House Democrats from Maryland, including Rep.-elect Adrian Boafo (D-5th), who was elected to succeed Rep. Steny Hoyer next year, voted for Jeffries.
“I firmly believe we cannot go back to a Congress of the past,” Rep. Sarah Elfreth (D-3rd) said in a statement, “which is why I am working with Speaker Jeffries and all of my colleagues to ensure that House Democrats use every tool, gavel, and subpoena power to relentlessly deliver on behalf of the American people.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Deputy Health Secretary Briskin stepping down in December, as state braces for Medicaid changes
description: Deputy Health Secretary Perrie Briskin, the top official for the state's Medicaid program and healthcare financing, will step down at the end of the year, as the state grapples with Medicaid changes under HR 1. But experts say she is leaving a strong team behind.
text:
Deputy Secretary Perrie Briskin giving an overview of how Medicaid operates in Maryland during her first week on the job in August 2025. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters).Deputy Health Secretary Perrie Briskin, the top official for the state’s Medicaid program and healthcare financing, will step down from the position at the end of the year, officials with the Maryland Department of Health announced this week.
Maryland Health Secretary Meena Seshamani notified department staff of Briskin’s departure in an email Tuesday, thanking the deputy secretary for “her service and commitment to advancing health coverage across the state over the past two years.”
“Over her tenure, Perrie has provided exceptional leadership and dedication to Maryland Medicaid, guiding critical policy and operational initiatives that serve more than 1.4 million Marylanders,” Seshamani said in the email.
Deputy Medicaid Director Rayva Viginkar will “serve as Healthcare Financing and Medicaid interim leader during this transition,” the department said in a statement Wednesday.
Briskin said she is planning to step away at the end of December to spend time with her family.
Health official warns that future Medicaid cuts could lead to $2.7 billion loss in federal funding

The announcement comes as the state braces for new Medicaid eligibility requirements Congress approved in the 2025 budget reconciliation legislation known as HR 1 – sometimes referred to as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.”
Medicaid is a joint federal-state healthcare plan for low-income households, with state officials administering the program. Come January, Medicaid recipients will need to prove that they’re working at least 80 hours per month, unless they meet certain exemptions, and they need to renew their coverage twice a year instead of annually, among other changes.
Those changes are expected to force thousands of Marylanders off the Medicaid rolls, due largely to administrative churn. Federal officials recently gave states an extra six months, until July, to prepare for the changes, but advocates said job No. 1 for Briskin’s replacement will be to ensure that as many people as possible retain coverage in the face of the changes.
“It’s a tough job,” said Gene Ransom, CEO for MedChi, the Maryland State Medical Society.
Vincent DeMarco, president of the Maryland Healthcare for All Coalition, echoed those concerns.
“The next person will have a very tough job to continue to protect Maryland from the attacks from the federal government,” he said. “Medicaid is important for the people on it and for all of us, because when everyone has healthcare, we all benefit.”
But DcMarco said he believes Briskin has built a strong strong framework to ease the transition.
“She and her team at MDH have done a terrific job of protecting Marylanders from the horrors created by HR 1 and the Trump administration’s attacks on Medicaid,” he said.
Briskin started with the department in January 2025 as chief of staff for Maryland Medicaid, and became deputy secretary for healthcare finance and director of Maryland Medicaid in August 2025.
Before her time with the state, she was the senior adviser to the director of Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program Services at the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.
Administration gives states 6 more months to implement Medicaid work requirement

Briskin started her tenure as deputy secretary at a transitional time for the health department. Several high-level officials had stepped away, including her predecessor, Ryan Moran. State officials were starting to untangle how steep cuts to Medicaid and similar programs under HR 1 would impact Marylanders. And the Maryland hospital system was transitioning to a new payment model after long negotiations with federal officials.
In her time as deputy secretary, not only has she overseen the administration of Maryland Medicaid and helped guide the health department through frequent federal policy changes, she also helped to improve internal administrative processes for Medicaid eligibility and fill leadership vacancies within the department.
“I am incredibly proud of the work we have accomplished at Maryland Medicaid and grateful for the opportunity to serve Marylanders alongside such a dedicated team and so many committed partners,” Briskin said in a text Wednesday.
“I have tremendous confidence in the team’s leadership and ability to carry this work forward, and I know Maryland Medicaid’s commitment, priorities and work will remain unchanged through a smooth transition,” she said.
While that may be, DeMarco said she will still be missed.
“She’s just done a terrific job at MDH, had really hard times,” he said. “We’re going to miss her and wish her well on her new endeavors.”

title: House keeps most of leadership, committee posts intact for upcoming legislative session

text:
House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk, left, speaks with Chief Clerk Sylvie C. Siegert. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Democrats appear to have gained four more seats in the House of Delegates, raising their supermajority from 102 seat in the 141-member chamber this year to an unassailable 106, but little else will be changed when lawmakers return in January for the 2027 legislative session.
House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel) released a list of leadership and committee chair positions Wednesday that are largely intact from the 2026 session.
“We have a challenging year ahead, with difficult budget decisions and consequential issues facing our state,” Peña-Melnyk said in a statement on the appointments. “Meeting that moment requires strong leadership, experience, and perspectives that reflect the people and communities from every corner of Maryland.”
Peña-Melnyk once again tapped Del. Luke Clippinger (D-Baltimore City) to serve as speaker pro tem, Del. David Moon (D-Montgomery) as majority leader and Del. Ashanti Martinez (D-Prince George’s) the majority whip.
The chairs and vice chairs for six of the eight standing committees will remain in place from this year’s 90-day session:
Meet the new bosses, same as the old bosses: Senate reelects leaders for next session


Appropriations Committee: Del. Ben Barnes (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel) as chair and Del. Anne Kaiser (D-Montgomery) as vice chair;
Economic Matters: Del. Kriselda Valderrama (D-Prince George’s) as chair and Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery) as vice chair;
Environment and Transportation: Del. Marc A. Korman (D-Montgomery) as chair and Del. Michele J. Guyton (D-Baltimore County) as vice chair;
Government, Labor and Elections: Del. Melissa Wells (D-Baltimore City) as chair and Del. Kenneth Kerr (D-Frederick) as vice chair;
Judiciary: Del. J. Sandy Bartlett (D-Anne Arundel) as chair and Del. Debra Davis (D-Charles) as vice chair; and
Ways and Means: Del. Jheanelle Wilkins (D-Montgomery) as chair and Del. Jessica Feldmark (D-Howard) as vice chair.

Del. Heather Bagnall (D-Anne Arundel) will continue serving as chair of the Health Committee, with Del. Terri L. Hill (D-Howard) moving into the vice chair slot to replace outgoing Del. Bonnie Cullison (D-Montgomery), who has served in the House since 2011.
The eighth standing committee, Rules and Executive Nominations, will be chaired by Del. Marvin Holmes (D-Prince George’s), who moves up from vice chair. Del. Anne Healey (D-Prince George’s), who decided not to seek reelection, ends a House career that began in 1991. The new vice chair will be Del. Emily Shetty (D-Montgomery).
A few other changes in the House include Del. Cheryl Pastuer (D-Baltimore County), who will be deputy speaker pro tem. Pasteur replaces Del. Dana Jones (D-Anne Arundel), who will serve as the Democratic Caucus chair, replacing Shetty.
Del. Jared Solomon (D-Montgomery) will serve as the parliamentarian to replace Sen.-elect C.T. Wilson (D-Charles), who moves across the hall, where he was assigned Wednesday to that chamber’s Finance Committee.
Dels. Jackie Addison (D-Baltimore City) and Teresa Woorman (D-Montgomery) will serve as the two chief deputy whips. They replace Del. Vaughn Stewart (D-Montgomery) and Sen.-elect Tiffany Alston (D-Prince George’s). Stewart will be chair of Economic Matters’ Banking, Consumer Protection and Commercial Law Subcommittee, while Alston has been assigned to the Senate’s Education, Energy and the Environment Committee.
“I am confident in the team we have assembled, and I am especially proud of the women serving in leadership roles across the House,” Peña-Melnyk said. “Together, we are ready to meet the challenges ahead and deliver for Marylanders.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Commentary: Lasting legacy of lame-duck Florida governor: Refusal to deal with climate change
description: Did you see what happened last week in Delray Beach? It was a hoot! The city council reviewed the anti-diversity measure that Gov. Ron DeSantis signed into law and concluded it could no longer use public funds to support the city’s popular St. Patrick’s Day Parade. If you can’t spend public money promoting any ethnic […]
text:
Heavy rains and king tides caused massive floods all up and down Florida's East Coast, including in this neighborhood in Indian River County. (Photo via Indian River County Sheriff's Office)Did you see what happened last week in Delray Beach? It was a hoot!
The city council reviewed the anti-diversity measure that Gov. Ron DeSantis signed into law and concluded it could no longer use public funds to support the city’s popular St. Patrick’s Day Parade. If you can’t spend public money promoting any ethnic group, then that must include the Irish.
Faith and begorrah, me lads and lassies, it kicked off quite a kerfuffle!
Of course, they should have focused their Eire — er, I mean ire — on the legislators who passed this law thinking it would only affect people who looked different from them, and the governor who apparently signed it with both eyes closed.
DeSantis reacted to this perfectly logical legal conclusion with what my Cracker grandmother used to call “a conniption fit.” He accused Delray Beach of committing the horrible crime of “malicious compliance.”
Isn’t that hilarious? It’s like a state trooper pulling you over and yelling at you for driving the speed limit. How dare you obey the letter of the law! I bet you’re such a sicko you renewed your license and registration in a timely manner!
When I stopped giggling, though, it dawned on me that “malicious compliance” could be the best way to deal with the biggest legacy of our lame-duck governor. I am speaking, of course, of climate cha — oh wait, he doesn’t want us to talk about that.
But we sure have been talking about the effects lately. Take that combination of record rainfall and king tides that’s led to massive flooding along the Atlantic coast.
“King tides and strong northeast winds are causing significant flooding concerns across Northeast Florida, with impacts that a National Weather Service forecaster says resemble those of a tropical storm,” WJXT-TV in Jacksonville reported. One resident captured footage “showing neighbors using kayaks to reach their homes.”
“Between 15 and 20 inches of rain have fallen in parts of Florida, turning roads into rivers, submerging cars and coming close to the state’s single-day rainfall record,” ABC News reported, focusing on Brevard County.
“Treasure Coast citrus growers are wading through what they described as the worst flooding event the local industry has ever seen,” the Treasure Coast newspaper chain reported.
“King tides are sweeping into South Florida more often, supercharged by sea level rise and other weather factors that are sending more saltwater into streets and buildings from Fort Lauderdale to Miami,” the Miami Herald reported last week.
And we’re not done. “Severe storms dumped as much as 8 to 10 inches of rain overnight in parts of Broward County, leaving neighborhoods underwater, flooding major roadways and forcing Memorial Regional Hospital in Hollywood to temporarily suspend visitation,” WPLG-TV reported Wednesday.
Bear in mind that this all-liquid blue wave happened without a hurricane hitting the state. It was influenced by a super-strong El Nino that was clearly a product of, well, you know.
Since we’re not supposed to mention that c-word, my Delray-inspired recommendation is that from now on we call it something equally descriptive: The DeSantis Effect.
Kayaks in the streets of St. Augustine via screen grab.
 The soggy state
Dirty emissions from the fossil fuels we burn in our power plants, factories, and cars began baking our world during the Industrial Revolution and continue to do so today. They’re why we’re warming up like we’re living in a frying pan.
As a semi-tropical, mostly flat state surrounded by water, Florida has long been on the front lines of that … uh … phenomenon the governor wants us to ignore.
We’re seeing lots of impacts. The list includes increased temperatures even at night, storm surges that go further inland because of sea level rise, hurricanes that became more intense more rapidly, a boost in the number of mosquito-borne diseases, and lots of toxic algae blooms, as well as a heightened acidity in the seas on both sides of us.
How bad is it? Last year, a Florida plant, the Key Largo tree cactus, became the first species in the world to be completely wiped out by that thing we’re not allowed to talk about. The cacti, known for their height (up to 20 feet), were washed away by rising seas.
We’re no longer the Sunshine State. We’re the Soggy State.
When DeSantis has mentioned the folks who would rather see Florida take action to counter this stuff than pretend it doesn’t exist, he’s complained that they’re members of “the church of the global warming leftists.”
Yet not too long ago, Florida had a Republican governor and Legislature that tried to fight back. No leftists in that congregation!
Former U.S. Rep. Charlie Crist, now mayor-elect of St. Petersburg. (U.S. House photo)
In his first State of the State Speech in 2007, then-Gov. Charlie Crist called the c-word “one of the most important issues that we will face this century,” After all, Florida ranked among the top 25 producers of greenhouse gases in the world.
Crist signed a series of executive orders imposing far-reaching changes for the state’s energy policies. Then he persuaded the Legislature to pass a bill calling for the state to set up a cap-and-trade system to limit emissions.
Unfortunately, wealthy healthcare executive Rick “I Wear My Navy Cap Because My Yachting Cap Looks Too Fancy” Scott replaced Crist and junked all that stuff. When scientists tried to talk to him about it, he refused to even discuss it.
DeSantis and Scott don’t like each other, but they’ve taken a similar approach to this issue: Silence is golden.
Now here we sit, 16 years later, needing kayaks to navigate our streets. If this place gets much wetter, Walt Disney World will have to cut a deal with Kevin Costner to change its name to “Water World.”
 More than mere words
Unlike Scott, DeSantis acknowledged that the cli — oops, sorry! — that thing we don’t discuss was changing. But he insisted that cutting our emissions would be bad for the economy, and instead we should burn MORE fossil fuels.
Hey Guv, you know what’s really bad for our economy? Repeatedly flooded streets, homes, offices, factories, and stores.
Not one person in state government should be surprised about this flooding. The website for the Florida Climate Center, at Florida State University, warns, “Extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent and intense as average temperatures rise.”
The only way FSU could have been clearer about that is if the ’Noles had set up speakers all around the Capitol to repeatedly play Bob Dylan’s “A Hard Rain’s Gonna Fall.”
Yet DeSantis didn’t just block the discussion about this. He vetoed a bill that would have spurred the state to buy more electric vehicles. He signed into law one that bars state and local governments from adopting net-zero greenhouse gas emissions policies. He even turned down $377 million in federal funding for energy efficiency initiatives.
Now can you see why I say we should call it the DeSantis Effect? He’s earned it!
 Harder to live here
When I have questions about that thing that starts with a C, one of the first people I call is John Morales, a TV meteorologist in South Florida since 1991. He’s now chief scientist for a company he founded called ClimaData.
John Morales via NBC6
When I asked him about the flooding along the East Coast, he reminded me that this was far from the first time it’s happened. Storms that hit Fort Lauderdale in 2023 dropped 26 inches in 24 hours, an amount so excessive it would make Noah start rounding up all the animals.
A warmer atmosphere tends to hold more moisture, he explained. That’s why Florida is being hit repeatedly by precipitation so destructive that people are calling it a “rain-bomb.”
Meanwhile, the rising sea level pushes king tides further inland, blocking the seaward flow of rain-swollen canals and other waterways, he said. It intrudes into the underground aquifer just as the rain is starting to soak into the ground and fill the aquifer.
The result: Flooding that keeps getting worse as well as more expensive.
Is it any wonder insurance costs are going through what’s left of the roof?
“It is increasingly hard to live in Florida,” Morales said.
 Settled science
Two years ago, in the wake of another rain-bomb flooding Hollywood, DeSantis angrily rejected any attempt at drawing a connection between the watery disaster and his hostility to … um, you know.
“Our energy bill that we did, it wasn’t about saying or not saying ‘climate change,’” DeSantis insisted, according to Politico. “It was a substantive piece of legislation to say that in the state of Florida our energy policy is going to be driven by affordability for Floridians and reliability.”
Ah yes, “affordability,” the big political catchphrase of the past election.
But Florida’s property insurance bills show that repeated weather-related disasters are making Florida less and less affordable. Just cleaning up after the flooding is hurting affordability.
Repairing your swamped car, peeling wet baseboard out of your house, cleaning the septic waste out of your bedroom — those all hurt homeowners’ ability to afford life in Florida.
These are all signs of the DeSantis Effect — increasingly destructive and expensive weather-related disasters.
Isn’t that the perfect term for it? Now that I think about it, calling it that really isn’t malicious compliance. I think it’s more accurate than that c-word thing. This is the effect that DeSantis has ensured we have to deal with.
Why is he so allergic to even discussing it? My theory is that he hopes to get financing from the oil companies for his next presidential run. That’s assuming he can make donors forget two years ago, when DeSantis campaigned in all 99 counties in Iowa and lost every one of them.
The good news is, in a couple of months, he’ll pack up his go-go boots and scoot out the door.
Dawn Shirreffs, Florida director of the Environmental Defense Fund, via EDF
Dawn Shirreffs, director of the Environmental Defense Fund’s Florida office, said she hopes his successor, Byron Donalds, and the new leadership of the Legislature will take up the challenge of making changes. They’ll ignore it at their political peril, she contended.
“This election showed what happens when the voters don’t feel heard,” she explained.
In 2023, when he was in Congress, Donalds told a committee that when it comes to climate change, “I don’t think that the science is settled.”
I hope the Florida scientists who tried to talk to Scott will tell Donalds that the c-word science actually IS settled, and it’s past time to do something about it.
After all, Donalds’ big promise is to make Florida more affordable. Stepping up to deal with all that expensive flooding would go a loooong way toward achieving that goal.
However, there’s one more aspect to the DeSantis Effect likely to cause problems.
 Tying their hands
While he was shutting down discussions of the double-C, DeSantis did spend a lot of the taxpayers’ money on “resiliency.”
That’s a bureaucratic buzzword that means “blowing big bucks on an infrastructure stopgap.” He handed out money for lots of pumps, pipes, and seawalls.
That’s a legitimate pursuit. A lot of stormwater facilities that were built in the 20th century can’t handle the ginormous quantities of runoff we’re seeing now. Unfortunately, whatever we add now probably won’t be able to handle the even larger quantities that will hit us in the next decade or so.
Jennifer Juraldo via Linkedin.
One person I called about this month’s rain-bombs was Jennifer Jurado, chief resilience officer for Broward County. She told me her county had scrambled to prepare for the deluge before it hit, managing water levels in canals, figuring out what storage was available and worrying about how much room is left in the aquifer.
The county has created a $20 million grant program to help municipal governments add infrastructure to deal with flooding caused by rising sea levels, she said.
“We are on the cusp of being able to get a suite of projects in the ground,” Jurado said.
Just one little problem: Amendment 3, the property tax “reform” measure DeSantis pushed to tie the hands of local governments and make them turn to Tallahassee for help.
Now that that measure passed, she said, “our ability to move forward with all of these projects is … substantially questionable. There is a question whether we will get any of it done.”
That’s another disaster we can chalk up to the DeSantis Effect!

name: Maryland Matters
title: Chamber report calls for fixing budget woes with improved business climate
description: Maryland's ongoing budget issues are linked to an economy that lags behind the nation over the last decade. A forthcoming report from an arm of the Maryland Chamber of Commerce argues that an improved business climate will grow state revenues over time.
text:
A new report from the Maryland Competitiveness Institute finds the state is falling behind when it comes to business climate. The institute is a new nonprofit research arm of the Maryland Chamber of Commerce. (Image courtesy Maryland Competitiveness Institute)Maryland’s ongoing budget issues are linked to an economy that has lagged behind the nation over the last decade. A forthcoming report from an arm of the Maryland Chamber of Commerce argues that an improved business climate will grow state revenues over time.
The report is the first from the Maryland Competitiveness Institute, a nonprofit research arm of the state chamber. Both will be officially introduced to the public during a chamber conference Thursday morning in College Park.
The report — the first in a series of expected data dives — comes at the same time that lawmakers and Gov. Wes Moore are looking at four years of project multibillion-dollar projected budget gaps.
“Our biggest concern is they’re going to start taxing businesses to pay for these decisions that were made years ago, and that is not the way to get out of this,” Maryland Chamber President and CEO Mary Kane said in an interview Tuesday. “Our goal is to grow the economy, not tax our way out of this. We will never win if that’s the only way we’re doing it.”
Maryland faces a series of significant budget challenges starting next year, when the projected budget gap approaches $3 billion. The projections worsen over the following three years.
Maryland Chamber of Commerce President and CEO Mary Kane. (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
Much of the problem is driven by increasing costs of the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future education program.
“When we budget with aspirations, which we should do, sometimes we find ourselves in a place where we look at now, where we have to have some very, very challenging discussions about what’s available, what additional resources may be available, and what has to be adjusted for growth to match what resources are there,” Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore) said during a Wednesday budget briefing.
Kane said improving the business climate must be coupled with realistic budgeting practices.
“It should always be realistic,” Kane said during Tuesday’s interview. “I’m sorry, budgets for states should not be aspirational. What they should be are realistic and attainable.”
The practice goes hand-in-hand with an improved business climate called for by the report, she said.
Among the findings, the report notes that Maryland’s economy grew less than 12% over the decade between 2015 and 2026. That compares with a 25% growth rate nationally over the same period.
“We have to have some realistic discussions about where we’re going forward because we’re losing businesses here,” Kane said.
“There are businesses that are leaving, and that is not the way we’re going to be able to fund our economy. It’s the business community that hires more people, that pay more taxes, that are actually going to grow us out of this problem.”
Additionally, the report finds the state lags behind others when it comes to businesses surviving past a critical three-year mark. It ranked the state 45th in startup businesses that convert into companies that hire new employees.
“Businesses are actually the thing that make for a healthy community,” Kane said. “When people have great jobs, when they can buy houses, when they can raise a family, that’s growing your community.”
The report points to Virginia as a potential model for improving Maryland’s economy. Both states were hit by cuts to federal employees. Maryland and Virginia each saw comparable cuts to federal jobs, though the hit to Maryland represented the biggest percentage of any state.
“A lot of the talk has been about DOGE, and that our economy has been drastically affected by DOGE,” Kane said of the Department of Government Efficiency, the Trump administration effort to slash the size of federal government.
“We went back 10 years,” she said. “Yes, our economy was affected by DOGE, absolutely, as was Virginia’s economy. But what happened? … Why isn’t Virginia in the same position that we are?”
Kane said the goal of the newly formed institute is to gather data to make the case to lawmakers that improving the economy and state revenue picture is inexorably linked to nurturing the business growth.
“Our pitch is competitiveness, and you are seeing them talking more about Maryland being more competitive, we cannot keep passing budgets that we don’t have money to pay for,” Kane said.
“You don’t grow the economy on nonprofits or on government,” she said. “You grow it on having healthy businesses here.”
Future reports will look at housing affordability and taxes in the state.
The relationship between state government and the Maryland business community is complicated.
More than a decade ago, the Augustine Commission found Maryland was a high cost of living state, too dependent on federal jobs, with high utility costs and other factors. And while some early recommendations were enacted, many others were left to gather dust.
Business leaders in Annapolis in 2025 said a proposed tax on services would make the state less business-friendly. (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
Elected officials acknowledge that economic growth is key to resolving some of the state’s stickier ongoing budget issues.
Business leaders — especially small business owners — say they are frequently vilified by lawmakers. Those same lawmakers then turn to them for new revenue in the form of fees, taxes.
In recent years, businesses have been hit with a series of policies that Kane and others say have made it difficult to compete including taxes on IT and data services and mandatory paid leave programs.
Kane, however, sees reason for optimism.
“When the Senate president stands up and he says, ‘I never forget the fact that people only live less than an hour away from another state if you live in Maryland,’ that’s come a long way,” Kane said. “They’re actually starting to think that way, and that’s our goal.”
