name: Connecticut Mirror
title: President in name only
description: Donald Trump thinks that naming and name-calling changes reality. But the more names he applies, the more obvious his deceit.
text:
What’s in a name? As Shakespeare’s Juliet mused, “That which we call a rose/By any other name would smell as sweet.”  The President of the United States evidently disagrees. He thinks that naming, re-naming, and even name-calling changes reality. But like his cosmetically altered features, the more names he applies, the more obvious his deceit.
Consider Trump’s pathological name-calling: He’s labeled Elizabeth Warren as “Pocohontas;” U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar as “garbage;” President Biden as “Sleepy Joe;” and Secretary of State Clinton as “Crooked Hillary.” He brands them with epithets to reduce them to “Trump” products. And though these ad hominem attacks convince some voters of Trump’s power, they also expose the pettiness, childishness, and prejudice of his appeal. A bully by any other name proves just as toxic.
The president, similarly, name-calls the media: “the enemy of the people,” “fake news,” “corrupt,” “human scum,” “failing,” and “phony.” Yet, when a compulsive liar falsely accuses the media of lying, it sounds a lot like the deflections of a guilty 5-year-old: “I’m rubber; you’re glue.”
Worse, Trump’s name calling often betrays his ugly racism, referring to African nations as “shithole countries;” Mexican immigrants as “criminals” and “rapists;” all Muslims as “Mohammad,” and Puerto Rico as a “floating island of garbage.” It explains an immigration policy that terrorizes, arrests, imprisons and deports the “huddled masses yearning to breathe free,” without any due process under the law.
The president has also tried to achieve dominance over the Western Hemisphere by unilaterally re-naming territories, bodies of water, and even nations. He declared that The Gulf of Mexico is now The Gulf of America; that Lake Ontario is now Lake America; that Canada is America’s 51st state; and that Greenland belongs to the US. Lately he has mused about changing the names of the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans to the Trump or American Oceans.  Are the planets next?
Of course, all of this nominal sound and fury signifies nothing except for Trump’s imperialist ambitions and America’s tarnished democratic standing. In fact, Trump’s counterfeit attempt to extend American hegemony and to intimidate neighbors has only alienated our allies and undermined their trust. Pretending to extend American power in name has curtailed its influence in substance.
Domestically, Trump has branded his name and likeness upon America itself, from its currency, passports, plaques, and warships to The Kennedy Center, West Palm Beach Airport, and the Institute of Peace. But like artless graffiti, his name has desecrated the reputation, association, and status of each symbol and institution he marks.
But President Trump’s most damaging misuse of naming has been his Orwellian subversion of language to whitewash his corruption, ill-conceived policies, and responsibility for their consequences.
Consider his naming a violent mob that attacked Capitol Police on January 6, 2021, “patriots.” However, the word, “patriots” in America refers to those that uphold the Constitution and protect the nation’s foundational institutions. Those that violently attacked the Capitol with stun guns, batons, and hatchets, that were arrested, tried, and convicted, justly are named “criminals” at best, if not “insurrectionists,” for violating the law and the institutions that uphold the law. Further, Trump’s pardon of these so-called “patriots” that amounts to a cosmetic cover-up of both his and their crimes that, ironically, highlights the depths of his corruption.
Consider, also, Trump’s unprovoked and illegal war in Iran that he prefers to name an “excursion” and “small potatoes,” terms that belie the danger of real soldiers and civilians in harm’s way. Nor does declaring Iran “totally defeated” mean that the Strait of Hormuz is open; that Iran will not pursue a nuclear bomb; that our Mideast allies are safe from Iran’s military power; or that global oil, gas, and grocery prices have fallen.
Preposterously, seven months after starting the war, Trump said he deserved the Nobel Peace Prize. In other words, according to the President’s lexicon, War is Peace, an equation right out of Orwell. Indeed, in Orwell’s essay, “Politics and the English Language,” the author observed, “The great enemy of clear language is insincerity.” “The great enemy” certainly is a title Trump has earned, in more than name only.
Overall, Trump’s proclivity for naming amounts to a case of magical thinking. Trump’s world exists in name only, where a war has been “won” but the fighting and dying goes on, where an election is “rigged” but it was actually lost; where the economy enjoys a “golden age” but the goods are unaffordable; where “America is Great Again” even as it falls apart; and where American autocracy wears the mask of democracy.
This year Trump named himself the “Greatest” U.S. president ever. I believe history will judge him as a president in name only. Or, with apologies once again to Shakespeare: That which we call a charlatan/ By any other name would be just as fake.
Thomas Cangelosi is a retired teacher from Avon.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The people have spoken. Women led the way
description: As President and Chief Executive Officer of YWCA Hartford Region, and as a member of the YWCA USA Board of Directors, I serve a mission to eliminate racism and empower women. I have never seen that mission come to life more clearly than it did this month. Recently many women wondered whether the ground beneath […]
text:
As President and Chief Executive Officer of YWCA Hartford Region, and as a member of the YWCA USA Board of Directors, I serve a mission to eliminate racism and empower women. I have never seen that mission come to life more clearly than it did this month. 
Recently many women wondered whether the ground beneath them was shifting, yet they did not lose hope. Rights and protections they had fought for came into question, so they organized. And when their value at work, in public life, and in their own families seemed open to debate, they decided to run. 

Adrienne Cochrane

And on November 3, they won. On election night in Austin, Gina Hinojosa, Texas’s first Latina governor-elect, told her supporters, “No one would have imagined that one day, a little girl from the RGV would stand before you here as the next governor of the greatest state, Texas.” Across the country, women who had been underestimated were elected.
Consider Amy Acton. As a young girl in Youngstown, Ohio , she spent one winter living in a tent. She grew up to become a physician, led her state through a pandemic, and in January will become the first woman elected governor of Ohio. She ran on housing and health because she has lived both. In New Mexico, Deb Haaland, a citizen of Laguna Pueblo , became the first Native American woman elected to lead a state, promising childcare families can rely on and homes they can afford.
 These women did not ask anyone to vote for them because they are women. They spoke to what every family talks about at the kitchen table. Can I see a doctor? Can I afford childcare? Will my rent go up again? Their message crossed lines of race, party, and region, and voters answered. 
And it was not one party’s story. In Tennessee, Republican Marsha Blackburn became the state’s first woman governor, promising a state “where hard work pays off, where families can put down roots, and where everyone has the opportunity to build a better future.” In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman ever elected governor in the United States, saying her win was “for the caregiver who can’t afford healthcare.” Two women from opposite parties, speaking the same language of families and opportunity.

Georgia Democrat Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks at an election night event, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Atlanta.   Credit: AP Photo/Brynn Anderson

A record 159 women will serve in the next Congress. For the first time, three Black women will serve in the United States Senate at once, and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota will be the first Native American woman elected to the Senate.
 Repeatedly I have heard Americans of every background say this month, “Thank you, Black women. Election after election, you showed up, organized and led. This year, you led the nation to new ground.” 
Connecticut answered with steady growth too. By our count, 71 women will serve in our next General Assembly, up from 68. In Greater Hartford, Maryam Khan moves up to the state Senate, and newcomers Tiffani McGinnis of West Hartford and Angie Parkinson, an East Hartford teacher, take their seats for the first time. Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz was reelected to a third term. And U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes, reelected to a fifth term, said she would start the very next day running to lead the House Education and Workforce Committee.
However, we know that the work does not begin in Washington or Hartford. It begins in our towns. Who serves matters. Through our 50/50 Campaign, YWCA Hartford Region works to make sure municipal boards and commissions reflect the communities they serve. Many of the women elected this month began on a school board or a planning commission. If you have ever wondered whether you belong at that table, know the answer is yes.
That is why this moment brings me such joy. In America’s 250th year, YWCA Hartford Region approaches its own 160th anniversary. Founded in 1867, it opened its doors to young women who came to Hartford for work and needed a safe place to live. At that time, they could not vote. This January, their daughters and granddaughters will lead states and take their places in Congress and our State Capitol. The needs these women ran on, health, housing, childcare, education, and good jobs, are the same needs that bring families through our doors every day. They are important to all.
 On election night, Deb Haaland said this moment is not only about history. It is about our future. The people have spoken. Women led the way. Now it is our turn. 
Adrienne W. Cochrane is President and Chief Executive Officer of YWCA Hartford Region, where she also serves ex officio on its board, and is a member of the YWCA USA Board of Directors.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Geography should not be a diagnosis in CT
description: If CT wants more physicians to choose practicing primary care, helping them afford their education is a practical place to start.
text:
In Connecticut, access to a primary care doctor often depends on where you live. The state’s 2025 rural health application demonstrates this gap: 97 primary care physicians per 100,000 residents in Fairfield County, compared with 56 in Litchfield County, and 45 in Windham County.
National Rural Health Day, on Nov. 19, recognizes the clinicians caring for communities like these. As a family physician who helps train rural doctors, I believe sustaining their work requires investing in the people who will follow them. Connecticut should fund medical scholarships tied to service so more students can afford to become the physicians our rural communities need.

Traci Marquis-Eydman MD

The need is already clear. Workforce data show that 34.1% of Connecticut physicians were older than 60. Yet among physicians who completed residency here from 2015 through 2024, only 46.7% were practicing in Connecticut. Connecticut must replace retiring physicians while addressing existing shortages, and it cannot assume the doctors it trains will stay to do that work.
For communities where patients already have few options, losing physicians can mean losing access to care. People in the Northwest Corner describe practices closing and offices that no longer accept new patients. As care becomes harder to find, screenings are put off, chronic conditions go longer without treatment adjustments, and manageable problems can become emergencies. Older residents are especially vulnerable. Staying well at home often requires regular medical care, and traveling farther for that care becomes more difficult as people age.
Preparing the next generation of physicians takes years, and the cost of that preparation can work against these communities’ needs. Some students leave medical school with debt approaching $400,000, while primary care pays less than most other specialties. Debt does not determine every career choice, but students considering family medicine must weigh substantial loan payments against lower expected earnings. If Connecticut wants more physicians to choose that work, helping them afford their education is a practical place to start.
That was a central conclusion of Connecticut’s Physician Recruitment and Retention Working Group, on which I served. Its May report made service-based medical scholarships its top recommendation. The group proposed one year of practice in a medically underserved Connecticut community for each year of scholarship support, with highest priority for family medicine and psychiatry.
This approach would give students financial support while establishing a clear obligation to Connecticut patients. Loan repayment programs remain valuable recruitment tools, helping physicians address debt already incurred. Scholarships help students finance their education while they are still forming career plans. They make primary care more affordable to pursue and connect the state’s investment to service in communities where physicians are needed.
That service can also give physicians an opportunity to build careers they want to continue after their obligation ends. In the family medicine residency program I direct, physicians spend their final two years training in Northwest Connecticut. They learn to care for rural patients, work with local colleagues, and understand the resources available in the communities they serve.
One national study estimated that, three years after residency, 50.9% of family physicians trained in rural programs were practicing in rural areas, compared with 18% of those trained in urban programs. Rural training and a service commitment offer different but complementary opportunities to establish professional and community connections. As physicians build patient panels, relationships with colleagues, and lives outside work, they gain reasons to stay.
Scholarships cannot guarantee lifelong retention, and keeping physicians will also require attention to their working conditions. The working group addressed those needs as well. But Connecticut can support the doctors practicing here today while helping students prepare to follow them. Funding scholarships tied to service would begin that work with a commitment to practice in underserved Connecticut communities.
The time required to prepare those students makes this a decision we should make now. A student entering medical school in 2027 would ordinarily complete a three-year family medicine residency in 2034. Starting two years later moves that completion date to 2036. Rural communities will need care throughout those years, and their physicians will continue retiring on their own schedule.
Waiting until access deteriorates further would leave those communities facing the same years of training with fewer doctors to care for them in the meantime. The state should fund these scholarships now, while it can still help students commit to practicing in the communities that need them. A child born in Winsted or Salisbury deserves the same chance at a healthy life as a child born in Stamford or New Haven.
Dr. Traci Marquis-Eydman is an associate professor of family medicine at Quinnipiac University’s Frank H. Netter MD School of Medicine and director of its Rural Family Medicine Residency Program. A primary care physician at Hartford HealthCare Medical Group, she also served on Connecticut’s Physician Recruitment and Retention Working Group in 2025.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Commission Keeps Maui Police Chief On Leave Amid Corruption Probe
description: The Maui Police Commission declined on Wednesday to reinstate Maui Police Chief John Pelletier, who was placed on paid administrative leave last month pending an investigation into his oversight of a department unit whose leader was arrested by federal authorities. Honolulu attorney Eric Seitz, representing Pelletier, demanded that the chief be allowed to co[...]
text:
The Maui Police Commission declined on Wednesday to reinstate Maui Police Chief John Pelletier, who was placed on paid administrative leave last month pending an investigation into his oversight of a department unit whose leader was arrested by federal authorities.
Honolulu attorney Eric Seitz, representing Pelletier, demanded that the chief be allowed to continue working while the investigation is carried out, arguing that placing the chief on leave harmed his reputation and amounted to disciplinary action. 
“Then I won’t have to sue you,” he told the commissioners after waiting seven hours to testify.
Honolulu attorney Eric Seitz, right, addressed the Maui Police Commission on Wednesday as Chief John Pelletier listened.  Hawaii News Now/Screenshot/2026
Toni Rojas and other volunteer members of the commission said the action was intended to ensure the integrity and independence of the investigation.
“It supports public trust and accountability, and it preserves due process and fairness,” Rojas told Seitz before the commission voted 6-1 to keep Pelletier on leave until the investigation is concluded. “I saw this as a temporary measure. We’re helping protect the chief’s employment rights, his livelihood, while the facts are all being reviewed.”
Commissioners also voted to instruct an outside investigator to expand the scope of an existing inquiry related to a high-profile property damage case to include the chief’s role in the department’s response. Additionally, they agreed to open another investigation into Pelletier’s comments and conduct since being placed on leave.
The actions were taken after commissioners heard hours of testimony from about 30 people, many of whom expressed support for Pelletier and said they believed he was committed to rooting out corruption within the department. Others voiced serious concerns about his leadership style and said the chief appeared to be overly defensive and reluctant to accept accountability.  
In October, the commission unanimously voted to place Pelletier on paid administrative leave while it investigates his supervision of the Criminal Intelligence Unit. The now-dissolved unit reported directly to the chief and was led by Lt. Michael Vaituulala, who is facing federal charges after prosecutors said he had been accepting bribes and using his police powers to protect cockfight organizers, drug traffickers and illegal fireworks distributors.
Two days later, Pelletier alleged during a press conference that Mayor Richard Bissen has for months been the subject of separate criminal investigations by the Hawaiʻi Attorney General’s Office and the Maui Police Department. The chief said he believed that Bissen retaliated by influencing the commission’s decision to place him on leave, a claim that the mayor denied. 
Maui County Prosecutor Andrew Martin has since said that Bissen is not the subject of a state criminal investigation into allegations of fraud and financial mismanagement.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska re-elects Republican Nick Begich to US House, showing limits of ‘blue tsunami’
description: Alaska has re-elected Republican U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III. Following a ranked choice tabulation Wednesday by the Alaska Division of Elections, Begich received 51.4% of the vote in the 2026 general election, ahead of independent challenger Bill Hill, who received 48.6%. Begich, first elected in 2022, became the most successful freshman lawmaker in the histor[...]
text:
Rep. Nick Begich, R-Alaska, addresses supporters on election night, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at the Hotel Captain Cook in downtown Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)Alaska has re-elected Republican U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III.
Following a ranked choice tabulation Wednesday by the Alaska Division of Elections, Begich received 51.4% of the vote in the 2026 general election, ahead of independent challenger Bill Hill, who received 48.6%.
Begich, first elected in 2022, became the most successful freshman lawmaker in the history of the U.S. House of Representatives, sponsoring seven bills and three repeal resolutions that passed a Republican-controlled Congress and the desk of President Donald Trump. 


“To the hundreds of thousands of Alaskans who made your voice heard this month, thank you for engaging in this important process,” Begich said in a victory statement. “Serving as Alaska’s sole representative in the U.S. House is an honor that my team and I take seriously. We work hard for the people of our state, and I look forward to serving all Alaskans: young and old; rural and urban; Republican, Independent, Libertarian, and Democrat alike. We’ve had success these past two years for our state, and we will endeavor to continue to build on that momentum as I serve you in the 120th Congress.”
Begich thanked his competitors in the election and said, “Alaska’s best days remain in front of us with opportunities for new responsible resource development, new infrastructure, and new industries and the jobs that come with them. As Alaskans we must continue this work together, to build a more abundant and prosperous state and ensure we fulfill Alaska’s promise: North to the Future.”
Though criticized by Hill for supporting Trump’s policies, Begich had more votes than any other Republican on the general election ballot. In the U.S. Senate race, incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan had over 4,000 fewer first-choice votes than Begich.
Independent U.S. House candidate Bill Hill waves to passing motorists on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in Midtown Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)
Amid a “blue tsunami” that saw Democrats elected in close races across the country this year, Begich was also helped by the fact that more than 22,000 Democratic voters chose Eric Hafner instead of Hill for their first-choice vote.
In a written statement, Hill said he has called Begich to concede.
“I wished him well as he continues representing Alaska in Congress, because all Alaskans have a stake in his success,” Hill said by email.
“This campaign has always been about taking power back from the DC elites and putting it in the hands of the hardworking people of Alaska. While we did not prevail in this election, we will continue that fight together.”



A sign erected by the Bill Hill campaign, seen Nov. 3, 2026, in downtown Anchorage, warns voters to avoid casting their ballots for felon Eric Hafner, a candidate for U.S. House. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
Who is Eric Hafner?
Eric Hafner is a perennial candidate who runs in elections across the country from his federal jail cell in New York state. Convicted in 2022 of threatening to kill officials in New Jersey, he is serving a 20-year term.
He has previously registered to run for federal office in Hawaii and Florida, among other states. 
In 2024, he ran for Alaska’s U.S. House seat as a Democrat. After the Alaska Division of Elections certified his candidacy, the Alaska Democratic Party sued, arguing that he was ineligible to run.
A lower court judge ruled against the party, concluding that although the U.S. Constitution requires someone to be a resident of a relevant state when elected, Hafner’s ability to run for office is protected by the First Amendment, even if he is unable to serve.
The Democratic Party appealed the lower court decision to the Alaska Supreme Court but raised only procedural arguments and not the Constitutional argument on appeal. The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Hafner in summer 2024.
Hafner’s mother, Carol Hafner, was a Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in this year’s election, finishing fifth in the primary election. She has argued on social media that her son’s candidacy is legitimate and he would be able to serve if pardoned by President Trump.



While Hill had the Alaska Democratic Party’s endorsement, Hafner — imprisoned in New York state for threatening federal officials — was the lone listed Democrat on the ballot.
Democratic candidate Matt Schultz, who had been favored by Alaska progressives, suspended his campaign and withdrew after the primary. Hill, despite getting the Democratic Party’s backing, declined during the campaign to say whether he would caucus with Democrats or Republicans if elected to the House. 
Alaska uses ranked choice voting in general elections. If no candidate has more than 50% of Alaskans’ first-choice votes, the lowest finisher is eliminated and their votes go to their voters’ second choices.
Rep. Nick Begich, R-Alaska, waves signs on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in Midtown Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)
Libertarian candidate Jim McDermott had 2.6% of the first-choice votes, and his voters split their second-choice votes somewhat evenly between Begich, Hill and no one; Hafner received less. Hafner, with 7.9% of the first-choice votes, was eliminated next, and almost half of his voters — 11,496 in total — picked neither Hill nor Begich as an additional option.
That margin was decisive: Begich defeated Hill by 7,385 votes in the final ranked choice tabulation.
More Alaskans voted in this midterm election than any other in state history, and turnout in the primary election was high as well.
Altogether, 15 candidates ran in the House race in the August primary. Begich finished first in the primary, followed by Hill, Schultz and Hafner.
Schultz withdrew to support Hill. Three other candidates — Democrat John Williams of Fairbanks, Republican Clay Strickland and Democrat Yaquelin Reynoso of Massachusetts — also withdrew, putting eighth-place finisher McDermott into the general election.
Begich’s campaign raised significantly more money than Hill’s campaign, but Hill benefited from millions more in spending by third-party groups, including one — Wheel Dog PAC — that spent almost $9 million. 
Hill and Wheel Dog PAC ran a two-pronged advertising effort to boost Hill’s name and raise awareness of Hafner’s status. Polling averages over the course of the campaign showed Hill shrinking the margin between himself and Begich, but he was never able to entirely eliminate it.
Begich served the first two years of his tenure as a member of a Republican majority in the House; he will return as a member of a shrunken Republican minority.  He will be the lone member of Alaska’s three-person Congressional delegation with friendly ties to Trump.
Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, is one of a few Republicans in the Senate to repeatedly oppose Trump and voted to impeach him after he encouraged the Jan. 6, 2021 insurrection at the U.S. Capitol, and Trump has criticized Sen.-elect Mary Peltola, D-Alaska.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska midterm turnout sets all-time record, beating marijuana-legalization year of 2014
description: More Alaskans voted in this year’s midterm election than any other in state history, according to preliminary figures published Wednesday by the Alaska Division of Elections. Wednesday was the deadline for the division to conduct a ranked choice tabulation and present preliminary results. Final, certified results are expected by Nov. 25.  According to Wednes[...]
text:
Voters are seen on the first day of early in-person voting in the midterm elections at a polling site in Juneau on Oct. 19, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)More Alaskans voted in this year’s midterm election than any other in state history, according to preliminary figures published Wednesday by the Alaska Division of Elections.
Wednesday was the deadline for the division to conduct a ranked choice tabulation and present preliminary results. Final, certified results are expected by Nov. 25. 
According to Wednesday’s tally, 290,323 Alaskans cast ballots in the primary, beating the prior midterm record of 285,449, set in 2014. 
That year’s election had a hotly contested U.S. Senate race and three popular ballot measures, including one that legalized marijuana for recreational use in Alaska. 


KHNS-FM in Haines reported that the village of Klukwan had the highest turnout of any individual precinct: 50 of 70 registered voters in the town cast ballots in the election.
In Alaska, voter turnout is higher in presidential election years than in midterm elections. Overall, this year’s participation is the seventh-highest overall: More ballots were cast this year than in the 2000 presidential election or any election before that. 
An unusual number of ballots were cast before Election Day as well: Only the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections saw a higher proportion of votes cast in advance of Election Day. 
Alaska’s atypically high voter registration rate means turnout measurements that use percentages are misleadingly low. 
Alaska had 605,433 people registered to vote for the election. The state has an estimated voting-eligible population of 543,594 people, meaning that the state’s voter registration rate is 111.4%. 
Federal and state laws make it significantly easier to register to vote than be removed from the state’s voter rolls, and Alaska has a transient population with large numbers of people moving in and out of the state annually. 
Many people registered to vote in Alaska are members of the military, college students or others who now live in other states but remain registered to vote in Alaska to preserve eligibility for the Permanent Fund dividend and to avoid state income taxes.

title: Commentary: Let’s hope better government isn’t just a dream
description: I had another weird dream, really weird. I actually would prefer that my dreams be less vivid, less memorable and less strange. It’s one thing to wake up with a dry mouth, a sore neck and wondering just where I set down my glasses. It’s an entirely different awakening when I sit up and wonder […]
text:
The Alaska State Capitol is seen on May 18, 2026. (Photo by Claire Stremple/Alaska Beacon)I had another weird dream, really weird. I actually would prefer that my dreams be less vivid, less memorable and less strange. It’s one thing to wake up with a dry mouth, a sore neck and wondering just where I set down my glasses. It’s an entirely different awakening when I sit up and wonder where I’ve been in my head.
I dreamed I was aboard the USS Missouri. Yes, the World War II battleship. The one that U.S. Army Gen. Douglas MacArthur used for the signing ceremony when Japan surrendered to end the war in the Pacific in 1945. The ship that now is a museum at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. That USS Missouri.
It’s almost three football fields long, so I know I would remember if I had been aboard.
I’ve never even been to Hawaii or on the battleship, or for that matter aboard any U.S. Navy vessel in my life, though I was aboard a German submarine as a kid.
The Museum of Science and Industry, near where I grew up in Chicago, has a German sub, the U505, parked outside, open for tours. There was no war in Lake Michigan; the sub was towed there after U.S. forces captured it in the Atlantic in 1944. Definitely the best part of the museum for a young boy. Climbing into a submarine beat studying science any day.
But back to my dream. I was aboard the USS Missouri and I think I was in charge, though I wasn’t wearing a uniform (and I can’t swim, but that never came up in the dream). The ship needed to aim its 16-inch guns at a target 24 miles away, the maximum range for the large turret-mounted guns. I have no memory of what we were shooting at. Which is good, it made my dream less violent.
The gun crew informed me that to hit a target 24 miles away required precision and perfect teamwork. Everyone and everything had to function to the max or the shell would start wobbling as it flew through the sky and would never reach its target.
Teamwork, the gunnery guy, or whatever his title, told me, that’s what’s needed to reach full potential. He even fired off a shell to show me how it wobbled when the team failed.
Even in my addled sleep, I remember standing on the deck of the ship and thinking that’s kind of like government. Unless everyone does their job and works together, plans never reach their target. Programs don’t reach the people they should, ferries don’t run and state agencies don’t get their work done.
 I’ll admit it’s a little strange to transition from a battleship gun to government mid-dream. I suppose it means I am spending too much time thinking about how government can be better. Maybe I should read the sports section instead of the news before I go to bed.
I wondered in my dream if maybe it was telling me that the new governor of Alaska and the new U.S. Congress would only hit their targets if everyone works together — both political parties, under new leadership and with better focus.
Then I woke up, back in my bedroom, with no seasickness from the ship. I wrote down what I could remember — who doesn’t keep a stack of Post-it Notes by their bed — and thought that while teamwork will be important for newly elected officials, they can skip the battleship training sessions. Take my word for it, the shells will wobble.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Denby Fawcett: Saving What Is Left Of Kāhala Beach From Severe Erosion
description: Sea level rise and seawalls are accelerating the damage.
text:
I grew up at 4523 Kāhala Ave. in the 1950s when the beach in front of our house was so wide and sandy my friends and I could ride our horses all the way from Black Point to Waiʻalae Country Club.
Today, that would be impossible. All the sand along our section of Kāhala Beach has disappeared, seized by increasingly strong storms, rising sea levels and the seawalls that seemed to spring up in large numbers in the late 1960s.
The concrete and lava rock walls hardened the coast. The sand that normally migrated in and out had nowhere to go except out to sea, never to return. There was no sand reserve to fill in what was lost. The beach in front of my family’s former house is now underwater, even at the lowest of low tides.
Some claim the erosion on Kāhala Beach accelerated after the city installed three storm water drain pipes that jutted from the shoreline out to the reef. They say that changed the flow of the currents and collected sand that was pushed out into deep water along with the storm water.
But coastal geologist Chris Conger says the erosion happening in Kāhala is occurring on beaches all over the state due to rapid ocean rise. Shallow fringing reefs that once protected coasts like Kāhala are gradually drowning beneath rising seas. Seawalls built or enlarged after the erosion intensified have made it worse.
Conger is vice president of Sea Engineering, a marine coastal and ocean engineering firm founded in Hawaii. He has worked on beach erosion issues for the last 20 years, many of those helping Kāhala owners with beach erosion issues.
Even though the beach where I lived is gone, there might still be time to try to stabilize other areas of the Kāhala shore.
“We as human beings have interfered with the ecosystem. We have messed it up,” says Lucinda Pyles, a Kāhala resident for 51 years. For decades, Pyles has photographed Kāhala beach and successfully lobbied for new state laws to halt the progression of beach erosion.
“The beach is a public trust asset. It belongs to all the people of Hawaiʻi. It is tragic not to take care of it,” she said one afternoon as we walked the beach.
At low tide, Lucinda Pyles photographs the wall and fence falling out of the eroded shoreline at 4663 Kāhala Ave. The property is owned by Far East Park Lane of Singapore, which was given notice in March 2026 to remove the wall and fence. (Denby Fawcett photo)
Part of Kāhala Beach that stretches from the public right-of-way at Hunakai Street to Waiʻalae Beach Park still has sand, but some parts of that section are severely imperiled.
“It’s a war zone. Kāhala has changed from one of the most beautiful beaches to one of the ugliest,” said Joe Correa, a contractor who has been working since 2010 to help two Kāhala homeowners stem erosion on their  properties in the 4600 block of Kāhala Avenue.
The once-white sand is often a beige color now from dirt washing off the homeowners’ eroding properties. The shore is dotted with clumps of vegetation and debris that has washed down from the property owners’ landscaping.



Ideas showcases stories, opinion and analysis about Hawaiʻi, from the state’s sharpest thinkers, to stretch our collective thinking about a problem or an issue. Email news@civilbeat.org to submit an idea or an essay.


Read More

One of the most alarming images of encroachment on public land is part of swimming pool sticking out on the beach at 4623 Kāhala from the diminishing front yard of the home owned by the Asagami Corp. of Japan.
The city’s Department of Planning and Permitting gave Asagami permission to build the swimming pool in 1992. The DPP said the pool was then legally situated just mauka of the then 40-foot shoreline setback.
I called the Asagami house to find out what the owner plans to do prevent more of his pool from edging out on the beach, A man who said he was Mr. Mizawa answered but his English was too limited to discuss the unusual situation or for me to properly identify myself as a reporter.  An email I sent to Asgami company president Kenichi Kimura in Tokyo remains unanswered.
This swimming pool was allowed by the city Department of Planning and Permitting at the request of Asagami Corp. of Japan in 1992. Then it was 40 feet back from the high tide mark.  (Denby Fawcett photo)
Earlier this year, the Department of Land and Natural Resources issued notices of violation to eight owners of properties from 4607 to 4663 Kāhala Ave. including the Asagami house for allegedly encroaching on the public beach with everything from collapsing seawalls and chainlink fences to rusting pipes, construction rubble and concrete stairs.
They were warned if they willfully disregarded the notice to remove the encroachments they could face fines of up to $15,000 a day.
In the violation notices, Michael Cain, administrator of the state Office of Conservation and Coastal Lands suggested that the property owners consider addressing the situation with vegetated sand dunes at the makai end of their properties to slow the erosion.
But former OCCL administrator Sam Lemmo thinks creating vegetated sand dunes will work only with the protection of a small groin on the beach to keep the sand built up in the dunes from escaping in super high tides. He says it is an option that should be considered.
Since then, some of the homeowners have removed the many of the  intrusions from what is considered part of the state’s conservation district regulated by the DLNR. On the coast that means all the area up to the highest reach of the highest tides at any time of year. 
Michael Cain, Office of Conservation and Coastal Lands administrator,  surveys Kāhala Beach to view properties that received notices of alleged violation. This uprooted palm tree is at 4615 Kāhala Ave., a property purchased by Alan Richter and Mary Widel. The tree was uprooted when ocean water swept into the propertyʻs landscaping when the home was occupied by the  previous owner. (Denby Fawcett photo)
The Kāhala property owners who received notices are also allegedly violating a state law  that guarantees the public free access to Hawaiiʻs beaches. 
Alan Richter and Mary Widel of 4615 Kāhala Ave. were among the landowners who received a notice in March for encroaching on the beach with debris and vegetation from their eroding yard that blocked peoples’ access to the sand.
Richter and Widel bought the property in April 2024 from a Japanese corporation that the state had been sending notices of violation since 2015.
Since they got the letter, they have removed the encroaching vegetation that was originally left on the beach by the prior owner. Richter has a master’s degree in coastal geology from the University of Delaware and says he is aware of the dynamics of seacoast erosion.
“DLNR has had problems with the previous owner of our property. We strive to address damage caused by storms and beach erosion,” Richter told Civil Beat.
Richter has hired coastal engineer Michael Foley of EA Engineering to design a dune restoration system on his property.
“I am hopeful that the 7 other neighboring Kāhala Beach property owners who received similar letters from the Board of Land and Natural Resources will also join in building a continuous dune that will be vegetated with a combination of robust native coastal vines and grasses,”  Richter wrote in an email. 
He says such a system will only work if his other neighbors buy in to make it a regional dune and if they can gain the support of government regulatory agencies and the community.
“It’s so important that we hear the ideas and perspectives of all in our community. This problem is greater than one property owner or even several can address. We, as a community, all need to work together to improve our coastal environment,” said coastal engineer Foley.
Kahala Beach in 1950 was one long ribbon of white sand.  (Courtesy: Hawaiʻi State Archives)
Tony and Sheryl Dong say they have lost land to erosion going 30 feet inland since they bought 4631 Kahala Ave. from Alexander & Baldwin 10 years ago. They are interested in joining forces with Richter to work with government agencies and the community to stabilize and restore Kāhala Beach.
“It is sad and tragic what has happened. I love the beach like everyone else. It is a public beach that unfortunately now has no sand but I think we can do something about it,” Tony Dong said in a phone call from Pontiac, Michigan.
Dong said he has been coming here for the last 30 years and plans to eventually make Hawaiʻi his permanent home. “All of us want the same thing, a healthy nice beach in Kāhala,” he said.
Other property owners like Far East Park Lane of Singapore have not yet addressed DLNR’s notice sent in March to ask it to remove a sea wall and fence that are now on  the public beach fronting 4663 Kahala Ave.
Property manager Riley Bloom texted that “the owner eventually will have to do something about the concrete wall … the only thing I have to say regarding the project is that it has been very difficult working with DLNR. They have not helped at all with educating, guiding and informing my client to make good decisions.”
Kāhala Beach can never return to what it was. It is the nature of beaches to change and more so now that the sea level is rising. But there is hope that collective action by the property owners might save what remains of the beautiful beach you once could ride a horse on for miles.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Lawmakers’ plan would restrain Utah data center development – and MIDA
description: Utah lawmakers facing intense outcry over data centers gave a first glimpse Wednesday of a wide-ranging plan to rein in development of the projects throughout the state.
text:
The sun rises over a part of Hansel Valley, in Box Elder County, near the proposed Stratos Project, a massive data center originally planned for 40,000 acres of land but later downsized to 20,000 acres, on Thursday, May 28, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Utah lawmakers facing intense outcry over data centers gave a first glimpse Wednesday of a wide-ranging plan to rein in development of the projects throughout the state. 
Part of the goal is avoiding a repeat of recent history. 
The massive Stratos data center proposal soared into a remote corner of northern Utah over the summer and crashed into a statewide wave of public resentment. It was seen as a driving force behind a stunning primary election loss for a top state lawmaker who supported the project, Senate President Stuart Adams.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Outcry over data centers has also been seen as a key contributor to a blue wave election that made landfall in Utah, doubling Democrats’ membership in the Utah House and shattering that chamber’s Republican supermajority for the first time in more than three decades. 
“It’s very clear we have to improve the process,” Rep. Paul Cutler told reporters Wednesday at the state Capitol. 
Cutler, a Republican from Centerville, said he’s sponsoring a proposal to prohibit “sweetheart” tax deals for the projects, force proposals into the open early on and put control in the hands of communities, not state authorities. Also off the table under his plan are any nondisclosure agreements for public officials. 
The details of the plan are still coming together, but the idea is to make the process more transparent and put issues of water quality and air pollution at the fore, Cutler said. 
Utah Rep. Paul Cutler, R-Centerville, and Sen. Chris Wilson, R-Logan, talk to reporters about their plans for data center legislation at the Utah Capitol on Nov. 18, 2026. (Annie Knox/Utah News Dispatch)
Last year, Utah’s Military Installation Development Authority (MIDA) worked with celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary on the Stratos project and gave the proposal its first round of government approval in Utah. 
Under Cutler’s yet-to-be drafted bill, an entity like MIDA couldn’t propose a data center. Only local land use authorities — counties, cities or towns — could do that, Cutler told members of the Economic Development and Workforce Services Interim Committee on Wednesday. 
At the local level, Box Elder County commissioners who approved the Stratos project have said MIDA didn’t need their support to pursue it. That would also change under Cutler’s proposal. 
During Wednesday’s committee hearing, Rep. Jim Dunnigan, R-Taylorsville, asked about MIDA and whether it would have “super authority” under the changes.
Cutler said entities like MIDA or the Utah Inland Port Authority could provide expertise and support, but the proposal must be endorsed by a local community, “so MIDA can’t override those.” 
A spokesperson for MIDA didn’t directly comment on the components of the plan but said “as a political subdivision of and independent entity in the state of Utah, we follow the general policy guidelines and specific statutory requirements provided by the legislature.”
Through reduced tax incentives, Cutler said his plan would route additional money to the surrounding community, water improvement projects and environmental mitigation. 
Community members protest ahead of a special Box Elder County Commission meeting to discuss the Stratos project, a massive data center proposed for an unincorporated area in Box Elder County, Utah, on May 4, 2026. (Photo by Alixel Cabrera/Utah News Dispatch)
There’s no bill filed yet and no draft to share as he and Sen. Chris Wilson, the Senate’s newly-elected majority leader and the bill’s floor sponsor, discuss their ideas with counties, cities, the governor’s office and others. The two lawmakers said they were assigned by House and Senate leaders to take on the issue.  
Cutler said public outrage has “given us a lot more leverage over some of the industry partners.” But he said the plan to come up with new policies for big industrial projects predates the Stratos controversy. 
He said he’s been clear with operators of hyperscale data centers that many tax incentives are going away. But he believes the effect will be that Utah only gets the sorts of development it really wants. 
“What we’re trying to do is separate the best projects — those with financial stability, those who are committed to environmental protections — from somebody who’s just trying to quickly, you know, do a development deal and flip a project to make money,” Cutler said. 
Rep. David Shallenberger, R-Orem, emphasized that the proposal is not a moratorium on the industry in Utah but rather, “we’re working with them to have these projects be successful and positive contributors into these local communities and the greater Utah economy.” 
Rep.-elect Kim James, D-Ogden, said after the hearing that while the bill sets a new process for evaluating data center proposals, she wants to have a different conversation. 
“Must we have them in Utah, where the lake is such a precious resource, where air quality is really terrible?” James said. 
The committee did not take any action or public comment on the proposal Wednesday. Lawmakers plan to take it up again during the 2027 legislative session, which convenes in January.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT prison health workers condemn staffing shortages, care delays
description: Healthcare workers for CT's Department of Correction say more state funding is needed to boost staffing and improve the quality of care.
text:
Two full-time optometrists for the more than 10,000 people incarcerated in Connecticut’s Department of Correction facilities. 
Mental health clinicians with caseloads of 80 to 120 patients. 
A single obstetrician for 27 pregnant women incarcerated at York Correctional Institution.
These are the conditions healthcare workers employed by DOC described during a Wednesday night rally in Hartford hosted by SEIU 1199, a union whose membership includes correctional healthcare workers. They say a lack of state funding is to blame.
“How can anyone find these numbers appropriate or sustainable?” Molly Haynes, a mental health worker at York Correctional, told attendees at the gathering, across the street from Hartford Correctional Center. “We are frustrated. We are struggling, and we are here because we need the state to step up and help.”
“As frontline healthcare workers, the state is setting us up for failure by refusing to provide us with the staffing and resources we need,” Thomas Lally, a registered nurse at Garner Correctional Institution, said during remarks to fellow workers at Wednesday’s rally. “The amount of young men that I have personally had to watch die preventable deaths in my four years on the medical team is unconscionable.” 
In an emailed statement Wednesday evening, Cathryn Vaulman, a spokesperson for Gov. Ned Lamont, said meeting the healthcare needs of people in the state’s correctional facilities “is a responsibility the state takes seriously.” 
“Every person in the Department of Correction’s care deserves quality health care, and every person who works in our facilities deserves to be safe on the job. Reliable care makes facilities safer for everyone,” Vaulman wrote in the statement.
She added that Lamont backed a roughly $8 million increase in funding for medical services in prisons between fiscal years 2026 and 2027 and that he will “closely review how medical services are being delivered in correctional services” as part of the upcoming biennial budget process.
DOC spokesperson Marci Moreau said in an emailed statement that the department is “working collaboratively” with state agencies and community partners to strengthen healthcare services and addressing the existing backlogs is “one of the department’s highest priorities.”
But demands from DOC healthcare workers, raised by many at Wednesday’s event, suggest they don’t believe those measures have gone far enough. They are proposing a new model of care that includes guidelines for frequency of appointments and proposed staffing ratios by specialty. 
“In order to achieve these standards, the State will need to apply far more resources and staffing to correctional healthcare,” reads a draft of the plan provided by an SEIU 1199 spokesperson. 
DOC healthcare workers said they are speaking up now because they feel they’ve been wrongly blamed for quality of care. They said their attempts to solve the problem internally have yielded limited results. 
The conditions healthcare workers described have been raised before. In March, the state Correction Ombuds, a state official tasked with overseeing DOC, published a report that found a backlog of over 2,300 specialty care appointments. A CT Insider investigation published around the same time detailed prisoners facing years-long waits for specialty care.
In May, DOC announced a slate of reforms focused on improving the quality of healthcare for people who are incarcerated, including a new director of medical services, a team to oversee the implementation of reforms and investments in technology advancements.
Legislators nearly unanimously passed a law containing several measures aimed at improving prison healthcare, including implementation of an electronic health record system within available resources and a guarantee that DOC would provide medically necessary procedures in “a timely and clinically appropriate manner.” 
But the legislation didn’t indicate a deadline by which DOC had to implement an electronic health record system — it just directed the agency to do so “within available bond authorizations.” 
“No More Excuses Fund DOC Healthcare” reads a sign during a Service Employees International Union press conference where Department of Correction healthcare workers shared concerns outside Hartford Correctional Center on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Lamont has also mentioned improving healthcare in prisons as a priority. During a press conference with reporters after the close of the 2026 legislative session, he raised the issue explicitly while mentioning some strides that have been made in criminal justice reform. 
“I’m proud of the fact that we have half as many people incarcerated as we had 15 years ago. Much lower recidivism rate,” Lamont said “Now we’ve got to work on healthcare in our prisons.”
Lally said funding needs to go hand in hand with reforms. 
“If they don’t put any resources behind those bills, then they are meaningless,” Lally said. “All they’ve done is put words on paper without giving us any resources to get the job done.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Departing Providence superintendent to receive nearly $200,000 in separation agreement
description: The Providence School Board approved a nearly $200,000 separation package for outgoing Providence Public School District Superintendent Javier Montañez at its Wednesday night meeting. Montañez’s resignation — first announced on Oct. 30 and formally submitted in a Nov. 4 letter — took effect at the end of the day Wednesday. The separation comes about seven […[...]
text:
Outgoing Providence superintendent Javier Montañez speaks with reporters on Aug. 29, 2024. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)The Providence School Board approved a nearly $200,000 separation package for outgoing Providence Public School District Superintendent Javier Montañez at its Wednesday night meeting.
Montañez’s resignation — first announced on Oct. 30 and formally submitted in a Nov. 4 letter — took effect at the end of the day Wednesday. The separation comes about seven months before his contract was set to expire. 
The separation agreement was approved in a unanimous 10-0 vote Wednesday night and provides the departing superintendent $152,706.92 in biweekly payments. The payments will begin on Friday and run through July 2, 2027. 
Montañez will receive an additional $46,968.35 for a little over 54 days of unused vacation time. The unused holiday pay will be disbursed in five installments through mid-January, with the first installment also arriving on Friday.
Montañez will also retain his health insurance through June 30, 2027, and he will be responsible for his share of premiums.
The end of Montañez’s superintendency concludes his 30-year career in the Providence school system that began in 1996 when he was a bilingual second-grade teacher at what is now Spaziano Elementary School. Montañez eventually became the school’s assistant principal and then principal, before heading to Leviton Dual Language School to serve as principal for a decade. 
He became superintendent in 2021, roughly two years into the state takeover of Providence’s public school system. The takeover ended on July 1, after nearly seven years.
In farewell remarks at the beginning of Wednesday’s meeting, Montañez urged board members to use their combined power to better the district and students alike.
“In order to hit greatness, you have to hit some bumps in the road,” Montañez said. “But you know what’s the difference between sitting there and becoming great is learning from those bumps. 
“You know you can do great things,” he continued. “You have power. Learn how to use that power to benefit you and benefit our kids.”
Montañez spent his own school days in Providence’s classrooms. As a teenager he experienced homelessness and struggled with illiteracy and dyslexia before ultimately dropping out of Hope High School. He went on to obtain his GED and eventually a doctorate in educational leadership from Johnson & Wales University.
“I was one of those students that you said, ‘Oh, pobrecito Javier, he can’t do it,’” Montañez said. “Don’t do that. Challenge them, because they will end up surprising you.”
The separation agreement notes that Montañez and the board are in harmony on the idea that the district needs a new leader during this time of transition.
“The Board and Dr. Montanez now mutually agree that it is in the best interests of the District that the Board have an opportunity to hire a Superintendent of its own choosing to lead the District post state-takeover,” the agreement reads.
The separation agreement stipulates that Montañez will stay available to the district in a consulting capacity, specifically to aid incoming interim Superintendent Lendozia Edwards as she adjusts to her new job, which begins Thursday. Montañez’s consulting services will be available through June 30, and the agreement does not require him to report to district offices or work a certain number of hours.
Lendozia Edwards named interim Providence school superintendent

Edwards was promoted from her current role as the district’s chief of schools to the interim superintendent position during a Saturday, Nov. 14 meeting of the school board, with the board formally approving her appointment at Wednesday’s meeting.
Edwards will serve as the district’s interim leader through June 30, 2028. Her salary is still being negotiated by the School Board. School Board President Ty’Relle Stephens said at the meeting that he expects a contract will tentatively be ready by the board’s December meeting.
To mark the change in leadership, Montañez ceremonially gifted Edwards with a big key Wednesday night.
“I would like to give you the keys to the kingdom,” Montañez said. “And it’s heavy. I usually say the crown is heavy, but that key is heavy.” 
Outgoing Providence Superintendent Javier Montañez presents incoming Interim Superintendent Lendozia Edwards with a ceremonial key at the Providence School Board meeting Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Screenshot from Providence School Board livestream)
Montañez’s contract with Rhode Island Education Commissioner Angélica Infante-Green was most recently renewed on July 1, 2024, and was set to expire on June 30, 2027. That contract stipulated the terms of his departure from the district, and allowed for the disbursement of Montañez’s remaining salary and benefits if he was terminated without cause, as well as compensation for up to 60 days of vacation time 
Under the agreement, Montañez cannot receive compensation from the Rhode Island Department of Education through June 30, 2027.
The agreement also releases the board from an assortment of potential legal claims by Montañez, which could include alleged violations of state and federal laws governing employment, discrimination, civil rights and open meetings.
Excluded from this release is a workers’ compensation case filed in September. It is subject to a separate settlement.
As is common in such agreements, a non-disparagement clause prohibits Montañez and board members from making “knowingly false” statements, or statements “made with reckless disregard for the truth,” that could be “reasonably calculated to harm the individual’s reputation.”
This provision outlasts the end of Montañez’s payments as well as current board members’ terms in office. 
“This provision applies from the beginning of the Parties’ relationship into the future, and the Parties agree that they shall never abandon this covenant,” the agreement reads.
But Montañez and the School Board had only good things to say about one another at Wednesday night’s meeting.
School Board President Stephens acknowledged his relationship with Montañez had not always been rosy.
“We haven’t always seen eye to eye, as we know, but the one thing that I’ve never questioned was your integrity, nor have I ever questioned your heart,” Stephens told Montañez.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa geologist: Groundwater monitoring needed if more data centers are coming
description: Data centers in Iowa currently have not had a huge impact on the state’s groundwater, but Iowa’s state geologist said Wednesday a more comprehensive groundwater monitoring network will be necessary if the state plans to have sustainable groundwater management while continuing to attract data centers and large users.  Iowa State Geologist Keith Schilling said[...]
text:
Iowa State Geologist Keith Schilling talks about data centers and groundwater use at the Iowa Nature Summit Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Data centers in Iowa currently have not had a huge impact on the state’s groundwater, but Iowa’s state geologist said Wednesday a more comprehensive groundwater monitoring network will be necessary if the state plans to have sustainable groundwater management while continuing to attract data centers and large users. 
Iowa State Geologist Keith Schilling said the state currently has about 50 “very poorly distributed” groundwater monitoring wells. He said more wells, placed at strategic locations, would give the state baseline levels to help inform decisions on, and later evaluate the impact of, large water users like data centers. 
“If we’re going to, again, be a state that encourages sustainable groundwater use for things like data centers or other large-scale users, what we need to do is get serious about getting a groundwater monitoring well network built,” Schilling said at the Iowa Nature Summit Wednesday. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Water use has been one of the top concerns among Iowans when it comes to data centers. As servers run at data centers to power things like artificial intelligence and online infrastructure, they generate heat. Part of the continuous operations at a data center includes cooling equipment. 
According to Schilling, the cooling process accounts for 30% to 40% of a typical facility’s total energy consumption. 
He explained most data centers have either open- or closed-loop systems. Open-loop systems commonly use evaporative technology, where they move water past their servers, the water absorbs the heat and a large portion of it ends up in the air via evaporation. A closed-loop system uses water, or a coolant like antifreeze, that is run through a heat exchanger and is able to stay within the system. 
Schilling said he has seen instances where data centers describe their cooling systems as “closed loop” even though they are using evaporative technology. 
Water sometimes comes from nearby rivers or ground wells, depending on the project. The Google data center operating in Council Bluffs withdrew 1.3 billion gallons of water in 2023, according to an environmental report from the company. Schilling said while that “sounds like a lot,” wells near the facility are the kinds of wells that are quickly replenished by the Missouri River. 
“But note that groundwater is not available at high enough capacity in many areas of the state for this sort of intensive development,” Schilling said.
Other areas, like southern Iowa, have more confined water systems that are less easily recharged.
While many deep aquifers have lots of water, that water can be “tens of thousands, if not a million years old” meaning tapping the well is like a “one-time use” of that water. 
“We’ve got to be really careful about using a deep aquifer like that for something like a data center or even ethanol plants,” Schilling said. “… That water is not coming back. It’s gone. It will never be seen again.” 
A groundwater monitoring program 
Schilling, who works with the Iowa Geological Survey, said researchers have come up with a plan for 92 groundwater monitoring wells, either in bedrock or sand gravel areas. This deployment, he said, would cost about $3 million and would occur over several years. 
He said the wells would allow groundwater levels to be monitored over time, which would give counties or cities that are considering permitting a data center a better understanding of their groundwater resources and whether they could support a large user.
Iowa’s current monitoring network, of fewer than 50 wells, is significantly smaller than surrounding states that have several hundred groundwater monitoring wells, Schilling explained.
Iowa House lawmakers put forward a bill in the past legislative session to retrofit existing private wells, in a partnership with the geological survey and Iowa Department of Natural Resources, to expand groundwater well monitoring. The bill advanced to an appropriations committee but not to the full body. 
“The best time to plant a tree was 50 years ago — or how about a monitoring well network?” Schilling said. “The time is now to start doing that because we’re going to have a lot of these issues start creeping up over the next handful of years, and we need to be ready to go.”
