name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Lawsuit: Farmers’ co-op CEO collected millions in unauthorized pay, benefits
description: An agricultural cooperative representing more than 5,500 farmers in Iowa and surrounding states is suing the organization’s former top executives, in part for allegedly routing $280,000 to the mistress of the group’s former CEO. The lawsuit also claims the farmers’ co-op paid for “a small army of full-time personal assistants to fluff (the CEO’s) pillows, […[...]
text:
A newly filed lawsuit alleges the Landus farmers' cooperative bankrolled this $10 million ocean-front home in Florida for the co-op's former CEO. (Main photo by Getty Images; inset photo via Google Earth)An agricultural cooperative representing more than 5,500 farmers in Iowa and surrounding states is suing the organization’s former top executives, in part for allegedly routing $280,000 to the mistress of the group’s former CEO.
The lawsuit also claims the farmers’ co-op paid for “a small army of full-time personal assistants to fluff (the CEO’s) pillows, tuck his heated blanket into his bed, and lay out his slippers and robe.”
Landus Cooperative, an agricultural cooperative owned by Midwestern farmers, is suing Matthew Carstens, who served as the group’s president and chief executive officer from 2020 to 2025, and his wife, Shanda, in Polk County District Court.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Also named as defendants are Landus’ former executive vice president and general counsel, Stephen Nielsen, and Landus’ former board chairman, Matthew Chambers.
The lawsuit accuses Matthew Carstens of breaching his fiduciary duties to Landus and unlawfully enriching himself and his family at Landus’ expense. It alleges Nielsen and Chambers helped Carstens carry out his scheme and, in the process, deceived the organization’s board of directors.
The defendants are alleged to have intentionally kept the full board of directors from understanding “key facts about Mr. Carstens’ compensation and benefits,” while Carstens and Nielsen directed employees to steer unauthorized payments and benefits to the Carstens.
In addition, Carstens and Nielsen are alleged to have hired full-time employees “to serve the Carstens family in their personal matters,” and of hiring “as a Landus consultant the woman with whom Mr. Carstens was having an affair, paying her $280,000 without evidence of anything more than de minimis services rendered to Landus.”
During his time as president and CEO, Carstens’ base salary allegedly surged from $625,000 to more than $4.4 million per year — an amount that was supplemented with hundreds of thousands of dollars in bonuses.
According to the lawsuit, employment agreements drafted by Nielsen committed Landus to paying $10 million for a house the Carstens used in Florida, plus $3.5 million to build his primary residence in Grimes, Iowa. Those agreements were never shown to, nor approved by, the full board, the lawsuit alleges.
Staff told to fluff cushions, tuck in CEO’s blanket 
The lawsuit asserts that Carstens would typically raise an issue in a board meeting, Nielsen would include in the board-meeting minutes a very general description of the issue and discussion, and then Nielsen would order Landus employees to take action far beyond what the board had authorized. In some cases, the lawsuit claims, Nielsen would draft an amendment to Carstens’ employment agreement that would “stretch the board’s discussion or authorization beyond all recognition.”
As an example, the lawsuit cites a March 2024 decision by the board to pay for individuals to help Carstens host Landus-related events at his Iowa home. Carstens then had Landus hire at least four full-time workers to serve his family, in one instance as the family’s personal wellness doctor. The lawsuit states Matthew Carstens’ wife, Shanda, allegedly proposed job titles such as “personal wellness assistant” for those employees to, in her words, “avoid labeling them house manager or personal assistants.”
The Carstens also are alleged to have sent one or more of their personal assistants to their Landus-funded Florida home days in advance of their arrival, to buy groceries and alcohol, also billed to Landus, for trips that were purely personal in nature.
Those workers allegedly cooked for the Carstens, cleaned their home and did yard work. One of the personal assistant’s checklists instructs the staff to place Shanda Carstens’ Ritz crackers and mini-can of ginger ale on the table between the recliners in their bedroom, and to make sure “all cushions are fluffed” in the living room, bar and patio area. Other tasks include: “Place Matt’s robe at the end side of his bed, and his slippers on the floor by the robe… Make sure Matt’s side of the heated blanket is tucked in.”
On one occasion in 2024, the lawsuit claims, the Carstens decided to use the Landus corporate jet to fly their entire family from Iowa to Florida for a week-long celebration of their daughter’s 21st birthday. “No board member was ever made aware of any of these facts at the time,” the lawsuit asserts.



Quotation







“In mid-2024, as Mr. Carstens continued to cause Landus to pay a small army of full-time personal assistants to fluff Mr. Carstens’ pillows, tuck his heated blanket into his bed, and lay out his slippers and robe, Landus’s financials started to trend downward.“


– Lawsuit filed by Landus Cooperative


As part of that birthday celebration, the lawsuit alleges, one of the personal assistants worked 80 hours in one week. A written list of tasks assigned to that individual, included as an exhibit to the lawsuit, details the time that assistant was to spend preparing meals and cleaning, as well as working until 2 a.m. “bar hopping in St. Pete” – a task that entailed driving the Carstens children and their friends to and from various bars.
Matthew Carstens also caused Landus to pay $904,000 to The Matt & Shanda Carstens Family Foundation for a “performance center” known as “the barn,” to be built on the Carstens family’s residential property, where farmers would receive physical and mental wellness services.
The performance center project was later abandoned after Polk County denied a zoning variance for its construction, but the foundation never returned any of Landus’s money, the lawsuit alleges.
At one point, the lawsuit claims, members of the board’s executive committee asked to see the amendments to Carstens’ employment agreement so they could understand his full compensation, but were told by Nielsen they “did not need to see them.”
Lawsuit: Carstens admitted to affair with consultant
With regard to the consultant with whom Carstens was allegedly having an affair, the lawsuit claims that in March 2025, Carstens admitted to the board that he had an extramarital affair with a woman Landus hired, at his direction, in 2020 to act as an independent contractor.
Under the terms of the hiring agreement, Landus was to pay the woman’s limited liability corporation $33.65 an hour for services that would be detailed in weekly reports to Landus. No such reports were ever provided, the lawsuit claims.
The limited liability corporation was paid a total of $180,000 for 40 hours of work per week from October 2020 through March 2023, plus $100,000 in severance pay. “No one at Landus has been able to confirm that the LLC performed any services of value to Landus beyond a de minimis data-migration effort,” the lawsuit states.
“In mid-2024,” the lawsuit states, “as Mr. Carstens continued to cause Landus to pay a small army of
full-time personal assistants to fluff Mr. Carstens’ pillows, tuck his heated blanket into his bed, and lay out his slippers and robe, Landus’s financials started to trend downward.”
Matthew Carstens’ relationship with Landus began to unravel in late 2024 when financial pressures forced the co-op to lay off 10% of its workforce. Days later, the lawsuit claims, Carstens sought to increase his own compensation, which at the time included $1.7 million in base salary plus up to $300,000 in bonuses, tickets to Iowa State University sporting events, a suite at the Wells Fargo Arena in Des Moines, payments for the $10 million Florida house and the $3.5 million Grimes house, and personal travel on a Landus-owned private plane.
Carstens’ base salary was then increased to $2.4 million per year, and several weeks later, in March 2025, his employment agreement was amended again to provide a total salary of $4.4 million. That agreement also included a $550,000 “fulfillment bonus” if Carstens stayed at Landus through March 8, 2025 — a date that had already passed before that particular amendment was even drafted, the lawsuit asserts.
By that time, the lawsuit states, tensions at Landus were high, particularly because board members were frustrated by a lack of clarity regarding Matthew Carstens’ total compensation. Carstens resigned on April 4, 2025, with Landus agreeing to pay him $1.5 million in return for a release of any claims Carstens might make against Landus.
When Landus entered into that severance agreement, the lawsuit claims, the co-op and its board “did not know the full extent to which Mr. Carstens had used his position as CEO and Landus’s assets for the personal benefit of himself and his family.”
The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages for fraud, unjust enrichment, conversion, breach of fiduciary duty, civil conspiracy and other alleged wrongdoing. The defendants have yet to file a response to the lawsuit and could not be reached for comment Wednesday.
In a written statement that coincided with the filing of the lawsuit, Landus said “pursuing this lawsuit is about living out our ‘Integrity in Action’ core value, which means doing what’s right for our farmer-owners and our employees even when it’s not easy. Our employees are deeply committed to the Landus mission and the farmers we serve. We are building a culture where employees feel safe, equipped and empowered to deliver the very best to our members.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: School funding reform could prompt constitutional convention, Greenwald says
description: Voters should approve eventual school funding reforms, the Assembly Majority Leader suggested during a panel discussion Wednesday.
text:
Assemblyman Lou Greenwald (D-Camden), pictured with Assemblywoman Eliana Pintor Marin (D-Essex), speaks about the $50.6 billion budget New Jersey lawmakers approved on June 29, 2022. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey should call a constitutional convention to include voters in the approval of a new school funding formula once a proposal is finalized, Assembly Majority Leader Lou Greenwald (D-Camden) said.
Though legislators and Gov. Mikie Sherrill in August began soliciting input for changes to the state’s funding formula, officials have said little about how their eventual proposal would differ from the funding formula enacted in 2008, and it’s not clear whether or how a formula enshrined in the state’s constitution would affect court precedent that demands New Jersey students receive a thorough and efficient education.
“I think ultimately this is going to need to lead to a constitutional convention and then a question that will include the voters as part of the solution because I think, ultimately at the end of the day, this is an issue that New Jersey has struggled with for generations,” Greenwald said Wednesday during a panel discussion at the New Jersey League of Municipalities’ annual conference.
In New Jersey, the state calculates how much each municipality must spend to provide their students a constitutionally sound education and how much those districts can raise on their own based on their residents’ incomes and property values.
State aid fills the rest, though not all districts raise enough revenue to meet the local spending — called a local fair share — needed to fully fund schools after state aid is added.
Some cannot raise enough revenue locally because of the state’s 2% cap on annual property tax levies, and others have been hammered by steep swings in state aid as the state in 2018 moved to begin phasing out aid meant to keep districts whole after the enactment of the 2008 funding formula.
At present, local governments in New Jersey look to property taxes to fund their share of school expenses, and Greenwald suggested that could change as a result of the yet-to-be-determined reforms.
“We need to understand that we are fixing a fundamentally broken tax system that dates back to the origins of this state as one of the founding states of this country,” Greenwald said.
New Jersey in 2024 tied with Illinois for the highest property tax rate in the nation, according to the Tax Foundation, and the average property tax bill in the state rose to a record high $10,570 last year.
It’s unclear what changes to the state’s funding formula lawmakers will eventually propose. The Department of Education last week said it would continue soliciting feedback from stakeholders at least through December.
Senate Majority Leader Teresa Ruiz (D-Essex) earlier told the Monitor she does not expect a proposal to be ready before the end of the current July-to-June fiscal year.
Among some other things, the reforms aim to better fund school transportation and extraordinary special education.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT greenhouse gas emissions are down, not enough to meet 2030 goal
description: CT is making progress in reducing emissions, but new projections show the state is unlikely to meet its target by 2030.
text:
Connecticut is making progress in reducing its greenhouse gas emissions, but new projections show the state is unlikely to meet its target by 2030 – making it harder to stave off the local impacts of global warming.
“Cutting greenhouse gas emissions is critical,” said Emma Cimino, acting commissioner for Connecticut’s Department of Energy and Environmental Protection.
“Preventing the worst impact of climate change is far, far cheaper than repairing the damage that more and more extreme weather events can have on our infrastructure, our natural resources, and our public health,” she said.
Cimino pointed to a rain bomb in September that dumped more than 7 inches of precipitation in Fairfield County, flooding homes, businesses and parts of I-95.
“When it rains, it can rain much harder. This means more pressure on roads, drainage systems, homes, businesses, and public infrastructure,” she said. “Addressing climate change is an affordability issue for our state.”
Connecticut’s greenhouse gas emissions are 28% less than what they were in 2001, but in order to meet its target by 2030, the state will need to bring that reduction to 45%. Current projections show the state is likely to miss that goal by about 9%.
What CT’s climate projections show
Greenhouse gas emissions from homes, commercial buildings and electric power decreased from 2023 to 2024, according to data released by the Governor’s Council on Climate Change in November.
Emissions from buildings are down as more people switch from home heating oil to natural gas, while the number of people using electricity has risen to approximately 20%. That’s according to Michael Malmrose, associate research analyst with DEEP’s Office of Energy Supply and Infrastructure.
Emissions from electric power are down as dirtier power plants are being replaced with gas generators and the Millstone Nuclear Power Station has been online for all of 2024, Malmrose said.(Reactors at Millstone were offline for 89 days for refueling in 2023).
Cimino called the emission reductions “real progress”.
“This is really significant because emissions continue to stay below pre-pandemic levels, even as Connecticut’s economy has recovered,” she said.
But emissions from transportation increased by approximately half a million metric tons from 2023 to 2024. That’s equivalent to the amount of gas emitted by more than 110,000 motor vehicles in an entire year, according to the Environmental Protection Agency.
“The numbers are a little daunting,” Cimino said.
What’s driving transportation emissions
A spokesperson for DEEP said the uptick was largely driven by increased gasoline consumption. Part of that was caused by a 2% bump in the number of miles travelled, but it’s not clear what else could be contributing to the rise.
One thing is certain – state environment officials don’t expect the issue to get any better now that the Trump administration has rolled back regulations on air pollution and fuel efficiency standards for new cars.
“Connecticut cannot meet our goals on our own. We need our federal partners to engage as well. Unfortunately, we’re seeing the opposite of that right now,” Cimino said.
The transportation sector is the highest source of greenhouse gas emissions in Connecticut, releasing more than twice as much carbon as residential buildings.
One way to fix that? Electric vehicles.
“EV adoption is going to be a key to getting those emissions down lower,” Malmrose said.
As of July 2027, more than 75,000 electric vehicles were registered in Connecticut, making up 3% percent of all motor vehicles on the road.
DEEP recently expanded the state’s EV rebate program, known as CHEAPR, to include more used electric vehicles. Under the new guidelines, used EVs with a purchase price of $35,000 or less may become eligible for the state’s Rebate+ Used incentive of up to $5,000.
“We continue to recognize, as a state, that some of the upfront costs are higher for those technologies,” Cimino said.
This story was first published Nov. 18, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: VTDigger
title: Gov. Phil Scott appoints new transportation, utilities leaders
description:
Greg Knight, the former head of the Vermont National Guard, will serve as interim secretary of transportation, while Brittney Wilson will lead the Department of Public Service.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Gov. Phil Scott appoints new transportation, utilities leaders.
text:
Greg Knight, former adjutant general of the Vermont National Guard, discusses his new role as special advisor to Gov. Phil Scott in Montpelier on Tuesday, September 8, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Vermont Gov. Phil Scott’s cabinet is going to look different when he takes office for his sixth term.
Shortly after Election Day, the governor’s office announced that two leaders in his administration were retiring: Joe Flynn, the longtime secretary of the Vermont Agency of Transportation, and Kerrick Johnson, commissioner of the Vermont Department of Public Service. 
Wednesday, Scott’s office announced their replacements. Greg Knight, the former adjutant general of the Vermont National Guard, will serve as interim secretary of the transportation agency. Brittney Wilson, currently the No. 2 at the public service department, will take over as commissioner.
The public service department oversees energy, telecommunications, water and wastewater infrastructure in the state. 
Scott’s office also said that Trini Brassard, a 30-year VTrans employee who most recently oversaw the agency’s rail, aviation and public transit programs, will serve as interim deputy secretary of transportation under Knight. Both Brassard’s and Knight’s appointments are expected to last about six months, according to a press release. 
Knight, a retired major general, left his post at the head of the guard earlier this year. He was later named a special advisor to the governor.
“I am truly honored to be appointed to this role and sincerely appreciate Governor Scott’s trust and confidence in me,” Knight said in the release. 
Wilson previously worked in Scott’s office as deputy chief of staff.
“Brittney has been a trusted member of my team since day one,” Scott said in the release. “She’s proven to be an effective leader, and I know she’ll continue to keep affordability for ratepayers at the forefront of PSD’s work.”
Last month, Scott announced a new interim leader at the Vermont Agency of Digital Services, Andrea DeLaBruere, who took over from Denise Reilly-Hughes after serving as the agency’s No 2. According to her LinkedIn page, Reilly-Hughes now works at Microsoft, where she also held multiple roles prior to joining state government.
In July, Scott appointed a new head of the state Agency of Commerce and Community Development. Tayt Brooks took over as secretary for Lindsay Kurrle, who is now set to be president and CEO of Vermont Gas Services starting Jan. 1.
There are 13 total positions in Scott’s cabinet, according to a list on his office’s website. That means about a third of the seats have turned over since the start of the year.

name: Delaware
title: New report raises three questions about Delaware’s freight growth
description: An examination of port expansion, warehouse development and roadside data collection asks what Delawareans can learn from the public records A report published Nov. 16 by former New Castle County Council President Karen Hartley-Nagle examines Delaware’s growing role in moving freight and asks what that growth could mean for taxpayers, nearby neighborhoods an[...]
text:
In The Corridor Was Built First, published by The Truthline Network, draws on transportation plans, project records, and spending figures. The report identifies $10B in transportation spending, with 20.8 million square feet of new warehouse space in 26 sites (18 in New Castle County), and a Bluetooth tracking system capable of collecting data from your family vehicle. Image created using A! on 10/17/2026
An examination of port expansion, warehouse development and roadside data collection asks what Delawareans can learn from the public records
A report published Nov. 16 by former New Castle County Council President Karen Hartley-Nagle examines Delaware’s growing role in moving freight and asks what that growth could mean for taxpayers, nearby neighborhoods and drivers.
In The Corridor Was Built First, published by The Truthline Network, Hartley-Nagle draws on transportation plans, project records and spending figures. She argues that decisions made across several administrations are turning Delaware into a regional freight hub, with few opportunities for residents to weigh the combined effects.
Gov. Matt Meyer has promoted the Port of Wilmington expansion as a source of union jobs and a way to make Delaware more competitive in trade. The Delaware Department of Transportation has published a draft statewide freight plan and invited public comment. The report brings those efforts together and raises three questions the public records answer only in part. Meyer’s State of the State address
How much public money is committed to freight?
The report puts the broader transportation figure at about $10 billion. It adds Delaware’s $325 million commitment to the $669 million Edgemoor container terminal, the $3.7 billion six-year statewide transportation program and about $6 billion in unfunded transportation needs. The six-year program covers roads, bridges and transit, too. The amount specifically committed to freight expansion remains an open question.
What happens when several warehouses open in the same area?
The report argues that reviewing warehouses one at a time can obscure the effects on neighborhoods when multiple sites share the same roads. The draft DelDOT inventory it cites lists 20.8 million square feet of warehouse and logistics space planned or under construction at 26 sites, including 18 in New Castle County. That figure measures building floor space. The local questions are how much farmland or open space could be converted, how much pavement could be added and how much truck traffic those sites could generate together.
What happens to the data roadside readers collect?
The report describes how DelDOT can match a detectable Bluetooth device, such as a phone or an in-car hands-free system, between two roadside readers. DelDOT says it uses those matches to measure travel times. A traffic-management study cited in the report describes indefinite storage of incoming data and lists road-segment information and travel times as Bluetooth inputs. The records reviewed leave open whether DelDOT keeps individual device identifiers today, how long it retains them and who can access them.
GO BOX | Read the report and check the records
Start with the full report. Read The Corridor Was Built First. Use its table of contents to jump to a topic or scroll to The Evidence File for the source list.

Public spending. Compare the Edgemoor funding announcement, DelDOT’s six-year capital program and May transportation funding task force minutes, page 5.
Warehouse growth. Look for Exhibit B-27 in the draft Delaware State Freight Plan. For a site-level example, see DelDOT’s traffic review for the proposed Jamison Corner Road warehouses.
Roadside data. Start with DelDOT’s explanation of Bluetooth monitoring, then read Table 5 and the paragraph below it in the traffic-management system report.

Pick the question closest to home and follow the records. Which conclusions do the documents support, and what would you still want officials to explain?

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Governor’s Council OKs two Healey pardons in under five minutes
authors: Katie Castellani | State House News Service
description: "Our justice system should recognize when people have taken responsibility and made meaningful changes in their lives. These pardons are about fairness and removing barriers to jobs, housing and other opportunities," Healey said in a statement when she recommended the pardons.
text:
THE GOVERNOR’S COUNCIL unanimously approved both of Gov. Maura Healey’s recent pardon recommendations during a brief meeting Wednesday.
The council voted 7-0 in favor of the pardon for Jayaar Gonzalez, who was convicted of selling cocaine in 1997 when he was 17. It was Gonzalez’s first offense, and he was sentenced to one to two years in state prison and released after 11 months, according to the governor’s office. 
After his release, Gonzalez earned a GED and an HVAC license and now hopes to start an HVAC business with his son, according to Healey’s office. Gonzalez sought a pardon so his conviction doesn’t limit where he can work, including in some state and federal buildings.
Councilors also voted 7-0 in favor of pardoning Brittany Reichmann, who was convicted of two counts of possession with intent to distribute a Class A substance in 2014 when she was 23. The governor’s office said Reichmann developed a substance use dependency after she was prescribed opiates for managing pain from a dental surgery during her senior year of high school. She was sentenced to six months in a house of correction, suspended, with four years of probation, according to the governor’s office. 
Reichmann completed her sentence in 2018, and Healey’s office said she has been sober since 2017. Since her release, Reichmann has worked in recovery, most recently as director of Recovery Friendly Workplace in Maine, which connects with businesses to help employees in recovery, according to Healey’s office. According to her LinkedIn page, Reichmann also founded Guiding Light Billing Solutions in October 2025. The small business helps behavioral health and substance use treatment providers navigate Maine’s Medicaid program. She is seeking a pardon to make sure her record doesn’t limit future employment opportunities or the ability to participate in her children’s school and sports activities, Healey’s office said.
“Our justice system should recognize when people have taken responsibility and made meaningful changes in their lives. These pardons are about fairness and removing barriers to jobs, housing and other opportunities,” Healey said in a November 10 statement when she recommended the pardons.
The governor has recommended 29 pardons since taking office in 2023. The Governor’s Council is responsible for reviewing and voting on the governor’s clemency recommendations and judicial nominations. 
Councilors did not discuss the pardons during Wednesday’s meeting, which lasted less than five minutes. Councilor Joseph Ferreira was absent.
Councilors also set a hearing for December 1 at 2 p.m. for Healey’s nomination of Elizabeth Rodriguez-Ross as an associate justice of the Housing Court. Another hearing for the renomination of former state Rep. James Kelcourse to the Parole Board was scheduled for December 1 at 3 p.m.
Rodriguez-Ross is an attorney at GLBTQ Legal Advocates & Defenders, where she has worked since 2024, according to her LinkedIn page. She has experience in Housing Court that includes representing a housing management company in legal matters, representing property owners and landlords, helping with code enforcement and creating a commission to manage and rehabilitate properties in Holyoke, according to Healey’s office. Rodriguez-Ross has also provided pro bono representation for those facing foreclosures and eviction orders. Rodriguez-Ross helped create the Volunteers for Justice — now named Lawyer for a Day — program in the Western Housing Court that’s meant to help low-income residents get legal representation. 
Kelcourse has been on the Parole Board since 2022. Before that, he ran a solo law practice in Newburyport and served four terms in the House as a Republican representing the First Essex District.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Online food influencers share Jackson’s gastronomic secrets
description: Food influencer Fallah Heard with a Stamps Burger she reviewed, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, in Jackson. Heard, known online as "Fallah the Foodie," is an online content creator who has acquired over 185,000 followers.
text:
Editor’s Note: Mississippi Today might be known for its investigative journalism and accountability reporting, but it won’t shy from performing another important public service: sharing the best eats around Jackson with the debut of a new food feature, Locals Only. Hosted by Jackson reporter Aaron Lampley, the series aims to introduce locals and visitors alike to Jackson’s culinary gems.



Jackson is known for many things, including its rich heritage as a city of the Deep South. What’s less known is its emerging food scene. The capital city has over 200 restaurants, four of which are Michelin recommended, sprawled across 113 square miles.


With an ever growing number of dining options, some might still be unfamiliar with the city’s gastronomic offerings. 
Joycelyn Lashae has worked to change that over the past year with her online food reviews.
Most fans know Lashae for keeping restaurants “on the clock” and getting their owners “on the line” — a catchphrase she uses at the beginning of her videos.
Food influncer Joycelyn Lashae poses with sweet potato fries and a porkchop sandwich from Ray’s to Go in a video posted to social media on Thursday, Feb. 12, 2026 Credit: Courtesy: Joycelyn Lashae
Lashae’s lack of confidence, however, prompted her to pause the endeavor. But she never let go of the idea. She began posting online food reviews in January following a breakup.“I found my purpose again,” Lashae said. “ I was like ‘Hey, I’m gonna do something.’”The Edwards native began selecting random restaurants to review in her spare time. Since then, Lashae has accumulated over 105,000 followers across her social media network and offers a smorgasbord of food reviews for the Jackson-metro area.
Nearly a decade ago, Lashae purchased a camera and lighting equipment for “mukbang” videos — a Korean word coined to describe people gorging on large amounts of food while being broadcast online. 
Lashae is not the only Jacksonian who is focusing their social efforts on the city’s food culture. 
Fallah Heard, also known as FallahtheFoodie, is also here to help.
“I go around finding all the good spots and putting y’all on,” is how she starts the food reviews she shares across social media. 
The Jackson-based food influencer boasts over 185,000 “fallawers” across major platforms, where she offers her take on restaurants, food trucks and festivals across the state.
Food influencer Fallah Heard, left, known online as “Fallah the Foodie,” chats with Phil Stamps Jr., at Stamps Burger, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, in Jackson. Heard is an online content creator who has acquired over 185,000 followers. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
The Byram native began creating social media content during the pandemic to promote her business selling home-cooked plates. She later experimented with trying food on camera, leading to her popular food reviews. 
Now Heard hops from eatery to eatery, hoping to serve as a guide for those who want to learn more about Mississippi’s food scene.
“I love to make it so that when they do come to Mississippi, they stop,” Heard said. “Even if they’re just getting off the highway right quick for some good food, they can check out my page and find some great food.” 
Both creators attribute their success to the growing food scene in Jackson and its potential to create connections between locals and undiscovered businesses. Their content also serves as a way to breathe life into struggling eateries.
Heard and Lashae say they pay for their own meals and typically don’t tell the owners they are coming.“I’m literally showing up to promote these small businesses because I know everybody is struggling in this economy,” Lashae said. “And if I could do this small thing for a business owner to make them have an influx of business, I feel like I’m walking in my purpose.”
The online creators hope  their work serves to shed more light on Jackson and increase its appeal to outsiders.
Visit Jackson offers a restaurant guide on its website that highlights some of the capital city’s more popular spots. However, official channels for Jackson restaurants end there — leaving the slack to be picked up via word of mouth or social media.
“It’s some things to do around here,” Heard said. “Take yourself out to eat. Take yourself out to find some fun to do. Find a festival. It’s so much more to Jackson than just the things we see on the news.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: As Pennsylvania’s measles-associated death toll rises, the CDC’s count lags. Why?
description: As the U.S. loses Measles Elimination status, a rift between the state and federal officials more broadly has experts concerned
text:
Ethan Turner holds his 14 month old son, Niko, while he gets the MMR vaccine from Raynard Covarrubio at a vaccine clinic put on by Lubbock Public Health Department on March 1, 2025 in Lubbock, Texas. (Photo by Jan Sonnenmair/Getty Images)On Tuesday, it was announced by the Pan American Health Organization that the United States officially lost the measles-elimination status it had earned in 2000. The virus, they determined, has now spread nonstop in the country for one year.
Pennsylvania has emerged as the epicenter of that outbreak, with nearly 1,600 cases and eight deaths reported by public health officials this year to date, more than any other state in the country.
But rifts between state and federal health officials have complicated the picture, and experts warn that could risk the spread of misinformation and confusion over how best to combat the disease.
The conflict is perhaps most apparent in how the state and federal government are counting deaths from measles. 
While Pennsylvania’s Health Department has recorded eight measles-associated deaths this year, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has only recognized six nationwide. Two others measles-associated deaths have been reported by Wisconsin’s health department and one by New York’s, but it’s unclear which deaths are or aren’t being counted by the CDC. 
Lizzie Harvey, deputy press secretary for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, which houses the CDC, said, for privacy purposes, the agency would not provide any details about the deaths to the Capital-Star, including what state or county the deceased were in.
The schism between the state and federal agencies  comes down to a recent change in CDC policy about how they define and count measles deaths. While they used to rely on data from state health departments, in September, the CDC said it would get its tally from the number of deaths reported by the National Center for Health Statistics where measles was listed as the underlying cause.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
It’s a change in longstanding precedent. Experts say the NCHS data, because it often lags, is better for retrospective study than understanding the scope of an ongoing outbreak. And it risks undercounting the number of deaths caused by measles.
Many states like Pennsylvania track what are known as “measles-associated deaths,” which the Department of Health defines as deaths that occur within weeks of measles symptoms emerging and not caused by unrelated incidents such as a car crash. This helps to capture deaths where the underlying cause may be another disease or infection that became more severe because of measles’ destructive impacts on the immune system.
Harvey told the Capital-Star using NCHS data “ensures accuracy by preventing the inclusion of cases in which measles may have been present but was not the cause of death. Including such cases could inhibit HHS from assessing the nationwide situation accurately and addressing it with precision.”
But, public health experts warn the change in policy upends decades of generally accepted best practices and risks downplaying the severity of the outbreak.
“I think there’s a generous and a cynical view here,” William Moss, an epidemiology professor at Johns Hopkins’ Bloomberg School of Public Health, said about the change in CDC policy. “The generous interpretation, I think, is that they’re being careful and wanting to make sure that the deaths that are being counted are truly due to measles … The more cynical view is it’s an effort to minimize the severity of measles, and that is consistent with some other messaging we’ve seen from the federal government. I don’t know how to adjudicate these views.”
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has a long history of spreading misinformation about vaccines’ proven efficacy and safety.
At the center of the rift between Pennsylvania and federal officials  sits Gov. Josh Shapiro and Kennedy, who have repeatedly criticized one another in public appearances and on social media.
Here’s a breakdown of what has changed so far in how the CDC counts deaths from measles, what it means for Pennsylvania, and why it has experts concerned.
A screenshot of the Pa. Department of Health’s measles dashboard showing cases by county as of Nov. 18, 2026
How it started
Pennsylvania recorded its first measles deaths of 2026 in late August, after an outbreak centered mostly in Lancaster County had already sickened more than 400 people in the state.
Shapiro announced the two deaths himself without providing much additional information, which officials said was to protect the privacy of the deceased and their families. 
Reporters were later told one victim was an infant whose primary cause of death was laceration to the spleen. The baby had contracted measles from its mother before birth, which can cause inflammation of the spleen and raise the risk of a rupture.
But with little information available to the public, Kennedy took to social media, saying the Shapiro administration may have “fabricated” the deaths. He cited Lancaster County Coroner Stephen Diamantoni,  who said that measles had not yet been determined as the underlying cause of death. He also accused the state Department of Health of failing to share data with the CDC, a charge the department and Shapiro’s office have refuted. The Atlantic reported that the baby’s parents believed the death was caused by measles.
The governor, for his part, had accused Kennedy on the same platform of “downplaying the severity of measles” and promoting misinformation that contributed to a decline in vaccination rates.
As the two leaders continued to go after one another over several days, the official stance of the CDC remained that no verifiable measles deaths had been recorded in the country in 2026. Reuters reported that Kennedy himself asked his CDC director not to count the Pennsylvania measles deaths in their nationwide tally.
Less than two weeks later, on Sept. 4, the CDC updated its webpage that tracks measles cases and deaths to note the CDC was “working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists (CSTE) to develop a standardized case definition for deaths due to measles. This work is intended to promote consistent classification and reporting of measles deaths across jurisdictions.”
Conflicting approaches to defining a measles death
As it stands, the CDC says it is still working on that definition of a measles death.
But Dr. Matt Ferrari, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Dynamics at Penn State, says public health officials already had a widely-accepted definition of what counts as a measles-attributable death based on one promoted by the World Health Organization. And it intentionally includes the deaths of people who died of subsequent health complications after contracting measles.
A little girl with measles. (Photo by Getty Images)
According to the WHO, a measles-related death is any death that occurs in an individual with a confirmed measles case within 30 days of symptom onset and is not due to an unrelated cause like acute trauma.
“The reason we use this definition of a measles-attributable death is because it is a prospective view of, ‘what is the value that the vaccine could provide,’” Ferrari said. “Whether or not that child died when they still had rash, or died because they were immunocompromised and subsequently infected with a bacteria that caused pneumonia or diarrheal disease, a measles vaccine would have prevented either of those outcomes.”
According to Rob Bonacci, a special advisor to Pennsylvania Department of Health Sec. Debra Bogen, the WHO definition almost exactly matches the one used by the state agency. Bonacci noted that the state has relied on definitions from the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists (the group CDC says it is working to define measles deaths with) when tracking outbreaks of other diseases. But the group had no such definition for a measles death.
“Part of that may be because measles has been so rare in recent years,” he said.
Despite the back-and-forth between Shapiro and Kenedy, Bonacci says state health officials still work closely with the CDC’s measles team.
“We meet with them on an every-other-week basis,” he said. “We have requested technical assistance from them many times. They have a lot of expert knowledge, and we’ve relied on that knowledge to provide assistance to our outbreak response here.”
Still, Shapiro has continued to criticize the head of the U.S. Health Department.
Rosie Lapowsky, a spokesperson for Shapiro, told the Capital-Star, “Conspiracy theorists like RFK, Jr. have no business leading our nation’s public health agencies. His deliberate choice to ignore medical experts and longstanding death reporting protocols puts lives at risk.”
Shapiro has often invoked Kennedy’s history of questioning the safety and efficacy of proven vaccines.
Before becoming U.S. Health secretary, Kennedy served as the chair of an anti-vaccine nonprofit called Children’s Health Defense. In that role, he advocated for alternative treatments for vaccine-curable diseases and spread misinformation about vaccine safety.
As head of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, he gutted and replaced a 17-person vaccine advisory council at the CDC, cut funding for vaccine research and has hired vaccine skeptics.
Roughly five years before the current outbreak, Kennedy spoke to a crowd of hundreds in Lancaster County, telling them that “the cure for measles is chicken soup and vitamin A,” and warning that “public health agencies and the pharmaceutical industry” were hiding science about the dangers of vaccines.
More recently, Kennedy has encouraged vaccination.called the MMR (Measles, Mumps Rubella) vaccine “the most effective way to prevent measles.”
“Under Secretary Kennedy’s leadership, CDC has mounted an aggressive response to measles outbreaks across the country,” said Harvey, the HHS spokesperson. “Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to recommend the MMR vaccine as the most effective way to prevent measles and protect communities from further spread.”
Children can receive their first dose of the MMR vaccine, above, after 12 months of age. The United States lost its measles elimination status in mid-November 2026 after more than 25 years. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)
Experts say vaccinations are the key
The measles vaccine is highly effective, and nearly universally considered the best tool we have to combat the ongoing measles outbreak. People with two doses of the MMR or MMRV vaccine have 97% protection against measles. Those with a single dose have around 93% protection. In the rare cases where vaccinated people contract measles, they are less likely to have severe symptoms or complications.
Of the nearly 1,600 people who have contracted measles in Pennsylvania this year, less than 1% were fully vaccinated, according to the state Department of Health.
Roughly one in five people who contract measles require hospitalization, with children, pregnant women and unvaccinated people at the highest risk. About one to three out of every 1,000 people who contract measles will die.
Generally, infants receive their first dose of the MMR or MMRV vaccine when they’re around a year old, and a second dose between ages 4 and 6. But the CDC recommends that parents of infants at heightened risk of developing measles, such as those living in areas where the disease is spreading rapidly, consider getting their child an initial dose as young as 6 months old.
However, infants under a year old with developing immune systems will receive less protection from the vaccine. Because of that, it’s recommended those who receive an early shot early still get two additional doses at a year old and between 4 and 6 years old.
“That’s the trade-off,” Moss said. “For 25 years we’ve had the luxury of having measles elimination status in this country. So the risk was low that these children could wait until they’re one year of age when a higher proportion will respond.”
Concerned parents should speak to their pediatricians.
Measles vaccines are widely available in Pennsylvania, including at 59 state health centers that provide them for free to uninsured or under-insured Pennsylvanians. Many county or municipal health centers are providing them as well. Those who are unvaccinated or unsure of their vaccination status are urged to talk to their doctors or visit these centers.

name: California
title: ¿Los últimos reclutas del Departamento de bomberos del condado de San Diego? Cientos de cabras hambrientas
description: Un rebaño de cabras pasta en un parque de San Diego, como parte del plan de prevención de incendios forestales del condado: "Son como un perro con cuernos, pero tan listos como un gato".
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Este mes, más de 500 nuevos miembros del cuerpo de bomberos trabajaron arduamente en Star Valley Park, en el condado de San Diego, limpiando la maleza y la hierba hasta dejar solo los rastrojos.
Al terminar, corrieron hacia el campo contiguo, empujándose unos a otros, saltando por encima de un perro pastor y mordisqueando la vegetación crecida.
 El proyecto, en la comunidad de Valley Center, es un programa piloto que emplea rebaños de cabras para eliminar la vegetación y reducir el riesgo de incendios forestales.
 “Es de gran ayuda para las agencias locales utilizar estas cabras, utilizar estos segadores vivientes aquí, para hacer que este lugar sea seguro”, dijo Jake Enriquez, gerente regional del Departamento de Parques y Recreación del Condado de San Diego.
Mientras los animales se agolpaban en el prado sin tratar, las madres guiaban a sus crías hacia los parches de hierba, y los animales más grandes se apoyaban contra un roble para comerse las hojas. Cinco perros blancos y mullidos —una mezcla de pastor de Anatolia y gran pirineo— patrullaban el rebaño. Varias cabras se acercaron para inspeccionar a los visitantes y que les rascaran la cabeza.
 “Son como un perro con cuernos, pero tan listos como un gato”, dijo Enriquez. “Son animales muy inteligentes, y se puede ver cómo interactúan, cómo siguen al perro”.
 Las cabras forman parte de la estrategia del condado para reducir el riesgo de incendios forestales en terrenos públicos, mediante la limpieza de la vegetación alrededor de las viviendas, a lo largo de las carreteras principales y en áreas que puedan ser necesarias como lugares de evacuación.
 Los devastadores incendios forestales que azotaron las zonas rurales de San Diego a principios de este siglo obligaron al condado a reformular su estrategia de lucha contra incendios.
Con viviendas dispersas entre la densa maleza en la zona rural, el incendio de Cedar en 2003 arrasó más de un cuarto de millón de acres, destruyó 2,820 edificios y causó la muerte de 15 personas.
En 2007, los cables de alta tensión azotados por el viento provocaron el incendio de Witch Creek, mientras que otros dos incendios de gran magnitud comenzaron el mismo día. En conjunto, arrasaron casi 300,000 acres, destruyeron 1,650 edificios, obligaron a la evacuación de medio millón de personas y causaron 7 muertes.
El fuego avanza hacia las casas en Scripps Ranch a lo largo de Pomerado Road durante el incendio Cedar en San Diego, el 26 de octubre de 2003. Foto de John Gibbins, The San Diego Union-Tribune vía Getty Images.
 Tras esos desastres, el condado de San Diego mejoró su capacidad de extinción de incendios desde el aire mediante la creación de una base Helitack de CalFire en la comunidad de Ramona, al este del condado, la incorporación de un avión cisterna C-130 Hercules de CalFire y un helicóptero Sikorsky S-70 CalFire Hawk, y la mejora de los sistemas de comunicaciones de emergencia.
Pero la prevención de incendios comienza en tierra. El condado limpia la maleza a lo largo de 1287 kilómetros de carreteras al año para garantizar rutas de evacuación seguras y realizó inspecciones de seguridad contra incendios en 15,000 viviendas el año pasado, según declaró Jeff Collins, director del Departamento de Bomberos del Condado de San Diego. Ahora, está incorporando cabras a su equipo de extinción de incendios.
Los funcionarios utilizaron fondos iniciales del condado para poner en marcha el proyecto piloto en Star Valley Park, y acaban de recibir una subvención estatal de 300,000 dólares para llevar el programa de pastoreo a otras zonas con alto riesgo de incendios.
 “Es una herramienta más en el conjunto de herramientas para intentar reducir el riesgo, tanto en incendios pequeños como en incendios a gran escala”, dijo Collins.
 Recientemente, las cabras se han unido a los equipos de bomberos en otras partes del estado y del condado. San Diego Gas & Electric utiliza cabras para la prevención de incendios , que se encargan de desbrozar la maleza cerca de las líneas eléctricas. En septiembre, la Estación Aérea del Cuerpo de Marines de Miramar lanzó la “Operación Cuerda de Cabra” para reducir el riesgo de incendios forestales en terrenos accidentados dentro de la base, en lo que, según los oficiales del Cuerpo de Marines, es la primera campaña de este tipo con cabras en una instalación militar estadounidense.
 Hace unos años, los bomberos de Glendale, California, trajeron cabras para limpiar la maleza seca de los barrios residenciales del condado de Los Ángeles. Asimismo, investigadores de Cal Poly, San Luis Obispo, desplegaron cerca de 1000 de estos animales para devorar la maleza y las plantas invasoras en la estación de investigación de la universidad en Swanton Pacific Ranch, en el condado de Santa Cruz, que fue arrasada por incendios forestales en 2020.
 Chad Hanson, experto en ecología del fuego y director del Proyecto John Muir, afirmó que las cabras pueden ser útiles, siempre y cuando se utilicen en los lugares adecuados. Advirtió que cualquier método de eliminación de vegetación en bosques y arboledas puede tener un efecto contraproducente al convertir esas áreas en pastizales más inflamables. En cambio, los administradores de tierras deberían centrarse en despejar el espacio alrededor de las viviendas y la infraestructura clave.
 “Lo que defiendo es centrar nuestros recursos y atención en crear comunidades seguras contra incendios, reforzar las viviendas y eliminar la vegetación que las rodea”, dijo Hanson.
 Star Valley Park es un antiguo rancho de aproximadamente 16 hectáreas ubicado en la comunidad rural de Valley Center, al norte del condado de San Diego, rodeado de casas y caminos públicos. Se encuentra mayormente sin desarrollar, y el condado está explorando ideas para nuevas instalaciones, pero mientras tanto, el parque es un centro para actividades ecuestres. Los vaqueros de Valley Center se reúnen allí para entrenamientos y eventos ecuestres, y el Valley Center Stampede celebra un rodeo anual en el lugar.
 “El Departamento de Bomberos del Condado se puso en contacto con nosotros y nos preguntó: ‘¿Tienen alguna propiedad en esta zona del Condado de San Diego donde realicen un manejo continuo de la vegetación?’”, dijo Enriquez. “Star Valley nos brindó una excelente oportunidad para poner a prueba este programa”. 
 Aproximadamente 525 cabras pastan en el Parque Star Valley en Valley Center como parte de un programa piloto para eliminar plantas que pueden alimentar incendios forestales. Foto cortesía del Condado de San Diego.
 Seleccionaron el parque como sitio piloto para el pastoreo de cabras debido a la combinación de riesgos y beneficios que presenta. Está rodeado de viviendas al norte, este y oeste, y de carreteras al norte y sur, todas las cuales serían vulnerables en caso de incendio.
Mientras tanto, la presencia de camiones y remolques en los eventos ecuestres representa un riesgo de ignición en época seca, dijo Johnny Gonzalez, gerente de operaciones de campo de Environmental Land Management, la empresa contratista del condado.
 Pero una vez despejado de maleza, el parque podría servir como lugar de evacuación para el vecindario en caso de incendio forestal, y como punto de concentración para equipos de bomberos, helicópteros, camiones cisterna, camiones de agua y otros equipos.
 “Tener una franja de vegetación aquí es muy ventajoso para los bomberos”, dijo Enriquez. “Les proporciona un espacio seguro desde donde trabajar… Hay muchas ventajas en tener un terreno limpio y bien mantenido, y estas cabras hacen un trabajo fantástico”.
 Según Collins, los bomberos del condado también utilizan segadoras, motosierras o quemas controladas para despejar la maleza y los arbustos crecidos en exceso. Sin embargo, las cabras pueden acceder a espacios reducidos y transitar por terrenos escarpados y rocosos. Además, mastican la vegetación hasta una altura mayor que la que alcanza la cuchilla de una segadora, por lo que el mantenimiento es más sencillo una vez que terminan su trabajo, explicó Enriquez.
 Según González, la naturaleza desnuda de los terrenos donde pastan las cabras permite que la tierra actúe como cortafuegos, en lugar de como fuente de combustible: “Esto es lo segundo mejor después de la tierra mineral, porque la tierra absorbe las brasas cuando estas se incendian en el campo”.
 Las cabras también ayudan a podar plantas invasoras como la mostaza, el cardo y la hierba rodadora, que les resultan más sabrosas que la vegetación autóctona, que es más alcalina.
 El uso de estos animales reduce el polvo y los gases de escape producidos por las motosierras y las cortadoras de césped, lo que resulta más respetuoso con el medio ambiente del vecindario. Además de sus balidos, las cabras hacen menos ruido que la maquinaria pesada.
 “Aquí, están gestionando la vegetación con discreción”, dijo Enriquez. “Se puede ver lo bien podada que la han dejado y lo limpio que está alrededor de los árboles. Como administradores de tierras, nos entusiasma mucho esto porque se necesita mucho tiempo, energía y trabajo para mantener una propiedad segura y limpia”.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: An eighth person has died with measles in Pennsylvania, Health Department says
description: An unvaccinated person died with measles in Clinton County, marking the eighth measles-associated death in the state this year, according to the state Department of Health.
text:
Children can receive their first dose of the MMR vaccine, above, after 12 months of age. The United States lost its measles elimination status in mid-November 2026 after more than 25 years. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)An unvaccinated person died with measles in Clinton County, marking the eighth measles-associated death in the state this year, according to the state Department of Health.
Few additional details were provided, including information about the person’s age, potential comorbidities or whether measles was recorded as the underlying cause of death. The department said the lack of information was to protect the privacy of the person and their family.
The Health Department defines a “measles-associated death” as a death that occurs within 30 days of confirmed measles symptoms onset and not due to unrelated causes, like a car accident.
The number of confirmed measles cases in Pennsylvania this year has also risen to 1,589, as of Wednesday. The state has recorded more measles cases and related deaths than any other in the country this year.
Of the nearly 1,600 people who have contracted measles in the commonwealth this year, less than 1% were fully vaccinated, and the ongoing outbreak has led to 315 hospitalizations, according to the state Department of health.
It’s official: Measles is endemic again in the US

Roughly one in five people who contract measles require hospitalization, with children, pregnant women, the immunocompromised and unvaccinated people at the highest risk. About one to three out of every 1,000 people who contract measles will die.
The best way to prevent measles infections is by being vaccinated. The MMR and MMRV vaccines are safe, and 97% effective at preventing measles with two doses.
Measles vaccines are widely available at Pennsylvania’s 59 state health centers, which provide them for free to uninsured and under-insured Pennsylvanians. Many county or municipal health centers are providing them as well. Those who are unvaccinated or unsure of their vaccination status are urged to talk to their doctors or visit these centers.
“We are saddened to hear of another death in Pennsylvania,” said Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.  “[The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention] deployed additional support to Pennsylvania to work alongside state and local health officials to investigate the outbreak, strengthen response efforts, and prevent further spread.”
She said the agency has provided the state nearly $4 million in one-time emerging funding to support measles response efforts in 2027.
As it stands, the CDC has not confirmed all eight reported measles deaths in Pennsylvania. While the agency has historically relied on states to collect the data, they changed their policy in September, shortly after U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. accused Gov. Josh Shapiro’s office of having possibly “fabricated” two measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania.
The agency now relies on data from the National Center for Health Statistics, counting cases where measles was confirmed as the underlying cause of death. The CDC has said it is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to develop a new standard definition for measles deaths.

name: VTDigger
title: Franklin County man admits to sexually assaulting and killing woman, faces at least 27 years in prison
description:
Darren Martell Jr. entered guilty pleas Wednesday as part of an agreement with prosecutors to three charges, including second-degree murder in the death of 82-year-old Roberta Martin in Enosburgh in July 2024.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Franklin County man admits to sexually assaulting and killing woman, faces at least 27 years in prison.
text:
Judge Mary Morrissey presides over a change of plea hearing for Darren Martell Jr. Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026 in Franklin Superior criminal court in St. Albans. Court screenshot by Nora Doyle-Burr/VTDigger

A Franklin County man charged with sexually assaulting and killing an 82-year-old Enosburgh woman more than two years ago has reached a plea deal that calls for a sentence of at least 27 years in prison.
Darren Martell Jr., 25, pleaded guilty Wednesday in Franklin Superior criminal court in St. Albans to a charge of second-degree murder in the death of Roberta Martin in July 2024. He also pleaded guilty to charges of sexual assault and obstruction of justice.
As part of the plea deal with prosecutors, Martell faces a sentence of 35 years to life in prison, all suspended except 27 years to serve. 
In addition, according to the plea agreement, Martell would be on probation for life after his release and be required to register as a sex offender. 
“The court is inclined to accept the agreement, recognizing that it has been negotiated in good faith by the parties in recognition of trial risk on both sides,” Judge Mary Morrissey said, setting a formal sentencing hearing for Jan. 13.
“There has been an attempt,” Morrissey added, “to balance public safety along with punishment for the offenses that have been charged here, as well as the fact that the family, understandably, reluctantly supports the agreement.”
Martell had initially faced a charge of aggravated murder, the most serious charge in Vermont, which carries a sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole. 
The plea deal heads off a trial that had been set for next month.
According to charging documents, Martell broke into Martin’s residence on Butternut Hollow Road early on July 17, 2024. Martell had been living at the time in a trailer on a property adjacent to Martin’s residence.
Martell also sexually assaulted and killed Martin, the documents stated. He removed Martin’s body from the home and took the remains to a wooded area where he grew marijuana plants about three-quarters of a mile away from Martin’s home and burned Martin’s body, the documents stated.
Alerted by Martin’s daughter who had not heard from her mother, neighbors arrived at the Butternut Hollow Road home later on July 17 to check on Martin but saw no signs of her. Inside the residence, court filings stated, they saw an unmade bed and a dresser drawer left open, the filing added.
“They advised this was very abnormal for Roberta because she was a very tidy and regimented individual who typically kept to the same schedule every day,” an investigator wrote in charging documents.Police also discovered duct tape on the floor of the bedroom and “dolly cart” tracks leading from the house to a neighboring property, the investigator added. 
Police searching for Martin found her remains about a week later. Martell was arrested soon after, and his DNA was reportedly located on Martin’s body, according to authorities.

READ MORE

Martell was listed Wednesday afternoon as incarcerated at the Northwest State Correctional Facility in St. Albans. 
Assistant Attorney General Franklin Paulino, a prosecutor, told the judge that Martin’s family was aware of the terms of the plea deal. 
“The family reluctantly supports this resolution,” Paulino said, adding, “The family seeks comfort in knowing what will happen, which is the plea agreement that’s stated.”
Paulino told the judge several of Martin’s family members are expected to give statements at the sentencing hearing. 
Jessica Burke, Martell’s attorney, also spoke in court in support of the plea deal.
“We think that this accurately balances the risks to both sides and is sufficient but not greater than necessary to ensure public safety moving forward,” Burke told the judge.
The judge detailed the terms of the plea deal to Martell during Wednesday’s hearing. 
“Yes,” Martell repeatedly replied when asked by Morrissey if he understood each provision of the agreement. 
Morrissey, the judge, ordered the state Department of Corrections to complete a presentence investigation ahead of that proceeding. The investigation leads to a report by a probation officer detailing several factors, including a defendant’s criminal history, to assist the judge in sentencing. 
The judge said at the close of the hearing Wednesday that unless that report comes back with information that “causes concerns about the plea agreement,” the proposed sentence would be imposed.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: School funding reform could prompt NJ constitutional convention
description: New Jersey should call a constitutional convention to include voters in the approval of a new school funding formula once a proposal is finalized, Assembly Majority Leader Lou Greenwald (D-Camden) said. Though legislators and Gov. Mikie Sherrill in August began soliciting input for changes to the state’s funding formula, officials have said little about how [...]
text:
NJ Assembly Majority Leader Louis Greenwald (D-Camden), shown at a news conference earlier this year in Trenton, says the state needs to hold a constitutional convention to approve a new school funding formula. He was speaking at a New Jersey League of Municipalities conference Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo / New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey should call a constitutional convention to include voters in the approval of a new school funding formula once a proposal is finalized, Assembly Majority Leader Lou Greenwald (D-Camden) said.
Though legislators and Gov. Mikie Sherrill in August began soliciting input for changes to the state’s funding formula, officials have said little about how their eventual proposal would differ from the funding formula enacted in 2008, and it’s not clear whether or how a formula enshrined in the state’s constitution would affect court precedent that demands New Jersey students receive a thorough and efficient education.
“I think ultimately this is going to need to lead to a constitutional convention and then a question that will include the voters as part of the solution because I think, ultimately at the end of the day, this is an issue that New Jersey has struggled with for generations,” Greenwald said Wednesday during a panel discussion at the New Jersey League of Municipalities annual conference.
In New Jersey, the state calculates how much each municipality must spend to provide their students a constitutionally sound education and how much those districts can raise on their own based on their residents’ incomes and property values.
State aid fills the rest, though not all districts raise enough revenue to meet the local spending — called a local fair share — needed to fully fund schools after state aid is added.
Some cannot raise enough revenue locally because of the state’s 2% cap on annual property tax levies, and others have been hammered by steep swings in state aid as the state in 2018 moved to begin phasing out aid meant to keep districts whole after the enactment of the 2008 funding formula.
At present, local governments in New Jersey look to property taxes to fund their share of school expenses, and Greenwald suggested that could change as a result of the yet-to-be-determined reforms.
“We need to understand that we are fixing a fundamentally broken tax system that dates back to the origins of this state as one of the founding states of this country,” Greenwald said.
New Jersey in 2024 tied with Illinois for the highest property tax rate in the nation, according to the Tax Foundation, and the average property tax bill in the state rose to a record high $10,570 last year.
It’s unclear what changes to the state’s funding formula lawmakers will eventually propose. The Department of Education last week said it would continue soliciting feedback from stakeholders at least through December.
Senate Majority Leader Teresa Ruiz (D-Essex) earlier told the Monitor she does not expect a proposal to be ready before the end of the current July-to-June fiscal year.
Among some other things, the reforms aim to better fund school transportation and extraordinary special education.
