title: Salesianum and Appoquinimink will Meet in 2026 DIAA Division One Boys Soccer State Championship Game after Semifinal Victories
description: Salesianum defeated Charter School of Wilmington, 6-0, and Appoquinimink defeated Cape Henlopen, 1-0, on November 17 punching their ticket to the 2026 DIAA Division One Boys Soccer State Championship game.   FREDERICA, Del. — Salesianum and Appoquinimink will meet in the state championship game for the first time since 2018 when the two teams play in the 202[...]
text:
The Salesianum boys soccer team celebrates their semifinal win with a group picture. The team will play Appoquinimink in the 2026 DIAA Division One Boys Soccer State Championship game on November 20. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
Salesianum defeated Charter School of Wilmington, 6-0, and Appoquinimink defeated Cape Henlopen, 1-0, on November 17 punching their ticket to the 2026 DIAA Division One Boys Soccer State Championship game.
 
FREDERICA, Del. — Salesianum and Appoquinimink will meet in the state championship game for the first time since 2018 when the two teams play in the 2026 DIAA Division One Boys Soccer State Championship Game, Friday, November 20.
Salesianum defeats Charter School of Wilmington, 6-0
Salesianum junior Bryan Perez-Herrera dribbled the ball down the left side of the field and settled about 15 yards away from the goal. Two Force defenders stood a couple feet away ready to defend the juniors’ attack. 
Perez-Herrera dribbled a little farther down the line then stopped his momentum and made a move to his right to evade the first Force defender. A second evasion got Perez-Herrera past a second defender and created enough space for a right footed shot. The shot curved left as it neared the goal and drifted past the dive of senior Scott Honisch in goal. It drifted so far the shot hit the left post. The ball bounced in on the right side of the net for the first score of the second half.
Perez-Herrera finished the half with a hat-trick that helped Salesianum defeat the Charter School of Wilmington Forces, 6-0, Tuesday night.
Sallies scored five goals in the second half starting with Perez-Herrera’s first in the 45th minute. Perez-Herrera struck again in the 49th minute with a shot to the middle of the net which was set up by an Esser assist, and his third came just two minutes later on a shot that snuck right between the goalkeeper and the right post. Perez-Herrera celebrated each goal by landing a flip, spinning in the air three times. Perez-Herrera said it was the first hat-trick of his high school career.
“It feels great,” Perez-Herrera said postgame. “Just proud of myself honestly.”
Esser scored for the Sals right after his fellow junior’s third goal and a goal by senior Sawyer Valle in the 64th minute completed Sallies’ total. Salesianum senior Nico Rossi scored the first and only goal of the first half on a shot to the back left of the net off an assist by Esser. The Sals’ finished the game with its sixth game scoring six or more points and the team’s tenth shutout of the season. 
“We switched our formation, but they have one guy who’s a game changer. We stayed tight on him in the second half,” Rossi said about the team’s defense. “Once we got on him, didn’t really do anything and kept it [a] clean sheet.”
The Sals are returning to the state championship game for the 17th consecutive season and will try to win their second straight state title in as many seasons. Salesianum has won 14 of the last 16 state championship games. 
Appoquinimink defeats Cape Henlopen, 1-0 (OT)
Appoquinimink sets up for a throw in during its semifinal game against Cape Henlopen. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
Appoquinimink senior Luke Talley placed the ball on the turf in the corner on the right side of the net. Talley took a few steps back, waited for the official’s whistle and served a pass into the box with three minutes elapsed from the first overtime period. 
Talley’s pass soared through the dark night sky and over the heads of Cape Henlopen defenders. The Vikings goalkeeper, Kasen Adams, leaped to try and deflect the pass but the ball flew over his outstretched arm. Jaguar sophomore Aiden Messinger made contact with the pass on an attempted header that hit his chest instead. The ball ricocheted into the air, off the crossbar and back toward Messinger in front of the goal. Messinger’s second attempt hit nothing but net. 
Messinger’s header in the third minute of overtime was the game winning score in Appoquinimink’s, 1-0, overtime victory over Cape Henlopen, Tuesday night.
“I saw the ball go up and first Gabe [Arbuet] on the back post hit it, hit crossbar, it went straight to me [and] I knew I had to put it in the back of the net to finish the game,” Messinger said. 
The game was evenly matched throughout the night. Neither team could gain much momentum and most of the game was played along the edges of the field. 
The Vikings had the best scoring opportunity in the first half on a shot by junior Kihara Ngido that went just high over the top of the goal. The Jaguars generated a corner opportunity late in the half, but the play was defended well and the two teams went into the half without a score.
The Jaguars attempted their first of two free kicks near the goal in the first four minutes of the second half, but the set piece was knocked away by a Cape Henlopen defender. The Jaguars kept the pressure on the Viking defense during the final 20 minutes of the half, but each time Appoquinimink looked like it might break through the Viking defense came up with a stop. Adams was integral to the staunch Viking defense, finishing the game with nine saves.
The Jaguars’ defense played just as well with strong communication along their back line, led in part by senior Reed Holliday. Appoquinimink only allowed a couple shots near the goal and each one was saved by Jaguar goalkeeper, Lincoln Neubauer. The Jaguars continued to create scoring opportunities in the final minutes of the second half, but were turned away by the Viking defense until Messinger’s game winning goal in the first overtime period. 
Appoquinimink is returning to the state championship game for the first time since 2022 and will try to earn the program’s first state championship title since 2020. The Jaguars beat the Sals for the championship title in 2020 and will have to do so again for the 2026 honor. 
The 2026 DIAA Division One Boys Soccer State Championship Game will be played at 7:30 p.m. on Friday, November 20, at DE Turf Sports Complex.

text:
New Zion United Methodist Church traces its roots to the 1830s and now supports youth programs in West Laurel. The public is invited to Friday’s unveiling.
LAUREL, Del. — The building that housed Laurel’s first Black Methodist congregation went on to become the town’s first school for Black children. On Friday, Nov. 20, the state will honor that history with a marker at New Zion United Methodist Church on West Sixth Street.
The Delaware Public Archives announced that the unveiling will begin at 11 a.m. at 1042 W. Sixth St. The ceremony is free and open to the public, with remarks planned from community members, local and state officials and Archives representatives.
From church to schoolhouse
Black and white Methodists in Laurel worshipped together in the early 1830s, according to a church history published by Operation West Laurel. As the Methodist congregation outgrew Zion Meeting House, its trustees gave the building to Black residents. In 1833, it was moved to Townsend Street, where it became their first church.
In the 1860s, the Black congregation bought a second church building, known as New Zion, and moved it to a site across from the present sanctuary. The Townsend Street building then became Laurel’s first school for Black children. A history preserved by the Delaware Public Archives says the school remained there until the county built a replacement and that the old building was torn down in 1924.
That same year, the congregation built the sanctuary it uses today under the Rev. D.G. Waters, according to the church history. The concrete-block building was known as Waters New Zion Methodist Episcopal Church. The adjoining cemetery connects the site to generations of congregants.
New Zion later became part of the Peninsula-Delaware Conference after the region’s separate Black and white Methodist conferences merged in 1965. The United Methodist Church was formed through a national denominational merger three years later.
Worship and youth outreach today
The Peninsula-Delaware Conference lists the Rev. Vanessa Stephens Lee as New Zion’s pastor and gives 10 a.m. as the church’s main worship time.
Outside of worship, New Zion supports Operation West Laurel, an interfaith group that formed after a series of fatal shootings involving young people in Laurel. The church provides space for some of the group’s programs and has helped fund its work, Operation West Laurel organizer Crystal Stevens told Spotlight Delaware in 2025.
The group’s SOAR program offers homework help and reading and math support for children in grades two through six who have been exposed to gun violence. Project RISE offers tutoring, mentoring and job preparation for high school boys. Operation West Laurel also organizes neighborhood prayer walks that give volunteers a chance to hear directly from residents.

title: Parents to ask Nevada lawmakers to mandate 45 minutes of recess in elementary schools
description: The first time her daughter came home saying she’d missed recess for “study hall,” Brandi Vesco thought nothing of it. On Wednesdays, […]
text:
Currently, Nevada law does not require elementary schools to provide any recess time. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The first time her daughter came home saying she’d missed recess for “study hall,” Brandi Vesco thought nothing of it. But as it continued to happen, she began to see skipped recess as a bigger problem.
Vesco found out the school was keeping kids from recess if they hadn’t finished their in-class work. On Wednesdays, the entire school skipped recess for additional instructional time.
When Vesco complained to the teacher and principal, they began allowing her daughter to go to recess and sending unfinished classwork home. Vesco eventually decided to enroll her daughter at a different public school, 5 minutes away, that gives students 45 minutes of recess each day.
She’d found a solution for her daughter, but one thought lingered: What about all the other kids?
“Children don’t thrive sitting and trying to learn for long periods of time,” said Vesco, a former ed-tech reporter and the founder of Washoe Parents Coalition. “It’s common sense to me. We all do better with some exercise and movement in our day.”
Vesco and the coalition are now advocating that all elementary students receive at least 45 minutes of recess during the school day. They also want to prohibit the withholding of recess for academic or minor disciplinary reasons.
An example of a Nevada public school with a policy of withholding recess. (Photo courtesy of Washoe Parents Coalition)
They have secured a bipartisan duo of lawmakers — Assemblymembers Alexis Hansen (R-Sparks) and Selena La Rue Hatch (D-Reno) — to sponsor a bill on the issue when the Nevada State Legislature meets next year.
Hansen, in a statement to the Nevada Current, said the legislation is a “commonsense, bipartisan effort” that will promote “healthier, happier students who are better prepared to learn.”
“Recess isn’t a luxury for children,” she continued. “It’s essential to their physical, emotional, and academic development. Every Nevada elementary school student deserves time during the school day to get outside, move, play, and recharge.”
Currently, Nevada law does not require elementary schools to provide any recess time. The Nevada Department of Agriculture’s Nevada School Wellness Policy, which schools that participate in the National School Lunch Program are supposed to adopt, states schools “must provide the opportunity for moderate to vigorous physical activity” for at least 30 minutes during each regular school day. That same policy states that schools shall not withhold opportunities for physical activity as punishment.
Vesco suspects the policy has little teeth, big loopholes, or both. The coalition has been calling on parents to report existing violations of that policy to the state Department of Agriculture or Washoe County School District, which formally adopted the wellness policy.
WCSD did not respond to the Current’s request for comment.
The coalition assembled a group of volunteers to call every WCSD elementary school to determine how much recess kids were receiving.
They gathered information from 58 of the district’s 66 elementary schools and found that 14 give students 45 minutes or more of recess. They also found that schools in low-income neighborhoods have fewer minutes of recess than schools in higher-income neighborhoods. Low-income schools are also far more likely to not have a physical education teacher.
The opportunity to play, to move and to be outside should not be limited to only certain neighborhoods, argues Vesco and other supporters of the national “Say Yes to Recess” movement. Recess is a valuable part of the educational environment, offering space for friendship and connection, problem solving and resilience.
“I think our school districts get so caught up on catching kids up on their proficiencies, which we should be doing, that we end up cutting things like recess,” said La Rue Hatch, a public school teacher and mother to an elementary schooler. “But every study actually shows us that if we are taking away their recess time, we’re actually taking away their ability to focus and their ability to learn, and we’re actually going to have significantly more harmful consequences as a result.”
While the coalition is based on Washoe, they believe limiting recess is a broader problem for the state. According to Vesco, initial calls to elementary schools within Clark County School District have revealed many offer 20 minutes or less each day. In Douglas County School District, recess time varies from 30 to 55 minutes.
But it’s not all school districts. In Carson City School District, every elementary school offers 45 minutes.
The coalition believes every school can incorporate 45 minutes of recess without making their school day longer or needing additional funding.
“It’s about scheduling,” said Vesco.
The language of the “Say Yes To Recess” bill has not yet been drafted. But the Nevada Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, Children’s Advocacy Alliance, and Nevada Cancer Coalition have already signed onto the cause. Vesco says other groups, including the Nevada State Education Association, which represents teachers and staff across the state, have also signaled support.
Advocates point to research showing that early elementary students who got 45 minutes of recess were “less off task and more focused in class” than students who got 30 minutes.
While the effort is still in its infancy, Vesco says initial response from parents and the public has been wildly positive: “Most people are like ‘Duh.’ Of course elementary school students can’t be sitting still without movement’” for long stretches.
Reporter Jeniffer Solis contributed to this article.

name: California
title: Calaveras County is a cautionary tale when California rural hospitals close maternity units
description: Almost every maternity ward loses money. Hospital leaders and California health officials should ask different questions when weighing a maternity unit closure.
text:
Guest Commentary written by

Maryal Concepcion
Dr. Maryal Concepcion is a family physician in Arnold and founder of My DPC Story, a podcast and education platform for doctors.


Health care officials recently decided Watsonville Community Hospital would close its maternity unit. Hospital leaders said the unit has lost the rural hospital about $10 million a year. 
Also in late October, California’s Rural Health Policy Council met and discussed spending federal funds earmarked for rural health care.
People in both rooms should listen to what’s happened in a county that has made this trip already.
I am a family physician in Arnold, in Calaveras County, in the Sierra Nevada foothills. For the past 10 years, there has been no place to give birth here. My husband and I are the only physicians in the county who provide prenatal care, and we no longer deliver babies.
Here is what a decade without a hospital labor and delivery unit looks like: Pregnant patients with insurance are told to find care in another county. Some keep a particular health plan only so they can deliver at that plan’s hospital, more than two hours away. 
Others plan to deliver in the next county over — if that hospital still accepts their insurance when the time comes. It hasn’t always.
Small tasks become long drives. Near the end of pregnancy, women must drive to another county to drop off urine samples, because there’s no longer a place near home to get blood or urine tested, unless you belong to one of the health system clinics there.
Emergency service gets slower. When a pregnant woman calls my office because she can’t feel her baby move, I can see her, put an ultrasound on her belly and show her the heartbeat. A woman without that kind of access goes to urgent care — which is not reliably open on nights or weekends — and then to an emergency room, if she has a way to get there.
Skills leave with the ward. Ten years on, the nurses who knew how to help with a delivery have lost that practice. Nobody can say for certain that anesthesia is ready for an obstetric emergency. 
There are no fill-in physicians who deliver and no backup plan, because there is no delivery service to back up.
Lastly, bringing maternity service back to an area is harder than keeping it. 
I recently talked with someone who helped restore obstetrics in Plumas County. A community that wants it and has the money to pay for it is not enough, they told me. If the hospital’s leadership won’t come to the table, the effort stalls. 
In my experience, that comes down to politics and dollars, not need.
My advice to Watsonville is to ask a different question than whether the unit loses money, because maternity does, almost everywhere. 
The American Hospital Association counts 331 hospitals that have stopped offering obstetric care since 2010. In California, nearly 60 hospitals have stopped delivering babies since 2012, largely due to financial challenges and population decline in rural areas.
Ask instead: Once a maternity ward closes, who will be trained to care for a pregnant woman who arrives bleeding at 9 p.m.?
And 10 years from now, who will be left to bring it back?
California leaders should help directly fund the people still standing in counties like mine. Independent rural physicians, nurses and clinics carry pregnant patients through the gap a closed ward leaves behind. Make sure they can apply for this money, not only hospitals and health systems.
In Calaveras County, the answer to “who is left” is two family doctors. California can do better than that.

name: California
title: San Diego County’s latest recruits to its fire-fighting ranks? Hundreds of hungry goats.
description: Goat herds are grazing a San Diego park, as part of the county’s wildfire prevention plan: “They're like a dog with horns, but they're smart as a cat.”
text:
In summary
Goat herds are grazing a San Diego park, as part of the county’s wildfire prevention plan: “They’re like a dog with horns, but they’re smart as a cat.” 


More than 500 new fire crew members were hard at work at Star Valley Park in San Diego County this month, clearing brush and grass down to bare stubble.
After they finished they raced onto the next field, jostling each other, leaping over a herding dog and chomping the overgrown vegetation.
The project, in the Valley Center community, is a pilot program employing goat herds to remove vegetation and reduce wildfire risk.
“It’s very, very helpful to local agencies to use these goats, to use these living mowers here, to make this place safe,” said Jake Enriquez, region manager for San Diego County Department of Parks and Recreation.
As the animals crowded into the untreated field, mother does guided their kids to patches of grass, and larger animals stood up against an oak tree to browse the leaves. Five fluffy, white dogs – a mixed breed of Anatolian Shepherd and Great Pyrenees – patrolled the herd. Several goats wandered over to inspect visitors and get their heads scratched.
“They’re like a dog with horns, but they’re smart as a cat,” Enriquez said. “They’re very intelligent animals, and you see how they interact, how they follow the dog.”
The goats are part of the county’s strategy to reduce wildfire risk on public land by clearing vegetation around homes, along key roads and in areas that may be needed as evacuation sites.
Devastating wildfires hit San Diego’s backcountry early this century, causing the county to revamp its fire-fighting strategy.
With homes scattered through dense chaparral in the backcountry, the Cedar Fire in 2003 burned more than a quarter million acres, destroyed 2,820 buildings and killed 15 people.
Then in 2007, wind-whipped power lines sparked the Witch Creek Fire, while two other massive blazes started the same day. Together, they charred almost 300,000 acres, leveled 1,650 buildings, forced evacuation of half a million people and caused 7 deaths.
Fire burns towards houses in Scripps Ranch along Pomerado Road during the Cedar Fire in San Diego on Oct. 26, 2003. Photo by John Gibbins, The San Diego Union-Tribune via Getty Images
After those disasters, San Diego County upgraded aerial firefighting capacity by creating a CalFire Helitack base in the East County community of Ramona, adding a CalFire C-130 Hercules air tanker and a Sikorsky S-70 CalFire Hawk helicopter, and improving emergency communications systems.
But the ground game is where fire prevention starts. The county clears brush along 800 miles of road per year to ensure safe evacuation routes, and conducted fire safety inspections on 15,000 homes last year, San Diego County Fire Director Jeff Collins said. Now, it’s adding goats to its fire-fighting lineup.
Officials used county seed money to launch the pilot project at Star Valley Park, and they just received a $300,000 state grant to take the grazing program to other areas with high fire risk.
“It’s one tool in the toolbox for trying to reduce risk, for both small and large-scale fires,” Collins said.
Goats have recently joined fire-fighting crews in other parts of the state and county. San Diego Gas & Electric uses fire safety goats to chew down brush near power lines. In September Marine Corps Air Station Miramar launched “Operation Goat Rope” to reduce wildfire risk in rough terrain on base, in what Marine Corps officials say is the first such goat-powered campaign at a U.S. military installation.
Fire officials at Glendale, California brought in goats a few years ago to scour dry brush from suburban neighborhoods in Los Angeles County. And researchers from Cal Poly, San Luis Obispo deployed nearly 1,000 of the animals to devour overgrown weeds and invasive plants at the university’s research station at Swanton Pacific Ranch in Santa Cruz County, which was scorched by wildfires in 2020.
Chad Hanson, a fire ecology expert and Director of the John Muir Project, said goats may be useful, as long as they’re deployed in the right places. He cautioned that any method of vegetation removal in woodlands and forests can backfire by converting the areas to more flammable grassland. Instead, land managers should focus on clearing space around homes and key infrastructure.
“What I advocate is to focus our resources and attention on creating fire-safe communities, to harden houses and remove vegetation around homes,” Hanson said.
Star Valley Park is a former ranch site of about 40 acres in the rural Valley Center community in North County San Diego, flanked by homes and public roads. It’s mostly undeveloped, and the county is exploring ideas for new amenities, but in the meantime the park is a hub for equestrian activities. The Valley Center Vaqueros meet there for drills and equine events, and Valley Center Stampede holds an annual rodeo at the site.
“County Fire approached us and said, ‘hey, do you have some property in this area of San Diego County where you have ongoing vegetation management?’” Enriquez said. “Star Valley gave us a really good opportunity to pilot this program.”
Roughly 525 goats are grazing at Star Valley Park in Valley Center as part of a pilot program to remove plants that can fuel wildfires. Photo courtesy of San Diego County
They selected the park as the pilot site for goat grazing because of its combination of risks and benefits. It’s surrounded by homes on the north, east and west, and surface roads to the north and south, all of which would be vulnerable if a fire broke out.
Meanwhile the presence of trucks and trailers at equestrian events presents an ignition risk in dry weather, said Johnny Gonzalez, field operation manager for the county’s contractor, Environmental Land Management.
But cleared of brush, the park could serve as a neighborhood evacuation site in case of wildfire, and as a staging site for fire-fighting crews, helicopters, tankers, water tenders and other equipment.
“Having a vegetation break here is very advantageous to the fire agencies,” Enriquez said. “It gives them a defensible space to work off of…There’s a lot of advantages to having a clean, well-maintained piece of property, and these goats do a fantastic job.”
County fire crews also use mowers, chainsaws or controlled burns to clear overgrown brush and weeds, Collins said. But goats can get into tight spaces and navigate steep, rocky terrain. And they chew vegetation down lower than a mower blade can cut, so it’s easier to maintain once they’re done, Enriquez said. 
The bare condition of goat-grazed ground allows the land to act as a firebreak, instead of a fuel source, Gonzalez said: “This is the second best thing to mineral earth because the land actually absorbs the embers as they light into the field.”
Goats also help prune invasive plants such as mustard, thistle and tumbleweed, which they find tastier than the more alkaline native vegetation.
Deploying the animals reduces dust and exhaust produced by chainsaws and mowers, making it more environmentally friendly for the neighborhood. Aside from their chorus of bleating, goats make less noise than heavy equipment. 
“Here, they’re quietly managing the vegetation,” Enriquez said. “You see how low they got it and cleaned up everything around the trees. As land managers, we kind of get excited about that because it takes a lot of time, energy, and labor to keep a property looking safe and clean.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Nevada health officials welcome delayed implementation of Medicaid work requirements
description: Nevada Health Authority officials “welcome the extra time” to implement new Medicaid work requirements after the Trump administration announced last week the implementation would be delayed by six months.  The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services told states on Nov. 13 that they can enter “an optional hold harmless period” to assess if recipients meet […[...]
text:
(Getty Images)Nevada Health Authority officials “welcome the extra time” to implement new Medicaid work requirements after the Trump administration announced last week the implementation would be delayed by six months. 
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services told states on Nov. 13 that they can enter “an optional hold harmless period” to assess if recipients meet Medicaid work requirements, and don’t have to deny applications or disenroll eligible individuals “solely for failure to meet the requirement” until June 30, 2027.
In a statement to Nevada Current, the Nevada Health Authority said pushing back the date “gives members another chance to keep their coverage while the state puts this new federal requirement in place.”
“Nevada plans to ask the federal government (CMS) for permission to use this option, and we are waiting for their approval,” the authority wrote in an email. 
President Donald Trump’s tax and spending bill signed into law in July 2025, known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” included significant cuts to food assistance and health care, including Medicaid. 
The bulk of those cuts, passed under the Republican controlled Congress, are expected to take place in 2027. Democratic lawmakers, who will control both chambers starting in 2027, have vowed to repeal parts of the law.
OBBA puts in place new requirements on Medicaid, requiring beneficiaries to reapply every six months rather than once a year. 
Recipients ages 19 to 64 will now also have to meet new work requirements, which could include at least 80 hours a month of work, job training, volunteering, or attending an education program. 
Even after the rules for work requirements take effect in 2027, Medicaid recipients will also be required to pay copays starting in October 2028. 
States had the option to choose between one month or three months of “consecutive compliance” for people to meet work requirements, said Ann Jensen, the administrator for Nevada Medicaid said during an interview.
Nevada selected a one-month “look back” period,  
“When you apply, it’ll be the month before you apply that we’ll be looking at,” she said. “When you renew, it’s just one month since the last time you renewed Medicaid coverage.”
The Nevada Health Authority hosted a public workshop in October to highlight the state’s approach to meeting federal requirements to work requirements. 
There are more than 261,000 Medicaid recipients as part of expanded Medicaid coverage for childless adults under the Affordable Care Act. About 158,000 will need to meet work requirements. 
During a public workshop earlier this year, Jensen said even if all the rules are “implemented perfectly” roughly 36,532 people could lose Medicaid coverage. 
Those deemed “medically frail” or a person with a significant health condition who is also impaired in their ability to work could be eligible for an exemption to work requirements.
Nevada health officials brace for new Medicaid work requirements

Multiple states with Democratic governors or attorneys general, including Nevada, sued the Trump administration in June, arguing that its new “medically frail” designation was too narrow and would make it too difficult for ill and disabled people to remain on Medicaid.
A U.S. District Judge sided with the lawsuit in October saying that Medicaid recipients who are disabled or have a chronic illness won’t have to prove they are medically frail. 
For other recipients who need to verify they’ve met work requirements, Nevada has chosen to self-attestation in 2027, Jensen said. 
Instead of providing specific documentation that shows how a recipient met work requirements – whether it was through employment or volunteering – the form allows them to self attest how those requirements were met. 
“We have chosen to do that in 2027 because we believe it helps limit the administrative burden, not only for members, but also on providers, community organizations, and employers who will have to provide documentation starting in 2028 for a number of these exemptions or compliance factors,” Jensen said during the public workshop.  
Medicaid recipients “must keep documentation available in the case of a federal audit on this work, but we won’t be asking for any documentation on those items in 2027,” she added.
Despite ever-changing requirements and litigation challenging rules, states were supposed to be fully compliant with all the changes to work requirements by Jan. 1. 
In its statement last week, CMS said the additional time period gives state governments more time to update their systems and improve the processes they have in place. 
“States have made real progress, and they’ve been clear with us about what it takes to get this right for beneficiaries—at scale and for the long term,” said Deputy Administrator and Director of the Center for Medicaid and CHIP Services Dan Brillman.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Post-blue wave, Utah conservation group says it’s rallying ‘red rock champions’
description: Voters delivered a national blue wave that reached into Utah. Now environmental advocates want them to key in on red rocks.
text:
Scott Braden, executive director of the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, speaks during a news conference at the Utah Capitol on Nov. 17, 2026. (Annie Knox/Utah News Dispatch)Voters delivered a national blue wave in the midterm elections that reached as far as some races in Utah. Now environmental advocates want them to key in on red rocks. 
Utah conservationists pushing back against President Donald Trump’s sharp downsizing of two national monuments are trying to keep the issue top of mind as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and expand their presence at the Utah capitol. 
The Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, one of many groups suing Trump and his administration over dramatic cuts to Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments, said Tuesday it’s making a new push to raise awareness and encourage local organizing.
Calf Creek Canyon in Grand Staircase Escalante National Monument near Escalante, Utah is pictured on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
“We’re rallying red rock champions in Congress from across the country, and we’re raising the alarm that yet another awful, awful precedent for public lands has emerged from Utah,” Scott Braden, the alliance’s executive director, told reporters at the state Capitol. 
Trump reduced the size of the monuments in his first term as president, but after they were restored slashed them much further in July — by more than 90%. The White House said he rightsized Bears Ears to allow for common-sense land use and mining of uranium, copper and other critical minerals. 
Patagonia, environmental groups revive old legal fights against new cuts to Utah monuments 

With billboards and other advertising, the wilderness alliance is rallying under the slogan “Keep Utah monumental” — a gentler message than retailer Patagonia took almost a decade ago when it declared: “The president stole your land.” 
When Trump ordered the cuts over the summer, Braden noted Utah’s all-Republican congressional delegation and governor stood with the president in the Oval Office and cheered the reductions. 
Democrat Ben McAdams, who will return to Washington, D.C., to represent Utah’s 1st Congressional District, has said he wants to defend the monuments. 
The state’s GOP officials have long called for tighter boundaries, saying Utah should control its own land. They also say the monuments established by past Democratic presidents Bill Clinton and Barack Obama are far bigger than needed to protect cultural and environmental treasures.
“I think the election two weeks ago helps to remind them that Utahns are watching their actions closely, that they chafe when things are being done behind their backs and against their interests, and that voters remember that when they return to the ballot,” Braden said.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Spending on speakers, concerts, more to prevent addiction spurs calls for oversight
description: To Bre Azanedo, the best addiction and overdose prevention fits neatly into her wheeled work tote, which looks like a cross between an airplane carry-on and a handyman’s toolbox. The “Rover” — as her group, Harm Reduction Inc., calls it — carries life-saving supplies like sterile syringes, naloxone, wound care supplies, and fentanyl test strips, […]
text:
Irvington township employees distributed Narcan and information about opioid addiction and treatment at a concert in June 2024. The township paid for the concert with national opioid settlement funds. (Photo courtesy of Irvington Township)To Bre Azanedo, the best addiction and overdose prevention fits neatly into her wheeled work tote, which looks like a cross between an airplane carry-on and a handyman’s toolbox.
The “Rover” — as her group, Harm Reduction Inc., calls it — carries life-saving supplies like sterile syringes, naloxone, wound care supplies, and fentanyl test strips, and makes it easy for Azanedo and her coworkers to reach drug users wherever they are.
Wheeled totes called Rovers are loaded with supplies to help people struggling with addition. (Photo courtesy of Reduce Harm Inc.)
Municipalities and counties across New Jersey, though, have interpreted addiction prevention so broadly that they’ve spent millions in opioid settlement funds on motivational speakers, “drug awareness” concerts and festivals, summer camps and retreats, graduation parties, household mailers, art and poster projects, and more.
Azanedo said she’s reluctant to accuse anyone of malicious motives, because she knows prevention and awareness can take many forms. But she said such spending underscores one message harm reductionists have tried to get across since the money started flowing in 2022 — that people with lived experience and those who work in impacted communities know best how to fight addiction and should be, but often aren’t, involved in spending decisions.
“There’s a lot of folks that are new to harm reduction in New Jersey, and so they don’t feel that it’s clear enough what to spend the funds on,” she said. “I think we’re super clear. We have been in the community, day to day, doing the work, reversing the overdoses, building the relationship with the community members. We have done the best work, and we have done it for years with little to no funding.”
Her group hasn’t gotten any of the millions pharmaceutical companies have paid to atone for the deadly opioid epidemic their drugs fueled. New Jersey, its 21 counties, and 241 of its biggest municipalities are expected to get $1.1 billion through 2038.
Several New Jersey lawmakers have introduced two bills to tighten oversight of opioid spending, but neither explicitly bars some of the things municipal and county officials have paid for in the name of prevention and education.
A New Jersey Monitor analysis of opioid settlement spending reports filed last month shows that local governments spent about $1 million in the fiscal year that ended June 30 on school speakers, curricula, scholarships, after-school programs, and other classroom programs for students as young as first grade. They described the spending as prevention and education.
Speakers typically were people who overcame drug addiction or lost loved ones to overdoses. But the topics of other talks offered no explicit link to opioid addiction, with speakers addressing cyberbullying, learning disabilities, life skills, leadership, drunk driving, cigarettes, vapes, marijuana, stress and anxiety, and mental health.
Elizabeth Burke Beaty, founder and CEO of Sea Change Recovery Community and Harm Reduction Center in Ocean County, said speakers can be effective, but she thinks students would be better served if they focused more on “reality” and practical information such as how xylazine and fentanyl are different and what kinds of overdoses naloxone can and cannot reverse.
“Can we please just accept the fact that kids need to be educated and not scared?” she said.
The spending reports show that counties and municipalities paid even more — close to $2.5 million — for community-based programs, events, summer camps, and services meant to prevent or educate residents about drug addiction.
Seniors were a frequent target audience, with several programs aimed at preventing misuse of medications.
But other spending angered advocates, with some officials squandering thousands on concerts, festivals, and parties even though former state Comptroller Kevin Walsh blasted Irvington last year for spending more than $600,000 on two drug awareness concerts.
Plainfield reported it spent almost $232,000 on a “House Music Festival” for 6,000 people. Paramus and Camden County also used opioid funds to pay for concerts, with the county dubbing its event a “Recovery Rocks sober tailgate and concert.” At least four communities spent more than $21,000, combined, on parties for graduating high-schoolers. Rahway spent $12,000 on an assembly for sixth graders that featured food, a photo booth, and an inflatable brain ordered off Amazon.
Others blew thousands on movie nights, ice cream events, drum circles, art and fitness programs, community dinners, brunch and tea series, writers’ groups, vigils and moments of silence, Girl Scouts, runs and walks.




Quotation







People are taking any little thing and using it as the reason for paying for big things. 'We had a table handing out naloxone at a concert, so now we’re going to pay for the whole concert.'


– Tonia Ahern, who lost her son to an opioid overdose



	Camden city officials sank more than $26,000 into a “street lighting inventory,” Passaic County paid a hospital system $70,000 for yoga classes to help 108 people in treatment manage their anxiety, and Camden County spent over $23,000 on a “Recovery Encouragement Athletic/Activity League” that featured golf, bocce ball, ice skating, horticulture, ceramics, a soap-making class, a sea-glass workshop, a St. Patrick’s Day social with karaoke, and a softball tournament.
“There’s nothing about soap-making that would benefit someone” struggling with addiction, Azanedo said.
Officials from Plainfield, Camden, Rahway, Paramus, Camden, and Passaic County did not respond to requests for comment.
But Dan Keashen, a Camden County spokesman, defended the county’s spending. The Recovery Encouragement Athletic/Activity League, or REAL Sports for short, does directly repair the harms of opioid addiction because it supports people who have beaten addiction — but who also might struggle to maintain sobriety, Keashen said.
“This would fall under the bucket of prevention for us, because these are people that have made it out to the other side. We want to keep them there,” he said. “Relapse is a part of recovery. REAL Sports was created so individuals don’t experience that relapse.”
An addiction awareness task force — with public health professionals, law enforcement, and people with lived experience as members — decides how to spend the county’s share of opioid settlement funds, Keashen added. The task force also has invested opioid funds in everything from sober living homes to social workers partnering with police on substance use calls, he added. Camden County has among the most overdose deaths and naloxone incidents statewide, typically lagging behind only Essex County, state data shows.
In Passaic County, spokeswoman Lindsay Reed said programs supported by opioid funds, such as the yoga classes, fit approved uses and are “chosen through a public process and are meant to work alongside, not replace, counseling and medications for opioid use disorder.”
“Our approach pairs established clinical treatment with complementary services that help people stay engaged in care,” Reed said. “We are committed to responsible stewardship of these funds.”
Advocates said fuller public reporting on spending could persuade them of the worthiness of the more questionable spending.
“If somebody wants to throw a yoga class and say it’s for people in recovery, that was not initially how many of these dollars are supposed to be used. It becomes a cash grab for low-hanging fruit,” said Mark Jenkins, Harm Reduction Inc.’s founder. “But if they’re having yoga classes and then somewhere before or after there’s a Narcan training, and you’re further reaching populations that may not be privy to it, then you can lock that in and call that prevention.”
Tonia Ahern of Upper Township joined critics’ calls for stricter guardrails and more comprehensive reporting on spending. She lost her 29-year-old son Rory to an opioid overdose in 2021 and still wonders if better prevention could have saved his life.
“People are taking any little thing and using it as the reason for paying for big things. ‘We had a table handing out naloxone at a concert, so now we’re going to pay for the whole concert,’ and those kind of things,” Ahern said. “It’s not really handling the opioid issue. It’s going to a concert. How is that helping anyone? It’s really not. And we give out naloxone everywhere. We don’t need to give it out at a concert.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: What can Washington lawmakers do about record-breaking lawsuit payouts?
description: When Washington lawmakers return to Olympia in January they’ll consider a variety of ways to address ballooning legal payouts hamstringing the budgets of the state and local governments. One option: transformative changes to the state’s legal system, such as capping skyrocketing damage payouts or limiting public liability. Conversely, attorneys who bring the[...]
text:
The state Capitol in Olympia, Washington on Aug. 10, 2026. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)When Washington lawmakers return to Olympia in January they’ll consider a variety of ways to address ballooning legal payouts hamstringing the budgets of the state and local governments.
One option: transformative changes to the state’s legal system, such as capping skyrocketing damage payouts or limiting public liability. Conversely, attorneys who bring the cases and other advocates want to focus on reducing the harm that leads to these cases.
After months of work by a state panel to come up with solutions, all ideas are ready for lawmakers to ponder — but competing voices appear no closer to consensus than when the Legislature finished its work for 2026 in March, and created the committee.
“It really is upon us to decide, given the menu of options, where we want to go,” said state Sen. Manka Dhingra, a Democrat from Redmond and chair of the Law and Justice Committee. 
Everyone agrees on one thing: Action is needed. 
“We need significant changes, and it has to happen now,” said Derek Young, executive director of the Washington State Association of Counties. “I just refuse to believe that this Legislature is going to allow their governments to fail.”
The claims leading to the fiscal crisis run the gamut from bungled child welfare cases to discrimination. Many involve childhood sexual abuse, especially in the foster care system. Governments have been found liable for failing to protect those children, and the cases often stem from decades-old conduct.
Court decisions over the past decade have opened up the state to more claims. At the same time, verdicts handed down from juries are growing. This spring, for example, a Pierce County jury ordered the state and a day care center to pay $130 million for the death of a toddler.
Last fiscal year, the state spent over $537 million resolving claims, a record-breaking annual figure that has jumped by hundreds of millions of dollars in the past few years. Beyond that, the state spent more than $90 million to defend the cases, including fees for insurance along with in-house and outside defense attorneys to handle litigation. 
This year’s costs are greater, so far. Through the first third of the fiscal year, from July through October, the state has spent $196 million on lawsuit payouts, and $41 million more on legal fees and insurance, for total costs of nearly $238 million, according to the state Department of Enterprise Services. The trend puts the state on pace for payouts nearing $600 million this fiscal year, which would set another record. 
Counties and school districts have similarly seen increases in payouts or insurance costs — money that would otherwise go toward typical public services such as police and fire departments, or education.
“I don’t know that the stakes could possibly be higher,” Young said. 
Rhea Yo, executive director of Legal Counsel for Youth and Children, is one of the advocates pushing governments to limit the traumatic episodes that lead to eye-popping verdicts in court.
“It’s not lost on me that when money is provided into these judgments, that the state has less money to provide and counties have less money to provide direct services, which then can potentially create more harm,” said “I understand the math of that. It is really a very difficult problem to solve.”
The Legislature this year spent $1 billion to shore up the state’s liability account, given the skyrocketing payouts and more on the way. But another massive infusion is likely needed. Lawmakers failed to pass proposed legislation earlier this year. It would have required arbitration to speed up cases; a red flag for trial lawyers, who opposed the idea at every step. Tyna Ek, general counsel for the Washington Schools Risk Management Pool, fears attorneys “will fight any recommendation that will in any way mitigate costs.”
After the bill stalled, the state spent $50,000 to set up the panel to study the issue and provide recommendations, all within a few months.
“This is a conversation that can’t be researched within like two months,” said Riddhi Mukhopadhyay, executive director of the Sexual Violence Law Center. “I understand what the purpose of the report was. I don’t know if it really accomplished what the initial hope was.”
Cost reduction
Most states have a cap on damage awards for cases against state or local governments. Washington does not.
Most members of the state’s committee, namely the government representatives, believe the Legislature should impose a damage cap, but they don’t specify a specific amount. A limit, they contend, would still allow plaintiffs to recover damages while preserving systemic fairness.
“Limiting non-economic damages would still allow claimants to be compensated. It would allow them to be more evenly compensated,” Ek said. “And it wouldn’t bankrupt the public resources.”

The argument will be a tough sell in the Democrat-controlled state Legislature.
“I personally struggle a lot with a cap on damages to survivors,” Dhingra said. “I don’t think you can put a dollar figure on the type of abuse.”
State Sen. Manka Dhingra, D-Redmond, listens to Gov. Bob Ferguson’s State of the State address on Jan. 13, 2026. (Photo by Bill Lucia/Washington State Standard)
Another issue for governments is a wonky legal concept called joint and several liability, which allows plaintiffs to bring their case against any party that is at fault, no matter how small their role in alleged misconduct. 
For example, if a drunk driver goes the wrong way on the freeway and kills another motorist, the state could be held liable because a “do not enter” sign wasn’t lit properly or placed in the right spot. In that scenario, the state, seen as a defendant with deep pockets, could be saddled with the entire penalty, even if its actual portion of the liability was small and the drunk driver was the real culprit.
Washington ranks as an outlier in such cases. Governments face expansive liability and no limit on damages that can be collected from them, according to the majority report from the committee.
“It effectively makes government the insurer for the misconduct of other people, so we don’t think that this is really all that difficult of an equation,” said Young, of the counties’ association. “This is the crazy part. If we were struggling with something that nobody else had figured out, I could understand. The thing is, we’re the only state with this problem.
Most of the state panel recommends prohibiting defendants such as the state from being held liable for the full amount of damages unless their responsibility for the harm rises above a certain threshold, such as 25%.
“I think there is appetite to take a look at the joint and several liability rules and where we may be able to make some changes,” Dhingra said. “I am agnostic on the details of it, but I do think there are some practical things we can do in that arena, so that you are being responsible on who needs to pay how much.”
Speaking of legalese, another difficult hurdle is sovereign immunity: the idea that a government cannot be sued without giving its consent. The state waives its immunity. Committee members recommend changing that, but it’s another idea sure to generate opposition from trial lawyers. 
Some panel members call for a fund to compensate certain victims with set amounts, limiting legal liability for claims involving historic child sexual abuse allegations, for example. Opponents fear that would pit survivors of abuse against each other for access to limited funds. 
Harm reduction
Attorneys who bring cases and allied advocates felt outnumbered on the committee, they said,  contending that their attempts to focus on limiting harm were given short shrift. 
They say the ideas brought by government affiliates would simply reduce access to justice for people harmed by public entities, rather than address root causes that could lower costs over time. So they brought forward their own suggestions.
“The primary focus is how do we make sure the judgments are lower,” Yo said. “The primary focus was not how do we make sure that we are not perpetuating this problem so that we’re dealing with this 10 years down the line.”
“It will save the state money in many different ways if they prevent the harm to begin with,” Yo added.
The biggest goal for harm-reduction advocates: finding ways for the state to limit trauma from government misconduct, such as record-high deaths in the child welfare system and overcrowding in youth prisons. Ideas include trauma-informed training for staff and volunteers, plus better staffing and lower caseloads for employees with the Department of Children, Youth and Families, the epicenter for Washington’s increased liability. Adversaries say that will cost more money, not less.
One recommendation calls for risk pools, which allow local governments to jointly manage their liability, to require participants follow prevention measures and review significant claims to ensure mistakes don’t recur.
On the court side, trial attorneys and advocates want to expand an early resolution program within the state attorney general’s office, with the idea of reaching quicker settlements and lowering litigation costs. 
Along the same lines, the committee’s minority hopes to limit the attorney general’s use of private law firms to defend the state in cases — a driver of rapidly increasing defense costs. A separate notion would require risk management decisions to be examined so governments don’t go to trial and get stuck with hefty verdicts that could have been avoided with lower-cost settlements.
State senators will be pushing legislation next year to protect survivors in K-12 schools by ensuring that employees and volunteers who commit misconduct can’t get other jobs in education, Dhingra said, comparing the idea to police accountability laws. Again, the goal is reducing harm, and thus lawsuits. A proposal aimed at college campuses seeks to ensure sexual assault survivors have access to resources.
Another policy would restrict companies that aggregate leads to sell to law firms that bring cases. 
Dhingra is hoping Gov. Bob Ferguson, the former three-term attorney general, will “lean in” to the thorny debate. She says she’s “really optimistic we will move the needle on this.”
A spokesperson for Ferguson said he is reviewing the recommendations. The 105-day legislative session begins Jan. 11.
“In order for the Legislature to fix the problem,” Ek said, “it’s going to take a lot of political will and courage.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers’ works and faith pave way for Scott Colom in Mississippi Senate election
description: Myrlie and Medgar Evers
text:
Two brothers began to crawl, the older one directing the way.
It was spring 1934, and Mississippi’s blustering U.S. senator, Theodore G. Bilbo, stood at the front of the courthouse in Decatur.
The children weaved their way through a forest of legs, dipping and dodging those in pants, jeans and overalls before arriving at the front of the crowd.
The subject of race arose, just as it always did when Bilbo spoke. He called on the crowd to “use any means to keep the n—s away from the polls.”
Bilbo spotted the brothers, 8-year-old Medgar and 11-year-old Charles Evers, and pointed at them. He warned the white men that if they failed to keep these “n—s” in their place, “then someday they’ll be in Washington trying to represent you.”
“Ain’t a bad idea, Charlie,” Medgar whispered to his brother.
Colom cites Evers as inspiration
Charles Evers shared this story with me. He said his brother, Medgar, wanted to serve his country one day in Washington but never got that chance.
In a campaign advertisement before Mississippi’s U.S. Senate election this month, Democratic nominee Scott Colom stood outside the home where Medgar Evers lived and was killed.
“There is a house in Jackson that everyone ought to walk through once,” Colom said. “It looks like every other house on the street, only it isn’t.”
The home was built without a front door. That was on purpose. Medgar Evers did that to keep his family from becoming easy targets.
“The children slept on the floor below the windows,” Colom said. “Their father taught them if they ever heard gunfire, they should crawl to the bathroom.”
Medgar Evers’ daughter, Reena Evers-Everette, who now directs the Medgar and Myrlie Evers Institute, said her father turned all of this into a game. He asked his children: What was the safest place in the house? 
They went from room to room, peering into closets and peeking under beds until they found the perfect place: the bathtub.
As a prosecutor for a decade, Colom said, “I’ve stood in a lot of houses like this one where something terrible happened. This isn’t any house. This isn’t any tragedy. This is where Medgar Evers died.”
Colom mentioned Evers’ military service. The Decatur native fought against the Nazis in World War II and became part of the famed Red Ball Express, which fueled Allied troops’ successful march through France and Germany.
“He came home to Mississippi,” Colom said, “and they wouldn’t let him vote.”
In 1946, after Medgar and Charles Evers returned home from war, they marched with other veterans to try and vote. White men with guns turned them away.
From that moment forward, Medgar Evers threw himself into the Civil Rights Movement. In 1954, he became the Mississippi NAACP’s first field secretary. The same veteran who once fought in Normandy now fought for the right of all Americans to vote.
Medgar and Myrlie Evers Home in Jackson.  Credit: Ashley FG Norwood, Mississippi Today
He faced what felt like a futile task. In 1954, a Justice Department survey of 37 Mississippi counties found that in 29 of those counties, less than 3% of African Americans had been able to register to vote.
On June 11, 1963, President John F. Kennedy delivered his first civil rights speech to the nation: “If an American, because his skin is dark, cannot eat lunch in a restaurant open to the public, if he cannot send his children to the best public school available, if he cannot vote for the public officials who will represent him, if, in short, he cannot enjoy the full and free life which all of us want, then who among us would be content to have the color of his skin changed and stand in his place?”
Evers and other civil rights activists had gathered to listen to the president on television. They marveled at his words and plotted their strategy.
Hours later, Evers returned home. As soon as he stepped out of his Oldsmobile, a Klansman shot him in the back.
His wife, Myrlie Evers, rushed outside, saw the blood and screamed. 
Reena and her brothers followed. “Daddy, get up,” she said. “Daddy get up.”
He never did.
“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said.
Two years after Evers’ assassination, leaders in Washington invoked his name in passing the 1965 Voting Rights Act, finally clearing the way for all Black Mississippians to be able to register to vote.
Thirty-one years after that assassination, a Mississippi jury convicted Byron De La Beckwith of Evers’ murder in the same courtroom where he had been tried three decades earlier.
After the clerk announced the “guilty” verdict, waves of joy could be heard cascading down the hall until they reached a foyer full of people, Black and white. They erupted in cheers.
“In Mississippi,” Colom said, “no one is above the law, and no one should be outside its protection.”
Keeping the faith
Colom became the first Black Mississippian elected to the Senate in history. More than 150 years ago, the state Legislature appointed two Black men to the Senate – Hiram Revels, who served just over a year, from 1870 to 1871; and Blanche Kelso Bruce, who served from 1875 to 1881.
U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during his election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Colom told Mississippi Today that he wants to make sure “it’s not another 150 years.”
After being declared the winner on Nov. 11, he spoke at Tougaloo College, a safe haven for civil rights activists in the 1960s. He talked of keeping the faith when few people appeared for rallies and potential donors wouldn’t answer calls.
“There are so many people who had faith in Mississippi at times where it seemed impossible — people like Medgar Evers,” he said.
The crowd of more than 1,000 clapped and cheered.
“I can’t help but think about Medgar Evers on Veterans’ Day,” he said. “A moment like this, where he served his country and came home to Mississippi, and they wouldn’t let him vote. But he had faith that Mississippi would make progress.”
Colom told the crowd that Evers had faith that “one day everybody would have the right to vote. He had faith that a day like today was possible.”
The crowd cheered.
“God bless you, Medgar,” Colom said. “God bless you, Medgar.”
Tears streamed down the face of Evers-Everette as she stood in the crowd. “God is so good,” she said afterward.
She telephoned her mother with the news that Mississippi had elected its first Black senator since Reconstruction. “What?! Are you serious?” Myrlie Evers replied before exclaiming, “Praise God!”
Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, speaks of her father’s life and legacy during a memorial tribute held at their former home Saturday, June 12, 2021, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
For Evers-Everette, Colom’s words sparked a memory of something her father said. “We are confident that we will achieve victory, not through violence, but through the channels provided by the Constitution of the United States of America,” he declared in a 1959 speech. “Our faith is invested in the law that is over and above man-made laws. We are dedicated to the cause of freedom and will continue to fight under God’s laws, without fear of consequences.”
She quoted from her father’s favorite prayer, saying these are words she seeks to live by every day: “Lord, make me an instrument of your peace. Where there is hatred, let me sow love; where there is injury, pardon; where there is doubt, faith; where there is despair, hope; where there is darkness, light.”
She wiped away tears. “The change we are witnessing is going to change the world.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri Republicans weigh another redistricting fight after voters reject GOP map
description: Missouri voters rejected a Republican-drawn congressional map earlier this month. But was that the end of the state’s redistricting fight? Some GOP officials are leaving open the possibility of trying again, potentially targeting a different Democratic congressional district or pursuing a map designed to give Republicans an even larger advantage. Whether the[...]
text:
Supporters of a referendum on Missouri's gerrymandered redistricting map rally at the state Capitol Building on May 12 after the Missouri Supreme Court heard arguments on two cases involving the redistricting map (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).Missouri voters rejected a Republican-drawn congressional map earlier this month. But was that the end of the state’s redistricting fight?
Some GOP officials are leaving open the possibility of trying again, potentially targeting a different Democratic congressional district or pursuing a map designed to give Republicans an even larger advantage.
Whether they can is far less certain. And after the results of the Nov. 3 election, so is whether another attempt would actually benefit Republicans.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Voters rejected the congressional map passed last year at President Donald Trump’s urging and approved Amendment 6, a constitutional change restricting lawmakers’ ability to enact legislation similar to measures rejected through a referendum.
Together, those votes raise questions about what options remain before the next census in 2030 — questions that could ultimately be decided in court.
State Sen. Nick Schroer, a St. Charles County Republican who will become Senate majority leader in January, has been among the most vocal advocates of revisiting congressional boundaries.
After the Missouri Supreme Court blocked the legislature’s 2025 map from taking effect, Schroer posted “8-0 2027” on social media, suggesting Republicans could pursue a map designed to defeat every Democratic member of the state’s congressional delegation.
But Amendment 6 has raised questions about how much freedom lawmakers will have to revisit decisions voters have already rejected.
Speaking more broadly about future ballot fights, Schroer acknowledged the uncertainty.
“Are we handcuffed by Amendment Six?” he said. “We’ve got several attorneys looking into this, myself included, to see what options are out there without wasting a lot of judicial resources, so we have to be strategic in what we do.”
Incoming Senate President Pro Tem Jason Bean, a Holcomb Republican, suggested his caucus may not be eager for another redistricting fight.
“I don’t think redistricting is high on our list of priorities,” Bean said.
Prop A and the fight over Missouri’s congressional map

And at least one incoming Republican senator believes lawmakers should abandon the idea altogether.
“The voters spoke,” Sen.-elect Mike Deering said during an interview with St. Louis Public Radio’s Politically Speaking podcast. “They want to keep the map as is, and that’s what we should do.”
Deering said lawmakers should stick to redrawing congressional boundaries once every decade rather than revisit an issue voters have already decided.
Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, meanwhile, has suggested lawmakers could have no choice but to revisit redistricting because of a recent U.S. Supreme Court decision.
“It may be forced on their hands because right now the 2022 map, according to the U.S. Supreme Court, is unconstitutional because it includes a majority-minority district,” Hoskins said after the election.
The Supreme Court did not declare Missouri’s map unconstitutional. Its April ruling involved Louisiana, where justices struck down a congressional district drawn predominantly on racial grounds. The decision could have implications for other states, but it did not order Missouri lawmakers to redraw their districts.
  A new legal obstacle

The most immediate uncertainty involves Amendment 6.
The constitutional amendment prohibits legislators from passing laws “similar in effect” to those rejected by voters through referendum. Lawmakers could send such a measure back to voters, but only with support from at least 80% of both legislative chambers.
That would require 131 votes in the House and 28 in the Senate, meaning Republicans would need substantial Democratic support.
But Amendment 6 does not define what constitutes legislation “similar in effect.”
Would a new congressional map targeting St. Louis rather than Kansas City qualify? What about an entirely different configuration of the state’s eight districts? And would the same restrictions apply if a federal court ordered Missouri to redraw its congressional boundaries?
Travis Crum, a Washington University law professor who specializes in election law, told The Independent in September that he believes another attempt before the 2030 census would fall under the amendment’s restrictions.
Amendment 6 could make another Missouri congressional gerrymander much harder

“A new map would be viewed as similar in effect to the map that was rejected,” Crum said, “and so therefore the 80% requirement would apply.”
But that interpretation has not been tested in court, and a new redistricting bill could produce another round of litigation.
Even if a new map survived scrutiny under Amendment 6, opponents could again use the referendum process to suspend it pending a statewide vote.
Republicans spent much of the past year unsuccessfully fighting that outcome in court.
There is also the question of whether another attempt would accomplish what Republicans want.
The 2025 map was designed to help the GOP defeat Democratic U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver of Kansas City, giving Republicans seven of Missouri’s eight congressional seats.
Instead, Cleaver won reelection under the state’s 2022 map, Democrats flipped a suburban St. Louis congressional seat and Republicans lost 16 seats in the Missouri House, ending their legislative supermajority.
And an analysis shared after the election by Republican pollster Titus Bond suggests the rejected map might have put additional GOP seats at risk.
Bond, president of Remington Research Group, calculated how the congressional contests would have looked under the boundaries lawmakers approved last year.
His calculations showed Cleaver narrowly defeating Republican Rick Brattin by 491 votes despite the attempt to make the district more favorable to Republicans.
Meanwhile, Republican U.S. Rep. Mark Alford would have defeated Democrat Jordan Herrera by fewer than 2,000 votes. Republican U.S. Rep. Bob Onder would have beaten Democrat Bethany Mann by about 10,700 votes.
But those hypothetical results assume voting patterns would have remained the same under different district boundaries. They cannot account for changes in campaigning, spending or turnout.
Incoming Senate Minority Leader Stephen Webber, a Columbia Democrat, said another redistricting push would suggest Republicans had failed to understand the message voters delivered.
“People are worried about affordability. They’re worried about their schools,” Webber said. “They are not worried about whether Republican politicians should try to gerrymander the congressional map.”
Richard von Glahn, executive director of the People Not Politicians campaign that organized the referendum against the 2025 map, said during an October interview on the Missouri on the Record podcast that lawmakers should move on to other priorities.
If Republicans try again, however, he indicated opponents would be prepared to launch another referendum campaign.
“Will People Not Politicians continue to exist?” von Glahn said. “I guess we will.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: New recess law has Oklahoma teachers wondering ‘What’s the point?’
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — A new Oklahoma law doubling minimum recess time, initially celebrated by cheering children at the state Capitol, has caused frustration among educators. The law, which requires elementary schools to offer at least 40 minutes daily of recess and prohibits taking it away as punishment, has prompted complaints that the policy comes at […]
text:
A soccer ball sits in the grass on the Wilson Elementary playground in Oklahoma City on June 29. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A new Oklahoma law doubling minimum recess time, initially celebrated by cheering children at the state Capitol, has caused frustration among educators.
The law, which requires elementary schools to offer at least 40 minutes daily of recess and prohibits taking it away as punishment, has prompted complaints that the policy comes at the expense of academic time and undermines teachers’ ability to discipline poor behavior. 
In its first year of effect, the law already has upended school schedules and raised concerns about the added cost of lengthening district calendars, particularly after the Oklahoma State Department of Education announced it would phase out a policy that allowed recess to count toward the instructional minutes of a school day.
Disciplining misbehavior has been “a struggle” ever since the law changed, especially when no one in a child’s home life will enforce accountability, said Jordann Hardin, a third grade teacher in a large Oklahoma City-area district.
“There’s not very many tools in a teacher’s toolbox for discipline, and they just took away a major one,” said Hardin, who’s been teaching for 15 years.
A child who’s thrown trash all over the school cafeteria can’t be held back from recess to clean up the mess, she said. Issues that Hardin normally would have addressed by taking away five minutes of recess time instead are causing her to make more phone calls home, leaving some parents baffled why they’ve been contacted over a minor incident.
Hardin said her school previously offered a sufficient 30 minutes of daily recess, which she called “quite possibly the most instructional part of our day” because students practice their interpersonal skills. 
Swings dangle on the playground at Eugene Field Elementary in Oklahoma City on June 29. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
This year, her school added another 10-minute play period to meet the new legal requirements, and while it seems to have made a minimal difference to students, the cost is more than just 10 minutes, she said.
“It’s the transition time going out to recess,” Hardin said. “It’s the lining up. It’s the coming back in. We’re losing so much instruction time just to be able to put in 10 more minutes of recess.”
Siomara Davis, president of the Edmond Classroom Teachers Association, said her union members have been wondering aloud, “What is the point?”
Edmond Public Schools had to rearrange its elementary schedules, start class five minutes earlier and convert a professional development day into a typical school day, all to add 15 more minutes of daily recess. 
Davis said many teachers already build in time for movement into their lesson plans, and the extra play period has been more disruptive than helpful. 
A class will “really be getting into the swing of the lesson for the day” and then have to stop for a recess break, she said. The teacher then has to allot time “for bringing kids back in and calming them down, getting that restroom break time, the drink time and getting back into the flow of things only to shortly after then go to lunch and recess again,” Davis said.
“I get a lot of, ‘When are they going to change this?’ I get a lot of, ‘Why do we have to do this?’” she said. “I also get a lot of, ‘Do you know what I could be teaching right now? Do you know how much I could get done in 20 minutes of class time?’”
While this law took effect, other legislation heightened pressure on elementary learning. Oklahoma lawmakers passed a bill this year that will hold back third graders from advancing to fourth grade if they score too poorly on state reading tests, starting in the 2027-28 school year. 
Sen. Ally Seifried, R-Claremore, an author of the recess law, has bills stacked high on her desk in the Senate chamber, a tradition on the final day of the legislative session, on May 14 at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Amid the added emphasis on testing, Sen. Ally Seifried, an author of the recess bill, has said extra time for play could help students burn more pent-up energy, allowing them to better focus in the classroom.
Seifried, R-Claremore, previously told Oklahoma Voice she has committed to looking at the law again during the next legislative session, which begins in February. She declined to comment further for this story.
Jenks Public Schools already provided 40 minutes of daily recess before the law. Superintendent Stacey Butterfield called it “an integral part of learning.” 
But if  the Education Department proceeds with its current plan to consider all 40 minutes as non-instructional time next year, even Jenks will have to add school days to compensate, Butterfield said. She estimated the longer school year will cost her district $2.7 million, despite the Legislature considering the recess law as having no fiscal impact.
“Oklahoma has one of the shortest calendars,” she said. “We need to be looking at adding to our calendar. But if we’re going to do that in Oklahoma, we have to pay for it.”
Jenks Public Schools Superintendent Stacey Butterfield speaks at an Oklahoma Watch education forum Nov. 12 at Oklahoma City Community College in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
The Legislature this year added $232 million to the state budget for public education while also adding seven days to the minimum length of a school year for districts with minutes-based calendars, a requirement that will take effect in the 2027-28 academic year.
Much of that $232 million, though, is earmarked for specific expenses, like teacher pay raises and reading programs, and can’t be applied to general operational costs.
State Superintendent-elect Robert Franklin said he expects lawmakers will need to revisit the recess law and that he’ll “have to wrangle with it” once he’s sworn into office in January. 
Until he’s taken the oath of office, he said he’s “not going to make any rulings at all” on whether he would change the Education Department policy on recess counting toward instructional time.
Franklin, a longtime educator, said recess is instructive for students, particularly on “how to get along with each other and share.” However, he said the intent of the legislation and its real-life application “are not lining up, and that’s where we’re going to have to figure out what’s next.”
“If we’re doubling the time dedicated to play and activity rather than the work of literacy development and math development, we’re sometimes getting the equation upside down,” Franklin said.
