name: Alabama Reflector
title: Commentary: Alabama’s school prayer amendment nudged us one step further down a slippery slope
description: Nearly 1 million Alabamians voted ‘yes’ to Amendment 3 on Nov. 3. Those in favor of student-led prayer in school outnumbered those opposed by a 25-point margin. For comparison, Tommy Tuberville beat Doug Jones in the governor’s race by only four points, meaning a sizable percentage of voters said yes to the Democratic gubernatorial candidate, […]
text:
A Bible on a school desk in a classroom. Alabama voters earlier this month approved a constitutional amendment requiring local boards of education to adopt policies on student-led prayer. (Getty Images)Nearly 1 million Alabamians voted ‘yes’ to Amendment 3 on Nov. 3. Those in favor of student-led prayer in school outnumbered those opposed by a 25-point margin.
For comparison, Tommy Tuberville beat Doug Jones in the governor’s race by only four points, meaning a sizable percentage of voters said yes to the Democratic gubernatorial candidate, flipped their ballots over, and also said yes to the Republican-coded question of school prayer.   
Given voters’ strong support for Amendment 3, it may seem like a fool’s errand to argue why it was a bad idea. But I’m going to do it anyway, because the debate over church and state runs all the way back to our nation’s founding. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The newly passed statewide constitutional amendment will require local boards of education to adopt two policies for K-12 public schools: One mandates the recitation of the Pledge of Allegiance at the beginning of each school day; the other authorizes student-initiated and student-led prayer.
Functionally, the amendment appears to be meaningless. Students already recite the Pledge every day, and student-led prayer has been enshrined in state code since 1993. Amendment 3 seems designed simply to show off legislators’ patriotism and burden local governments with a few extra lines of useless policy. The waste of time it took to get it passed is already a strike against it. Lawmakers should be focused on substantive issues, not grandstanding.
But the bigger problem is that it further smudges the already blurry line between Christianity and public education in Alabama. 
Many schools actively promote a cornucopia of Christian clubs and gatherings, from First Priority and Bible studies to Fellowship of Christian Athletes and See You at the Pole. While those gatherings are voluntary, students in grades 5–12 will soon face mandatory religious displays. When they return from winter break in January, they will find freshly minted copies of the Ten Commandments hanging in their history classrooms and common spaces, as required by a new state law.
If parents decide that’s not enough, and they’d rather send their children to religious schools instead of public ones, the CHOOSE Act ensures that they can use taxpayer funds to help pay their tuition.
When students feel moved to discuss their religious beliefs among their peers, the First Amendment protects their right to do so. But when schools dedicate resources to promoting Christian groups, then up the ante with clearly unconstitutional nonsense like the Ten Commandments law, the result is an educational environment that inappropriately elevates and exalts Christianity.  
Some parents would argue that all of this is good and necessary, that too many families today have lost their moral compass and need to be steered toward the guiding light of Jesus in whatever way you can reach them, up to and including through official school channels.
James Madison would heartily disagree. The founding father and author of the Bill of Rights would say that fudging the separation between church and state does not lead to each uplifting the other. Instead, both suffer. 
In 1785, he wrote: “The preservation of a free Government requires not merely, that the metes and bounds which separate each department of power be invariably maintained; but more especially that neither of them be suffered to overleap the great Barrier which defends the rights of the people.” The rulers who breach that barrier, he wrote, are tyrants, and the people they govern are slaves. 



Quotation







The founding father and author of the Bill of Rights would say that fudging the separation between church and state does not lead to each uplifting the other. Instead, both suffer.


If that sounds a touch dramatic, consider where Madison was coming from. Just across the Atlantic, Europe’s messy history was littered with centuries of deadly inquisitions and religious expulsions, fruitless Crusades and craven bishops—all the result of politics entwined with religion. He wanted none of that.
So when Madison wrote the Bill of Rights, he included the Establishment Clause and Free Exercise Clause right at the top of the First Amendment: “Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof.” Practice your faith to your heart’s content, he said, but don’t impose it on others.
That should have settled the matter, but the issue has come before the U.S. Supreme Court again and again. Litigants have poked and prodded at the First Amendment from various angles, testing its limits.  
In the landmark 1962 case Engel v. Vitale, as the country grappled with the Cold War and tried to distinguish itself from the Soviets through displays of Christian patriotism, the Supreme Court considered a New York law that had established a specific nondenominational prayer that public-school teachers could lead in their classrooms. 
The court struck down the law. Writing for the majority, Justice Hugo Black (formerly a senator from Alabama) summed up and reinforced Madison’s thinking beautifully. He said that first and foremost, the Establishment Clause “rested on the belief that a union of government and religion tends to destroy government and to degrade religion.” 
It may seem like an impossible leap to get from where we are today to some apocalyptic future where government has been destroyed and religion degraded. But consider our governor-elect: Tuberville has been hell-bent on persecuting law-abiding Muslim Americans, and he recently blasted Christian pastors for being insufficiently political. Imagine if the First Amendment weren’t around to keep him on a leash. Suddenly it’s not such a leap at all. 
There is a place for faith in public schools, just as there’s a place for it in every public space. The faithful are called to live out their beliefs not just in prayer, but in every word and deed. Kindness, generosity, mercy, honesty: All of these can be expressions of faith. And the First Amendment protects our right to frame those virtues in specifically religious language. It’s OK to talk about Jesus.
We just can’t co-opt the power of the state to do it. It violates both our country’s founding principles and the sanctity of faith.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: More than 1,000 acres of Kentucky’s highest mountain to become a nature preserve
description: Megan Falce’s earliest memories of Black Mountain were of trying to see the “golf ball,” a federal aviation radar dome that sticks out above the trees, on top of the mountain as her parents drove up twisting roads in Harlan County.  But as she grew up, she started to understand the “many layers” of Kentucky’s […]
text:
An aerial view of Black Mountain, Kentucky's tallest mountain reaching up to 4,145 feet. (Courtesy Kentucky Natural Lands Trust)Megan Falce’s earliest memories of Black Mountain were of trying to see the “golf ball,” a federal aviation radar dome that sticks out above the trees, on top of the mountain as her parents drove up twisting roads in Harlan County. 
But as she grew up, she started to understand the “many layers” of Kentucky’s highest mountain peak, reaching 4,145 feet above sea level along the Kentucky-Virginia border. It’s been an extensive resource for timber and coal mining, but it’s also a place with a breadth of ecological diversity — an ecosystem she believes has had limited protection over the decades. 
“Black Mountain is super special because of its high elevation,” said Falce, an outreach coordinator with the Kentucky Natural Lands Trust. “There’s especially plants that are on the mountain that are found nowhere else in the state due to how much rainfall it receives annually, the cooler temperatures.” 
That diversity will now be protected as part of Kentucky’s first nature preserve on the mountain, preserving 1,126 acres on the north side of the mountain. It’s an effort that the conservation nonprofit Kentucky Natural Lands Trust has worked on for years to piece together. 
The new preserve, named Black Bear Fold, is adjacent to more than 9,400 acres of other existing conserved land that the Berea-based land conservation nonprofit says serves as a key bird migration pathway across the continent. Not only is the land home to black bear habitat but also thousands of other species including Indiana bats, green salamanders and birds like the dark-eyed junco and Canada warbler. 
Canada warblers are known for distinctive black streaks across their bright throat and chest. (Courtesy Kentucky Natural Lands Trust)
The land is being purchased through a coalition of donors and foundations including the regional conservation initiative Appalachia Rising, the Nature Conservancy, the James Graham Brown Foundation, the Open Space Institute and the Imperiled Bat Conservation Fund. The preserve will also protect headwater streams that feed into the Cumberland River Watershed. 
Mark Burgett, a vice president with the national conservation nonprofit Re:wild that’s a part of Appalachia Rising, told the Lantern the Black Bear Fold is a part of critical work to “recenter nature as part of the region’s future.” 
Yellow lady’s slippers are a perennial orchid found in cool, shaded forest in Kentucky, including Black Mountain. (Courtesy Kentucky Natural Lands Trust)
“If you care about nature, if you care about the diversity of life on the planet that we have been bequeathed, then you’ve got to care about Appalachia and Appalachian forests,” Burgett said. “There’s room for economic opportunity, and there’s room for nature conservation that benefits not only species but benefits the people of the region.”
A legacy of extraction and advocacy
Falce said that Black Mountain has always been a place that’s worn “multiple hats.” Her family and friends are part of its coal mining history that stretches back to the early 20th century. The nearby city of Lynch was one of the country’s largest coal mining towns in the 1940s, with its own movie theater and hospital.
Although Black Mountain has been stripped of both trees and coal, it’s also had native reforestation, according to one of the families that owned the land set to become a nature preserve. There’s still an active strip mine next to the new nature preserve. 
Ed Parsons, a member of the Cawood family that’s owned Black Mountain land for more than a century, said his family is confident the beauty of the mountain “will be preserved for years to come.” 
“Black Mountain has been an important resource for America while also contributing to the beauty of Eastern Kentucky and the Central Appalachian region,” Parson said in a statement. 
Black Bear Fold is not the first tract of land that’s been preserved on Black Mountain. In 1999, Kentucky Gov. Paul Patton helped strike an agreement between coal operators and activists, including students at a local elementary school, concerned about the state’s tallest peak being strip-mined. The easements that resulted from the agreement protected thousands of acres, including Black Mountain’s summit from mining. 
Jacob Doyle was 13 years old at Wallins Creek Elementary School in Harlan County when he and his classmates wrote petitions and letters trying to protect the mountain. Doyle, 41, has had his perspective on Black Mountain evolve as he’s worked in the coal mining industry himself. He’s now a therapist and a pastor of a local church. 
Trees and undergrowth are a part of the dense forest that’ll be a part of the nature preserve on Black Mountain. (Courtesy Kentucky Natural Lands Trust)
He recognizes the importance of the coal mining industry to the area and the jobs it brings, though he opposes mountain-top removal — a form of surface mining where explosives blow up the top of a mountain to reach buried coal seams, a practice damaging to waterways and air quality. 
But he also still sees the importance of preserving the mountain, hoping the mountain and new nature preserve can be a place of education for children and maybe a place for religious purposes. 
“Crossing it first thing in the morning, seeing the fog lay down on the mountains, it looks like an ocean,” Doyle said. “When I see it, I see God’s creation. I see the beauty of what he did. And I think for most Harlan Countians, that’s what we think when we get on top of that mountain and look down and see the rolling hills.”
Falce, who still lives in Harlan County near the community of Big Laurel, said the preserve is personal to her because it’s protecting her “backyard”, a mountain top where her husband proposed to her among painted trilliums, her favorite wildflower. 
She likes to take trips to Black Mountain to see the “incredible spring ephemerals” among the forest, like the rose-twisted stalk or the yellow lady slipper among the dozens of species of wildflowers and flora on the mountain.  
Like Doyle, she also sees future opportunities for education through the nature preserve, with potential hiking trails and other activities, helping chart an additional path for Harlan County’s future economy through conservation. The Kentucky Natural Lands Trust states the land, which will be the nonprofit’s third-largest nature preserve, will initially be limited to scientific research of the area. 
“It’s a giant in so many ways for the state of Kentucky,” Falce said about Black Mountain. “I just really think that there’s a multitude of ways that this conservation can serve the local economy and serve the local people as well.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: North Baldwin voters send Danielle Duggar to Montgomery
description: A new Republican representative from Baldwin County hopes to use her experience as a legislative analyst and perspective as a mother of school-age children to legislate. “I’m still raising children and seeing what they’re being taught in school and what they’re dealing with in sports and friends, social media and everything that kids are going […]
text:
Construction of the new Alabama Statehouse as seen on July 29, 2026, in Montgomery, Alabama. Voters in House District 96 elected Danielle Duggar, a Republican from Spanish Fort, to be their representative for the next four years. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector) 
 This the first of a series of profiles of new Alabama legislators.

A new Republican representative from Baldwin County hopes to use her experience as a legislative analyst and perspective as a mother of school-age children to legislate.
“I’m still raising children and seeing what they’re being taught in school and what they’re dealing with in sports and friends, social media and everything that kids are going through today that’s different from when I was growing up. I’m exposed to that. I see it in my home and in my family,” said Danielle Duggar, R-Spanish Fort, in a phone interview Wednesday. “I feel I have a unique perspective that I can bring to the Legislature, living through it as a mom.” 
She has three children; a 23-year-old son, a son in high school, and a daughter in sixth grade. 
Voters in House District 96 chose Duggar over Democratic nominee Terri Osborne in the general election. Duggar got about 11,400 votes (64.1%), and Osborne got almost 6,400 votes (35.7%), according to unofficial returns.
Rep. Danielle Duggar, R-Spanish Fort, is the newly-elected representative for House District 96. (courtesy of Duggar)
Duggar defeated two-term Rep. Matt Simpson, R-Daphne, in a close Republican primary in May Simpson was one of eight incumbent lawmakers that lost their seats in the primary. Simpson filed a cease and desist against the Alabama Values political action committee (PAC) for making false claims of his voting record on campaign fliers. He has threatened legal action against the PAC for the false statements.
Duggar, 42, is one of 14 new representatives joining the 105-member body. There will be a 74-member Republican supermajority in the lower chamber, and Democrats will have 31 members.
New members are thinking of committees they hope to serve on for the next four years. Duggar said her top three are the House Health, State Government and Education Policy committees.
“I ended up working as a legislative analyst and stopped teaching,” she said. “I loved it, but ended up going with legislative analysis because the whole medical freedom thing is really my ultimate passion.”
Duggar has been a legislative analyst for the National Vaccine Information Center (NVIC) since 2024. The center’s mission, according to its website, is to prevent vaccine injuries and deaths, and advocate for vaccine exemptions. The center promotes “informed consent” of vaccines on its website, highlighting the potential risks and dangers of vaccines, but not the prevention of contracting disease.
According to a 2015 study, scientists at the Immunization Safety Office of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) found no concerning pattern in deaths following vaccines studied between 1997 and 2013, most of whom were children under 12 months old. 
The center is widely considered anti-vaccine, but Duggar disputed that in a text Friday evening.
“NVIC promotes informed consent to medical risk-taking. So they want individuals to have all the info on vaccines before deciding to take one aka “informed consent” which all physicians are supposed to obtain from their patients prior to any medical procedure including vaccination,” she said. “NVIC is anti-mandate, not anti-vaccine.”
Duggar said she wants to pass a bill in her first term that would ensure no discrimination at any workplace based on an individual’s vaccination status.
“I really feel confident that we can do that,” she said. “It doesn’t prohibit mandates, but it does prohibit discrimination.”
Similar legislation has been filed in recent years by Sen. Arthur Orr, R-Decatur, and Rep. Mack Butler, R-Rainbow City, to allow religious vaccine exemptions over the last three legislative sessions. 
Orr’s bill in 2025 got approval from a House committee two weeks before lawmakers left for the year, but never received final passage.
Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville also supports religious exemptions for vaccines, and has filed federal legislation to withhold funding from public schools that do not recognize the exemptions. 
The push for vaccine exemptions comes as the United States has faced its first outbreak of measles, a highly contagious disease, since it was declared eliminated in 2000. Three Alabamians have tested positive for the disease since the onset of the outbreak last year.
As of Friday, the CDC has confirmed almost 5,200 cases of measles in 2026 across the country. About 96% of the confirmed cases were not vaccinated against the disease. There were almost 2,300 confirmed cases in 2025, where about 93% were unvaccinated.
According to the CDC, 94.3% of Alabama kindergarteners are vaccinated against the disease for the 2025-26 school year. In the 2024-25 school year, 95.2% of kindergarteners were vaccinated. Herd immunity can be reached with a 95% vaccination rate. 
Local issues
The port city of Mobile, Ala., sits at the head of Mobile Bay and is a key link in shipping goods in and out of the U.S. (Lee Hedgepeth/Inside Climate News)
Duggar said that, like most Alabamians, affordability is a top concern for her constituents. A new bridge that will connect Baldwin and Mobile counties across the Mobile Bay is expected to have $3 to $7.70 per trip tolls to repay a $2.52 billion federal loan.
The tolls were largely unpopular among candidates of both parties during the campaign. Duggar said she wants to propose a dollar-for-dollar tax refund for tollpayers.
“We have like 20,000 daily commuters from Baldwin County and Mobile County driving across the Bay. I’d love to see that money come back into our pockets,” she said.
The Mobile metro delegation will have four Republicans and three Democratic lawmakers. Duggar said that the local issues seem bipartisan and looks forward to working with everybody.
“There hasn’t, that I know of, really been a lot of conflict there between what one party wants, what the other. It seems to be that they’re willing to vote on whatever is going to be good for the district,” she said.
Tuberville and Republican leadership have vowed to eliminate the state sales tax on food in 2027, which is currently 2%. It has been reduced over the last three years. Democratic lawmakers have also advocated for the elimination of the state sales tax on food for years. 
Duggar said that while taxes are part of life, she wants to reduce them wherever possible.
“I’m big on reducing tax burden on our citizens, making sure that if we can cut the grocery tax the rest of the way, let’s do it. Let’s give the people some relief,” she said. “As a conservative, I don’t want to pay any taxes, but I get that this is a part of the government that we’ve built, and it’s how we fund government.”

name: National
title: States struggle to impose new Medicaid work rules, even with 6-month reprieve
description: Last week the federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services extended the deadline by six months to June 30, 2027, for state Medicaid programs to impose work requirements on their enrollees, but states still face a slew of unique challenges keeping people on the rolls.  Among the many logistical challenges states are figuring out are […]
text:
Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, speaks at the Department of Health and Human Services in Washington, D.C., in December 2025. Despite a six-month reprieve, many states will struggle to implement new Medicaid work requirement rules. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)Last week the federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services extended the deadline by six months to June 30, 2027, for state Medicaid programs to impose work requirements on their enrollees, but states still face a slew of unique challenges keeping people on the rolls. 
Among the many logistical challenges states are figuring out are how to communicate the many different exceptions to enrollees for work rules, overhauling their eligibility systems to have people seeminglessly turn in their paperwork to verify income and hiring more staff to review those documents. 
Last week, after months of hearing from state Medicaid programs that meeting the former Jan. 1 deadline would be too challenging and expensive, Daniel Brillman, CMS’s deputy administrator and director, offered states in a Nov. 13 letter a reprieve, which he called a “hold harmless” period, offering states another six months without penalty. 
Still, some states, such as Montana and Nebraska, rolled out their work requirements early and have already hit some roadbumps. Jeremy Nordquist, president and CEO of the Nebraska Hospital Association representing the state’s hospitals, said he’s been working with the state to reach Medicaid enrollees and noticed that the biggest barrier has been communication. 
‘Medically frail’ Medicaid enrollees won’t have to prove their inability to work to keep coverage

“It’s really important to try to get down, you know, as deep into the community as possible. Typically these folks aren’t watching local news as much as the general population. They’re not following healthcare policy,” Nordquist said. 
According to Nebraska state data, by August 2026, around four months after the state began enforcing work rules on May 1, the state had already denied 557 new Medicaid applicants due to the new requirements. But among those the vast majority — 466, or 83.7% — had simply failed to provide documentation needed to prove compliance or an exemption from the rules. 
Another 533 people who were renewing their Medicaid were also denied. Of those, 490, or 91.9%, also failed to provide documentation. 
Overall that meant at least 956 people lost their Medicaid because of paperwork, which many experts have said would be the biggest challenge. 
“Early on, we saw the state send a letter to Medicaid recipients with a high-level overview of what would be needed, and it was really written at a 14th-grade reading level,” Nordquist said. “That’s really not something that’s easily comprehensible or easily followed up on by Medicaid populations.”
And in Montana, Dr. Aaron Wernham, CEO of the Montana Healthcare Foundation, a healthcare policy and investment group, said even before work requirements in the state, it was already hard to get enrollees help if they were struggling with paperwork. 
“We have long wait times in the Medicaid call center, high rates of call abandonment by people trying to call in to get help and also very high rates — among the nation’s highest — of renewal applications taking more than 45 days to process, that was before all the work requirement stuff,” Wernham said. 
Different states, different problems
Every state is dealing with its own set of circumstances, and so are enrollees. Federal work requirements state that adults under the age of 64 and who are able-bodied earning up to 138% of the federal poverty line (around $22,000 for an individual) would have to volunteer, go to school or work for at least 80 hours a month or meet a minimum household income of $580 a month ($6,960 for a household year) in order to be eligible for Medicaid. 
But among the 41 states plus the District of Columbia that expanded Medicaid to adults with lower incomes, as well as those that partially expanded through waivers such as Georgia, Tennessee and Wisconsin,  31 have minimum wages that are higher than the federal government’s minimum wage of $7.25 and would have to work fewer than 80 hours. And across 20 states plus D.C., enrollees are eligible for Medicaid if one person in their household works at least 40 hours a month.
So, each state will have to consider its own minimum wage standards every year while calculating enrollees’ eligibility. Many states shift their minimum wages every year. 



Quotation







It's just an additional administrative burden, not only on the Medicaid agencies, but also on providers who have to chime in to help.


– Jennifer Evans, an attorney at Polsinelli working with healthcare providers and former Medicaid director for Colorado


“They might be checking if they have pay stubs or other data sources that might show hours worked or connections with education hubs to see education status,” said Amaya Diana, a health policy analyst at health research group KFF. “And then, if they don’t have data on file, that’s where they may ask for additional documentation from an enrollee, and that is where they might be submitting extra documents to the state.” 
Given that enrollees can meet the requirements or seek an exemption in many different ways, Rebecca Kellenberg, a principal at Health Management Associates, a firm that helps organizations implement health policy, said states will have to really focus on their communication strategies so enrollees don’t think they are unqualified when they actually are. 
“I think states are anticipating that the majority are already working or will meet some exclusions based on their circumstances, and that the challenge is documenting that work,” Kellenberg said. “It’s a communication challenge to figure out what the documentation requirements are … that will be the biggest challenge for ensuring individuals don’t lose coverage when they are in fact eligible and meeting requirements.” 
In Nebraska, Nordquist said his biggest takeaway for states and hospitals is to start early. 
“We created Spanish language resources that our hospitals could use in their communities doing outreach to try to explain the requirements that were coming but also make sure to tell people to keep their information current,” Nordquist said. “This Medicaid expansion population tends to move more frequently than the general population, so physical mail isn’t always the best. 
“That’s why it’s so important we find ways to break down those barriers and get people’s contact information updated as frequently as possible.” 
Most enrollees already working
Most people on Medicaid are already working, and states already check income for Medicaid eligibility. While meeting a smaller standard of just 40 hours or less may not be a challenge for many, the paperwork of providing proof of income twice a year will be the actual significant and unnecessary burden to people who are working, said Jennifer Evans, an attorney at Polsinelli working with healthcare providers and former Medicaid director for Colorado.  
Data from KFF shows 63% of adults on Medicaid work 80 hours a month or attend school. 
Doctors and hospitals to see lower Medicaid payments in three dozen states

“It’s just that they don’t make enough money, or they don’t work in a location that offers health insurance. … These are low-wage earners, and so I don’t think that the fact that the dollar number is less is going to have a material impact,” Evans said. “It’s just an additional administrative burden, not only on the Medicaid agencies, but also on providers who have to chime in to help.”

In Washington, D.C.,  for example, the Medicaid program will have to distinguish between District workers and federal workers. While people under federal law minimally earn $7.25 per hour, District workers earn $18.40 per hour, almost three times as much. 
“The biggest challenge will be ensuring that District residents are reporting all their income so that DHCF (Department of Health Care Finance) can accurately determine their total income and subsequently, their compliance with the work requirements,” Melisa Byrd, senior deputy director of D.C.’s Medicaid program, wrote to Stateline. “DHCF’s goal is to utilize electronic sources for income verification whenever possible — but we will accept any other documentation showing earned income.”
Byrd wrote that the department estimates that of the approximately 75,000 Medicaid adult enrollees without children who would be subject to work requirements, nearly a third appear compliant based on their household income of at least $580 in a month. 
That means states and municipalities will still face a host of challenges keeping Medicaid recipients on the rolls who may be working inconsistently, facing unemployment or dealing with unforeseeable circumstances. 
“Many people on Medicaid have little to no income, and little to no taxable income,” said Jennifer Wagner, director of Medicaid eligibility and enrollment at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan policy research group.
“Many people turn to Medicaid in a time of crisis, such as when they’ve lost a job and are in between jobs, or they’ve had a medical crisis that’s caused them to take time off of work,” Wagner said. “Their annual income might be higher, but when they apply for Medicaid, they may be very low income.” 
Wagner said states will face confusion and paperwork issues around people who are in school, medically frail, caregivers, or fall under other exclusions. Enrollees taking care of kids under the age of 14 are also exempt from the work rules. 
In June, 25 Democratic-led states plus the District of Columbia sued the Trump administration over the work requirement, largely on the basis of their decision to change “medically frail” guidelines to ask enrollees to prove they are too sick to work. In late October, a U.S. district judge struck down that part of the rule, saying it would cause significant harm to enrollees and create costs for states, but granted some concessions to the federal government in other areas. 
Specifically, the court upheld the federal government’s new rule requiring that states look back at 12 months of claims data to determine whether an enrollee meets the medical frailty exemption at all. 
States also have to look back at least a month at an enrollee’s work history for them to apply at all. In the past, states did not have to do this, Wagner said. According to KFF, right now 31 states have opted to look back one month to determine eligibility, but five states plan to look back two to three months. Another two will look back three months after a quarterly compliance check. 
“This idea of looking back at a month instead of what your current circumstances are is not a concept in Medicaid,” Wagner said. “It’s not the way applications are structured. It’s not the way eligibility systems are structured, and so this is a totally new thing.” 
Stateline reporter Shalina Chatlani can be reached at schatlani@stateline.org.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Commentary: Trump voucher program would use taxpayer dollars to fund religious education
description: Scholarship-granting organizations are central to implementing President Donald Trump’s federal school voucher plan, officially called the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit, or Education Freedom Tax Credit. Beginning in 2027 in at least 31 states, including Colorado, the program allows taxpayers to redirect up to $1,700 of their federal tax liability to qualify[...]
text:
(Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Scholarship-granting organizations are central to implementing President Donald Trump’s federal school voucher plan, officially called the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit, or Education Freedom Tax Credit. Beginning in 2027 in at least 31 states, including Colorado, the program allows taxpayers to redirect up to $1,700 of their federal tax liability to qualifying SGOs, which award scholarships for private school tuition and other eligible educational expenses.
On Oct. 1, the Treasury Department released proposed and temporary regulations for the program. According to Treasury estimates, the program could generate nearly $26 billion annually, supporting nearly 2.2 million scholarships. Education Secretary Linda McMahon said the program would help parents “flee” failing schools, and Trump called it a major expansion of school choice for families seeking schools that share their values.
Critics warn the regulations limit states’ ability to protect civil rights, oversee scholarship organizations and ensure equitable funding. Brookings researcher Jon Valant characterized the program as “Title I for rich kids,” questioning whether benefits would reach students most in need.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Others raised concerns about church-state separation and the program’s implications for funding public education. The regulations also lack clarity on how funds will reach public schools or what safeguards will protect participating students. 
Treasury estimates more than 600 SGOs could qualify by 2030. Competition to attract donors is already underway. Chalkbeat reported that billions could be spent marketing the tax credit nationwide.
A financial incentive
Denver-based ACE Scholarships is one of the largest K-12 scholarship organizations in the country and is expanding nationally. Co-founded by Walmart heir John Walton, ACE has awarded more than 121,000 private school scholarships worth $395 million over 25 years. Walton believed public schools would improve only if parents could “leave ineffective schools and take the money with them.”
According to Education Week, “almost 75 percent of private schools in the U.S. are religious,” and ACE’s scholarship awards fit that statistic. In a legal brief filed in Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue, ACE reported that approximately 88% of its 673 partner private schools nationwide were religiously affiliated. 
In May 2026, ACE launched EmpowerEd, a platform handling applications, eligibility, awards, donor tracking and compliance for participating organizations. Federal rules allow SGOs to retain up to 10% of contributions for administrative expenses. ACE states it will return 3% of qualifying contributions to organizations in its partner network, including schools, professional associations, financial and tax advisers, nonprofits and faith-based organizations. This financial rebate incentivizes individuals and groups in ACE’s partner network to contribute through ACE’s platform, thereby earning money to use for their own purposes. 
Churches will play a major role
ACE’s partners include Turning Point USA, PragerU, the Herzog Foundation, the Archdiocese of Denver, the Chesterton Schools Network, UEL Education, Aequitas Education and the Association of Classical Christian Schools.  This partner network gives ACE access to religious communities that can promote the tax credit, encourage contributions and connect families with private schools. 
ACE’s partnership with Turning Point USA extends to TPUSA Faith’s Make Heaven Crowded Tour, a series of faith-centered events at churches and other venues. TPUSA says ACE’s sponsorship creates opportunities to share information about scholarships and the federal tax credit with attendees. TPUSA reports more than 12,000 churches, 22,000 trained pastors and 6 million congregants are engaged annually.
Public good or private marketplace?
If successful, ACE and other well-funded SGOs could redirect billions in federal tax credits toward private education, much of it religiously affiliated. This raises several key questions: Should public education function like a private marketplace driven by individual consumer choices, or a public good that serves the entire community? Does the federal tax credit voucher plan violate the constitutional principle of separation of church and state?
Public education is a shared public responsibility and a cornerstone of democracy. Public schools bring together students from different communities and prepare young people to live in a democratic society. They are obligated to educate every child, regardless of background, ability, religion, values or family income.
By allowing taxpayer dollars to expand faith-based school enrollments, the federal program creates a workaround for SGOs like ACE Scholarships to send taxpayer dollars to fund religious education while eroding support for public schools. Public education should not become a marketplace in which private organizations manage educational resources. It should remain a public commitment to serving all children and the communities they share.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: In Dominion-NextEra merger opening arguments, parties clash over potential risk, protections
description: The legal case of the historic proposed merger of Virginia’s largest utility provider, Dominion Energy, and Florida-based NextEra Energy began Tuesday at the State Corporation Commission, with attorneys representing over 30 intervenors presenting their opening arguments in Richmond.  The crux of the debate is whether the $67 billion merger should be approved[...]
text:
Inside a State Corporation Commission courtroom in Richmond, where on Nov. 16 opening arguments in the proposed Dominion-NextEra merger unfolded. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)The legal case of the historic proposed merger of Virginia’s largest utility provider, Dominion Energy, and Florida-based NextEra Energy began Tuesday at the State Corporation Commission, with attorneys representing over 30 intervenors presenting their opening arguments in Richmond. 
The crux of the debate is whether the $67 billion merger should be approved, creating the largest regulated utility in the world. State regulators must decide whether “adequate service to the public at just and reasonable rates will not be impaired or jeopardized” by the deal.
Several clean energy advocates and other interested parties in the case insisted that Dominion and NextEra have not proved that the deal wouldn’t risk rate increases. 
Opponents also said the companies need to back up their claims that the deal’s boost to the companies’ energy infrastructure buying power will benefit customers. 
“Petitioners have failed to provide any real evidence or analysis to support these claims or any enforceable conditions to ensure that customers will in fact benefit,” Appalachian Voices attorney Nate Benforado said.
The utilities argue that the law is narrow in requiring the companies to “do no harm,” and that the scope of the merger case should focus on the efforts to maintain reliable service. 
Some intervenors have pushed to include NextEra’s  alleged involvement in political campaigns in past years as part of the evidence in the case.
Clean energy groups have also asked for a more robust plan of how the companies would work to meet the state’s Clean Economy Act mandates, as power demand continues to grow under the buildout of data centers across the commonwealth.
“This case, in our view, is simply not the one to litigate that cost of service, and nor is it the case to litigate who’s paying their fair share, and ensuring everybody pays their fair share, including the data centers,” Joseph Reid, representing Dominion, said.
Intervenors outline concerns, potential risks
The companies said if they’re allowed to combine, their ability to bulk-buy energy infrastructure will bring down the cost of the energy projects. 
The Sierra Club and other intervenors said Tuesday those savings would not be quantifiable or guaranteed.
In pre-filed testimony, SCC staff wrote that NextEra’s “unregulated, competitive business” exposed Dominion to additional risks. NextEra Energy Resources (NEER) produces energy infrastructure and is valued on the market value of power – which can be a volatile calculation.
“Rates that carry another company’s risk are not just and reasonable,” said Greg Habeeb, an attorney representing Clean Virginia in the case.
Bill increases are one of the top concerns the intervenors identified. 
Dominion Energy customers have already seen a steep increase in the average monthly bill over the past two decades. 
In a report to the Energy Commission of Virginia, the SCC reported that the average monthly Dominion residential bill “was $90.59 as of July 1, 2007. The bill has increased by $90.20, or 99.57%, to $180.79 per month as of July 1, 2026.”
The joint petitioners have offered a monthly bill credit of $10 a month for up to four years. Gov. Abigail Spanberger and Chief Energy Officer Josephus Allmond have asked for that rate to be increased to $29 and to have a base rate freeze for six years. 
The attorney representing the governor’s office also urged commissioners to implement enforcements in the deal, to ensure that all that is being promised in the case by the two companies actually is implemented if the merger is approved.
“The commission has broad authority, under Virginia law, to impose civil penalties, require specific performance, and when necessary, unwind a transaction,” Matthew McGuire, on behalf of Spanberger and Allmond, testified.
Reid stated that the bill credit is meant to be a bridge between the current cost of bills to when the potential benefits of the merger would kick in. Clean Virginia’s attorney testified that these conditions don’t get to the heart of the risk that has been outlined in staff testimony.
“Every condition offered treats the symptom, but leaves the cause. The source of the jeopardy is NextEra’s control, and NextEra’s other businesses that are untouched by any proposed condition,” Habeeb said.
Reid pointed to the list of recommendations and policy changes that were recommended by SCC staff and the Attorney General’s office that the agencies felt would put the merger deal in a better position to advance. 
The utilities agreed to the majority of the protections, but offered alternate plans in regards to separating finances and resources, otherwise known as ring-fencing, in specific “trigger events” as well as other policy shifts.
“We hope that there’s some sort of peace in the valley here because the petitioners made an effort to make those conditions even more protective and robust than staff proposed,” Reid testified.
Other participants in the case have brought their own list of recommendations and policies that they want the utilities to consider.
Cliona Mary Robb, representing the Virginia Energy Purchasing Governmental Association, testified that the group was frustrated Dominion and NextEra did not address their list of recommendations in their rebuttal testimony.
The utilities also didn’t remark on the governor’s recommendations in their filed rebuttal testimony.
The hearings for the case are anticipated to run through the Thanksgiving holiday. A decision must be made by the three commissions on the merger by Jan. 11.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia lawmaker, advocates push to expand local authority under home rule proposal
description: A proposal to grant Virginia localities more authority is gaining momentum, as advocates, labor unions, and community and immigrant rights organizations seek to expand local government powers beyond what the commonwealth currently allows. Virginia is a Dillon’s Rule state, meaning local governments can exercise only powers specifically granted by the state, [...]
text:
The Virginia state Capitol in Richmond on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Markus Schmidt/Virginia Mercury)A proposal to grant Virginia localities more authority is gaining momentum, as advocates, labor unions, and community and immigrant rights organizations seek to expand local government powers beyond what the commonwealth currently allows.
Virginia is a Dillon’s Rule state, meaning local governments can exercise only powers specifically granted by the state, or those that are reasonably implied or necessary to carry out their responsibilities. 
Home Rule, on the other hand, would give local governments more freedom and flexibility to make decisions based on the needs of their communities, as long as those decisions do not violate state or federal laws. 
Dillon’s Rule originated in the 19th century, when Iowa Supreme Court Judge John F. Dillon developed the legal doctrine during a period of rapid urban growth, railroad expansion, and growing concerns about municipal spending, public borrowing, and rising local government debt.
Del. Marty Martinez, D-Loudoun, is introducing the Virginia Home Rule Act proposal, which would let localities act on local issues unless the state expressly limits or prohibits them, rather than requiring them to seek permission first. 
“We now have an opportunity to build a more responsive system of government,” Martinez said during a call with reporters on Monday.
Nearly 80% of local officials say Dillon’s rule limits their policy options, according to survey data collected by the Municipal Research Lab at Old Dominion University, which included 301 responses from every Virginia locality. 
More than half have abandoned potential policies because they expect the state to stop them.
Bruce McDonald, the lab’s director, presented the data on Monday, reporting that 73% of respondents said Dillon’s Rule restricts their ability to meet community needs and that over 60% of respondents support the concept of Home Rule.
Additionally, a study from the University of Virginia School of Law analyzed 33 local government legislative agendas containing 979 requests for the 2026 General Assembly session, finding that 45% concerned expanding local authority and 76 agendas sought more power over taxing and land use.
“Our bill makes one fundamental change: Instead of asking whether Richmond gives a community permission to act, we would ask: Has the commonwealth prohibited or limited that community from acting?” Martinez said.
Advocates for the Home Rule Act argued that current restrictions impact immigrant families and working-class residents facing housing instability and rising costs. Enacting the proposal law would allow cities like Alexandria or Fairfax to address specific regional emergencies without waiting for Richmond’s approval.
Carmen Daugherty, executive director for the Advancement Project, said Home Rule would preserve statewide civil-rights protections while giving communities more say in local decisions. 
“Statewide protections should serve as a floor for people’s rights, not an unnecessary ceiling on local progress,” Daugherty said.
Boaz Young-El, statewide campaigns director for New Virginia Majority, added: “The people closest to these problems should have a meaningful voice in developing the solutions, and that means local governments need meaningful authority.” 
Opponents have pushed back against proposals to modify the state framework, concerned about how that would affect statewide consistency, the business environment, and public safety and environmental standards.
But Home Rule would not mean every locality can do whatever it wants, Martinez and others said. Rather, it would mean the legislature can set boundaries, retain authority over statewide matters and identify areas where uniform policies are necessary.
The delegate from Loudoun also said he expects challenges in the legislature, given state leaders’ reluctance to alter state control.
A copy of the proposal was not available during a call with reporters on Monday, and is still under review by the Division of Legislative Services.
According to recent data collected by the National Association of Counties, if successful, Virginia would join most states across the country with less restrictive state powers.
Virginia is one of seven states with the most restrictive powers: Delaware, Nebraska, Texas, Vermont, West Virginia and Wyoming. 
Martinez said he expects to introduce the proposal for the upcoming General Assembly session, which begins in Richmond on Jan. 13.
Del. Dan Helmer, D-Fairfax, recently introduced a resolution to study Dillion’s Rule, but it was continued. No action has been taken on the measure.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Commentary: Can Democrats now compete for votes in Republican rural Virginia?
description: If Democrats are ever going to win Virginia’s Republican-held 5th, 6th and 9th Congressional Districts, 2026 presented their best chance in decades. First, they tried changing the boundaries with a mid-decade, statewide gerrymander in response to the same strategy Republicans had already taken in Texas and elsewhere. Legislative Democrats hastily proposed an[...]
text:
Southwest Virginia’s rolling Appalachian mountains, seen here in Wise County near Big Stone Gap. This part of the state is  in the 9th Congressional District, represented by Republican U.S. Rep. Morgan Griffith. (Photo by Ben Paviour/Virginia Mercury)If Democrats are ever going to win Virginia’s Republican-held 5th, 6th and 9th Congressional Districts, 2026 presented their best chance in decades.
First, they tried changing the boundaries with a mid-decade, statewide gerrymander in response to the same strategy Republicans had already taken in Texas and elsewhere.
Legislative Democrats hastily proposed an amendment to the Virginia Constitution that would have temporarily decommissioned the bipartisan Virginia Redistricting Commission that voters had approved in 2020 to rid their state of partisan reapportionment. 
In April, the voters approved the reversal, but the courts nullified it for illegally cutting corners.
Had it gone into effect, the revised districts would have plausibly given Democrats a strong chance to prevail in 10 of Virginia’s 11 U.S. House districts – all but the 9th.
But with the redistricting plan stopped, Democrats entered this month’s election with the next best thing: an intense disapproval of President Donald Trump and a GOP-ruled Congress on which voters placed blame for inflation born of the president’s tariffs and high fuel prices caused by the war Trump launched on Iran.
Democrats won in the most challenging of environments: Texas (a Senate seat and the governor’s office); Kansas (where no Democrat had been elected senator since 1932); and a shocking upset in Mississippi, where Democrat Scott Colom’s Senate victory made him the first African American elected statewide since Reconstruction.
In Virginia, Democrats extended their dominance of the U.S. House delegation from 6-5 to 8-3. They also hold both U.S. Senate seats.
Democrat Tom Perriello fell about 5,748 votes (or 1.5%) shy of Republican U.S. Rep. John McGuire in the 5th District, while fellow Democrats ousted GOP incumbents in the 1st and 2nd districts. Republicans comfortably won reelection in the 6th and 9th districts, respectively.
Outside of another ill-considered redistricting power play, are those districts beyond the Democratic Party’s reach?
Elections are about the conditions the electorate experiences. If they aren’t afraid and struggling, the incumbent usually prospers. If they are, challengers have an advantage, as they did this year.
“From the outset, it was very clear that the main priority for the Republicans in the state was to hold the five districts, that we were not going to be expanding the map beyond that,” Republican Party of Virginia Chairman Jeff Ryer said during After Virginia Votes, a panel discussion sponsored annually by the Virginia Public Access Project and the Schar School of Policy and Government at George Mason University.
GOP resources were focused on holding the most competitive seats — the 1st and 2nd districts. That left strongholds —like the rural 6th and 9th Districts and  prohibitive long shots like Bert Mizusawa’s bid to unseat Democratic U.S. Sen. Mark Warner — to fend for themselves, Ryer said.
If things don’t improve in rural Virginia, the path for Republicans gets more challenging.
Trump convincingly won congressional districts in those areas in each of his presidential runs, though he failed to carry Virginia in any of them.
This fall, Republicans in every district — including the 5th, 6th and 9th — significantly underperformed Trump’s 2024 margins but remained strong enough to prevail, according to Virginia Department of Elections data.
Rural Virginia’s economy has been hit particularly hard by Trump and GOP policy actions. If they continue or worsen, Democrats could find a foothold and become competitive, at least in the 5th and 6th districts.
In this year’s midterms, the rest of the country learned what Virginia has known for a while

Zack Golden, a Democratic strategist who managed Warner’s campaign this year, said in his After Virginia Votes appearance that Trump’s policies could eventually “lead to a political realignment in the rural areas.”
“If these gas and diesel prices keep going up … farmers are going to have something to say about that, more than they did in 2026,” he said. “If these Medicaid cuts are continued — are allowed to go into effect — and more rural hospitals close, and people have to drive hours and hours to get healthcare, they’re going to take a second look at their political representation that has allowed this to happen.”
Through the middle of the 20th century, Democratic dominance in those rural areas was unchallenged. 
Republicans didn’t gain that dominance  overnight. Policies and actions of both parties at the state and federal level fostered it over decades. The same would likely be true for another realignment.
Rural and farming communities also face economic disadvantages resulting from trade policy. 
There is a huge disparity compared to urban and suburban Virginia that are better able to fund schools and attract better employment opportunities. Cuts to Medicaid and Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits disproportionately penalize residents near or below the poverty level in rural areas where good jobs are scarce.
Politicians who listen to those people’s stories and help them can, over time, gain their trust and their votes. 
The groundwork for Democratic gains in rural Virginia has been set. The question is whether the party can build on its electoral successes in 2026 with public policies that effectively address rural Virginia’s needs.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland’s 1.15 million family caretakers need more support, advocates say
description: Advocates say that Maryland’s family caregivers need more support as they take on economic and emotional tolls while providing billions in unpaid labor helping family members through chronic conditions, injuries and other challenges.
text:
Advocates say that Maryland’s family caregivers need more support as they take on economic and emotional tolls while providing billions in unpaid labor helping family members through chronic conditions, injuries and other challenges. (Photo by Halfpoint Images/Getty Stock photo)Advocates say that Maryland’s family caretakers need more support as they take on economic and emotional tolls while providing billions in unpaid labor helping family members through chronic conditions, injuries and other challenges.
From providing for a spouse with dementia to helping aging parents with their medications and mobility needs, the labor that Maryland’s estimated 1.15 million family caretakers provide would equate to, collectively, 1 billion hours of unpaid caretaking services valued at $24 billion.
But instead, family caretakers report taking financial hits when they move into caregiving duties such as paying for groceries, providing or arranging transportation or even making home modifications to support their loved ones, according to a report Tuesday by the AARP Maryland.
It’s for that reason and more that a coalition of healthcare advocates and family caregivers gathered in Annapolis Tuesday to push legislation that provides greater protections for Maryland’s caretakers and bolsters the state’s long-term care system.
“Family caregivers are the backbone of Maryland’s long-term care system, but right now we’re asking them to shoulder an enormous responsibility largely on their own,” Sara Westrick, AARP Maryland Advocacy Director, said at the press conference. “The Our Care agenda that we’re launching today is about making sure that caring for someone you love does not mean sacrificing your own financial security, health or future.”
The AARP Maryland report shows that 43% of Marylanders aged 30 and older provided unpaid care for a family member or a friend in the last year. The report is based on a survey of 1,018 Maryland residents aged 30 or older, from Aug. 5 to Aug. 26.
It found that about 45% of all caregivers in Maryland were between the ages of 45 and 64, while 35% were 30 to 44 years old. The other 20% of Maryland caregivers are 65 or older.
About 61% of caregivers live with a partner or spouse, and approximately 60% of caregivers in Maryland are women, the survey found.
“Behind every one of these statistics is a daughter helping a mother with her medications, a husband caring for a spouse with dementia, or an employee trying to get through the workday after staying up all night providing care,” Westrick said. Also joining the AARP Maryland were members of Service Employees International Union 1199.
Del. Lesley Lopez speaks a meeting of the the Women Legislators of Maryland. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
Overall, two-thirds of Maryland caregivers reported working a job while taking on caregiving duties. They are concerned about unfair treatment in the workplace, with four in 10 reporting that they had not told \their boss about their caregiving responsibilities, and 8% of respondents saying they felt penalized or discriminated against because of caregiving.
It’s why Del. Lesley J. Lopez (D- Montgomery) plans to reintroduce legislation that would protect caregivers against workplace discrimination.
“Being a caregiver does not mean you are not doing a great job at your regular job. It does not mean that your are going to be any more late, any less present at your workplace,” Lopez said at Tuesday’s event. “We have to understand that there are accommodations that need to be made, but most importantly, people should not be discriminated against because of their status.”
That said, the data shows that portions of the caretakers had to cut back on hours or stop working entirely to take care of their family members.
A quarter of caregivers surveyed took a leave of absence from work, while 19% moved from full-time to part-time work. About 10% of caregivers reported turning down a promotion, while about 7% retired earlier than planned. Additional costs needed to support family members can also take a toll. New out-of-pocket spending can whittle down savings accounts and lead some caretakers to take on debt.
That’s not factoring the emotional challenges that can arise from caretaking. The legislative priorities include bolstering access to resources for people with dementia and similar conditions.
It’s a sadness that Del. Ashanti Martinez (D-Prince George’s) knows personally, recalling his experience of watching his great-grandmother forget him and other family members as her dementia progressed.
“There are few things more heartbreaking than watching someone you love slowly forget the people and memories that made up their life,” Martinez said. “That experience has stayed with me and has shaped how I understand our healthcare system, how I approach my work in Annapolis.”
Del. Ashanti Martinez (D-Prince George’s) listens during a committee discussion on proposed 2026 legislation. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
It’s why he plans to sponsor legislation to ensure that Marylanders have better access to Alzheimer’s treatments.
“With early detection, access to those treatments, and family knowing that options exist – it can make a world of difference,” Martinez said.
He also plans to sponsor legislation that would provide greater transparency and accountability on how nursing homes spend their money, to ensure that the funds are being used to provide the best care for patients in those facilities.
Members of 1199 SEIU are also pushing legislation to protect staffing levels for long-term care facilities. They also want legislation that penalizes large employers for each employee who receives healthcare coverage through Medicaid, thereby freeing up taxpayer dollars to support other state healthcare programs.
“When taxpayers are forced to pay for healthcare coverage for large companies’ employees, those companies should shoulder the cost.” said Ricarra Jones, political director for the union.
“When a large employer does not provide affordable health coverage, the bill doesn’t just go away. It doesn’t disappear. It gets sent to us as Maryland taxpayers,” she said. “We cannot continue to allow large corporations to continue to shift that healthcare cost onto us.”
With lawmakers and advocates alike gearing up for the 2027 session, they’ll need to grapple with a looming $3 billion budget shortfall that threatens both existing programs and the success of any new initiative with a large price tag.
In an interview last week, Westrick said that she hopes the new data can help sway lawmakers to support the legislative package amid the challenging fiscal year.
“We wanted to find the data to make our case to legislators,” Westrick said in a recent interview. “And because of the magnitude of this infusion of care means for the state’s economy – it’s not just a family issue, it’s a workforce issue. This is an economic issue.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: UL System board might have violated Open Meetings Law when hiring new president
description: The University of Louisiana System Board of Supervisors is the subject of a complaint alleging it violated the state’s Open Meetings Law with its last-minute, improperly noticed meeting in which it hired a new president.  The complaint was filed by James Finney with East Baton Rouge District Attorney Hillar Moore, whose jurisdiction is where the […]
text:
The University of Louisiana System announced it will hire state education superintendent Cade Brumley, left, to replace Rick Gallot as its president. (Photos by Allison Alsop/Louisiana Illuminator, UL System)The University of Louisiana System Board of Supervisors is the subject of a complaint alleging it violated the state’s Open Meetings Law with its last-minute, improperly noticed meeting in which it hired a new president. 
The complaint was filed by James Finney with East Baton Rouge District Attorney Hillar Moore, whose jurisdiction is where the UL System board met Friday to name state education superintendent Cade Brumley its next president. The published agenda for the meeting did not meet the law’s requirement that it be reasonably specific, according to the complaint. 
The agenda item called for “consideration of personnel actions for the UL System” and did not specifically mention the board would hire a new system president, a process that usually takes a monthslong search and involves multiple opportunities for public comment.
Finney, a Baton Rouge resident and longtime government transparency advocate, said he filed the complaint because he has no tolerance for public officials who treat the law as open to artistic interpretation rather than guidelines for conducting the public’s business. 
“There is absolutely no excuse for the agenda to be as vague as it was,” Finney said in a statement to the Illuminator. “Clearly the architects of Dr. Brumley’s coronation to his prospective new job didn’t want the public to have any clue as to the actual topic of the special meeting.”
Other government watchdogs agreed the notice was vague. 
“The public should not have to guess what ‘consideration of personnel actions’ means, particularly when hiring a system president,” said Steven Procopio, president of the nonpartisan Public Affairs Research Council of Louisiana. “Clearly informing the public is a simple step. A vague agenda only invites more scrutiny and undermines confidence in the process.” 
The UL System board’s steps to hire Brumley run into other issues with the state’s Open Meetings Law. In addition to its vagueness, board members failed to provide the agenda to members of the press and the public who have formally asked to receive meeting notices. 
Scott Sternberg, an attorney who specializes in First Amendment and government transparency law, said the Open Meetings Law requires public bodies to give notice of their meetings and what’s on their agendas with “reasonable specificity.”
“The reason that it is that way is so that people can look at the agenda and decide whether they need to go to the meeting. So if the average person can’t look at the agenda and say what the meeting is about, then in my opinion, that is not reasonable specificity,” said Sternberg, who has represented the Illuminator. 
The board’s meeting notice also was not posted to the webpage where it usually publishes its agendas and was instead placed in a secondary location on the website. The law requires that the notice be posted to the website but does not stipulate the location. 
Any action taken during proceedings in which the Open Meetings Law is violated can be thrown out by a judge, according to the law. Also, members of public bodies who participate in meetings that a judge determines to be in violation of the law may be penalized up to $100 per violation.
“The point of the whole exercise is so that citizens get to participate in the goings on of their government. Knowing what’s on the agenda is an essential portion of that,” Sternberg added. 
Brumley, UL System board chairman Mark Romero, spokeswoman Katie Dawson and DA Hillar Moore have not yet responded to requests for comment on the complaint. 
The UL System board moved to replace its current president, Rick Gallot, less than 24 hours after The Advocate broke a story about a tax lien filed against him for more than $350,000 in unpaid taxes. Gallot, who has said his accountant is responsible for the tax issue, submitted his resignation Friday.
Gallot was also hired without a search in 2023, but the notice for that meeting did specify the UL System board would be hiring a new president. Its members moved quickly to replace Jim Henderson after he stepped down to become president of Louisiana Tech. Members of the board at the time were all appointees of Gov. John Bel Edwards, a Democrat who was on his way out of office. 
Incoming Gov. Jeff Landry, a Republican, initially pushed back on Gallot’s appointment but ultimately approved the hire. Gallot, who had been president at Grambling State University, a historically Black university, was previously a Democratic lawmaker. 
Gallot has not yet responded to a request for comment from the Illuminator. 
Brumley is a socially conservative Republican and ally of Landry who backs the governor’s K-12 school voucher program that directs public dollars toward private schools. He is also credited for Louisiana’s recent improvements in early elementary literacy rates. 
Brumley is expected to officially become the new UL System president Dec. 1.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana gets EPA approval to permit waste disposal at coal-burning power plants
description: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has given Louisiana the final go-ahead to oversee its own permitting and regulation of waste that coal-fired power plants generate.
text:
Cleco's Brame Energy Center in Rapides Parish is one of three coal-burning power plants in Louisiana. (Photo courtesy of Cleco)The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has given Louisiana the final go-ahead to oversee its own permitting and regulation of waste that coal-fired power plants generate. 
The program’s approval, made official Monday, will allow the state Department of Environmental Quality to assume responsibility for the proper disposal of coal ash in landfills and the use of the material for some forms of construction, such as adding it to asphalt for roadwork. 
The clearance comes a year and a half after the federal agency announced it would roll back regulations on the disposal of coal waste byproducts and allow states to take over the EPA’s responsibility of ensuring waste is disposed of in a way that follows federal rules. 
Louisiana is the seventh of 10 states to receive approval for its own coal combustion residuals permitting program, alongside North Dakota, Wyoming, Virginia, Oklahoma, Georgia and Texas. Applications from Alabama, Wisconsin and Indiana remain under review. 
EPA Administrator Lee Zeldein lauded the decision as “a win for cooperative federalism and for Louisiana” in a news release announcing the agency’s decision, saying that handing over authority to the state ensures that oversight would be in the hands of those “who understand their communities and their energy industry best.”
Louisiana has three working power plants at least partially powered by coal in the state: Entergy’s R.S. Nelson plant in Westlake, Louisiana Generating LLC’s Big Cajun 2 plant in New Roads, and Cleco’s Brame Energy Center in Rapides Parish. 
Another plant in Louisiana that used coal to generate electricity, Cleco and Swepco’s Dolet Hills power plant in Mansfield, was retired in 2021 after 30 years in operation and is in the process of being fully decommissioned.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
When coal is burned to generate electric power, it produces harmful byproducts with contaminants such as mercury, cadmium and arsenic, which the EPA monitors. If not properly disposed of, they can leech into the ground and surface water and pose health risks to humans and wildlife. 
Changes to the EPA’s coal combustion residuals rules and regulations began in March 2025, when the Trump administration announced deregulatory measures on coal-fired power plant pollution. The move mirrored policy changes at multiple federal agencies toward the large-scale deregulation of environmental standards. 
Environmental and consumer rights groups in Louisiana decried the EPA decision to approve state oversight of permitting on coal ash disposal, saying the Department of Environmental Quality has a poor track record when it comes to ensuring proper enforcement of pollution regulations. 
“Our state regulators are dangerously inadequate in their oversight and enforcement of polluting industries, which has already cost Louisiana our safe air and water, ” Logan Burke, executive director of the consumer rights group Alliance for Affordable Energy, said in a news release after the EPA’s final decision was announced. 
“We simply don’t think LDEQ can handle even more responsibilities they won’t take seriously,” she added. 
The Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality did not respond to emails, text messages and phone calls requesting comment on the groups’ claims and the EPA’s decision to allow the permitting program. 
The Alliance for Affordable Energy, Sierra Club and Earthjustice submitted comments to EPA during its public feedback period, arguing that LDEQ’s permitting plan “lacked important aspects” and had “weaker standards” than federal rules. 
The organizations also alleged the state has continuously failed to ensure that federal standards for coal combustion residual disposal were met at all Louisiana power plants, with groundwater contamination measured at all four sites in operation, according to analysis from Earthjustice and the nonprofit Environmental Integrity Project using industry data provide to the federal government. 
The EPA also held a hybrid in-person and remote hearing in July for public comment on the rule change. The only person who spoke at the meeting was Mychal Ozaeta, an attorney with Earthjustice. 
Citing industry data, Ozaeta detailed the amount of coal ash stored at three landfills and six coal ash surface impoundments, or ponds, in Louisiana. The disposal sites are located at Big Cajun II, Brame Energy Center, Dolet Hills and R.S. Nelson. Together, they contain more than 25 million cubic yards of coal ash, he said.
“That’s equivalent to a football field piled over 2 miles high with coal ash,” Ozaeta said. 
In addition to the landfills and ponds at power plants, the EPA began regulating 10 other coal ash disposal sites in 2024 under revised rules. The amount of ash at these sites hasn’t been reported by industry, according to Ozaeta’s testimony and Earthjustice’s submitted comments.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Rogers continues push for environmental literacy framework, reconnecting students with the outdoors
description: As the Michigan Legislature heads into its lame duck session following the Nov. 3 election, a Kalamazoo Democrat is renewing her push to improve education on environmental issues.  Last week, state Rep. Julie Rogers introduced House Bill 6465, which would establish a 13-member task force to adopt an environmental literacy pathway for students from prekinderg[...]
text:
State Rep. Julie M. Rogers (D-Kalamazoo) in 2025. (Michigan House Democrats photo)As the Michigan Legislature heads into its lame duck session following the Nov. 3 election, a Kalamazoo Democrat is renewing her push to improve education on environmental issues. 
Last week, state Rep. Julie Rogers introduced House Bill 6465, which would establish a 13-member task force to adopt an environmental literacy pathway for students from prekindergarten through 12th grade.
This framework is intended to prepare students to understand and address environmental issues in their community, contribute to healthy lifestyles by making outdoor experiences a regular part of school curriculum, and teach students about jobs in fields like alternative energy, renewable fuels and materials science that can help protect the environment. 
The framework also includes education about equity, disproportionate impacts, cumulative impacts and the unique needs of individual communities facing environmental challenges. 
Speaking with Michigan Advance, Rogers, who was elected to the state Senate on Nov. 3, said she’d been working on the bill for quite a while, introducing a previous version in 2023.
“My sister is a educator, and she had had several other educators talk to her about climate change and also the fact that we have so many youth facing mental health issues with screen time and not really getting outdoors,” Rogers said.
She stressed that her proposal was not a mandate for teachers, but a framework for teaching environmental literacy, allowing districts to decide whether they’d like to opt in.
Climate literacy in crisis: Why understanding climate science matters now more than ever

“My kind of vision is to have several touch points throughout K through 12,” Rogers said. “In Julie’s perfect world, it would be a touch point in elementary school, a touch point in middle school and another time in high school. And this would not be a separate class. It would be designed to embed with current existing curricula to weave in some of this information.”
In addition to the environmental literacy pathway, the bill instructs the task force to develop a guidance document to identify professional development opportunities for teachers, explain how to implement their environmental literacy pathway, and showcase ways to encourage educational agencies and schools to participate in programs that support environmental education. 
Between the initial version introduced in 2023 and the recently-reintroduced policy, Rogers has added some stipulations on the makeup of the task force. In the most recent version, one member of the task force must be from an urban school district, while another must be from a rural school district.
“One of the things that’s no secret is in some of the more urban, heavy industry areas of Michigan, there’s been quite a bit of air quality issues and environmental justice impacts….And then Michigan has such a rich agricultural history with many farms, and they sometimes have their own set of environmental challenges,” Rogers said when asked how these differing perspectives could enrich the task force’s conversation around local environmental impacts.
The task force would also include a seat for a student appointed by the state superintendent, who would act as an advisor rather than a voting member.
Rogers pointed to Michigan Youth Leaders For Environmental Stewardship, as among the bill’s supporters, later reflecting on testimony during a 2023 committee hearing for the bill where a student activist discussed the anxiety that can arise when students are not educated about climate change and its solutions.
Alongside helping students build a personal relationship with their environment, Rogers said she also hoped to expose students to different career pathways, pointing to the state’s 2023 clean energy policy, which aims to shift Michigan’s grid to a 100% clean energy standard by 2040.
