“I think over the next eight to 10 years, we’re going to see Michigan’s energy sector transformed, and we are going to need students trained to go into those fields, whether it be wind or solar,” Rogers said. “I just think as we’re diversifying our energy portfolio in Michigan, there’s going to be a whole new range of jobs to fill, and so it’s never too early, in my opinion, to start exposing students to those fields and career paths.”
While speaking with youth activists about their concerns, climate-related tragedies like the record flooding the state experienced earlier this year was a key concern, Rogers said. 
“With that brings major devastation. It’s also very expensive, and then the state has to step in, or sometimes even the federal government,” Rogers said, noting that the activists she spoke with were passionate about taking a forward-thinking approach rather than simply reacting to these disasters.
Serving on her county’s brownfield redevelopment commission for more than 10 years, Rogers said she’s been in the position of reacting to environmental messes. Now, she says it’s exciting to be in a leadership position where she can work to try and mitigate environmental harm through education.
While the Michigan House is controlled by a 58-52 Republican majority, Democrats were able to win control of the chamber this past election. With Democrats retaining control of the Senate and current Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson winning the governor’s seat, a Democratic trifecta will control the executive seat and both chambers of the state legislature.
With little over a month and limited session days remaining on the House’s schedule, the clock is ticking for lawmakers to take action on Rogers’ bill. If the year comes to an end without any movement, Rogers said she plans to reintroduce the policy in the state Senate, where she’ll take office in the coming year.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: New Hampshire housing market is stagnating. Some see a silver lining
description: When New Hampshire’s housing market was at its hottest in recent years, the conversation Josh Greenwald might have had with a client selling their home was simple: List the home, and sit back and wait for the offers.  “All you had to do was list your house for sale, and somebody’s going to want it, […]
text:
Even as the housing market appears to be cooling for sellers, it is not exactly a picnic for buyers. (Photo by Cappi Thompson/Getty Images)When New Hampshire’s housing market was at its hottest in recent years, the conversation Josh Greenwald might have had with a client selling their home was simple: List the home, and sit back and wait for the offers. 
“All you had to do was list your house for sale, and somebody’s going to want it, you know, and they’ll pay through the nose to get it,” said the Keene Realtor and president of the New Hampshire Association of Realtors.
That “seller’s market” persisted years after the out-of-state buying frenzy in 2020 and 2021 drove a spike in New Hampshire home prices and caused a severe shortage in inventory. Even as prices went higher and listings became more unaffordable for residents, the demand refused to die.
This fall, that might be finally starting to change. Years of high mortgage rates and list prices — in addition to inflation and cost-of-living hardships — have squeezed buyers in New Hampshire, leading to a slowdown in sales. 
Homebuying in New England typically falls off in the fall and winter months, picking up with the warmer weather in spring and summer. But this year, the drop-off appears to be exceeding the usual slowdown and is noticeable on the ground, Greenwald says. And the conversations he is having with sellers are more sobering. 
“We have to now tell our clients it might take a week or two before we get a showing,” he said. “And they’re like, ‘Well, how come we’ve only had three or four showings?’ I’m like, ‘There’s not as many buyers right now.’”
That conversation often leads in only one direction: Lowering the price. It could be the difference between the house selling or sitting on the market for a year. 
As the real estate market heads into winter, new numbers from the New Hampshire Association of Realtors show home prices remain stubbornly high, and affordability is worsening. 
Yet the tough news could come with a silver lining, Greenwald says: The state’s housing price frenzy might finally be running out of gas. With enough price corrections, the market could eventually find its elusive balance.
“I consider 2027 to be more of a return to normalcy in the market where buyers have their power back, and I think that that’s the way it ought to be,” he said.
Affordability issues persist
Even as the market appears to be cooling for sellers, it is not exactly a picnic for buyers. 
The median price for a single-family home in the state was $543,223 in October, 1.5% higher than the year before, according to the monthly reporting from the state association. Townhouse-condo properties rose by 6% from 12 months before; the median price for one of those properties is now $430,000.
The climbing prices continue to put homeownership out of reach for many families. New Hampshire’s housing affordability index, which weighs the prices of homes against median household income, has dropped 10.2% from a year ago, according to the association.
For single-family homes, the index is now 53. That means the state’s median household income, $106,759, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, is just 53% of the earnings needed to afford the median home price in New Hampshire. The metric assumes families would spend no more than 30% of their income on housing and pay a 20% down payment.
“New Hampshire’s housing market has entered a period of prolonged stagnation,” wrote Rob Dapice, executive director and CEO of New Hampshire Housing, a quasi-state agency, in the agency’s annual report this month. “Rents and home prices may no longer be rising at the extraordinary pace of recent years, but they remain far beyond reach for many residents.”
New Hampshire homes weren’t always so unaffordable. Between 2007 and 2022, the affordability index was at more than 100, meaning for 15 years the median income could afford the median home price. In 2012 and 2013, the index was more than 200. 
But skyrocketing prices during the COVID-19 pandemic and an inability for inventory to meet the demand in the years since have widened the gap between what New Hampshire families earn and how homes are priced. 
The findings come as interest rates and low inventory continue to plague the state. 
Nationally, the average mortgage rate on Tuesday was 7.3%, according to the Mortgage Research Center. For a family buying a home at the state median price of $543,000 and putting down 20%, or $108,600, that would require a monthly payment of about $3,000.
The continuing high prices tell only part of the story. Fewer people in New Hampshire are putting their homes on the market than last year, the data indicates. 
And those who put their homes on the market continue to struggle to make a sale, the numbers suggest.
The total number of homes for sale last month is up 18.6% from a year earlier. But that increase measures the cumulative total of all homes that were at some point listed. 
The number of pending sales in New Hampshire fell 4.2% last October compared to a year before, while the number of new listings dropped 8.6%.
While more inventory is usually good for prices and buyers, in this case the numbers suggest a glut of homes that are not affordable and not selling — potentially a casualty of the persistently high interest rates. 
“It’s not necessarily because many more people are listing their homes,” said Greenwald. “It’s the ones that are on the shelves that are not getting bought.”
Tools to help
As market conditions continue to harm first-time homebuyers, New Hampshire Housing is increasing its attempts to help. 
The agency, which helps disburse New Hampshire’s Department of Housing and Urban Development funds, distributed $7.5 million in down-payment assistance to home buyers in the 2027 state fiscal year, a 38.9% increase from the fiscal year before, according to its annual report. It has expanded the number of first-time homebuyers receiving mortgage assistance from 1,000 to 1,345 over the past year. 
“This work is rarely glamorous, and it will not command the same attention as tomorrow’s headlines about the next AI breakthrough,” Dapice wrote in the annual report. “But we are proud of every success story we help make possible, and we remain committed to carrying this mission forward.”
Lawmakers have enacted a number of new laws meant to spur housing growth and improve affordability, from expanded rights to build accessory dwelling units to requirements that municipalities allow mixed-use housing in most commercial zones. Many are just starting to take effect, and new housing made possible by the laws could be years away.
New Hampshire Housing is providing funding to help support multifamily developments in the state; the agency used low-income housing tax credits to help build 850 new apartment units in the last year, the report states.
Greenwald, like many real estate agents, sees inventory as the primary obstacle. He compared the housing experience to musical chairs: Buyers can try to secure a dwindling number of seats, but the better solution is to add more chairs.
“I think that is going to take many years to bear fruit,” Greenwald said of the legislative approach. 
For now, he added, the short-term relief might come from supply and demand.
“As we see inventory levels increase, we have more buyer options, and that’s going to (tamp) down price increases,” he said. “Which is going to have a snowball effect.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Majority of NJ hospitals earn an A in hospital safety
description: More than half of New Jersey's hospitals got an A grade on a new safety report, leaving the state ranked 3rd nationwide for high-quality facilities.
text:
Hospitals in New Jersey scored well on the latest Leapfrog safety report, with 36 of the 67 facilities included in the study receiving an A grade. New Jersey ranked 3rd nationwide for the number of A-rated hospitals. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey now ranks third in the nation in hospital safety, according to the latest review by a nationally recognized team that compares acute care facilities nationwide based on the number of medical errors, accidents, injuries and infections. 
The fall 2026 letter grades released Wednesday by the Leapfrog Group show that 36 of the 67 New Jersey hospitals that were graded received an A, seven more than in the spring, when the Garden State ranked sixth nationwide for the percentage of highest-grade hospitals. Only Connecticut and Utah had more A-ranked hospitals this time. 
New Jersey Hospital Association President and CEO Cathy Bennett welcomed the news. 
 “New Jersey’s 3rd-place national ranking for patient safety underscores our hospitals’ longstanding commitment to accountability, value and continuous quality improvement. We’re proud of how hospital teams across New Jersey work together in the spirit of collaboration so patients in every community benefit from what we learn,” Bennett said in an email to the New Jersey Monitor. 
Leapfrog uses data from several sources, including a hospital survey it conducts and the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, some of it dating back several years. New Jersey has the highest percentage of hospitals participating nationwide. Only Bergen New Bridge Medical Center in Paramus was not graded because of insufficient data from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, according to the Quality Institute.
“Every one of our hospitals voluntarily reports its safety and quality data to Leapfrog,” said Linda Schwimmer, president and CEO of the New Jersey Health Care Quality Institute and a Leapfrog board member. “Patients and employers need clear information about safety and quality to make good decisions about their.”
The Quality Institute serves as a regional leader for Leapfrog to help people understand the safety data. 
Making hospitals safer for patients takes continuous work, said Adelisa Perez-Hudgins, also with the Quality Institute. “It can take time for those improvements to show up in publicly reported data. What matters most for patients and their families is that the commitment to safer care continues,” she added. 
Some Garden State hospitals still struggle on the rankings. Nine facilities received a C grade in Leapfrog’s latest report, one fewer than the spring survey. Two got D’s — Hoboken University Medical Center and Carewell Health Medical Center, in East Orange — the same grade they got six months ago. 
Overall, 84% of New Jersey’s hospitals received an A or B grade in the fall survey. Seventeen hospitals have received A grades for five straight years. Eleven hospitals improved by at least one letter grade, two declined and 54 held steady.
Nationwide, the number of A grades ranged from more than 64% of the hospitals in Connecticut to zero percent of facilities in five states: Iowa, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont and Wyoming. Pennsylvania ranked 16th with nearly 34% of its hospitals getting an A, while New York was 18th with 29%.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Disability advocates rally at Indiana Statehouse to preserve in-home Medicaid supports
description: Hundreds of Hoosiers with disabilities and their caregivers rallied at the Indiana Statehouse Tuesday to protest changes to Medicaid eligibility assessments, caregiver supports and waivers designed to keep disabled people from being institutionalized. Their message for lawmakers: preserve assistance for Hoosiers with disabilities to remain in their homes and[...]
text:
A rally in support of disability rights coincides with Organization Day, the annual swearing-in ceremony for incoming lawmakers at the Indiana Statehouse Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Hundreds of Hoosiers with disabilities and their caregivers rallied at the Indiana Statehouse Tuesday to protest changes to Medicaid eligibility assessments, caregiver supports and waivers designed to keep disabled people from being institutionalized.
Their message for lawmakers: preserve assistance for Hoosiers with disabilities to remain in their homes and prioritize funding to move people off waitlists for these services.
Disability advocates are worried about a series of changes to Medicaid, including waitlists, paid family caregiving and an algorithm the Indiana Family and Social Services Administration introduced this year to assist with level-of-care assessments for Medicaid home and community-based services.
The waivers are a popular alternative to institutionalization for Hoosiers who need support with daily tasks, but advocates report a surge in denials and coverage reductions since Indiana started using the interRAI algorithm for these assessments.
Disability advocate Luke Labas shares his story during a disability rights rally at the Indiana Statehouse Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
“We want to be contributing taxpayers,” said Luke Labas, a disability advocate who spoke at the Statehouse Tuesday. “We want to invest in our community.”
The home and community-based services waiver enabled Labas to find a job at The League in Fort Wayne, as he could now hire an aide to assist with daily tasks like getting out of bed.
Now, Labas said his waiver only covers 125 hours a month for personal care — less than half the 400 hours a month of help he once relied on.
“Too often policymakers look at Medicaid and waivers as a single line item,” he said, “but without home and community services, I end up in the hospital. Then look at the hospitalization bills that come from that. Then with me not being able to work … I then need housing assistance, utility assistance and what have you. Meanwhile, the goal should be economic self-sufficiency.”
Dr. Mary Ciccarelli, a primary care physician in Indianapolis, said the waivers are designed to be cheaper than institutionalization.
“We’ve never actually allowed waivers here in Indiana to reach all those who need them,” she told the crowd, lamenting what she described as a lack of outreach and lengthy waitlists that at times result in preventable hospitalizations due to lack of community supports.
“Home and community-based services should be a win-win for our state,” Ciccarelli said.
The Arc of Indiana estimates 932 families, people with disabilities and advocates registered to attend Tuesday’s rally.
Disability advocates watch a rally at the Indiana Statehouse Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
In attendance were former Lt. Gov. Suzanne Crouch and current Reps. Robin Shackleford, D-Indianapolis, and Lori Goss-Reaves, R-Marion, who spoke in support of home and community-based services.
“Right now, decisions are being made inside these chambers about the state’s priorities and our state’s budget,” Shackleford said. “And let me be crystal clear: we cannot and we will not balance Indiana’s budget on the backs of people with disabilities in their communities.”
Also spotted wandering around the atrium: FSSA Secretary Mitch Roob.
Chants of “home, community, choice” echoed through the Statehouse atrium as lawmakers returned for their annual Organization Day.
Protesters carried signs saying: “Don’t balance the budget on the backs of the disabled,” “the worst disability is a lack of empathy” and “disabled not disposable.”
In response, FSSA spokesperson Marcus Barlow said the agency “values the important efforts of its partners and those with lived experience supporting and advocating for Hoosiers with disabilities.”
He added, “We will continue to collaborate with our stakeholders such as The Arc of Indiana, to create a model of care that empowers individuals to live independently, work, and thrive in their communities.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: 40 million people will be watching. No pressure, UConn.
description: The UConn Marching Band will perform at the 100th annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade for the first time in the university’s history.
text:
At first it was the low hum of sousaphone, the drums providing a crisp, steady heartbeat. Then, a trumpet kicked in, inviting the woodwinds along as it trilled its high hello. 
At one end of a huge asphalt lot, student Arlo Tucker stood straight-backed atop a ladder, hands slicing through the cool, wet air. In full layered harmony, Bill Withers’ “Lovely Day” exploded around them.
Tucker, a junior studying music education at the University of Connecticut, is a member of the UConn Marching Band, a 130-year-old tradition that this month will perform at the 100th annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade for the first time in the university’s history. Over a year after submitting its first application, the group is preparing for the event with an expected audience of 40 million people between the streets of Manhattan and their television sets at home. 
The UCMB, often billed as the “Pride of Connecticut,” will perform as part of a musical lineup that also includes the University of Alabama’s Million Dollar Band, the University of Illinois’ Marching Illini, and five high school marching units from as close as Massachusetts and as far away as Hawaii. 
“You know, it’s a huge stage, and we understand the gravity of this moment,” said Jessica Dickerson, a twice-over UConn alum who is the first woman to direct the university’s athletic bands. “I think we are all feeling tremendously excited, with a nice healthy dose of [being] anxious underneath that, because this is such a big moment in the history of the program.” 

UConn Marching Band Color Guard members work through a flag routine during practice at their practice field in Storrs. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror


While UConn has a history of national and international marching band performances — in 1992, two decades after taking its sound to Europe and the U.K., it was tapped to play at President Bill Clinton’s inaugural parade in Washington, D.C. — the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade feels exceptional, Dickerson said. As a kid, and then a member of the UConn marching band herself, she grew up watching the parade and knows that many of her students did too. 
To get there, students have been practicing for seven to 10 hours a week, on top of performing at sporting events like football, basketball, and hockey games (Assistant Director of Athletic Bands Justin Daly recently asked them to “rehearsalmaxx,” which they seem to have taken to heart). Band members have also raised $126,000, which will help cover the cost of travel and lodging for more than 350 students.
“We are really leaning into the difficulty of preparing for this,” Dickerson said. “In life, great opportunities are hard. Great opportunities require hard work, require commitment. We’ve long framed ‘talent, unity, pride’ as kind of a mantra of ours … ‘Unity,’ for us this year, is like everybody in all the time.”
At a rehearsal last week, students’ enthusiasm was palpable as they arrived on the gently sloping sides of the university’s practice field, setting out water bottles and instrument cases as the clock ticked past 4 p.m. and the sun began its slow descent. As they spread out, sections materialized. Drums rumbled and rolled to life at a corner of the field, and members of the school’s color guard began to stretch, as if they had just been waiting for a beat. Marimbas and vibraphones appeared with a bouncing, bright sound by the university’s soaring field tower. Across the lot, the electronic automated beep of a metronome came from somewhere among a row of trumpets, the horns glinting in the late afternoon light.

Members of the UConn Marching Band play in formation during practice at their practice field in Storrs on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Tucker, a French horn and mellophone player who was named one of the band’s drum majors this year, buzzed between classmates, sometimes running to one side of the lot to field a question or get ready to conduct the group. Every so often, Dickerson called out their names, and students followed, with ebullient cheers of “Arloooo!” that filled the air.  
Born and raised in Hartford, Tucker fell in love with music through the violin, and then the piano, and then the French horn by the time they were in fourth grade. After singing in the high school choir and playing in the orchestra, they realized that “I’m a band kid through and through.” So when they joined the UCMB their freshman year, something clicked right into place. 
The marching band is a place where things just make sense, Tucker said as they handed off their white gloves to senior Kevin Bueno so he could conduct for a moment. But the band’s appearance in the parade is a fact that they still can’t wrap their head around. Every other Thanksgiving has found them curled up by the television with their younger sister, watching the parade unfold through a screen. 
“That it’s gonna be us this year. It’s kind of surreal,” Tucker said. 
That feeling is true among many band members. Twirler Lauren Aliberti, a sophomore who is studying to become a speech pathologist, said she can’t fully believe that the band is headed to a parade she’s watched every year. She expects the performance to fully register only after the parade is over. 

Lauren Aliberti, features twirler with the UConn Marching Band, practices at their practice field in Storrs on Nov. 5. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

At Thursday’s rehearsal, she brought her A game. As Tucker and fellow drum major Morgan Mettica climbed atop two ladders at opposite sides of the lot, more than 320 students moved into formation. Above, long, gray clouds had started moving against a rose-colored sky. Tucker held up a hand for a moment, casting their gaze toward the center of the lot as brass swelled and then quieted just as quickly. 
At the front of the lineup, students had begun moving forward, flutes and clarinets leading the way. Dancers, not missing a beat, rolled their arms, do-si-doed, and grooved in sync to the trumpets, feet criss-crossing the space. Behind them, musicians stepped from side to side, their bodies rocking as they worked the keys, slides, mallets and embouchures on their respective instruments.  
From his place on the field tower, a mic in his hand, Daly nodded along. As horns blared, dancers Jessica Attah, Cassidy Battaglino and Kayla Gilibertie linked arms, spun around giggling and then stood back-to-back in a pose inspired by the original Charlie’s Angels.
“We’re held to a high standard, and we’re able to create something special,” said senior Ben Robinson, a mechanical engineering major who leads the tenor drums. Since his freshman year, the marching band has made him more accountable to his peers and teachers alike. He has to show up for the other drummers — and they have to show up for him. 
“I think for right now I’m just excited,” he said. “It really feels like we can be pushed to be productive.”          

By the first bars of Diana Ross’ “I’m Comin’ Out,” arranged by Associate Director of Bands Ricardo Brown, Aliberti was leaping in time with the drums, her whole face a smile. In “I Wanna Dance with Somebody,” students moved breezily past each other, instruments raised and ready beneath a deep blue night sky and stadium-bright lighting. When Dickerson raised her arm and gently asked “C to E, please,” the trumpets came back with a galloping shriek. 
For Dickerson, who has been on staff for a decade but only in the role for a year, it’s about more than just parade day. As she walked to her car for a quick break before rehearsing with the pep band, she remembered her own experience playing mellophone in the Pride of Connecticut before graduating from UConn with a degree in music (her specialty is the French horn, although she can play a little bit of everything) in 2011. 
“Above all, I learned to work with people,” she said. She couldn’t stay away for long: By 2014, she was back on campus for her graduate studies in instrumental conducting. When she finished her degree, she stayed on as the associate director of athletic bands, a role that she held until a leadership transition less than a year ago. 
“You’re forced to enter a headspace of ‘I am one of many,’” she said. “It fortifies you. These students come here, and we really challenge them. We push them, and there’s a period of personal growth … that’s what we learn here, empathy.”  

UConn Marching Band works through a song during practice at their practice field in Storrs on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Just minutes earlier, Kevin Bueno had remembered how playing in the marching band has helped him feel more at home in his own skin, and the words resonated as the lot emptied out and wisps of music hovered in the air. A junior studying music education, he grew up in Cheshire, playing in the school band from the time that he was able to. 
But something changed when he joined the marching band and began to gel with other students. 
“It’s about being a leader,” said Bueno, who was among the UConn students who traveled to New York last year, where the cast of the Today Show announced that they would be part of the 2026 parade. “I think a lot of that stems from the experiences we have together. It does test us at times, but we really collaborate with each other.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Commentary: NH shouldn’t confuse regulating dangerous kratom-labeled products with banning an entire plant
description: Recently, there have been talks about New Hampshire once again debating how to address kratom, but this time the proposals seem considerably more sweeping. One proposal involves legislation that would classify kratom, the plant, as a Schedule I controlled substance. This would place it in the same legal category as heroin and other illicit drugs. As […]
text:
"Some of these products marketed as 'kratom' bear little resemblance to traditional botanical preparations, containing compounds not naturally present in the plant and, in some cases, acting exclusively on opioid receptors in the brain." (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)Recently, there have been talks about New Hampshire once again debating how to address kratom, but this time the proposals seem considerably more sweeping. One proposal involves legislation that would classify kratom, the plant, as a Schedule I controlled substance. This would place it in the same legal category as heroin and other illicit drugs.
As an addiction psychiatrist with national expertise in kratom and its impact on clinical populations, I certainly see the concerns driving this proposal. A significant proportion of today’s marketplace consists primarily of highly concentrated, semi- and fully synthetic products labeled as “kratom,” which pharmacologically and safety-wise resemble nothing of the kratom plant itself. The kratom plant has been used for centuries in Southeast Asia without much concern, but the products we have here created legitimate public health concerns. 
Recognizing a problem and choosing the appropriate solution are two separate entities. As a state, we should be careful not to erroneously treat every product labeled “kratom” as pharmacologically equivalent, and most importantly not to assume that blanket prohibition is the most effective way to protect the public.
Here are several key considerations that should inform the development of any legislative approach.
The kratom market has evolved in recent years
Traditional kratom refers to the dried leaves of Mitragyna speciosa, a tropical tree native to Southeast Asia. Historically, leaves have been used for various remedies, to assist with pain management, enhance endurance, and as part of traditions and ritual ceremonies. Typical consumption involves either chewing the leaves or brewing them as a tea, or, to a lesser degree, smoking them. 
In the United States, early use largely involved powdered leaf consumed in capsules or mixed into beverages by those looking to self-manage various ailments, to get off illicit substances, or promote general well-being, among other reasons.
Over the years, manufacturers developed concentrated extracts, enhanced and even blended formulations that deliver increasingly potent doses, and have raised concerns about adverse effects.
Today, what we have available are semi- and fully synthetic compounds, highly concentrated 7-OH products and chemically modified derivatives. Some of these products marketed as “kratom” bear little resemblance to traditional botanical preparations, containing compounds not naturally present in the plant and, in some cases, acting exclusively on opioid receptors in the brain. These products should not automatically be treated as interchangeable by virtue of their shared marketing label.
Schedule I classification warrants careful examination
Schedule I classification is the most restrictive drug-control designation, and it carries significant consequences for possession, distribution, access and, most importantly, research. It also serves as an evidence-based determination that a substance has a “high potential for abuse and no currently accepted medical use.”
Comparing everything sold as “kratom” to opioids and calling it “gas station heroin” makes for a very catchy news headline and political sound bite, but it does not substitute for rigorous scientific and regulatory assessments.
A blanket classification may create unintended consequences for numerous individual consumers. Over the past decade of studying this botanical, I have encountered patients using botanical kratom preparations to self-manage pain, often being able to avoid opioid therapy, as well as to address other conditions for which FDA-approved treatments were ineffective or not tolerated. Making botanical kratom a Schedule I may prompt some of these individuals to turn to less regulated alternatives, seek products through illicit channels or substitute for other substances. For some consumers anecdotally using kratom for relapse prevention, this could mean losing a tool that they have found helpful in preventing a return to conventional opioids.
I am not making the argument that kratom should be used for the treatment of opioid use disorder, as a substitute for FDA-approved therapies or as a recommended therapeutic intervention for any condition. Rather, I suggest that policymakers should consider the real-world consequences of prohibition, which historically have included unintended substitution and reduced product oversight.
Other states are approaching kratom differently
It is important to recognize that we do not have to choose between unregulated retail sales and an overall blanket ban. Other states have implemented several regulatory models worth examining.
Last month, I was invited to be part of a panel in Rhode Island and had a chance to learn about how officials there are approaching kratom. After previously banning kratom, the state reversed course and in April of this year implemented the Rhode Island Kratom Act. The law established a tightly regulated marketplace to replace the outright ban.
Under this framework, the oversight is done by the Department of Health through its Center for Food Protection, which licenses and enforces requirements for manufacturers, distributors, importers and retailers. Sales to individuals younger than 21 are prohibited. Products sold must meet labeling and packaging requirements, as well as the state-established restrictions on how concentrated these can be, while also banning semi- and fully synthetic products. In addition, Rhode Island also imposes a 15% tax on the wholesale cost.
Since this was just implemented earlier this year, the overall efficacy and safety of this approach is too early to claim. What is important to emphasize here is the state has created a framework through which products, manufacturers and retailers can be identified, monitored and held accountable.
Other states have pursued variations of this approach, with most having enacted age restrictions, registration requirements and prohibitions on certain synthetic compounds. There are, of course, states such as Massachusetts that have taken a more restrictive approach, temporarily placing all forms of kratom, including botanical, under Schedule I.
We have an opportunity here to evaluate which policies actually serve the public and align with public health goals, rather than assume that the most restrictive policy is the most effective.
So, what does the research actually tell us?
A 2026 Centers for Disease Control and Prevention analysis revealed that between 2015 and 2025 there has been a 1,200% increase in kratom-related exposure reports. Unfortunately, the data do not establish that botanical kratom was responsible for these outcomes as the investigators could not reliably distinguish it from concentrated or chemically modified “kratom” products.
A separate 2026 observational study examined poison center-reported kratom exposures from 2010 through 2023 and compared states with different regulatory approaches. States with full kratom bans had lower reported exposure rates, severe outcomes, hospitalizations and healthcare utilization compared to states where kratom remained legal. This study found no statistically significant differences among states with consumer protection laws, local restrictions and states with unrestricted access.
This study does not establish that prohibition is superior, or that consumer protection laws reduce kratom-related harm. This data stems from poison center reports, which are highly variable in terms of reporting patterns, differences in enforcement and other state-level characteristics. What this study calls out for, however, is the need for better outcome data, and cautions against presenting regulation as an already proven solution. Rhode Island provides an opportunity to collect those data prospectively, and New Hampshire should learn from those outcomes as they become available.
New Hampshire needs a thoughtful approach
Earlier this year, Senate Bill 557 and other proposals attempted to address semi- and fully synthetic “kratom” products, but lawmakers failed to reach agreement. As we move forward, we need to make the distinction between botanical kratom and the increasingly potent derivatives.
As an addiction psychiatrist I have no interest in minimizing the risks of kratom or defending an inadequately regulated industry. My concern is that policy should be driven by pharmacology, clinical experience and measurable public health outcomes rather than blanket assumptions about an entire category of products. Rather than classifying all kratom as Schedule I, I encourage legislators to consider a comprehensive regulatory framework that includes:

Age restrictions: Individuals should be 21-plus years of age to purchase. 
Product testing: Require independent, third-party, laboratory testing for concentration limits, contaminants, adulterants and synthetic compounds. 
Transparent labelling: Require the disclosure of composition per serving and per container. 
Potency limits: Establish evidence-based limits on concentrated products.
Manufacturing standards: Require licensing, traceability and accountability throughout the entire supply chain. 
Targeted prohibitions: Restrict semi- and fully synthetic “kratom” products and products blended or adulterated with other constituents. 
Ongoing surveillance: Periodically track poison-control-related exposures, emergency department visits and other public health outcomes to determine whether the framework is working. 

New Hampshire has an opportunity to develop a policy that acknowledges risks, potential benefits and protects consumers, while holding manufacturers accountable without automatically criminalizing every product labeled as “kratom.” 
There are plenty of other options other than an unregulated marketplace or a blanket prohibition, and these involve thoughtful, evidence-informed regulation that can be longitudinally evaluated and refined as better data become available.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Baltimore County schools, police sued for AI software ‘bag of chips’ mistake
description: After an AI program mistakenly identified a Baltimore County high school student's bag of chips as a gun, county police and school officials turned that mistake into a "terrifying" and "life-threatening" encounter for the four teens involved, a new lawsuit says.
text:
The Baltimore County Circuit Courts Building in Towson. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)After an artificial intelligence program mistakenly identified a Baltimore County high school student’s bag of chips as a gun, county police and school officials turned that mistake into a “terrifying” and “life-threatening” encounter for the four teens involved, a new lawsuit says.
The suit was filed in Baltimore County Circuit Court Tuesday, a little more than a year after the confrontation at Kenwood High School. The 31-page complaint claims police officers inflicted pain and suffering on Oct. 20, 2025, on Taki Allen, then 16, and his three friends – Yui-Osa Ogbeide, Devon Thompson Jr.  and Keith Winfield III – all now 18.
The incident began about 6:30 p.m., as the four were talking and waiting outside the school for a ride after football practice. Allen had a bag of Doritos that his coach had given him after practice, a bag that the school’s Omnilert Gun Detection identified as a gun, alerting school officials.
Three officials who received the alert recognized the mistake and canceled the alert within minutes. But the school’s principal, Catherine Smith, “never acknowledged the Alert’s cancelation or took any steps to verify whether the Alert remained active,” the suit says.
Instead, more than 10 minutes after the alert was canceled, she sent a screenshot of video footage of Allen “holding the chip bag” and sent a text message to the school resource officer, who forwarded the screenshot to the police department, prompting “an armed police response.”
The alert went out about 7:05 p.m. By 7:21 p.m., six police cruisers surrounded the teens and officers got out, “many with guns drawn,” according to the complaint. They forced the teens to the ground, cuffed and searched them, according to the suit, which shows a picture of the boys with their arms raised outside the school.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
After they determined there was no gun, one officer told the students that “AI is not the best,” and another muttered “stupid AI cameras” and “[expletive] Omnilerts,” according to the complaint. “Yet officers relied on the Alert to initiate this painful encounter with the students,” it states.
One of the officers, Corp. Michael Foehrkolb, allegedly told the teens, “Hey, thanks for not running away, that would have been a real problem,” the suit says. It shows a text message from the principal to school staff and administrators that “made light of the incident.”
The text states: “No worries. SRO (school resource officer) had patrol car roll through. It was a bag of chips.” The message included four emojis crying from laughter.
Freya Jamison, an associate counsel with the Lawyers’ Committee’s Criminal Justice Program, said in an interview Tuesday there’s been no public apology from the school’s principal to the teenagers or their families. Jamison said Smith remains at the school.
“We can’t ignore the potential consequences of an armed police encounter, especially with young Black men like Takei, Osa, Devon, and Keith,” Jamison said. “They survived the encounter, but their safety never should have depended on luck.”
“As AI is on the rise around the country, it’s critical that technology companies and public officials are held accountable when they use that technology to violate constitutional rights,” she said. “We simply can’t outsource human judgment to machines, and this case shows exactly why.”
Omnilert spokesperson Blake Mitchell said in an email Tuesday that the company, named as a defendant, “cannot comment on lawsuits.” Baltimore County police and county school officials also declined to comment on pending litigation.
‘Failure’
The complaint notes that Omnilert’s AI weapon detection system was patented in 2022, “barely a year before it was deployed” in Baltimore County Public Schools, which was among “the first of its initial deployments.”
Richard Henry, the Maryland Office of Inspector General of Education, said in December on the “C4 and Bryan Nehman” radio show on WBAL that Omnilert works in Baltimore County schools. Henry attributed the Kenwood High situation to “human error” when looking at video and still images on a cell phone.
“In this case, this occurred in the evening hours, so it was low light,” Henry said on the show. “The student had the bag next to their hip, and they had the way that their hand was situated [with] a couple fingers in, a couple fingers out. That movement was detected, and it was just more or less, this is an alert. It could be a possible threat.”
But the complaint notes that Omnilert’s AI software suffered from false negatives before, including in January 2025 when it failed to detect a shooter’s gun at Antioch High School in Nashville. Two students died, including the shooter, and another was shot in the school’s cafeteria in that incident.
All four teen in the Kenwood High incident remain friends, the complaint says. Allen is still at the school, while Ogbeide, Thompson and Winfield, who graduated earlier this year, plan to visit the school on breaks from college and attend basketball games and other activities.
But with the current AI system in place and without adequate training for police and school staff, there remains concern for all four teenagers’ safety.
“The policies, customs, and training failures that produced this incident also remain in place, putting all four Plaintiffs at ongoing risk of being detained and searched without reasonable articulable suspicion,” the complaint states.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: As Kansas hunters fan out to search for deer, how should we value our vanishing wilderness?
description: As the Kansas deer hunting season unfolds, I have been thinking about the increasingly common practice of feeding and baiting deer among Kansas hunters. It diminishes the value of hunting and frays the already tenuous link between Kansans and wild things.  My reflections upon this issue began not with deer but with a much larger […]
text:
A young buck searches for a snack at dusk on June 21, 2025, on a hill south of Lawrence, Kansas. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)As the Kansas deer hunting season unfolds, I have been thinking about the increasingly common practice of feeding and baiting deer among Kansas hunters. It diminishes the value of hunting and frays the already tenuous link between Kansans and wild things. 
My reflections upon this issue began not with deer but with a much larger prairie ungulate: the American Bison. 
Frontier Park on the outskirts of Hays is home to what is charitably called the Hays Bison Herd. The herd is just a few animals, remnants of a species that once roamed the plains in the tens of millions.
I often take my dog for walks around the fenced field that contains these great furry beasts. When we approach the fence, one of the bison will usually stop chewing grass to share a long stare with my dog. I imagine them silently discussing their experiences of domestication. 
The drive home is melancholic as I think about the prairie that used to be, when bison roamed free and native grasses and wildflowers danced uninterrupted across the plains. 
The alterations to the American prairie over the last century are best observed from above. Looking down from the window of a plane, one can see a lattice of roads separating farms and ranches, as if a great net had been drawn up from beneath the soil and laid to rest upon the earth. 
In this new, parceled-out prairie, Kansans have little access to wild places. Those rare spots that have not been turned into crop fields lie hidden behind fences and property lines while publicly accessible areas of “preserved prairie” are often hours away by car. 
In an ideal world, reduced access to wilderness would be treated as a public health crisis. Spending too much time surrounded by the fingerprints of our own species can, strangely, make us feel less human. Getting outside and outside of ourselves makes us humbler beings. 
For many Kansans, deer hunting offers an opportunity to do just that. Hunting requires the hunter to step outside themselves and imagine the mind of the animal they are pursuing.
A Kansas hunter may stalk in the furrows of a plowed field or sit within earshot of cars passing on a country road and yet still experience some of the benefits of immersion in the wild because they are engaging with something that is wild. For hunters and non-hunters alike, a skunk ambling over a country road or a deer leaping over a fence are reminders that wild things still exist and resist our domination of the landscape. 
White-tailed deer are wily and elusive creatures. A hunter may spend many frosty autumn mornings catching only an occasional glimpse of one as it vanishes into a cornfield. 
Yet the difficulty and frustration of deer hunting can compel a hunter to turn to feeding and baiting. 
On the surface, the practice makes sense. White-tailed deer in Kansas are already supplementing their natural diet of forbs and grasses with fallen corn and other agricultural leftovers. Establishing feed sites makes deer movements more predictable. Therefore the creatures becomes easier to spot and kill. Feeding also provides more calories to the deer, which yields more meat for the freezer and a more impressive set of antlers for the mantelpiece. But is this all that a hunter is pursuing?
Feeding and baiting improves the chances of killing a deer and the likelihood that it will be a more impressive specimen. But, over time, it diminishes what is most valuable about hunting: engaging with something wild and outside of our control. 
Consider the following advice from Tractor Supply Co. on deer feeding: 
“The best way to attract wild game to your land is to provide a steady and nutritious supply of wild game or deer feed throughout the seasons. This will ‘train’ whitetail deer and other big game to visit your property often, giving you the chance you’ve been waiting for.”
“Wild game feed” and “wild game training” are obvious contradictions. The more control we exert over a wild animal, the less wild it becomes. 
Steven Rinella, host of the popular hunting show “MeatEater,” once said he values the idea of deer more than the deer itself. The value of a deer may be measured in the size of antlers and the quality of its meat, but the value of the deer lies in its separateness from us. That distance is worth preserving. 
This is to say nothing of the ethics of shooting a deer over a feeding pile. President Theodore Roosevelt once said that this type of hunting can “only be justified on the plea of hunger.” 
What about the deer themselves? While it may seem like they are getting a free lunch, concentrating deer around feeding sites disrupts their natural patterns of movement and brings them into unnatural proximity. This can increase the spread of diseases such as Chronic Wasting Disease. Kansas wildlife biologists recently estimated that “somewhere between 33% and 48% of 2.5-year-old bucks in northwest Kansas counties now have the disease.”
As more deer congregate on farms and in other areas where feed is provided, hunters who would otherwise abstain from baiting can find their access to deer diminished. The result is a kind of arms race, where even hunters who would prefer not to bait may feel compelled to do so to compete with those who do.
Whether it is fields of corn, family dogs, cows or the caged bison on the edge of town, there is no shortage of examples of human control over animals and land in Kansas. 
What we are desperately short of is wild places and wild things. 
The prairie is unlikely to be restored to its wild past, but if Kansas were to join the 27 other states that have outlawed intentional deer feeding, it would help to ensure a healthier population of deer on the plains while preserving the idea that something wild remains out there amongst the crops and crisscrossing roads.
Sam Foglesong is a scholar of African Studies and a writer who lives in Hays. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Union supporters at 2 mental health clinics want resolution as labor law challenges drag on
description: Seven months ago all but a handful of nurses, therapists and other mental health providers at two Rogers Behavioral Health clinics in Wisconsin voted for union representation with the National Union of Healthcare Workers. They have yet to get a contract or even to get to the bargaining table to start negotiations. A federal official […]
text:
A passerby speaks with supporters of a union campaign at Rogers Behavioral Health outside the Pfister Hotel in Milwaukee on Thursday, Nov. 12, where a fundraising gala for Rogers was being held. (Photo courtesy of National Union of Healthcare Workers)Seven months ago all but a handful of nurses, therapists and other mental health providers at two Rogers Behavioral Health clinics in Wisconsin voted for union representation with the National Union of Healthcare Workers.
They have yet to get a contract or even to get to the bargaining table to start negotiations.
A federal official with the National Labor Relations Board has reviewed and rejected the objections Rogers raised to the vote outcome at one of the clinics, in the Milwaukee suburb of West Allis. Now Rogers is appealing that finding to the NLRB itself in Washington, D.C.
The same official has also issued a complaint against Rogers, charging that the mental healthcare provider illegally fired a half-dozen West Allis clinic employees in retaliation for organizing the union. A hearing was scheduled to start in mid-December, but has now been postponed until February, a union spokesperson said.
The delays have frustrated union supporters at Rogers and contributed to persistent tensions at Rogers Behavioral Health, a nonprofit that operates in 10 states and is based in Oconomowoc.
“We’ve waited so long,” said nurse Stephani Lohman, who helped organize the West Allis clinic union and whose firing is part of the NLRB case. She’s taken another nursing job while waiting for the complaint to be resolved.
On a chilly Thursday night last week, Lohman was one of a few dozen Rogers union supporters and community allies who stood outside the Pfister Hotel in downtown Milwaukee, holding candles and handing out leaflets to people attending Rogers’ annual fundraising gala at the hotel.
“Many of our former patients came to the event to help hand out flyers,” Lohman said.
She saw a variety of reactions from the people arriving for the gala. Some brushed past the small crowd of protesters, with or without one of the leaflets. Others stopped and heard about the grievances that led majorities at the two clinics to vote for the union back on April 22.
“It was a mixed group,” Lohman said. “Some people seemed interested and some people seemed genuinely not interested.”
The union had announced its plans for the vigil and protest outside the fundraising event two days earlier, on Tuesday, Nov. 10.
“Nobody should be celebrating Rogers when its leaders have turned their backs on patients and workers,” Rogers therapist T’Anna Holst said in the union’s announcement. Services were “severely understaffed,” she added, “because Rogers executives fired our coworkers for supporting our union.”
Late Thursday morning, about six hours before the gala was scheduled to begin, Rogers issued a written statement attributed to Rogers CEO Cindy Meyer.
“We are pleased to announce that the National Union of Healthcare Workers (NUHW) has agreed to mediate the concerns in the state of Wisconsin,” Meyer stated. “We will participate in this process in good faith seeking resolutions and understanding.  We respect the right of individuals to express their views and we believe the mediation process is the place to work thru concerns to reach solutions.  As always, we are committed to our communities, patients, and families.”
The statement did not explain its reference to mediation. It also didn’t define the “concerns in the state of Wisconsin” that are to be the subject of discussion. Officials and members at the healthcare workers union say they didn’t know it was coming or what it referred to.
Rogers had agreed to mediation in October, said Sal Rosselli, the NUHW president emeritus — not to settle contracts for employees at the two clinics, but to resolve the NLRB complaints over the six fired employees. But he said there had been no date set for talks, and Rogers officials said they would not be available before February.
Meyer’s statement was “misleading” and “appears to be intended to draw attention away from a protest workers are holding this evening outside Rogers’ ‘Celebrate the Light Gala’ in downtown Milwaukee,” Rosselli said. The protest would go on, he declared.
“As of now, Rogers is still refusing to begin contract negotiations in Madison and still refusing to recognize the union election in West Allis, both of which took place in April,” Roselli said.
He added that union supporters at the Wisconsin clinics “have always been open to mediation or any reasonable settlement that will result in Rogers following federal labor law and bargaining contracts in good faith, rather than spending additional patient care dollars on lawyers when its treatment centers remain seriously understaffed.”
In the aftermath of the union’s statement, the Wisconsin Examiner sent a series of questions Thursday to Rogers’ communications and marketing executive Maureen Remmel.
The questions ask what were the subject or subjects of the mediation referred to in Meyer’s statement, the timeline for that mediation, and whether Meyer’s statement was issued in response to the protest scheduled for that Thursday evening. The Examiner also asked whether Rogers planned to recognize the union at the West Allis clinic or to begin contract negotiations at the Madison clinic.
Remmel said Friday morning that a response to the questions would be forthcoming. Follow-up reminders were sent late on Friday and again on Monday, but there was no further response.
Lohman hopes the demonstration outside the Pfister last week might yet put “public pressure” on Rogers to shift its stance.
“If they really want to settle the issues, they should go to the bargaining table,” Lohman said. “I hope that Rogers sees that their position is so unpopular and makes a rational choice for once. I would really like to see this chapter be behind us and for the workers to have a contract.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Report examines opportunities, shortcomings of Wisconsin treatment courts
description: Treatment courts are intended to offer accountability and encouragement for people who have a substance abuse issue and also a pending criminal charge. The carrot for those who complete the requirements of the court, show progress toward sobriety, is the criminal charge will be avoided or there will be leniency. Treatment courts, also called drug […]
text:
Treatment court offers a path to recovery and and alternative to a punitive criminal justice approach. But just over half of participants in Wisconsin make it through the process. (Getty Images creative)The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
Treatment courts are intended to offer accountability and encouragement for people who have a substance abuse issue and also a pending criminal charge.
The carrot for those who complete the requirements of the court, show progress toward sobriety, is the criminal charge will be avoided or there will be leniency.
Treatment courts, also called drug court or wellness court, veteran courts and OWI court, are well-established in many Wisconsin counties.
A new report prepared by the Wisconsin Policy Forum, commissioned by Vital Strategies, a global health nonprofit, examines the 104 treatment courts in the state, including 61 that receive Treatment Alternatives and Diversion (TAD) funding from the state that require data reporting from each court.
Besides the TAD courts, the report obtained data from 53 treatment court coordinators in 43 counties and treatment court information available in manuals and web sites.
The report notes that drug and narcotics violations were involved in nearly 25% of arrests in 2023, highlighting the importance of treatment courts to address the deeper problem of addiction and substance abuse.
At a press conference Tuesday, the report’s authors discussed some of its notable findings. One interesting fact is that only 54% of those in TAD treatment courts between 2019-2024 successfully graduated.
“It’s worth noting that sometimes there’s a misconception that treatment court is easy or that it doesn’t ask a lot of participants,” said Jason Stein, president of Wisconsin Policy Forum, “and you can see here that the data tell a different story, in terms of who makes it through to the end.”
 Stein said data from the National Treatment Court Resource Center report the graduation rate nationwide is higher, at 60.7%.
“Treatment court is the hardest thing participants have ever done,” said Milwaukee County Circuit Judge Carl Ashley at the press conference. “They appear regularly before a judge. They are drug tested. They attend treatment. They must be honest, and when they fall short, they have to recognize that. What they also get for the first time in their lives is a team that believes they can change: a judge, a prosecutor, a defense attorney, treatment provider, law enforcement, case managers, and for veterans, mentors who have worn that same uniform. That combination of accountability and support is what makes the difference.”
Stein noted that TAD data shows a racial disparity: 82% of people referred   to treatment court are white, versus 7.6% for Blacks and 6.9% for Native Americans. As the process moves forward into eligibility and then admittance to graduation the percentage of white participation expands but for both Blacks and Native Americans it declines.
“These desperate outcomes make this an important area for policymakers, treatment court teams and the general public to keep track of,” he said of the racial disparity.
He also noted 26 of 40 treatment coordinators said there are fewer people in their treatment courts today versus 2019, but 11 said they had more than in 2019.
 He also noted at 60 of 61 TAD courts use jail as sanction for participants such as when a treatment court participant is re-arrested or when they re-use.
“Most court officials say they do not use jail as a response to a positive drug test alone, but 10 of 45 respondents, or one-fifth, did use short-term sanctions in that circumstance,” said Stein. “It’s worth noting the importance of that because individuals when released from jail are at a heightened risk of an overdose.”
He added, “On this point of when to employ jail as a sanction, a broader discussion within the state treatment court community could be valuable given that the National All Rise Adult Treatment Court best practice standards stress the importance of using jail as a tool for protecting public safety rather than as a response to substance abuse.”
From the report findings, Adrienne Hurst of Vital Strategies made several recommendations.
First, she said, punishment for drug use is not treatment and more should be done to avoid “punitive systems that punish predictable setbacks for people in drug treatment.”
She added, “More than 20% of reviewed treatment court manuals report using jail-based sanctions in response to a positive urine test. More courts apply a jail-based sanction if a participant reported no use, but a urine test comes back positive; 29% of survey responses said that reoccurring use was a reason to terminate treatment court participation. And let’s be clear: termination of participation means return to jail.”
Second, she encouraged deferring prosecution versus requiring a conviction or a guilty plea to be qualified for treatment court.
“Deferring prosecution could also mitigate some of the knock-on effects of a criminal record that make achieving lasting recovery difficult,” she said
She also said courts should “strengthen” their “evaluation and oversight to reinforce best practices,” but be wary of adding too many regulations that results in “rigidity that reduces access and increases punitive responses…While I applaud the idea that stronger practice requirements and additional oversight will result in evidence-based practices that promote wellness, treatment courts should avoid policies that increase the intensity of court requirements on participants.”
Fourth, she recommended the use of methadone and buprenorphine for opioid treatment.
“Most courts who responded to the survey allow methadone or buprenorphine, which are the standards for treatment for opioid use disorder,” she said. “Naltrexone is FDA approved but is significantly less protective against overdose than buprenorphine and methadone. Medication choice should be based on a discussion between a medical provider and the participant and requires the availability of all options.”
 She also recommended that treatment courts evaluate fines and fees so they don’t create barriers to participation, and to consider those at high-risk for recidivism because research has shown they could benefit the most from “intensive programs like treatment court.”
“In addition, 41% of survey respondents report the courts exclude people who sell drugs, but low-level drug sales is a common form of survival economics for people with substance use disorder,” Hurst said, “and the exclusion of these offenses is a missed opportunity to support individuals who could benefit from the treatment court model, especially the employment and other social determinant of health supports Wisconsin courts provide.”
Eli Corbin, harm reduction coordinator for the Bad River Band of Lake Superior Chippewa, said at the press release that treatment court had helped him turn his life around because his relationship with the key players – judge, district attorney and others – went from a punitive relationship to positive interaction that provided accountability and a community of support.
Judge Ashley said treatment courts reduce recidivism by as 58% and save up to $6,000 per individual with fewer arrests and court cases and days in jail.
“That is money we can return to the community,” he said, “but the real savings are harder to count: the crime that never happens; the overdose call that never comes; the child who never enters foster care.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: New taxes, changes to property tax exemptions among recommendations to Maine Legislature
description: A state task force is recommending that Maine double its homestead exemption to $50,000 and allow municipalities to set local sales tax to alleviate property tax burdens around the state.  The Real Estate Property Tax Relief Task Force held its final meeting Tuesday, and despite meeting for over a year, the group had no shortage […]
text:
The Legislature's Taxation Committee hears public feedback on bill proposals in Augusta. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)A state task force is recommending that Maine double its homestead exemption to $50,000 and allow municipalities to set local sales tax to alleviate property tax burdens around the state. 
The Real Estate Property Tax Relief Task Force held its final meeting Tuesday, and despite meeting for over a year, the group had no shortage of discussion as the meeting carried on for more than seven hours.
The task force, which is composed of legislators, municipal and county leaders and business representatives, began its work in September 2025. It issued interim recommendations in February, and its final report is due to the Legislature by Dec. 15.
​​Property taxes have long been a concern in Northeast states, which tend to rely more significantly on them for revenue to fund public institutions such as schools, but the issue has gotten even more challenging since the pandemic when property values were upended.
Throughout the meeting, task force members debated if they could meaningfully relieve the pressure on property taxes without increasing revenue elsewhere.
Portland Attorney Phil Saucier said he was unsatisfied with shifting things around and leaving the burden on municipalities.
“While it’s more targeted relief for the same money, it’s still raising the mill rates for municipalities,” he said. “The municipalities and the other property taxpayers, will be funding these changes, not the state. That’s the problem I have with the funding mechanism part of it.”
Without new revenue, the task force is left to reallocate money from one program to another, ultimately not reducing the total amount that Mainers pay in property taxes.
“It’s not straight out property tax relief,” said Dick Woodbury, an economist and former state senator for Cumberland County. “We’re going to raise just as much from property taxes as we did before. We’re just going to reapportion it a bit in a way that feels a little bit fairer — not a little bit, a lot fairer — and you know that to me is a good is a pretty amazing accomplishment if we could pull it off.”
Woodbury said he didn’t think new funding was guaranteed, in which case he’d still like to see state programs help the people that need assistance the most. 
“I am not optimistic,” Woodbury said. “And therefore I put in there what I still think is a significant improvement to the system.”
But not all members of the task force were sold on creating new taxes to pay for property tax relief.
“The danger of adding new taxes is that they will just become extra money, and it will do nothing to help with the property tax,” said Rep. Robert Nutting (R-Oakland). 
To that end, the group ultimately agreed on a few recommendations that would generate new funding, such as expanding revenue-generating options for municipalities, such as a local sales or lodging tax. 
Another suggestion is legislation to allow municipalities to issue a service charge to properties that are exempt from taxes. For example, a town could charge a state building for the cost of providing trash removal, or another municipal service. 
The group also recommends that the Legislature look to find better ways to support larger communities such as Bangor and Portland that have facilities such as hospitals and state offices that are used by people who don’t live and pay taxes in those cities.   

Other recommendations

Document how many municipalities have impact fee ordinances — a fee charged to a new development, for local governments to pay for infrastructure improvements needed because of that development project
Establish ongoing and regular reviews of exemption programs
Update minimum assessing standards, and create financial supports for municipalities to reach compliance with new standards
Reduce revenue sharing for municipalities that do not move toward assessing compliance within three years
Study underfunded mandates, the requirements for municipalities in state law that get some funding support but not enough
Fund a program to share information about the Property Tax Fairness Credit
Coordinate with the taxpayer advocate on educational efforts and how programs are being utilized 
Review audit and financial disclosure requirements for municipalities and school districts
Direct the ​​Maine Office of Community Affairs to provide an annual report on regionalization efforts for local services. 


Changes to existing programs
One of the major recommendations focuses on the homestead property tax exemption and the Property Tax Fairness Credit — which provides refunds for property taxes or rent paid.
The group recommends that the state increase the homestead exemption to $50,000. It suggests the Property Tax Fairness Credit be amended to create a two-tiered system for taxpayers who pay more than a certain percentage of their income for property taxes or rent. The modified program should also remove any distinctions based on age or family size, so the only factor is property tax bills as a percentage of income. The details will be left up to legislators to determine.
The program was already expanded in 2024, alongside the creation of the Property Tax Deferral Program, to soften the blow from the short-lived Property Tax Stabilization Program that allowed older Mainers to freeze their property taxes. 
The Legislature repealed that program after just one year, following skyrocketing cost projections, concern about wealthy property owners taking advantage due to a lack of income restrictions and the administrative burden on municipalities.
Also included in the task force recommendations is the Property Tax Deferral Program, which allows Mainers who are 65 and older or permanently disabled to defer paying property taxes until they die or their property is sold.
The group recommended that lawmakers remove the limit on the number of acres eligible for the deferral program and the requirement that a landowner must have less than $150,000 in liquid assets.
The members also agreed that the program should be amended to allow a landowner to apply any time of year for the program, and direct the Maine Revenue Service to develop educational information about the program for municipalities, who in turn would be required to share that information with delinquent taxpayers.
The group would also direct the Maine Revenue Service to issue a report to the Legislature in 2032 on participation in the deferral program and any trends. 
Task force members discussed how to protect the state’s investment in these properties, and how that investment is made whole at the end of the program. 
But Sen. Nicole Grohoski (D-Hancock) pointed out that losing some money to keep someone in their home is still less expensive than the state paying for them to be in a nursing home or homeless shelter.
“I think the money lost would probably still ultimately be money saved elsewhere,” she said.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Years after scrutiny, Black drivers still dominate Bratenahl traffic stops
description: This article was first published by The Marshall Project, a nonprofit news organization covering the U.S. criminal justice system. Sign up for their newsletters, and follow them on Instagram, TikTok, Reddit and Facebook. BRATENAHL, Ohio – For years, Black Clevelanders complained they bore the brunt of traffic citations in this wealthy neighboring village, bu[...]
text:
Stock photo from Getty Images.This article was first published by The Marshall Project, a nonprofit news organization covering the U.S. criminal justice system. Sign up for their newsletters, and follow them on Instagram, TikTok, Reddit and Facebook.
BRATENAHL, Ohio – For years, Black Clevelanders complained they bore the brunt of traffic citations in this wealthy neighboring village, but only had anecdotes from a local court where long lines of Black people waited to face prosecution and pay fines.
They now have definitive proof: Black drivers have been stopped and ticketed more often than White drivers as they traveled through the village since 2024, according to traffic stop data gathered by The Marshall Project – Cleveland.
Officers didn’t consistently record race during traffic stops before 2022, but started doing so after a Marshall Project investigation into racial disparities in enforcement. By 2024, the department was collecting racial data, and the village ordered officers to undergo racial bias training.
In 2024, Black drivers accounted for approximately 70% of traffic stops and of citations. In 2025, they made up roughly 65% of both. Through September of this year, those numbers returned to roughly 70%, according to the village records.

Since 2024, the village has collected close to $400,000 in fines, court costs and other revenue from the Mayor’s Court, which primarily handles traffic violations, records show.
The 1,400-resident village of waterfront estates and mansions, including one recently purchased by pop superstar Taylor Swift and NFL star and Cleveland Heights native Travis Kelce, is notorious among Clevelanders. For decades, they said officers targeted Black drivers to raise revenue, and nicknamed the citations the “Bratenahl tax.”
Cleveland Councilman Kevin Conwell, who represents areas near Bratenahl, said he was stunned and “so disappointed” at the numbers since the village’s mayor had pledged to curtail the stopping of Black Clevelanders.
“I am not happy about this,” Conwell said, adding that he wants to meet with Mayor Keith Benjamin. “This must stop.”
Bratenahl officials, including Benjamin and Chief of Police Charles LoBello, have said officers do not racially profile drivers. Benjamin acknowledged recently that the data doesn’t bode well for the village’s reputation and said he took the concerns seriously.
The mayor vowed to do a thorough review of the stop data.
“Racial profiling is unacceptable, and a concern about it deserves a careful, respectful review,” he said. “Even when the facts have not yet been established, the perception of unfair treatment matters because it affects people’s trust in our police and our community.”
Benjamin suggested this type of analysis needed to take into account the race of the tens of thousands of drivers who pass through the village daily on Interstate 90.
“That’s an important missing piece,” Benjamin said. “We need to understand the traffic population as well as the decisions officers make.”
During a recent visit to Mayor’s Court, the majority of the attendees were Black or Hispanic residents of other cities.
“There’s no type of justice here,” Eon Fawcett said Sept. 29, after leaving with $345 in fines, fees and court costs for speeding and not using a turn signal.
“People just get screwed here. Everyone is found guilty.”
The village’s officers patrol side streets and a 3-mile stretch of Interstate 90 that runs along the village’s southern edge.
In late 2022, the police force did not record the race of drivers stopped by officers, and The Marshall Project – Cleveland analyzed records from Mayor’s Court to estimate that the majority of those stopped were Black residents.
As a result, LoBello ordered officers in early 2023 to log the race of all drivers in traffic stops.
LoBello, the most tenured officer on the force, stressed that officers do not use race as the reason for the stops. If the department were doing improper policing, the number of Black drivers being stopped would have decreased after the scrutiny, he said.
“It is truly based on the demographics of people who drive through the village,” he said. “The numbers have been consistent the past four years.”
Bratenahl is surrounded by Cleveland and shares a ZIP code with Glenville, one of Cleveland’s poorest neighborhoods — hundreds of feet away from towering iron security gates, privacy fences and opulent yards.
Chief executives, professional athletes and team owners have called the village home. While they pay property taxes, many of the wealthiest residents do not live there full-time, prohibiting the village from collecting income taxes.
Earlier this month, Bratenahl drew national headlines when Swift and Kelce became its newest residents.
Kelce purchased the 3.5-acre property for $5.35 million in March, months before marrying Swift. News reporters swooped in to paint picturesque scenes of the village, but none mentioned the decades-old friction over disproportionate traffic stops.
On Sept. 29, after leaving the court with a $260 payment plan for speeding and expired plates, Cleveland resident Brandon Shelley said the traffic stops in the village are a fact of life that will not change.
“This goes on in our world on a daily basis,” he said. “I just put my hands up and live.”
Editor’s note: This story has been updated to clarify that Bratenahl officers weren’t consistently gathering racial data before 2022, and that they were doing so by 2024.

title: Report raises additional questions about Kroger data gathering in Ohio, nationally
description: As Kroger works to complete its purchase of Giant Eagle, an antimonopoly group says it will make groceries even more expensive, particularly in parts of Ohio.  Perhaps more ominously, the group worries that a merger will further enhance a surveillance program that earns Kroger huge sums by selling customer data.
