text:
A Kroger store in Columbus, Ohio. (Photo by Marty Schladen/Ohio Capital Journal)As Kroger works to complete its purchase of Giant Eagle, an antimonopoly group says it will make groceries even more expensive, particularly in parts of Ohio. 
Perhaps more ominously, the group worries that a merger will further enhance a surveillance program that earns Kroger huge sums by selling customer data. There are also fears that Kroger will use the information to support a “dynamic-pricing” program that would increase prices even further, said the group, the American Economic Liberties Project.
“Buying bleach or yogurt now comes with the prospect of being scanned, tracked, and profiled,” the report said. “With every store Kroger buys, the data and surveillance apparatus grows, and Americans become more and more accustomed to an increasingly inhumane and demoralizing shopping experience.”
Kroger didn’t immediately respond to questions for this story.
But in its report, the economic liberties project said that a purchase of Giant Eagle would raise concerns similar to those raised by the proposed merger with Albertsons that failed in 2024. Without enforcement of relevant antitrust law, competition goes down as Kroger grows, and remaining stores can increase prices, the argument goes.
That would be particularly true in Central Ohio if Kroger’s purchase of Giant Eagle goes through next year, according to the American Economic Liberties Project report.
“In Columbus, Ohio, Kroger already controls 43% of the grocery market,” it said. “In three instances, Giant Eagle and Kroger sit directly across the street from one another. If this deal goes ahead, it would turn head-to-head competitors into a single company, controlling nearly 50% of the market.”
But also raising concerns is Kroger’s huge customer surveillance program through a subsidiary called 84.51°.
Every time its 63 million loyalty customers use their Kroger cards, the company archives that information and sells it, generating more than a third of company profits, Consumer Reports said last year.
The American Economic Liberties Project report said Cincinnati-based Kroger’s data-gathering operation is drawing scrutiny on Capitol Hill.
“In a recent Senate hearing on AI surveillance pricing, (U.S.) Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri described Kroger as ‘not just a grocery store,’ but a “data-selling megacorporation,” the report said. 
The report further quotes Hawley as saying “Last year, Kroger earned over $500 million from selling data that it harvests from its loyal customers and giving it to other corporations … That accounts for 43% of its income last year.”
“Giant Eagle operates its own loyalty program, which Kroger would absorb and add to its already extensive dossier of customer information,” the report stated.
It’s not just Kroger’s sale of customer data that critics find concerning. There are also suspicions that the grocery giant will use it to jack up prices and profits.
Taylor Warren of the Center for Responsible Food Business last month told the Capital Journal that 84.51° builds customer profiles estimating income, family size and things like whether they have pets. It can also monitor customer behavior and make educated guesses about the maximum amount one is willing to spend on an item and price it accordingly, he said.
The American Economic Liberties Project said Kroger is making other moves that might enable dynamic pricing, including plans to implement electronic self-pricing labels across all of its locations by the end of 2027.
“While (the labels) allow Kroger to change prices instantly through a software program, Kroger denies using the technology for customer surveillance and dynamic pricing,” according to the report. “In September, however, the supermarket altered its privacy policy to include facial recognition technology as part of the biometric data the company collects on its customers at select stores.”
The report added that the surveillance begins when customers enter the parking lot and extends well beyond that. It mentioned Kroger’s partnership with Cooler Screens, “a digital smart screen company whose AI-powered cameras utilize data on a customer’s ‘presence, dwell time, and door opens,’ and facial analysis to serve personalized advertisements and make inferences on a customer’s demographics.”
“Sensory data, which includes photos, CCTV recordings, and the use of automated license plate readers, is also listed as information collected by the supermarket,” the report stated.

 Catching Our Eye

• Ohio House. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Sarah Donaldson is reporting, “Huffman should hold onto speakership, Ohio House GOP caucus votes.”
House Speaker Matt Huffman (R-Lima) has for now fended off a challenge to his speakership, following a vote held behind closed doors Tuesday evening.
Rep. Tex Fischer (R-Canfield), 30, ran against Huffman, 66, but lost. The Ohio House GOP did not release the vote total, which is counted on secret ballots.
Huffman, who’s held the speakership the last two years, won the gavel with the unanimous backing of the caucus in November 2024.
• Cultural sites. WOUB Public Media’s David Forster is reporting, “Concerns about cultural sites lead to the downsizing of proposed locations for a Pike County data center complex.”
The company planning to build a massive data center complex in Pike County has reduced the size of the proposed project area by half in its permit application.
At least some of this has to do with concerns over sensitive cultural sites.
SB Energy initially was planning to build the data centers on more than 1,000 acres of private property just south of Piketon.
But according to its latest filings with the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency, it is now looking to build on less than 500 acres.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT could have saved $1 billion on electricity. Here’s what comes next.
description: Are CT residential customers buying electricity in the most cost-effective way possible? It would appear not.
text:
What if Connecticut residential electric customers could have saved $1 billion over the past decade simply by changing how we purchase electricity?
That’s the question raised by new research I requested from Synapse Energy Economics. And at a time when families are struggling to pay their electric bills, it’s a question we cannot afford to ignore.

State Rep. Raghib Allie-Brennan

Eversource is seeking approximately $727 million in additional annual distribution revenue, a proposal that could increase a typical residential customer’s monthly bill by roughly $33 if approved. Families are already feeling nickel-and-dimed by rising costs, and another increase would only add to that burden.
As a member of the General Assembly’s Energy and Technology Committee, I believe we have a responsibility to examine every component of the electric bill, not just the charges that receive the most attention.
For years, Connecticut’s energy affordability debate has focused heavily on public benefits charges. Those costs deserve scrutiny, and we took steps to address them in 2025. But we also need to ask a fundamental question: Are we buying electricity in the most cost-effective way possible?
Earlier this year, Synapse published a study estimating that Connecticut residential Standard Service customers paid approximately $1.8 billion in wholesale supplier premiums between 2016 and 2025.

A chart from the Synapse report showing how much Connecticut consumers might have saved collectively using an alternative wholesale purchasing system. Credit: Synapse Energy Economics Inc.

These aren’t profits collected by Eversource or United Illuminating. They’re costs associated with suppliers taking on the financial risk of selling electricity at predetermined prices.
Fixed-price contracts provide stability, but that protection comes at a price.
After reviewing the findings, I contacted Synapse’s researchers and invited Representative Tracy Marra, the Ranking Member of the Energy and Technology Committee, to join our discussion. Electricity affordability shouldn’t be a Democratic or Republican issue.
I subsequently requested a Connecticut-specific analysis to better understand whether alternative purchasing strategies could have reduced costs for ratepayers.
The results deserve attention.
Using historical data from 2016 through 2025, Synapse estimated that purchasing 25% of Standard Service electricity through a spot-market model, with subsequent cost reconciliation, could have saved residential customers approximately $500 million, averaging $42 per customer annually.
At 50%, the estimated savings increased to $1 billion, or approximately $86 per customer annually.
Let’s be clear: Saving $42 or $86 a year won’t solve Connecticut’s affordability challenges. But for families facing rising electricity costs, insurance premiums, property taxes, and grocery bills, every dollar matters.
And when those individual savings add up to hundreds of millions of dollars statewide, we have a responsibility to examine whether customers are paying more than necessary.
Perhaps most notably, both scenarios produced lower modeled electricity rates in 86 of the 120 months examined, with slightly less month-to-month bill volatility.
That challenges the assumption that greater participation in wholesale markets necessarily means less predictable bills.
These findings are based on a simplified historical model, not a guarantee of future savings. There were months when customers would have paid more, and wholesale markets carry risks that must be managed carefully.
But the research raises a serious question about whether our traditional purchasing strategy has placed too much emphasis on price certainty at the expense of potential savings.
Importantly, Connecticut has already begun addressing this issue.
In 2025, I supported bipartisan energy affordability legislation, Senate Bill 4, which became Public Act 25-173. Among other reforms, it required utilities to develop the capability to purchase at least 25% of Standard Service electricity through more flexible wholesale-market arrangements.
That legislation preceded the Connecticut-specific analysis I requested. The new findings provide additional evidence for examining how that flexibility should be used.
In October, the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority approved an updated procurement framework with a nonbinding 20% wholesale-market purchasing target and flexibility to go higher when conditions and safeguards justify it.
An updated procurement plan is due February 1, 2027.
We’ve created the opportunity to purchase electricity differently. Now we need to determine whether that opportunity is producing real savings.
As we approach the 2027 legislative session, I intend to work with colleagues on both sides of the aisle, regulators, and consumer advocates to examine how these reforms are implemented.
How much electricity is actually being purchased through wholesale markets? Are ratepayers saving money? Are adequate protections in place against price spikes? And do the results justify further changes?
Those questions should guide our next steps, rather than rushing to introduce another law before the existing reforms have been tested.
Eversource’s pending rate case concerns electricity delivery, while this research addresses electricity supply. They are separate costs, but both appear on the same bill families struggle to pay.
No single reform will make electricity affordable overnight. But that cannot become an excuse to overlook opportunities for savings.
Connecticut families deserve more than explanations for why their electric bills are high. They deserve evidence that we’re doing everything reasonably possible to bring them down.
That means looking beyond the usual arguments, following the data, and holding ourselves accountable for results.
Raghib Allie-Brennan represents District 2 (Bethel and parts of Danbury) in  the Connecticut House of Representatives.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: AI can be a useful tool for students who struggle
description: Learning when AI is helpful and when it crosses the line into doing the work for you could actually be an important skill.
text:
I have struggled with a lot of assignments in college, and sometimes I feel like I need a little extra help to get started or understand what I am supposed to do. My parents have told me that I could use ChatGPT to give me a small boost, but I have usually said no because I have been told that I am not allowed to use it for school. 
There have been many times when I have been tempted to use it, not to do the whole assignment for me, but just to help me understand the directions, organize my thoughts, or get started. I think AI could be a useful tool for students like me who struggle in school, as long as it is used to support our learning instead of doing the work for us. 
For me, one of the hardest parts of an assignment can be just getting started. Sometimes I understand the topic, but I don’t know how to put my thoughts together or what the teacher is asking me to do. I can sit there looking at an assignment for a long time without knowing what to write. This is where I think AI could help. I could use it to explain the directions in a different way or help me come up with ideas. That would still mean that I am doing the actual thinking and writing. I would just have something helping me get started. 
I also think there is a difference between using AI as a tool and having AI do your assignment. If I put my whole assignment into ChatGPT and tell it to write everything for me, then I am not really learning anything. I don’t think students should use AI that way. But if I ask it to explain something I don’t understand, help me organize my ideas, or give me an example of how to start, I don’t think that is the same thing. It is more like getting extra help from a tutor. The student still has to make the decisions and complete the assignment. 
I did not use AI for this essay. These are my own thoughts. I just wanted to discuss how AI can be useful in small doses rather than the whole essay.
Some people might say that students should not use AI because it is cheating. I understand why teachers are concerned about this. It can be hard to know if a student actually wrote something or if AI wrote it for them. (I did not use AI for this essay. These are my own thoughts.)  
I also think there should be rules about how students can use it. But I don’t think banning it completely is the best answer. Students already have different levels of support. Some students can get help from parents, tutors, friends, or other resources. For students who struggle with school, AI could be another way to get some support when they are stuck. 
Another reason I think this is important is because AI is probably going to be part of the future. Students are going to see it in college, jobs, and everyday life. Instead of only teaching students that AI is bad or that they can’t use it, I think schools should teach students how to use it responsibly. Learning when AI is helpful and when it crosses the line into doing the work for you could actually be an important skill. I would rather learn how to use AI correctly than be completely afraid to use it because I might get in trouble. 
I am not saying that students should be allowed to use ChatGPT to write every assignment. I am saying that there should be a difference between using AI to get answers and using AI to get help. For students who struggle with learning, organization, or getting started, that little bit of help could make a big difference. I know that if I could use ChatGPT just to understand directions, organize my thoughts, or get unstuck, I would still want to do my own work. 
I just think having that extra support could help students like me show what we actually know instead of getting stuck before we even get started. 
Sammy Clay is a student at Mitchell College in New London.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The Regents and CSCU: A 15-year fiasco
description: The primary problem facing CSCU is not years of bad leadership but rather the flawed premises the system is built on.
text:
The recent string of scandals that has embarrassed the Connecticut State Colleges and Universities system and the Board of Regents (BOR) that oversees this system are simply the latest chapters in a long tale of failure and woe. 
Since Gov. Dannel Malloy and the Connecticut General Assembly created the BOR and CSCU in 2011 by forcing the four Connecticut state universities, the 12 community colleges, and Charter Oak State College into a single administrative and oversight structure, problems have followed, one after another, about as regularly, and almost as predictably, as the rising and setting of the sun.
Given the resignation of CSCU Chancellor Terrence Cheng (July 2025), followed by that of his successor, Interim Chancellor John Maduko (April 2026), the suspension of Maduko’s successor, System General Counsel Karen Buffkin (May 2026), and the resignations of BOR Chair Marty Guay (May 2026) and Vice Chair Juanita James (September 2026), as well as that of Central Connecticut State University President Zulma Toro (also September 2026), each under a cloud of controversy, it is obvious that the system has a leadership problem. 
This is nothing new. The first CSCU President, Robert A. Kennedy, lasted a year before several ethically dubious decisions cost him his political support and forced him to resign.  Kennedy’s successor, Gregory Gray, alienated legislators as well as the faculty at most of the system colleges and universities, who voted no confidence in him. He lasted two years. 
Mark Ojakian, a veteran state bureaucrat who headed CSCU from 2015 through 2020, survived as long as he did not because of his desire to collaborate with faculty (rumor has it he had a plaque on his desk engraved with the phrase “sometimes the squeaky wheel gets replaced.”) or his ability to win their support (he did not: faculty voted no-confidence in him as well) but because he maintained the backing of Malloy, who appointed him, incoming Gov. Ned Lamont, and other key powerbrokers in Hartford. Having set in motion a merger of the 12 community colleges into a single Connecticut State Community College (a shotgun consolidation, as it were, within the larger system merger), steadfastly opposed by the large majority of faculty, he retired. 
In addition to turnover at the highest executive levels, CSCU has seen a musical chairs of college and university presidents, CEOs, regional presidents, system provosts, vice-provosts, vice-presidents, associate vice-presidents, directors, deans, acting this and interim that, coming and going, being hired or appointed, and either leaving or being forced out. 
Ill-conceived, ineffective, and dysfunctional organizations (and CSCU has demonstrated, over and over again, that it is all of the above) rarely attract capable leaders, good managers, or the best possible employees in general. Skilled and talented people tend to steer clear of the wreckage of such organizations and go to where they are able to put their skills and talents to good use. 
The primary problem facing CSCU, however, is not leadership but rather the premises the system is built upon and the manner in which it is constructed. These may be summarized as follows:

Since education funding is not considered a fixed cost in Connecticut and fixed costs (e.g., Medicaid, debt service, retiree health care and pensions) account for over half the state budget, increase each year, and must be paid for, the Governor and General Assembly will regularly prioritize spending on other agencies, programs, and initiatives over spending on public higher education. Thus, savings and efficiencies must constantly be squeezed out of college and university budgets.
The only way to achieve savings and efficiencies, as well as achieve stated secondary goals (reduce administrative costs, largely by consolidating “back-office” functions; plow savings into teaching and “student-facing” services; improve student “success rates,” especially for socio-economically disadvantaged students), is to organize 17 colleges and universities into a single system, assemble a central office of managers and bureaucrats in Hartford to run this system, then destroy 12 community colleges and combine them into a sub-system within the greater system and create a second central office of managers and bureaucrats in New Britain to run the sub-system. 
CSCU must be structured as a centralized, top-down hierarchy. Primary authority will reside at the central offices in Hartford and New Britain, not at the colleges and universities. Bureaucrats who do not teach, do not work at a campus, rarely if ever see a student, and do not know the citizens who live in the respective service areas of the colleges and universities will make (for the community colleges), or greatly influence (for the universities), the key decisions about every matter of significance (budgetary, personnel, academic, curricular, initiatives and priorities) for every campus.
Decades of direct legislative oversight of the community colleges, Connecticut State Universities, and Charter Oak State College were a failure. Thus, CSCU will be overseen by a Board of Regents composed of 13 political appointees and two students, all volunteers, few possessing any higher education experience save as students, and most with full-time jobs or commitments elsewhere.

So, what could possibly go wrong with such a creative, innovative plan? Not surprisingly, everything — for 15 years and counting. 
By Governor Lamont’s own admission, the CSCU merger has achieved not a penny of savings to date. Nothing. As the merger has saved no money, there has been no money to reinvest into teaching and student services. Is it conceivable that 17 autonomous colleges and universities, each with an administration in control of its own budget, would have done no worse than this, and perhaps done better? 
And who could have possibly predicted that expanding the number of managers 22.8 percent (including a 35.9 percent increase for the community colleges), mostly to staff the two system offices, would save no money? 
Conversely, since 2012 the number of full-time faculty has declined 11 percent (14.3 percent at the community colleges). Between FY 2013 and FY 2023, the number of full-time classified staff fell 22.3 percent (38.3 percent at the community colleges). Over the past three years, the number of part-time and contingent faculty and staff positions, those most vulnerable to the budgetary axe, has increased 21.5 percent.
Regarding secondary goals, centralizing administrative functions such as accounting, information technology, human resources, payroll, and purchasing has simply diminished the quality, reliability, and timeliness of these services on every campus. There seems to be little evidence that any system initiative —more importantly, any initiative that required combining seventeen institutions to implement—has significantly improved student success, however defined. In Spring 2026, enrollment, which plummeted during the COVID-19 pandemic, stood at 87.5 percent of what it was seven years earlier, lagging the enrollment rebound at the University of Connecticut and the state’s private colleges and universities. Since Fall 2020, the four Connecticut State Universities have had greater full-time equivalent (FTE) enrollment than the consolidated community college, which may reflect well on the former but does not reflect well on the latter. Between 2017 and 2025, the number of students enrolled in community college non-credit courses declined 64.6 percent. [4]
A 2024 report on the new Connecticut State Community College detailed a slew of “bureaucratic inefficiencies, communication gaps, budget constraints, and operational shortcomings” that hinder students and do nothing to help the socio-economically disadvantaged. An evaluation of the CSCU system, commissioned by the Office of Policy and Management, highlighted similar failings and concluded that the BOR is “. . . ill-equipped to provide  . . . necessary guidance and  . . . appropriate oversight and accountability . . . .” Assuming faculty and staff—the people on each campus who teach, advise, mentor, know, and work directly with students—had had use of even a portion of the over $600 million the system office withheld from the constituent institutions, the $100 million (perhaps more) that was squandered to replace twelve community colleges with one, and the nearly 8 percent of the state block grant that is spoken for by system bureaucrats, is it possible that students might have been helped in some way? [5]
To merely hire a new chancellor, appoint 15 new regents, or tinker with the existing structure of CSCU will be to do nothing but reinforce failure. The current structure is fundamentally disordered, unwieldy, and unworkable and was from the moment it was conceived. It needs to be razed to the ground and rebuilt, probably along the lines of what existed prior to 2011, which served students and the public tolerably well for decades. 
If the incoming Governor and General Assembly actually give a damn about both students and taxpayers, they will take decisive action to fix this mess. And if they do not, rest assured that the fiasco, and the scandals and controversies, will continue.
Francis Coan is a Professor of History Emeritus at Tunxis Community College and Representative Emeritus on the Board of Regents Faculty Advisory Committee.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Peltola elected to fill Alaska US Senate seat, becomes Senate’s 56th Democrat nationally
description: Alaskans have elected Mary Peltola, a Democrat, to one of the state’s two U.S. Senate seats. She will replace incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, a Republican, according to preliminary, partial election results published Tuesday by the Alaska Division of Elections. Peltola will return to Congress as the 56th Democrat in the U.S. Senate when it convenes […]
text:
Mary Peltola greets supporters on election night, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at a Mary Peltola watch party in downtown Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)Alaskans have elected Mary Peltola, a Democrat, to one of the state’s two U.S. Senate seats. She will replace incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, a Republican, according to preliminary, partial election results published Tuesday by the Alaska Division of Elections.
Peltola will return to Congress as the 56th Democrat in the U.S. Senate when it convenes in January after a tsunami of pro-Democratic election results saw Republicans evicted from the Senate’s governing majority.
She was the first Alaska Native woman to serve in Congress when she was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in 2022 and will be the one of the first Indigenous people to serve in the U.S. Senate.
“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my career to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first,” she wrote on Facebook on Tuesday evening. “Thank you, Alaska. Let’s get to work.”
With 209,003 ballots counted through Tuesday evening, Peltola had 50.1% of Alaskans’ first-choice votes, more than enough to avoid a ranked choice runoff election.
 



How Alaska elections work
In Alaska, all candidates for an office run together in an August primary election, and voters pick their favorite candidate. The top four vote-getters advance to the November general election.
If there are four or fewer candidates, all advance to November.
In November, voters rank the four candidates in order of preference. If one candidate has more than 50% of the first-choice votes, they win. If none have 50%, the person with the fewest first-choice votes is eliminated, and their votes are redistributed to their voters’ second choices.
Eliminations and redistributions continue until two candidates are left. The person with the most votes wins.
 



The Associated Press called the Senate race for Peltola shortly after elections officials confirmed she had more than 50% of the vote.
Sullivan had 45.8% of the first-choice votes, followed by Republican challenger Gerald Heikes with 2.1% and independent challenger Dan J. Sullivan with 1.7%.
Final preliminary results are expected Wednesday, and the Division of Elections is planning to publish a certified result on Nov. 25.
In a statement issued Monday morning, Sullivan campaign spokesman Nate Adams said that “Alaskans deserve a complete and accurate count, and we will let that process run its course until every legal vote is counted and certified. The Division of Elections has work left to do, and we respect the Alaskans doing it. We will not be commenting on individual ballot updates or outside projections in the meantime.”
Peltola’s participation in the Senate race wasn’t a surprise: National Democrats tried to recruit her as far back as 2025, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer playing a key role. 
After announcing her run for office in January, Peltola campaigned with the slogan “Fish, Family, Freedom,” emphasizing an anticorruption platform, limits on commercial trawl fisheries and a politically moderate stance that includes support for development and oil and gas drilling on federal land in Alaska. 
One of 16 candidates in the August primary election, the former Alaska U.S. House Representative instantly became Sullivan’s leading challenger.
Another candidate, Dan J. Sullivan of Petersburg, immediately drew public attention for having the same first and last name as Sen. Sullivan.
The Alaska Division of Elections ruled Dan J. Sullivan ineligible to run, citing irregularities in his candidacy that indicated he was running only to confuse voters, but Dan J. Sullivan appealed the decision and the Alaska Supreme Court ruled in his favor.
Dan J. Sullivan finished third in the primary. Fourth-place primary election finisher David Leslie, a progressive Democrat, withdrew after the final result. That promoted Heikes into the general election and concentrated the Democratic vote around Peltola.
Republican and Democratic campaigners collectively spent more than $100 million to promote Peltola and Sen. Sullivan, making it the most expensive election campaign in state history. Final tallies won’t be available until early next year.
Shortly before the primary, Peltola fired her campaign manager, Elisa Rios, and made other major staffing moves. Rios subsequently told the New York Times that Peltola was physically and verbally abusive toward staff and was a key source in a Times article that said Democratic campaigners worked to recruit independent Dan J. Sullivan as a spoiler candidate to help Peltola defeat Sen. Sullivan.
Peltola herself has denied knowing about the recruitment, but Republican officials — including President Donald Trump — have called for legal action against Peltola and her campaign.
The FBI and the Alaska Department of Public Safety are investigating whether Democratic campaigners committed a legal violation. No charges have been filed.
The U.S. Department of Justice filed a civil lawsuit against the Division of Elections, seeking to prevent it from certifying Peltola as the winner of the election, but a federal judge in Alaska dismissed the case. That ruling is now on appeal to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.
Part of the federal case was based on the idea that confused voters might have chosen Dan J. Sullivan instead of Sen. Sullivan. Peltola now has more votes than both Sullivans combined.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Convicted Killer Indicted For Murder Of Transgender Prisoner
description: Jason McCormick is accused of attacking transgender prisoner Denise Foster at Hālawa prison.
text:
An Oʻahu grand jury on Tuesday indicted two-time convicted killer Jason Lee McCormick for a third murder in the beating death of transgender inmate Denise Foster at the state’s largest prison last summer.
Foster was killed at Hālawa Correctional Facility, a men’s prison, on Aug. 4 after McCormick allegedly attacked her in her cell. The indictment accuses McCormick of first-degree murder.
Foster, 55, was a non-violent minimum security inmate inmate who was serving a five-year prison term for theft and unauthorized control of a propelled vehicle. Foster’s niece Queenair Bulawan said Foster had expected to be released in September or October.
The prison system has not explained why Foster was housed in an area of the prison where she had contact with McCormick, 52, who is a maximum security inmate.

Denise Foster was reportedly beaten and strangled in a cell in Hālawa prison on Aug. 4. (Courtesy photo/2022 ) Courtesy photo/2022

McCormick was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole in 2013 for the murder of visiting University of Pittsburgh Professor Robert Henderson in 1996.
He also pleaded guilty to premeditated first-degree murder in Arizona in the 2015 strangulation death of his cellmate Jonathan Namauleg, 21, at the Saguaro Correctional Center. That conviction carries a life sentence without parole to be served after McCormick completes his life sentence for the Henderson murder.
The indictment gives no details about the case, but sources with ties to the state correctional system said a video camera recorded McCormick and Foster arguing outside Foster’s cell before the killing, and McCormick allegedly wrote a profane message in blood on the wall of Foster’s cell directed at Hālawa Warden Shannon Cluney. 

Civil Beat: 
Another Hawaiʻi Prison Death Has Family Seeking Answers

Two online petitions circulated after Foster’s death calling on the state to create safeguards for transgender and vulnerable inmates. The petitions together garnered over 300 signatures.

Jason Lee McCormick (Courtesy Hawaiʻi Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation/2026)

“No one should be beaten to death because the system refused to ask whether they were safe,” one petition reads. “Demand gender-affirming, safety-based housing policy in Hawaiʻi’s prisons before another life is lost.”
Bulawan said her family has heard nothing from the prison system about what led to Foster’s death, and was not told about the indictment before it was made public. “Ever since she passed, nobody said anything,” Bulawan said. “We don’t know.”
Bulawan said Foster will be missed during the months ahead. “It’s hard, especially coming the holiday part where she always goes to family houses,” she said. “That’s the part that everyone miss about her. She always tried to give something to everybody.”
Toni Schwartz, public information officer for the state Attorney General’s office, said in a written statement McCormick is still being held at Hālawa prison, without bail.
The first-degree murder charge carries a sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Reporter Taylor Nāhulukeaokalani Cozloff contributed to this story.

title: Utah lawsuit accuses Stake of running ‘illegal online casino,’ seeks to recover Utahns’ money
description: In its latest legal move against online gambling working around the state’s comprehensive ban, Utah is suing the overseas companies behind Stake, alleging its all-hours online casino violates state law and harms Utahns. In a 43-page complaint filed in 3rd District Court Tuesday, Utah Attorney General Derek Brown and the Utah Department of Commerce’s Division[...]
text:
The office of the Utah Attorney General at the Capitol in Salt Lake City is pictured on Tuesday, Jan. 16, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)In its latest legal move against online gambling working around the state’s comprehensive ban, Utah is suing the overseas companies behind Stake, alleging its all-hours online casino violates state law and harms Utahns.
In a 43-page complaint filed in 3rd District Court Tuesday, Utah Attorney General Derek Brown and the Utah Department of Commerce’s Division of Consumer Protection are asking a judge to declare the site has violated Utah law and prohibit it from operating in the state. The lawsuit also demands Stake return the money it has made off of Utahns and pay fines.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The complaint names Sweepsteaks Limited of Cyprus and Easygo Group Holdings Pty Ltd of Australia, which operate Stake.us. 
The lawsuit comes less than three weeks after the state filed criminal charges against the founders of Kalshi, including felony counts of online gambling promotion, over the prediction market allowing Utahns to use the platform despite Utah’s gambling ban. 
Meanwhile, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission has in turn filed a legal challenge against Utah, asserting the federal government has sole jurisdiction over derivatives markets and aiming to block the state’s restrictions on companies like Kalshi.
In a news release Tuesday announcing the lawsuit against Stake, Utah Gov. Spencer Cox said “Gambling addiction destroys lives and tears families apart.” 
Utah files criminal charges against Kalshi over operations within the state

“Companies like Stake are putting a casino in every pocket, even targeting children. Gambling is illegal in Utah, and we intend to keep it that way. We will do everything in our power to protect Utah families and hold these companies accountable,” Cox said.
The state’s complaint points to the harms of addiction, particularly for children and teens, saying the site is deliberately trying to draw in young users.
“Stake’s predatory and deceptive tactics are a direct assault on Utah’s values and laws that protect our community, particularly our children and vulnerable populations. By glamorizing gambling through colorful promotions and appealing themes targeted at kids, they exploit impressionable young minds, leading them towards financial peril and addiction,” said Margaret Woolley Busse, commissioner of the Utah Department of Commerce, in the news release.
Stake offers casino-style games, including slots, table games like blackjack, roulette and poker, live dealer games, and proprietary games, according to its app store description. iGamingFuture called it “one of the most recognized sweepstakes casinos in the US, backed by a globally established brand.”



Let us know what you think...


 


The site is a “sweepstakes” or “social casino” where users don’t bet real currency, but users must purchase the platform’s virtual currencies in order to play, leading to real losses, the complaint claims. 
On Nov. 13, less than a week before the case was filed, Stake added Utah to its list of prohibited states, according to the complaint, though investigators from the consumer protection division were still able to access and use the platform as recently as Nov. 16. When investigators logged in that day, a banner informed them the site will only be accessible in Utah until Dec. 7, the complaint says.
Court records did not list an attorney for Sweepsteaks Limited or Easygo Group Holdings. Stake did not respond to an email seeking comment about the lawsuit.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Jackson Council censures Councilman Kenneth Stokes after recent outburst
description: Jackson Ward 3 City Councilman Kenneth Stokes sits in silence during a press conference on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, after a disruption he caused at the Nov. 3 council meeting.
text:
The Jackson City Council censured Councilman Kenneth Stokes on Tuesday for remarks he recently made during a contentious debate over data centers, in which he called one woman a “bitch” and told another woman, who was wearing a hijab, to “take the rags out y’all hair, y’all not Muslim.”
The council did not debate the resolution, which was adopted in a 5-1 vote, with Stokes the sole vote against. The censure was a rare rebuke to the longest-serving member of the City Council. Stokes has a history of chaotic statements and insulting those who disagree with him. 
A smattering of applause broke out in the council chambers after the vote. The resolution did not impose a monetary penalty against Stokes but declared his comments “rude, disrespectful, insulting and indecent.” 
Last week, Stokes responded to a letter from City Council President Vernon Hartley asking for an apology by threatening to sue his colleagues if they adopted the resolution. At a press conference, Stokes’ attorney, Dennis Sweet III, said the censure would violate the councilman’s right to free speech. 
Attorney Dennis Sweet III, left, sits next to his client, Jackson Ward 3 City Councilman Kenneth Stokes, as they prepare for a press conference on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026.  Credit: Aaron Lampley/Mississippi Today
Stokes doubled down on his refusal to apologize two days later in an interview with WLBT.
“Hell no. Hell naw. Hell to the naw,” Stokes said. “Kenny ain’t apologizing for nothing because I have done nothing wrong.”
Stokes did not arrive at Tuesday’s council meeting until after the public comment period, during which a number of Jacksonians addressed the council, urging members to pass the resolution. 
“Black women should never have to fight for their humanity in the very chambers where our ancestors fought for our representation,” said Candace Abdul-Tawwab, the executive director of the nonprofit Mississippi for a Just World and the woman who Stokes told to take off her hijab.
Norma Michael, a neighbor of Stokes who organized a petition calling on the council to censure him for comments he had made to Councilman Brian Grizzell, spoke during the public comment period. 
Jackson City Councilman Kenneth Stokes speaks during a council meeting at City Hall in Jackson on Tuesday, April 21, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“Citizens should be able to participate in local government without being subjected to personal insults, humiliation or attacks on their faith,” she said.
Wanda Evers, a Hinds County Supervisor, called Stokes a “coward” for not attending the public comment period. 
Stokes, known for wearing oversized suits and a hat emblazoned with his last name, was first elected to the City Council in 1989. Since then, his comments have repeatedly made national news and whose style has often drawn comparisons to President Donald Trump.
Tuesday’s censure is not the first time Stokes has been reprimanded for his statements during council meetings. In 2003, Stokes’ colleagues censured him after he claimed that an unnamed member had requested a bribe from a permit applicant, according to archival news reports. 
Earlier in the evening, the council voted against Stoke’s ordinance lifting a moratorium on data centers.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: RI House panel advances nomination of Matos for Supreme Court
description: Luis M. Matos on Tuesday affirmed his support for abortion rights, telling lawmakers he has considered himself pro-choice for many years as he seeks to get a lifetime appointment on the state’s highest bench. “That wasn’t always my perspective,” the 62-year-old Rhode Island Supreme Court nominee  told members of the House Committee on Judiciary. “But […]
text:
Luis M. Matos, nominee for the Rhode Island Supreme Court, arrives at the State House basement for his vetting by the House Committee on Judiciary on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Luis M. Matos on Tuesday affirmed his support for abortion rights, telling lawmakers he has considered himself pro-choice for many years as he seeks to get a lifetime appointment on the state’s highest bench.
“That wasn’t always my perspective,” the 62-year-old Rhode Island Supreme Court nominee  told members of the House Committee on Judiciary. “But that is my perspective today and that’s my personal opinion — I am not making any statement about what the law is and what that what the law is not.”
Those assurances were enough for the Democratic chair of the House Judiciary Committee to join the panel in unanimously advancing Matos’ nomination to the full chamber for consideration.
Gov. Dan McKee nominated Matos in August to fill the Supreme Court seat vacated by Justice Maureen McKenna Goldberg, who retired in March after almost 29 years on the bench. The nomination was formally submitted to the House and Senate for advice and consent Nov. 4, triggering a 60-day window for lawmakers in both chambers to act.
Before Matos’ formal nomination, members of the House and Senate judiciary committees received an email from a Baltimore woman who became pregnant while dating Matos in the 1990s and claimed he had opposed her decision to have an abortion.
The Oct. 10 email from Amanda Nelson to the House and Senate Judiciary committees described her relationship with Matos in Washington, D.C., in 1994, when she said she became pregnant and he urged her not to have an abortion. Nelson said she ultimately terminated the pregnancy after Matos declined her offer to raise the child as a single father.
Rep. Carol Hagan McEntee, a South Kingstown Democrat who chairs the House Committee on Judiciary, asked Matos whether Nelson’s account called into question his personal views on reproductive rights — and whether lawmakers should have concerns about how he might defend or adjudicate those rights as a Supreme Court justice.
“We fought long and hard for the right to choose, for the women’s reproductive rights in this body,” McEntee said.
Matos responded that he had tried throughout his career as a prosecutor, civil servant and judge to keep his personal opinions out of public discussion. He said that was important both to ensure he ruled impartially and to maintain the appearance of impartiality.
Matos has served as an associate justice on Rhode Island Superior Court since 2012, when he was appointed by then-Gov. Lincoln Chafee. A Providence resident who immigrated to the U.S. from Portugal as a child, Matos previously worked as a federal prosecutor in Rhode Island and Delaware.
“I never lost the sensation, the utter sense of pride when I would walk into the courtroom the first time … and I stood in front of the judge and I introduced myself and I said that I was there to represent the United States of America,” Matos told lawmakers.
He spent much of his introduction looking back at the journey that brought his family from Portugal to Providence — and the sacrifices his parents made to give him opportunities they never had.
He recalled growing up in Fox Point’s Portuguese immigrant community, learning English in a bilingual elementary school and watching his parents work factory and domestic jobs to support the family. 
When his mother developed lupus while he was in high school, his parents still found a way to help him attend Brown. 
“I went to a place that was in my old neighborhood’s backyard, but could not have been further from any universe that I was familiar with at the time,” he said.
Rep. Carol Hagan McEntee, chair of the House Committee on Judiciary, stands behind the committee dais with other panel members before a Nov. 17, 2026, hearing on the nomination of Superior Court Associate Justice Luis M. Matos to the Rhode Island Supreme Court. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
Praised by judges
McKee repeatedly praised Matos as the “most qualified” of the five applicants he interviewed when he announced his judicial selection Aug. 12. 
Top federal and state judges echoed those sentiments in letters of support for Matos’ nomination. Many reiterated those comments in the State House basement Tuesday.
“Justice Matos has demonstrated an intellectual honesty throughout his judicial career,” Rhode Island Supreme Court Chief Justice Paul Suttell told the committee.
Suttell highlighted Matos’ work on the Judiciary’s Committee on Racial and Ethnic Fairness in the Courts, particularly his efforts to establish a debt review program that reduced court-related debts for formerly incarcerated people based on their ability to pay. 
“Justice Matos has been an invaluable member of that committee, displaying a resolute commitment to the principles of equal justice for all persons,” Suttell said.
Superior Court Presiding Justice Joseph A. Montalbano vouched for Matos’ honesty, saying his colleagues could rely on his representations about his beliefs.
“Without a doubt, Justice Matos is an honest judge,” Montalbano said.
Goldberg, whose seat Matos is seeking to fill, stopped by the State House basement for the hearing. Matos said he was humbled by her presence, praising her as “a true lioness” of the legal profession and saying her contributions would be missed.
“The fact that she is here has truly humbled me,” Matos said. “I will forever be grateful to her for her being here today.”
The full House is scheduled to vote on Matos’ nomination Dec. 1. The Senate Judiciary Committee is scheduled to hold a hearing on his nomination Nov. 30.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Jeta: Hawaiʻi Can’t Make Arts Education Soar If It Is Flying Blind
description: The people of Oʻahu have spoken: Data stewardship belongs in local government. This month, 71.1% of voters said “yes” to Question 15, establishing a permanent Office of Data and Innovation under the Honolulu City Charter. The office gives the City and County of Honolulu’s chief data officer a charter-protected home, shielded from the whims of […]
text:
The people of Oʻahu have spoken: Data stewardship belongs in local government.
This month, 71.1% of voters said “yes” to Question 15, establishing a permanent Office of Data and Innovation under the Honolulu City Charter. The office gives the City and County of Honolulu’s chief data officer a charter-protected home, shielded from the whims of future luddites in the mayor’s office.
The outcome signals a growing appetite for data-driven government. For Hawaiʻi’s arts, however, that enthusiasm came with more strings attached in the Legislature.
Consider the failed House Bill 2117, which would have established the Mapping of Arts Data for Education (MADE) task force to inventory arts programs on a public geographic information system (GIS) map: who’s offering what, where, and to whom. The data could expose gaps in K-12 arts education and inform funding decisions.
Despite the bill’s demise, the initiative survived through a sister measure: House Concurrent Resolution 162, introduced in the session’s final weeks and later adopted.
Same task force. Same ambition. Only this time, the resolution requested a task force rather than mandating it by law. A weaker legal commitment, but a common fallback for bills that fail to pass on their first attempt.
Now, the newly assembled task force must make the case for investing in itself before it can make the case for investing in the arts.
From Bass to Bill
HCR 162 calls for 13 representatives from Hawaiʻi’s arts, education, government, and data sectors, with room for additional members, to build the state’s first arts education database.
Randy Wong, president and CEO of Hawaiʻi Youth Symphony (HYS), is designated to convene and chair the task force. For Wong, 45, the mission is personal.



Ideas showcases stories, opinion and analysis about Hawaiʻi, from the state’s sharpest thinkers, to stretch our collective thinking about a problem or an issue. Email news@civilbeat.org to submit an idea or an essay.


Read More

Growing up in Honolulu, he struggled with a severe speech impediment and was teased for his slight frame and “stick legs.”
“If you don’t feel sure of yourself, if you’re worried about what people think of you, you don’t want to participate in class,” Wong said. “It’s hard to feel like you really have any self-worth.”
That began to change in third grade, when he picked up the double bass in his required music class. All it took was a simple request from the teacher.
“Randy, will you pluck the string of the bass?” he recalled his teacher asking. “Do it again. I like that.”
For the first time, Wong felt comfortable participating. Someone genuinely wanted to hear his voice.
Wong went on to play bass in HYS, study music at Boston’s New England Conservatory, and earn a master’s degree in Arts in Education from the Harvard Graduate School of Education.
He returned home in 2012 as HYS’s executive director and joined the Hawaiʻi Symphony Orchestra.
Chamber Music Hawaiʻi performs with Hawaiʻi Youth Symphony students at Moanalua Public Library.  (Courtesy: Hawaiʻi Youth Symphony)
“I’m back home, and I feel like it’s my duty,” Wong said.  “It’s my calling to help other kids access music because of what it did for me, and what it did for so many of my friends.”
That sense of purpose planted the seed for the task force.
Nearly a decade ago, Wong sought to identify music “deserts” across Hawaiʻi, only to discover that neither the Department of Education (DOE) nor nonprofit arts leaders had comprehensive data on K-12 arts offerings.
Wong brought the problem to lawmakers in 2025, including Rep. Jeanne Kapela, chair of the House Committee on Culture and Arts. The following session, she introduced HB 2117 and later HCR 162, both proposing a task force to establish a statewide arts education database.
Connecting the Dots
The other organizations named in HCR 162 bring different perspectives and expertise to the task force, helping ensure no single organization’s interests dominate.
The State Foundation on Culture and the Arts (SFCA) and Hawaiʻi Arts Alliance (HAA) contribute knowledge of existing arts programs. The DOE, along with private and charter school representatives, offers a fuller picture of arts education across the islands.

ESOL students work on identity-based self-portraits under the guidance of teaching artist Zoe Liu during an Artists-in-the Schools residency at Stevenson Middle School.  (Courtesy: Hawaiʻi Arts Alliance)

And because the goal is a GIS map, Hawaiʻi Data Collaborative (HDC) and the state’s GIS program manager get seats at the table, too.
Rep. Kapela and Sen. Chris Lee, who helped advance the measures through the Legislature, are also represented on the task force through their positions as arts committee chairs.
All task force members are volunteers.
Thomas Lee represents HDC, a nonprofit promoting data access and public decision-making. As director of government partnerships, Lee submitted the charter amendment proposal that became Question 15.
Lee’s background is in data, not the arts, but his experience with HYS drew him to the task force.
“I personally advocated for it just because I grew up playing music,” Lee said. “I know if someone is exposed to music in the DOE system or in a private school, you’re more likely to succeed in school. But we don’t have a lot of data to support that locally.”
For Lee, data helps move beyond intuition when evaluating policies.
“No one’s just basing it off gut or experience,” he said. “We want the data to help us inform whether or not policies or initiatives are actually making the impact that they’re intended to.”
Gaye Humphrey, HAA’s executive director and task force representative, wants arts mapping to expose disparities in access. HAA expands arts education through programs like Artists-in-the-Schools, in partnership with SFCA.
Gevanie-Denise Reyes, a Nanakuli Elementary School fourth grader, rehearses in the Nanakuli High and Intermediate School Multi-Purpose Cafe in 2024 in Waianae.  (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2024)
“With data, we can really understand where opportunities are for arts learning, where the gaps are,” she said. 
“Does a child growing up on Molokaʻi have access to the same range of arts opportunities as a child in Honolulu? If the answer is no, then we need to be thinking about how we can solve that.”
The task force also hopes to break down institutional data silos. Until now, no statewide effort has attempted to bring records together for public access.
“It’s natural that certain organizations or systems collect data for their own purposes and use it only internally,” Wong added.
“There just hasn’t been really a thinking around what it will look like when we have open data and use it for a larger purpose than just internal metrics.”
Deadline Without a Dime

Teaching artist Zoe Liu (center) guides ESOL students through painting techniques during an Artists-in-the Schools residency at Stevenson Middle School, supported by the State Foundation on Culture and the Arts and Hawaiʻi Arts Alliance.  (Courtesy: Hawaiʻi Arts Alliance)

Neither HB 2117 nor HCR 162 provided funding, although Rep. Kapela’s committee asked House Finance to consider an appropriation.
Under HCR 162, the task force is expected to deliver initial findings on Hawaiʻi’s music and dance programs before the 2028 legislative session, followed by a comprehensive report on all arts disciplines before 2030.
The resolution is nonbinding, with no clear consequences if named organizations stop participating. Still, Wong says attendance and engagement have remained consistent since monthly meetings began in September.
Members have begun designing a survey to inventory arts programs and consolidate the information into a statewide GIS map. But getting that information won’t be straightforward.
Lee says some organizations may be reluctant to share data for community use. Wong and Humphrey say even DOE representatives struggle to extract arts education information from the department’s systems.

Sculptures and drawings created by students in the Kahauiki Village After-School Arts Enrichment program, which provides arts instruction during after-school hours and school breaks.  (Courtesy: Hawaiʻi Arts Alliance)

With little arts education data publicly available on DOE’s website, much must be gathered directly from schools.
While middle and high school music programs are easier to identify, elementary offerings are harder to track. Many schools rely on general education teachers or visiting artists rather than dedicated arts specialists, leaving much of that instruction unaccounted for in DOE staffing records.
Even basic questions, such as which schools employ arts specialists, what disciplines they teach, and how many students they serve, take considerable effort to answer.
Despite these challenges, Wong remains optimistic.
“It’s going great, great, great,” he enthused. “We’re making progress every month. This is a very thoughtful and action-oriented group of people.”
To make the case for future funding, though, the task force must first demonstrate what it can accomplish. Can dedication alone carry volunteers meeting once a month through their first report?
In the end, the data will tell us.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Yellowstone National Park could increase bison removal
description: Advocacy groups say Yellowstone National Park plans to cull 1,500 bison from the park, an effort to control the population they say goes too far. There are about 6,000 bison in the park. Slightly more than 900 bison were culled from Nov. 1, 2024, through Oct. 31, 2025, according to the Interagency Bison Management Plan […]
text:
Bison move north out of Lamar Valley in Yellowstone National Park (Photo by Jacob Frank of the National Park Service | Photo via Flickr). Advocacy groups say Yellowstone National Park plans to cull 1,500 bison from the park, an effort to control the population they say goes too far.
There are about 6,000 bison in the park. Slightly more than 900 bison were culled from Nov. 1, 2024, through Oct. 31, 2025, according to the Interagency Bison Management Plan annual report.
The park culls because of worries about how many bison the park can support and fears of transmission of disease from the bison to cattle on the outskirts of Yellowstone National Park. 
But advocacy groups say the park is making decisions that are not based on best available science.
They note there is no confirmed brucellosis transmission from bison to cattle, and they argue the park itself estimates a much higher capacity for bison.
Yellowstone National Park announced the target during a meeting last month of the Interagency Bison Management Plan, a group made up of state, federal and tribal officials, according to advocacy groups whose members attended and spoke to the Daily Montanan. The Mountain Journal also reported the same number.
A video of the meeting was not available on the interagency website, and Yellowstone National Park did not return a Daily Montanan request for comment regarding the number of bison expected to be culled. 
A timeline for culling also wasn’t immediately clear, but the park has previously said it can take place over a single winter or can be further spread out. 
The bison management plan is the subject of a lawsuit brought by Alliance for the Wild Rockies and Council on Fish & Wildlife, which says the park can hold as many as 10,000 bison and the national park isn’t using the best available science in the plan. Advocacy groups have said the 10,000 number comes from the park itself, and wildlife researchers have said the same thing. 
“The Park Service’s bison management plan is based on outdated assumptions that thousands of bison need to be slaughtered to stop brucellosis infections in cattle,” Alliance for the Wild Rockies Executive Director Mike Garrity said in a press release. “That is no longer accepted science.”
Yellowstone National Park states its target bison population is from 3,500 to 6,000.
“Bison are not allowed to move freely outside Yellowstone due to fears they might transmit brucellosis to cattle and out of concerns about competition with cattle for grass, human safety, and property damage,” a National Parks Service webpage says. “Elk are also infected with brucellosis, but their movements outside the park are not restricted.”
In press statements, Roam Free Nation blamed the state’s cattle industry for pushing for the increase in bison removal, particularly around brucellosis, a disease that impacts bison and elk and can be spread to cattle. However, there have been no documented transmissions of brucellosis from bison to cows.
In court documents filed in the bison management suit, Alliance For the Wild Rockies has argued there has been a significant reduction in cattle close to Yellowstone since the late 1990s.
The Daily Montanan reached out to the Montana Cattleman’s Association this week about its position on bison and cattle, but those requests for comment went unreturned. The Daily Montanan also reached out to Gov. Greg Gianforte, who has pressured the park to reduce the size of its bison herd. Those media requests also went unanswered. 
Gianforte has previously said the National Parks Service has not listened to concerns the state needs to protect its cattle industry.
But Roam Free Nation said the cattle industry has undue influence.
“Yellowstone just can’t help but cave under pressure from Montana’s livestock industry,” Stephany Seay, cofounder of Roam Free Nation, a bison advocacy group, said in a press release. “It’s not ‘what’s best for the buffalo as a species,’ it’s not ‘what do the people want?’ Yellowstone just wants to get Montana’s cattle interests off their backs, to hell with the damage.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: ‘Handing them out like candy’: NC GOP lawmakers give new jobs to outgoing colleagues
description: North Carolina lawmakers approved a package of appointments Tuesday, handing eight outgoing Republicans in the General Assembly jobs on public boards and other powerful positions. The appointments bill passed the Senate by a 28-17 vote. The House of Representatives approved the measure with 80 members voting in favor and 34 opposed. The bill includes dozens [...]
text:
NC Senate leader Phil Berger, R-Rockingham, is surrounded by other Republican senators as he talks about a bill suspending the state's gas tax. (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)North Carolina lawmakers approved a package of appointments Tuesday, handing eight outgoing Republicans in the General Assembly jobs on public boards and other powerful positions.
The appointments bill passed the Senate by a 28-17 vote. The House of Representatives approved the measure with 80 members voting in favor and 34 opposed.
The bill includes dozens of appointments recommended by Senate President Phil Berger, R-Rockingham, and House Speaker Destin Hall, R-Caldwell. Among those named are eight sitting members of the General Assembly, including six representatives and two senators, all Republicans who lost their seats Nov. 3.
The top parting gift went to outgoing Rep. Michael Schietzelt, R-Wake. Schietzelt, an attorney, was given a special Superior Court judge seat until 2034.  He clerked for former Republican N.C. Supreme Court Chief Justice Mark Martin, but has no experience on the bench.
The House appointments include Rep. Timothy Reeder, R-Pitt, a doctor, to the North Carolina Institute of Medicine Board, and Rep. Dennis Riddell, R-Alamance, a former GOP party official, to the State Ethics Commission.
Other House members named include Reps. Anna Ferguson, Brian Biggs and Hugh Blackwell, who were appointed to boards or commissions focused on higher education and public schools.
Democrats appear to win the NC House majority and gain seats in the Senate

Hall said most of the appointments are volunteer positions, and he worked to identify members he thought had strong backgrounds and would make good appointees.
“It’s always the case when you have outgoing members, and even former members, who go on to some of those boards and commissions,” he said.
But some Democrats questioned the appointments, calling them political favoritism and accusing Republicans of cronyism. Sen. Democratic Leader Sydney Batch, D-Wake, called it “frustrating.”
“After an election ends the way it did, then all of a sudden everybody gets an appointment,” Batch said. “They’re handing them out like candy.”
In the Senate, Berger recommended Sen. Lisa Barnes, R-Nash, for appointment to the state Board of Agriculture, and Sen. Michael Lee, R-New Hanover, to the North Carolina High School Redesign Board.
Berger said Sen. Lee had a long track record on education policy, and Sen. Barnes had been “deeply involved” in agriculture for years.
But on the floor, Sen. Val Applewhite, D-Cumberland, said she was surprised to see so many names of elected officials who lost their races resurfacing as appointees.
“I don’t know if this is a tradition that we do here,” she said. “It feels to me that the voices of North Carolinians are not being heard.”
Both the Senate and the House also unanimously approved two nominees from Gov. Josh Stein, Caitlin Poe and Richard Worf, to serve as special Superior Court judges.
The appointments follow the midterm elections earlier this month, in which Democrats gained enough seats in the House for a majority and flipped four in the state Senate.
Democrats have not held a majority in the House since 2010.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Military veterans to feds: no data centers on public lands
description: Add military veterans to the growing force demanding a data center reckoning.  A national coalition called Veterans for Public Lands is calling on federal powers to immediately pause data center development on public lands until safeguards are in place.  “These are our lands,” said Gregg Bafundo, a senior advisor of the coalition and former ranger […]
text:
An explosion of data center facilities, including the one pictured here in northeast Oregon on May 18 have been built along the Columbia River Gorge during the last few years. (Photo by Jordan Gale/Oregon Capital Chronicle)Add military veterans to the growing force demanding a data center reckoning. 
A national coalition called Veterans for Public Lands is calling on federal powers to immediately pause data center development on public lands until safeguards are in place. 
“These are our lands,” said Gregg Bafundo, a senior advisor of the coalition and former ranger of the Okanogan Wenatchee National Forest. “If the government’s going to do anything with these, they have to ask the permission of the American people. And right now, the American people don’t want data centers on our public lands.”
The coalition launched on Veterans Day, a week after the November midterm elections where at least 69 veterans won election to Congress.
“The reality is that veterans themselves … we’re not just a piece of the American pie, we are the American pie,” Bafundo said. 
“We’re here to protect (public lands) just like we protected (them) in the United States when we were on active duty. The mission, in many regards, hasn’t changed.” 
U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum speaks on May 19. 2026, at the Alaska Sustainable Energy Conference in Anchorage. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
The coalition is calling on U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to begin an immediate moratorium. Burgum, a former North Dakota governor, reportedly has tens of millions of dollars invested in AI companies, according to a Propublica investigation. 
Last week, Burgum’s department vowed to sell off public lands to states or tribes in a five-year strategic plan. 
“Of course he wants to sell them. I mean, the corruption is absolutely blatant,” Bafundo said, noting that Burgum has not responded to the veterans’ request. 
“They want to dump these lands to the states knowing full well that states have to balance a budget,” he said. 
Veterans for Public Lands is also calling on the upcoming Congress to advance moratorium legislation on federal public lands within its first 100 days in office. It also wants guardrails in place during development, which include public input, environmental review and tribal consultation. A bipartisan bill slated for a passage vote in the U.S. Senate this week would weaken those protections. 
Veterans for Public Lands is opening the doors for other veterans to get involved in advocacy work. It is now accepting applications for its Defenders Corps, which trains veterans how to use their voices to help protect and tell the story of America’s public lands.

title: Hand count in southwest Georgia legislative race confirms Republican incumbent’s win
description: Election officials in Seminole County completed a hand count of a southwest Georgia House district’s election results after a review from the secretary of state’s office found a discrepancy between the number of voters who checked in and the number of ballots cast. Local election officials discovered a memory card that had not been properly […]
text:
A voter card is shown inserted into one of Georgia's ballot-marking devices. Election workers in Bartow County, Georgia, conducted their pre-election tests of the voting equipment on Oct. 6, 2026. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderElection officials in Seminole County completed a hand count of a southwest Georgia House district’s election results after a review from the secretary of state’s office found a discrepancy between the number of voters who checked in and the number of ballots cast.
Local election officials discovered a memory card that had not been properly uploaded. 
Republican state Rep. Gerald Greene of Cuthbert was initially trailing Democratic contractor Harry James by less than 100 votes, but after the totals had been updated with the additional votes, Greene took the lead by 260 votes.
The county’s hand count confirmed those results.
“The Elections Superintendent requested an additional Seminole County Elections audit for the State House of Representatives District 154 race; a hand count of all ballots and the votes cast in that race. The ballot results matched the numbers Seminole County Certified last Friday, November 6, 2026,” said Seminole County elections supervisor Ronald D. Foskey in an email.
Foskey added that he “felt it was of utmost importance to convey transparency and demonstrate integrity in our election system.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Foskey said that six Seminole County citizens participated in the hand count and that all citizens physically touching ballots were sworn in to count ballots. Two were appointed by the county Superior Court, one was Republican leaning and another was Democratic leaning, and the remaining two were volunteer citizens. 
He also provided a list of people who were in attendance for the hand count, which included James himself and two representatives for Greene, representatives from the Carter Center, a representative from the Seminole County GOP and a representative from the Donalsonville News.
Harry James. Contributed photo
Despite the results of the hand count, James said he is not conceding, at least not yet, citing an ongoing investigation from Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger looking into the root of the error.
“Until that due process finishes,” James said, “I won’t make no prejudgments on what I should do or need to do. We’ll wait till we get all the facts and we make decisions based on facts, not based on what we think or feel.”
James said that his campaign will explore avenues outside of the courtroom to challenge the results, such as asking for a recount once the results are certified because he feels that deciding to concede before knowing exactly what happened won’t address mistrust in the election system among voters in the district. He said that the error is contributing to that mistrust and that this election is no longer about him, saying that whether he wins or loses “is not the issue for [him] anymore.”
“There’s a lot of questions that people out there that they ask me that I can’t answer. The general public has a lot of questions on how this happened. I can’t answer any of it, and there’s a lot of raised questions about how the results were reported,” James said.
He pushed back when asked if his refusal to concede after county officials’ hand count confirmed the results feeds into that mistrust, saying that “people had that distrust before this election ever happened.”
Gerald Greene. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
“This race did not create that doubt. This race did not start that doubt. In a lot of people’s minds, this just confirmed what they were thinking,” James said.
Greene called it an “an unfortunate situation in Seminole for those individuals.”
“Nothing points to any problem – that it was intentional or anything,” Greene said.
Raffensperger, who is a Republican, announced on the Friday after the election that his office would examine how the memory card was overlooked and what steps can be taken to avoid a similar incident in the future.
“This oversight didn’t just affect the numbers – it changed who was leading an election. That is unacceptable, and we intend to find out exactly how it happened,” Raffensperger said earlier this month.
House Democrats currently hold a fragile 91-seat majority with this race and two others still pending. Another southwest Georgia race is headed to a Dec. 1 runoff.
