name: VTDigger
title: ‘I just wasn’t thinking it through’: Ex-deputy permanently banned from police work for racist message
description:
The Vermont Criminal Justice Council imposed the sanction over arguments by the former officer’s attorney seeking a lesser punishment.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘I just wasn’t thinking it through’: Ex-deputy permanently banned from police work for racist message.
text:
Rutland County Sheriff Department on January 28, 2026. Photo by Greta Solssa/VTDigger

A former Rutland County Sheriff’s Department deputy fired earlier this year for sending a racist message in a group chat to fellow deputies has now been banned from working as a law enforcement officer in Vermont.
The Vermont Criminal Justice Council, the body that regulates police in the state, voted unanimously Tuesday to permanently revoke Ryder Paskevich’s law enforcement certification. 
The vote followed a hearing where Paskevich and his attorney pushed for a lesser sanction of a written warning or revocation of his law enforcement certification with a chance of recertification in the future.
The meeting took place with some members in person at the Vermont Fire Academy in Pittsford and others appearing by video.
Paskevich had admitted that his conduct represented misconduct by engaging in an “egregious act that demonstrates discrimination based on race,” according to a stipulation reached ahead of the hearing, leaving the only contested matter the sanction to be imposed.
Christopher Perkett, the council’s associate general counsel, argued for permanent revocation of Paskevich’s law enforcement certification in Vermont. 
“This wasn’t just a tasteless joke. This was overt racism,” Perkett told council members. “This was a caucasian individual as a police officer in a white hood shaped like a KKK hood opining that every Black individual that they saw was a criminal.” 
According to a stipulation reached between the parties ahead of the hearing, Paskevich admitted he was part of a Facebook chat group with other members of the department called “Mulligans” that was used to arrange golf outings and “other chitchat.”
Paskevich sent a message in January to the group that was an “animated video where a white male in a pointed white hood talks to another officer, explaining that he can identify a criminal just by looking at them,” according to the stipulation.
“The people this man identified as criminals were all black individuals,” the document stated. “The other officer was chiding the officer with the hood for his arrest record of all black individuals.” 
Another deputy in the chat group then confronted Paskevich, writing, “Where in the actual f— do you find s— like this!” adding, “This is racist and discriminatory you bigot a–h—,” according to council records.
Paskevich then responded with the dismissive message, “womp womp,” the records stated. 
Paskevich later deleted both of his messages, and all the officers left the chat, according to the documents. The incident was reported by other members of the chat to superiors, and following an internal investigation, Paskevich was fired, according to the documents.

Ryder Paskevich, a former Rutland County Sheriff’s Department deputy, far left seated at table, testifies Tuesday during a hearing before the Vermont Criminal Justice Council. Screenshot  by Alan J. Keays/VTDigger

Lisa Ryan, community inclusion director for the Vermont Criminal Justice Council, testified Tuesday that permanent revocation should be imposed. 
“In your opinion,” Perkett asked Ryan, “how would a written warning be seen by the community?”
“I think it would be seen as inadequate and as a slap on the wrist,” Ryan replied. 
“And in your opinion, how about the ability to become reinstated?” Perkett asked.
“I think the public would see that there’s no integrity, that there’s no accountability,” Ryan responded. 
Wendy Radcliff, Paskevich’s attorney, argued for a lesser sanction rather than permanent revocation.
“Ryder is a 23-year-old that made a bad mistake,” Radcliff told the council members. 
“You should not foreclose all opportunity that he would have in the future to retrain and be certified again, recognizing that this will trail him forever,” Radcliff added. 
Paskevich also testified during the hearing, telling the council he understood it was a serious matter.
“I am not disagreeing that it was inappropriate to share,” he said. “I stipulated to that — that it is a violation — and I am remorseful for it.”
Asked why he posted the message, he replied, “To put it simply, I just wasn’t thinking it through. I had an initial perception of the content of which I was sharing that very shortly thereafter realized was not how it was perceived, was not how the video was, and upon realizing that, I attempted to take steps to rectify it by shortly thereafter deleting the video.”
Paskevich also talked about the impact the incident has had on him.
“It’s something that I will live with and carry throughout my life, especially in a small community like Vermont,” he said, adding, “I live with that, with that, with that shame, with that guilt of having done this, for the rest of my life.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘I just wasn’t thinking it through’: Ex-deputy permanently banned from police work for racist message.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota lawmakers receive award for bipartisan work on school lunch bill
description: State Rep. Kadyn Wittman, D-Sioux Falls, and state Sen. Brandon Wipf, R-Huron, received the Cherisse Eatmon Collective Impact Award on Monday from the Future Caucus, a bipartisan group supporting millennial and Gen Z lawmakers. “These leaders remind us that politics doesn’t have to be a zero-sum game,” said Layla Zaidane, president and CEO of Future […]
text:
South Dakota State Rep. Kadyn Wittman, D-Sioux Falls, left, and state Sen. Brandon Wipf, R-Huron, pose with their Cherisse Eatmon Collective Impact Awards from the Future Caucus on Nov. 16, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Photo courtesy of Future Caucus)https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/111726-School-Lunch-Bill-Award-web.mp3
 Listen to an audio version of this story produced by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: See below for a downloadable version with a host intro script.
State Rep. Kadyn Wittman, D-Sioux Falls, and state Sen. Brandon Wipf, R-Huron, received the Cherisse Eatmon Collective Impact Award on Monday from the Future Caucus, a bipartisan group supporting millennial and Gen Z lawmakers.
“These leaders remind us that politics doesn’t have to be a zero-sum game,” said Layla Zaidane, president and CEO of Future Caucus, in a news release. “These lawmakers show what’s possible when we prioritize practical solutions.”
The South Dakota lawmakers successfully co-sponsored House Bill 1082, which stops school districts from charging students’ families for breakfast or lunch if they qualify for reduced-price meals under federal income guidelines. The law shifts those costs to state government and will cost the state about $593,000 a year, according to an estimate prepared by the state’s Legislative Research Council. Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden signed the bill into law earlier this year.
The Future Caucus celebrated Wipf and Wittman in Washington, D.C., for their across-the-aisle work, including the use of a procedural maneuver to force a full vote of the Senate after a Senate budget committee tabled the bill.
Support from governor means state will cover gap in reduced-price school meals

Wittman had proposed similar legislation over the prior three years, including bills for students on reduced-price meal plans in 2024 and 2025. In 2023, she attempted to make school lunches free for all students in the state.
“I have big plans and goals to expand this policy in the future to serve more kids and families. But just for now, to have received this recognition and to know that we crossed the finish line,” she said, “it’s a crazy feeling, to be honest.”
She also thanked the advocates who supported the legislation and Wipf for “being a champion for school lunch in the Senate.”
Wipf said he “played a small role” with this year’s legislation and thanked Wittman and advocates who spoke in support of the bill throughout the legislative process.
As a first-time lawmaker trying to persuade other legislators, Wipf said he wanted to emphasize the small cost, which he previously said seems like “pennies compared to the enormous investment that we make in education.”
“I just tried to get them to see this as a small thing that we could do to protect the investment that we were making every year in our children, and I think that when kids are fed well, they learn better,” Wipf told South Dakota Searchlight. “And that argument found purchase with a lot of my colleagues.”
Prior to the new law’s passage, students whose families meet income qualifications for the reduced-price program paid 30 cents for each breakfast and 40 cents for each lunch. The rest of the cost is covered by the federal government, which also covers the entire cost of free meals for students whose families meet stricter income limits.
More than a third of the state’s public school students receive free or reduced-price school meals, according to the South Dakota Department of Education.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas lawmakers propose repealing 2025 measure on utility projects that’s drawn criticism
description: A bipartisan group of Arkansas legislators hopes to repeal a 2025 law on utility projects that was hailed by supporters as needed to attract data centers and other businesses but has been blamed by critics for higher energy bills. Eight Republicans and two Democrats co-sponsored legislation filed this week to repeal the Generating Arkansas Jobs […]
text:
(From left) Sens. Clint Penzo and Ben Gilmore listen to their colleague Sen. Jonathan Dismang, during a meeting of the Arkansas Senate on March 6, 2025. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)A bipartisan group of Arkansas legislators hopes to repeal a 2025 law on utility projects that was hailed by supporters as needed to attract data centers and other businesses but has been blamed by critics for higher energy bills.
Eight Republicans and two Democrats co-sponsored legislation filed this week to repeal the Generating Arkansas Jobs Act of 2025, which allows utilities to charge ratepayers for power generation that has not yet been built.
The law was signed last year by Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders and praised by utility companies but has faced questions in the Legislature over the past several months. 
The legislation allows electric utilities to recover the costs of building new power generation before it comes online via a “strategic investment rider,” which shows up on bills as an extra charge. Before the law, the utilities couldn’t recover those costs until after the power plants were completed.
Arkansas lawmakers question utility on data center projects, impact on ratepayers

Senate Bill 2, which was introduced by Springdale Republican and Senate Majority Whip Clint Penzo would repeal the law — including its provisions for the strategic investment riders.
The Generating Arkansas Jobs Act’s supporters said the law insulates Arkansas ratepayers from rapid increases in power bills by allowing utilities to gradually add the costs associated with building new generation to the bills. But opponents of the law have said it puts ratepayers on the hook to finance expensive power projects that may never see completion, and that the law ultimately benefits utilities at the expense of consumer protection.
Sam Dubke, a spokesperson for Sanders, did not say whether the governor supported the effort to repeal the law in a statement.
“Arkansas’ energy infrastructure is aging and needs to be upgraded or replaced to maintain the grid our citizens rely on, and Governor Sanders looks forward to working with the legislature to make those necessary investments while still keeping Arkansas’ utility rates among the lowest in the nation,” Dubke said.
The 2025 law’s main sponsor, former Republican Sen. Jonathan Dismang of Searcy, resigned from his seat this year to take a job as the vice president of external affairs for Arkansas Electric Cooperatives. Entergy Arkansas’ former CEO, Hugh McDonald, currently serves as Arkansas’ commerce secretary.
Entergy Arkansas spokesperson Matt Ramsey said the utility would monitor the bill but did not say whether the company opposes it. 
“Our priority is to work with the members of the General Assembly to answer questions and address any concerns about how the law works and the benefits it provides to customers,” Ramsey said in a statement.
Lauren Waldrip, the executive director of the Arkansas Advanced Energy Association and a longtime skeptic of the law, said concerns about the 2025 law have “only grown” since its passage. A full repeal of the law, she said, is necessary — as is “a broader conversation about energy policy.”
“Arkansas needs laws to enable market-based solutions that encourage new generation, protect existing ratepayers, and ensure we can meet growing energy demand without sacrificing affordability,” Waldrip said in a statement.
Lawmakers have also expressed reservations and outright regret about the law in recent months after the first extra charges under the act to pay for three power generation projects began to appear on the bills of Entergy Arkansas customers. 
One of those projects is slated to provide power to Google’s West Memphis data center. Google is paying hundreds of millions to Entergy to cover the costs of supplying electricity to its facility, but the utility isn’t directly applying those payments to the construction of power generation, which prompted questions from lawmakers in September. 
Republican Sen. Steve Crowell of Magnolia, one of several Republicans who initially declined to vote for the Generating Arkansas Jobs Act before voting for an amended version, on Tuesday called the law a mistake that had to be corrected. He joined Texarkana Republican and SB 2 cosponsor Sen. Jimmy Hickey in expressing his regret for voting for the law.
“I thought we had fixed it, and obviously, we hadn’t fixed it,” Crowell said. 
Crowell is not a cosponsor of the repeal proposal, and said he was waiting to see what other legislation gets introduced.
“I don’t know if there’s anything we can do but repeal it,” Crowell said. “Again, I think it’s prudent to think about all the options, but I don’t feel that the people of Arkansas are going to want us to keep this in place.”
Besides Penzo and Hickey, the bill’s other sponsors are Republican Sens. Ronald Caldwell of Wynne, Terry Rice of Waldron, Ricky Hill of Cabot, Missy Irvin of Mountain View, Mark Johnson of Ferndale and Bryan King of Green Forest. The Democratic cosponsors are Sen. Jamie Scott of North Little Rock and Sen.-elect Tara Shephard of Little Rock. The bill does not list any House cosponsors.
The legislation was introduced  Monday, the first day to file bills for the 2027 legislative session. Legislators will return to session Jan. 11, with lawmaking set to run through April at the earliest. The Generating Arkansas Jobs Act is only one of the topics weighing on the Republican-dominated Legislature, which just saw Democrats make strong gains in the House amid national frustration over the cost of living.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Audit: Millions in Ag Department grants went to ineligible recipients; commissioner disagrees
description: Millions of dollars issued under a North Dakota bioscience grant program went to ineligible recipients, according to an audit released Tuesday. Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring, whose department manages the grant program, said the money was properly granted and that he disagrees with the audit’s interpretation and a related press release. State Auditor[...]
text:
Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring listens during a meeting of the North Dakota Industrial Commission on Oct. 30, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)Millions of dollars issued under a North Dakota bioscience grant program went to ineligible recipients, according to an audit released Tuesday.
Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring, whose department manages the grant program, said the money was properly granted and that he disagrees with the audit’s interpretation and a related press release. State Auditor Josh Gallion said he stands by the audit report and that his team did excellent work. 
North Dakota Republican State Auditor Josh Gallion addresses the Legislative Audit and Fiscal Review Committee on Sept. 22, 2026. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)
The audit of the North Dakota Department of Agriculture looked at the Bioscience Innovation Grant Program during the 2023-25 budget cycle. The program is for boosting bioscience technology and jobs in North Dakota. The 2019 Legislature created the grant program, which received increased funding in 2021 and 2023 but was not funded in 2025, according to the audit.
In the 2023-25 period, the grant committee made 39 grants totaling $10.9 million. The recipients used $8.4 million. The remaining $2.5 million went back to the state government’s main operating account, the general fund.
Initially, the audit sampled nine grant recipients regarding eligibility requirements and found six couldn’t show they met a requirement of annual sales below $2.5 million, the report said. One recipient was awarded $1.1 million despite never opening an intended Fargo location. Another was paid nearly $100,000 of its $240,000 grant before it established its North Dakota location. Another recipient was granted $125,000 for a purpose that wasn’t in state law, according to the audit.
Those findings prompted the audit team to look at the physical locations of all 34 grants that got payments. The audit found nine more recipients didn’t have locations in North Dakota, the audit said.
The grants included more than $2.5 million to businesses with no physical location in the state, the audit found.
State law doesn’t say anything about having a “bona fide” presence in North Dakota, but does require the businesses to be registered with the secretary of state, “and they were,” Goehring said.
The law mentions bioscience businesses “operating in the state,” the audit said.
The grant committee encouraged companies to establish a presence and bring their company to the state, Goehring  said. Many companies developed relationships in the state, set up labs and did testing in North Dakota, he said.
The Ag Department “did not require grant applicants to submit information to validate eligibility requirements were met,” the audit said.
North Dakota Veterans Home audit questions meal prep in wake of choking death

Goehring said his department was “dinged” for not having a checklist or a more formal process in place, but did verify all the information. A third-party contractor, the Bioscience Association of North Dakota, was supposed to do all the front-end work and report to the ag department, Goehring said. One agency staffer did help administer the program, he added.
He also said his agency inherited the program from the state Commerce Department and he sought to have more clarification in the law about responsibilities, duties and accountability, but lacked support in the Legislature and the industry.
The Ag Department canceled one grant award and reached a settlement agreement that cost the state about $82,000, the audit said.
Goehring said his agency did recoup money from a company that left the state before it completed all of its work and was sold to someone else.
“We followed the law and we reimbursed for work that was done, for devices that were developed, for programs, for software, for the work that was accomplished in the medical field, and where we had one issue, we recovered that money,” Goehring said. 
The longtime agriculture commissioner said he will appear in front of the Legislature’s audit review committee to answer questions about the audit. 
The state auditor said, “Our focus is making sure that we’re looking at these grants, these programs to make sure that we are complying with statutes, that we are making sure that funds are distributed in accordance with the laws, the rules, the policies.”
The audit also found some site visits and performance reviews weren’t done. 
In its audit response, the Ag Department said it agrees with recommendations of ensuring grant applicants meet the eligibility requirements before receiving the money, evaluating whether recovery of any money is necessary and clearly defining the grant requirements.
The Ag Department also said it has put formal eligibility verification procedures in place and added monitoring controls to the grant administration process, and is reviewing past grants to see if any recovery actions are necessary.
Sen. Terry Wanzek, R-Jamestown, who introduced the 2019 bill creating the grant program, said the audit creates questions and officials need to learn more. 
“I’m not ready to be judgmental yet. I want to hear more about what happened,” Wanzek said. 
The Legislative Audit and Fiscal Review Committee meets Nov. 30.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Jackson police need more evidence against one suspect in Tasia Fortune’s death, judge says
description: Christy Spivey, right, speaks with the media Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, in Jackson after the preliminary hearing for Earnest Lloyd Jr., who is accused in the death of her daughter, Tasia Fortune. Lloyd did not attend the hearing, and Circuit Judge Johnnie McDaniels sent Lloyd's case back to Municipal Court after finding that police have not presented enough evi[...]
text:
A judge ruled Tuesday that there is not enough evidence to proceed with the preliminary hearing for one of the three men arrested in the death of Tasia Fortune, whose body was found hanging from a tree in the backyard of a Jackson home in August.
Hinds County Circuit Court Judge Johnnie McDaniels speaks in court on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, in Jackson, during a preliminary hearing for Earnest Lloyd Jr. The judge sent Lloyd’s case back to municipal court, saying police need more evidence to connect Lloyd to the death of Tasia Fortune. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Hinds County Circuit Judge Johnnie McDaniels sent the case against 25-year-old Earnest Lloyd Jr. back to Jackson Municipal Court to give the Jackson Police Department additional time to investigate the death. 
During a hearing in the Hinds County Courthouse in Jackson, McDaniels learned that Lloyd’s attorney, Nicholas Coleman, hadn’t had the chance to speak to his client, and JPD did not have enough evidence against Lloyd to send the case to the Hinds County grand jury.
Lloyd is one of three people arrested on charges in the death of Fortune, a 29-year-old mother of four. Fortune, who was Black, was found hanging from a tree outside a vacant home in west Jackson. Her race and the manner her body was found invoked memories of Mississippi’s history of racial terror lynchings. All of the suspects arrested are Black, and authorities said they believe Fortune was killed in retaliation for stealing drugs.
A makeshift memorial for Tasia Fortune is seen in the backyard of a vacant home in the 500 block of Road of Remembrance in Jackson on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. According to authorities, Fortune’s body was found hanging from a tree in the backyard of a vacant home Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
After court, Fortune’s mother Christy Spivey said she was not surprised by the outcome. She said she had lost trust in JPD’s ability to get justice for her daughter. She said the department has not been transparent with the family about the investigation, adding that she believes JPD officers are spread too thin.
“It’s hard,” Spivey said, eyes filling with tears. 
“I don’t even know how she died.”
Spivey started a petition to investigate the Jackson Police Department, and has been supporting a petition to get federal authorities to investigate Fortune’s death. She said she is just trying to get answers.
When asked what JPD could do to regain her trust, Spivey replied, “I don’t know that they can.”
JPD’s public information officer Tommie Brown said he could not respond until talking with investigators. Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney previously said all three suspects had a “known association” with Fortune. 
The first person arrested in Fortune’s death was Jarques Ratliff, 51. A judge found probable cause in September to send the case against him to a Hinds County grand jury.
The second man arrested was Lloyd, who missed his preliminary hearing Tuesday because he was being transported from a jail in northern Mississippi. He was denied bond during his initial appearance.
Bond for the third man, Eric Derrell Clark, 45, was previously set at $5 million.

In his lawsuit, Lloyd cl[...]
text:
The Newton Correctional Facility in Iowa's Jasper County. (Photo courtesy of the Iowa Department of Corrections.)An Iowa prison inmate is suing state corrections officials over alleged sexual harassment by a female jailer and retaliation by the jailer’s colleagues.
Vincenzo Sabastiano Lloyd is suing former state corrections officer Samantha Kimmel, also known as Samantha Wilson, as well as 12 other employees of the Newton Correctional Facility.
In his lawsuit, Lloyd claims that in the summer of 2023 he was walking in the prison yard when Kimmel began acting flirtatiously toward him, telling him he was living rent-free in her head. Over time, the conversations became sexual in nature, the lawsuit alleges, and then “became physical and sexual.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the lawsuit, the interactions between the two “were primarily kissing and groping” in a storage room, a “chemical closet,” and a pizza supply closet. At some point, Kimmel began spending time in the pizza supply closet with another inmate, the lawsuit claims. Kimmel also sent Lloyd money “many times,” through Western Union, the lawsuit alleges.
The lawsuit also asserts that when the staff at Newton became aware of Kimmel’s actions, they told Lloyd to stop interacting with her or he’d be placed in isolation or “shipped out” to another prison — comments that Lloyd took as an indication the Newton staff was trying to “protect” Kimmel.
The lawsuit asserts that with their relationship cooling, Kimmel became “aggressive, demeaning and revengeful” toward Lloyd, demanding multiple times per day that he show her his penis and then later physically groping him.
In September 2025, the lawsuit asserts, Lloyd filed a formal Prison Rape Elimination Act, or PREA, form complaining of Kimmel’s conduct. Although the lawsuit doesn’t state when, Kimmel allegedly searched Lloyd’s cell and took “all of the love letters” the two had exchanged.
After the PREA investigation was launched, Lloyd was allegedly placed in solitary confinement for three days. In October 2025, Lloyd allegedly received a letter informing him that the PREA investigation had been completed, and the staff had concluded there was sufficient evidence to substantiate Lloyd’s claim of sexual harassment.
According to the lawsuit, Lloyd later filed grievances alleging Kimmel had retaliated against him for having reported her conduct, and that after Kimmel was allegedly fired, some of her former colleagues retaliated against him — in part through unwarranted disciplinary action, and in part by informing other inmates he was a “rat.”
The lawsuit seeks $500,000 in damages for sexual assault, sexual harassment and retaliation.
In response, attorneys for the state have denied wrongdoing, and argued that to the extent that any harassing behavior occurred, Lloyd failed to take advantage of any preventative or corrective opportunities to address the situation.
The state also says the defendants in the case were not “deliberately indifferent” to Lloyd’s situation and that any harassment that may have occurred was neither intentional nor severe.
A trial date has yet to be scheduled.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC film grants get $31M boost in controversial spending bill
description: The grants are part of a 62-page omnibus spending bill that wasn’t made public until moments before it was debated Tuesday afternoon.
text:
The grand staircase at  the NC Legislative Building (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) North Carolina lawmakers voted Tuesday to set aside $31 million for film grants, boosting the state’s entertainment industry. 
The grants support movies and television shows in the state. Many are filmed along the coast, like R.J. Decker, a crime television show shot in Wilmington. Grants are agreed upon at the beginning of a project but aren’t paid out until after post-production, leading to multiple years of future financial commitment.  
Managed by the Department of Commerce, the grant program underspent its $31 million annual budget for four years, leaving a reserve fund. But program officials said this summer the reserve had been fully committed, leaving them unable to make additional grants until 2028 at the earliest.
Some Republican lawmakers initially accused Commerce officials of mismanaging the funds and declined to add more money for the program to the state budget. But on the campaign trail this fall, Sen. Michael Lee, R-New Hanover, promised to secure $31 million more to keep the grants going. 
“This is a statewide effort,” chief Senate budget writer Brent Jackson, R-Sampson, said Tuesday.
Gov. Josh Stein told reporters Tuesday morning that North Carolina needs to stabilize the film grants program.
“It’s a growing dynamic industry all across the state,” Stein said. “We have to make sure that we have enough resources to replenish the programs to keep it going, because thousands of people work in the industry.”
North Carolina seeks $40 million to help schools cover rising fuel costs

The bill also includes $40 million in extra money for fuel for school buses, and another million for fuel for drivers’ education vehicles. School districts’ fuel budgets for the year were busted by the high gas and diesel prices caused by the Iran war.
The grants are part of a 62-page omnibus spending package, Senate Bill 177, that wasn’t made public until moments before it was debated Tuesday afternoon. 
The measure appropriates or redirects over $100 million to various entities across the state, and also includes many special provisions making changes to state programs, from SNAP to water policy.
The Senate voted 26-19 in favor, and the House approved it 66-49, with most Democrats opposed.
Democrats criticized Republican leaders for not allowing more time for lawmakers and constituents to read and understand the bill. They also said the spending and policy parts of the measure should have been broken down into separate proposals, instead of lumped into one. Sen. Jonah Garson, D-Orange, said there are good provisions in the bill, but they’re outweighed by the negatives.
“Unfortunately, those good things like fuel relief for our school systems are held hostage to a number of bad provisions,” Garson said. “I would hope that this body can come back in December and address some of these emergency relief items in a responsible and appropriate way, but for the reason that the good is held hostage to the bad, I’ll be voting no.”
House Democrats argued that the measure was too rushed, saying there should have been some opportunity for the public to weigh in on it in committee hearings. 
“You’re asking us to vote on this now, to spend well over $100 million of the people’s money without any public involvement, without any notice, without any chance for even the members responsible for voting on behalf of their districts to have a say in it, let alone to read it,” Rep. Phil Rubin, D-Wake, said. “This is just not the way that this body should be run. It’s completely inappropriate.”
House Speaker Destin Hall, R-Caldwell, told reporters that members had been working on the bill “for some time,” but that last-minute changes delayed its public release.
“There’s tweaks here and there that you’ve got to fix,” Hall said. “You don’t always have all this stuff, you know, days and weeks ahead of time.” 
The bill now goes to Gov. Josh Stein for his signature.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Lawmakers call for forensic audit of Georgia child welfare agency’s spending
description: A bipartisan group of Georgia lawmakers is calling for a new third-party audit of the Division of Family and Children Services, the state agency tasked with protecting vulnerable children. “There is still so much that we don’t know, and we don’t know what we don’t know, and the only way we can get that is […]
text:
Sen. Kay Kirkpatrick and Rep. Beth Camp listen to a foster parent talk about their experiences during a study committee meeting on Oct. 22, 2026. Jill Nolin/Georgia RecorderA bipartisan group of Georgia lawmakers is calling for a new third-party audit of the Division of Family and Children Services, the state agency tasked with protecting vulnerable children.
Rep. Katie Dempsey. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
“There is still so much that we don’t know, and we don’t know what we don’t know, and the only way we can get that is a deep, forensic audit,” said Rome Republican state Rep. Katie Dempsey.
Dempsey said lawmakers should look at starting the process “tomorrow.”
Dempsey was speaking Tuesday at a hearing of a joint House and Senate committee tasked with evaluating rising costs in Georgia’s foster care system. The committee was convened after the agency faced a shortfall of about $85 million, which led to service cuts and terminated contracts with nonprofits.
After the committee was formed, new reporting from the Center Square raised questions about the department’s spending, including nearly $1 million on an SUV equipped with high-tech surveillance gear including a device that can tap into cellphones.
The committee approved 10 recommendations including proposals like making better use of federal funds, identifying resources for foster parent recruitment, reviewing insurance coverage for foster youth, and improving early diagnosis and treatment of autism for foster children.
The recommendations did not include the audit called for by Dempsey and other members of the committee. Whether agency spending contributed to the deficit was beyond the committee’s purview.
Rep. Esther Panitch. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
An amendment to one of the recommendations from Sandy Springs Democratic state Rep. Esther Panitch states that a future legislative panel should examine agency spending.
“These were things that were actually coming up while we were meeting in committee but were not addressed, so this will allow us to move forward to deal with the elephant in the room, which is the DFCS scandal,” Panitch said, referring to the agency’s purchase of the SUV and other controversial spending.
Panitch added that she would support a forensic audit in addition to further legislative oversight.
“Obviously, DFCS had some significant major problems that the Legislature was not warned about, and we cannot allow that to happen again,” she said. “The kids suffer when it happens, and those kids are our priority, not the administrators.”
A September audit requested by the House Appropriations Committee and published by the state auditor’s office found that spending on 20% of children in foster care, typically those with complex needs, accounted for 70% of the increase in spending.
The cost of providing out-of-home care for foster children in Georgia increased by $155 million, or around 42%, between 2022 and 2025 while the number of children has remained steady and inflation was only 18%.
“Costs increased due to numerous related factors, including increased spending on children with complex needs, reduced foster home availability, limited psychiatric residential treatment facility capacity, greater reliance on higher-cost placements and contracted providers, and rate increases,” the report found.
Rep. Beth Camp. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Concord Republican state Rep. Beth Camp, who co-chaired the study committee, said a forensic audit would provide more access into DFCS’ spending than the state audit.
“The forensic audit is different because it basically goes from this date back, and it does a very deep dive into where the money went,” she said.
“It doesn’t add up, especially when we had the commissioner of DHS addressing us last year about this time and indicating to us that there was an $86 million shortfall,” she added. “It’s just not adding up for most of us. If we were running our household budget like this, we’d all be in trouble.”
Camp said a forensic audit should be performed by a third-party agency not involved with the government and said it would need to be initiated by the executive branch, most likely Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, who is set to take office in January.
“It’s been communicated to her transition team,” Camp said. “This is something that probably needs to take place sooner rather than later.”
Speaking to reporters in the Capitol Tuesday morning, Bottoms said she was continuing to review budget and policy recommendations but indicated she was not opposed to a full forensic audit.
“What I would support is making sure that we can get to where we need to be on fully funding foster care, and if that means that an audit is in order and, and a top-to-bottom review, we’re going to do whatever we need to do to make sure that our foster children are cared for and they have the resources that they need,” she said.
In an emailed statement, spokesperson Kylie Winton indicated the state agency would not oppose the audit.
“DHS adheres to all applicable laws and policies, and we will gladly work with any person or firm auditing or investigating our agency’s budgeted funding and expenses,” Winton said.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: ACLU questions presence of Milwaukee DA staff at Election Day polling places
description: The American Civil Liberties Union of Wisconsin is raising questions about the deployment of investigators from the Milwaukee County District Attorney’s Office to polling sites during the 2026 midterm elections. In a Tuesday press release, the ACLU said that it had filed a records request to learn more, noting that the non-partisan organization Election Prot[...]
text:
Voting rights activists and others gather at the Midtown Center in Milwaukee on the first day of early voting in 2022. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)The American Civil Liberties Union of Wisconsin is raising questions about the deployment of investigators from the Milwaukee County District Attorney’s Office to polling sites during the 2026 midterm elections. In a Tuesday press release, the ACLU said that it had filed a records request to learn more, noting that the non-partisan organization Election Protection received numerous reports of armed individuals patrolling around and entering polling places in Milwaukee County on Nov. 3. 
The ACLU has requested records involving the use of Milwaukee County DA resources including any plans, policies, training, staffing information, firearms permits, communications and complaints. 
Tensions were high as the midterm elections approached after Trump administration officials did not rule out  deploying armed federal agents near polling locations. Those fears did not materialize, and Democrats across the country achieved historic victories on the state and national level.  
But apparently the Milwaukee DA did deploy armed people to the polls.
“The program conducted by the District Attorney’s office appears to have needlessly caused significant confusion and apprehension among voters and poll workers, with, as we understand it, at least one Chief Inspector calling the police to report unidentified individuals with guns at their polling place,” said Ryan Cox, ACLU of Wisconsin’s legal director. “We have significant concerns about the propriety of this program — which would certainly be illegal if federal law enforcement engaged in similar conduct — and we need to know the facts.”
Jeffrey Altenburg, chief deputy district attorney at the Milwaukee DA’s office, pushed back against the ACLU’s criticism in an email statement to the Examiner. Altenburg said that the DA’s office “regularly engages in election integrity monitoring for major elections.” The program has been ongoing for over 20 years, Altenburg said, and involves sending selected attorneys and DA investigators who’ve received election-related training to polling sites “to ensure there is no interference with individuals’ voting rights.” 
Alternburg said  the DA’s office notifies municipal clerks prior to visits, and communicates and trains with community groups, political parties and organizations like Election Protection in the lead-up to Election Day.
Altenburg added that the ACLU has been involved in these trainings as well. He rejects claims in the ACLU’s press release that DA staff were armed, stating that only DA office investigators are armed as they are considered active law enforcement. He said that DA staff checked in with the chief inspector at individual polling sites, and that their appearances were brief. 
The Milwaukee Police Department did not respond to a request for comment. However, during an Election Day check-in on Nov. 3, MPD told the Examiner that DA staff accompanied officers to a call involving people handing out election materials too close to a polling place near a university. Those individuals were gone by the time officers and DA staff arrived.
“The intent of this program is to provide support to the community in making elections fair and accessible to individuals in the community,” said Altenburg. “Prior iterations of the program have routinely generated positive responses from the community.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Panel: Arkansas families receiving subsidized childcare have until July to choose between programs
description: Dozens of Arkansas families whose infants and toddlers receive subsidized childcare will have to choose between two programs by July 1, the Early Childhood Commission agreed Tuesday. Ideally the change will free up funds to allow 243 families from the state’s waitlist of more than 3,500 to receive childcare, said Ashelyn Abney, director of the […]
text:
Photo by (Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent)Dozens of Arkansas families whose infants and toddlers receive subsidized childcare will have to choose between two programs by July 1, the Early Childhood Commission agreed Tuesday.
Ideally the change will free up funds to allow 243 families from the state’s waitlist of more than 3,500 to receive childcare, said Ashelyn Abney, director of the Office of Early Childhood in the state Education Department’s Division of Elementary and Secondary Education.
Arkansas’ early childhood education challenges were highlighted last year when the state faced pushback over plans to address the waiting list by updating reimbursement rates for the School Readiness Assistance program, which helps low-income Arkansans afford childcare.
The state spends about $3.67 million per year, or $306,000 per month, in grant money from the federal Child Care Development Fund to support families in the Early Head Start program, Abney said. This funding has been “layered” with the School Readiness Assistance program.
Abney said she hopes all 243 families that currently benefit from both programs will continue to receive childcare.
Commissioners expressed concerns during Tuesday’s virtual meeting that families will have to find other sources of childcare during hours of the day that are no longer subsidized. Early Head Start programs usually care for children from the morning to early afternoon, and School Readiness Assistance-funded care covers the later afternoon.
Child care costs preventing Arkansas mothers from seeking or retaining full-time work, report says

The commission, a group of childcare providers and advocates,  advises the Office of Early Childhood on how best to support early childhood development in Arkansas. The commission considered asking families to choose a program by Jan. 1, but decided giving them until July was easier on everyone involved.
Democratic state Rep. Denise Garner said she was concerned about the “most vulnerable families that may not be able to work because of childcare.” High costs and a provider shortage prevent Arkansas mothers from seeking and retaining full-time employment, according to a March report from the Women’s Foundation of Arkansas.
Garner, who will be Fayetteville’s state senator in January, also said the changes to the funding streams are likely to foster distrust among childcare providers, just over a year after a task force came to the School Readiness Assistance program’s rescue.
Childcare providers raised the alarm in September 2025 that the Arkansas Department of Education’s plan to change the School Readiness Assistance reimbursement rates and families’ copayments would make childcare unaffordable for families and unsustainable for providers.
The adoption of a plan to keep the program workable for all parties came during a federal government shutdown last November that froze School Readiness Assistance funding and strained childcare centers.
Abney said Tuesday that 20 centers have closed since October 2025, four for financial reasons.
Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders proposed directing $20 million annually to early childhood education in her balanced budget for the fiscal year starting July 1. What the Office of Early Childhood does with that new recurring funding source is up to the Legislature, Abney said.
“My dream and my vision is looking at serving the maximum number of children that we possibly can, and so I think that is the first thing that we need to work on, just to see if we’re all in agreement with that,” Abney said.
Republicans control both chambers of the Legislature, but this month’s elections saw Democrats win enough seats to break the GOP’s House supermajority. Most budget bills will now require bipartisan support to pass the House.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Federal permitting bill splits South Dakota Republicans, causing some to align with Democrats
description: Federal legislation that could accelerate permitting for large energy and infrastructure projects has scrambled political allegiances in South Dakota, leading two Republican U.S. senators to vote differently while splitting Republican state lawmakers and causing some of them to align with Democrats. Fifty state lawmakers and lawmakers-elect from South Dakota[...]
text:
The South Dakota House of Representatives meets at the Capitol in Pierre on Feb. 10, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)Federal legislation that could accelerate permitting for large energy and infrastructure projects has scrambled political allegiances in South Dakota, leading two Republican U.S. senators to vote differently while splitting Republican state lawmakers and causing some of them to align with Democrats.
Fifty state lawmakers and lawmakers-elect from South Dakota — including 37 Republicans, 12 Democrats and one independent — sent a letter on Monday to Republican U.S. Senators John Thune and Mike Rounds urging opposition to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. It would streamline federal review and approval for projects including power plants, transmission lines and pipelines. It would also require data centers to cover their electrical infrastructure costs. 
Supporters say the changes would reduce project delays and costs, while critics say they would weaken environmental oversight, local control and public input.
The letter says economic development, affordable energy and infrastructure investment “must not come at the expense of environmental protections, agricultural interests, private property rights, tribal sovereignty, local control, or the health and well-being of our communities.”
State senators Joy Hohn, R-Hartford, and Red Dawn Foster, D-Pine Ridge, were the first two signers of the letter. Foster is a member of the Oglala Sioux Tribe. Hohn, who won reelection earlier this month, is a vocal opponent of a carbon-capture pipeline that was proposed to run through eastern South Dakota. 
“This bill is an incremental erosion of our fundamental rights,” Hohn told South Dakota Searchlight.
Other letter signers include a county commissioner and various Republican Party officials.
Sen. Joy Hohn, R-Hartford, speaks on Feb. 11, 2026, in the South Dakota Senate at the Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)
Lawmaker disagreement
State lawmakers sometimes approve resolutions urging support or opposition of federal actions. A news release from Hohn and Foster about the letter said that because lawmakers don’t begin their annual legislative session until January, they “do not have the opportunity to formally address this issue through a legislative resolution.”
“Recognizing the concerns being raised by constituents throughout South Dakota, participating legislators have come together through a joint letter to ensure those voices are heard at the federal level,” the news release said.
Judging solely by the signatures, the letter does not have enough support to pass as a resolution, partly because some of the signers lost their bids for reelection or did not run for another term. The letter has 20 signatures from state House members who will be in office in January, short of the 36 needed for a majority, and 12 signatures from state Senate members who will be in office in January, short of the necessary 18.
Sen. Casey Crabtree, R-Madison, the state Senate’s majority leader-elect, did not sign the letter. Nor did any other member of the incoming Republican legislative leadership teams in the state House or Senate. 

Sen. Casey Crabtree, R-Madison, speaks in the South Dakota Senate on Feb. 11, 2026, at the Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)

Crabtree said he supports the federal permitting legislation and said lawmakers should commend U.S. Senate Majority Leader Thune for working in a bipartisan manner to “deliver affordable electricity, fix our roads and bridges, upgrade our telecommunications systems and maintain strong protections for South Dakotans.”
“The American people are united behind the issue of affordability,” Crabtree said. 
All of the members of the incoming Democratic legislative leadership teams in the state House and Senate signed the letter. That includes both of the party’s Senate members who will be in office in January, and 10 of the 12 Democrats who will be House members in January. 
Senate Minority Leader-elect Erik Muckey, D-Sioux Falls, said trying to cut red tape for infrastructure development may sound great on its face. 
“But the thing is, you can accomplish that without having to have very drastic, negative impacts on environmental law, the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act, all the way to the utter disregard of tribal sovereignty, local control and even, frankly, the state Public Utilities Commission,” Muckey said. 
House Minority Leader-elect Eric Emery, D-Rosebud, acknowledged that federal permitting needs work. He said the bill goes too far. 
“As a Native legislator from Rosebud, I can’t get past what this bill does to tribes,” he said. 
Emery said the bill narrows what states and tribes can review under the Clean Water Act, and it allows 150 days to challenge a federal permit in court, which he said is too short. He also opposes what he described as a watering-down of tribal consultation requirements. The Great Plains Tribal Chairmen’s Association and some other tribal organizations oppose the legislation.
“Consultation on sacred sites and cultural resources is part of what the United States owes tribal nations under the treaties. It shouldn’t be optional,” Emery said. “This is one issue where I agree with a lot of my Republican colleagues here at home. Local control and tribal sovereignty don’t belong to one party in South Dakota.”
Rep. Eric Emery, D-Rosebud, sits at his desk in the South Dakota House of Representatives during the 2024 legislative session. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)
Not just lawmakers opposed
South Dakota Public Utilities Commission Chair Chris Nelson, a Republican, said the commission is “adamantly opposed” to provisions that would allow transmission line developers to seek federal approval if state regulators deny a permit or impose conditions developers consider too burdensome.
“What it really does is it takes away the South Dakota PUC’s ability to evaluate projects fairly under our statute and to work with landowners here, to work out their concerns, and make a final decision here,” Nelson said.
Nelson also raised concerns about federal eminent domain authority and whether federal regulators would be required to consider landowner objections. Eminent domain is a legal power granted to some developers for gaining access to land without landowner consent, while paying just compensation to the owner. It’s been a divisive issue in South Dakota the last several years because of a proposed multi-state carbon capture-pipeline that would have passed through the eastern part of the state. The Legislature and Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden banned eminent domain for carbon pipelines last year.
Bill moves forward in D.C.
Sen. Rounds was the only Republican to cast a procedural vote against the legislation earlier this month. Afterward, he posted comments on social media expressing some of the same concerns expressed by Nelson. Rounds said at the time that he hoped to work with his colleagues to address the concerns.
The bill passed that procedural vote 73-25 and awaits a final vote in the Senate.  
Permitting overhaul splits SD’s US senators but advances with tepid bipartisan support

Thune voted to advance the bill and has said permitting reform is necessary to lower energy costs, create jobs and prevent infrastructure projects from being delayed for years by federal bureaucracy.
“Too often, projects are bogged down in bureaucratic delays for months, and often years, at a time,” Thune said during a Tuesday speech in the Senate. “Delays cause project budgets to balloon, which then leads to higher costs for American consumers.”
Thune said the bill would also reduce permitting burdens on farmers and ranchers, provide technical assistance to communities considering a data center, and require data centers to cover their own energy-related costs.
“Whether that’s their operating and construction costs or the cost of grid improvements needed to accommodate them,” he said. “This legislation ensures those costs don’t show up on household utility bills.”
Thune’s office told South Dakota Searchlight the legislation would not override South Dakota’s ban on eminent domain for carbon pipelines.
U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, R-South Dakota, shared his support for the bill last week on social media, calling it “the most important affordability bill in decades.”
“If we want lower taxes, lower energy bills, better roads and bridges, we have to right-size our regulatory approach,” Johnson said, adding that the bill “does that while protecting property rights and forcing data centers to pay their fair share.”

description: TOPEKA — The lead headline on the front page of the Marion County Record’s Aug. 16, 2023, edition read in big, bold font: “SEIZED…but not silenced.” The paper’s weekly issue came five days after local law enforcement seized computers, cellphones and materials from the Record, its reporters and editor Eric Meyer’s home. An HBO Original […]
text:
Copies of the Aug. 16, 2023, edition of the Marion County Record rest on a countertop in the newspaper office. Staffers pulled an all-nighter to get the newspaper out after their equipment was seized by law enforcement. (Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The lead headline on the front page of the Marion County Record’s Aug. 16, 2023, edition read in big, bold font: “SEIZED…but not silenced.”
The paper’s weekly issue came five days after local law enforcement seized computers, cellphones and materials from the Record, its reporters and editor Eric Meyer’s home.
An HBO Original documentary, “Seized,” traces the raid, the lawsuits that ensued, and the staff that remained to continue covering the community.
It will debut at 8 p.m. CT on hDec. 1 on HBO and will be available to stream on HBO Max.
The documentary, directed by Sharon Liese, premiered at the Sundance Film Festival in January.
“Told with humor and candor, the saga of The Record raises salient questions about the role of local newspapers, often underfunded, under attack, and disappearing fast,” a press release said. “The film is an affectionate portrait of small-town America and how one small town became a flashpoint in the global discourse about the urgency of independent journalism.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: As Dems take control, advocates see opportunity to upend the energy status quo
description: With Wisconsin sitting on the precipice of total Democratic control of state government and voters in the state more focused than ever on both their rising utility bills and the system behind them, the state’s Citizens Utility Board held a forum on energy affordability Tuesday to discuss policy solutions for bringing those costs down.  Residents, […]
text:
Solar panels in Boone, Iowa. Participants at a Citizens Utililty Board meeting in Madison on Tuesday said an integrated resource plan is crucial to bringing down utility costs in Wisconsin. (USDA photo)With Wisconsin sitting on the precipice of total Democratic control of state government and voters in the state more focused than ever on both their rising utility bills and the system behind them, the state’s Citizens Utility Board held a forum on energy affordability Tuesday to discuss policy solutions for bringing those costs down. 
Residents, advocates, policymakers and experts gathered at the Park Hotel in Madison where the results of the election earlier this month were cast as an opportunity to upend an energy status quo. In recent years, participants said, Wisconsin has prioritized the development of fossil fuel burning plants, investment returns to utility shareholders and the needs of tech companies building massive data centers over the finances of regular citizens.
Kristy Nieto, a member of the Wisconsin Public Service Commission — the regulatory body that oversees the state’s utility companies — said at the event that Wisconsin was previously a national leader in regulating utilities in ways that benefited regular people and the environment. She argued that the commission should be given the staffing, budget and authority to restore that leadership. 
“We have to fundamentally rethink how we approach affordability and the tools that we have to mitigate rate increases,” she said. “Business as usual won’t cut it, but despite the challenges that we face, I think there’s something important that Wisconsin has going for it right now. We have an opportunity to lead again. Sometimes we’ll hear the argument that the commission shouldn’t do something because the commission hasn’t done it before, or because other states don’t do it …  Wisconsin would be an outlier. I say that when done thoughtfully, competently and rationally, being an outlier can be a good thing. We were an outlier when we established modern utility regulation in the progressive movement, in environmental stewardship, and we shouldn’t be afraid to be an outlier again.”
Nieto said that to successfully make energy in Wisconsin more affordable, the state should pull three levers — establish a more holistic planning process for the state’s energy portfolio, give the PSC more tools to prioritize lowering costs when setting electric rates and increase the capacity of PSC’s staff to regulate an increasingly complex industry. 
Policy advocates speak at the Citizens Utility Board’s Nov. 17 energy affordability forum in Madison. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)
In the weeks since the November election, during which Democrats were swept into power on promises to  increase the affordability of basic needs such as energy, lawmakers, environmental groups and affordable energy advocates have settled on “integrated resource planning” as a top priority for Democrats once the legislative session begins in January. 
Integrated resource planning means the state’s utility companies would have to submit their future plans to the PSC for approval, forecasting how much power a company will need to generate, where that power will come from and how it will pay for that generation. That process will include public input and, advocates say, will help lawmakers push the utility companies toward building more renewable energy sources. 
Wisconsin is one of just a few states that doesn’t already have an integrated resource planning requirement. 
Emma Heins, who works on Wisconsin policy for the clean energy trade group Advanced Energy United, said that as data centers put stress on Wisconsin’s energy system, the state needs a way to address the broader energy landscape rather than tackling energy demand issues on a case-by-case basis. 
“Wisconsin is really, really overdue for an integrated resource plan,” Heins said, adding that the system has benefits for the regulators, who would be able to see the whole picture at once, for the utilities, who would have more regulatory certainty, for labor, which would be able to plan for 20 years of job opportunities, and for lawmakers, who would have a clearer picture of the decisions being made. 
A number of speakers at the forum argued that once the planning process is in place, the Legislature needs to keep the  pressure on the utilities and that regulators need the tools necessary to do their job. 
“The Legislature, you all have the bully pulpit. You have the microphone, the voice, to get out to the media, to leverage your constituents and to apply pressure in a holistic sense to utilities and what they are requesting of commissions,” Tremaine Phillips of the energy affordability group Powerlines said. “The other way is on personnel. Our commissions as well as consumer advocates are outgunned, outmanned in these proceedings.” 
The Legislature, he said, needs to give regulators adequate staff and resources to do their job. 
Beyond structural change to the planning process and the potential benefits of giving the PSC more manpower and teeth to regulate the state’s utility companies, a number of advocates at the forum said the state can save a lot of money by supporting energy efficiency programs and giving residents incentives to use less power and lower demand on peak energy days. Wisconsin has a number of existing programs that help people make their homes more energy efficient. Forum speakers said these could simply be given bigger budgets to achieve larger results. 
“I think there’s still a misconception that it’s not enough, or it’s so marginal that it doesn’t actually help the situation,” Heins said of the state’s existing energy efficiency programs. “So I think people think about, well, in my own home, I didn’t see 30% savings because I replaced LED light bulbs or something like that. And so then they extrapolate that to the grid and say, ‘Well, how much could energy efficiency actually do?’ When we know it’s a lot.”
If Wisconsin fully takes advantage of its available programs to reduce energy demand, the state could save up to $1.5 billion on energy costs, according to Citizens Utility Board analyst Jeff Adams.
“I mean, you factor in commercial and industrial and kind of multiply things to the scale of an entire grid — it can fix a lot of problems,” Heins said.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota students try on legislative roles, tackle AI
description: North Dakota students brainstormed answers to AI and technology use this week, hoping state lawmakers will take up the baton in January. Nearly 50 student senators from across North Dakota debated and advanced bills on artificial intelligence and student technology use during the first Student Legislative Summit at the Capitol. The students met on Monday […]
text:
Adam Said, a junior at Sheyenne High School, speaks on the Senate floor during the first Student Legislative Summit at the Capitol on Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota students brainstormed answers to AI and technology use this week, hoping state lawmakers will take up the baton in January.
Nearly 50 student senators from across North Dakota debated and advanced bills on artificial intelligence and student technology use during the first Student Legislative Summit at the Capitol.
The students met on Monday and Tuesday to form committees, subcommittees, debate and vote on both topics as bill drafts were created from their work. The bills will be made available to state lawmakers as they begin the 2027 legislative session Jan. 5
“It was a lot of debates. A lot of, not heated discussion, but respectful discussion around topics that truly matter,” Adam Said, a junior at Sheyenne High School in West Fargo.
Said said it was a unique experience and he believes the students did a good job putting their viewpoints into the summit’s bill drafts. He also hopes state lawmakers take their opinions to heart.
“Parents and students do actually have a voice and our voices should matter, especially with AI that changes how education is viewed and how education is operated,” he said.
Thomas Unser, a student at West Fargo High School, speaks on the Senate floor during the first Student Legislative Summit at the Capitol on Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Superintendent of Public Instruction Levi Bachmeier said one of his favorite units as a state government teacher was the mock Congress and thought he could recreate that type of environment at the Capitol with high school students.
“I genuinely have appreciated and learned so much from these students,” Bachmeier said. “Just having the opportunity to hear from such thoughtful and passionate young people has helped develop my thinking and I hope that lawmakers view it the same way.”
He said the goals of the summit were to expose student leaders to the legislative process, but also give the student perspective on issues that state lawmakers may need to grapple with.
“They are smart and they are engaged,” said Sen. Kathy Hogan, D-Fargo, of the students attending the summit. 
Hogan said she hopes the students will stay involved and come back to Bismarck to sit with their representatives during the regular legislative session.
Kierstin Hurtt, superintendent of Valley-Edinburgh School District, and parent of one of the students participating, said she was watching the next generation of engaged leaders in North Dakota, in real time.
Brody Kramer, a senior at Bismarck Legacy High School, speaks on the Senate floor during the first Student Legislative Summit at the Capitol on Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
“It’s inspiring. It’s hopeful. It’s massive,” Hurtt said. “You are really learning what it’s like to be a stakeholder and how everything is about building a relationship with other stakeholders to achieve a common goal.”
She said she was impressed that students were asking each other for clarity on their different points of view and opinions.
Hurtt added she hopes student senators will be able to use the voting board and the proceedings will be live-streamed in the future.
Brody Kramer, a senior at Bismarck Legacy High School, said it’s good for students to interact with others from across the state and expressing viewpoints constructively on complicated topics is an important skill to learn.
“I think the bills we’re talking about should be pushed into the legislative session and talked about there,” Kramer said. 
He said the committee work and debating with other students inspired him to consider running for public office.
The bill outlining rules for artificial intelligence use in schools passed on a 40-8 vote.
The bill would allow students to use artificial intelligence tools beginning in ninth grade, unless under the direction of a teacher during classroom instruction. However, it would not allow students to use the tools to complete assignments.
Hazel Albert, a student from Hope-Page High School, speaks on the Senate floor during the first Student Legislative Summit at the Capitol on Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
The bill would also require teachers to list when AI use is permitted and not permitted as part of course instruction. Teachers would not be able to use AI to input grades into a gradebook or assign final grades, but they can use AI tools to assist with grading assignments and to create lesson plans.
A bill regulating the use of technology during the school day was approved on a 47-0 vote.
The school technology bill outlines that school districts must use technology as a support to learning and not a replacement for essential instruction. It also requires the technology must be used in a “manner reasonably suited to a student’s academic level, age, accessibility needs, and educational circumstances.”
“The seeds are being planted to have good public servants and there’s a whole Senate full of them right now,” Hogan said.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

title: New ‘Opportunity Zones’ designated in Idaho, allowing tax breaks for new development
description: The U.S. Department of the Treasury approved all of Idaho’s 25 requested areas to be eligible to receive federal tax incentives to spur development.  The agency on Tuesday announced that the areas, which are located in 14 Idaho counties, are designated as Opportunity Zones. The federal program allows certain housing or economic development projects to […]
text:
A construction crew works outside a new development in Boise. Five of Idaho's new "Opportunity Zones" will be located in Boise. The designation allows for certain developments there to receive tax breaks. (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun)The U.S. Department of the Treasury approved all of Idaho’s 25 requested areas to be eligible to receive federal tax incentives to spur development. 
The agency on Tuesday announced that the areas, which are located in 14 Idaho counties, are designated as Opportunity Zones. The federal program allows certain housing or economic development projects to qualify for tax breaks. 
The Opportunity Zone program was created under the first Trump administration through the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. Congress last year made the program permanent through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Idaho’s Republican Gov. Brad Little gives an interview to a reporter during a GOP election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Downtown Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
“Idaho is committed to encouraging private investment, creating good-paying jobs and strengthening communities across our state,” Idaho Gov. Brad Little said in a press release.  “Our first round of Opportunity Zones brought millions of dollars in investment to Idaho. With these new designations, we have another opportunity to build on that success, support rural and urban communities alike and ensure Idaho continues to be a place where businesses can grow and families can thrive.”
Nine of the 25 designated zones in Idaho are considered rural and will qualify for enhanced tax breaks, according to a press release. The most new zones are located in Ada County followed by Canyon County. 
Five of the designated zones will be in Boise, two in Nampa, two in Pocatello and two in Moscow. There will be a zone designated in Caldwell, Emmett, Twin Falls, Post Falls, Rexburg, Jerome and Lewiston, and other cities and unincorporated areas. 
U.S. Sen. Mike Crapo, R-Idaho, talks with attendees of the Idaho GOP election night watch party at the Grove Hotel in Boise, Idaho, on Nov. 8, 2022. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun)
“By making Opportunity Zones permanent and strengthening incentives for rural communities, we’ve laid the groundwork to attract long-term private investments to Idaho in areas that need it most,” U.S. Sen. Mike Crapo, R-Idaho, said in the release.  “This is about generating economic growth in our communities and creating opportunities for Idaho families to prosper.”
The new designations take effect Jan. 1, 2027. 
Here are some of the new zones: 

Boise: Areas off West Main Street downtown, south of downtown and Shoreline Drive, in West Boise near the Boise Towne Square Mall, off South Broadway Avenue, and near Boise State University and West University Drive. 


Nampa: Downtown around 12th Avenue South and First Street South, as well as the 11th Avenue North corridor. 


Pocatello: The downtown Main Street corridor and Portneuf River area and areas around Yellowstone Avenue, Pole Line Road and West Quinn Road. 


Moscow: North of Main Street, along Highway 8 and Highway 95, and south of Moscow near the University of Idaho campus and Schweitzer Engineering Laboratories. 
Twin Falls: Downtown, near Main Avenue and Shoshone Street. 

The area in Twin Falls was home to Idaho’s first Opportunity Zone project, a food hall.

 Results of previous Opportunity Zones are hard to measure 

In 2025, U.S. Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner traveled to Idaho with Crapo to discuss housing issues in the state. Turner, who led the first iteration of the program, said it would be a continued focus for developing more housing to meet the needs. 
Idaho to submit ‘Opportunity Zone’ proposals seeking tax breaks for economic development 

Turner said at the time 700 new housing units had been built inside Idaho Opportunity Zones and 4,000 new jobs had been created.
The first version of the program didn’t have reporting requirements, according to the Idaho Department of Commerce. 
A 2021 Brookings Institution analysis of the program nationally found some increased economic activity in urban areas, but not in rural areas, Stateline reported. However, that study’s data was limited by the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The updated program, called Opportunity Zones 2.0, provides larger incentives for rural investments compared to urban ones and has a reporting requirement.
