name: North Carolina Newsline
title: After election gains, NC Democrats and advocates push for voting rights, redistricting reforms
description: For the first time since 2010, Democrats will control one chamber of the North Carolina General Assembly, and voting rights advocates are already pressing the incoming legislature to pass a state Voting Rights Act and establish an independent commission to draw voting districts. On Tuesday, Democratic senators and representatives of several advocacy groups g[...]
text:
Sen. Kandie Smith speaks during a press conference at the North Carolina Legislative Building in Raleigh on Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Ahmed Jallow)For the first time since 2010, Democrats will control one chamber of the North Carolina General Assembly, and voting rights advocates are already pressing the incoming legislature to pass a state Voting Rights Act and establish an independent commission to draw voting districts.
On Tuesday, Democratic senators and representatives of several advocacy groups gathered at the legislature in Raleigh to outline the changes they want lawmakers to pursue when the new General Assembly convenes in January.
Speakers cast the proposals as a response to voters’ demands after the election, but many of their ideas will likely face an uphill battle in the Senate, where Republicans maintain a one-vote majority.
Voting rights
Forward Justice Executive Director Caitlin Swain called on North Carolina to lead the South by adopting a state Voting Rights Act, saying the measure is necessary to protect voters’ rights.
“We believe that this is not only possible — that it is structurally necessary to preserve the rights of our people,” said Caitlin Swain, executive director of Forward Justice. “We don’t think that it needs to be a partisan issue.”
More specifically, advocates are calling for automatic voter registration, and changes to how state and county election boards are appointed and funded. They said the legislation could also change how election directors are hired and paid and increase pay for poll workers.
Asked about that idea, outgoing House Speaker Destin Hall, R-Caldwell, said he doesn’t think it’s necessary. 
“It looked to me like most of their voters didn’t have a tough time voting this time around,” Hall quipped to reporters Tuesday, but added, “You can always improve things, of course, and so, you know, we can listen to that.” 
NC House Dems elect Reives, Butler to 2027 leadership roles

Redistricting
Tyler Daye, program manager for Common Cause North Carolina, called for an independent commission to draw legislative and congressional districts, criticizing both parties for using redistricting to their advantage when in power.
“The only path forward for redistricting in this state is an independent commission, taking the power out of the hands of politicians and putting it back with the people,” Daye said.
Daye said the commission should include equal numbers of Republicans, Democrats and unaffiliated voters. The commission should also be required to keep communities together and prohibited from using partisan data to draw districts.
Daye noted that outgoing Republican Senate Leader Phil Berger supported independent redistricting when Republicans were in the minority in the state legislature before 2011. But in late 2025, Berger was the chief proponent of redrawing the state’s congressional map to give Republicans an 11-3 advantage. 
“The party that is out of power wants reform. The party that is in power thinks the system is fine,” Daye said.
That 2025 redistricting backfired earlier this month, and Democrats won 11 seats to Republicans’ three, flipping the delegation. But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Berger, R-Rockingham, defended the redraw, blaming the flip on the national blue wave. 
“Reality is, we didn’t redraw the map in South Carolina. We saw similar situations in South Carolina,” Berger said. “We saw just a wave election. Those things happen from time to time.” 
Affordability 
Affordability was one of the top issues for voters this past election, and the senators at Tuesday’s event said lowering costs will be high on their agenda next year.
Sen. Natalie Murdock, D-Durham, said Democrats are preparing a package of legislation aimed at lowering everyday costs. “An agenda that helps people afford housing, healthcare, child costs, energy bills, groceries. An agenda that raises wages, strengthens public schools,” Murdock said. 
Murdock said Democrats may be able to find common ground with Republicans on housing and public education. 
Berger won’t be returning to the Senate next year — he lost his seat in the primary. But he said he expects opportunities for Republicans and Democrats to work together on some issues. 
“There’ll be a wealth of opportunities for folks to reach agreement on things,” Berger said, “and there likely will be some things where folks will say, ‘We’ll just have to really disagree,’” he said.
Sen. Val Applewhite, D-Cumberland, said she had received calls and emails from Republican constituents asking for help with policies advanced by their own party because they felt their voices were not being heard. She said Democrats need to remember that lesson next year.
“The power we hold is borrowed power,” Applewhite said. “It belongs to the people.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Hy-Vee claims $5 million in losses for non-reimbursed COVID-19 vaccinations
description: The Hy-Vee grocery chain is suing a Texas billing company over $5 million worth of COVID-19 vaccinations, the cost of which was never reimbursed by the federal government. Hy-Vee Inc. is suing Omnisys, a Texas limited liability company also known as XiFin Pharmacy Solutions, in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa. Hy-Vee, […]
text:
The Hy-Vee grocery chain is suing a Texas billing company over $5 million worth of COVID-19 vaccines that didn’t qualify for reimbursement by the federal government. This Hy-Vee Pharmacy is located at 410 N. Ankeny Blvd. in Ankeny, Iowa. (Photo via Google Earth)The Hy-Vee grocery chain is suing a Texas billing company over $5 million worth of COVID-19 vaccinations, the cost of which was never reimbursed by the federal government.
Hy-Vee Inc. is suing Omnisys, a Texas limited liability company also known as XiFin Pharmacy Solutions, in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa.
Hy-Vee, whose food stores typically include full-service pharmacies, alleges that during the COVID-19 pandemic, the nation’s pharmacies were required, by the federal government, to provide vaccinations at no cost to patients in an effort to stem the spread of the virus. The federal government agreed to reimburse those pharmacies for the cost of administering the vaccinations to the uninsured and the underinsured.
Hy-Vee alleges it was eligible to receive $40 per vaccine, and that it administered “hundreds of thousands of COVID vaccinations at no cost to the target patient populations” pursuant to the federal program.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In March 2022, the federal government announced the reimbursement program would stop accepting claims after April 5, 2022, due to concerns that funding for the program was running out.
According to the lawsuit, Hy-Vee and many other pharmacies contracted with Omnisys to act as a “clearinghouse” for the submission of reimbursement claims to the federal government, and paid Omnisys for each claim that the Texas company processed and submitted.
Hy-Vee claims that while most of its claims were accepted and reimbursed, some were rejected, with Omnisys asserting that the reason for some of those rejections was lack of funding for reimbursement.
Through Freedom of Information Act requests, Hy-Vee now alleges, the company learned directly from the federal government that the reimbursement program did not run out of money to pay any eligible claims submitted before the April 5, 2022, deadline. In addition, the information obtained by Hy-Vee indicated that some claims were rejected after being submitted after the deadline.
Hy-Vee’s lawsuit suggests Omnisys is to blame for rejected claims the grocery chair had turned over for processing – although, because Hy-Vee’s court petition is heavily redacted, the precise nature of Omnisys’ alleged failures isn’t clear.
For example, the publicly filed lawsuit states: “Despite receiving claims from Hy-Vee for processing, Omnisys failed to [redacted] … Omnisys also failed to [redacted] … Omnisys failed to [redacted], resulting in millions of dollars of losses to Hy-Vee … On June 23, 2022, Omnisys admitted that it timely received over 100,000 claims from Hy-Vee but failed [redacted].”
Hy-Vee alleges the redacted information, if made public, would violate the terms of confidentiality provisions written into its contract with Omnisys.
The specific allegations concerning Omnisys’ alleged failures, while redacted from public view, fall within two separate categories the lawsuit labels as “late claims” and “unsubmitted claims.” Hy-Vee alleges its own investigation of the matter has “uncovered that Hy-Vee timely submitted more than 150,000 claims to Omnisys that were not reimbursed” due to the Texas company’s alleged failures.
The lawsuit claims Hy-Vee’s total losses exceed $5 million. The grocery chain is suing Omnisys for breach of contract and negligent misrepresentation.
Omnisys / XiFin Pharmacy Solutions has yet to file a response to the lawsuit. Calls and emails to the company’s media relations office and its public relations firm were not immediately returned on Tuesday.
On its website, the company says it is dedicated to “empowering healthcare providers to achieve financial strength,” in part through medical billing services and claims management.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC Ports sees October cargo jump, favorable ruling in open-records lawsuit
description: The Port of Charleston had an increase in containerized cargo last month as freight promised by businesses earlier in the year started to materialize, although the port continues to lag year-over-year numbers.
text:
Cargo containers are moved at the Port of Charleston’s Wando Welch Terminal in Mount Pleasant. The State Ports Authority had a year-over-year increase in containerized cargo in October. (Photo by Matthew Peacock/Courtesy of the S.C. State Ports Authority)MOUNT PLEASANT — The Port of Charleston had an increase in containerized cargo last month as freight promised by businesses earlier in the year started to materialize, although the port continues to lag year-over-year numbers.
Charleston’s container terminals handled 119,494 boxes of all sizes in October for a 5.4% increase over the same month a year ago. Still, the number of containers is down by nearly 3.9% for the fiscal year, which started July 1.
“We saw an uptick in October,” Micah Mallace, president and CEO of the S.C. State Ports Authority, said during the agency’s board meeting Tuesday.
“Now, certainly some of that is market driven,” he said. “However, a sizable portion of that is also due to the awards, the business that was awarded early in the year that we have reported on, and that we are now seeing start.”
Mallace announced during his annual State of the Port speech last month that manufacturers and other businesses have committed to bringing an additional 159,000 containers through the port in the coming year.
Charleston port chief says recovery underway, but more work must be done

That is roughly 6% of the port’s annual total. Mallace said businesses — like Isuzu, which is moving freight for its Upstate truck plant through Charleston’s port — are picking the port because of financial and operational improvements that have been made.
Ports nationwide, including Charleston’s, have experienced a longer-than-usual peak shipping season as retailers prepare for the holidays.
Jonathan Gold, vice president of the National Retail Federation, said ports have seen strong numbers “even as the season winds down.”
“Consumers should find shelves well-stocked with a wide range of choices to meet their needs and budgets for the holidays,” Gold said.
The retail trade group is forecasting a nationwide 1.4% increase in imports for the calendar year.
FOIA lawsuit
Tuesday’s board meeting follows a court ruling earlier this month in which a Charleston County judge said the authority did not violate the state’s Freedom of Information Act when it held an unscheduled closed-door meeting in August 2025 to discuss the employment of former CEO Barbara Melvin.
Mount Pleasant resident and open-records advocate Frank Heindel sued the authority three months ago alleging the maritime agency broke state law by failing to inform the public ahead of time about the specific reason for the closed-door meeting. Instead, the agency provided a vague explanation that didn’t hint at any executive shakeup.
Melvin abruptly resigned from the authority’s top job two days after the closed-door meeting, receiving a severance package that totaled nearly $1 million.
Facing a lawsuit, SC Ports ratifies former CEO’s severance deal a year later

A judge said the authority’s actions were legal because it did not take a vote during the closed-door meeting.
But the ruling ignored the key point of Heindel’s case – that prior public notice was required by law.
“The (judge’s) order answers a question I didn’t ask,” Heindel told the SC Daily Gazette. “I never claimed the board took a secret vote. My claim was that South Carolina law requires a board to tell the public the specific reason it’s going behind closed doors.”
An authority spokeswoman declined to comment on the judge’s ruling.
The board’s attorney agreed during the court hearing that there is room for improvement in the way the agency handles closed-door meetings.
“I agree, and I hope the board acts on that without needing another lawsuit,” Heindel said. “Too many public bodies in this state use the same vague language, and the public deserves better.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Lower your expectations: House majority leader does not think Legislature will finish every bill stuck in negotiations
description: Any bills that do not reach Gov. Maura Healey’s desk before the legislative term ends on January 5, 2027, will expire, and lawmakers must start from scratch once the new one begins.
text:
THERE’S A LOT of pressure on lawmakers to make final decisions about dozens of policy proposals still lingering after the election, and top House Democrats have begun floating the idea that maybe some of their work will just have to wait ‘til next year.
Rep. Michael Moran, the House majority leader and a chief deputy to Speaker Ron Mariano, on Tuesday said he does not believe the Legislature will finish its work on all 12 of the bills that already won approval in both chambers and now need to be shaped into compromise versions.
“I think you’ll see some move. I don’t believe you’ll see all of them move, but I think you’ll see some move,” Moran told reporters when asked about the prospects for the dozen conference committees working to strike House-Senate accords. “That’s just negotiations. The good thing is we have next session to go right back at it.”
His comments, made after lawmakers convened a public hearing where they faced often-stinging feedback about their internal processes, are the clearest reflection yet that the Democrats who wield supermajorities in both the House and Senate are struggling to set aside their differences as the 2025-2026 term nears a close.
More than 40 discrete policy changes are at stake in the dozen bills bottled up in conference committees, ranging from zoning reforms to spur more housing production to energy efficiency program cuts aimed at reducing utility bills. The House and Senate have each approved separate versions of the bills, but nothing can reach Gov. Maura Healey’s desk until negotiators agree to final drafts that reconcile differences.
Any bills that are still pending by the time the term ends on January 5, 2027, will expire, and lawmakers will need to start the process from scratch after the next Legislature is sworn in the following day.
Typically, it takes several months for the Legislature to begin advancing weighty bills after starting a new two-year session, but they have moved more quickly on rare occasions. In 2021, lawmakers sent then-Gov. Charlie Baker a wide-reaching climate bill on the penultimate day of the term. With no time left to propose amendments, Baker vetoed the package altogether. Legislators then refiled and reapproved the bill in the next term, sending it back to the governor less than four weeks later.
“You’ve seen in the past sometimes we came right out the next session and did one of those bills immediately,” Moran said. “It may be slowed down in the process now, but it doesn’t mean it’s completely over.”
It’s not the first time a high-ranking House Democrat has tried to tamp down expectations about the remaining seven weeks of the 2025-2026 lawmaking term, the first in decades in which lawmakers granted themselves permission to tackle thorny, complex topics this late in the cycle. Rep. Aaron Michlewitz, who chairs the House Ways and Means Committee and sits on three of the negotiating panels, told The Boston Globe last week that it’s “too early to tell” if lawmakers will “bat 1.000” on everything that remains unfinished.
Good-government activists, many of whom spent Tuesday afternoon at a committee hearing directly urging Moran and other lawmakers to embrace further changes in the name of efficiency and transparency, responded to the darkening outlook with exasperation.
“Good grief,” said Scotia Hille, executive director of the group Act on Mass, when told of Moran’s comments.
“My first thought is of the rank-and-file representatives who voted on that legislation on behalf of their constituents. I’m sure they’ll be disappointed to hear legislation they worked on that they thought would move us forward might once again die in the black box of the conference committee,” Hille added.
For three decades, lawmakers set themselves a deadline to complete all major business by July 31 in the term’s second year, allowing only routine measures or those with unanimous support to move after that date.
The goal of the summer target was to avoid anything consequential or controversial during election season or in the lame-duck stretch afterward, but over time, legislators began leaving significant piles of work to finish in a last-minute sprint.
In both 2022 and 2024, the final sessions started late in the morning of July 31 and stretched overnight well past sunrise on August 1. The chaos — and the smoldering wreckage of bills that remained unfinished despite the all-nighters — prompted lawmakers to give themselves an extension this term.
Under rewritten rules adopted last year, as long as the House and Senate had each approvedtheir own bill by July 31 of the term’s second year, they could keep negotiating over a final accord all the way until the term ends.
Lawmakers hoped the change would smooth out friction and reduce some of the deadline-induced pressure, but some are beginning to sour on it.
Senate President Karen Spilka last week called the “prolonged inaction” on bills stuck in negotiations “unacceptable,” and signaled she might not support the same deadlines in next term’s rules package. Republican Rep. David Muradian of Grafton said during Tuesday’s hearing that moving the due date for conference committees “did nothing more than move the goalposts or kick the can down the road.”
“I don’t think there is any reason why we can’t get all these major pieces of legislation done,” Sen. Michael Moore of Millbury, a Democrat, told CommonWealth Beacon. “But I think anyone would be hard-pressed to say they’re happy that it has gone on this long.”
Still, while some frustrations ooze into public view, House Democrats have remained the most supportive of the new timeline. “Getting 200 people to agree on complicated issues can be challenging, so I’m not so worried about the deadline more than I am the substance,” Moran said.
He took a friendly tone toward his counterparts in the other chamber, too. Asked if House-Senate relations have declined in recent years, he replied, “I wouldn’t say that.”
“I have nothing but great things to say about the people I’ve served on conference committees with,” he said.
Hille linked the prospect of collapsing negotiations to another common frustration aired at Tuesday’s hearing: the Legislature’s reliance on larger omnibus bills as vehicles for legislating specific policy issues. Lawmakers defend the practice as more efficient, while critics knock it as a policymaking stick that higher-ups use to stifle dissent from rank-and-file members whomight be loath to sink an entire package over concerns with one section.
“We’ve seen this before when legislation can only pass as part of a massive, multi-subject political grab bag,” Hille said. “When it’s unsuccessful, we as Bay Staters are left without progress, relief, or even a clue where it went wrong, because it’s all happening behind closed doors.”
Jordan Wolman contributed to this report.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Lawrence among newly elected progressives doubling down on calls for federal data center moratorium
description: Outside of the U.S. Capitol building, standing behind stacks of bankers boxes, a number of progressive representatives gathered with labor advocates, political organizers and environmentalists to demand a pause on data center development until regulations can be put in place.  During a Tuesday press conference, Jim Walsh, the policy director for Food & Water[...]
text:
U.S. Rep.-elect William Lawrence (D-Lansing) joins organizers, labor advocates and environmentalists in Washington, D.C. demanding a federal data center moratorium on Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo Courtesy of Food and Water Watch)Outside of the U.S. Capitol building, standing behind stacks of bankers boxes, a number of progressive representatives gathered with labor advocates, political organizers and environmentalists to demand a pause on data center development until regulations can be put in place. 
During a Tuesday press conference, Jim Walsh, the policy director for Food & Water Watch said they intended to deliver 250,000 petitions to Congress seeking immediate action on a federal data center moratorium.
“The American public resoundingly rejected data centers two weeks ago, and Congress needs to follow their lead,” Walsh said, “Hundreds of organizations, hundreds of communities across the country, hundreds of thousands of people and millions of voters are saying no to data centers.”
The buildout of data centers – facilities that house servers and technology needed to power the internet and develop artificial intelligence tools – has become a flashpoint issue for communities throughout the country. 
Michigan is no exception, as an ever-growing number of data center proposals bucks up against community concerns of how these resource-demanding facilities will impact their electricity rates, their access to drinking water, and the state’s ability to meet its 100% clean energy standard by 2040.
U.S. Rep. James McGovern (D-Massachusetts), who is among the lead sponsors of the Artificial Intelligence Data Center Moratorium Act introduced by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), argued that the White House is asleep at the wheel when it comes to AI policy, calling for an immediate change to the status quo.
Will Lawrence rolls out plan for regulating Big Tech, data centers in Michigan and beyond

“People are sick of big, powerful tech companies squashing competition, controlling how we use the internet and driving up prices for everyday people,” McGovern said. “They want us to fight back, and they want us to take action immediately. The American people are done getting screwed over by unelected, unaccountable big tech oligarchs.”
McGovern also questioned the tactics data center developers have used to advance projects in American communities.
“Let’s get real, if this AI infrastructure is so great, why are they making shady deals without community input,” McGovern asked. “If it is so profitable, why are they begging for government subsidies? And if it’s so popular, why are the voices of people so loud begging them to stop?”
“And I’m going to tell you why,” McGovern continued. “Because they’re lying.”
With Democrats set to take control of the Republican-led U.S. House and U.S. Senate in the new year, McGovern said change is coming, and that they would reassert Congress’s power over the issues that matter to the American people.
Among the incoming members of Democrats’ newly won majority is U.S. Rep.-elect William Lawrence of Lansing, who defeated U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte). SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Lawrence made data centers and accountability for tech companies a cornerstone of his campaign, calling for a moratorium on both data center and advanced AI development.
“This was not an issue that was on many of our radars, you know, 15 months ago, and it wasn’t mine, but I’m trained as an organizer. As an organizer, the first thing you learn is to listen,” Lawrence said, noting that his district has seen several hyperscale data centers proposed over the past year and a half.
“I’m not somebody who, you know, thinks that there’s no potential use for AI,” Lawrence said. “I mean, it’s a marvelous technology. It’s the sum distillation of human language that now has been trained to talk back to us, and it is capable of amazing things. Maybe we could make medical advances and things of this nature.”
However, Lawrence stressed that in its current form, AI technology is not being built in service of the people.
“We know for certain that under the current incentives, it is going to be used to put people out of work, to harm the environment, to undermine our democracy, and to put us all at terrible risk,” Lawrence said, reiterating his support for a moratorium.

name: California
title: Bonuses tick up at California pension funds with 3 executives landing $1 million+ in incentives
description: California's biggest pension funds, CalPERS and CalSTRS, award bonuses every fall. Performance incentives increased as a run of good investment returns continued.
text:
In summary
California’s biggest pension funds, CalPERS and CalSTRS, award bonuses every fall. Performance incentives increased as a run of good investment returns continued.


The investment staff at California’s two biggest public pension funds received larger performance incentives this year, with three executives landing seven-figure bonuses, according to newly released summaries of the extra pay. 
Both funds beat their investment targets for the last three years, accounting for some of the bonus pay. 
The California State Teachers’ Retirement System earlier this month disclosed it paid $21.8 million in incentives to investment staff, up from $20.3 million last year.
CalSTRS Chief Investment Officer Scott Chan received a $1 million bonus in addition to his $576,000 salary; CalSTRS Chief Executive Officer Cassandra Lishnock earned a $750,000 incentive on top of her $500,000 salary.
Chan’s bonus in the previous year was $881,000, while Lishnock’s was $675,000.
The California Public Employees’ Retirement System disclosed this week that it distributed $37.9 million in bonuses to its staff, up slightly from $37.7 million in incentives last year. 
As previously reported by CalMatters, the biggest bonuses went to Chief Executive Marcie Frost at $1.1 million and Chief Investment Officer Stephen Gilmore at $1.7 million. Frost in the previous year earned a $766,000 performance incentive and Gilmore took home a $1.5 million bonus.
Both funds characterize the bonuses as essential to recruiting and retaining investment staff. They’re also sensitive to the perception that the bonuses are excessive. 
Each system described the incentives as a small fraction of the funds’ earnings in reports to their boards. 
CalPERS included an artificial intelligence-generated graphic that depicted the incentives as the equivalent of 6 cents for every $1,000 the fund held in its portfolio as of July 1, when its assets were valued at $637 billion. It provides retirement plans for about 2 million people.
CalSTRS as of last month had a portfolio valued at $415 billion. It provides pension plans to about 1 million people.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Mum is the legislative word on public school funding changes
description: A top Republican legislative leader gave no insights Tuesday afternoon about how the Florida Legislature may deal with public school funding and the “myriad of accountability problems” uncovered in a 2024-2025 school year state audit. Republican Sen. Don Gaetz championed a proposal (SB 318) during the 2026 session to significantly change the state’s school c[...]
text:
House Speaker Sam Garrison provided no insights on public school funding and vouchers during a question and answer session with reporters at the Florida Capitol. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)A top Republican legislative leader gave no insights Tuesday afternoon about how the Florida Legislature may deal with public school funding and the “myriad of accountability problems” uncovered in a 2024-2025 school year state audit.
Republican Sen. Don Gaetz championed a proposal (SB 318) during the 2026 session to significantly change the state’s school choice programs, improve student tracking, ensure funding follows the student, enhance budget predictability, and create consistency across scholarship programs.
School daze: Rapid expansion of voucher program leaves public, private schools underpaid

During budget negotiations over the state fiscal year 2026-27 budget, the Senate had proposed for accounting purposes that money for the school choice scholarships programs be separated from the Florida Education Finance Program (FEPF), the mechanism that funds traditional public schools, and expand the education stabilization fund, which shores up their financing amid enrollment fluctuations.
The Senate’s push to put the funding in different silos reflects a recommendation from a state audit of the 2024-25 academic year that showed “funding did not follow the child” — the rallying cry of school-choice proponents that education dollars need to follow students and not schools.
There was no House companion to SB 318 and the House refused during budget negotiations to bifurcate the funding as recommended by the audit.
When asked Tuesday whether the House would be open to shifting its position in the 2027 regular legislative session, House Speaker and Fleming Island Republican Sam Garrison was coy.
“On Day Zero, it’s hard for me to give you an answer to that,” Garrison said, adding that he “knows” House Appropriations Committee Chair Traci Koster, a Tampa Republican, and Senate Appropriations Chair Sen. Jay Trumbull, a Panama City Republican, will “work hard on these issues.”
He added: “Obviously, you know, when I say our goals in the House are a strong economy, safe streets, and quality schools — well, quality schools require consistent funding, so the money follows the vision we have for excellence.”
Gaetz told the Phoenix earlier this year that, until the Legislature takes action, “Everything will get worse. There will be more students who won’t be able to be tracked. Taxpayers will be paying for them but we won’t know where they are. We won’t know if the right money is going to the right place or the right student. More families who are relying on family empowerment scholarships to support homeschooling will be waiting for payments for weeks and months longer than they should,” Gaetz said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: New CT therapeutic arts pavilion breaks ground: ‘A living laboratory’
description: Silver Hill's new space will host its therapeutic arts, a mental health and addiction treatment offering considered integral by the hospital.
text:
Clinicians at Silver Hill Hospital in New Canaan, who treat patients for psychiatric issues and substance abuse disorders, have watched the benefits of art and horticulture therapy up close for decades. 
On Tuesday, the hospital held a groundbreaking for a $3.5 million therapeutic arts pavilion that will transform an existing building and affirm its commitment to the creative arts and horticulture in its therapeutic milieu.
“The creative arts specifically show benefits to patients who are recovering from mental illness and addiction. And we’re not talking about a nice thing to do while you’re waiting for the meds to kick in. We’re talking about treatment that goes right to the core of what the illness is,” said Dr. Andrew Gerber, president and medical director at Silver Hill. 
Because patients arrive at Silver Hill “to get the most cutting-edge evidence-based treatment for mental illness and addictions,” these treatments must be part of those offerings, he said.
Silver Hill is a nonprofit inpatient, outpatient and residential treatment facility that was founded in 1931. Designed by GMI Architects, the new pavilion will “immediately be best in class” for a psychiatric facility like Silver Hill, Gerber said.
Silver Hill President and Medical Director Andrew J. Gerber, MD, PhD, speaks to guests during a groundbreaking at Silver Hill Hospital’s new Therapeutic Arts Pavilion at its Martin Center in New Canaan on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Silver Hill already offers a variety of arts programming, including painting, yoga and gardening. But currently those activities take place wherever there is space on campus. Gerber said the ambitious new pavilion will be a huge leap forward. That’s in part because, by gathering patients together under one roof, the center will offer a second powerful therapeutic component: community. 
The benefit of being part of a community or large family has been known for a long time in psychiatry, Gerber said, but can be challenging for institutions to reproduce in a hospital setting.
“You need that space where our patients and their therapists can come together and feel that bond, feel the way that their togetherness actually changes their brain,” Gerber said. “So for me, what we’re creating here is truly a living laboratory.”
Damara Toohey, the project’s lead architect, said the new center will be in a renovated building from the 1960s, a timber frame structure with large windows that currently houses a swimming pool that has been underutilized by patients. The renovation will retain the structural features of the original building but will have state-of-the-art studios for painting, movement, and other arts activities, as well as a greenhouse area for horticulture.
Toohey said her firm spoke with staff who provide those therapeutic services, and those staff members also sought patient input.
“Creative art is a wonderful way to explore who you are, your relationship with the world and how you leave here to go back to your normal life while still bringing these skills,” Toohey said.
A rendering of Silver Hill Hospital’s new Therapeutic Arts Pavilion at its Martin Center in New Canaan by GMI Architects is seen during a groundbreaking on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Cheryl Bundy, Silver Hill’s director of spiritual care and patient development, spoke about the moments patients would soon experience inside the new space.
“We welcome a young adult who hasn’t felt joy in months; a parent who lost the thread of who they were; a professional who has spent years holding everything together for everyone else and has finally asked for help for themselves,” she said. “Someone will pick up a paintbrush for the first time since childhood. Someone plants a seed and comes back the next day to see if anything changed at all. And someone who has very little to look forward to may find themselves actually looking forward to coming back tomorrow. That is a small thing to say aloud at the groundbreaking, but it’s an enormous thing in a life that’s going through recovery.”
Gerber said in an interview with The Connecticut Mirror that the pavilion gets to the heart of questions about how effective various forms of psychotherapy are compared to medication or physical interventions like electroconvulsive therapy, or ECT.
“Psychotherapy, when done well, has more efficacy than our best biological treatments,” he said. “That doesn’t mean I’m against biological treatments — I’m a psychiatrist, we give medication, we do ECT. But to think about the psychotherapy as the anchor, and the medications and the other things as adjunctive and helpful, is actually much more my approach.”
More recently, in the past 10 to 15 years, Gerber said, therapeutic arts clinicians have done studies to measure the efficacy of their treatments. “And one by one, those studies have shown efficacy for those therapies that is equal to other forms of psychotherapy or medication, believe it or not,” he said. “So for us to be a cutting edge place, we want to integrate all of it.”

title: Center for Intellectual Freedom director to set center strategy, memorandum of understanding
description: The Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa’s first permanent director has been tasked with developing its long-term strategy and establishing its place within university operations. According to the offer letter sent from the Iowa Board of Regents to UI political science professor and new center director Brian Lai, provided over email by [[...]
text:
Panelists speaking Dec. 6, 2025, at the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa, from left, are center Interim Director Luciano de Castro, U.S. Assistant Secretary for Postsecondary Education David Barker, state Rep. Taylor Collins, state Sen. Kerry Gruenhagen and Regent Christine Hensley. Brian Lai has taken over as the center's permanent director. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa’s first permanent director has been tasked with developing its long-term strategy and establishing its place within university operations.
According to the offer letter sent from the Iowa Board of Regents to UI political science professor and new center director Brian Lai, provided over email by board Senior Communications Director Josh Lehman, Lai started his five-year tenure as director Nov. 13. Lai was announced as the new director at the board of regents’ Nov. 12 meeting.
Responsibilities for Lai listed in the letter include developing the center’s five-year strategic plan, completing this year’s speaker series and developing one for 2027, preparing a revised annual budget, bolstering “stakeholder engagement” and establishing an Academic Memorandum of Understanding for the center with the UI and board of regents office.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Lehman stated in his email Lai’s current academic year salary is $117,394, but with the new director role his roles will shift to 30% center work and 70% work through the UI College of Liberal Arts and Sciences, meaning the center will fund 30% of his salary with the university covering the rest.
Compensation for his director work includes an academic year administrative stipend of $29,349, $5,000 for research and two months of summer payments totaling $26,088, according to the offer letter. Lai’s total compensation with his new position comes out to $177,831.
In addition to the responsibilities laid out in the letter, Lai will also have to abide by the law that established the center in 2025, which codifies his ability to manage hiring and firing of center staff and faculty among other duties. He will report directly to the board’s center committee chair, Regent Christine Hensley.
“In your role as the Director, it is the Board’s expectation that the duties described in Iowa Code Chapter 263C be fulfilled in the order set forth in the statute,” the offer letter stated. “Any questions regarding the interpretation or application of the statute should be directed to the Chair of the CIF Committee.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Legislators to tackle property taxes — again — in 2027
description: LouAnn Hansen said her property tax bill on a small second home with access to Flathead Lake jumped 93.24% in one year — and she can’t even stay there half of the year. The parcel is 0.06 acres — 2,490 square feet — and it has a manufactured home and a small shed, Hansen said. […]
text:
Photo illustration by Getty Images.LouAnn Hansen said her property tax bill on a small second home with access to Flathead Lake jumped 93.24% in one year — and she can’t even stay there half of the year.
The parcel is 0.06 acres — 2,490 square feet — and it has a manufactured home and a small shed, Hansen said.
She said her land isn’t lakefront property despite access to it, and the state Department of Environmental Quality mandates a winter closure due to its sewage system.
At a legislative committee meeting Monday, Hansen said her taxes jumped to $2,167.80 after the property’s assessed value went from $131,602 to $270,339, and its taxable value increased 105% in one year.
Hansen said other residents of the 121-lot Paradise Cove Resort in Polson are in a similar situation, and many are Montana seniors.
“Property owners I know have discussed how they perhaps will not be able to afford their property taxes and may have to sell, which will most likely be to more wealthy out-of-state owners,” Hansen said.
At the final meeting of the Revenue Interim Committee before the 2027 Montana Legislature, Hansen asked lawmakers to make a property tax fix a top priority for the upcoming session, and to be sure they had adequate time to consider any bills.
In the 2025 session, lawmakers worked on reducing property taxes, but they disagreed on the best approach and didn’t pass a pair of bills that did so until the final day.
One bill, Senate Bill 542, faces a couple of legal challenges, including one alleging it was cobbled together out of the public eye, a violation of the Montana Constitution.
One result of 2025 legislation was 80% of Montana homeowners saw property tax decreases, according to earlier estimates.
But some people such as Hansen, who own second homes, saw increases, and others, such as owners of long-term rentals, didn’t get access to a rebate.
“I would really like to see this kind of legislation that affects every single Montanan to not be dealt with right at the end of the session,” Hansen said.
At their meeting Monday, legislators heard some of the work that still needs to be done to help Montanans pay rising property taxes, and they also heard a plea to ensure any new legislation doesn’t undo solutions from 2025.
Heather O’Loughlin, head of the Montana Budget and Policy Center, said if legislators make policy changes “around the edges,” they should consider impacts on Montanans paying property taxes at the median rate.
“You all provided a pretty substantial property tax decrease for primary residences at the median, so we hope that we can continue to hold that,” O’Loughlin said.
Rep. Mark Thane, D-Missoula, pointed out one outcome that meant disparate treatment of similar property owners.
Thane showed how a young couple coming from outside Montana who purchased property in the state in August 2026 would be treated differently than another couple in a similar situation when it came to a property tax rebate — based on the status of the home under its previous owner.
If the previous owner had applied for a reduced property tax rate under the new legislation, the new couple would receive the benefit, but if the previous owner hadn’t qualified, the new owner would miss out, Thane confirmed through the Department of Revenue.
“Is there any latitude or capacity within the rules to afford that young couple safe harbor and qualify for the rebate?” Thane asked.
Bryce Kaatz, with the Department of Revenue, said the plain reading of the law requires a property owner to have lived in their principal residence for at least seven months, so the couple coming from outside Montana would not be eligible.
Rep. James Reavis, D-Billings, said he’s been receiving complaints from people who are not professional landlords but have been renting long-term rentals to others and missed the refund application deadline.
“Does this require a legislative solution?” Reavis said.
Kaatz said the plain language of the refund provision is specific to a principal residence, and the Department of Revenue does not have latitude to extend it to long-term rental properties.
Kaatz said he didn’t see obstacles to legislation that would apply the refund to long-term rentals, but he also said it would take some time to implement.
In public comment, Sen. Mary Ann Dunwell, D-Helena, said many of her constituents benefited from legislation in 2025, but she sees Montanans with property tax problems that need attention.
“Many, however, keep me up at night,” Dunwell said. “Their faces and their despair haunt me, and I’m sure you’re in a similar position. The bills we passed hurt them, really, really a lot.”
Sen. Greg Hertz, R-Polson, is one of the plaintiffs in two lawsuits against SB 542, one of the key property tax bills from 2025.
Also a committee member, Hertz said remarks in the meeting demonstrate the difficulties with such a bill.
“This discussion obviously illustrates what happens when you try to pass a very complex bill, no matter what it is, in a matter of a couple days, and you don’t see all the unintended consequences,” Hertz said.
But Bob Story, with the Montana Taxpayers Association, said any piece of legislation ends up needing work after it takes effect.
“No matter how much time you put into it, you never fix all the holes, and you find out a lot of unintended consequences when it actually gets implemented,” Story said.
Chairman and Rep. Larry Brewster, R-Billings, said Tuesday the committee opted against bringing its own property tax bills to the 2027 session, partly to first see how litigation is resolved.
Brewster said some bills might try to do away with legislation from 2025, and he anticipates others that would “nibble away at the worst parts” to help more property owners.
More than a dozen bill drafts are in the works to address property tax laws, although not all are related to residential taxpayers, and some are on hold.
“There’s a lot of different ideas among members about what they think we should do,” Brewster said.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Power transformer manufacturer to open $328M factory near Gaffney
description: A company that makes transformers for the power grid plans to open a manufacturing plant near Gaffney, pledging to hire 400 people.
text:
An electric transmission substation pictured in Bismarck on April 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)A company that makes transformers for the power grid plans to open a manufacturing plant near Gaffney, pledging to hire 400 people.
LIMiK International, headquartered in Ukraine, has been engineering and building power transformers for 25 years.
Now it plans to bring manufacturing operations to the United States, investing $328 million in Cherokee County, the company announced Tuesday.
It will move into a warehouse northeast of Gaffney town limits where Hart brand power tools previously stored and shipped products.
How SC plans to boost its profile in the energy industry, bringing in new companies and jobs

“At a time of rising costs and growing demand for electricity, this plant will supply utilities, manufacturers and businesses across the Southeast and the United States with the transformers they need, while supporting South Carolina’s economy and American energy dominance,” LIMiK International LLC Co-owner Igor Lon said in a statement.
Ken Moon, director of the Cherokee County Development Board, said there is a dire need for transformers across the country, with many utilities waiting 18 months or more for delivery. That need is what’s driving the investment.
The company expects to begin operation in early 2028.
Moon said wages paid by the company will start at $28 per hour for entry-level positions and will average $37 per hour across the plant. The company will need managers, sales professionals, engineers, welders, electricians and mechanics, as well as assembly workers on the manufacturing line.
In exchange, county council approved the company for property tax breaks. The council passed the incentives without making the details of the deal public, Moon said.
County Council Chairman Tim Spencer, in a statement, called the announcement a “significant milestone in the continued growth and diversification” of the county’s industrial base and “exactly the type of investment that moves Cherokee County forward.”
The 400 new jobs more than makes up for the 114 positions lost when the tool distribution center closed in May 2024.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont public schools expect the lowest health insurance increase in years. For districts, it’s only a small relief.
description:
Statewide efforts to push down healthcare costs have lowered insurance increases for public schools. Still, school boards are budgeting for a litany of rising expenses amid tight spending caps. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont public schools expect the lowest health insurance increase in years. For districts, it’s only a small relief..
text:
Signs posted in many Vermont communities call for property tax changes. Photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger

Vermont school districts expect a break from more than a decade of steep hikes in staff health insurance costs, but they still face tough choices as they craft their budgets.
After seeing premiums increase more than 200% since 2020, the nonprofit group that coordinates public school employee benefits, the Vermont Education Health Initiative, announced that it expects premiums for employees’ health insurance to increase an average 2.5% for fiscal year 2028, which begins July 1.
Those premiums are “definitely welcome news when compared to the double-digit increases that we’ve had in recent years,” said Sue Ceglowski, executive director of the Vermont School Boards Association.
This year’s projections disrupt a trend of climbing prices, but they don’t necessarily mean that districts will be able to achieve lower overall budgets. 
Public school spending on healthcare premiums is approaching $400 million a year across the state, according to Ceglowski. While the costs have downstream effects on taxpayers, they make up only a part of the state’s more than $2 billion in education costs. The spending on healthcare has become a high-profile piece of budgets that some lawmakers and school leaders have billed as a way to curb expenses and offer relief to property tax payers.
School boards are expecting an especially difficult budgeting year. As Vermont starts transitioning to a state-directed education funding model, the state has pushed districts to curb costs, and it plans to impose tax penalties on residents if the district’s spending exceeds a set cap. Meanwhile districts have rising costs to cover, such as food, gas and heating fuel.
Anticipating any downstream effects of projected healthcare costs on taxpayers is difficult at this point, according to Ceglowski, because districts are still drafting budgets, most of which go to voters for approval on Town Meeting Day. 
The effect on districts
In the Washington Central Unified Union School District, which enrolls about 1,300 kids and operates six prekindergarten and K-12 schools in five towns surrounding Montpelier, board members are still in the early stages of writing next year’s budget. Members expect to see an initial budget draft in a meeting this week, according to Chair Diane Nichols-Fleming. 
“While (the small projected health insurance increase) is a huge break, it isn’t keeping up with other things that aren’t following typical trajectory, you know, like fuel prices have skyrocketed,” Nichols-Fleming said. 
Unlike the modest health insurance increases, the rising price of essentials such as diesel for school buses, heating fuel and food are difficult for districts to manage, Nichols-Fleming said. Winter can also bring unpredictable costs, she said, including plowing and building maintenance.
The small increases expected next year are on top of already high base premiums. A silver plan — the least expensive option available to public school employees — is expected to cost a total $1,244.59 a month for coverage of one person, while a silver-rated plan for an employee and their spouse would be $2,489.20. A silver plan for parents and children would cost $3,541.72. Schools split the overall premium cost with their employees, covering roughly 80% of the base premium, with some variances depending on the employee and plan. 
Last year, VEHI requested cost increases of 7.3% overall. The year before, plans grew by 11.9%. The 2.5% increase is still awaiting approval from the Vermont Department of Financial Regulation.
The premium growth for school employees’ plans follows smaller premium increases for plans on Vermont Health Connect, as lawmakers, regulators, hospitals and insurers all try to jointly curb increasing healthcare costs.
Many of the same factors driving down the marketplace’s premium increases are also working to keep public school insurance costs lower. Those include orders from the state’s main hospital regulator to shrink hospital revenue, a 2025 cap on the cost of certain prescription drugs and BlueCross BlueShield’s new contract with the University of Vermont Health network, which VEHI said will save over $12 million.
“The actions that the Legislature and the Green Mountain Care Board have taken with respect to addressing the affordability crisis in healthcare — lowering prices, rationalizing hospital budgets — all of that has had a very positive impact on VEHI,” Mark Hage, the trust manager for the group, said. 

READ MORE

Changes made over the last two years have allowed the group to reduce their expenses by $44 million, he said. 
Additionally, VEHI limited coverage of GLP-1 drugs, such as Ozempic, to patients with Type 2 diabetes and certain cardiovascular conditions, which has yielded $16 million in savings since the start of this year. 
VEHI also negotiated a new contract with its pharmacy benefit manager that coordinates drug prices and procurement. VEHI said the new plan should save $5.3 million in the coming year.
On top of paying for their share of premiums, public schools end up paying for much of the out-of-pocket expenses their staff incur.  
In addition to an employee’s regular insurance, the employer pays for a set amount of an employee’s out-of-pocket claims through these reimbursement cost-sharing accounts, called HRAs and HSAs, which are available to any employees on VEHI plans. 
Districts will contribute up to $1,900 a year toward medical costs for an individual and up to $4,000 for couples and families of “licensed” staff, such as teachers and principals. For unlicensed staff (those who don’t need professional certification to do their jobs) schools pay even more into those accounts. For most of the HRA plans, the district covers most out-of-pocket expenses toward an employee’s deductible, at which point, the insurer covers the costs. 
Those additional benefits become costly for districts to take on. One 2025 calculation from Ceglowski found that districts spent $33 million covering claims in 2023 for employees on one mid-tier plan type — a separate expense than the premiums for those plans themselves. 
A piece of a bigger budget puzzle 
In the Washington Central district, board members are expecting to face tough budget decisions for the second year in a row, as the district feels the effects of statewide education reform efforts, Nichols-Fleming said.
Vermont is in the process of overhauling how it pays for education by moving to a state-directed funding model called a foundation formula. That model allows the state to decide how much it spends to educate each student, with certain added funds for students who are more expensive to educate, such as those with learning disabilities or those from low-income families.
As Vermont studies school consolidation and transitions to a state-directed funding system, it’s urging districts to rein in spending. The state sets a spending cap that allows districts to spend a set percentage above what it costs to educate each student on average. If a district spends above that spending cap in per-student costs, the state can double taxes on residents. 
Legislation passed this year lowers that spending cap on per-student costs year by year, pushing districts to spend less and less annually.
Last year, Washington Central struggled to propose a budget that would spare residents from tax penalties, according to Nichols-Fleming. And this year, districts are budgeting within even tighter limits. 
“It’s not going to be easy and, you know, we’re going to be very saddened if we go into it thinking it’s going to be very easy,” she said. 
“It would be foolish to not be worried.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont public schools expect the lowest health insurance increase in years. For districts, it’s only a small relief..

name: National
title: Black mothers around US say pregnancy, postpartum needs are often unmet
description: The majority of a group of over 1,600 Black mothers of infants and toddlers across the country said they lacked access to continuous and comprehensive reproductive health care before, during and after pregnancy and have often felt ignored or discriminated by medical professionals, according to a report co-produced and released Tuesday by several groups that [...]
text:
Affordable childcare advocate Danielle Stewart gets ready for the day with her daughter, Marilyn, on June 15, 2026, at their home in Ladue, Mo. Like many of the 1,600 Black mothers who answered a national survey, Stewart said she wasn’t fully listened to by doctors at the hospital. (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).The majority of a group of over 1,600 Black mothers of infants and toddlers across the country said they lacked access to continuous and comprehensive reproductive health care before, during and after pregnancy and have often felt ignored or discriminated by medical professionals, according to a report co-produced and released Tuesday by several groups that advocate on behalf of women.
Many of respondents’ concerns and experiences are related to structural racism and social inequities, said Amani Echols, senior policy analyst for maternal health at the National Partnership for Women & Families. The partnership conducted the survey along with two other advocacy groups, Black Mamas Matter Alliance and MomsRising.
Research has shown that Black women face disproportionately high rates of injury and death related to pregnancy and childbirth compared with other racial groups, and that a majority of those deaths are preventable.
Birth centers are linked to better health outcomes, research shows, but 10 states have none

“The issues that Black moms are experiencing are not due to individual failures or individual behaviors, but a reflection of systemic failures and inequities,” Echols said. “Over and over again, we heard moms share their experiences of disrespectful maternity care where they felt ignored, not listened to, their requests for timely care were not prioritized.”
Black mothers reported among their top concerns receiving unwanted labor and birth interventions. About 31% of respondents said they experienced little to no shared decisionmaking around having their pregnancies induced with medication or invasive procedures. Among respondents with a cesarean birth, 63% were unplanned, compared with 46% among white respondents. But the report also points out that within the same group of C-section deliveries, 75% of Black women, a larger percentage than other racial groups, experienced regular labor contractions beforehand, “raising questions about the benefits and necessity of surgery.” 
“I feel angry about my C-section because it wasn’t the experience I wanted or expected,” reads an anonymous quote in the report. “I felt like the decision was out of my control, and that loss of choice left me frustrated and disappointed.
There have been recent reports of Black women forced by court order to have C-sections. 
One mother with a life-altering birth injury is Danielle Stewart from Missouri, who in 2014 experienced a failed epidural that left her paralyzed from the waist down. 
“Imagine walking into a hospital to have your first child and leaving on a stretcher alone, paralyzed from your waist down,” Stewart told the Missouri Independent, alleging the anesthesiologist had dismissed her pain concerns. She sued the hospital, which settled, and has since become an advocate for affordable child care. 
The Listening to Black Mothers survey is the latest in the National Partnership’s ongoing, intermittent Listening to Mothers survey series launched in 2002. This one reached Black mothers 18 and up in all 50 states and the District of Columbia, who answered in-depth questionnaires about their experiences around hospital births in 2023, 2024 and 2025.  
Among their other top concerns was limited access to family planning. Only 37% of Black respondents intended to become pregnant when they did, compared with 52% of white respondents. 
Support during pregnancy and labor from doulas and midwives has been linked to better outcomes for Black women and babies. But just 7% received most of their maternity care from midwives, though 73% expressed they would want to consider such care for future pregnancies. About 17% of respondents said they received doula support.
Another concern was lack of access to treatment for mental health issues during and after pregnancy, which were high among Black mothers. Among respondents with symptoms of anxiety or depression, 58% said they received no treatment during pregnancy, and 53% said they received no treatment after pregnancy. 
‘It’s a safe space’: Mobile midwifery clinics meet patients where they are

Relatedly, many Black respondents reported gaps in insurance coverage before, during and after pregnancy. Looming federal Medicaid cuts are expected to disproportionately affect Black families. Among the survey respondents, Medicaid was the primary payer for the prenatal care of 57% of Black respondents, and Medicaid paid for the childbirth of 62% of respondents. 
The report zooms in on the impact of climate change on Black mothers: 34% of Black mothers reported experiencing a weather-related disaster during pregnancy, with one respondent saying she had no power for two weeks when she was about four months pregnant. And it delves into discrimination faced by Black and multiracial Black mothers. The majority of Black respondents said they felt safer with providers who shared their race, ethnicity or heritage, but only 1 in 4 always had maternity providers who did. Many in the Black community practice self care to deal with the issues they face.
The report comes just two weeks after Democrats swept the midterm elections nationwide, with the help of high Black voter turnout in states such as Georgia and throughout the South, ushering in many Black mothers into office. They include Georgia Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, Virgin Islands Democratic Gov.-elect Stacey Plaskett and Democratic U.S. Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton, of Illinois.  
Echols said she hopes federal and state lawmakers work to enact some of the policies recommended in the report, and that Congress can slow or prevent some of the federal health cuts slated to go into effect early next year. 
“The number of Black female legislators is a big win for the maternal health space, but also the record number of healthcare professionals and scientists who campaigned on prioritizing healthcare also makes me really optimistic,” Echols said. “I’m also hopeful that there’s an ability to focus on maternal health in a much more expansive way than we have been able to.”
Other recommended congressional policies would provide funding to establish racism and discrimination training for maternity care staff, require state Medicaid programs to cover doula and midwifery services, and increase federal support for Medicaid and public health systems.
Efforts to expand access to doulas and birth centers to improve Black maternal mortality outcomes are under way in states such as New Jersey and North Carolina. 
Stateline reporter Sofia Resnick can be reached at sresnick@stateline.org.

title: NJ Supreme Court weighs jail credits for time on home confinement
description: Prosecutors argue the 246 days a Hudson County man spent on 24/7 home confinement shouldn't count against his jail sentence.
text:
Chief Justice Stuart Rabner asks questions during arguments in a clergy sex abuse case on April 28, 2025, at the Richard J. Hughes Justice Complex in Trenton. (Dana DiFilippo | New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey’s Supreme Court will determine whether time a Hudson County man spent on home confinement with an ankle monitor under the supervision of the county’s Department of Corrections should count as time served against his sentence for aggravated assault.
The high court on Tuesday took oral arguments in Jason Edwards’ appeal, which seeks 246 days in jail credits for time he spent in the Hudson County Department of Corrections’ home confinement program that lower courts ruled should be denied because he was not physically in jail for that time.
“The problem with the state’s argument is that Mr. Edwards was never released from the custody of the Department of Corrections despite the order releasing him on pretrial monitoring,” said Assistant Deputy Public Defender Alyssa Aiello, who represented Edwards.
The dispute centers around a court rule that states defendants must get credit for time served for any time spent in custody of a jail or state hospital between the time of their arrest and sentence.
The county operated a home confinement program but it was not meant to serve individuals the court ordered released pretrial but was for the county jail’s inmates, she said.
Edwards in briefs argued he was in the department’s custody even while outside the county’s correctional facility, noting his name appeared on a daily population list and that others on Hudson’s GPS home confinement program had been arrested without warrant and returned to jail without a hearing when the department determined they’d violated the conditions of their house arrest.
The latter point, especially, distinguished the county’s home confinement program from the court’s own because the court’s system guaranteed those on home confinement greater due process, including a hearing for a bench warrant, Aiello said.
Attorneys for county and state prosecutors said there was no guarantee that would be the case because Edwards committed no violations while under electronic monitoring and so never tested the issue.
They added jail officials previously contacted him to see if he had committed a bonafide violation when he stepped out onto his porch rather than immediately remand him back to the Hudson County Correctional Facility.
In the case of an actual violation, he would still get due process after being remanded, said Assistant Hudson County Prosecutor Colleen Signorelli.
“At that point, the state would have considered moving to revoke, there would be a violation of monitoring hearing,” she said. “If no motion to revoke was filed, the court would not be able to detain him.”
In briefs, Edwards’ attorneys said jail officials warned he could be returned to jail if he did not immediately go inside of the home when he went out onto his porch to smoke.
An agreement between Edwards and the county’s Department of Corrections said any violations “shall result” in Edwards being returned to the department plus appropriate sanctions.
The justices spent much of their focus on whether Edwards’ home confinement was equivalent to jail time in the eyes of the court rule that governs jail credits.
“At home, the defendant has the ability to choose when to go to sleep, when to wake up, what to eat, when to eat, who they can visit with and when the guests may arrive — those are differences from confinement within a jail,” Chief Justice Stuart Rabner said.
Prosecutors cited those and similar differences — like the monitoring of telephonic and electronic communications of inmates — to argue Edwards shouldn’t get the credit because jail places far more restrictions on a person’s privacy and liberty than home confinement.
Aiello argued house arrest amounted to custodial confinement in Edwards’ case because while home confinement might be more comfortable than confinement in a correctional facility, he was not free to leave in either case, including because he could be charged with escape for doing so.
“I think because it’s hard for us to understand how being at home should be treated as the same as being in jail, that we often lose sight of what an extraordinary deprivation of liberty it is to be confined 24/7,” she said.
The record is silent on whether Edwards was ever told he could be charged with escape for leaving his home while confined there, but prosecutors argued house arrest pretrial could never satisfy that charge.
“You have to be in official detention to be prosecuted for escape, but the definition of official detention specifically excludes constraint incident to release on bail,” Signorelli said. “Because electronic monitoring was a condition of the defendant’s release, he was not in official detention and therefore could not be prosecuted for escape.”

SEAFORD, Del. — Delaware Technical Community College’s Seaford Innovation Center is bringing trade and health care training closer to western Sussex County residents while giving a former shopping center a new role in the local economy.
The 30,600-square-foot facility at the Nylon Capital Center offers welding, heating and air conditioning, dental, phlebotomy, sterile processing and certified nursing assistant training. Students began attending in June, with the full program lineup starting this fall. The college held its ribbon-cutting Oct. 9, according to its Oct. 12 announcement.
College President Mark T. Brainard said the center would help residents train closer to home and “help more Delawareans gain the education and skills needed to meet the demands of the state’s workforce.”
The two-story center includes medical training spaces designed to resemble workplaces, computer workstations and classrooms. The college also announced plans for high school dual-enrollment classes and public conference-room rentals.
For prospective students, the next step is finding a course that fits their schedule and career goals. Delaware Tech’s July-December workforce catalog lists Seaford offerings alongside those at its other locations, with course hours, tuition and prerequisites.
The catalog also describes a welding apprenticeship route that connects classroom instruction with a separate employment step: Students apply to registered sponsors, and an employer oversees the on-the-job training required for a registered apprenticeship. Completing classroom training is one step in that process.
Students should contact the center about upcoming classes, available seats and financial assistance.
The college’s arrival is part of a broader effort to reuse the former Nylon Capital Shopping Center on Stein Highway.
Delaware’s 2026 Capital Projects Fund performance report describes the redevelopment as combining workforce education, health care, business incubation and family services. The report lists Delaware Tech and The Mill coworking space as operational, with TidalHealth construction approaching completion at the time of the update.
Public money has helped finance that transformation. The state report lists a $20 million federal American Rescue Plan Act Capital Projects Fund budget for the broader Seaford project through Tri-State Community Partners Inc. That figure covers the larger community redevelopment and does not establish the cost of Delaware Tech’s facility alone. accountingfiles.delaware.gov
An earlier state announcement, issued in December 2022, identified initial redevelopment commitments of $3.1 million from Seaford, $2 million from the state and $500,000 from 9th Street Development Co.

name: National
title: Black politicians win newfound power across state, federal governments
description: Black politicians will wield unprecedented amounts of power following this month’s seismic midterm elections. Black representation will reach new heights across state and federal governments: In Washington, the U.S. House is set to seat its first Black speaker and the U.S. Senate will include a record seven Black members.  Black leaders also set new levels [[...]
text:
Georgia House speaker-nominee Rep. Carolyn Hugley, a Democrat, speaks at a news conference on Nov. 12 at the state Capitol in Atlanta announcing the caucus’ picks for leadership roles. Black politicians will wield unprecedented levels of power following this month’s midterm elections. (Photo by Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder)
Black politicians will wield unprecedented amounts of power following this month’s seismic midterm elections.
Black representation will reach new heights across state and federal governments: In Washington, the U.S. House is set to seat its first Black speaker and the U.S. Senate will include a record seven Black members. 
Black leaders also set new levels for state representation, according to an analysis by The Collective Political Action Committee, which works to build Black political power by increasing Black representation in state and local governments. 
A record five states and the U.S. Virgin Islands will be led by Black governors. And voters are poised to send a record nine Black lieutenant governors, eight Black attorneys general and nine Black state House speakers to office in 2027. 
“Now, you’re actually going to see Black leaders in positions to drive policy, to determine what policy issues get debated, what policy issues get attention, and also what policy issues get covered by the media,” said Quentin James, founder and president of The Collective PAC. 
Fueled by Democratic gains, women will hold a record of state legislative seats

In total, the political action committee expects between 850 and 900 Black lawmakers in state capitols next year once election results are finalized. That’s poised to set a record and represent more than 11% of the nation’s 7,386 state lawmakers.
“For one election cycle to do what we haven’t done in 250 years, I think it’s more than historic,” James said. “It is kind of a cultural shift in terms of what it means to now be a Black elected official.”
Not every legislative chamber has selected leaders for upcoming sessions. But so far state House chambers in Colorado, Delaware, Georgia, Maryland, New York, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Texas and Virginia are expected to be led by Black speakers.
In Illinois, embattled House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch recently announced he would not seek another term leading the chamber. Citing unnamed sources, FOX Chicago recently reported that the Illinois Legislative Black Caucus would only support one of its own members as successor. That means as many as 10 state Houses could be led by Black speakers next year. 
After flipping control of the lower chamber, Georgia House Democrats last week nominated Rep. Carolyn Hugley for House speaker. If approved by the full House, she would become Georgia’s first Black speaker.
In a news conference, Hugley described the new Democratic leadership as “a team that looks like Georgia.”
In Georgia, Black women will hold at least nine statewide executive offices — up from one currently. Nationally, Black women will hold at least 19 statewide executive offices, according to The Collective PAC.
The number of Black lieutenant governors is expected to nearly double from five to nine. In Kansas, Oklahoma, New York and South Carolina, voters elected their state’s first ever Black lieutenant governors. 
Democrats romped in state elections. What will they do with their newfound power?

As with the record number of women elected this year, the rise in Black representation was largely driven by Democratic gains. 
In Florida, Byron Donalds will become the state’s first Black governor and the nation’s first elected Black Republican governor. 
Following the midterms, only one Black Republican will serve in Congress, U.S. Sen. Tim Scott, of South Carolina. 
James said Black Republicans such as Donalds and Scott have a chance at recasting what it means to be a Black Republican in the post-Trump era. While his organization works to elect Black Democrats, he said it’s important to have representation on both sides of the aisle. 
“That’s a way where we could find more political equity,” he said, “because yes, there are African Americans who are conservative. They should be represented as well. But I don’t think the MAGA movement is the best place for that representation to occur on the right.”
