name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Aging water, transportation systems pull Pennsylvania’s infrastructure grade down to a ‘C-’
description: Pensylvania's infrastructure got a passing grade in a 2026 report card but experts warn the state needs to invest millions more to get ahead.
text:
Raccoon Creek Bridge construction on Frankfort Road, Route 18, in Beaver County. (Photo by John Beale/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)The commonwealth got a passing grade for its infrastructure in a 2026 report card, but experts warn the state needs to invest millions more to get ahead of the curve. 
At the Capitol on Tuesday, the state chapter of the American Society of Civil Engineers unveiled Pennsylvania’s C- grade, emphasizing the importance of maintaining and upgrading bridges, parks, roads and transit to keep Pennsylvanians safe and productive.
“These systems also serve as the backbone of Pennsylvania’s economy. Infrastructure affects the lives of everyone on a daily basis,” said Brent Basom, the president of ASCE’s Central Pennsylvania section. “When an engine is functioning as planned, it is often out of sight and out of mind. But when infrastructure encounters a critical, serious problem or a system fails, the consequences can affect people’s quality of life and have serious, widespread economic impacts.” 
From left: Brent Basom, the president of ASCE’s Central Pennsylvania section, and Justin Komp, who chaired the Pennsylvania 2026 infrastructure report card, share findings at a Nov. 17, 2026 press conference. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Justin Komp, who chaired the Pennsylvania 2026 report card, highlighted some of the positives and negatives across 17 categories, each of which were assessed by a team of civil engineers. 
“This report is a snapshot of our infrastructure conditions and serves as a tool to start a conversation about where we are and what can be done to improve infrastructure in Pennsylvania,” said Komp. “I want to emphasize this report is a reflection of the condition and capacity of the systems we have in place … (And is) not a reflection on the people and agencies who work hard to operate and maintain those systems with the resources made available to them.” 
Carol Haddock, the incoming national president of ASCE, pointed to last weekend’s events as evidence of infrastructure’s importance. Upgrading communication technology at a remote Arkansas airport over the weekend accidentally triggered a nationwide failure, grounding flights for hours nationwide. 
“The ASCE infrastructure report card translates complicated, discipline-focused data and analysis into something digestible, so that our decision makers and the general public … have information to help them make decisions and to help guide the investments that we make,” Haddock said.
She noted that it would take an estimated $3.7 trillion over the next ten years to close the nation’s infrastructure investment gap to meet a “good repair” standard. The state report doesn’t include an overall number, but has estimates for individual categories.
 Report specifics

Pennsylvania has some of the nation’s oldest infrastructure. Shirley Clark, a professor at Penn State Harrisburg and a technical director with ASCE, noted that excavators still routinely uncovered 100-year-old wooden pipes made from hollowed out trees. 
“My area of interest has been everything in water that’s buried underground: drinking water, wastewater and stormwater,” Clark said. 
All three categories she mentioned received a D, the second-lowest grade, which Clark said is an improvement from previous years but impressive considering the state’s patchworked and aged system.
Pennsylvania’s grads across 17 different infrastructure categories, as determined by the American Society of Civil Engineers. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“(There’s) this idea that when it’s out of sight, it’s out of mind. And that has been one of the challenges,” Clark continued. “Water is interconnected. Drinking water is not separate … from wastewater. From stormwater. Because they all come together in what we call the Susquehanna (River) or the Juniata (River) or the Delaware (River) or any of the other rivers in the state.”
Clark said the Susquehanna River, one of the world’s oldest, is “one of the most flood-prone rivers in the United States,” traveling 300 miles within Pennsylvania’s borders. Along its length are low head dams, where water runs over the construction, creating a circulating current that can be dangerous for swimmers.
“At certain flood times, they’re drowning machines,” Clark warned. “We know there are ways to fix it. We know there are ways to prevent this from happening. But it takes investment.”
Dams were an area of improvement from the state’s last report card, moving up to a C due to federal investments, though more than 30% are over 100 years old.
“We must recognize that water is vital. Water is critical to public health and well-being,” Komp said. “While increased federal funding … was helpful, it was not sufficient to address the massive backlog of work to be done. New legislation must close the infrastructure gap through sustained capitalization and grants for small systems and disadvantaged communities.”
The state’s worst score was transit, where it earned a D-.
Komp encouraged stakeholders to think about transit, roads and bridges as one, interconnected system — rather than separate areas. He noted that the average bridge in the state is 59 years old, while the national average bridge is 47. Most bridges are designed to last for 50 years.
“You can’t just only fund roads and bridges, and you can’t just fund only transit,” Komp said. “Not everybody can take public transit, but also not everybody can drive.”

Read the full Pennsylvania report from ASCE here, including grading breakdowns for each category.

On the plus side, Komp pointed to energy, one of three categories to get a B-, which is the state’s highest individual grade and far above the national D+ average. 
“The reason for this discrepancy is Pennsylvania’s role as one of the leading energy producers in the nation, exporting 87 million megawatt hours of electricity in 2024 and supplying nearly 20% of U.S. natural gas production,” Komp said. 
The state also leads when it comes to producing nuclear and coal, he continued, but increased demand for power — driven, in part, by data centers — warrants continued improvement, he added. 
“Outages are also on the rise, meaning more investment in the grid and resilience measures are necessary,” Komp concluded.
Other areas with B- grades include aviation and hazardous waste. 
 Funding and workforce challenges

Presenters credited the nation’s “C” grade last year — the highest awarded since ASCE report cards started in 1998 — to the $1.2 trillion in federal investments under the Infrastructure, Investment and Jobs Act, which former President Joe Biden signed into law in late 2021. 
“(The act) provided Pennsylvania more than $22 billion,” Komp said, and “helped address decades of underinvestment across our infrastructure networks.”
Additionally, Act 89 of 2013 generated nearly $2.4 billion over 10 years for transportation revenue by increasing the fuel tax. But gaps remain, especially in transit systems like the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority (SEPTA). 
People board a Pittsburgh Regional Transit bus in downtown Pittsburgh Oct. 19, 2026. (Photo by John Beale/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“SEPTA faces a more than $10 billion funding gap, while Pittsburgh Regional Transit is facing more than $2 billion in deferred capital needs,” Komp continued. “Pennsylvania transit agencies provided more than 528 million passenger trips in 2024, demonstrating the system’s critical role in supporting mobility, access to jobs, healthcare and education.” 
Transit funding gaps stalled budget negotiations last year until Gov. Josh Shapiro announced that $394 million from the Public Transportation Trust Fund could be used for operating expenses. The transfer bought legislators two years to identify a new, ongoing funding source for transit, which is a priority for the incoming Democratic trifecta. 
“Stopgap measures and temporary funding, though valuable, are not sustainable solutions,” Komp said. “The development of long-term funding streams for transportation would enable agencies to reliably plan for the future.”
Komp also noted the looming workforce crisis for civil engineers, with more people retiring each year as the number of incoming students dwindles. 
Drinking water systems alone saw a 16% drop in the number of state operators compared to twenty years ago, he said. 
“Most of the infrastructure we rely on was built in a time where we did not have an understanding of how prominent and severe flooding, wildfire and wind events would be,” Komp added. “Not only is the infrastructure old and must be modernized, but the designs must adapt to current and future weather conditions.”

name: WyoFile
title: Campbell County blames meth, denies excessive force in fatal jail restraint lawsuit
description:
Kenneth Durrah's family sued for civil rights violations after he died naked and strapped to a restraint chair in the county's jail crying out that he couldn't breathe. 
The post Campbell County blames meth, denies excessive force in fatal jail restraint lawsuit appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
In Campbell County’s first detailed response to allegations that county jail staff violated the civil rights of Kenneth Durrah, who died naked and strapped to a restraint chair, defense attorneys argued his death was “self-caused” by methamphetamine. 
The civil rights lawsuit, filed Aug. 31 in federal court by Durrah’s family, alleges law enforcement used excessive force and showed deliberate indifference to his medical needs before he died in the Campbell County Detention Center on Dec. 1, 2022. 
Campbell County denied these allegations Monday, arguing that Durrah’s death was caused by his own concealed drug ingestion and not deputies’ use of force or inadequate medical care.

Kenneth Durrah and his sister, Ashley, in an old photo. (Courtesy photo)

Video of the 2022 incident — obtained by WyoFile and the Gillette News Record through a public records request — showed the hours before Durrah died naked, strapped to a restraint chair. The nearly three-hour video begins in the early hours of Dec. 1, 2022, with Durrah — who’d been held in the Campbell County jail for about a week on drug and firearm charges and parole violations — complaining of chest pains. Jail deputies took Durrah from his cell to booking where he was cleared by two EMTs. Then, back in a cell, Durrah appeared to ingest methamphetamine from a small bag. Deputies entered the cell, pushed Durrah against the back wall and commanded him not to swallow whatever he put in his mouth. 
Durrah pushed through the cell door out into the booking area. 
Several guards forced Durrah to the floor, cuffed his hands behind his back and restrained him face down. The officers carried him to a padded booking cell where four guards again pinned Durrah on his belly to the ground, this time for several minutes. One guard kneeled on Durrah’s head and hip while another kneeled on his back. Two other guards restrained his legs, sometimes kneeling on his lower legs and ankles. 
Using trauma shears, guards cut Durrah’s orange jumpsuit from his body. 
While pinned, Durrah periodically strained and resisted. He complained that he could not breathe. Four guards then lifted Durrah from the ground and placed him in a restraint chair. A guard tightened a strap across his waist then another removed the handcuffs. Officers placed straps across his arms and chest, which they retightened before wheeling him into a cell. 
Durrah pleaded with deputies that he couldn’t breathe in the restraint chair. “It’s too tight, please,” he can be heard saying on the video. Some 40 minutes after strapping him in the restraint chair, deputies found him unresponsive. 
Kenneth Durrah tells Campbell County Sheriff’s Detention Officer Samuel Boyles, “it’s too tight, please,” before he’s left in the cell strapped to the restraint chair. (screenshot of Campbell County Detention Center video)  
An autopsy described Durrah’s cause of death as “sudden cardiac death, consistent with ‘excited delirium’ due to Methamphetamine Overdose,” but the lawsuit argues the use of restraints produced a fatal chemical imbalance. “Instead of summoning medical aid, the deputies left Mr. Durrah tightly strapped in the restraint chair for half an hour as he died,” the complaint states. “As a result of the strenuous prone restraint and Mr. Durrah’s inability to sufficiently respirate during and after the initial restraint, when he was tightly strapped in the restraint chair, he could not clear the dangerous buildup of carbon dioxide and lactic acid in his system.”
Campbell County’s recent court filing frames deputies’ actions as necessary and lawful because Durrah resisted efforts to remove the drugs, assaulted a deputy and forced his way out of his cell. The strip search and restraint chair were justified by the suspected contraband and continued resistance, the filing argues. 
After witnessing Durrah ingest suspected methamphetamine, none of the deputies “took any other action to mitigate the effects of a potential drug overdose” or call for medical help, according to the complaint. The county, however, disputes the claim that they were deliberately indifferent to Durrah’s medical needs and did not provide adequate care while in the jail’s custody. Deputies placed Durrah on a “special watch,” observed steady, non-labored breathing and performed a capillary-refill test, a quick test to check blood flow, the county argues in its response. When they found Durrah unresponsive, deputies began CPR, applied an AED and called EMS, the response states.
The defense asked the federal court to rule in favor of Campbell County and the deputies involved in Durrah’s death and dismiss the case against them.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Environmentalists outline blue-trifecta energy priorities in Capitol rally
description: Conservation Voters and environmental justice group Penn Future unveiled a plan setting a 100-day agenda for the new legislative session focused on reining in big tech, creating opportunities for renewable electricity and protecting consumers from skyrocketing energy costs.
text:
Molly Parzen, executive director of Conservation Voters of Pennsylvania, speaks at a rally on legislative priorities on energy Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Pennsylvania’s divided legislature has proven frustrating for environmentalists and lawmakers who have seen legislation to place guardrails on data center development, expand clean energy and lower utility bills marooned in the Republican-controlled Senate.
With Democrats set to take control in both chambers of the General Assembly, they now hope those legislative efforts will reach Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro’s desk. 
“Pennsylvania voters went to the polls and they delivered an unmistakable mandate for change,” Molly Parzen, executive director of Conservation Voters of Pennsylvania said Tuesday in a rally at the state Capitol.
In the blue wave election that swept legislative races earlier this month, Democrats expanded their one-seat majority in the state House to 13. Democrats also flipped four seats in the state Senate to take control of the upper chamber. And Shapiro skated to a second term, defeating Republican state Treasurer Stacy Garrity.
The legislative session starting in January will be the first without a Republican majority in the Senate in more than 30 years. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Voters from across the commonwealth demanded an end to the endless gridlock we’ve seen in Harrisburg these last few decades. They demanded a comprehensive agenda to address affordability, and they demanded that their elected representatives deliver on policies that will make real and tangible improvements to their lives,” Parzen said. 
Conservation Voters and environmental justice group Penn Future unveiled a plan setting a 100-day agenda for the new legislative session focused on reining in big tech, creating opportunities for renewable electricity and protecting consumers from skyrocketing energy costs.
Patrick O’Donnell, president and CEO of PennFuture, noted that many of the initiatives detailed in the agenda have already passed in the House but languished in the Senate. 
House Energy Committee Chair Elizabeth Fiedler (D-Philadelphia) speaks Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, at a state Capitol rally on energy policy. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“There were no hearings on these bills. There was no discussion on the floor about these bills,” O’Donnell said. “It’s more than just the votes. It’s the voice of people not being able to be heard in that chamber, and it’s important that we’re able to finally have that voice heard in both chambers of our legislature.”
Data center speculation across the commonwealth has contributed to increased electricity bills, bitter fights between developers and communities and concerns about pollution as energy producers look to fossil fuels to quickly increase supply. 
The agenda calls on lawmakers to ensure that 100% of the cost of connecting data centers to the grid is paid by developers and that utility regulators have the power to enforce consumer protections. It also cites the need for a ban on non-disclosure agreements between tech companies and government officials.
And it asks lawmakers to pass strict requirements for data center developers to supply their own clean power from sources in the commonwealth and prohibit data centers from running on polluting diesel and natural gas backup generators.
Incoming Senate Energy Committee Chair Carolyn Comitta (D-Chester) said the election also marked an end to fossil-fuel-first energy policy in the General Assembly.
“When it comes to priorities, renewables are at the top of our list,” Comitta said, noting that solar energy is the least expensive way to add new capacity to the grid. But as utilities have satisfied state quotas for renewable energy production, installation of new wind and solar energy facilities has plateaued, she said.
The environmental groups say lawmakers must pass bills that promote renewable energy by requiring all warehouses and distribution centers to be built ready for solar panels to be installed. They also call for legislation establishing state targets for utility-scale battery storage to capture solar energy during the day and release it into the grid during periods of high demand.
Other priorities include bills allowing renters and others in multi-family dwellings to subscribe to community solar power projects and enabling smart-grid technology to allow consumers to link residential batteries and electric vehicles to supply power to the grid during peaks in demand.
The agenda also calls for a 30% tax credit on the cost of manufacturing clean energy products in Pennsylvania, which proponents say will drive economic growth and the creation of union jobs. And it calls on lawmakers to hold utility companies accountable by limiting profits, curbing rate hikes and expanding assistance for people who can’t afford their energy bills.
House Energy Committee Chairperson Elizabeth Fiedler (D-Philadelphia) said the chamber has passed a “tremendous amount” of legislation related to energy, consumer protection and the environment that has already been vetted with stakeholders. Often, those bills have had bipartisan support, she noted. 
“A lot of the work that we’ve done over the last two years sets us up really, really well to come out of the gate strong on energy,” Fiedler said, adding that it’s among the topics, such transit funding and raising the minimum wage, both the House and Senate Democratic caucuses plan to tackle early next year. 
“All of us recognize this is a huge opportunity, and we need to be on the same page … and have real meaningful conversations about how we can improve people’s lives,” she said. “I feel tremendously optimistic. It is a lot of work, but we are very lucky to have the chance to do this.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Outgoing Rep. Don Bacon wants Republicans to reclaim their values after midterm shellacking
description: Bacon blames Trump for what Republicans experienced on election night, saying the Republican Party followed Trump “off the cliff.”
text:
Rep. Don Bacon speaking in Omaha on Oct, 29. 2026. (Juan Salinas II)OMAHA — Outgoing Nebraska 2nd Congressional District U.S. Rep. Don Bacon saw Democrats win states they haven’t in decades during a watch party for Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts earlier this month. 
Bacon had expected the 2nd District race to replace him to be a barn burner. But it was over an hour after the polls closed, with Democrat Denise Powell winning by more than 10 points. 
Bacon himself, who is no stranger to the camera, made news last week, saying he’s willing to step up to run for the 2028 GOP presidential nomination. It wasn’t the first time he’s suggested he’d consider running.
Bacon told the press in the same call that he will test his message around the country. The retired Air Force brigadier general sat down with the Examiner to discuss that message and the future of the Grand Old Party, which he says needs to reclaim the values of federalism and free markets. 
He blames President Donald Trump for what Republicans experienced on election night. Bacon said the Republican Party followed Trump “off the cliff,” pointing to policies that he disagrees with the president on.
“This is not me being anti-Republican,” Bacon told the Examiner. “This is me being a Republican … this is me being the Reagan Republican. … I never abandoned my values.” 
Bacon has been highly critical of the second Trump administration — he criticized Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, Trump’s handling of Ukraine and how the administration treats American allies, including Europe and Canada. Politico had referred to Bacon as a “YOLO Republican” with nothing to lose during his last year in Congress.  
In 2022, Trump and his campaign team actively tried to recruit a Republican challenger to Bacon. The then-former president came to Nebraska for an unrelated campaign rally and attacked Bacon, who ultimately defeated Democrat Tony Vargas in the general election.
Bacon defended Nebraska’s most politically divided and diverse congressional district for Republicans for about a decade. But he acknowledged to the Examiner that he would have been “unlikely” to keep the seat this cycle. 
“Abraham Lincoln would have lost here,” Bacon recalled saying earlier this month on election night. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Bacon believes that Americans are “expecting too little, and they’re demanding too little” of the highest office in American politics, as it’s “unacceptable” to have had the last four presidents target their political opponents using the “DOJ, FBI (and) the IRS.”
He also criticized Trump and former President Joe Biden for enriching “their families in the White House.” 
A Harris poll and other polls leading up to Election Day indicated that government corruption was one of the top issues for midterm voters. Another issue viewed as having caused the “blue tsunami” was the Iran war. 
Vice President JD Vance blamed the GOP losses on the war in a lengthy social media post after Election Day. Bacon, who has supported the war, told the Examiner he acknowledged the war and its unpopularity played into the losses. But he pushed back at Vance, saying the U.S. relationship with Israel was one of the reasons for the major GOP losses. 
“He’s a Tucker Carlson guy, and a lot of his Republicans don’t like that,” Bacon said of Vance. Carlson is a conservative commentator who has been highly critical of the Iran war. 
Bacon said Trump’s mistakes before launching the war were failing to make a case to the public and failing to build bipartisan support, adding that there was a case to be made for the war. 
Asked about his message, Bacon said the country is dealing with four “threats” that will take bipartisanship to solve if the U.S. wants to remain a world superpower. Those threats are the national debt, figuring out legal immigration, the cost of healthcare and national security. 
Bacon emphasized that those issues can’t be solved by only Republicans or Democrats, as he believes the U.S. is “living in a house of cards financially.” 
On the 2028 presidential bid, Bacon once again said he is willing to run if he feels no one is running on that message, but emphasized his bid as a last resort because it’s not about him. 
He said former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin, Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Nikki Haley are some on the GOP bench who he thinks could wear the mantle of leading America and secure its position as a “superpower and the economic engine of the world” for the next generation.
Populism has emerged as a driving force in today’s politics, as some voters have lost faith in institutions. It’s credited with Trump’s rise in politics, and now economic populism is credited with helping  Democrats win big across the country. 
Bacon said he doesn’t “subscribe” to populism because it “doesn’t have a moral compass,” adding that he wants to know someone’s “ideology and values.”

“Populism sort of goes where the compass goes, or where the wind blows,” Bacon told the Examiner. “I am more of the Reagan guy. I’d rather be optimistic and positive, draw people in. … Populism is all about anger.”
Bacon is expected to speak Thursday at the National Press Club in Washington, D.C., about this pitch for the future of the GOP, emphasizing he wants to start a conversation. 
“I have zero doubt in what I’m saying is right,” Bacon said.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: More Than Half Of Hawaiʻi Households Living On Financial Brink
description: People report having trouble sleeping and focusing at work as numbers in trouble jump dramatically.
text:
There are about 500,000 households in Hawaiʻi — and more than half of them are struggling financially, a steep jump from just two years ago. 
That’s according to a new report unveiled Tuesday morning that depicts a state where hundreds of thousands of people are living beyond their means just to get by.
The rising cost of living, plus wages that are too low and rising too slowly, is driving people into debt and eating up money they’ve set aside, forcing them to rely on credit cards, sell belongings and work more than one job, the report from Aloha United Way shows. 
“It’s definitely straining the social and cultural fabric of our state,” Michelle Bartell, president and CEO of Aloha United Way, said of the financial burden so many Hawaiʻi residents are living under. 
The impact goes far beyond the financial. The survey found that people below the ALICE threshold are more likely to report trouble sleeping or focusing at work and more tension in the home. 
For those on fixed incomes, there’s added strain. Kathy Fujimoto and her husband both worked steady jobs before retiring. Both receive social security, and her husband has a pension from his time working as an accountant for the City and County of Honolulu. 
But social security places a limitation on how much they can earn from part-time jobs. After their rent doubled last year, they’re just scraping by.
Fujimoto said coupons at places like Safeway and Longs are a lifesaver. But digging for discounts in the stores’ apps adds a lot of time to her shopping.
 “You almost have to almost have a second job doing that,” she said.
The nonprofit’s new report, based on a survey of 1,810 full-time Hawaiʻi residents, follows earlier versions, in 2022 and 2024. It assesses the needs and circumstances of people living at the edge of their financial rope. That includes people below the poverty line, but also those above it who still endure financial hardship, a group referred to as ALICE: asset limited, income constrained, and employed.
The federal poverty level for a family of four in Hawaiʻi is just under $38,000 a year. What Aloha United Way’s ALICE Initiative refers to as the household survival budget — enough to cover basic necessities such as housing, child care, food, transportation, health care, taxes and phone plans — is $45,804 for a single adult and $112,000 for a family of four. 
In 2024, 40% of Hawaiʻi households lived below the ALICE threshold. In 2026, that number rose to 52%. For Native Hawaiians, who fared the worst among ethnic groups surveyed, 74% said their household isn’t making enough money to get by.
Bartell noted that the current threshhold is based on 2024 numbers, so it is possible that the true numbers of those falling behind is even higher.

Graphic 1: 






Cole Mijo works three jobs as a flight instructor, a cashier and a bookkeeper, but that still puts him below the roughly $46,000 threshold Aloha United Way estimates he’d need to cover his basic costs living on his own. 
“I can’t afford two rent payments, so I’ll just pay one.”Cole Mijo, who works three jobs
The 25-year-old lives with his parents and two siblings on ​​Oʻahu while he pays down his $900 a month loan for flight school. And that’s after he refinanced it down from $1,500 a month.
“So basically a rent payment,” he said. “I can’t afford two rent payments, so I’ll just pay one.”
There’s not just one factor that is making Hawaiʻi’s economy untenable for residents, according to economists at UHERO. Increased costs driven in part by the war in Iran, inflation that has recently been higher than the rest of the nation and the long-lasting effects of pandemic are all likely contributing. That’s on top of longer-term trends that have led to a stagnant economy. 
“We have essentially been battered by shock,” Carl Bonham, the executive director of UHERO, said. “The new normal is chaos in the economy.”
This makes it difficult for economists to pinpoint precisely why it’s costing more to make ends meet and why more families are falling behind.
“Regardless, it’s going in the wrong direction,” Bonham said.
But Bartell said the latest rise in the number of people struggling was so startling that the firm that did the survey — Anthology/Finn Partners —  was asked to “rerun the numbers because nobody wanted to believe it” and Aloha United Way also checked its findings with the national United Way ALICE research project.
“We really wanted to make sure that before we put out data that was this shocking,” she said, “that we were all confident.” 
How much worse and why
By pretty much every metric, more Hawaiʻi residents are having a harder time financially than  two years ago. More than one in three households find it tough to afford enough food. One in four spend more than their income each month – by a median amount of $700 – to cover essential bills, often taking on debt just to get by. Emergency savings are dwindling. 
More than a third of households are above the federal poverty level but still fall short of the ALICE threshold, meaning they struggle to cover the cost of basic necessities, even though they’re employed. 
Mijo said he limits his spending. Fujimoto’s husband drives farther for cheaper gas, and she finds inexpensive but healthy recipes on social media.
At a Tuesday morning news conference to unveil the findings, speakers commended how scrappy local residents are in finding ways to get by. 
“We know that our families, our households here, are incredibly resilient,” Kayla Keehu-Alexander, a vice president at Aloha United Way, said at the press conference. “But we shouldn’t have to rely on the resilience of our families to make this economy better. We should be relying on our willingness to come together and do all of that for them, so no one has to continue to struggle.”
Derek Kurisu, executive VP for KTA Superstores, walks past the dairy chiller, which features local Mountain Apple milk on the bottom two shelves, at the KTA Superstore at in Hilo .  (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026) Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026
The burden falls disproportionately on certain groups. In addition to almost three quarters of Native Hawaiians surveyed saying they don’t make enough to cover basic costs, about 68% of families with children under 18 also reported a household income that falls short of what Aloha United Way estimates is needed to cover necessities such as housing, food and childcare.
Nearly two thirds of young adults surveyed live in a household that falls below the ALICE threshold, an increase of almost 10 percentage points from two years ago. More than half of these 18 to 34-year-olds said that they frequently don’t have enough food but lack the cash to buy more. 
Renters, those without a college degree and people living on neighbor islands are also more likely to find it difficult to cover their basic costs.

Neighbor islands 

While the survey measures hardship, not its causes, Bartell said the findings reflect two difficult years.
Over the 12 months ending in July 2026—midway through the Aloha United Way survey—Honolulu inflation surged to 5.6%, while inflation-adjusted wages grew by just 1%, according to the University of Hawaiʻi Economic Research Organization.
Bartell pointed to a string of economic hits including disruptions to federal funding, such as the temporary suspension of SNAP benefits in 2025, the loss of several thousand federal jobs, surging energy prices due to the war with Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the Kona lows in March, and the impacts of Hurricanes Lala and Lowell.
A year of turbulent storms has impacted Mijo’s income as a flight instructor. The work pays minimally while he’s working his way up in the industry. Severe weather means fewer hours.
“Those months are squeaking a little bit,” he said. 
The origin of this year’s pain date back several years, too. Hawaiʻi was slower to come out of the Covid-19 era and pandemic inflation had a delayed impact in the state, compared to the rest of the country, according to Bonham at UHERO. 
As prices rose, wages continued to lag, UHERO found,  only slightly outpacing inflation.
“We’ve had, definitely, a long string of disruptions that happened before the survey was in the field,” Bartell said, “and at the same time paychecks just haven’t kept pace.” 
And while over the past decade the poverty rate for the Native Hawaiian and other Pacific Islander population improved more than other groups — decreasing from 20.5% in 2015 to 15.9% in 2025 according to some estimates — it remained the highest, contributing to their overrepresentation among the homeless population.
At the press conference, the CEO and president of Hawaiʻi Community Foundation said the striking results should be a call to action.
“There’s three ways that we can react to this disturbing set of data. One is to blame somebody for it. Let’s blame government. Let’s blame bureaucracy. Let’s blame corporations. Let’s blame the system,” Terry George said. “A second way is to just hope somebody else will solve it.
“And the… third way is the only way that we all must respond to this. Roll up our sleeves, work together, and do something about it for the sake of our friends and neighbors, and the communities that we love.” 
More People At The Precipice 
While Aloha United Way found that the gap between what people make and their essential costs has shrunk slightly overall in the last two years, more people are staring down the reality that they can’t make ends meet. The median household fell about $700 short of covering their monthly costs this year, down from $1,000 in 2024. 
More Hawaiʻi households are seeing a mismatch between their income and their expenses. About 28% of households surveyed reported bills totaling more than their income, up from 24% two years ago. About half of young adults surveyed said they struggle to pay every one of their bills on time. 
It’s driving people to the brink of financial distress. More three quarters of households surveyed reported tapping into their savings, about the same percentage that had also relied on credit cards. Almost half – 47% – said they had overdrawn their checking account.
For those whose costs exceed their income, it’s hard to dig out of that hole. About 37% of households below the ALICE threshold find it difficult to pay off debts, compared to 21% of households above that income level. 


That leaves little financial wiggle room to cover the cost of an unexpected emergency. More than half of Hawaiʻi households don’t have enough set aside to cover their expenses for three months, up 9 percentage points from two years ago. One in 10 households said they couldn’t afford a surprise $400 bill, and almost a fifth of households below the ALICE threshold said they wouldn’t be able to pay that bill at all. 
Keehu-Alexander said some interventions are helping, listing the increase in the minimum wage, income tax cuts to households under the ALICE thresholds and better access to preschools and childcare subsidies.
But those initiatives need to be made permanent because more than half of the state’s households cannot plan financially for the future at all, which she called “one of the clearest signs of economic stability.”
“Hawaii’s households are making difficult trade-offs to get by. At times, those sacrifices can come at the expense of health and well-being, or even long-term financial security,” Keehu-Alexander said. “The effects extend far beyond just household budgets.”
Since the 2023 Maui wildfires, Maui Food Bank increased its full-time staff by 50%.  (Courtesy: Maui Food Bank/2023) (Courtesy: Maui Food Bank/2023)
Finances Forcing Tough Decisions 
Dire financial straits are forcing families to make hard decisions. 
Almost half of households below the ALICE threshold bought less fresh food. One in three reported relying on credit cards, loans or pawnshops, and a quarter picked up additional jobs or extra shifts to increase their paychecks. Almost a fifth said they had delayed medical treatment. 
More people are also relying on federal assistance such as SNAP or Medicaid to help cover the costs of food and medical care, compared to 2024. The last year has been marked by confusion over proposed requirements for people receiving aid, a gap in federal funding last fall that forced the state to step up and cutbacks in which food markets in the state can take SNAP benefits. 
While experts feared people would fall out of the program as a result, Aloha United Way’s report found a slight increase in the percentage of households receiving assistance. 
Falling behind in so many ways contributes to another sad reality in Hawaiʻi: outmigration — an uptick in long-time residents leaving the state. It’s particularly grim for Native ​​Hawaiians, more of whom now live in the rest of the United States than in Hawaiʻi, according to UHERO.
“For many, the cost of living is making that decision for them.”Kayla Keehu-Alexander, VP Aloha United Way
The trend manifests in elderly with no one to care for them, parents missing their children, siblings living far apart. With ʻohana – extended family – such a foundational element of life here, that phenomenon contributes to what the United Way’s Bartell characterized as a strain on the social and cultural fabric.
About 44% of survey respondents below the ALICE threshold said someone in their home has considered leaving the state in the last year. Most say the cost of living and the price of housing is driving them to weigh a move, despite family ties and a cultural connection. 
“For many, the cost of living is making that decision for them,” Keehu-Alexander said.
But many can’t afford to leave, even if the price of living here makes it hard to envision staying. Households below the ALICE threshold are three times more likely to say that the cost of the move is one factor keeping them here.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: New House and Senate leaders see Amendment 3 as major challenge next year
description: Florida Republican leaders all but closed the door on Gov. Ron DeSantis’s push for a special legislative session before he leaves office to implement a “tax payers bill of rights,” tied to passage of a far-reaching property tax proposal known as Amendment 3. “We believe that there’s time later on during the regular session, and […]
text:
Changing of the guard: New Florida Speaker of the House Sam Garrison (left) takes the gavel from former Speaker Daniel Perez on Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix).Florida Republican leaders all but closed the door on Gov. Ron DeSantis’s push for a special legislative session before he leaves office to implement a “tax payers bill of rights,” tied to passage of a far-reaching property tax proposal known as Amendment 3.
“We believe that there’s time later on during the regular session, and give it the time and attention it needs through the committee process and then certainly the floor discussion and debate,” newly installed Senate President Jim Boyd said Tuesday.
Byrd and new House Speaker Sam Garrison had previously declared that the amendment is “self-implementing” and didn’t need to be worked on before it becomes law on Jan. 1. That’s because nothing will really change on that day, but that the true impact of the measure will come later in the year, when cities and counties prepare their fiscal year budgets with reduced revenues.




Florida Democrats vow to make their (limited) numbers count in 2027




Byrd and Garrison spoke during a press conference following an organizational session in which they delivered acceptance speeches to the newly elected House and Senate members in the Capitol. These sessions come every two years following general elections.
Amendment 3 is the constitutional provision passed by more than 62% of Floridians on Election Day. The measure will increase the non-school homestead property tax exemption from $50,000 to $150,000 beginning next year. In 2028, it will increase to $250,000.
While that tax break will undoubtedly benefit homestead property owners through lower property tax bills, it also is expected to cut revenues to local government by billions of dollars in its first year, increasing in following years.
“It puts thousands of dollars back into people’s pockets and it makes good on a promise this House made to our voters to reduce the tax burden on Florida homeowners,” Garrison said. “But as someone who never met a tax he didn’t want to cut, let me be clear: The laws of economics remain undefeated, and there is still no such thing as a free lunch.”
He continued: “From Dixie to Duval to Dade, Amendment 3 impacts each of our 67 counties differently. This is the biggest fiscal challenge our state has faced in a generation. It will be difficult, very difficult, it will take time, but failure is not an option.”
Byrd called passage of Amendment 3 a “clear message” from Florida voters: Property taxes are out of control.
He acknowledged the Senate would need to address those reductions in revenue, especially in rural areas. “I look forward to working with you to determine our next steps,” he said.
Garrison mentioned two other priorities for the two years he is slated to serve as House speaker.
One is regulating AI. Confessing he is “an analog guy in a digital world,” Garrison said the more he learns, the more he worries: “We may have gained the world but lost our souls.”
Led by DeSantis, the Legislature passed a bill in the 2026 session regulating AI data centers, but the House failed to move on an “AI Bill of Rights” that the Florida Senate overwhelmingly approved.
That’s because then-House Speaker Daniel Perez was following the influence of Donald Trump, who did not want states to write their own AI regulations.
“The White House’s position on AI and the House’s position on AI … are on the same page,” Perez said at the time. “We do believe that the federal government should take care of AI and in whatever legislation or policy has to pass on a national level as opposed to doing it on a state-by-state basis.” (Trump later rewarded Perez by nominating him for U.S. Ambassador to Brazil).
Garrison maintained the House last year had “rightly” ceded to Congress the opportunity to lead, but, “to the surprise of no one, they failed.”
That’s why he has established an Advanced Technology and Digital Security Committee to provide “a comprehensive, in-depth analysis of the risks and opportunities artificial intelligence poses to Florida citizens, our economy, and all levels of government,” he said.
Senate President Jim Boyd addresses the Florida Senate on Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)
The new leaders
Garrison, 50, is an Illinois native who moved to Florida in 2001. He’s an  attorney from Fleming Island in Northeastern Florida who was first elected to the Florida House in 2020.
Byrd, 70, is a veteran in the Legislature. A lifelong resident of Manatee County, he served in local government and worked in the insurance industry before first winning election to the Florida House in 2010, where he served until 2018. He was elected to the Senate in 2020.
Attending both speeches was the man they’ll work with closely over the next two years: Gov.-elect Byron Donalds. Garrison said he and Boyd believe it’s their job to make Donalds “the most successful governor in America.”
“That does not mean we’ll always agree,” he cautioned.
For his part, Boyd noted the results of the midterm elections nationally and in Florida by saying it is “imperative that we tackle affordability. What good is a beacon of opportunity if you cannot build a good life here?”‘ he asked.
“From rent and mortgages, to utilities, gas, daycare, and grocery bills, we are faced with the harsh reality that post-Covid-era inflation has completely realigned the cost of consumer goods and services — not just here in Florida but across the country and around the world,” he said.
“It’s challenging to build a good life when folks are struggling to make ends meet. While we don’t have the ability to change the national and global economy, we do have an important role to play in keeping Florida affordable. Families have made hard adjustments, and they expect government to do the same.”
Like most of the Florida Republican establishment, Boyd said the Legislature has already “instituted  major reforms to offer homeowners more choice and lower costs” in the insurance market. He promised the Senate would “continue to pursue every opportunity that can offer more choices and lower rates to Floridians, allowing them to save more of their hard-earned dollars, while maintaining the integrity and reliability of the industry we’ve worked so hard to reform.”
The third focus for Garrison is restoring public trust in government. To that end, he said he is reestablishing the House Public Integrity Committee “to investigate public corruption and hold public officials to account.”
Additionally, he said, the House Appropriation subcommittees will renew focus on how public money is spent.
State lawmakers will next return to Tallahassee for the first of their committee weeks on Nov. 30. The start of the regular session will take place on March 2, 2027.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Drought causing spike in Jackson water line breaks, utility warns
description: JXN Water crews making repairs to the city's water distribution system.
text:
Jackson’s drinking water system is experiencing a spike in line breaks in its distribution network because of ongoing drought conditions, the city’s water provider warned on Tuesday. 
JXN Water, the federal receiver overseeing the city’s drinking water and sewer systems, said it has responded to more than twice the usual number of water main breaks in the city over the last six weeks.
As of the most recent update on Nov. 10, 100% of Hinds County experienced “severe drought,” and 89% of the county was in “extreme drought” according to the U.S. Drought Monitor. 
“Drought conditions are putting real stress on the pipes under our streets, and our crews are out every day meeting it. We are putting the breaks that take water away from homes, hospitals and schools at the front of the line. If you have already reported a leak, it is on our list, and we will get to it,” said Terrance Byrd, chief operation officer for JXN Water.
Dry soil around water lines will shrink and shift, the utility explained, and that movement puts more stress on the pipes underground. 
JXN Water didn’t disclose how many line breaks it was dealing with or where, but its website shows nine ongoing boil water notices affecting a total of 284 connections, or meters. Click here for a list of JXN Water’s ongoing boil water notices.
From July through the end of September, the utility issued 61 precautionary boil water notices, according to JXN Water’s latest quarterly report. That was slightly down from 64 notices in the previous quarter.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Woonsocket ran out the clock responding to public records requests. Now time’s up, AG says.
description: At least 27 times over the last three years, the city of Woonsocket failed to fill public records requests on time. Or at all. That’s why the Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha’s office has given the city notice of legal action for “willfully and knowingly” violating Rhode Island’s Access to Public Records Act (APRA), […]
text:
Woonsocket faces an up to $2,000 fine for 27 instances of public records violations, the Rhode Island Attorney General's office says. Pictured is City Hall on Main Street. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)At least 27 times over the last three years, the city of Woonsocket failed to fill public records requests on time. Or at all.
That’s why the Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha’s office has given the city notice of legal action for “willfully and knowingly” violating Rhode Island’s Access to Public Records Act (APRA), according to a letter sent Monday. A copy of the letter was obtained by Rhode Island Current. 
The pending state Superior Court lawsuit, which comes with a maximum fine of $2,000, marks the third time Neronha has pursued legal action against a public body for violating state records law during his eight years in office, according to information provided by Neronha’s office. 
“Time and time again, the City violated the APRA in virtually the same manner, and it has largely refused to remedy its error unless and until this Office directed it to do so,” Patrick Reynolds, special assistant attorney general, wrote in the 13-page letter to city attorneys.
He also called the city’s decadeslong history of violations a “pattern of systemic failure,” rejecting the “same tired excuse” of staffing shortages that the city has provided in response to previous rebukes and lawsuits over public records violations.
“It’s the most searing takedown of a public body I’ve ever seen from the AG’s office,” said John Marion, executive director for Common Cause Rhode Island.
Attorneys Michael Lepizzera and Allan Fung, who represent the city and to whom the letter is addressed, did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday. Mayor Christopher Beauchamp also did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Mayor-elect Dan Gendron, the sitting council president who defeated Beauchamp in the nonpartisan November mayoral election, said he had received the letter but was waiting to hear from the city solicitor.
Of his administration, Gendron said, “We do plan to implement a more detailed recording of APRA requests to make sure they are answered in a timely fashion. Obviously, there appears to be some breakdown somewhere.”
The 1979 law gives public bodies 10 business days to provide public information to the person who asked for it, with a 20-day extension for large amounts of records or those that might be difficult to find and fill quickly.
The city of Woonsocket routinely fails to meet the deadlines, often not responding to requests for months, until after delays are appealed to the attorney general’s office, according to the letter. In a few cases, requests for public information dating back several years remain partially, or wholly, unfilled.
The letter outlines 27 examples of APRA violations spanning 2024 to 2027: requests from residents, lawyers, landlords, and even the former city council president, seeking employee salaries, city contracts, and tax information, among other public data.
The Rhode Island Office of the Attorney General rarely invokes legal action to enforce public records law. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current)
18 years of problems
The city’s history of failing to answer records requests on time dates back decades. In 2009, then-Attorney General Patrick Lynch filed a lawsuit on behalf of the Woonsocket Fire Fighters Association and its president over a 2008 public records request that went unfilled and unacknowledged for six months. Woonsocket paid a $1,000 fine under a consent judgement entered in 2010, court records show. 
In 2013, the attorney general’s office filed a legal complaint against the city for failing to respond for nearly 10 months to records requested by a private practice attorney.
A series of four records requests in 2022 and 2023 by a reporter at The Public’s Radio — now Ocean State Media — also went unanswered until an appeal to the AG’s office, which threatened court action and a $1,000 fine unless the city responded.
“This finding should have marked the end of the City’s practice of blatantly ignoring APRA requests and engaging in dilatory tactics when this Office attempted to investigate such violations, but instead it sadly marked only the beginning of the City’s misadventure in violating the APRA and often being non-responsive to our efforts to investigate such violations,” Reynolds wrote.



Quotation







It’s the most searing takedown of a public body I’ve ever seen from the AG’s office.


– John Marion, executive director for Common Cause Rhode Island


In every case, the city said staffing shortages were the reason for delays or lack of response to public requests. The city has struggled to hire qualified staff to complete mandatory financial audits and other responsibilities, prompting citizen lawsuits and two major credit ratings agencies to withdraw their bond ratings. 
The letter notes that the city no longer employs two attorneys who handled public records requests.
Instead, Lepizzera, who took over as city solicitor in late 2022, and Fung, who was brought on to help in early 2024, have full responsibility for all city legal matters, in addition to their work for other private practice clients.
Reynolds said the decision not to use clerks or non-legal staff to handle records requests was “deliberate,” amounting to a “willful and knowing or reckless” violation of state law.
“It is troubling that the City appears to have been unable to figure out how to resolve its staffing issue despite these issues persisting for at least 18 years since the City was previously sued for these same types of failings,” he said.
Reynolds also flagged a problem in how records requests are submitted and processed by the city, with no clear way for records to be submitted directly to Lepizzera and Fung. Instead, it relied on the AG appeal process to notify attorneys of public records requests.
“This not only violates the APRA, but it also deprives the public of meaningful and prompt access to public records and places an unnecessary administrative burden on this Office,” Reynolds said.
There is no timeline for when the AG’s office intends to file the complaint. Neronha, who is term-limited, leaves office in early January. Neronha was unavailable for comment Tuesday. 
Attorney General-elect Kim Ahern did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The wait continues
Reynolds’ letter is also addressed to a dozen people who have appealed to the AG’s office after their attempts to obtain city records were not filled on time, including three who never received them. 
One is Gregory Rice. A landlord and developer with Pawtucket-based Nexus Property Management, Rice filed three separate records requests with the city in January, April and September, seeking tax records for properties similar to the church on Orlo Street that his company bought and converted into luxury apartments. 
As of Tuesday, he’s still waiting to hear back on all three requests, which were supposed to help his company challenge what it believes is an unfair property valuation of the church-turned-apartment development.
His company sued the city over the property assessment even without the requested tax information, but having it could help the case, Rice said.
“The city is extremely sloppy, inefficient and understaffed,” Rice said, calling the pending lawsuit a “monumental step forward.”
John Ward, a former city council president who ran unsuccessfully for mayor in 2024, is also among the letter’s recipients, having had three separate requests from May 2025 to October 2026 left unanswered for more than 10 days. 
“Frankly, very, very simple requests were being ignored for days and weeks at a time,” Ward said Tuesday. 
Now retired, Ward said he used the public records law to help get information he no longer had access to since he left the council, sometimes prompted by resident complaints on social media.
“It’s a situation that didn’t have to happen,” Ward said of the forthcoming lawsuit, noting the worsening financial situation, especially as the city moves to close its regional wastewater treatment plant. 
‘The city just doesn’t prioritize transparency’
Good government advocates including Marion have long fought for overhauling the state’s public records law, which was last updated in 2012 and offers many loopholes for public agencies to deny or overcharge people for public records. But Marion did not think there was a legislative fix to force a routine law-breaker like Woonsocket to comply.
“This is really the biggest hammer in the toolbox of the AG’s office when it comes to enforcing the law,” Marion said of civil litigation. “At a certain point, over so many years, dozens of violations, it’s inescapable that the city just doesn’t prioritize transparency.”
Neronha’s office also sued Pawtucket and West Warwick for public records law violations in 2020 and 2019, respectively. And in 2019, he took the Woonsocket City Council to court for violating the state’s Open Meetings Act.
The Woonsocket City Council paid a $5,000 fine to settle the complaint over vague meeting agendas. West Warwick also reached a settlement but the agreement is not public.
The Pawtucket case was dismissed after the legislature moved to exempt the requested records — where city police officers live — from being made public.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ sues federal immigration officials for ‘stonewalling’ Delaney Hall probe
description: NJ Attorney Jennifer Davenport sued U.S. Department of Homeland Security officials for not complying with a subpoena for Delaney Hall records.
text:
A detainee is seen in a window of Delaney Hall, the Newark detention center, on June 5, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey accused the Trump administration in a new lawsuit Tuesday of failing to comply with a civil rights investigation into medical care and confinement conditions at Delaney Hall, a federal immigration jail in Newark.
Attorney General Jennifer Davenport said U.S. Department of Homeland Security officials have failed for months to respond to a subpoena seeking information about the treatment of detainees at the 1,196-bed facility. At least three Delaney detainees have died in federal custody and people held there waged a hunger strike over treatment by guards last summer, prompting critics to call for its closure.
The Geo Group, the private prison group that owns and operates Delaney Hall, has said it cannot respond to the subpoena without authorization from Homeland Security, Davenport said. The subpoena sought records on medical care provided to detainees and was part of a broader probe into potential civil rights violations Davenport’s office launched in early August.
“There are far too many reports of inhumane treatment of the people held at Delaney Hall. But what we have received for months from both GEO Group and DHS is plain stonewalling,” Davenport said in a statement. “We will continue to do all we can to ensure that these civil detainees are treated with the dignity and decency that all people are entitled to under the law.”
Davenport wants a federal judge to declare Homeland Security in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act for unreasonable delays in its response to the subpoena, and set a deadline for department officials to respond.
The lawsuit names as defendants Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, David J. Venturella, a senior official in Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and their respective agencies.
Homeland Security spokespeople did not respond to a request for comment.
The new lawsuit comes five months after the state sued the department for barring state health inspectors from inspecting Delaney Hall. Litigation in that case remains ongoing.
Yolanda N. Melville, director of the Division on Civil Rights in Davenport’s office, said Delaney detainees and the families of those who died have shared “extremely troubling accounts.”
“Individuals housed in an immigration detention facility do not waive their constitutional and legal right to receive adequate medical care or to be protected from violence,” said Melville said in a statement. “The federal government’s silence in response to our lawful requests for information speaks volumes.”
Geo Group doesn’t need permission from Homeland Security to comply with subpoenas, because it’s a private business operating on its own property, the lawsuit says. But investigators also tried to obtain information directly from Homeland Security officials, with no response, the complaint says.
Geo Group spokespeople did not respond to a request for comment.
Investigators already have found problems with the facility’s medical intake and screening, failures to provide medications for detainees with chronic conditions, inadequate responses to medical emergencies, failures to protect detainees from physical and sexual harm, denial of accommodations for individuals with disabilities, and routine denial of language interpretation services, the lawsuit says.
Detainees also have complained of buggy or improperly prepared food and insufficient contagion controls that allow illnesses to spread.
Those findings, along with Homeland Security’s suggest detainees face “a serious risk of further harm,” including death and disease, the lawsuit says.
They also fit a pattern of resistance to oversight, it says.
Homeland Security and Geo Group officials have prevented Newark leaders from inspecting the facility to ensure it met safety codes, barred state health inspectors, refused Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s request to speak with detainees on a controlled tour of the jail in June, and rebuffed other officials looking to carry out their oversight duties there, the lawsuit says.
“DHS’s failure to respond is part of a troubling and repeated pattern of stonewalling requests for information regarding conditions at Delaney Hall,” Davenport wrote to Homeland Security officials in an Oct. 20 letter appended to the lawsuit.
Amy Torres, executive director of the New Jersey Alliance for Immigrant Justice, applauded the lawsuit as “a great development.”
“Even though it doesn’t give any answers, it shows that the attorney general’s office is using all levers of the law to pursue answers about what is happening at Delaney Hall and how we can release people immediately to get them out of those unsafe conditions,” Torres said.
Amy Torres, the executive director of New Jersey Alliance for Immigrant Justice, speaks outside Delaney Hall on Dec. 23, 2025. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
The lawsuit came one day after Davenport, in a separate court filing, told federal judges that Homeland Security officials have refused to release information about an immigrant jail it plans to open in Roxbury.
That prison was put on hold pending an environmental review, but state officials fear federal immigration authorities are proceeding with renovations despite the court-ordered pause, Davenport said.

title: Neighbors as community: Cohousing expands across Vermont
description:
Residents co-own shared spaces to foster togetherness.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Neighbors as community: Cohousing expands across Vermont.
text:
Residents at Bristol Village Cohousing enjoy a meal together. Photo courtesy Jim Mendell

Natalie Bankmann is a reporter with the Community News Service, part of the University of Vermont’s Reporting & Documentary Storytelling program.
BURLINGTON — On a recent Monday in October, Burlington Cohousing East Village resident Sharyl Green followed a winding stone path past a shared common building and conjoined townhouses. She continued on to the luscious common garden, where she picked a tomato.
It wasn’t her tomato. Her neighbor, who was away on vacation, told the whole community to take whatever they like.
Green is one of 56 neighbors who share more than just tomatoes. They share a kitchen, green space and, every other night, dinner.
“It’s a dynamic way to live. So that includes all the ‘Oh my goodnesses’ and the pleasant surprises,” Green said.
Burlington Cohousing East Village is one of 12 cohousing communities in the state. That’s up from just one in 1995, according to the National Cohousing Alliance.
Vermont ranks seventh in the number of cohousing communities — more than many larger states.
Cohousing helps curb loneliness while helping residents live more sustainably, said Jim Mendell, vice president of the National Cohousing Alliance Board.
“It is a way of dealing with a lot of problems in the world today,” said Mendell, who lives in Bristol Village Cohousing, a 14-unit development 45 minutes south of Burlington.
Cohousing began in Denmark in the 1960s as a way to eliminate the loneliness and isolation of the modern world.
It’s a shared model of living that is built to provide a strong sense of community. Residents own their individual properties and collectively own shared spaces.
Many cohousing communities adopt a form of organizing called sociocracy, where decision making is decentralized.
For example, at East Village, the community is split into six committees including land, building and home. Bristol Village Cohousing has a similar system.
“Everyone has a job. Every month we have work time, so we all get together and do projects together. Sometimes it’s painting a building, doing some weeding, gardening or fixing things that are broken,” Mendell said.

Residents at Bristol Village Cohousing landscape the garden. Photo courtesy Jim Mendell

Besides dinners, various events are also hosted in the common spaces of East Village Cohousing. Recently, a group of residents gathered in the common area to hear Progressive/Democratic candidate Amanda Janoo’s campaign for governor.
“You couldn’t do this without our common community space,” Green said.
At both East Village and Bristol Village, those common spaces are powered by solar power. The model of cohousing encourages sustainability by having shared equipment like lawn mowers, cars and even children’s toys.
“I’ve got some toys that my kids have outgrown. ‘Can anyone use them?’ That’s what cohousing can provide,” said Liz Ryan Cole, a former member of the National Cohousing Alliance.
Cole lives in Pinnacle Cohousing in Lyme, New Hampshire, across the Connecticut River from Vermont.
She says one thing that defines cohousing communities as opposed to other types of living arrangements is “intentionality.”
Some choose to have a room for yoga, while others might have farm spaces on their property. The community decides how its property is used.
Many cohousing organizations save money by having shared spaces such as a guest room, piano room or game room.

Residents at East Village Cohousing have dinner in their shared kitchen space. Photo courtesy Sharyl Green

Still, cohousing is not always cheap. One of the biggest criticisms of cohousing is the cost effectiveness, Cole said. The properties can be expensive to design and build to zoning standards, she said.
Some of the homes at East Village Cohousing are designated as affordable housing. These properties are listed and sold by Champlain Housing Trust.
The National Cohousing Alliance is working on finding more ways to make cohousing more accessible, Mendell said.
“One of our big questions is how to keep it more affordable,” Mendell said.
Cohousing’s model can be expensive and can’t curb loneliness alone, but Cole said it can be a transformative way of life.
“It’s not a utopian community,” Cole said, “but it is a cooperative one.”

title: After calling for a ‘new generation’ of leadership, SC Sen.-elect Andrews is undecided on her vote
description: After emphatically saying she would not back New York Democrat Chuck Schumer as U.S. Senate majority leader, Sen.-elect Annie Andrews said Tuesday she’s undecided on who will get her vote. Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for a decade, is being challenged by Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen following midterm elections that put Democrats back […]
text:
U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., center, poses for a photo with newly elected Democratic senators in his office in the U.S Capitol on Nov. 9, 2026 in Washington, D.C. From left to right: Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio, James Talarico of Texas, Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, Josh Turek of Iowa, Roy Cooper of North Carolina, Juliana Stratton of Illinois, Chris Pappas of New Hampshire, Annie Andrews of South Carolina, Troy Jackson of Maine, Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Adam Hamilton of Kansas. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)After emphatically saying she would not back New York Democrat Chuck Schumer as U.S. Senate majority leader, Sen.-elect Annie Andrews said Tuesday she’s undecided on who will get her vote.
Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for a decade, is being challenged by Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen following midterm elections that put Democrats back in charge of the upper chamber. Andrews’ win was among at least eight flips for Democrats in the U.S. Senate, with a ninth possibility in Alaska, where the race has yet to be called.
“On the campaign trail, I really stressed that I think it’s time for generational change, and I stand by that statement,” Andrews told reporters on a virtual call Tuesday.
“The way I assess the situation as it is right now is that the generational change is represented by this incredibly dynamic incoming freshman class of senators, and the generational change goal is something we’ll achieve, you know, as we move forward,” she said.
Andrews said she’s meeting with Schumer, 75, and Van Hollen, 67, before deciding who she’ll support. The closed-door caucus vote is set for Dec. 1.
Ahead of her win, Andrews said she would not vote for Schumer.
“No, I think it’s really clear that both parties are ready for a new generation of leadership,” the 46-year-old Democrat said in an Oct. 29 TV interview with Fox News anchor Bret Baier, who asked her directly whether she would vote for Schumer as majority leader.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Two days after the election, he asked her again.
“I still very much believe that it’s time for a generational change on both sides of the aisle,” she told Baier during a televised interview Nov. 5.
Schumer, who was previously majority leader from 2021 to 2025, is considered likely to keep control of the caucus.
While Van Hollen is not a new generation, his uphill challenge is backed by prominent progressives. They include Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent who identifies as a democratic socialist and caucuses with Democrats, and Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who made history as the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate.
Andrews said she’s part of the freshman class of senators who will break the “norms of the way the Senate functions” to deliver for Americans.
A look at how SC voters’ support shifted to flip the US Senate seat

They will be sworn in Jan. 3.
“It’s clear to me that Americans are ready for change. I think my election is a big shining symbol of that fact, so I continue to believe we need generational change. I continue to believe that we need to act with urgency,” Andrews told reporters.
She said she’s optimistic that Democrats will “get to work to solve problems” after the leadership election, regardless of who wins.
Schumer’s been in Congress for 46 years. New York voters first elected him to the U.S. House in 1980, then the U.S. Senate in 1998. That compares to 24 years total on Capitol Hill for Van Hollen, who was first elected to the U.S. House in 2002 and the U.S. Senate in 2016.
The freshmen are eager to “deliver on the promises we made on the campaign trail,” Andrews said. “I think we’re going to push as hard as we can to get the job done” once the majority leader is chosen.
Andrews defeated U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed in July to fulfill the remaining term of her late brother, Lindsey Graham.
She is the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from South Carolina since Fritz Hollings’ last re-election in 1998.
Conversations are ongoing, she added, about keeping on some Graham staffers.
