name: Mississippi Today
title: With his PGA Tour job on the line, Fulton’s Chad Ramey reaches deep inside for a huge win at Austin
description: Chad Ramey hits on the fairway on the first hole during the third round of the 3M Open golf tournament at the Tournament Players Club, Saturday, July 27, 2024, in Blaine, Minn.
text:
Someone once asked Lee Trevino, a former caddy-turned-hustler-turned-golfing-legend, about the pressure of playing his sport with tens of thousands of dollars on the line. Trevino answered there’s little pressure playing for what he called “other people’s money.”
Rick Cleveland
“Pressure,” Trevino said, “is playing for five dollars when you only have two dollars in your pocket.”
And that may well be the case. But Mississippian Chad Ramey of Fulton played golf Monday in Austin, Texas, with a whole different, perhaps higher, level of pressure.
That’s right. Ramey played golf with his livelihood on the line. What’s more, he won. Ramey shot a final round, 7-under-par 65 to win the inaugural Austin Championship and the $1.2 million paycheck that comes with it.
Ramey entered the Austin event at No. 137 on the 2026 FedEx Cup standings. Only the top 100 earners keep their PGA Tour privileges for 2027. The victory vaults the 34-year-old Ramey to No. 68 on the list and guarantees him PGA privileges through the 2028 season.
Ramey summed up the situation best in his first comments in the post-tournament press conference: “I was battling for my job.”
“My life went from not knowing what I was going to be doing in January to now knowing what I will be doing for the next two years,” Ramey said.
Ramey’s clutch victory becomes even more meaningful when you realize the PGA Tour purses will escalate by millions and millions of dollars in 2028.
For an athlete in any sport, playing your best when it matters most is a valuable characteristic. Some coaches call it the “it” factor. Some have “it.” Most do not. 
Clearly, “it” is present in Ramey, the former All-SEC Mississippi State golfer, who hadn’t won a tournament in four years.
Ramey entered the final round in Austin, which was supposed to have been played Sunday, in a three-way tie for second place, one shot out of the lead. Heavy thunderstorms inundated the Fazio Canyons Course, delaying the final round until Monday. That meant Ramey had an extra 24 hours to sit, watch the rain and marinate in the pressure of the career-defining circumstances.
Chad Ramey (with Austin Championship trophy, flanked by his dad Stanley, his wife Kelly, and son Nolan after his big victory. (Photo courtesy PGA Tour.)
“It’s unbelievable,” Ramey said. “It seems like for whatever reason I play my best golf when my back is against the wall. It’s very rewarding. I’m very thankful.”
It was his first top 10 finish in 2026, but Ramey said that part of his record is somewhat deceiving.
“I’ve been so close,” he said. “I’ve probably made more cuts this year than I ever have. For whatever reason, I just haven’t put it together on Saturdays and Sundays. But I was playing well, doing the right things. I just kept working at it. This week, my putter just got hot. I’ve worked my butt off for this.”
Ramey shots rounds of 68, 68, 67 and then the 65 to finish 20-under par, two shots clear of runner-up Ben Kohles and three shots better than third-round leader Trace Crowe. Blades Brown, the 19-year-old sensation who recently became the Tour’s youngest winner in 92 years, finished fourth.
Ramey is one of two native Mississippians currently on the PGA Tour. Hattiesburg’s Davis Riley, the other, missed the cut at Austin, shooting 74-74. And now, Riley, 29, finds himself in much the same position Ramey was in before Austin. Riley, a two-time Tour winner, currently sits at No. 125 in the FedEx standings heading into this week’s RSM Classic, the last PGA Tour event of the season, at Sea Island Golf Club in St. Simon Island, Georgia. Since finishing third in the Rocket Classic in late July, Riley has missed five of seven 36-hole cuts, including three straight. He will need a strong finish at Sea Island to make the top 100.
Riley has shown the “it” factor often in the past. He needs reach deep inside and re-discover it this weekend. Ramey, who also plans to play at Sea Island, has showed how it’s done.

name: VTDigger
title: Study finds it’s rare for big investors to swoop in to buy Vermont homes
description:
Fears about corporations crowding out everyday homebuyers have animated political debate nationwide and in Vermont. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Study finds it’s rare for big investors to swoop in to buy Vermont homes.
text:
Houses viewed from Barre Town on Oct. 4, 2026. Daniel McCullum / Courtesy
Carly Berlin covers housing and infrastructure for Vermont Public, in partnership with VTDigger.
How many of Vermont’s homes on the market end up in the hands of big investors? 
Very few, according to a report published last week by Vermont’s Department of Housing and Community Development. The study, requested by lawmakers earlier this year, sought to find out how large a footprint “institutional real estate investors” have had in the homebuying market in recent years. Critics have worried the presence of such investors in Vermont could be crowding out everyday homebuyers. 
“We are not seeing any significant buying either by private equity, outside corporations, or even individuals here in Vermont,” said Housing Commissioner Alex Farrell. 
The question of corporate home ownership has animated political debate nationwide and in the Green Mountain State. Yet national research has suggested that large real estate investment firms have generally avoided buying up single-family homes in northern New England; their holdings tend to be more concentrated in Sun Belt housing markets like Atlanta and Phoenix. 
The Vermont report looked at tax data for the sales for single-family homes and duplexes between January 2022 and December 2025. The authors focused on “high-frequency buyers” – companies or individual people involved in three or more purchases in a given year. 
The report found just 14 entities who fit that criteria during the four-year span. Altogether, those companies and individuals conducted 108 property acquisitions, out of nearly 30,000 that occurred during the timeframe. Most of the entities purchased five homes or fewer.
The data includes both year-round homes and seasonal ones, including short-term rental properties counted as residences. The report’s authors did not track down whether entities bought properties under multiple names or LLCs, a gap they want to dig into in the future, Farrell said.
A single company bought 43 properties flagged in the report: the Newport-based homebuilder and remodeling company Tanguay Homes. Yet Farrell said the company’s behavior did not match the concerns driving the study – that large companies are buying up homes and adding them to rental portfolios. 
The report found that in most instances, Tanguay Homes bought a property and then resold it within a year at an average gain of about $110,000.
Tony Tanguay, the company’s owner, said Tanguay Homes purchases properties in cash that a homeseller is eager to get off their hands quickly or that they’d struggle to market. Often, the homes have considerable maintenance issues that might deter a bank from writing a mortgage or an insurance company issuing a policy, like faulty wiring or a dilapidated roof, he said.
The renovation and resale work constitutes about half of Tanguay’s business, he said. He began buying existing homes in the wake of the 2008 housing market crash, when the math for building new homes no longer penciled, and he wanted to keep his construction crew busy. The homebuying work has only picked up as the cost of homebuilding has soared since the COVID-19 pandemic, he said.
He knows some might view his work as taking advantage of people, but he sees it as a way of giving people an option aside from foreclosure. 
“What I’m trying to help people out with is, you know, contact me before you get to that point. So they don’t have a foreclosure on their credit report,” he said.
State tax data indicates that there were about 7,400 “corporation owned” residential properties in the state in 2025, or about 3% of all residences, including seasonal homes and apartment buildings. That’s a broad category that includes properties owned by an LLC or a nonprofit or government entity.
Farrell, the housing commissioner, suspects Vermont’s relatively old, high-priced, and scarce housing stock has likely dissuaded large-scale investment firms – who want to buy many homes at a fairly low cost – from making inroads in the state. 
Vermont did see a spike in “investor” purchases of homes in 2021, mirroring a nationwide trend when interest rates were low, according to reporting by VTDigger. That window fell outside the timeframe the state examined, though Farrell said officials may look at it in subsequent reports.  

READ MORE

A new federal law passed this summer restricts large institutional investors that own at least 350 single-family homes from buying additional ones beginning in January.
Rep. Emilie Krasnow, a Democrat from South Burlington, introduced legislation earlier this year that would have forced large-scale investors to wait 90 days after a home is listed before purchasing it, among other restrictions. That bill, modeled off of similar legislation in New York, was tabled and ultimately resulted in the housing department study.
Krasnow sees the report’s findings as good news. But she disagrees with the recommendation of officials like Farrell that the state should not pursue regulatory action now, and instead should keep monitoring the issue. She plans to reintroduce a new bill aimed at reining in investor purchases come January as a proactive measure. 
“If we don’t have things in place before it becomes a problem, then it’s often harder to regulate and get ahead of it,” she said.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: West Virginia Attorney General wants school funding lawsuit dismissed
description: The office of West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey is asking the state Supreme Court to dismiss a legal challenge over the state’s school aid funding formula.
text:
(Greenleaf123/Getty Images)The office of West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey is asking the state Supreme Court to dismiss a legal challenge over the state’s school aid funding formula.
In a motion filed Friday on behalf of state officers named in the lawsuit, attorneys with McCuskey’s office argued that the state Supreme Court does not have authority over Senate President Randy Smith and House Speaker Roger Hanshaw, the two lawmakers named in the suit. They ask the court that the two be dismissed from the lawsuit. 
They also argue the petitioner, a sixth grade student in Lincoln County identified only as M.D., has not met the burden of showing standing to sue anyone. They separately asked the court to dismiss the lawsuit. 
“Her first theory — direct harm to M.D.’s education — fails because the Petition never ties that alleged harm to anything the State Officer Respondents did or anything a writ could make them do,” they wrote. “The second theory,  taxpayer standing, fails because M.D.’s mother hasn’t provided any evidence that she pays taxes to the State (let alone that M.D., the actual Petitioner, does).”
The lawsuit was filed in September on behalf of M.D. and the student’s parent, Lakin Patten, in an attempt to require state lawmakers to “correct the school funding formula.” The student is represented in the case by the American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia. 
The lawsuit lists as defendants Hanshaw, R-Clay; Smith, R-Preston; Auditor Mark Hunt; Tax Commissioner Matthew Irby; Treasurer Larry Pack; the state Department of Education; the state Board of Education, the School Building Authority, State School Superintendent Michelle Blatt, as as well as Lincoln County school board officials and county officials.
State officials have asked the court to pause the case until April, giving lawmakers time to address the funding formula during the upcoming legislative session, when the formula is expected to be a focus. 
West Virginia public school poor finances have prompted a wave of school closures across the state. The West Virginia Department of Education says it will take a $410 million increase in state aid for public schools to meet needs in special education, enrollment stabilization, personnel and more. 
State school officials have agreed with the motion to delay the case, while officials for the Lincoln County school board took no position. 
Attorneys with the ACLU, on behalf of M.D., have argued against delaying the case, in a response filed Nov. 9.
“For years, West Virginia’s students and schools have been given false hope and empty  promises concerning reform to the school aid formula, always being told that an adequately funded education is right around the next corner….,” the attorney wrote. “The present action is before this Court because the wait was too long, the cost of inaction too high, to permit another legislative session to proceed without  clear guidance from this Court as to what is constitutionally required of the Respondents.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana struggles to add, monitor stores that accept WIC benefits, audit finds
description: At the end of September, there were 391 authorized WIC vendors in the state serving more than 69,000 families, according to Louisiana Department of Health data. That’s down from 406 stores a year earlier.
text:
A new Louisiana Legislative Auditor report highlights deficiencies with the state health department’s oversight of the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children, better known as WIC.  (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Families with young children in Louisiana that depend on federal food benefits can’t always easily redeem them because state officials have fallen short on monitoring and adding stores that accept them, a state audit concludes.
A new report from the Louisiana Legislative Auditor highlights deficiencies with the state health department’s oversight of the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children, better known as WIC. 
The U.S. Department of Agriculture issued a moratorium on Louisiana approving new vendors from 2014-17 related to a lack of oversight. The audit noted the state lost nearly 57% of its vendors under the moratorium and has only added back about one-fourth as of mid-2026.
At the end of September, there were 391 authorized WIC vendors in the state serving more than 69,000 families, according to Louisiana Department of Health data. That’s down from 406 stores a year earlier.
The USDA provides WIC resources to states for low-income pregnant and breastfeeding women, infants and children under age 5. States put the rules and procedures in place to distribute the benefits that can be redeemed for healthy foods and infant formula. The program also offers access to nutrition education and postpartum support services.
“The availability of vendors for participants to easily redeem WIC benefits is important because of the health benefits of the program, and because LDH only draws down funds its uses, leaving unspent funding with the USDA rather than being used in Louisiana’s economy,” the audit report states.  
The audit highlights barriers to adding more WIC vendors and procedural weaknesses within the health department that result in fewer participants being able to redeem benefits. Only 18% of Louisiana’s low-income neighborhoods have convenient access to WIC vendors, according to the report, compared with 43% nationally. 
The state health department agreed with the auditor’s recommendation that it work with potential vendors to increase WIC access in low-income areas. Health Secretary Bruce Greenstein said his agency will develop and launch a vendor recruitment strategy by January to expand participation and strengthen vendor retention.
Health officials also plan to take steps to modernize WIC access by making the benefits available for online shopping, according to Greenstein.
The audit also suggested the health department better explain exceptions to WIC rules that could lead to more nontraditional vendors, such as a pharmacy or convenience store, taking part in the program. 
The auditor’s review noted that the health department didn’t conduct a compliance investigation or routine monitoring visit 64% of its vendors from 2023-26, although it points out the USDA does not require the state to monitor its WIC vendors at least once over a defined period. Routine monitoring ensures vendors are providing proper services to WIC participants, the audit report said.
The health secretary said the agency will put a rotating monitoring schedule in place to increase the number of vendors reviewed and cover as much of the state as possible.
A December 2025 audit report on the program found that because WIC-approved items account for a small portion of purchases, many retailers choose not to accept the benefits even though participants pay for them with electronic benefit cards similar to those the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program uses.
The December report also found only 37% of eligible state residents took part in the WIC program, and that Louisiana was one of 45 states that did not draw down all of the WIC money the federal government allotted for the state in fiscal year 2024.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Feds propose allowing seismic oil surveys to disturb polar bears
description: Operators of a planned seismic survey intended to help search for oil in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain would have permission to disturb polar bears under a proposed rule released Monday by the Trump administration. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is proposing to issue an incidental harassment authorization to the Alaska Industrial […]
text:
Polar bear cubs are seen emerging from their den in 2010. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service says a seismic survey program planned by the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority for the coastal plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge will cause only negligible disturbance to polar bears, including denning bears. (Photo provided by the U.S. Geological Survey)Operators of a planned seismic survey intended to help search for oil in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain would have permission to disturb polar bears under a proposed rule released Monday by the Trump administration.
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is proposing to issue an incidental harassment authorization to the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority, or AIDEA, the state development agency that holds six active oil leases in the coastal plain.
AIDEA is seeking to conduct a seismic survey, through contractors, as early as this winter. The proposed incidental harassment authorizations is set to be published in the Federal Register on Tuesday, kicking off a mandatory 30-day public comment period. Incidental harassment authorizations allow for activities that disturb species like polar bears that are managed by the Marine Mammals Protection Act.
If granted, the incidental harassment authorization would bring AIDEA a step closer to actual oil exploration work in the refuge.
The refuge’s coastal plan has been the subject of a decades-long national debate between development advocates and conservationists, with different Alaska Native groups on either side.
Seismic surveys use soundwaves sent through the ground to map out geologic features and help identify potential deposits of oil and gas. The loud sounds associated with seismic operations pose potential hazards to polar bears and other noise-sensitive animals.
But the Fish and Wildlife Service, in its proposed authorization, said it has concluded that the seismic surveys planned by AIDEA will result in only minimal and short-term disturbances to polar bears.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

AIDEA’s holdings in the refuge comprise six leases acquired in a January 2021 sale conducted at the end of the first Trump administration, plus three more leases the agency acquired in a U.S. Bureau of Lane Management auction in June.
AIDEA’s plan, as described in the proposed incidental harassment authorization, is to conduct aerial infrared surveys to locate polar bear dens that should be avoided, followed by on-the-ground surveys with seismic equipment and supported by worker camps.
Supporters of oil drilling in the refuge coastal plain have characterized AIDEA’s seismic program as a necessary step toward responsible development that will help the state.
AIDEA in May approved an expenditure of up to $190 million for exploration work in the refuge, mostly for the seismic program. At the time, Gov. Mike Dunleavy described it as “a major investment” in Alaska’s future.
“ANWR represents one of many opportunities to secure long-term economic prosperity for future generations of Alaskans while strengthening American energy security,” Dunleavy said in a statement released by AIDEA.
AIDEA had planned to start its survey work as early as this month, according to the Fish and Wildlife Service’s proposed authorization.
However, AIDEA now expects the program to start no earlier than January, according to a status report the development agency filed earlier this month in federal court as part of a pending legal case that seeks to block oil exploration in the refuge.
Opponents of oil development said Monday the Fish and Wildlife Service’s analysis vastly understates the impacts that seismic exploration would have on the Arctic environment.
Opponents who weighed in include the Gwich’in Steering Committee, which represents Gwich’in Athabascan tribes in Alaska and Canada, and Earthjustice.
“The Gwich’in Steering Committee is appalled by the level of industrial and human activity that AIDEA is outlining in their request,” Kristen Moreland, the organization’s executive director, said in a statement. “Seismic testing, and everything that comes along with it, would have far-reaching and devastating impacts on the Coastal Plain.”
The Gwich’in Steering Committee and a coalition of conservation groups represented by Earthjustice are plaintiffs in the pending lawsuit seeking to prevent AIDEA from carrying out its planned exploration.
Scientists with the University of Alaska Fairbanks have cautioned that seismic surveys in the refuge coastal plan will likely damage tundra and permafrost terrain and harm the area’s wildlife. Winter snow cover in the coastal plain is too patchy to provide protection from heavy equipment moving across the ground, and freshwater sources are too scarce in that part of Arctic Alaska to support temporary ice roads that are used for winter work, the scientists concluded in a 2020 report.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida Democrats vow to make their (limited) numbers count in 2027
description: Despite losses in the top 2026 races, Democrats in the Florida Legislature are fired up. Democratic leaders in the state House and Senate delivered rousing speeches Tuesday, as the House and Senate reorganized following the midterms, promising a return to relevance as party members worked their way out of superminority status. In her acceptance speech […]
text:
House Democratic Leader Christine Hunschofksy (center, blue dress) with fellow Democrats in the House chamber on Nov. 16, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)Despite losses in the top 2026 races, Democrats in the Florida Legislature are fired up.
Democratic leaders in the state House and Senate delivered rousing speeches Tuesday, as the House and Senate reorganized following the midterms, promising a return to relevance as party members worked their way out of superminority status.
In her acceptance speech as the new Senate Democratic leader, Sen. Tracie Davis of Jacksonville encouraged members: “Join us, or be left behind.”
“A revolution is what happens when millions of people stand up to say enough is enough. A revolution happens at kitchen tables, in community centers, and at front doors, and at the ballot box,” Davis said. “So, to my colleagues across the aisle, I hope you took notice of what happened two weeks ago. I hope you’re putting together an agenda now that reflects the needs of the people we are elected to serve, not the ambitions of politicians or the input of corporate donors.”
She added: “I hope you can put partisanship aside and show Florida that there’s more that unites us than divides us, because that revolution started Nov. 3.”
Florida Democrats lost races for governor, the U.S. Senate, and three Floria Cabinet seats. However, they netted 16 additional seats in the Florida House, giving the chamber the largest number of Democrats since 1998. In the Senate, they flipped one seat.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Climbing out of superminority status in the House confers more than bragging rights. It means if Democrats can stick together, they can deny Republican legislative leaders two-thirds votes on legislative procedures such as waiving the rules, placing constitutional amendments on the ballot, and overriding vetoes by the governor.
“We know we cannot accomplish everything on our own, but we should never underestimate what 50 committed voices, united by shared values and a common purpose, can accomplish,” House Democratic Leader Christine Hunschofsky of Parkland said in a 20-minute speech Monday night. “We don’t need to hold the majority to make a difference.”
She added that while the Democrats remain in the minority in the 120-member House, those 50 voices have “a responsibility to lead, to advocate, to offer solutions, and to make sure that the people we represent are heard in this chamber.”
“While we may not hold the majority, we must never confuse being in the minority with having a limited responsibility or a limited ability to lead. Floridians didn’t send us to Tallahassee simply to hold press conferences or political points or engage in partisan fights. They sent us here because they are looking for solutions. They want their elected leaders to focus on the challenges they face every single day. And that is exactly what we must do.”

title: US Senate seeks to restore campaign finance watchdog during lame-duck session
description: The U.S. Senate took a first step Tuesday toward reviving the moribund Federal Election Commission, holding a confirmation hearing on President Donald Trump’s nominees to lead the campaign finance watchdog after it was sidelined for the midterm elections.The FEC has lacked a quorum for more than a year, preventing it from taking action on complaints or issui[...]
text: The U.S. Senate took a first step Tuesday toward reviving the moribund Federal Election Commission, holding a confirmation hearing on President Donald Trump’s nominees to lead the campaign finance watchdog after it was sidelined for the midterm elections.The FEC has lacked a quorum for more than a year, preventing it from taking action on complaints or issuing advisory opinions. As its backlog of work has grown, candidates and political groups have been left uncertain about when — or if — the FEC will take action on alleged violations of federal campaign finance law.The Senate Rules and Administration Committee on Tuesday weighed the nominations of two Republicans, Ashley Stow and Andrew Woodson, to join the FEC. Only two commissioners, both Democrats, are currently serving and the agency needs a bipartisan quorum of at least four to take official action.“Restoring the commission’s ability to function is especially important following the 2026 midterm elections,” said Sen. Bill Hagerty, a Tennessee Republican who chaired the hearing.Hagerty pointed to the backlog of complaints and the need to prepare for the 2028 presidential race. Restoring a quorum will allow the FEC “to resume its essential responsibilities,” he said.The FEC enforces federal campaign finance laws and assists candidates and donors in complying with them. The FEC, which marked its 50th anniversary in 2025, also makes public a vast trove of campaign finance data.The hearing marked an effort by Republicans to end the FEC’s dormancy during the Senate’s lame-duck period before Democrats take control of the chamber in January. At that point, Democrats will have much more power to demand that the White House nominate individuals acceptable to Democrats or block Trump’s nominees.Democrats support restoring a quorum on the FEC, but they question whether Trump will allow commissioners to act independently.In February 2025, Trump fired the Democratic chair of the FEC, Ellen Weintraub, who had been a commissioner since 2002. Weintraub has said she doesn’t view the firing as legally valid, though she hasn’t challenged the dismissal in court. The move against Weintraub came after Republican Sean Cooksey resigned before Trump’s inauguration. In April 2025, Republican Allen Dickerson also resigned, creating a lack of a quorum that has persisted.Sen. Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, said Tuesday the FEC was established in the post-Watergate era to be evenly balanced between Democrats and Republicans and politically independent. Padilla is the ranking Democrat on the committee but will likely chair the panel beginning in January."It's absolutely critical that any commissioners who sign on to help lead this agency commit to restoring and defending that independence. Full stop,” Padilla said.The Trump administration has broadly sought to bring independent agencies created by Congress under the control of the White House. The U.S. Supreme Court in June allowed the president to fire members of the Federal Trade Commission without cause. It’s not clear how that decision would apply to firings of members of the FEC.Pledges of neutralityStow and Woodson promised to act impartially and emphasized the importance of the bipartisan nature of the FEC. But they evaded questions about how they would specifically act toward Trump’s political operation, MAGA, Inc. because complaints about the super PAC could come before the commission.“Should I be confirmed, I pledge to discharge my duties with impartiality and unwavering commitment to the First Amendment and enforcement of the law as enacted by Congress and interpreted by the nation’s courts,” said Stow, a longtime FEC lawyer from Texas.Woodson, a Virginia lawyer focused on campaign finance at the law firm Wiley Rein LLP, worked at the FEC from 2013 to 2015. He said the FEC must always act with sensitivity for First Amendment rights, and that its guidance and regulations should “promote freedom, not frustration.”“Everyone that will come before me, I will treat exactly the same — impartially,” Woodson said, whether they hold “the highest office in the land” or are “just an ordinary congressperson.”Trump nominated Stow and Woodson in February, but Tuesday’s hearing marked the Senate’s first public step toward advancing their nominations.Push for quorumOn Nov. 5, a dozen former Republican FEC commissioners wrote to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a South Dakota Republican, asking that he prioritize their confirmations before the end of the current Congress. The FEC’s situation is “increasingly untenable,” the former commissioners wrote. In addition to being unable to take action on complaints and issue guidance about campaign finance law, the group noted that hackers had targeted the FEC, crippling its online system for reporting campaign finance information in the closing days of the midterm elections.The former commissioners wrote that the incident offered a “stark reminder” that the FEC is responsible for maintaining critical systems that allow the American public to receive campaign finance information.“An agency carrying responsibilities of that magnitude should have a functioning Commission at its head,” the group wrote.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Providence police chief to retire when Morales takes office
description: Providence Police Chief Col. Oscar L. Perez plans to leave his post leading the capital city’s police department the very day its new mayor will be sworn in. Perez formally submitted his resignation letter to Mayor Brett Smiley on Tuesday morning, saying he intends to retire after 32 years with the Providence Police Department on […]
text:
Providence Police Chief Col. Oscar Perez during a press conference on the Brown University shooting investigation on Wednesday, Dec. 17, 2025, in Providence. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Providence Police Chief Col. Oscar L. Perez plans to leave his post leading the capital city’s police department the very day its new mayor will be sworn in.
Perez formally submitted his resignation letter to Mayor Brett Smiley on Tuesday morning, saying he intends to retire after 32 years with the Providence Police Department on Jan. 4. 
“This is not an easy message to write,” Perez wrote. “I never imagined I would have the privilege of leading this department. It has been the greatest honor of my professional life.”
Perez did not cite a specific reason for his departure in the letter. 
Mayor-elect David Morales, who defeated Smiley in the Sept. 9 Democratic primary, said in a statement Tuesday that Perez told him he planned to leave to spend time with his wife and focus on her care as she faces serious health challenges.
“I respect his decision to put his family first, and I’m grateful for his decades of service to Providence,” Morales said.
Perez, who oversees a department with 441 sworn officers and a $120.1 million fiscal year 2027 budget, was appointed by Smiley in February 2023, nearly three decades after joining the department as a police recruit in 1994. In his resignation letter, Perez reflected on his journey as a young immigrant from Colombia who grew up in Providence and went on to lead the department he had dreamed of joining.
One of the defining challenges of his tenure came on Dec. 13, 2025, when a gunman opened fire in the engineering building at Brown University, killing two students and wounding nine others. The shooter then fled the campus, leading to a six-day manhunt. Providence police coordinated with state and federal law enforcement agencies to track down surveillance footage and determine the killer’s true identity and location. 
Perez called the shooting one of the most heartbreaking experiences of his career, writing that the victims, their families and the community deserved “answers, accountability and justice.” He also thanked the officers, first responders, law enforcement partners and community members who came together in the aftermath.
“My goal was always to make our city safer for our children and families and to ensure that every young person growing up here could see a future full of possibility,” Perez wrote. “No police chief can prevent every tragedy, but I hope that my service made a meaningful and lasting difference.”
Smiley in a statement praised Perez’s leadership, pointing to reductions in crime, the department’s community policing efforts and investments in public safety. Under Perez’s watch, the city reported a 16.6% decrease in violent crime and 17.2% drop in property crime between 2023 and 2025.
“I am forever grateful for his partnership, his steady leadership during some of our city’s most challenging moments and his unwavering commitment to the people of Providence,” Smiley said.
Perez’s departure comes as Morales prepares to take office with a stated intention to end the city’s use of automated license plate readers — a position at odds with the police department’s defense of the technology. Morales has pledged to cancel the city’s contract with Flock, while the City Council is considering an ordinance that would ban the cameras.
Perez had pushed back against the proposed restrictions, arguing in an Oct. 15 statement to Rhode Island Current that police should have been consulted before councilors drafted the ordinance affecting criminal investigations and department operations. He said he respected elected council members’ authority to set policy, but believed decisions of that magnitude should be informed by the officers responsible for carrying them out.
The City Council’s Special Committee on Health, Opportunity, Prosperity and Education unanimously advanced the proposed ordinance to the full chamber during its meeting Monday evening. The full council is expected to take its first of two required votes Thursday, Council President Rachel Miller confirmed in a text message to Rhode Island Current.
Deputy Police Chief Cmdr. Tim O’Hara defended the technology before the committee on Nov. 11.
“We need every legal advantage to keep this city safe, provide answers, and reduce the fear of crime on our neighbors,” O’Hara told the committee. “We believe here in Providence we have the proper safeguards in place to protect the confidentiality of our information.”
Perez’s departure follows another pending leadership change in the city’s public safety departments. Providence Fire Chief Derek Silva announced on Nov. 10 that he would retire after three years leading the department.
Perez earns an annual salary of $244,725. Silva earns $220,339 a year.
Morales said his administration will begin searching for the city’s next chiefs of police and fire in the weeks ahead. 
“I’m committed to ensuring that our Providence Police Department has the resources, support, and strong, steady leadership our officers need to serve our communities effectively and keep our neighborhoods safe,” Morales said.
The incoming mayor said he is also seeking an “experienced leader in fire and emergency medical operations” to replace Silva.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: New Jersey invests $8M to expand midwife workforce
description: New Jersey is investing $8 million to expand the midwifery workforce to help improve maternal and infant health outcomes.
text:
Sarah Simmons, a midwife and co-owner of Maple Street Birth Center in rural Omak, Washington, is pictured holding a newborn. New Jersey announced Monday it will invest $8 million to expand the midwife workforce, something advocates say can help improve health outcomes for moms and babies in a state that still struggles with high maternal deaths and massive racial disparities. (Photo courtesy of Sarah Simmons)New Jersey will invest $8 million to expand scholarships and provide professional support for midwives as part of its ongoing effort to strengthen the maternal health workforce and improve outcomes for moms and babies. 
Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced the commitment late Monday with the Rutgers School of Nursing, which she said will oversee the three-year community workforce pilot program designed to make it easier for people to be trained and thrive as midwives in New Jersey. 
“Every New Jersey mother deserves that support, regardless of her ZIP code,” Sherrill said. 
While New Jersey has one of the nation’s lowest infant mortality rates and preterm birth rates have also declined, it still has an above-average maternal death rate, and racial disparities that leave Black moms and babies at far higher risk than white women. On average, hundreds of babies and roughly two dozen moms die here every year during pregnancy, childbirth or in the year after, according to state data. 
Midwives are clinically trained primary care providers whose involvement in birthing has been shown to reduce the number of maternal and infant deaths and need for surgical intervention, while improving breastfeeding and child immunization rates. Midwives also care for newborns and provide reproductive healthcare for people at any age. 
There are about 450 licensed midwives in New Jersey, where they attend to 1 in 10 births, but experts say more are needed to really improve outcomes. Nationwide, midwives participate in about 12% of all births. 
“New Jersey needs more midwives, particularly in communities where access to maternity care is limited,” said Angela Starkweather, dean and professor at Rutgers School of Nursing, which started its graduate midwifery program more than 50 years ago. 
Dr. Michael Warren, chief medical officer with the March of Dimes, which advocates for healthy moms and babies, agreed that expanding access to midwives could boost outcomes in this country, which seriously lags other developed nations. 
“We’ve seen some promising trends in more parts of the United States, with more and more births every year attended by midwives, and those are associated with improvements, like lower rates of C-sections,” Warren told the New Jersey Monitor. 
“We need to continue to make this investment,” he said.  
New Jersey committed at least $500,000 to midwifery scholarships in the current annual budget. The new money will expand this financial assistance to cover more graduate students, officials said, and enable the state to help midwives establish new practices, particularly in high-needs communities. In return, they would need to agree to work in the Garden State for at least five years. 
Funding will also be used to provide grants to recruit and train instructors and support student mentors, officials said, and allow Rutgers to work with community organizations to see if it makes sense to establish an associate degree program at a community college in New Jersey to bolster the midwifery pipeline. 
“Investing in midwives is a way to advance equity and improve New Jersey’s health,” said Julie Blumenfeld, director of the school’s nurse-midwifery program.
Work will be guided by an advisory council of midwives, educators and community leaders, officials said, and the Rutgers School of Public Health will oversee research and evaluation.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Meet the 27-year-old Jackson native behind Scott Colom’s viral ‘pick another protein’ campaign ad
description: Ryan Sayles, pictured left, smiles for a photo with Democratic Sen.-elect Scott Colom at Colom's campaign office in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026.
text:
When Ryan Sayles first picked up his camera to film the now-viral “pick another protein” ad that spotlighted Democrat Scott Colom’s U.S. Senate campaign to the nation, he wasn’t looking forward to the work.  
It was the Friday of homecoming weekend at Alcorn State University, Sayles’ alma mater, he was tired and he had to drive over three hours to Columbus to film the ad. 
“But thank God I did,” Sayles told Mississippi Today in an interview. 
Ryan Sayles. Credit: Courtesy of Andrew Johnson
Sayles, 27, is a freelance videographer and photographer from Jackson, who graduated from Murrah High School. He had never worked on a campaign before, and now political pundits are calling his ad one of the best of the midterm election cycle. 
E.J. Dionne Jr., a longtime columnist and commentator, praised the ad in a guest essay in The New York Times, describing it as a creative way to make “economic issues front and center.” 
After Gerard Henderson, Colom’s campaign manager, and Andrew Colom, the soon-to-be senator’s twin brother, wrote the script, Sayles filmed the ad that helped define Colom’s campaign against Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, which ended with Colom winning the seat.
At this point, most Mississippians are familiar with the ad. Hyde-Smith is asked by a WLOX journalist about the high cost of beef, and the senator, who is a cattle farmer, responds that there are “so many proteins to choose from.” 
The 30-second Colom spot features Mississippians reacting to Hyde-Smith’s comment, and the line that stuck was that they’d rather pick another senator.  
“Pick another protein? Shiiii-, I’d rather pick another senator instead.”
“Pick another protein? She done lost her damn mind. I’d rather pick another senator.”
Colom, who will become Mississippi’s first Democratic U.S. senator in over four decades and whose victory shocked the nation, called Sayles the “breakout-star” of the election. 
“He’s going to be a giant in the media consultant game,” Colom wrote in a post on X. “He did GAME CHANGING work with SO little.” 
Sayles initially came to the campaign casually. Early in Colom’s run, he said, the campaign asked him to take some photos and shoot a video. They liked the results, and the work grew from there. 
The first ad he produced showed Colom at a Mississippi State University football game, lamenting that rising grocery costs have made tailgates more expensive.  The campaign was so small at the time that Henderson held a microphone in the background. 
While the campaign’s ad strategy grew more sophisticated, it still kept the scrappy, gritty core that it had since its inception. Sayles said he works best alone, anyway, with creative control and a “run and gun” approach. 
Sayles thinks the “pick another protein” ad resonated because it focused on a pressure people were already feeling and let ordinary Mississippians say what they thought, elongated curse words included.
“I think a lot of everyday people felt that way and just weren’t saying it,” Sayles said.  
The Jackson native also came up with the title “Sinators” for another viral campaign ad, a parody of the film “Sinners” starring the Colom twin brothers that made Hyde-Smith a vampire in the Mississippi Delta.
Sayles said the election result shouldn’t surprise people. “What I think a lot of people missed is that Mississippi isn’t a lost cause. It’s been a betrayed cause,” he said. “People have been so close to winning.” 

I’m sure everyone will enjoy the moment that changed Mississippi forever!! @scott_colom I guess Mississippi Matters now huh?? 😂🔥 pic.twitter.com/tQSklV9E63— Ryan Sayles (@RyanSayles_) November 14, 2026

“Now that we’ve broken through, a lot of people are scratching their heads,” he said. “But all it took was a little bit more investment. I think that came in part because of the ad.”
He said the campaign saw campaign donations rise after the ad came out. 
Sayles dislikes the negative image Mississippi sometimes gets and hopes this moment shows what’s good about it. People who disliked Colom, he said, mostly disagreed with him on party, not personally.
Since the election, Sayles has received a lot of messages from people who want to meet with him. He said he doesn’t know whether those new contacts will lead to work or what will come next, and he isn’t making commitments.
Still, his heart will always be Mississippi.
“I love Mississippi, and that’s where my heart is,” Sayles said. “I would love to continue to be helpful to bring about change in Mississippi and in the South for sure. That’s what I would desire to do. Mississippi matters.”

title: Just over one week left: Keep Vermont informed and provide 10 meals
description:

text:
Dear Reader,
The dust is settling from the general election and now it’s time to start looking ahead to the legislative session that will begin in January. Your continued support now, during our year-end member drive, is critical. 
Donate by Thanksgiving and your gift will power our statehouse reporting and provide 10 meals to the Vermont Foodbank.

Donate and send 10 meals

What does your support make possible? It funds rigorous reporting about the choices that affect us all. 
My colleagues and I worked hard to bring our readers in-depth stories ahead of Election Day on the policy debates that made this year’s race for governor so interesting, from taxes to big tech to universal primary care. Those stories required hours of research and lengthy interviews not just with the candidates themselves, but also outside experts who could weigh in objectively and cut through the political bluster. 
On top of those policy stories, we hit the road to bring our readers interviews with people all across the state on the issues that matter most to them.
It isn’t always easy to write and report these stories, but we know that tens of thousands of Vermonters rely on them to inform who they’ll vote for and why. If our work helped you better understand Vermont’s election this year, I hope you’ll donate to support our work.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: As prices soar, Alaskans choose between food and fuel
description: As winter descends over Alaska, many residents are facing tough choices: Should they buy groceries, pay for gasoline to power their snowmachines or purchase enough heating oil to stay warm through the season? These decisions are made even tougher in rural areas, where resources are in short supply and dollars simply don’t stretch far enough […]
text:
Noatak, Alaska. (Photo by Brian Adams/HCN)As winter descends over Alaska, many residents are facing tough choices: Should they buy groceries, pay for gasoline to power their snowmachines or purchase enough heating oil to stay warm through the season? These decisions are made even tougher in rural areas, where resources are in short supply and dollars simply don’t stretch far enough to cover everything.
In Alaska’s most remote communities, people are paying up to four times more for gas than people in the Lower 48 do. The Iñupiaq community of Shungnak garnered national attention in August after gas there hit $26 per gallon.
Due to the state’s distance from the continental U.S., costs have always been higher in Alaska. The coming winter is looking particularly challenging, however. “This is the first time I’ve seen it like that,” said Merle Custer, an Iñupiaq Elder and tribal council member from the Native Village of Shungnak, located north of the Arctic Circle in the state’s northwest region. “Hard times are hitting us big-time now.”
“I think we’re past the point where you can call this a (price) spike, but that’s the big question,” said Steve Colt, a research professor of energy economics at the University of Alaska Fairbanks. “The worst could be yet to come.”
Winters in Shungnak are long, with snow, strong winds and freezing temperatures that periodically plummet below minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Coastal communities usually see slightly warmer temperatures, especially with this year’s Super El Niño, but for much of the state, 2025 was one of the coldest and most extreme winters on record.
Custer and other council members are feeling pressure from locals who are asking for help. “I don’t decide the price of gas,” he said.
In the short term, Custer said, people are trying to cut back on non-necessities. “Twenty-one bucks a pack,” he noted as he pulled some Marlboros from his jacket pocket. Maybe it’s time to switch to chewing tobacco, he joked.
More than 80% of Alaska’s communities are not connected by roads. Shungnak is one of them, and food and fuel are delivered there by plane or barge.
Mary Ann Rainey, a member of the Tlingit Petersburg Indian Association, lives in Petersburg. A mother of six, she’s now retired and lives on her monthly Social Security payments. “If I didn’t have my children helping me, I’d be in big-time trouble,” she said. “An elderly person can’t afford to live on their own unless they have help. At least that’s what I found out.”
Chris Graves, Rainey’s daughter, explained: “Everything is freighted in on a barge, because the container ships that come up to Anchorage can’t make it into Petersburg.” As a result, she said, food prices in the small Southeast coastal community can be three times as high as in Alaska’s largest city.
But in recent years, a changing climate means dozens of communities can no longer receive deliveries by barge. The permafrost-rich soils along riverbanks are deteriorating, and as they slough off and slump, the waterways become less navigable and barges are unable to land.
Up to 95% of food in Alaska’s grocery stores is shipped in from out of state, and the rising cost of the fuel needed to transport it is reflected in higher prices.
More than 160 miles northwest of Shungnak, Hannah Onalik, an Iñupiaq Elder from the Native Village of Noatak, said prices have more than doubled in the past three years in Noatak. Onalik, 72, works as a cashier at the local store, where she says ground beef now costs $11 per pound and a bag of boneless chicken breasts is $20. “It’s getting scary,” Onalik said. “I’m so terrified to quit work. We won’t survive.”
Noatak, Alaska. (Photo by Brian Adams/HCN)

HISTORICALLY, THE WAY to avoid high grocery costs was to source food locally. Custer, Rainey and Onalik are Alaska Native, and they and their families, friends and neighbors rely on subsistence harvest of game, fish and plants as their main sources of food. What’s at stake is more than just food. Subsistence is also an important part of the cultural heritage and Indigenous identity in Alaska.
Hunting and fishing trips require boats, four-wheelers and snowmachines, and those all take gas too. In Noatak, Onalik said even when people spend the money to go hunting, fewer and fewer are getting caribou. The size of the Northwest Arctic Caribou herd that locals rely on for food has declined by 75% since the 1980s.
Even still, Custer said people are pooling their resources to go hunting out of Shungnak. Caribou is a main source of meat for the community. “Everybody’s really concerned about it,” he said. “We had a meeting to get the whole town together and see how we’re going to survive the winter again.”
In other parts of the state, the salmon that has long sustained communities through the winter has become less abundant too.
SURVIVING A LONG, DARK WINTER in Alaska also requires a reliable heat source. Reliance on home heating oil as a primary source of heat in Alaska is seven times the national average.
Onalik said almost everyone in her community uses heating oil, and many supplement it with wood. She said the young men who go out to collect the wood charge $200 for a load, which will last about four to five days.
In Bethel, a hub community on the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta where trees are few, 90% of households rely on heating oil as their primary source of heat, according to KYUK Public Media. Farther west, toward the Bering Sea, where there are no trees, people often burn scraps from delivery pallets and pieces of lumber left over from building projects. In some cases, they burn garbage.

Jeremiah John is Yup’ik from the Native Village of Newtok, which has relocated to Mertarvik, a coastal community more than 90 miles west of Bethel. This fall, he used his snowmachine to look for driftwood along the coast of Nelson Island; he spent about $400 on 50 to 60 gallons of fuel to gather driftwood along a 40-mile coastal route. This was still cheaper than trying to access firewood at the treeline, which would have required an additional 20 gallons of fuel. John said the driftwood he gathered will last about six months and supplement his family’s home heating oil.
DESPITE THE HIGHER FUEL PRICES and harsher winters in Alaska, the state lacks access to assistance some other U.S. states enjoy. In October, for example, the U.S. Department of Energy agreed to release up to 315,000 barrels of home heating oil from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve to protect Mainers from the financial burden of high fuel prices.
There is no federal fuel reserve for Alaska. Nor is there a state-owned stockpile of fuel or home heating oil for emergencies, though Alaska does have a loan program to assist small communities in purchasing bulk fuel and paying for shipping. This year, lawmakers raised the cap for loans, but state law also requires the loans be paid back within a year.
“It is wrong that fuel prices are so high,” said U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski in an address during the Alaska Federation of Natives convention in Anchorage in October. She blamed the war in Iran, which she said she has consistently voted to end. “We know that high prices are a threat to everyone, from Wasilla to Wrangell,” Murkowski said. “I fear that many Alaskans will struggle to keep warm this winter.”
Murkowski said her goal was to “bring down prices for good,” though she did not propose any concrete plans to meet that goal. “We can push for greater federal assistance,” she said.
In previous years when energy prices have soared, state lawmakers have agreed to help. In 2008, under then-Gov. Sarah Palin, legislators agreed to a one-time $1,200 energy relief subsidy for Alaskan residents who qualified for the state’s annual permanent fund dividend. This year, lawmakers agreed to offer Alaskan residents $200 in energy relief, enough to buy about 25 gallons of home heating oil in Anchorage or Bethel. According to a 2015 survey, a household in Fairbanks uses on average about 1,200 gallons of heating oil each year, though it can vary across the state, and depends on home construction and the availability of other heat sources.
Economics professor Steve Colt said short-term solutions include financial assistance for consumers and taxes for the petroleum industry. “The fastest long-term solution,” he said, is to “somehow reduce the amount of diesel that needs to be burned.” The cheapest and easiest way to do that, he added, is through weatherization and energy-efficiency investment for existing homes and buildings. But winter is fast approaching; in some communities, it has already arrived.
Shungnak, Alaska. (Photo by Brian Adams/HCN)

ARTHUR AND FRIEDA PANAMAROFF are Alutiiq from the Native Village of Larsen Bay, a small Kodiak Island coastal community off Alaska’s southern coast. There’s no school, no store and no road to get there, so everyone pays to fly in supplies. Freight costs $1.10 per pound, so every apple, onion or chicken breast the Panamaroffs buy costs that much more. “We all have to pay it,” Arthur said. “Otherwise, we starve.”
The Panamaroffs are both retired and say they no longer practice subsistence. As winter sets in on Kodiak, the couple said they’re paying $9.27 per gallon of oil to heat their home. They’re trying to save, Frieda said, by cutting back on travel: “We just stay home now.”
The Panamaroffs are still helping their 18-year-old granddaughter, Katie, who moved to Kodiak to finish school. She graduated in May and worked a few odd jobs to make ends meet.
“It’s kinda hard,” Katie said. “I haven’t worked too much lately.” She said gas is her largest expense, and without reliable income, her grandparents are helping her with other expenses.
Arthur said they also try to help friends and neighbors when they can. “Sometimes we have to share what we got,” he said. “It makes it hard when they don’t have any money to order their food, or even go out hunting.”
“They can’t afford shells or gas,” he added. “The only way we can survive is to share anything we have, if we can.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Sal Monarca, guilty of bribing Kosta Diamantis, avoids jail time
description: Sal Monarca faced years in federal prison for bribing Konstantinos Diamantis, the former head of the CT school construction office.
text:
The owner of a Connecticut masonry company was sentenced to three years of probation on Tuesday for bribing Konstantinos Diamantis, the former leader of the state’s school construction office. 
U.S. District Judge Stefan Underhill allowed Salvatore Monarca, the former president of Acranom Masonry, to avoid a federal prison sentence. 
The federal charge that Monarca pleaded guilty to in court carried a maximum sentence of up to 20 years in prison, and the federal sentencing guidelines recommended that he receive 30 to 37 months in prison. 
But Underhill offered leniency to Monarca, who testified during Diamantis’ criminal trial last year and explained to jurors how he bribed the former state official to win multimillion-dollar contracts for school construction projects in Tolland and Hartford.
Before the judge handed down the sentence, David Grudberg, Monarca’s defense attorney, directly compared his client to Diamantis. He noted that Monarca chose to face his criminal sentence in court, unlike Diamantis, who fled the country and absconded to Greece earlier this year before he could be sentenced to seven years in prison.
Grudberg also argued that Monarca has already faced significant backlash because of his involvement in the high-profile bribery scheme. His company, which his son is now president of, has been removed from state contracting lists. 
“He’s been the subject of significant publicity, scrutiny and scorn,” Grudberg told the judge. 
Assistant U.S. Attorney David Novick acknowledged that Monarca’s testimony helped federal prosecutors convict Diamantis, who also served as Connecticut’s deputy budget director. But he noted that Monarca admitted to bribing Diamantis only after prosecutors obtained incriminating evidence from his cell phone.
“The defendant did not come clean immediately,” Novick said.
Grudberg, however, repeatedly noted that Monarca was remorseful, and he argued that prior to meeting Diamantis, Monarca was an upstanding business owner. 
Monarca’s parents emigrated from Italy to the United States, Grudberg explained, and Monarca went on to build a successful masonry business despite dropping out of high school and struggling to read and write. 
“Mr. Monarca is very much what we have classically thought of as the American dream,” Grudberg said. 
Grudberg argued that Monarca privately expressed reservations about paying bribes to Diamantis in order to win contracts on school construction projects. And he said Monarca’s hesitancy later elicited threats from Diamantis. 
Underhill, who has served as federal judge since 1999, was not so certain that Monarca acted purely out of fear, however. 
“I don’t know if you feared losing business,” Underhill said. “I worry a little bit that it was the greed that got you here.” 
When Monarca stood to address the court, he said that he was deeply ashamed for agreeing to bribe Diamantis. And he acknowledged that he had nobody else to blame but himself. 
Underhill responded by telling Monarca that he should feel an overwhelming sense of guilt for the crimes that he committed. 
“Bribing a public official is conduct that is not only illegal, but is very harmful to our state,” Underhill said, adding that it creates general distrust among the public. 
“I’m glad frankly that you feel a sense of shame,” Underhill said. “You should.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: Lung cancer has an awareness problem. It’s just not the one you might expect.
description: Every November, we set out to help people understand why lung cancer is a disease we can’t afford to ignore. We call it raising awareness. We do it through mortality statistics, memorials, and stories of families forever changed. We’ve made our point. People know what’s at stake. For nearly two decades, national surveys have consistently […]
text:
November is Lung Cancer Awareness Month (Getty Images)Every November, we set out to help people understand why lung cancer is a disease we can’t afford to ignore. We call it raising awareness. We do it through mortality statistics, memorials, and stories of families forever changed.
We’ve made our point. People know what’s at stake.
For nearly two decades, national surveys have consistently shown that most Americans associate cancer with death. In that same timeframe, among adults who smoke, awareness that smoking causes lung cancer has long exceeded 90%.
People aren’t just aware of the danger. They’re afraid of it. In fact, fear of finding out is among the most commonly reported barriers to lung screening.
What if the problem isn’t a lack of awareness about lung cancer? What if people understand the urgency, but not what they can do about it?
I’m not a surgeon. I can’t read your CT scan, and you certainly don’t want me determining your treatment plan. (I’ll leave that to the clinicians at Markey Cancer Center—Kentucky’s first and only NCI-Designated Comprehensive Cancer Center.)
My expertise is words.
I’m a strategic public health communication researcher. That means I spend a lot of time thinking about what makes people recognize the urgency of a problem and what moves them to do something about it.
And that’s where our awareness efforts sometimes fall short: Too often, we reinforce what people already believe instead of giving them reason to believe their future could look different.
The story we’ve told about lung cancer is true, but it’s incomplete.
Consider how much has changed: Today, we can find it earlier. We have more ways to treat it. And more people are surviving it. Advances in immunotherapy and targeted treatments are changing not only how long some people live with lung cancer, but what ‘living with it’ can look like. That can mean more time to enjoy life on their own terms.
Lung cancer hasn’t gone away. But it doesn’t look the way it did a generation ago. And that changes what awareness needs to accomplish.
Knowing something is dangerous is only part of what moves people to act. People also need to believe that something can be done, that those actions can make a difference, and that it’s within their reach.
If I spend all my time convincing you that a problem is serious but never show you a way forward, I haven’t necessarily motivated you. I’ve just made you really, REALLY aware of how big the threat is.
And when the threat is cancer, giving someone one more reason to be afraid may also give them one more reason to look away.
 Tell the Rest of the Story
This Lung Cancer Awareness Month, I’m not asking us to stop honoring those we’ve lost. I’m asking us to tell the rest of the story.

 Tell people lung cancer is serious—but also what early detection can change. 

Large clinical trials have shown that low-dose CT screening reduces lung cancer deaths by approximately 20% among people at higher risk. Screening creates an opportunity to find cancer earlier, when treatment is more likely to be successful.
That’s not just another statistic about cancer. It’s evidence that the future isn’t necessarily predetermined.

 Tell people who’s at risk—but also what they can do. 

Screening happens before symptoms, while life is still happening.
Ask a doctor whether screening is right for you. You don’t have to wait until something feels wrong, and you don’t have to be ready to quit smoking to be ready for screening.
That’s not simply a story about searching for illness. It’s a story about protecting health before illness can interrupt everything else.

 Tell stories about people we’ve lost—but also about lives still being lived. 

We should make room for people to see themselves not as potential patients, but as people with lives still unfolding around them. Another birthday. Another afternoon on the lake. Another sleepover with the grandkids. Another completely unremarkable Tuesday with someone you love. Sometimes the most compelling reason to take care of your health isn’t the disease you’re trying to avoid. It’s the life you want to keep living.
These aren’t distractions from the serious business of lung cancer care. They’re the reason the serious business matters.
Before we publish another awareness message this November, let’s ask, “What will someone believe is possible after seeing this?”
We’ve spent decades showing people what lung cancer can take from them. Let’s make sure they also understand what earlier detection and better treatments might help them keep: more time for the people and moments that matter most.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Recount confirms Republican Clement flipped Lewiston House seat
description: Republican Kerryl Lee Clement was officially declared the winner of House District 96, defeating Democrat Luke Jensen by less than 30 votes following a Tuesday recount.  According to the Maine Secretary of State’s Office, the final tally was 2,232 votes for Clement and 2,208 for Jensen.  Clement had a 32 vote lead in election night […]
text:
Staff of the Maine Department of the Secretary of State work during the final day of ranked choice voting tabulations  at the Maine Department of Public Safety in Augusta on June 18, 2026. (By Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)Republican Kerryl Lee Clement was officially declared the winner of House District 96, defeating Democrat Luke Jensen by less than 30 votes following a Tuesday recount. 
According to the Maine Secretary of State’s Office, the final tally was 2,232 votes for Clement and 2,208 for Jensen. 
Clement had a 32 vote lead in election night results, according to the secretary’s office. The Lewiston district is currently represented by outgoing Democrat Michael LaJoie.
The district is one of very few that Republicans flipped in the election, while Democrats won several new seats, securing a strong majority in the Maine House of Representatives and a supermajority in the Maine Senate. 
The Maine Secretary of State’s Office released its first recount result Monday, confirming Democrat Elizabeth Bosworth the official winner of Maine Senate District 18. Bosworth, who will replace independent Rick Bennett defeated Republican John Andrews by slightly more than 50 votes.There will be one more legislative recount tomorrow, and a recount for a Kennebec County Commission seat Thursday. 
The recounts are  all open to the public at the Maine Public Safety Building in Augusta and live-streamed on the secretary’s office Youtube page.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Maine Transportation Commissioner Doughty to retire at the end of the month
description: Commissioner of the Maine Department of Transportation Dale Doughty is retiring Nov. 28 after three decades in public service, Gov. Janet Mills announced Monday.  “Dale Doughty has dedicated his career to creating safer, more efficient transportation and public works systems across Maine,” Mills said in a statement. “As commissioner, Dale directed investment[...]
text:
A Maine transportation worker directs traffic at a project site. (Photo via Maine DOT)Commissioner of the Maine Department of Transportation Dale Doughty is retiring Nov. 28 after three decades in public service, Gov. Janet Mills announced Monday. 
“Dale Doughty has dedicated his career to creating safer, more efficient transportation and public works systems across Maine,” Mills said in a statement. “As commissioner, Dale directed investments in our roads, culverts and bridges and expanded access to rural communities. In the face of severe weather and unprecedented natural disasters, Dale focused on what mattered most: improving safety for Maine people.”
Doughty was appointed deputy commissioner in the department in 2024, and was appointed acting commissioner the following year. He was confirmed as commissioner in January 2026. 
“I’m grateful to Gov. Mills for her trust and support, and to the colleagues and partners who work every day to keep our communities connected and our transportation system reliable,” Doughty said. “As I prepare to retire, I take the greatest pride in the people of this department and their commitment to Maine.”
He first joined the department in 1996, holding several roles in the Office of Environment and the Bureau of Planning and later rising to work as director of the Bureau of Maintenance and Operations. He left the department in 2018 to work for the city of Lewiston as public works director and later deputy city administrator. 
Doughty and Mills will discuss the appointment of an acting commissioner before his last day. Meanwhile, Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree and her transition team will be conducting interviews for all cabinet positions.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kentucky has highest rate of new lung cancer cases, according to new report
description: Kentucky has the nation’s highest rate of new lung cancer cases, according to the American Lung Association’s annual “State of Lung Cancer” report, released Tuesday.  According to the report, Kentucky has a lung cancer rate of nearly 84  per 100,000 people; The national rate is 52 per 100,000.  The commonwealth is also third in the […]
text:
Air pollution, including smoking, can cause health problems, including asthma and cancer. (American Lung Association)Kentucky has the nation’s highest rate of new lung cancer cases, according to the American Lung Association’s annual “State of Lung Cancer” report, released Tuesday. 
According to the report, Kentucky has a lung cancer rate of nearly 84  per 100,000 people; The national rate is 52 per 100,000. 
The commonwealth is also third in the nation when it comes to smoking — an improvement from 2025, when the report found Kentucky was the second-highest. Smoking can cause cancer, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and other health problems. 
Report: Kentucky worst in nation for new lung cancer cases, second worst for smoking

“Overall, our report reveals positive news—more people in the U.S. and in Kentucky are living longer after a lung cancer diagnosis than ever before, and more people are getting screened for the disease,” Shannon Baker, director of advocacy for the American Lung Association, said in a statement. “While these findings give us hope, more still must be done to end the burden of this devastating disease on families throughout Kentucky.” 
Other rankings from the report include: 

Kentucky is 38 out of 43 in the nation for lung cancer survival. 
Kentucky is 22 out of 40 in the nation for surgical treatment of lung cancer.
Kentucky is 29 out of 47 in the nation for lack of treatment. 
Kentucky is 18 out of 50 in the nation for lung cancer screening. 

“We need to continue to increase screening rates among those at high risk to catch the disease early when it’s more likely to be curable and improve access to clinical trials and the best lung cancer care,” Baker said.

title: ​Third Trump-appointed judge confirmed to serve on powerful Denver-based federal court
description: A third Trump-nominated judge will serve on the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals after the U.S. Senate voted to confirm him Monday.  Judge Daniel Domenico of the U.S. District Court of Colorado will join the 10th Circuit’s powerful panel of 12 judges after the Senate voted 51-46 to confirm him. Colorado’s two U.S. senators, Michael […]
text:
Daniel Domenico, chief judge of the U.S. District Court in Denver, refuses to state who won the 2020 presidential election during his confirmation hearing before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee on June 24, 2026. (Screenshot from U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee broadcast)A third Trump-nominated judge will serve on the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals after the U.S. Senate voted to confirm him Monday. 
Judge Daniel Domenico of the U.S. District Court of Colorado will join the 10th Circuit’s powerful panel of 12 judges after the Senate voted 51-46 to confirm him. Colorado’s two U.S. senators, Michael Bennet and John Hickenlooper, both Democrats, voted against his confirmation. 
President Donald Trump nominated Domenico for the court of appeals in May. Trump also nominated Domenico for the U.S. District Court of Colorado during his first presidency in 2017. Domenico briefly served as chief judge of the Colorado district this year.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A spokesperson for Hickenlooper said Domenico’s judicial record and responses during a judiciary committee hearing on his nomination raise concerns about his fitness for a lifetime appointment. Domenico declined to answer when a senator on the committee asked him who won the 2020 election. Hickenlooper’s office said that refusal and his record on immigration “were troubling and inconsistent with the high standards we should expect from federal judges.”
The 10th Circuit hears appeals of district court decisions from Colorado, Oklahoma, Kansas, New Mexico, Wyoming and Utah, as well as portions of Yellowstone National Park in Montana and Idaho. Appeals from the 10th Circuit, based in Denver, go to the U.S. Supreme Court.
Besides Domenico, Trump appointed 10th Circuit Judges Allison Eid and Joel Carson during his first term. 
Judge Timothy Tymkovich announced earlier this year that he would retire as an active judge on the appeals court to serve as a senior judge, creating the vacancy Trump appointed Domenico to fill. Domenico clerked for Tymkovich in 2003. 
Domenico served as solicitor general for Colorado, arguing cases before the U.S. Supreme Court, the 10th Circuit and the Colorado Supreme Court on the state’s behalf across three governors. 
In 2022, Domenico had the fourth-biggest backlog of pending motions of all district and magistrate judges across the U.S.
Trump will nominate a replacement for Domenico on Colorado’s federal district court. U.S. senators are typically involved in the nomination process for district court judges in their state.
